# THE ARGUMENTS OF THE BOOKS
### On the Harmony of the World <note>original: "De Orbis Concordia"</note>.

First, the tenets of the Christian religion <note>original: "religionis Christianæ"</note> are taught through philosophical reasoning.

Second, the life, upbringing, and customs of Muhammad <note>original: "Muhamedi"</note>, the lawgiver of the Arabs <note>original: "Arabum"</note>, and his followers are related; finally, the Quran <note>original: "Alcoranum"</note> is examined and refuted from beginning to end <note>A Latin idiom, "from head to heel"</note> from the original Arabic.

Third, what the whole world holds in common, both by human law and divine law.

Fourth, by what skill false beliefs about God or the gods may be drawn toward the truth without civil unrest.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing a circular frame depicting a man seated in a landscape, wearing a long garment and a cap, appearing to study or speak.</image-desc>“What will this boaster produce that is worthy of such a wide-open mouth?” <note>original: "Quid tanto dignũ feret hic promissor hiatu?" Postel quotes the Roman poet Horace’s *Ars Poetica*, mocking writers who promise more than they can deliver.</note> I am pleased to use this verse from Horace, O Princes and most upright assemblies, lest I be preempted, to address certain people who I do not doubt will immediately say—from the work's title and the argument of the first book—that he who promises such arduous and unheard-of things will perform them either unwisely, or without sufficient holiness and perfection. This is especially so since, in handling even the smallest matters, powers that have not been sufficiently weighed often fail. Furthermore, a matter of the highest importance in the whole world—and one that could occupy everyone to the greatest degree—is being undertaken to be explained by a man of thin <note>or slight</note> erudition. Indeed, both reason and authority resist such a treatment, preventing it from being completed. 

When I attempt to prove and confirm the reasons for the Christian faith <note>original: "fidei Christianae rationes"</note>—already confirmed by men of the highest genius and by divine and human authority—with reasons not foreign to the opinions of the most excellent philosophers, I will seem to some to contravene the opinion of Saint Gregory <note>original: "D. Gregorij Ro. pont." Referring to Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD).</note>, the Roman pontiff. For he left it written: “Faith has no merit where human reason provides proof.” <note>original: "Fides nõ habet meritum, ubi humana ratio præbet experimentum." This was a standard theological argument: if you can prove God exists via logic, you aren't using "faith."</note> 

Although something consistent with reason could be brought against this axiom, nevertheless, so that we may receive it as proven, it will be enough to show that I do not withdraw from the common opinion received in the Church of Christ to this day. To those who, imbued with the sacred mysteries, are moved by the Spirit of God (although they ought to persuade themselves of this one thing above all: that God, the author of reason, commanded or taught nothing, however arduous or obscure, without reason), faith is not to be confirmed by reasons, as they already hold it sufficiently persuaded. Therefore, I have not undertaken this work so that I might play the Christian philosopher among you. For what else would this be in such an erudite age—with disciplines partly awakened and partly restored, with such illustrious geniuses, and such a great abundance of learned men—than, according to the proverb, “owls to Athens”? <note>original: "γλαῦκας εἰς ἀθήνας" (glaukas eis Athēnas). A Greek idiom similar to "carrying coals to Newcastle," meaning to do something redundant, as Athens was already full of owls (the symbol of Athena).</note> 

But for those who are foreign to our persuasion, but who use and rely on their own authority in divine matters—an authority different from ours—certainly that reason <note>original: "ratio"</note> must be set forth which we believe has flowed from God, the author of truth. For what end will there ever be to arguing, and stubbornly defending one's own position by simple authority, unless the reason of the true and the false makes a distinction, and settles it between the litigants like an arbiter? It is permissible for me, therefore, since the cause of the nations wandering from the true goal of happiness... <meta>The text continues on the next page, beginning with the word "scribere" (to write).</meta>

# THE PROOF OF THE TRUE RELIGION, THAT IS,
## THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION, DRAWN FROM
## PHILOSOPHY, BOOK I.

<image-desc>A large woodcut decorative initial letter 'E' at the start of the first paragraph. The scene within the letter depicts a scholar or monk seated at a desk, studying an open book. A window behind him shows a hilly landscape.</image-desc> Although it is difficult and beyond human capacity to treat anything that does not fall under the senses—since even things widely admitted find a place in many people's minds with difficulty, and many withhold their agreement from the most obvious truths, while things usually perceived by the senses are known only on the surface—reason is ineffective for weighing all things, and especially divine matters separated from this filthy matter <note>The author refers to the physical, material world as "filthy matter" (*feculenta materia*), contrasting it with the purity of the divine.</note>. Nevertheless, driven by a zeal for trying and a desire to achieve the highest things, I judge it better to test what human powers can do than to leave unattempted, through laziness and dejection of spirit, that which brings no small benefit to this mortal life even by the mere thought of achieving it. For while the mind is occupied in the contemplation of great things, even if it does not usually attain what it proposed for itself, yet while it is held by the zeal for attaining it and is entirely occupied in contemplating, it must necessarily lack many troubles. For when it is carried so completely into the thought of the matter that it is plainly snatched away by that very passion, it happens that it does not even feel those troubles by which others are weighed down. Just as someone intent on blood and vengeance does not feel the wounds he receives unless he settles down, because his passion itself carries him away; so too might he see other successes only through a lattice-window <note>The phrase *per transennam* (through a lattice or screen) implies seeing something only partially or in passing.</note> and marvel at them, like someone who, with the goal of happiness set before him, looks at or cares for nothing else at all until he has reached it.

Therefore, since I see that <term>happiness</term> <note>original: *felicitatem*. In this context, it refers to "beatitude" or the ultimate fulfillment found in God.</note> is the goal of this life, which all things naturally seek, and it has been cut into various parts by various judgments—while one person proposes one part for himself and another busies himself to obtain many parts—everyone seeks a solid happiness. By debating about that very thing, as it can be thought of as the highest and absolute goal, I have decided to treat it in such a way that, from those sensible traces, shadows, and conjectures, I may come into knowledge (as far as it is permitted for a mind closed in the prisons of the body to reach) and demonstrate the divinity of the supreme deity and the creator of all things. Thus, by this labor—which meanwhile calls me away from other things—while I strive to satisfy myself, even if the argument handed down to this age could be of benefit, I might indeed seem to have done a great service. To repeat this from a slightly higher point, I judge that one must begin from the contemplation of all nature, daring to approach this not without the favor and grace of Him whom we seek. I therefore pray and beseech Him with every vow that the knowledge concerning Him which He has deigned to open to us by His mercy through the holy scriptures and His son Jesus Christ, the <term>God-man</term> <note>original Greek: *Θεάνθρωπον* (Theanthrōpon), a theological term emphasizing Christ as being simultaneously fully God and fully man.</note>, He might allow and cause that same knowledge (as if reclaimed from His authority) to pass for a short while into the power of reason.

As long as innocence lasted, ambition was banished, deceit did not creep into sacred places, and providence—the avenger of crimes and the producer of miracles—was present and revealed itself sufficiently to the world; whatever sacred religion proclaimed in His name was accepted. But these dangerous times, which Peter predicted, receive nothing of sound doctrine; they laugh at authority, turn toward fables, and recoil from all authority of antiquity to follow their own dreams. I wish these things to be set forth so that they may be without excuse, and may rightly be separated from the number of men if they do not listen to truth joined with reason. Indeed, if this work is to be of benefit to others besides myself, I desire it to be written so that those who have been occupied with false authority until this day may take up the truth. I do not truly pity many of them so much, who after acknowledging the truth

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

...either attack it with words and deeds, or they completely reject it by their way of life. I am moved by the error and unhappiness of so many peoples who, although they are far from the truth and follow falsehoods, nevertheless omit nothing of those things which they are convinced lead to the highest happiness, so that they might finally obtain it. For who would not weep that so many labors perish? That so many noble efforts are lost when vice is admitted and accepted in place of virtue? Who would not weep that the sweetest liquids are ruined by the mixture of wormwood <note>Wormwood is a proverbially bitter herb; the author uses it here as a metaphor for how false beliefs embitter a well-intentioned life.</note>, and that a life lived in the constant company of death never truly lives? One man claims the opinion of Moses for himself; another approves of Muhammad <note>original: *Muhamedem*</note> as the author of the law; for many others, the foul image of a demon presents itself to be worshiped. Some are terrified by ghosts <note>original: *lemuribus* — spirits or shades of the dead</note> and perform sacrifices to them; whatever else is offered to the rest is held in the place of God.

And meanwhile, the truth itself lies hidden among us; it remains concealed by our sloth, unknown by many names. Truly, it is primarily because of our way of living that even if there were some who would voluntarily submit to that law—which we prove and assert depends on the highest happiness—they would be drawn in a completely different direction. For it seems unjust that the common conduct of life should differ so much from the holy precept. The primary examples of neglected persuasion are not sought from the common people, nor are they found only in lawless military service, nor do they show themselves in the courts of princes in such a way that they are not also by far the worst among the initiates <note>original: *mystis* — referring here to the clergy or those "initiated" into the mysteries of the faith</note> themselves. 

Dire ambition and the pursuit of vain reputation <note>original: *fumorum captatio* — literally "the catching of smoke," a metaphor for seeking empty honors</note> torment those removed from the common noise of human affairs and from more splendid usage. Pride and arrogance drive the rich astray; the middle class, increased by the vices of their elders, think everything is permitted to them. In short, ignorance, vanity, and greed infect the entire social order, so that those who correspond to so holy a name—whom I wish were untouched—are very rare. Other nations leave no stone unturned to sow the seeds of their false persuasions wherever they can; they entice with gifts, lure with friendship, compel with authority, pull with force, and strive to join everyone to themselves by persuasion. But we, idle and sluggish, sleep deeply, considering it enough to possess the most noble thing like misers: having it without the use of the use itself <note>The author means that Christians possess the "treasure" of faith but do not actually put it into practice.</note>.

The third cause lies in the difficulty of the matter, which not infrequently repels the most excellent men. For although we may be well-disposed toward the things themselves, and faith itself—a gift of God devoid of reason and supported by divine authority—ought to produce belief by itself, yet while authority offers itself everywhere, the right of all seems entirely the same unless you make a choice by reason. For all either seek God while thinking they have Him, or they profess Him. Jews, Muhammadans, and Indians <note>original: *Indi* — likely referring to the peoples of the East Indies or the Americas known at the time</note> either worship or acknowledge one creator of heaven and earth; we do the same. Imagine you are a stranger who has never heard anything about God (whom you nevertheless judge should be held by nature): it is certain that you would be in doubt as to whom among all you should believe, unless reason compels you to turn toward one side rather than the other. If authority alone makes the law, the reasoning for all will be equal, since there will be none. Surely no mortal would not greatly approve of our precepts if he understood everything from the very beginning.

But since difficulty alienates many of the pagans, and all the Jews and Muhammadans from us, I judge that we must deal with them by reason, both in all things and especially in those which they cannot persuade themselves to believe. Such as these:
<margin>1</margin>
That not only must injury be forgiven, but it must be repaid with benefits instead of retaliation—which must be done not only by him who embraces peace in this life, but by every Christian man. But what wonder if a Jew, a Turk, a Persian, or a Moor refuses to believe this, when we ourselves are accustomed to observe that most holy precept only with our lips? Indeed, we even persuade others that this—which is the basis and proof of a truly pious man—is a matter of counsel, not a command <note>The author critiques the theological view that "loving enemies" is an optional "counsel of perfection" rather than a mandatory commandment for all Christians.</note>. We must therefore deal with the Jew and Muhammadan with reasons, so that they may judge that forgiveness is to be preferred above vengeance in every way, except insofar as it pertains to the punishment of the laws. Now indeed, the most holy Trinity itself has made both Moors and followers of Moses strangers to Christ, because it seems by no reason...

## GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.

<note>The text begins here by concluding a thought on the nature of God's unity.</note> ...it may seem that the same most simple thing is also three; and conversely—although it is difficult to demonstrate and almost beyond human capacity—I will nevertheless strive, as far as reason can support authority, to bring this forth from the most holy inner chambers of philosophy, to point it out by its tracks, and to offer it to the sharp vision of the mind. Regarding the necessity and reason for the coming of Jesus Christ, I will make an attempt if anything can be held that an experienced judgment of human affairs might not easily conceive and approve; although I must deal with those (I mean the Jews and Muslims <note>original: *Moisaicos & Mahumedicos*</note>) whom I could overcome by the very authority of their own legislators. The immortality of souls, being consistent with reason in its proper place, will be proven by a necessary argument. The crowning conclusion <note>original: *coronis* — a Greek-derived term for a finishing touch or a flourish at the end of a work</note> will be that we engage with philosophical arguments against the philosophers, and show that the resolution <note>original: *catastrophen* — used here in the classical sense of a final outcome or "turning point" of a plot</note> of this entire present life must lead to the immortality of souls, the resurrection, eternal life, and the transformation of matter. For even the greater part of the Jews are persuaded of this, and the Muslims read it countless times <note>original: *fexcenties* — literally "six hundred times," a Latin idiom for a very large, indefinite number</note> in their Quran <note>original: *Alcorano*</note> and believe it.

So that our defense might be armed on all sides against those falsely claiming the name of philosophy, we shall come to the first cause from the very causes of the world, and we will attempt to demonstrate and persuade that the world has its origin from God and must be referred back to that same end. Everything else that does not seem at first glance to have self-evident principles—and therefore earns belief with difficulty—we shall hand down here in the first book. In the second, the life of Muhammad and the persuasion of the Quran will be presented and examined, and things still unknown to us will be translated from their own writings. And so that nothing is lacking from this argument, I will subjoin in the third book those principles of both secular and sacred laws in which all people agree, of whatever persuasion, provided they are mature and cultivated, so that even in this part I might not seem to have failed our people. For it is not enough to have asserted and demonstrated the truth itself, unless you also explain, defend, and clearly vindicate and claim its freedom wherever it may differ. However, once I have taught from their own doctrines what the Jews, the Moors <note>A common early modern term for North African Muslims</note>, and the Pagans <note>original: *Ethnici*</note> ought to feel about their own persuasion, and by what reasons they should transition to ours—having refuted their vain opinions and substituted our own—I shall make an end of speaking, noting and examining what in each persuasion serves the matter at hand. Now indeed, we must first deal briefly with the sum of all things: namely God and the world.

---

### ON THE WORLD AND GOD. CHAPTER I.

<margin>☞</margin>
I do not think I should call into doubt whether there is only one world or many, or which is more excellent; since it is now most proven among the princes of philosophers—as if received by the decrees and judgment of all—that there can be neither many nor diverse worlds. So far am I from this that I do not judge that I should use any division before I define the term.

For although I think I must act with reasons and demonstrations, nevertheless, because I judge that the opinions <note>original: *placita*</note> of Aristotle, Galen, and Averroes <note>original: *Abenreis* — the Latinized name for the 12th-century Andalusian polymath Ibn Rushd</note> hold the place of reason for everyone, it is certain that their authority ought to be held as reason, since it is approved by everyone. Therefore, the "multiple worlds" introduced by Democritus—lest he seem to know nothing more than the others—are exploded by these reasons. For absurdities would follow in both cause and effect: it would follow that there are multiple authors, either equal or unequal. If equal, they are superfluous. If dissimilar, they would be in perpetual strife, which is repugnant to the first cause. In effect, however—or in matter—nothing would seem higher or lower; with everything collapsing confusedly in every direction, it would be a chaos rather than a distinction of worlds. By these and many other reasons, the greatest philosophers refute the opinion of empty men born for trifles and contentions. Therefore, if anyone doubts that there is one world, and that it is finite, he is not to be held among the seekers of truth. There was once another reason for doubting everything, primarily due to two causes: the obscurity of things...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
### Book I

...[uni]ty, the ancients were driven to call all things into question—not out of a desire for conflict, but out of a zeal for the truth. For although nature has made the signs of truth almost innate to our souls, difficulties have arisen both from the things themselves and from the weakness of our senses, preventing us from being perpetually held in its possession. This was debated among the greatest leaders of philosophy until they attained it as far as it can be grasped by our judgment. After this obscurity and difficulty, there followed the stubbornness of certain men who were hunters of glory through their opinions. While they refuse to accept those things subject to reason, they spontaneously recoil from the truth, devising, thrusting forward, and bringing forth new ideas—partly to seem as if they discovered them themselves, and partly to avoid appearing to subscribe to another’s opinion. This was the cause of searching for the truth for so long and following various opinions. For here, one man affirms that all things can be known; another withholds assent from everything; a third makes all things doubtful. Some would rather cast off their humanity than admit that things manifest to the senses are as they appear; even though they themselves are forced to confess that they know at least this: that they know nothing. This was the cause of the truth remaining hidden for so long. Since, therefore, those doctrines of vanity have been hissed off the stage, and we know that faith must be placed in the senses and in reason (which is like the eye of the mind), there is no reason for us to be moved away from established and fixed demonstrations by the opinion of a few who deny that reason exists within them.

->The world, therefore, is one, finite, and in every part most perfectly adorned.<-

That it is adorned is signified by the etymology <note>original: *etymon*</note> used by all nations, and the reality itself makes it clear. <note>The Latin word *mundus* means both "the world" and "clean" or "adorned," mirroring the Greek *kosmos* which implies "order" and "ornament."</note> Whatever is adorned, however, must necessarily depend upon a cause, be ruled, and be set in motion; from which it follows that it is finite. For nothing infinite can be held by any power. We assert, therefore, that the world is this "temple of nature," which embraces all things whatsoever that are subject to the senses. Whether some call it the "universe" or others call it "whatever this is," they differ in words, not in reality. But since the recklessness of fortune (I meant to say the recklessness of insane opinion devising "fortune"), the continuous change of corruptible things, ignorance of the truth, and the lust for lying place fortune, chance, and I know not what other monsters among the causes of such a great mass (although no philosopher allows this), and since some would cast God out of his own heaven with words—God, who is the author of a work so great and truly worthy of himself—we shall show in a very few words, by following the argument, that the world itself is ruled by the judgment of providence. We shall then add a discussion on eternity: whether the world is to be eternal in its form, or in the cause of its form, or even in its matter, or whether indeed both joined together shall be an eternal nature. If we had to attend to and satisfy every objection of every person, we would linger longer on the side-issue <note>original: *parergo*</note> than on the main work. Therefore, leaving aside the question of whether the world is animated, or a living creature, or whether it has a cause outside itself (which will be treated in their proper place), I come to demonstrations sought from the innermost parts of philosophy. I demonstrate that God exists in this way: from the contemplation of truth and nature, from the composition of all things, from motion, from distance, from order, from the perfection of the good, from happiness, and from the purpose of all things.

1. I believe it is confessed by all that **truth** exists in the nature of things and is manifold; for there is the false, and that which is falser than the false. That truth is greatest in which the sense or the intellect of all—but especially of the wise—does not wander when weighing it, and whose very assertion bestows the most faith because it is most truly so. For example: he who says there is light in "sub-bright" darkness touches the truth to some extent; he who brings a greater light brings a little more; he who speaks of the light of the moon speaks more truly; finally, if he should speak of the light of the sun (as far as it pertains to the sense of the eyes) as the truest light, he will undoubtedly not err. From this it appears to us that what is the greatest and most perfect **being** <term>original: *ens* — a central philosophical term for "that which exists" or "essence"</term>, and in which judgment cannot be deceived, is the truest. Thus, those things which are commonly thought to be the greatest are "hardly true." Things that are coarse are merely present and dreg-like; those things which both exist and live are worthier and truer. More worthy still are those which also possess sense and life. Far truer are those to which intellect is added, infused into matter. Truest of all are those things devoid of body; they prevail and flourish by intellect alone, among which that is the worthiest and truest, whose...

<summary>Postel argues that the world is a finite, "adorned" temple ruled by divine providence rather than chance, and begins a philosophical proof for God's existence based on the hierarchy of truth and being.</summary>

# THE BOOK OF GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I

the mind runs through all things. God Himself is therefore truth, and the target of all truth; He is all the more true the more He exists by Himself. For since these lower things <note>Referring to the physical world of matter.</note> are not from themselves, it is certain that they depend on a most true starting principle. For the basis of all things—namely, "being"—exists within a cause of the most perfect perfection, which is entirely devoid of matter. Therefore, that supreme truth is sought not through the senses, like other things, but through **privation** <note>original: *privationem*; in medieval philosophy, this is the "way of negation," understanding God by defining what He is *not* (e.g., He is not finite, not material).</note> and the removal of all other things. We can barely touch it, though we know it truly exists (even if only by its effects).

Indeed, the nature of our soul indicates this most clearly, as it never ceases from contemplation and the desire for truth, even though it has grasped all those things subject to the senses as far as they can be grasped. For Nature—and God Himself, the parent of Nature—would never have created a soul so greedy to progress further unless a goal had been set for it where it might find rest; a goal which, by its immensity and the glory of being known, would satisfy that desire. We see in all other things that move us to desire (whether from within or without) that we set a limit to our longing once we have attained them. Therefore, God is the truest and most perfect cause of all, from whom all things come, through whom all things stand, and toward whom all things finally tend, as if toward rest and happiness.

### 2
The perfection and composition of all things also argue that there is a **Mind** that adorns everything. Since all things consist of **matter and form** <note>Postel uses the Aristotelian concept of hylomorphism: "matter" is the raw stuff, and "form" is the organizing principle that makes a thing what it is.</note>, and since formless matter cannot move toward form on its own and cannot exist by itself, it is certain that their connection depends on something else. For even the celestial bodies, even if they were to lack motion, still consist of matter—made of a **fifth element** <note>original: *quinti elementi*; the "Aether," which ancient philosophers believed filled the universe beyond the terrestrial sphere.</note> known only through privation—and the form that we see. Who truly would believe that these moist things could be joined with the dry, or the hot with the humid, unless they were fused into one by some supreme and most powerful cause? And how could they last, except as long as they preserve that connection conceived by the **spirit** that penetrates all things?

God, therefore, is everywhere. This was surely the reason why certain philosophers said the world was alive and called God the "Soul of the World" <note>original: *anima mundi*</note>, wanting an infinite power to be contained within a place. To refute their opinion (if they mean God is restricted by place), I will offer nothing other than what would follow: namely, that all things would be eternal if they were held within the arms of the substance of the divinity. For the **intellect** assimilates all things to itself; since it is an eternal substance, it would make all things eternal. Therefore, although He is supremely powerful and penetrates all things, He acts upon these lower things primarily through the ordered movements of the higher bodies, while remaining most remote from matter.

### 3
I think no one is so stupid or stubborn as to doubt the motion of the world (after the manner of certain ancients) or to deny that anything moves, since the contrary is obvious to the senses and to experience. Whatever is moved, however, is moved by something else—whether from birth to decay, or the reverse, or in any direction or arrangement; for motion is manifold. Truly, as it fits its category, motion is a successive change according to place or state. Or, more briefly: **it is the action of the mover upon the moved.** (**Aristotle, Physics, Book 3**).

It is established that whatever exists in the nature of things moves by a certain constant motion, whether in act or in potential. For heavy and light things, although they are at rest in their place of repose, are only so to a greater or lesser degree; they are born to tend toward that point as long as they are away from their true point of stability. It is certain that those things which possess life receive their motion from a vital principle. It is also clear that whatever is moved is moved from elsewhere. For otherwise, if anything moved itself, it would be partly at rest and partly in motion; then the whole itself (of which a part rests) could not be said to move by its own nature, but only by the nature of a part. And if that moving part were to rest, the whole would rest. He whose rest depends on the rest of another must also follow that other's motion. Therefore, nothing is moved by itself, but from elsewhere. Simple beings are moved by an aptitude proceeding from the **First Mover**; animate beings are moved by the soul...

## ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...souls from a certain supreme mind. For unless motions were halted in something constant and perpetually immovable, and took their beginning from there, it would be necessary for all things to proceed into infinity. From this, many inconsistencies would follow. For everything that is moved must be divisible. And everything divisible is finite; it would be moved, and would move others, within a finite time. Therefore, those infinite things—both the movers and the moved—would be moved in a finite time, each in its own certain time, which is impossible. Therefore, there is a certain **First Mover** <note>original: *primus motor*; a concept from Aristotle’s *Physics* describing the primary cause of all motion in the universe.</note>, who is God. The Greeks call Him *God* <note>original: *θεὸν* (*theon*)</note> because His act runs through all things from a constant principle, bestowing motion. For they name Him thus from the phrase *running through all things* <note>original: *ἐκ τοῦ διὰ πάντα θεῖν* (*ek tou dia panta theein*)</note>, based on an eternal course. That it is impossible for movers to proceed into infinity is also evident by this reason: among such things, there would be no "first mover." But where there is no first mover, there is no motion; therefore, nothing would be moved. It is necessary, therefore, since motion exists, that there be one First Mover. Thus, God exists.

4. A demonstration is also made from moved things in this way: that which is born to be moved in the manner of an instrument must be moved by a primary and principal cause. This happens mutually to some extent, until we reach some "first" thing, which is the First Mover. For otherwise, the first inconsistencies mentioned above would follow. Corruptible things act by the power of the heavens; the heavens act by the power of the First Impeller, who is God Himself.

5. The work itself serves as an argument for the skill of the craftsman. For although things demonstrate their author and cause by even a slight indication, we can easily judge which was more excellent by a comparison of all their effects. For he who has built a house complete in every detail must certainly be judged greater than one who has merely erected huts, dug out caves, or constructed shacks. For he who accomplishes what is greater is permitted also to perform what is lesser, but not the other way around. Therefore, the greater and more constant the order seen in things, the more skillful the craftsman must be considered. And yet, one can find nothing more ornate, or with greater and more constant order, than the world. Therefore, the world has a most prudent and most wise cause: God.

But when I speak of order and constancy, and argue that all things act in a most orderly fashion, there will immediately arise those who assert that fortune, chance, and rashness preside over human affairs in the place of **Fate** <note>In this context, Postel uses "fate" or "providence" to mean the divine plan.</note>. You can cure these people with all the more difficulty, as they are less likely to acknowledge their own disease and its cause. Although I know they are moved to these objections more by a disease of the soul than by the nature of things, and I am persuaded they are driven by a lust for contention and resistance rather than a love of truth, we must nonetheless attempt to deal with their reasons in a few words. Their sayings must be refuted, not so that those who wish to be so persuaded might repent, but lest their poison creep into more people.

According to the opinion of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle, known for walking while they discussed philosophy.</note>, the types of causes are manifold. For some are "near" and some are "remote"; some are "manifest" and others "hidden"; some are "antecedent" and others "consequent." We must deal chiefly with these here, for to deal with the entire genus of causes would be another work entirely. In the whole number of causes, it is accepted that there are four, of which no natural thing can be deprived. For nothing that falls under the senses can be the cause of itself.

Therefore, the primary cause, which is called the **efficient cause**, is in the first place. Since it is confessed that all things consist of some matter, we shall place the **material cause** in the second place. The third will be that which takes its name from the **form** <note>The "formal cause" refers to the design, pattern, or essence of a thing.</note>. Truly, it is certain that all things act for the sake of an **end** <note>The "final cause" or purpose.</note>. For all other things would be present in vain unless all things were made for the sake of some use. 

For example: before a house is made, there must pre-exist builders and architects who are not unskilled, who conceive the thing in their mind before it is made. If the resources—the stones, cement, beams, and so on—are lacking, nothing happens. The work itself can be distinguished from any other and made fit for use; but the other things are present in vain, unless for the sake of some useful end. The two middle causes <note>Material and formal.</note> are near and connected. The extreme causes <note>Efficient and final.</note> are separate, and proceed from the mind of the craftsman or the owner. From this place it necessarily follows that all things exist by the cause of the First Author, and...

# THE WRITINGS OF GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I

...of that one to whom the thing belongs; for it is certain that those things which are made, are made for the sake of their Author. Indeed, there are not infrequently several preceding causes before the "artful" or "efficient" cause <note>Aristotelian terms: the "efficient cause" is the agent that brings something about; the "artful" cause refers to the design or skill involved.</note>, but one is necessarily the highest: the "final cause," for the sake of which the end exists. And so we see that those things subject to the senses consist of matter and form—such as the elements—which it is established have already coalesced from some necessary cause, and exist for the sake of those things composed from them. For from the elements, all things subject to change are born, and to them they return. From this, life is composed: things devoid of sense tend toward the use of living beings; living beings toward the use of intelligent beings; and intelligent beings themselves necessarily toward their own use, their happiness, and the honor of the **First Cause**. While that Cause, being blessed and happy in itself and in need of nothing, draws all things to itself, it then bestows happiness and the ultimate goal upon them. For there is a goal for "separated substances" <note>original: *substantijs separatis*; refers to purely intellectual beings like angels or the human soul when considered apart from the body.</note> in the contemplation of the First Cause, just as there is for a house and other things in the use of their master. But if insensible things were capable of any happiness, they would then at last enjoy themselves with the greatest joy, being placed in their highest end. Therefore, in these causes, there is as yet no fortune, no rashness. Thus, the entire order of nature is mostly free of them.

But in the realm of causes, antiquity placed fate, fortune, and chance. It placed them there certainly, but in a way where one may see **Fate** itself—which some called *Heimarmene* <note>original: *εἱμαρμένην*; the Greek term for ordained fate or destiny.</note> and others *Heirmon* <note>original: *εἱρμὸν*; a Greek term meaning a "string" or "sequence," referring to the chain of causes.</note>. This is nothing other than that eternal and once-prescribed order of things of which we have spoken; and even if we do not see its causes, it is nonetheless no less in order despite our ignorance. For our knowledge stands in relation to the truth of causes no differently than the eyes of an owl toward the sun <note>A classic Aristotelian metaphor suggesting that human intellect is blinded by the "brightness" of supreme truths.</note>. For the things most known to nature are most obscure to us, and vice versa.

It remains to speak of **Fortune** and **Chance**. Chance and fortune have this in common: they are properly said to happen in those things which do not occur according to one's will, and which produce an effect different from the goal of the agent acting from deliberation. Thus, they happen rarely and by accident. They differ, however, in that chance comes from elsewhere, while fortune comes from the agent. For example: I go to the city; it happens by "chance" that I am struck by a falling tile <note>original: *lateris*; literally a brick or side-piece.</note> so that I am harmed and distracted from my goal; or, if I fail myself through negligence—the first accident is from chance, the second from fortune. Therefore, the **Philosopher** <note>Aristotle.</note> rightly placed the location for this "monster of fortune" in the soul—that is, in opinion—and said it was a quality of a noble life, for it is not customary in the order of nature. 

But because it frequently happens in those matters that depend on human choice, and is tossed before the eyes of those men who rarely or never weigh the first and certain cause, they perpetually propose fortune to themselves, even though it is furthest away. Therefore, they do not hesitate to assert with the greatest impiety that the world is ruled by fortune. Kings meditate on kingdoms, wealth, victories, glory, smoke, and fame; they apply themselves to any arts whatsoever so they may attain what they desire. And as if their will and choice imposed laws on things, they are not afraid to immediately ascribe everything to fate, fortune, or chance unless it succeeds according to their lust. While they follow their own dreams, they make themselves unhappy by their own laws and resolve to overthrow **Providence**. Someone meditates and imagines for himself—on account of his merits—priesthoods, dignities, and rewards; if he is forestalled in these by anyone, you would immediately hear: "There is no God; fortune dominates." It is as if the whole nature of things should be changed based on the frustrated lust of a most wicked scoundrel, for this one reason: that no one sets a limit on his own greed. This is the reason why you hear nothing else from the impious: "All things depend on chance and fortune." O unbearable blindness! 

Yet they claim authority from what is said. For in **Solomon** (they say), a practitioner of the Old Testament, this sentiment is held: *There is one chance for all* <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 9:11. Postel notes that others translate the word *casus* as "event" or "occurrence."</note>. Therefore, they argue, their opinion should not be condemned. Let them weigh in that passage what the subject is, what follows, what precedes, and what the context is: it will be clear that he does not ascribe all corruptible things to chance, but to fate and the laws of ending, from which neither wealth, nor strength, nor wisdom can exempt anyone. Therefore, that passage does nothing for the impious, who, having itching ears, twist everything into their own opinion. Just as that most unspeakable scoundrel **P. Pomponatius** <note>Pietro Pomponazzi (1462–1525), a philosopher who sparked controversy by arguing that the immortality of the soul could not be proven by reason alone.</note> did, for the sake of a certain...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...demonstrates, where he treats the winds. Just as we perceive through our very senses that there are four elements in corruptible matter—fire, earth, air, and water—so too is there a fifth, from which the nature of the heavens and the stars consists. According to Aristotle, whom some call the "god of philosophers," even the origin of our souls is carved from this fifth element <note>Original: *quintum [elementum]*. This refers to the "Aether" or "Quintessence," which was thought to be the unchanging material of the celestial spheres.</note>. Beyond these five bodies, nothing can be found in the nature of things that presents itself to our senses, except for what is made from their composition. Thus, whether it be a mathematician or anyone else—even if he were to scour the entire globe, carving and polishing, attempting a thousand times to shape all metals and liquids into other regular forms consisting of identical parts—he could still form nothing entirely regular except for those five bodies <note>These are the "Platonic Solids": the tetrahedron, cube (hexahedron), octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note>. From this, it is clear that there is a plain affinity of form between these first principles, just as there is an affinity of number.

Therefore, antiquity rightly compared these bodies, which are produced from the triangle, to the five elements. When I reflect on this, I realize that although the human intellect can achieve much on its own, I cannot believe that the first person to pass these truths to posterity received them by any way other than divine inspiration. No one could have surpassed our natural lifespan ten times over, even by constant thinking and shaping of forms, to discover this. This is especially true because if you were to prescribe a single diverse mixture of bases to even the most skilled artisan, he could not produce a single trial of it in ten whole years—as is proven by experience. For many craftsmen have dared to attempt this, but after trying for a very long time, they finally came to their senses and acknowledged both the truth and their own rashness.

Now, we must most attentively weigh how well these shapes correspond to the nature of things. Just as the triangle is the smallest of all regular surfaces, so the <term>tetrahedron</term>—that is, a shape of four bases rising from equilateral triangles—is the smallest of all regular bodies. It is impossible by any logic to admit any other surface into it. For if a square were added to the triangles, it would become a <term>pentahedron</term> (five-sided); if a pentagon, it would become a <term>heptahedron</term> (seven-sided); if two squares, a third must necessarily be added along with two triangles to make it a pentahedron. Thus, no smaller regular body can exist. For this reason, the ancients compared it to **fire**, which is the thinnest among the elements; unless there is matter to feed or preserve it, fire escapes our senses. However, when it acts upon matter, even flames represent the pyramid of a tetrahedron, stretching from a wider base to a sharp point.

But the primary consideration must be paid to the bases. Because **earth** itself shares the quality of "dryness" with fire, they placed its symbol in the second position as the <term>hexahedron</term> <note>original Greek: *ἑξάεδρον*. This is the six-sided cube.</note>. This is the most stable of all figures, having six sides or "tiles" <note>original: *tesserā*—referring to the six-sided dice used in games.</note>, just like a cube. Upon whichever side it falls, it stands unmoved. Gamblers know this best. There is no doubt that a square consists of two opposing isosceles (equal-legged) triangles. Therefore, the most stable figure is suited to earth, the base of all elements—not merely for the sake of the shape, but for its properties.

The <term>octahedron</term> (eight-sided) is compared to **air**, because air is already far more prone to motion than earth, yet far duller in its heat-action than fire. To **water**, they assigned the <term>icosahedron</term> <note>original Greek: *εἰκοσάεδρον*. A twenty-sided shape.</note>, because it is well-suited for motion, yet possesses a very dull action. For although water is the source of moisture, it is far "moister" in potential than in act. Unless it is moved or dissolved by the force of air and fire, it has no action at all; thus, water is usually more easily confined to a place.

Air itself penetrates everything, even moistening rocks and metals, which is evident in "sweating" and the contraction of things. For drops flow from solid and polished bodies. Indeed, after great cold, when the moisture is dissolved by the force of heat, the very rocks and bronze columns tend to "sweat"—not because of water, which could not be admitted into solid bodies, but because of air, which mingled with the bodies due to its thinness and then returned to a liquid state. This agrees with the three elements mentioned above, because the figures adapted to them rise immediately from triangles.

...due to the greater speed of action and passion, while the earth is formed mediately. For a square consists of two opposing isosceles triangles, as has been said; but the earth consists of six squares <note>This refers to the cube, the geometric solid associated with the element of Earth, which has six square faces.</note>. But since, by hypothesis, there are only five regular bodies, one cannot progress beyond the pentagon for their formation. Thus, from twelve pentagons, a body of twelve bases is composed, which they call the **dodecahedron**, and they adapt it to the heavens for this reason: just as the circuit of the sky consists of 360 degrees, so this body consisting of twelve pentagons yields the same number. 

For each pentagon is made of five triangles, each of which consists of six scalene triangles; this number, multiplied by itself, produces the 360 degrees of the "great circle" <note>12 faces × 5 triangles × 6 scalenes = 360. Postel is using geometric numerology to link the dodecahedron to the 360 degrees of the zodiac.</note>. Therefore, I believe it came to pass that this number of degrees—although discovered by the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian astronomers and mathematicians.</note> and by divine men (whoever they were) rather than by human reason alone—has held its place throughout the whole world. For although the calculation of years has varied, it was necessary to preserve the year according to that number of degrees. 

Now, therefore, it is seen that the four elements and the **entelechy** <term>entelechy: from the Greek *entelecheia*, referring to the vital principle or the "actuality" that makes a thing what it is.</term> entirely correspond with the five regular bodies. There remains the figure which is easily the chief of all in capacity, form, and motion, embracing all those others within itself: the **circle**. Although it is not seen by the eyes <note>Postel likely refers here to the "perfect" geometric circle or the sphere of the universe, rather than a drawn line.</note>, yet because it exists in the nature of things beyond the other shapes, it necessarily has its own archetype and image, with which it must agree in many, if not all, things; and this image is God himself, who corresponds to the circle in every possible way. 

For a circle is born to move up and down simultaneously; it proceeds forward and backward in a single action, and it encompasses whatever exists in other things and forms—even contradictions (such as motion and rest, and in a word, all things)—which consist of presence and not of lack. It has a beginning, middle, and end everywhere; yet it has no beginning, middle, or end. Nothing can be added to it or taken away without destroying it, unlike other forms. 

But it differs most from the other regular bodies in that their size can be grasped by a certain measure and reduced to a "squaring" <note>Original: *quadraturam*. This refers to "squaring the circle," the ancient mathematical challenge of constructing a square with the same area as a given circle using only a compass and straightedge.</note>, by which all things can be measured. But the squaring of the circle will be perpetually "potential" in knowledge; it cannot be precisely measured by anyone. Thus, the elements themselves and the celestial orbs fall within our grasp, except for the line from the center; but no thought can ever grasp the measure of the immense God, since there is no proportion between the finite and the infinite. 

Therefore, all other things can be called "imperfect," because while their name remains the same, something can be added to or taken from them. You can take nothing from a circle, nor add anything, without overturning it. Thus, that first circle is most perfectly aligned with Unity; it is perfect and least subject to matter. Even **Aben Reis** <note>Original: *Aben reis*. This is Averroes (Ibn Rushd, 1126–1198), the influential Andalusian philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note>, the greatest seeker of truth through the intellect, says that the substance of the sphere has neither matter nor form. How true that is, let him see! For concerning those things which we know only by what they are not—such as all celestial things and the First Cause—we can assert nothing <margin>*</margin> except from their effects. 

Averroes would certainly have been by far the most outstanding of mortals if he had wished to spend as much effort proving the First Cause and the belief in God received throughout the world as he labored to tear it out of the minds of men. The cause of this was the most absurd persuasion about God which **Muhammad** left in writing (as will be clear in its proper place). Imbued with this from childhood and diligently instructed in it, as befits a man of high standing—which he was—when he came to the knowledge of truth, he did so not through the prescriptions of a foolish and wicked law, but by the guidance of reason. 

He burned with such a fire against that absurdity and imposture—under which he had long been a miserable captive buried in the darkness of ignorance—that he not only took up arms against that religion, but attempted to overturn all religions. He tried to thrust upon the world a certain fate and a most "powerless" God—that is, one destitute of free will. He did this for one reason: because he saw many people approving the decrees of that persuasion, especially a certain **Gezel** <note>Original: *Gezelem*. This refers to Al-Ghazali (1058–1111), the Persian theologian who famously attacked the philosophers in his work *The Incoherence of the Philosophers*.</note> who argued against the philosophers...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...love, most loving. Since He truly loves all things in Himself in the highest degree (for in Him is the life consisting of that love), He does so through the greatest unity of love. For just as He is most perfect, so He unites most perfectly. Since He is the highest love, in Him is the very equality of love (for otherwise He would love nothing, unless the equality of love represented itself to Him from within Himself) responding to the one loving, so that in Him there is the lover and the beloved, from whom proceeds a common love. The loving friendship holds the place of God the Father; the friendship by which all things flourish is the Son; and the love proceeding from the lover and the beloved is called the Holy Spirit. The whole friendship is in the lover, the whole in the beloved or the lovable, and the whole is in the love: and yet there are not three friendships, but one friendship. For while God knows Himself in Himself, He loves Himself in the knowledge of Himself with a most uniting love (just as one who sees himself in a mirror loves himself most because he greatly prizes his own form) and generates a "beloved love," whom we call the Son of God: from these two proceeds a bond <note>original: *nexus*</note>, and these three things are one. It is just as water is one and the same, differing only by "before" and "after," as it flows from a fountain through a river into a pond. For the channel proceeds from the fountain, and the pond from the fountain and the channel. And to demonstrate by a clearer example: a fountain returning waters to itself and sending them forth can be compared to God. Let the water spring up in one place, and let it pool; finally, let it be soaked back into the veins of the earth—it is one and the same water springing up, pooling, and receding, in which there is no "before" or "after." For it acts as one, if we observe carefully. We do almost nothing in which a single will, action, and passion <note>In the philosophical sense, "passion" refers to the state of being acted upon.</note> do not concur: as if, driven by bile, I strike a man, my will, the blow, and his suffering all concur as one. *

<margin>*</margin> Human love also imitates the divine. For it is impossible to love without there being a lover, a beloved, and a love proceeding from both: of which we shall speak later.

->FOURTH<-

That there is a multitude and a number in the things of the universe, there is no one who doubts. Yet, before every number and multitude, a most simple unity must precede. For if that were removed, number could not arise. Therefore, God is the sacrosanct and primordial unity. Among created things differing in number, there is necessarily a certain inequality. For otherwise all things would be one and similar. Furthermore, nothing is so similar to another even under some specific appearance that it does not differ in some way. Since, therefore, there is a difference and inequality between individual things, before the creation of all things there was **equality**; for the mind knows nothing as unequal, neither in reality nor in the soul, unless it first knows the equality by which it may judge the unequal. Therefore, before all things, there is also equality, which is also the one God, equal to Himself.

All things, insofar as they represent themselves to the perception of the senses by themselves, are separate. For no pure notion can be had of confused things. But before every separation, a bond <term>nexus: a joining or connection that holds disparate things together</term> precedes, by which things are what they are. In nature, conjunction precedes separation, nor can one exist in the sense without the other. Therefore, that eternal bond is called God. Since He is thus one and most simple, yet He also has equality and the bond within Himself, and there is in unity a likeness and a bond; in the bond, equality and unity; in equality—where there is neither less nor more—are the species and forms, and there is also a bond and unity. Three in one, and one in three, existing together, neither confused nor separated.

->FIFTH<-

Individual things, whether made by nature (meaning God) or by art, are accustomed to bear witness to their author (as is commonly said) and to reflect his **vestiges** <term>vestiges: from the Latin *vestigia*, meaning "footprints" or "traces" left by God in the physical world</term>. Hence the skill or lack of skill of craftsmen is usually discerned from their works. Since, therefore, all natural things are produced by God as the First Cause through the path of nature and artifice, He testifies to the nature of the author in this: that just as He is one, and yet has a Trinity in persons so that He cannot exist without it, so also individual natural compounds have His image so closely connected within them...

<summary>Postel argues that God’s triune nature (Unity, Equality, and Bond) is a logical necessity that precedes all creation and is mirrored in the physical world through "vestiges" or traces. He uses the analogies of a water cycle and the relationship between a lover and beloved to explain how God can be three persons in one essence.</summary>

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.

...origin, so that it cannot perish from it without the things themselves perishing. Just as, therefore, from the eternal power of God there proceeds from eternity His wisdom, and from both benevolence and love toward Himself and created things; so also in individual things there is, according to their own nature, a fruitfulness or power for acting, from which there is an inexhaustible progression of their action and virtue, which through a love of acting never ceases from its nature, and as it were, makes a choice <note>original: *delectum*, suggesting both a selection and a natural delight</note> in acting. For example: As long as pepper is pepper, it has an inexhaustible power of acting—that is, of heating or burning—from which proceeds that burning or action, naturally loving to act. For as long as it is pepper, it can burn the tongue if it is rubbed; nor does that force ever fail it as long as it exists, but it proceeds and acts in its own way from where it began to go forth, as if making a choice. For it acts upon sweaty skin rather than upon skin where pores are not open, upon flayed skin rather than whole skin, and upon a tongue suited for taste rather than upon the other parts of the body. Likewise fire, however small its quantity may be, has an untiring power, from which flows an unceasing progression of heating and burning, also having its own choice and delight in acting. Thus the smallest spark is of such great force that it could burn forests and the world, and it makes its choice with such delight and love of acting that it prefers straw and thin dry bodies to moist and thick ones, and thus chooses in such an order that it is never deceived. So in us the vital, natural, and animal faculties act upon those things which are added to or taken from the body, such that nothing more powerful, nothing more fruitful and abundant, and nothing more prudent seems possible. Thus trees are nourished, animals are preserved, and the natures of all things exist with that holy Trinity giving life to all, so that when that force and image has perished in them, they are no more. The entire force of things consists in power, the whole in progression, the whole in choice and love; and yet they are not three things, but one, just as power, wisdom, and love are only one God.

### PROOF FROM CREATED THINGS, AND
->first from minds and souls.<-

I see that no one doubts that man consists of body and soul. Let us speak first of its most excellent part: so that since it is most especially one and simple, escaping the senses of the body and accessible only through its effects, we may nevertheless see the image of God within it. The soul, as it is called by a general name, is one, and consists of three parts or properties: the vital life, the sensitive life, and the discerning life—although some claim there is a soul in plants having attractive, retentive, and expulsive faculties <note>A common Aristotelian classification of biological functions</note>. The life of brute animals consists of life, sense, and choice. The first acts while the second and third are at rest. From the first proceeds the second, and the third from both. When I grant "choice" to brutes, I do not mean free will or intellect, but the knowledge of fleeing and seeking; without which faculty they could not prolong life nor provide for themselves. These three parts are also common to humans. For a person living in sleep lives and is animated by the vital life. Sensation proceeds from there, and without it, one does not choose. Therefore, that choice proceeds from the vital and the sensitive, and not the other way around. But reason, approaching the same, consists of intellect, reasoning, and remembrance. For in brutes there is found apprehension, thought, and memory; but that they should understand those things which are more remote from the senses of the body, or reason and gather, or remember through discourse like a human, is impossible. The Father is like apprehension—that is, the source. The Son—that is, the progression from apprehension—is thought. The Spirit is memory itself, which proceeds from both faculties. In the same way reason, mind, or intellect, or soul (for these differ in name, not in essence) produces reasoning and wisdom: these procreate remembrance. For (as the Philosopher <note>Referring to Aristotle</note> says) in this dreg-filled matter <note>original: *feculenta materia*, referring to the physical world of decay</note>, nothing can be found of understanding, gathering, and remembering...

For this reason, he traced the origin of souls back to that **entelechy** <note>original: *entelechiam*; an Aristotelian term referring to the full realization or "actuality" of a potential being</note> and the **fifth element** <note>also known as the quintessence, the pure substance of the heavens</note> (from which perfection comes to things); from this, it is certain that they are immortal. If prudence is present, the image of Divinity also appears in reason: so that we can call the mind, "reason"; the collection or induction of thoughts, "reason"; and even recollection, "reason." Certainly, we cannot act prudently without this likeness to Him. For if reason does not grasp what it intends to deliberate upon with a firm and constant image, and if it does not calculate that the power to act is within itself, a person will never undertake anything by their own will. For a person would want in vain what they neither knew nor had the power to do. Thus, more things happen by the guidance of nature than by our own intellect. For our will is frequently hindered, while nature is never—or rarely—obstructed.

### FROM BODIES.

7 Now, from the body itself, which falls under the reach of the senses, the arguments will be even more manifest. No body can be found in the whole nature of things that is not both "one" in itself and composed of **form** and **matter**. Therefore, Plato said that there were three principles of all things: **Matter, Form, and God**. Aristotle, contradicting him as if he had thought up something brilliant, put **privation** <note>Aristotle's term for the absence of a form that a thing should naturally possess</note> in the place of God; let those who are led by reason rather than authority judge how well he did so. Both would have spoken better and more appropriately if they had named **Form, Matter, and Divine Unity**. Plato, however, is closer to the truth. Thus, the Form itself, giving "being" to the thing, places the Matter into existence; from these two proceeds the "Composite" <note>the finished object or creature</note>. It is not possible to separate Form from Matter, nor vice versa, nor the whole Composite from its parts, except by the intellect itself. For if you separate them, the thing no longer exists. From this, the mystery of the Holy Trinity and Unity is clear—how one is three, and three are one. Rightly, therefore, that atheist Lucian <note>a Greek satirist known for mocking religion</note> and Julian the "Deserter of Holy Reason" <note>Emperor Julian "the Apostate," who rejected Christianity</note> are not only to be hissed out of the company of us Christians, but even out of the company of philosophers, for they could never grasp such clear arguments, or else refused to acknowledge them once known.

### FROM THE PARTS OF BODIES.

8 But perhaps matter, once dissolved from its composite and separated, or the parts inherent in the whole, do not possess this image of the Trinity. Let us consider this. Certainly, when a man has perished, the most excellent form—namely the mind and the soul—departs; yet even the breathless corpse consists of its own form and matter. Matter and form cannot be deprived of unity until the body loses its "principle of generation" <note>its basic biological structure</note> and returns its parts to the elements. The same must clearly be felt regarding the parts of a body, whether they are simple or complex: everywhere there is matter, form, and a unity or "bond" <note>original: *nexus*</note> connecting them. You may see this in a familiar example: the **magnet**. That stone consists of one southern part and another northern part; if you touch and rub iron needles with them, one part will be forced to turn toward the north, the other toward the south. Cut whichever part you wish from the whole, and try to separate the southern part from the northern part—you will never be able to. Cut a slice however thin from any part: both parts will be in it, just as in the whole, whichever way you cut it. Thus, in all human affairs, the **triune** <note>original: *unitrina*; three-in-one</note> power of the Creator is most evident. For (as in the magnet) two different parts are so connected that their bond cannot be torn away from them.

### FROM THE NATURE OF LIGHT.

9 Nothing greater or more famous regarding the nature of light can be brought forward than the **Sun** itself; the Creator has placed nothing more admirable before the eyes of mortals for contemplation. For that reason, it is less surprising that men ignorant of the Creator held the sun to be God, since even those who especially claimed the name of "prudence" preferred scoundrels and lost souls to the sun, placing men hardly worthy of sewers in the heavens and adorning the greatest pests of the world with noble names. To such an extent does the power of Satan blind the miserable minds of men, so that they delight in their own miseries. But back to the point.

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK I.

<margin>Some have used the example of the sun in this way: the radiance is the Father, the light is the Son, and the heat is the Holy Spirit.</margin> No one denies that the sun itself is a body, acting as a center of light, nor that rays proceed from it. It is well established that the rays and the power of the light differ greatly, for the rays spread out very widely, while the body itself is quite small. Furthermore, the effect—whether it be the brightness, the ripening of fruit, or whatever utility comes to us—also differs from the sun itself. Therefore, the center of the sun is like the Father, holding all things in his power, eternally generating rays from himself; by both of these, everything in the heavens and the elements is nourished, whatever is born to be moved, helped, or changed by his power. This is indeed a most clear example. First, the center or body, like the Father, procreates the Son as a ray from eternity, in whom he places the power over all things, just as he has it in himself. The effect itself is not "born," but is seen "proceeding" from the body and the rays. It is therefore necessary to admit that the **archetype** <note>the original model or divine pattern of God</note> is of a similar nature and a most simple **hypostasis** <term>hypostasis: a theological term referring to a distinct person or individual reality within the one essence of God</term>, since an example of it is never lacking.

->FROM THE REASON OF THE UNIVERSE<-

10 No eminent philosopher denies that heaven itself is moved by a perpetually constant and stationary power, and that it necessarily obeys, having no choice in how it is moved. From this it is clear that the universe also consists of a triple **hypostasis**. For although the power, majesty, and act of God are spread everywhere (needing no specific place), yet because of the excellence of his essence, he is properly said to be "above the heavens," where his greater and nobler operation is seen. In the second place is the "middle world," namely the celestial region; the ancients called it "middle" because countless separate substances <note>referring to angels or celestial intelligences</note> are established there, and from there, motion, action, and the changing of things flow down into the lower realms. Third is this corruptible world known to us, the most imperfect, depending on the first and second. If we see this world as admirable, what must we judge concerning the excellence of the others? This world, were it not for the **forms** <note>the organizing principles of matter</note> mixed within it and the spirit nourishing all things, would not quite fit the comparison. But if we look at the forms and the vital force, it matches in every way. It is as if the higher world were the Father, the middle world (eternally generated by the Father) were the Son, and the lower world were the Holy Spirit—not born, but proceeding. It has been sufficiently demonstrated by all parts of the universe that the Author must necessarily have within himself a most perfect unity in trinity, and trinity in unity. But perhaps someone will object that such demonstrations have a place in the constant things of nature, but that human actions are exempt from this pattern. Truly, whatever comes from deliberation—however poorly weighed or useless—it is impossible for it to exist without a trinity necessarily being present from the very power of the thinking mind.

->FROM THINGS MADE BY HUMAN INDUSTRY<-

11 Whatever we ever attempt, it must proceed from the mind's cognition, wisdom, and will. For unless I understand and have the faculty, how could I will anything freely? For to will and not be able is slavery, not freedom of choice. Before we even come to the work, even outside the mind, there is a need for a craftsman, tools, and matter. Without these, the work does not arise. In friendship there is the lover, the beloved, and the love that is the bond of both. For the lover is not the beloved, nor vice versa; nor is the love the same as either, though it proceeds from both. This is also clear in neutral actions. Just as in a "run" there is the action, the passion <note>original: *passio*; here meaning the state of being acted upon or the physical experience of the act</note>, and the "running" itself which is the bond of both. Hence it becomes less a thing to wonder at when, in Divine Goodness, action and passion are the same thing; for although the most simple Being can suffer nothing, we speak this way because He reflects upon himself whatever qualities are most excellent, in a manner unknown to us.

->FROM THE ORDER OF MAGISTRATES<-

12 Although human nature itself was otherwise happy—alas, destined to be eternally happy if it had preserved the innocence given by the Creator—it was forced by imperfection, necessity, and vice to establish the order of magistrates to preserve humans in turn...

ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...to protect: nevertheless, because it was forced to find a remedy for human affairs by the guidance of reason and intellect, it could not happen otherwise than that the Holy Trinity itself gave the beginning. Even when things flourished in false religions estranged from God, the Trinity formed an order in its own image. Thus, all magistrates <note>Magistrates here refers to any person holding public office or authority.</note> were divided into three types. For they manage the care of either souls, bodies, or external things: namely, priests, judges, and kings. These three "persons" were one in the first institution of Republics. For when few peoples were gathered and the ambition for ruling was unknown, the same person was priest, judge, and leader. Hearing cases based on sacred laws, when necessity arose and sacred rites were performed, he was a successful leader for his soldiers—defending his own people’s property, not lusting after the property of others.

<margin>
Christ, being abundantly sufficient for governing all things, gave equal power to the Apostles and apostolic men, each in his own Church and province. This is noted so that no one might perhaps think that their own tyranny is approved by this argument.
</margin>

When affairs eventually increased, three levels of men were introduced for each office. In sacred matters, one leader, now made superior, established others in different places. If a dispute arose among them, so they would not labor too much by seeking a legal ruling from so far away, he willed there to be certain officials of "middle power," to whom he granted his authority as far as he wished. Thus, all power began to be in the highest, all in the middle, and all in the lowest; and yet they are not three powers, but one power. Those second from the first, and those lower than the first and middle, use their own authority. The same is true in military matters, concerning the king, the commanders, and the soldier; likewise for judges, with the highest, middle, and lowest authority—total in each individual and total in the whole group: a unity in trinity. In short, there is nothing that does not represent that most sacred property of the divinity. In all things, there is a beginning, a middle, and an end. In motions: upward and downward, forward and backward, to the right and to the left. For these do not differ except because they consist of an impulse and three straight intersecting lines. The nourishment of things is drawn inward, outward, or both ways. Time consists of past, present, and future. In geometry, no regular, angular shape exists before three straight lines meet; in the composition of regular solids, only three surfaces can meet: the triangle, the square, and the pentagon. In summary, nothing is free from the mystery of that triad.

### THE TESTIMONY AND AUTHORITY OF PHILOSOPHERS
### concerning the Trinity.

13 Aristotle, the philosopher of truth, writes as follows about the trinity in the first book of *On the Heavens and the World* <note>original: "de Coelo & mundo"</note>: "Knowledge," he says, "concerning nature is mostly occupied with bodies and magnitudes, and their attributes and motions, and concerning principles, as many as are of the same substance. For of those things that consist of nature, some are bodies and magnitudes, others are body and magnitude, and others are the principles of these. Therefore, the continuous is always divisible, but a body can be divided in every direction. Furthermore, magnitude can be divided into one part, like a line; into two, like a surface; or into three, like a body. And beyond this there is no magnitude, because all things are three, and the trinity is everywhere. For as the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who believed numbers were the essence of all things.</note> say, the universe and all things are bounded by three. For the beginning, middle, and end have the number of the universe." I understand here the number of the trinity. Therefore, receiving from nature as if her own laws, we use this number in sacred rites and give the names of numbers to it. For we do not say "all" for two, but "both"; however, for three, we say "all."

And likewise in the eighth book of the *Physics*, he says the world is ruled by three: the unmoved mover, the moved mover, and the moved non-mover <term>unmoved mover: Aristotle's concept of a primary cause of all motion that does not itself move; Postel identifies this with God the Father</term>. This is as if he were to say: the uncreated Father generates the eternal Son, from whom and from the Father proceeds the Holy Spirit, in whom is the end of the divinity—if it is permitted to compare corruptible things to eternal ones, and finite to infinite. If I were to write down what should be ascribed to me concerning the Divine Mind and the Creator in the works of Plotinus, Porphyry, Proclus, Maximus, Amelius, Iamblichus, Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a syncretic combination of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth; seen as a source of ancient wisdom.</note>, and their teacher Zoroaster, there would undoubtedly be no end. For nothing was more persuasive to learned men in all ages than that there is necessarily a Mind proceeding from the highest Parent. Therefore...
