# THE BOOKS OF GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK 1.

Leaving aside their opinions and authorities regarding this mind, let us see what the most divine of philosophers, Plato, thought of our triad. He revealed it through a famous enigma addressed to the tyrant Dionysius <note>Dionysius II, the ruler of Syracuse, to whom Plato addressed several letters.</note>. "Concerning the nature of the first (that is, of God)," he said, "I must speak to you in riddles, so that if these letters are intercepted, they may not be understood by anyone else. Hear it thus: All things are around the King of all, and all things are for His sake, and He is the cause of all good things. A second group of things is around the second, and a third group around the third." After Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who was often critical of Christianity, though Postel argues he recognized Christian truths.</note> had learned how to explain these words from the Christians, he interpreted them as referring to the Triune God: the first **hypostasis** <term>hypostasis: a technical term for a "person" or "substance" within the Trinity</term> is the Supreme God; the second is the Maker of all things; the third is the Mind of the soul. Since that wretched man [Porphyry] had come to know this, it is a wonder he valued human glory so much that he recoiled from the very truth he was forced to admit—and like Maximus, Amelius, and Plotinus, he took his best ideas from our own people. 

In the meantime, we must not omit what is said of Amelius: when he had read the Gospel of John, he exclaimed from the very beginning, "May I perish if that barbarian <note>original: "barbarus ille"; Amelius uses "barbarian" to refer to the Apostle John, who was not a Greek philosopher.</note> has not briefly captured exactly what Plato and Heraclitus <note>The text says "Heraclius," likely a variant or error for the philosopher Heraclitus.</note> taught regarding the divine Reason, the Principle, and the Arrangement of things." There is no doubt that Plato would have brought forth far more concerning the Holy Trinity—which he had surely learned from the prophets—had he not considered it a religious duty to keep the holy mysteries secret. He had obtained them with difficulty and wished to keep them for himself alone. He did not even wish to reveal them to the tyrant from whom he had received great favors. Thus, ambition lost the truth and drove it away from our company. 

What would the great Pythagoras not have declared after seeing the Gymnosophists <note>literally "naked wise men," referring to ancient Indian philosophers.</note>, the Magi, the Egyptians, and the divine prophets, had he not wished to keep those things quiet so as to remain an object of wonder? To avoid revealing the Holy Trinity, which he had read about in the works of Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary figure to whom many ancient mystical and philosophical texts were attributed.</note>, he thrust upon his disciples the **tetractys** <term>tetractys: a symbolic triangular figure of four rows of dots, totaling ten; here, Postel suggests it was a "veil" for the number three plus the unity of God.</term>. By this "four-fold" he hinted at the same truth, but covered it in wrappings. For the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were God; the Begetter, the Mind, and the Begotten; and the Soul of the World was God or the Cause—one single thing. For this reason, the Greeks used the term **thrice-blessed** <note>original: "tris-makares"</note> for those who were absolutely happy and lacked nothing. They understood gods clearly worthy of this title. The Latins say "thrice-blessed" in the Platonic manner, and "four-times-blessed" in the Pythagorean manner. 

According to Damascius the Platonist, the Egyptian sages would cry out to the deity three times in their religious rites, and they had an altar dedicated to Minerva in whose temple this was written: *I am all that has been, and is, and shall be, and no mortal has yet uncovered or revealed my veil.* <note>original: "ἐγώ εἰμι πᾶν τὸ γεγονὸς..."</note> Those worthless Greek poets—Orpheus, Linus, Homer, and the rest—by attributing such things to their various gods while concealing the true source of their knowledge, have shaken the world and paved the way for every kind of error. But now we must come to the principles set down in the writings of religion.

## PROOF FROM THE OLD TESTAMENT
### and the Kabbalah and the Talmud.

<margin>
† There are indeed things in the Law to be observed until the "time of correction" [Hebrews 9:10], serving as a teacher leading us to Christ, who perfects all things.
</margin>

Because the † Mosaic Law was like a first rudiment of the divine law—in which remedies for sin were sought but not found, where the fault was shown but not removed—many things were permitted to the Jews themselves because of the hardness of their hearts. These were things that not only Christ himself removed, but even the prophets more than six hundred years before him already seemed to disapprove of. 

<margin>
It cannot be denied, however, that the entire mystery and theology of Christ was handed down by Moses.
</margin>

In that Law, to put it briefly, God acted with Israel as the best teacher does with a very young student; because of his tender age and ignorance, the teacher permits the usual games along with the roots of learning. Because, I say, that Law is the first authority of God (existing in writing) in which He opened Himself to His servants, there will be no better method than to confirm from that source, in a reverse order, the things that have been proven from philosophy. I said "reverse order" because, even in the teaching of disciplines, authority comes before reason. Hence it is rightly written: *Unless you believe, you shall not understand.* <note>A common Latin translation of Isaiah 7:9.</note> This applies not only to sacred matters, but also to the humanities...

->ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-

Here we have God, the word of God, wisdom, and His spirit. He writes the same opinion a little earlier, and in the same words. For he says: "And we gave to Jesus, son of Mary, wisdom, and we formed him from the holy spirit." <note>Postel is likely paraphrasing or quoting a version of the Quran (possibly Surah 2:87 or 4:171) available to him in Latin translation to argue that Islamic tradition inherently acknowledges the Trinity.</note> Here is God who gives, the wisdom which is given, and the Holy Spirit. But since God is the most unified One, and yet sends from Himself wisdom (or the Word) and the Holy Spirit, it is necessary—even according to your own prophet—to infer a Trinity in Unity and a Unity in Trinity, as we demonstrated from necessary principles at the beginning. For if there were only one single quality, nothing at all would come into being, unless, having been conceived by the Father through His wisdom (which He eternally generates), He had created all things in spirit and will. For as has been shown, you imagine in vain unless you know and are wise; and you think and know in vain unless you also will. For it is necessary, as we have said, that all things concur, just as our own intellect—unless it becomes three-and-one in the act of thinking—will never produce anything from its own movement. For it must think, know, and will before it produces an effect. Therefore, you alone of all mortals (O most excellent minds of the world, as long as you judge freely) ought not to resist manifest reason and the proof of all wise men without cause, even if your own persuasion contradicts it. But when you see that reason supports us in this matter, and that God admits and approves of wisdom and His spirit, how much more should you approach and "offer the herb" <note>original: "herbam porrigere" — a Latin idiom meaning to admit defeat or acknowledge the truth.</note> to the truth?

The Muslim <note>original: "Musfulmanus"</note> will say: "Our Law <note>Postel uses "Law" to refer to the Quran or Islamic jurisprudence.</note> fights against this elsewhere, where it says God does not beget, nor is He begotten, because He has no females, and because there are no male or female spirits in heaven." <note>This refers to Surah 112 (Al-Ikhlas): "He begetted not, nor was He begotten."</note> It is certain that God, in our human manner and through the instruments of nature, neither begets nor is begotten. But as we have seen, it is so necessary for Him to eternally generate the Son, who is Wisdom, that the world itself could not otherwise stand. For the Son of God is not a corporeal thing, insofar as He is God, but a purely spiritual thing; and this generation is necessary. Thus both points will hold firm, as I shall reveal more fully in its proper place when explaining the life of Muhammad <note>original: "Muhamedis"</note> and your Law. You see then (O followers of Muhammad, whom I love the more because you were a part of us that perished) that by both divine and human reason, by the authority of all philosophers, of Moses, and of your own, our faith concerning the Trinity is most true, and that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, the Word, and Wisdom: which He joined here to humanity for the sake of the salvation of all. But concerning these things, in their proper place.

### ON THE CREATION OF THE WORLD, AND WHETHER THE WORLD IS
### from eternity. CHAPTER IV.

Up to this point, the entire crowd of philosophers, of whatever sect they may be, has seemed to favor me. For all find it necessary to admit a cause of this universe (which is in itself indeed corruptible) from which, through which, and in which all things consist—or else they must assert that the nature of things is nothing at all. But now, I must declare war on the entire tribe of philosophers, and finally settle a peace with them. First of all, there is a great dissension among them all, so that if it could have happened by the nature of the case, you would have seen here as many opinions on the constitution of the world as there are men. In truth, there could not be more than these five positions. 

For as pertains to the universe, not a few—and those who bind many to the oath of their authority—assert it is eternal on both sides: that is, it had no beginning and will feel no end. It pleased others that it indeed had an origin, but will not perish. Some held that it had indeed been eternal from the beginning, but would finally and gradually fail. We ascribe its origin and its end to the will of the Mover <note>Postel refers to God as the "Motor" or "Mover," a common Aristotelian and Scholastic term for the Creator.</note>. If there are any who attribute these same things to its own nature, I know not; certainly, if there be any such, they are in great error and deprived of common sense, who affirm that this order of things and such a great mass lack a cause. To judge among all these, as it does not lack the greatest difficulty in the whole world, so it seems to me as if some members of a prince's household...

### BOOK I OF GUILLAUME POSTEL

...about His majesty, they argue in such a way as if they were dealing with their own most familiar affairs. Through either ignorance or an inability to grasp His majesty—or even through sheer contention and desire—they cast Him down from His own empire by their own opinions, while they are either unable to defend His rights or even attempt to subvert them. It is certain that this nursery of discord was sown in the seat of truth by the adversary of the human mind <note>The "adversary" refers to Satan or the devil.</note>, so that wretched men might be perpetually engaged in arguing while seeking the truth, and might contend for glory. Their goal is not to gather more votes for the truth, but to foist their own dreams onto posterity and to testify that they lived through their wicked crimes. I do not deny that the love of truth and the zeal for seeking it has made many men perplexed; but far more have been driven astray by lust. It is certain that we owe this to *Greece* (as we owe many good things), so that even the most excellent thing [philosophy] might not be without its own plague. These opinions must be scrutinized more carefully and not concluded in an irreligious manner. 

Regarding the opinion of the *Peripatetics* <term>Peripatetics: The followers of Aristotle, so named because they reportedly walked about while discussing philosophy.</term>, which is first in authority and position (since it has more who approve and defend it as being more plausible), it must be discussed in the final place, after applying reasons and authorities from both sides. *Plato* agrees with us in part; his axiom holds the second place. For, compelled by necessity, he knew that this matter had an origin—or at least that it was inferior to the First Cause by being posterior to it. For whoever posits a cause (as all learned men do) will necessarily say that it differs from the effect; otherwise, the cause and the effect would be one and the same, which is contrary to the senses. For nothing can produce itself. And furthermore, the matter of the world would then be a part of God, and the causer would not differ from the thing caused—which is altogether absurd. 

Therefore, *Plato* necessarily ascribed a Beginning to the world. As for the fact that he withheld from it an end and destruction, he does not prove this by arguments or tricks drawn from the nature of things, but affirms that it will be so by the favor of the Creator, because He is good and does not begrudge His goodness to anyone. For this reason, he likewise attributes this to separate and immaterial substances <note>These "separate substances" are what Postel identifies as angels and demons.</note>, saying that they are mortal by their own nature, unless they are granted a longer life by the will of the Creator through His kindness. 

Truly, in my judgment, he did not consider carefully enough the nature of demons—whom we call both good and bad angels. For since they are pure immaterial forms, it is impossible for them to perish while the First Cause remains vital and non-perishing. But he did this, in my judgment, not so much from a false opinion conceived about these things, but because he considered it a religious duty not to subtract anything from the will and power of the Creator. That good man did not notice, as I judge (saving any better opinion), what he himself often asserted: that evil is "non-being" <note>original: "non ens"</note>, which is not made by the Creator but happens on the part of matter through the privation of good and essence. 

Thus, he agrees with us, except regarding the transformation of matter, which we hold by our religion will surely happen. For although we grant the world a beginning, we do not admit its destruction, but rather its transformation—which both God and nature perform—affirming it will be entirely for the better, so that all corruption may be absent in the future. Indeed, regarding this point, we later agree with both [philosophers] on the fact and the manner of the beginning; but regarding the end, we differ only in the manner, being equal in the reality of the thing. He believes in eternal corruption <note>Plato views the physical world as naturally subject to decay, preserved only by God's will.</note>, while we believe in eternal incorruption, which is far more worthy of the majesty of the Creator. But if the philosophers, those lovers of truth, deny this to me, I will necessarily extract it from their own principles in the Chapter on Transformation. 

Those who affirm that the world is corruptible only at the end, and that it is firm and constant from eternity up to a certain period, agree on one side with *Aristotle* and on the end with us—except that they introduce "corruption" in the place of "transformation" and "perfection." I shall "paint both walls with one stroke" <note>This is a translation of a Latin idiom meaning to address two problems with a single solution or argument.</note> when the beginning is discussed. We hold to what the nature of things carries, as is already clear and will be made more clear. Just as they are entirely destitute of reason, so...

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

<meta>catchword: God</meta>

Nor do those people need a refutation who have arrived at such impudence and rashness that they ascribe things which are most constant and orderly to fortune and chance. They claim that atoms—with their tiny hooks—are wiser than God and nobler than all of nature, and they attribute "choice" to these atoms so that they can choose one another, connect together, and generate things from that union. <note>Postel is mocking the Epicurean theory of "hooked atoms" (*uncinis*) which suggested matter combined by chance without a divine creator.</note> I am weary and ashamed of this opinion. I hesitate even to call them "men" who, in their pursuit of a little glory, preferred to deny that reason existed within themselves rather than subscribe to the common sense and consensus of the rest of mortality. Nature produced such monsters only so that we would not grow sluggish once the truth was found. 

Now I come to **Aristotle** and the students of his sect. Listen, whoever you are, you who think that assent should not be withheld from manifest truths. The Cause, which we all prove and affirm to preside over this world, necessarily preceded the effect, at least in respect to time or by the logic of order. For whether a cause is antecedent and remote, or conjoined and near, it precedes the thing of which it is the cause. The *efficient* and *final* causes are prior in time; the *formal* and *material* causes precede the effects at least in the understanding. <term>Efficient Cause: The agent that brings something into being; Final Cause: The purpose for which a thing exists; Formal/Material Cause: The essence and the physical substance of a thing.</term> For although matter pre-exists in things that can decay, yet while the thing does not yet exist—before the matter is joined to it—the matter is not said to "pre-exist" the thing itself. 

But so there is no occasion for doubt, I speak here of the *efficient cause*, not the others, unless we also admit a similarity to the *formal cause*. Therefore, no matter how continuous and eternal you make the world, you must necessarily admit it is posterior to its cause; otherwise, you would call it either the cause itself or a part of the cause, which is most absurd. For you know that the cause and the effect differ, and nothing can be called a cause except in respect to what is caused. Furthermore, the cause would necessarily be creating a part of itself if it were joined [to the effect]. All these things are manifestly absurd, inconsistent, and impossible. 

Therefore, the world had a beginning, however ancient you make it. I am not lingering on the question of "time" now, for I will deal with that in its proper place. But whatever had a beginning (provided it consists of form and matter) is certain to experience ruin as far as its own nature is concerned. Aristotle proves this regarding inferior and elemental matter, but it must also be understood regarding the heavens. For in the heavens—whether **Averroes** <note>original: "Aben reis," the Latinized name for the 12th-century Islamic philosopher Ibn Rushd.</note> likes it or not—there is matter and form, a point Aristotle does not disprove. Therefore, by reason of its "body" (which, though not having form annexed to matter in the same way as these lower things), it must still follow that because it is a body, it is apt for corruption and subject to a beginning. 

This is also evident by the logic of quantity. For whatever things are "bodies," because they are finite, they are by their very nature subject to corruption, unless sustained by an infinite moving power. That the heaven is finite is evident even to the eyes; it is demonstrated by the nature of a finite circle (that is, a physical body) and is established by the Greek etymology. For the Greek word for heaven is *ouranos*, which means "the boundary of the things above," as **Plato** rightly says. <note>original: "οὐρανός ὄρος τῶν ἄνω" (ouranos oros tōn anō). Postel uses Plato's Cratylus to argue that the very name of heaven implies a limit or "boundary."</note> Whatever is of such a nature is finite, and therefore corruptible. Indeed, the Philosopher <note>Common medieval/Renaissance shorthand for Aristotle.</note> himself affirms this in the eighth book of the *Physics*, the twelfth of the *Metaphysics*, and the second of *On the Heavens and the World*; even **Averroes** proves it in the third book of *On the Substance of the World*. **Alexander of Aphrodisias** does not shrink from this opinion either. 

Furthermore, whatever things possess "potentiality" are also by their nature subject to corruption, since nothing can be eternal of itself unless it is **Pure Act**. <term>Pure Act: A philosophical term for God, meaning a being that is fully realized and has no "potential" to change or be anything else.</term> But here, by chance, I have touched upon a knot more than Gordian, <note>The "Gordian Knot" refers to an unsolvable problem, famously cut by Alexander the Great.</note> and one which even Alexander’s sword could scarcely loosen. For because God is "Pure Act" or "Power" (philosophers understand "power" as the capacity to act or not act, not as regarding the power of nature, for God is most powerful), a great difficulty arises from this. Therefore, the nature of God himself must be sought—not from the authority of the Divine Will, but from the prisons of the philosophers who constrain Him with bars and bolts—so we may see whether, since other things are necessary, it might be possible (even through the faculties given to God by the philosophers) for the same things to be called true, so that what is evident to the senses might also be established by reason. For wretched...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument against the Aristotelian idea of an eternal universe. Having previously discussed the "efficient cause," he now addresses the freedom of God's will against the "necessity" argued by certain philosophers and commentators like Averroes.</meta>

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK I.

God, unless the philosophers permit it, would not even be able to reign according to His own will. Certainly, if He acts out of necessity upon matter, and does so unwillingly—unable to be moved except by some external object—then the impious have won: reason will throw up its hands and surrender. But the opinion of that man who seemed somewhat unjust and semi-impious toward the First Cause (which he attempted to bind to matter in the manner of a "form" or "soul"), **Averroes** <note>original: "Aben reis." Postel is referring to the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd, known in Latin as Averroes.</note>, even grants to God by his own authority that which we attribute to Him according to reason. And he grants this specifically to **Al-Ghazali** <note>original: "Algezeli." Al-Ghazali was a Persian theologian who famously critiqued the philosophers' view of an eternal world.</note> with these words in the 2nd doubt of the 3rd Disputation: "It is clear therefore from these things," he says, "that the argument of Al-Ghazali does not strike the philosophers. For they always judged that the action of God proceeds from knowledge, without a necessity inducing Him to act. Whether from Himself, or from some intrinsic thing, He acts instead from pure goodness. And therefore He necessarily wills and chooses in the most excellent manner of willing and choosing. For He never commits an error in those matters, such as we do here in this world." These are his words.

From this passage, I must take this point: Since He possesses the will and the choice of acting, it is certain that He possesses them universally—that is, both in respect to the thing and the time (if He were subject to time, though He is far superior to it). Therefore, when He willed, He acted, and in the manner that He willed. Thus, it was not necessary for Him to act upon matter from eternity, even though He is **pure act** <term>Pure Act (actus purus): A scholastic term for God, meaning He is fully realized and has no "potential" to become something else; He is constant and perfect.</term>. 

But you will say: if He is pure act, then (suppose Him to have been subject to time before there was motion or time, just to satisfy yourself) it was necessary for Him to act perpetually. I admit this. But I deny it was necessary to act *on matter*. For if He could not act except with matter, He would be more powerless than a soul or separated substances. In what, then, did He act and rest for so long? In the contemplation of Himself and in His wisdom, which encompasses all future beings; in this wisdom, His will was not forced to act according to the perfection and "idea" which He saw within Himself. For if He saw all things in Himself—as He certainly did—no perfection could come to Him from matter being brought into existence from His mind, such that He is now "helped" by it. Otherwise, imperfection would complete perfection, which is contrary to reason. 

From this it is established that by His perpetual action He can act happily by Himself, even if the whole world were to perish; for His perfection does not depend on it, but rather the opposite. Otherwise, you immerse God in things and make Him subject to corruption if He requires matter. The world, therefore, is not from eternity, but has a beginning, as we have shown. 

But you will say to me: "What was He doing in such an eternity of self-contemplation?" Surely you are imagining "time" for yourself where and when there is none. But suppose it exists; I am willing to grant it. While He Himself ought rather to satisfy you in this part with His own singular wisdom (certainly, if it were necessary for the salvation of man—for whose sake He made all corruptible things when He willed—He would have opened and satisfied that knowledge), nevertheless, I will try to satisfy you in this difficult matter by a certain not-unfit comparison. 

For you know that the principles of all arts must be taken up without great inquiry and received as proven. For if anyone asked a teacher why fire is hot, snow white, earth dry, a line a line, or a point a point, he could say nothing else than because it is so, and it holds this from the First Cause. So in these questions concerning the simple Supreme Good, one could say nothing else except that it is so. 

But pay attention, and test this in yourself. If there were some kingdom for you to both form and rule, or any other great task to be undertaken (since those things would add nothing to your happiness except regarding glory and the display of your virtue), is it not possible that you could be held for a long time in the contemplation of it, with a pleasure supreme and plainly equal to the finished work? (If it were permitted to seek pleasure outside yourself). Could not that pleasure of thinking be drawn out even for infinite ages? Finally, you could perform the work itself according to your judgment when the time seemed right—not for the convenience of the kingdom (which does not yet exist), but out of mere liberty.

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

### BOOK I.

...and decreed by your will? It is certain that we are daily held by similar pleasures and can be most greatly affected by them, yet we delay until it seems right to us. For the fact that we lack the capacity to fulfill many of our desires is a fault of our own, having nothing in common with God. For we, when wisdom is present in our minds, necessarily act if the will and the capacity are also present. But God, acting in the eternal Trinity, with a mind comprehending the forms of the nature of things through wisdom, had the will as a perpetual companion, which indeed always willed that things exist. But since He had free choice of the time in which He willed them to be made, it was placed in this: that He might create when He willed that which He was considering within Himself through eternal meditation and joy; meanwhile, He was never lacking in either the capacity or the will. For there are also two ways of willing in us. For we either will a thing simply, without any regard for time, or we will it at such or such a time.

But you, who are affected by the weariness of human affairs, tossed by the motion of the heavens, moved by births and decays, and who measure the condition of all things by the length of time calculated from the motion of the heavens, you cannot yourself weigh how, above and before motion, **a thousand years are like one day, and one day is like a thousand years** <note>original: "mille anni sint sicut dies unus, & unus dies sit ut mille anni." Postel is quoting a famous biblical principle from Psalm 90:4 and 2 Peter 3:8 to explain that God’s perspective on time is not the same as ours.</note>, as Peter left written along with David. Satisfy yourself, then, with these reasons if you can; or seek better ones, and consider that your own perfection in the deliberation of what is good is not greater than divine providence.

Furthermore, it should not be said that there is a "new" will in God because He willed to produce the world at some pre-fixed time, since the divine will is not new simply because new things are born daily which He previously did not will to exist. But you will object: "Why then did that God remain hidden for so long?" Or you will say He suffered from either **sloth** <term>socordia: a state of sluggishness or neglect</term> or **envy** <note>original: "inuidia." In this context, "envy" or "jealousy" refers to the idea that God might have been "stingy" by withholding the gift of existence from the universe for so long.</note>, because He kept such a magnificent thing in His mind for so long. Sloth cannot exist except where there is a delay or neglect of a designated and necessary duty. Neither could exist in God. For things which did not yet exist could not bind Him; no one could prescribe a duty to Him. Envy was not an obstacle, because nothing existed besides Him. 

But to impart immediately what you have is a divine quality. **For the more common a good is, the more divine it is.** <note>original: "Bonum enim quo communius, eo diuinius." This was a standard axiom in medieval and Renaissance philosophy, suggesting that goodness naturally seeks to share itself with as many recipients as possible.</note> How much worldly things benefit us who possess them, and how eager He ought to have been in giving and creating, must be considered from these points. 

A wide field indeed opens up here. I proceed with the comparison already begun concerning our capacity. When you think of that kingdom of yours and are happily fed by the knowledge of it, you are very often refreshed far more than by the work itself. If that work (which can make you neither better nor more perfect, and is prepared only for the sake of your honor and glory) consists of the labor and diligence of certain people who, while they carry out your work to please you and strive toward you as if toward their highest happiness, would have to undergo the greatest unhappiness through the difficulty of administration for their whole life—so that they could never be happy in the work itself—would your delay not be envy? Not at all. 

Furthermore, those servants who are in your work must be gifted with freedom, so that they can act or not act, in order to be more attentive to the matter. For he who acts without free choice must be good or bad without his own merit or fault. Therefore, since you yourself would not be envious if you delayed gifts mixed with punishments for future subjects—especially when the future reward will be equal for all, even after hundreds of thousands of years, and those refusing or ignoring authority would pay equal penalties—would you not want the blessed, most just Creator to be in a worse condition while He delayed those punishments of life and those rewards which He disposed from eternity, especially since there is no loss in the delay, whether He exhibits them later or sooner? 

See, then, that the Creator Himself neither ceased from perpetual action even when the world was absent, nor [was He moved by] sloth or en-

<meta>This page continues Postel’s defense of God’s timing and methods in Creation. He moves from the concept of God’s "delay" to the problem of why God created a world containing imperfection, decay, and the potential for human sin.</meta>

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.

...you would have labored, since in human judgment—in which the power of recognizing equity resides—you assert that you would not have sinned in those last two points by delaying, nor would you have ever ceased from the first action for a longer time when considering all things; it is indeed certain that a person is able to do this for a long time. Acquiesce, then, acquiesce to the omnipotence of the Creator, whose manifest signs and riddles we discern in our own souls and deliberations. 

But, to persist still in the example: how could it be that that supreme wisdom, from which it was impossible for anything future to be hidden, would want to create humans who would voluntarily decline into future miseries and vices—turning entirely toward wickedness away from their liberty and acting against what was prescribed? How, I say, could it be that He willed them to be created under such a condition? Would it not have been far more excellent not to be created at all than to be made in a condition where one could perish and fall away entirely from the Creator? For it is better not to have been born than to have been born to perish miserably. 

Consider diligently which of two men would be more perfect or imperfect: the one who, out of fear of ruin—which is necessarily present as a companion to **matter** <note>original: "materiae"</note> (whence evil does not proceed from the Author himself)—would never attempt anything noble, lest the fault of matter should have to be restored too often; or the one who, having recognized the imperfection of matter, would nonetheless establish noble works, intending to restore everything until they achieve their end? 

It is clear that the latter is far more excellent, spirited, brave, and good—the one who nonetheless performs noble deeds, even though they must be constantly renewed and repaired. It is established that the first is cast down by faint-heartedness, useless and abject, and as if nothing. Therefore, it was far more excellent to have produced man—who is the **apex and target of the lower world**—even if he must be daily corrected and renewed, than to have left the world a desert out of fear of error and vice. Thus, He both foreknew and willed it. 

But evil would not have been in the world if He had made matter perfect. Matter is not evil in itself, since "all things are very good" when made by the Best. But so that the first life in this murky world would not be immortal and take away the <term>free choice of man</term> <note>original: "arbitrium hominis"</note>—who, if created from the most perfect matter and a form similar to God without choice, would not have been able to sin—therefore God willed matter to be not evil, but "fluid" or "fleeting." He did this so that through the resistance between matter and form, the victory of great things would be achieved through difficulty. Meanwhile, the entire mass of the elements is being purged, to be led at the end entirely beyond corruption, so that through eternity all things may obtain the happiness necessary for bliss. 

You will easily learn that evil does not proceed from the Creator or from matter itself by this analogy: if you place water, clay, stones, or anything else good in itself into a well-constructed building, and it collapses due to the injury of time, the fault is not yours, nor is it in the material itself, but in the condition of things and in **motion**, which daily renews and corrupts lower things. For it is necessary for matter itself, following whatever forms it takes, to be daily cut into various parts, joined, and changed. 

From this, it happens by innumerable chances that composite things themselves are weakened and affected, so that sometimes matter even seems victorious, and covers over certain forms so that you do not easily recognize them in an individual, as in <term>monsters</term> <note>original: "monstris." Postel is using the classical etymology where a "monster" is a "demonstration" or "sign" from the Latin *monstrare*, "to show."</note>; which are so named because they **show** something by their own truth. I believe the nature of things would lack these if we were moved by a just estimation of things to acknowledge God's benefits and wonders. 

For when common things become cheap to us, then we are moved only by the rare; not indeed that rare things possess any more majestic or greater nature than a common shape, or a little herb, or any other thing, but because of our negligence and contempt for common things. For whatever we are ignorant of, as soon as it appears—if it has an unusual life, size, or property—we are stunned by it; and because that feeling proceeds from our ignorance, we often believe it to be something "new" to nature and the omniscient Creator. Yet I would think that those things which we do not know surpass in number, magnitude, and power to infinity those things which were known even to the greatest philosopher of the whole world. Because what I have never seen happen or exist...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...you should not be troubled. If your misfortune is moderate, you are perhaps "healthier" by half because of it, since the instrument for sinning is missing, and the tools for making amends are provided by necessity. I am struck in the body: the sooner you perish, the sooner you are happy. I am gradually consumed by a lack of resources: I am all the more dear to God, who seeks out **purified bodies** <note>original: "defecata corpora." In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to a body cleansed of earthly dross or refined through suffering.</note> for souls. Therefore, unless you fail yourself, nothing should be counted as an evil. For this reason, certain learned men have thought and affirmed that evil has no **subsistence** <note>The philosophical idea that evil is not a "thing" in itself, but merely the absence or "privation" of good.</note>. Since God is the author of things, and not of "privation," He cannot be the cause of evil. Rightly, therefore, did Plato—who is closest to the Divine Scriptures—write that God is not the author of evil. Since we have seen by many arguments that the world once did not exist, and that God is **pure act** <note>A Scholastic term meaning God is fully realized and eternal, with no unfulfilled potential.</note>, yet free, and an eternal agent in Himself without matter—neither lazy nor envious, but good in all things so that He is not the author of evil—and that the nature of evil itself does not subsist, it remains for us to proceed to the confirmation.

### FROM THE CONTEMPLATION OF MATTER, AND FIRST FROM THE
<gloss>nature of air, it is proven that the world had a beginning.</gloss>

Although I think I have already done more than enough regarding the creation of the world in the previous discussions, having stated things that are partly necessary and partly not contradictory (which cannot be opposed with reason), I nevertheless think it should be confirmed by several following arguments. The first is from the consideration of matter itself, which is open to the eyes. For those things which are presented to the **senses** <unclear>sensibus</unclear> provide a stronger argument for the common people than those which are usually persuaded by reason alone. I say, therefore, that the world had a beginning and was not eternal; or, if it was not created [from nothing], it must have been restored from scratch quite often—not just by a "renewal of the old" (which the philosophers admit), but by a restoration and **increase** <unclear>incrementis</unclear> of the total matter. I proceed to prove it thus: we see by a sensory argument that the elements themselves are not only altered, but perish entirely through mutual action, with fire acting most powerfully. The first argument will be from **air**, which is usually consumed by fire. For through the [medical] **cupping glass** <note>A "cucurbita" or cupping glass was used in medicine; by heating the air inside and placing it on skin, a vacuum was created as the air cooled/contracted.</note> and the invention of **aeolipiles** <note>An aeolipile is an early steam-powered device or a metal vessel with a small opening used to demonstrate the power of heated air/steam.</note> by physicians and mechanics, we see this. When fire is applied to such a small amount of air as fits in a cupping glass and the vessel is closed, the fire dies when "breathing" is lacking; and as much air as it consumed, the nature of the fleshy body pulls in to prevent a vacuum, and thus occurs the "attraction of humor" for the sake of scarification. That the air is almost entirely consumed is indicated by that force of attraction, which is so powerful and inflicts such pain that no greater force can be proven by pliers or any other instruments. Air can indeed be compressed a little and forced by a heavy blast to be smaller in volume than nature allows—as we prove with <term>medical egg-vials</term> <note>original Greek: "ὤοις ἰατρικοῖς" (ōois iatrikis). These were egg-shaped glass instruments used for suction or as primitive syringes.</note>, in which some air is admitted by sucking and emitted by squeezing—yet that quantity is small and does not consume the substance. But fire needs air so much to thrive that without the use of it, there is no fire except what is latent and potential. This is far clearer in aeolipiles. For the air in them is so entirely exhausted and destroyed that, through a narrow hole and a thin passage, they draw in as much water as the capacity of the vessel. For whatever air remains is very thin and most like fire. Thus, it is not only consumed, but it makes the residue so rare that it occupies the space, unless a dense and cold body like water enters. If we can touch these things with our fingers in daily experiments, can we doubt that the same happens in the rest of the air, and that much is consumed daily from above, and restored gradually from watery matter? That fire also needs air to act is proven by the fact that it is ignited when air is moved and more powerful, and extinguished when air is absent. Flames, therefore, are airy parts released from water. Since these things are certain regarding air, it is sure that it can be diminished and finally consumed—and consequently water and earth as well. Therefore, the world would have failed long ago if it had existed from eternity; and there would have been a need

...often recreated; which no one would admit. For if they deny that it was created once, they will deny it even more two or three times. But floods and **conflagrations** <note>Great fires or burnings. Postel refers to the ancient idea that the world is periodically purged by water or fire.</note> have purged it. Fire can indeed decrease matter, but it cannot increase it; and the greater the fire, the more it consumes. Water must either be multiplied from this nature or be created anew by the Creator; for water alone can restore nothing, except for a small amount of air.

->FROM EXPERIMENTS WITH WATER.<-

Here, too, nature must be confined into a space where nothing can perish that might escape the senses, so that we may clearly see what happens to a substance when fire acts upon it, how it is altered, or what it becomes. Let a certain quantity of water be placed in any vessel made of the most solid material, which admits no **perspiration or expiration** <note>leaking or evaporation through the pores of the container.</note>. Let this vessel be a **distillatory** <note>original: "distillatorium." A vessel used for distilling liquids.</note>, which we call by the Arabic name **alembic** <term>alembic: a chemical apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube, used for distilling volatile substances</term>, smeared on every side with strong **lute** <note>original: "luto." A clay or cement used to seal chemical apparatus to make them airtight.</note> so that no air may evaporate. Finally, having applied fire beneath the vessel, let us ensure that what flees from the fire distills into another vessel that is also closed and joined to the first, so that no air escapes (although air that is not under pressure does not seek the lowest places by its own motion). Then, once the water is distilled, we will see that not even an eighth part remains. Therefore, the fire has consumed the rest, since it could not have been consumed anywhere else than in the fire, or have slipped into the lower vessel. What of the fact that we experience the same thing daily in all boiling water, when all its parts are consumed? Must we not judge the same of the whole world? For it is certain that a part of that moisture which is raised into rain from the heat of the sun—from the whole nature of water—is consumed, by this one argument: that its **exhalation** <note>In Aristotelian science, "exhalations" were vapors rising from the earth that were thought to fuel celestial phenomena.</note>, which is raised on high, sometimes feeds the fires in the highest region of the air for a long time, from which various "impressions" are made. Truly, that thick and putrid air can be set on fire is proven by the miseries of our own bodies, with boys as witnesses who light foul flames from the **wind of the belly** <note>A polite reference to flatulence being flammable.</note>. From this, in that region of the air, are seen comets, **bothyni** <note>original: "bothyni." An Aristotelian term for meteors that look like glowing trenches or pits in the sky.</note>, **beams** <note>original: "trabes." Meteors or auroras appearing as long wooden beams.</note>, and countless other likenesses of things. From this come falling stars, and from this lightning and flashes. If the world had existed from eternity, it would have reached its end many times over by now. Who does not know that from dry and burning wood, watery tears come out at the ends, and from there a watery smoke, plain and thick, into which place the flame immediately rushes once the thicker moisture is driven out, so that they succeed each other until the moisture has sweated out entirely? This was so approved by many philosophers that they even falsely affirmed that the stars themselves were fed by some lower exhalation. Indeed, this consumption and diminution of water is also seen in marshy places, where it putrefies and is consumed, infecting the air as if by dying, so that from there **epidemic diseases** creep everywhere. Thus, it does not only perish, but does so at the expense of the neighboring areas. Springs vanish daily in higher places and are found with difficulty in lower ones (since all waters naturally tend to find their own **level** <note>original: "libellam." A water-level or balance.</note> in the earth), which is a sign of diminution. But there is no more manifest argument for the decrease of waters and their daily consumption than the fact that in many places there was once sea where there is now land; and it was once very deep where it is now shallow, which Aristotle confirms with histories in his *Meteorology*. Indeed, I can enrich this with many examples. It is established by the elementary order that the globe of the earth should naturally have been surrounded on all sides by the nature of water, in the manner of the other elements and heavens, like the layers of an egg or an onion embracing themselves; but it is certain that by the command of the Creator it receded, and not by a natural motion. For there is no prudence in the elements, nor could an insensible nature provide for the safety of living creatures. Water, therefore, once surrounded the whole globe, as you may see in all places. For there is no part of the earth in which you will not find the **traces of all kinds of oysters** <note>original: "ostreorum omnium generum vestigia." Postel is identifying fossilized seashells as evidence of a global flood.</note> (unless where the ground has rotted away), as in the sands or in the harder rocks. That enclosure was also present at the time of the Flood. Thus, the earth was not entirely covered before that. But I shall prove by many histories that even since that time, the sea has been greatly diminished. To me indeed, in

### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

Aristotle admits that locations are altered; however, I shall demonstrate that they are also diminished. For now that the whole world is open to us, we may draw a conjecture regarding the entire terrestrial globe. First, indeed, Homer testifies that Egypt was once submerged by waters, a fact which Aristotle records; <note>original: "refert Aristoteles." Aristotle discusses the silting of the Nile delta in his work *Meteorology*.</note> now, part of it is drier than is level. That the region of the Venetians, which they commonly call the Paduan and the March of Treviso, was once the sea is evident from this: when you dig deep (even twenty miles from where the sea now is), fragments of submerged ships are found there. Even in our own age, near the **city of Antenor** <note>Padua, which according to legend was founded by the Trojan prince Antenor.</note>, this was proven when the bed of an aqueduct was being dug. This ought not to seem a wonder, since a foundation made of oak and alder, and many other woods, becomes eternal, as some write hyperbolically. Unless the Venetians today took diligent care so that the channels were frequently cleared to save the lagoons and the city, the city of Venice would have been on dry land long ago. Fifteen hundred years ago, Ravenna was entirely similar to Venice, for it was possible to travel through it by bridges and boats. Now, however, it stands nearly two miles from the sea; such is the result of human industry. Venice, founded more than 1,100 years ago, has avoided by its diligence what happened to the people of Ravenna in that same period of time. Ptolemy had diligently searched the Adriatic and Aegean seas; yet far more islands are seen in both than he, or Pliny (drawing from Strabo), wrote of. From this, it is clear that the sea has subsided. In the lower coastal places of Asia Minor, and likewise in Africa, the same has occurred. And not only does the salt water in the sea vanish, but marsh water does as well. For many regions once uncultivated due to marshy places are now inhabited, the waters having dried up. This is evident in the farthest coasts of Gaul and Germany, where they turn toward the Ocean; the tides do not proceed as far as they once did. In Greece itself, the arguments are the same. **Mount Athos** <note>Postel refers to the canal dug through the Isthmus of Athos by the Persian King Xerxes; he argues that if the land hadn't dried, the traces of the canal would be more obvious or unnecessary.</note>, having been dug through (except for the scrapings of Mount Haemus), was once surrounded by water; otherwise, if it had been as it is now, it would have been a promontory; nor is the trench visible, since everything has dried up. In the Peloponnese, there are very many signs. What was more famous than the kingdom of Tyndareus? Yet today almost the entire peninsula is sterile, showing the "bones" of the earth. What shall I say of the Argives and Mycenaeans, who showed that immense marshes dried up within more or less four hundred years? **Lake Maeotis** <note>The Sea of Azov.</note> was so changed in the span of sixty years during the time of Aristotle that it could support far smaller ships than before; now, indeed, it carries nothing besides skiffs, except along the channel of the river **Tanais** <note>The Don River.</note>. Aristotle also grants that rivers are changed and dried up, which is certain. For in the third year before this one—that is, the year of Christ 1539—there was such a burning heat in summer that many rivers in Gaul vanished, and all the waters of the wells subsided by more than the space of a cubit; in some places by six or ten feet, which is a certain sign of a diminished elemental quantity consumed by fire.

But they object: "We do not deny that it diminishes, but we affirm that it moves elsewhere and floods certain regions unknown to us; just as we see the sea let in between the most famous parts of the world." I marvel at the impudence, or certainly the listless negligence of men who profess the knowledge of truth, yet are so accustomed to swear by the words of storytellers in certain matters that they despise the reason of things after them. If the sea was at some time admitted at the **Pillars of Hercules** <note>The Strait of Gibraltar.</note>, before it was admitted, where did the Ebro, Rhone, Po, Danube, Dnieper, Don, Phasis, Thermodon, Nile, and Bagradas—all the greatest rivers—place their waters? One of these, the Danube, carries sixty navigable rivers with it; another, namely the Nile, runs from near the winter tropic to our own. I stay silent about more than three hundred others, all navigable. Where, finally, did those waters go before that "illustrious God" <note>A sarcastic reference to the Ocean or the forces of nature acting as a deity.</note> let in the sea? Hey you! Are you not ashamed of such follies? Since all waters are necessarily placed at a level in the vicinity (for I am not ignorant that the globe is made of water and earth), how could it happen that those waters did not fill the basin and that place where the sea [withdrew]...

# BOOK I BY GUILLAUME POSTEL

...by the coming of that God, I believe from eternity, it preserved that miracle for itself: and the waters vanished against nature. O the vanity of Greece! O the madness of the philosophers who give credit to those trifles. I do not name them here, lest they be noted for their folly. It was certainly necessary that, by the command of the Creator, the water always remained at its level; it is so far from being admitted from the Ocean into our sea <note>The Mediterranean</note> that, on the contrary, our sea overflows into the Ocean, and with such violence that it drives mills of every kind by its most rapacious force from the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara</note>. This is the reason why the nature of the Ocean's reciprocal tide is not seen in our sea—a subject of so many arguments among philosophers. The force of our overflowing waters wards off the tides of the Ocean, preventing them from meeting except in the very straits. For at the Pillars of Hercules <note>The Strait of Gibraltar</note>, the tide is almost equal to the Ocean’s. Further inside, near the Spains and Mauritanias <note>North Africa</note>, it gradually diminishes, so that at Rome and Carthage, the greatest tide is scarcely seen to be a foot and a half. In Venice, when the master of the Adriatic blows <note>original: "arbitro Adriæ flante," referring to the prevailing winds</note>, it becomes a little larger; otherwise, it is usually raised by barely half a foot. In the Black Sea and the Sea of Marmara, it is not even felt, except when the waters are thickened and raised by the blowing of south winds. Thus, water is not admitted [into the Mediterranean], but emitted. How has this been falsely understood for so long? By the mixing of the other, that which might be lost by fresh waters is restored. Therefore, the water is saltier at the straits than in the interior. This is why on the whole shore of the Ocean, the water is dried into salts by the power of the sun, a thing which does not happen within the sea beyond Italy.

And yet it is certain that water is sometimes admitted into the land. I do not deny that by the force of a storm or the will of the Creator, water is sent in as a punishment for crimes; but if it happens by natural motion, the water immediately recedes, as it seems, after a few years. For that quantity of water which has already been lost over so many thousands of years in our world—since the waters themselves, though fouled and agitated by the winds, are set at a level—ought to overflow in a perpetual course, flooding now these people, now those, so that nothing would be more familiar than a flood. Or at least, it should be raised into a mound in certain places and exceed its level, neither of which is seen. Therefore, the water is consumed.

You will say, "Floods do not recede immediately, for the island of Atlantis, once situated before the Pillars of Hercules, perished by a deluge." This is an excellent Egyptian fiction <note>original: "Egregium commentum Ægyptiacum"</note>, and unworthy of being left in writing by Plato in his *Atlanticus* <note>The *Critias*</note> and *Timaeus*—a man who is otherwise quite far from the rashness of asserting falsehoods. It is as if that which is no longer visited had perished, or perhaps that which never even was. But suppose it did exist, and that Plato, in order to grant his citizens a most ancient origin, spoke the truth. Even today there is a very great continent, a part of the furthest part of Asia seeking the west from the east through the antipodes. It is certainly most wide, and—unless he understood it to be this very land—it has been opened in our time beyond the memory of all literature by the work of the kings of France, Portugal, and Spain, and surveyed; yet it has not perished <note>Postel is identifying the Americas with the "lost" Atlantis, arguing they were never submerged but merely "lost" to European memory.</note>. But it is necessary that the Egyptian fiction, or Plato’s authority, place it a little further from the straits of Hercules. Certainly, since it extends from pole to pole, it cannot but be set against the strait of our sea. Therefore, nothing is submerged there.

Who would deny that certain cities are swallowed up, shaken by earthquakes, and finally enveloped by waters? Yet these things happen more frequently in low and humble places. Elsewhere, after short intervals of time, the waters return to their channel, a fact which even Greek triflings will not deny. For those floods which Greece fashioned for itself, it devised in imitation of the divine Flood of which it had heard; in every matter, Greece was an ape of others' inventions—but truly an "ape," which is to say, a distorter. It was necessary, therefore, that such a mass of water from that place should immediately cause floods elsewhere, especially in our sea, which is not capable of holding such a mass. I am easily led to believe that divine providence (for otherwise it cannot happen by natural motion) punished those peoples who were going to pervert the world with false opinions and become instruments of demons with a flood of waters. But these things are enough to make it clear that waters lost from here do not pass into floods, but are gradually consumed by exhalations; while they are dissolved in the air, the air itself becomes the fuel for flaming fire.

# THE FIRST BOOK OF GUILLAUME POSTEL

...by the arrival of that God; from eternity, I believe, He reserved that miracle for Himself, and the waters vanished against their own nature. O, the vanity of Greece! O, the madness of the philosophers who give credit to such trifles! I shall not name them here, lest they be noted for their folly in this place. It was certainly necessary that the water always remained at a level balance <note>original: "ad libellam," referring to a level or plumb-line used in surveying</note> by the command of the Creator. So far is it from being true that water is admitted from the Ocean into our sea <note>The Mediterranean</note>, that on the contrary, our sea overflows into the Ocean, and so violently that near the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara</note> the current drives mills of every kind with a most rapacious force. This is the reason why the nature of the Ocean's reciprocal tide does not seem to exist in our sea—a subject of so many disputes among philosophers. The force of our overflowing waters wards off the tides of the Ocean so that they do not harmonize, except at the very mouth of the strait. For at the Pillars of Hercules <note>The Strait of Gibraltar</note>, the tide is almost equal to that of the Ocean. Further inward, near the coasts of Spain and Mauritania <note>North Africa</note>, it gradually diminishes, so that the highest tide at Rome or Carthage is scarcely seen to be a foot and a half. At Venice, by the will of the blowing Adriatic, it becomes a little greater; otherwise, it is usually raised scarcely half a foot. In the Pontic Sea <note>The Black Sea</note> and the Propontis, it is not even felt, except when the southern winds blow in the Propontis and it is raised by the thickness of a span <note>original: "spitamae," a measurement of about 9 inches</note>. Thus, water is not being admitted, but emitted. 

How could such a falsehood persist for so long? What might be lost through the evaporation of fresh waters is restored by the mixture of another. Therefore, the water is saltier at the mouth of the strait than in the further recesses. This is why, along the entire shore of the Ocean, water is dried into salt by the power of the sun, which does not happen beyond Italy. Yet it is established that water is sometimes admitted into the land. I do not deny that by the force of a storm or the will of the Creator, water is sent in as a punishment for sins; but if this happens by natural motion, the water immediately recedes, as is seen, a few years later. For that quantity of water which has already been lost over so many thousands of years in our world—since the waters themselves, when settled and quiet from the agitation of the winds, are set at a level—ought to perpetually flood now these people, now those, so that nothing would be more familiar than an inundation. Or at the very least, the water should rise into a mound in certain places and exceed its level, neither of which is seen to happen. Therefore, the water is consumed.

You will say that floods do not recede immediately, for the island of Atlantis, once situated before the Pillars of Hercules, perished in a flood. This is an excellent Egyptian fiction <note>original: "Egregium commentum Aegyptiacum"</note>, and unworthy of being left in writing by Plato in his *Critias* <note>referred to here as the "Atlanticus"</note> and *Timaeus* (who was otherwise quite averse to the rashness of asserting falsehoods). It is treated as if it truly perished because it is no longer visited, or perhaps because it never existed. But suppose it did exist, and that Plato spoke the truth in order to grant his citizens a most ancient origin. Even today, there is a very great continent, the extreme part of Asia reaching toward the west through the antipodes. It is certainly most wide, and beyond the memory of all literature (unless Plato understood this to be Atlantis), it has been opened in our time by the efforts of the kings of France, Portugal, and Spain; it has been surveyed, and it has not perished. Truly, this Egyptian fiction, or the authority of Plato, must place that land a little further from the mouth of Hercules. Certainly, since it stretches from pole to pole, it cannot fail to be set against the strait of our sea. Therefore, nothing was submerged there. 

Who would deny that certain cities are swallowed up, shaken by earthquakes, and finally enveloped in waters? Yet these things happen more frequently in low and depressed places. Elsewhere, after a short interval of time, the waters recede into their channel, which not even Greek trifles can deny. For those floods which Greece fashioned for itself were devised in imitation of the Divine Flood <note>The Biblical Deluge of Noah</note> of which they had heard; for in nothing were they not an ape of the inventions of others—but a true ape, which is to say, a distorter. It would have been necessary for that mass of water to immediately cause floods elsewhere from that place, especially in our sea, which is not capable of holding such a mass. I am easily led to believe that Divine Providence (for otherwise it could not happen by natural motion) punished those people who were destined to pervert the world with false opinions and become instruments of demons with a flood of waters. But these points are sufficient to show that the waters lost from here do not pass into other floods, but are gradually consumed by exhalations while they are dissolved into the air; the air itself is the fuel for the flaming fire. Whence, both by the air and by the...

...and its nature is clear: the world has not existed from eternity, for it would have been consumed long ago.

### FROM THE CONTEMPLATION OF THE EARTH.

The earth is steadily wasting away by the force of rains; it is carried elsewhere by the course of torrents and rivers, gradually vanishing and finally leaving behind what are like its naked bones <note>original: "ossa nuda," a metaphor for the rocky bedrock or mountains exposed by erosion</note>, as seen in areas near torrents and rivers. Indeed, we perceive by our senses that something is worn away every year—a fact which even <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE) whose views on the eternity of the universe Postel is challenging</note> does not deny. Therefore, if these same actions had been lasting from eternity, the earth would have perished many times over; and since it exists now, it must have been created anew. 

The philosophers are unwilling to concede this based on this single argument: they cannot conceive in their minds what God Himself, the <term>self-originated</term> <note>original Greek: αυτοφύης (autophyes), meaning existing of oneself or "self-natured"</note>, was doing for so long in that eternal vastness. Truly, if they wished to be fair judges of the reason they claim to seek, they would find it far more difficult to conceive how the world itself—whose parts are entirely perishable—could persist for so long in the nature of things, than to conceive how that eternal Providence, happy in itself and needing nothing, subsisted from eternity without this filthy matter. 

Come now, let us learn from an example, so that we may understand the infinite from the finite. Suppose someone builds a sheepfold, or a hut, or a <term>hovel</term> <note>original: "mapale," a term used by ancient writers like Sallust to describe the portable huts of Numidian nomads</note>, or anything else that is transitory by the nature of its material. Suppose we see with our own eyes that its parts perish daily, so that the house necessarily suffered from the decay of its material from the very beginning, and we judge that it cannot last for ten years. If someone then asserted that it had already lasted fifty years because the one who built it is of an age where he could have built it, which would you find easier to conceive? Since that builder is free and was not forced to make it, is it easier to believe the house has lasted fifty years alongside its author, or that the author lived happily by himself without a house for forty years and finally built that fragile dwelling? 

If you say you cannot grasp that reasoning, I shall appeal to the consensus and judgment of the whole world. But they are so inflamed with a desire to corrupt the truth—while they confess God in words and acknowledge Him in His works and effects—that with all their effort, in writings, words, and their very way of life, they deny His existence. For if they acknowledged Him as omnipotent, most perfect, free and not compelled, infinite, most happy, and a perpetual act driving all things within Himself (whether they exist or not), as they are forced to do in words, they would never join this matter to Him as if it were necessary for His completion. His happiness is equal before matter was created, during its creation, and after it has been changed and purified or released from action. They wish to add the mass of matter to the Most Perfect as if to add perfection. O stupid and blind men! How rightly did our <term>Paul</term> <note>The Apostle Paul, quoting from the Epistle to the Romans 1:21-22</note> say, being privy to the secrets of heaven:

> Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and vanished in their own thoughts, and their foolish heart was seized by madness. For when they had known God, they did not glorify Him as God.

Therefore the wisdom of the flesh is death, an enemy to God. Since, then, it is certain that the earth itself is gradually wasting away, it must necessarily be judged that eternity is lacking in its very nature. Thus, the mass of the four elements would have perished by now: the caverns of the earth themselves dripping with water, vapors usually being drawn from the earth daily by the work of the sun, water turning into air, and air usually being consumed by fire (whenever the fuel and base for flames is present). Nothing would have been left long ago. 

But when I assert (what is obvious to the senses) that the mountains themselves are gradually worn away and perish by the flow of waters and other injuries of time, and that slopes are washed and swept clean by rains, that <term>circumcised</term> <note>original: "recutitus," a Latin epithet for Jewish people. Postel is referring to Philo of Alexandria.</note> Philo will object to me. I marvel that he, though steeped in the prescriptions of the Holy Law, wished to depart from those holy prescriptions because of these trifles which he ascribes to <term>Theophrastus</term> <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle</note>. "It is indeed true," he says, "that mountains are worn down and consumed; but meanwhile, others are born from the force of fire shut up within the earth. While the fire tries to break out, they emerge as it exits, the earth itself following the erupting fire." O, a figment worthy of Theophrastus! Thus do those who wish to lie with impunity ascribe their nonsense to great authors. Who would believe that so learned a disciple of Aristotle, whom he [Aristotle] judged to be the most outstanding of the school...

# THE FIRST BOOK OF GUILLAUME POSTEL

...to be governed by the most excellent [nature], has he come to such a point of impudence against the decrees of his teacher <note>original: "praeceptoris placita," likely referring to Aristotle</note> as to assert that the flow of the earth follows the motion of fire? That one movement in the air might draw another, and fire might draw fire, and perhaps water might draw water to avoid a vacuum, can be admitted. But that the earth, a solid and hard body, should suffer the same—who is so shameless as to imagine it? 

Truly, let him hold his own opinions as proof of his judgment. Mountains are accustomed to being dissolved daily by active fire, and all things are broken by it. He wishes them to be born and to consist of the same fire; yet active fire cannot exist except within matter, such as in sulfurous substances. Such is the case in Iceland, Sicily, and Mount Vesuvius, and many parts of the world—where fire does not bind things together, but consumes them. 

That distinguished man was unable to discern the difference between <term>potentiality and act</term> <note>These are key Aristotelian concepts: "potentiality" is the capacity to become something, while "act" or "actuality" is the fulfillment of that capacity</note>. It is true that in the entire bond of earthly nature there is a certain **spiritual fire** mixed in; from this, through the mediation of the spirit, all things on earth are created by outflows and vegetation. But that this fire should ever burst forth or use force is a far cry from the truth. 

But I proceed to other matters: **the invention of the arts**. For it is certain that the earth is being consumed, and the objections of <term>Philo</term> <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Jewish philosopher who argued that the world appeared young only because periodic catastrophes like floods and fires destroyed human records</note> are frivolous. How is it that the invention of arts emerges daily, and that all things were not long ago either handed down by hand or recorded in writings? Even the most necessary things are of recent invention, created by men only lately deceased. Various types of crops emerge daily; species of fruits are seen as human ingenuity assists nature, adding to its natural power. 

What more? They will say that general floods and <term>conflagrations</term> <note>great fires that consume the world</note> wipe away all human memory. Hence, everything must be sought and learned anew from the beginning. Therefore, they say, all are equal in that potential, and if there are any of greater talent, they are more excellent. 

How does it happen then, that the Greeks—a race of men born under a lucky star, and who (as <term>Aristotle</term> wished it written) never lacked the best forces of heaven, soil, intellect, or body—being far more excellent than other mortals, did not discover those things which serve human life and enrich nature long before all other mortals, especially the Athenians? Why was it that a thousand years after the **"barbarians"** (as they called the <term>Chaldeans</term> <note>Ancient people of Mesopotamia, famous for astronomy</note>, the **Magi**, the **Egyptians**, the **Prophets**, and that sort), religion, arts, and letters reached the Greeks, having been previously unknown? From whence did that opinion arise, that whoever was distinguished in Greece traveled to the barbarians for the sake of learning? This was observed in Athens 1500 years ago, where that divine force of intellect, which is surpassed by the barbarians, is taught and formed. 

Therefore, since after the general flood of <term>Deucalion</term> <note>The Greek mythological figure who survived a great flood; Postel argues this is merely a Greek name for the biblical Noah</note>—as the Greeks changed the name of **Noah** so as not to seem to have borrowed anything from foreigners—the condition of all men was equal. Since the "barbarians" are more unrefined than the Greek authors, how could it be that they possessed so many types of the greatest disciplines so much earlier in time? 

**"Grecians, you are always children,"** <note>original Latin: "Graeci Graeci semper pueri estis," a famous quote from Plato’s *Timaeus* where an Egyptian priest tells Solon that the Greeks have no ancient history</note> and there is no ancient learning among you (as that man said). It was necessary, therefore, that those men survived the flood—as the sacred records hold—and received from their ancestors those disciplines which were immediately cultivated, and from there were gradually spread into the whole world over many centuries thereafter. 

But those same people, whose decrees must necessarily be believed, handed down that the world had a beginning, and that the knowledge of divine things was given to them by the Deity before their time. Other arts, being not as necessary for life, were discovered by posterity as necessity taught them. But those earlier men learned everything using the foundations of things received from their fathers. From them the Greeks later learned, and then the Latins. 

Since, therefore, they had survived the waters in Asia, they had certain knowledge of past events. Thus, the more humane arts—which the prior age, occupied with better things (namely, the divine), had not yet discovered—remained hidden even at that time. Therefore, the world had a beginning. Philosophers must therefore subscribe to the **sacred authority** which handed down these things without attached reasoning, which must be true, since reason, laboriously sought, leads us there even against our will. 

But enough regarding the world for now. For since all things in it are seen to be corruptible and recent, it is certain that it had an origin.

He concludes that both reason and the Bible prove the world has a beginning.</summary>
