# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

## THAT THE WORLD WAS CREATED FROM NOTHING. Chapter V.

Whoever admits that the world depends on a cause, and that God is above the nature of all things and is **self-sufficient**, **self-born**, and **blessed** <note>original Greek: "αὐταρκῆ, αὐτοφυᾶ, εὐδαίμονα"</note>—to put it in a single word, blessed in every part—that person does not need to be persuaded that the world was brought into being from nothing. But if one must deal with a person who removes cause and providence from the universe—who is neither moved by their own senses, nor admits necessary reason, nor approves the authority of any name or judgment no matter how great, following nothing but their own dreams—certainly, the effort would be wasted; it would be like "beating the air." Therefore, so that some light may be added to the obscurity of the preceding matters, and the nature of truth may gradually reveal itself, we will treat these things. For we shall confirm for good and pious men those things that have already been handed down, and we shall pave the way for what follows. 

To make this easier, all the causes of things must be listed again. There are, therefore, two types of causes and "con-causes." The **primary causes**, without which the secondary cannot exist, are the **first agent** (or providence) and the **end** (or purpose). The **con-causes** <note>The Latin "concausæ" refers to secondary factors that must be present for an effect to occur, but do not initiate the action themselves</note> are those so connected to things that they can in no way exist without them: namely, **matter** and **form**. The metaphysician considers the first and second, while the mathematician and the artisan consider the second and third. Although the secondary causes cannot exist without the effect of the primary ones, it is not always necessary for them to be joined. For though a house is not made without the mind and work of an artisan, nor except for the sake of some use, a house once built can be devoid of the artisan’s presence and be uninhabited. However, unless there is a certain "form" of habitation and it is made of some matter, it is no longer a house. 

Regarding the logic of the universe, the same must be held: that there is one Artisan by whom matter is laid beneath form itself, for the sake of some end. If, therefore, there is a **first mover** and **providence** of the universe—as there necessarily is—then He created all things from nothing. For if He had material already formed beforehand, He would not be the first cause. Since nothing exists without a cause, that matter (whether formed or unformed) would come from another cause, and that from another, and so on to infinity. Thus, there would be no first cause, which is most absurd. 

But perhaps that matter arose from itself? Yet it is impossible for anything to create itself. For if it is not from nothing, it must be from another, or from itself, or part of God and the first cause. The first two are false, and therefore so is the third. For that "part of God" would then be creating itself, which is absurd; it would mean God makes matter, and that which is **most simple** <note>In Renaissance theology, "divine simplicity" means God is not composed of parts or pieces; therefore, God cannot be "divided" to create matter</note> would be made divisible. Therefore, the matter and mass of the world were fashioned out of nothing. 

But the human mind does not grasp how something can be made from nothing. It cannot, because our knowledge is "nocturnal" <note>Postel uses the image of an owl (noctuina) whose sight is strong in the dark but weak in the light; our human intellect is similarly dim when trying to perceive divine truths</note>, proceeding from the things less known by nature to those better known to itself, through material experiments accustomed to this globe of the world; it cannot grasp what it has not seen by example. Yet from those things which daily reach our senses—which we would never have believed before we saw them—we clearly recognize, if we compare the unknown part with the known, that we know plainly nothing of the whole universe if you look at the underlying reason of the whole. 

But we know the four principles <note>The four elements: fire, earth, air, and water</note> from which all things come: "that is the labor for those above" <note>original: "is superis labor est." A poetic way of saying this knowledge belongs to a higher realm</note>. For we know all things just as a man who, because he knew the letters of the alphabet of any language, would profess knowledge of all the disciplines written in those characters. He could perhaps read all the syllables and words, but what he would gain, you judge. In the same way, because philosophers know that fire is hot and dry, earth cold and dry, air hot and moist, and water cold and moist—as if reciting a history of nature—they think they can know the reason why it is so, or how many species can come from it. First, they will never know the **reason why** <note>original Greek: "τὸ διότι," an Aristotelian term for the "reasoned fact" or the cause behind a phenomenon</note>, and they will never recognize it except through admiration of providence; and if they do recognize it, it will be such that they conceive it in the mind but cannot explain it in words. Furthermore, they will learn the rest through the experiments of the senses. And they wonder if they do not grasp how that God, who in His goodness has subjected these things to our eyes for His honor and praise and gave us the senses by which we might know them, could [have created them]...

<summary>Postel argues that if one accepts a self-sufficient God, one must accept creation from nothing (ex nihilo), as the alternative leads to an impossible infinite regress of causes. He acknowledges that while humans can observe the elements of nature, we are like people who can read letters but do not understand the language, unable to grasp the "why" of creation without divine providence.</summary>

Postel then moves from theoretical arguments to a famous empirical observation—a precursor to the "willow tree experiment"—to illustrate how matter can appear to increase through divine influence rather than just the consumption of existing earth. Finally, he begins Chapter VI, addressing the nature of Divine Providence.</meta>

->WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK I.<-

[signature mark: d 4]

...[could] produce something from nothing. Although there is no example in the lower <note>earthly or material</note> realms by which it can be shown to the senses that something is made from nothing, I will nevertheless add what can be offered as the closest thing in nature. Take three thousand pounds, or any other weight of fertile earth, and water it as much as you can before you weigh it, so that it is at the highest degree of heaviness, such that nothing of the same quantity and kind could be heavier. From this, make a hanging garden <note>hortus pensilis</note>, with a stone, metal, or any other body placed underneath that will for a long time prevent connection with any other soil, and ensure that nothing sensible <note>detectable by the senses</note> is lost. Finally, sow any kind of seed, but especially those of a luxuriant nature, in that garden, so that you may complete the experiment more quickly. Every year, collect the leaves, the bodies of the plants, and the fruits; weigh them, and you will see that before many years have passed, you have taken a large part of weight away from that garden. Then, weigh the watered soil again as you did before; you will find nothing in it has been diminished. 

Think, therefore, where those fruits came from, since nothing at all was lost from the earth. But you will say: "It came from the air and rains, and grew by watering." It is certain that Moses did not leave it written without reason: *And the Spirit of the Lord was carried over the waters* <note>Genesis 1:2. Postel implies that water, influenced by the divine spirit, can become solid matter.</note>. For although the four elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note> concur in the generation of all things, water claims such a large part for itself in all things that the work of the others, if compared to it, does not appear; it carries matter from elsewhere in parts that escape the senses. 

But if you give those things which grew without diminishing the earth to fire—the purifier of all things—there is no doubt that there will be a large quantity of ash, especially if you planted trees or shrubs. Philosophers admit that ashes are pure earth. For while fire, as the active agent, consumes the water and air, it cannot entirely destroy the earth, even if it diminishes it somewhat. See, then, where that earth came from, since you blocked the path of any neighboring soil and none of your own was lost. Certainly, you would say it was created from nothing, were we not dealing with the material part of the world. 

O lover of truth and true wisdom, take up the reasoning from this example and place the whole nature of things before your eyes: you will see many things created as if from nothing. Or at least, if they are not created from nothing, you will never grasp how a thick and sensible body creeps into the composition of nature. Do not, therefore—do not, because of your ignorance—attack God with your blasphemies or diminish His power, since it far surpasses those things which you know. For your "knowing" is merely to recount His works.

## THAT GOD CARES EVEN FOR
### particulars. Chapter VI.

Not a few philosophers, while they admit that providence gives a beginning to human affairs and acknowledge it even against their will, nevertheless remove it from the care of the universe. They believe that after things are brought forth, God no more cares whether they preserve their being well or ill than a craftsman who, having finished his work, usually neglects it. 

But this is held with too little accurate consideration of things. For when by our art we apply a certain form to any matter, it subsists by the power of the matter, according to the nature of the thing, the place, and the time, so that our industry is not needed for its primary parts; for how long it can endure is not determined by us, except in those parts usually changed by the injury of time and place. And when we restore something, we do so using matter taken from nature, which is destined to last in that work for a prescribed time. We, being corruptible, require rest, motion, and alterations; but Divine Providence, since it is **pure act** <note>original: "purus actus" — a theological term meaning God is eternally active and fully realized, with no potentiality or need for rest</note>, never resting, undoubtedly always leans upon the power of matter, whether mediated or immediate. If the world consisted entirely of stone, or any thick matter which, even if it had no sensation, still participated in elementary matter, once the parts of these bodies were bound together, it could last for some time as far as...

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

...they would be dissolved and act quietly. But besides the fact that those things which lack sensation are usually brought forth gradually—some by addition, others by connection—so that we may everywhere recognize the traces of a divinity who is always active, He willed that far more perfect things should come into the open. For these [lower things], he intended them to serve as a basis, and then to place others upon them, until the fourth level was reached.

For some things in the whole of nature are most dense and devoid of life; these we say simply *exist*, such as the elements themselves, stones, gems, metals, and other things which we see possess a great part of earth and water, and which do not exist for their own sake. In the following order are those things conceived from seeds which, by the power and presence of God and from seeds sown long ago, draw nourishment from those first [inanimate] things. These things live and rise up in greater bulk until they reach the period of their own nature and serve the following order. This [third] order, besides life, also possesses sensation and motion; it is increased by that same power until the period of its life or the end of its use, which it does not have within itself (for it is certain that things and their ends always differ), but rather in the following order, and it follows the greatest of all mortality.

This fourth step, embracing all four natures, exists with the stones, lives with the plants and animals, feels with the animate beings, and is **man**, the goal <note>Latin: *scopus*</note> of all nature. Since he could not have been generated for his own sake, it is necessary that he have his end in a higher degree. Therefore, besides the soul common to other living creatures, he is endowed with an immortal intellect, by which he can frequently contemplate heaven, the origin of souls, and God. His chief end in this life is mutual labor with other men as if they were brothers; in the future life, it is the knowledge of God and the perfect vision of all things in Him. Thus, the efficient cause of all things, creating all for His own sake, then returns their purpose to them when man passes into and remains in the recognition of his Creator.

Does it seem that such an order could endure, even in the smallest things or for a moment of an hour, unless that Moderator were perpetually present, preserving and binding the forms in matter and caring for all things? Certainly, it is impossible. For dying nature would never be replaced unless a preserving form were always present, commanded to be there by the Creator. Therefore, because these things could never subsist by themselves if deprived of a ruler, Plato rightly said they "do not exist." What is it (he asks at the beginning of the *Timaeus*) that is always being born and never *is*, or what is it that is never born and always *is*? By those things which are "always being born" and never subsist, he means these lower individual things, which in truth now subsist through Him. For forms, although they are never seen except in matter, nevertheless always exist; thus God is everywhere.

But if there is need of authorities to confirm these reasons, no one (except perhaps the <note>original: "λογοὶ" (logoi), likely referring to mere 'talkers' or those relying solely on human logic</note> and the **Epicureans**) from the entire assembly of pagan philosophers will be found wanting—not even **Averroes** <note>Latin: *Aben reis*, the 12th-century Islamic philosopher known as "The Commentator" on Aristotle</note> himself, who is as unfair as can be toward God. Therefore, regarding the knowledge of God, one must see what he thinks. For unless God knew all things, and through one science knew them all simultaneously and at once, He could not have care for all of them. Thus he [Averroes] speaks of this in many other places, but most especially in his work against **Al-Ghazali** <note>Latin: *Algezelem*, an 11th-century Persian theologian</note> (from whom I take this authority more willingly, because he [Averroes] would hardly wish to grant him even the most just points).

In the sixth discussion, in the solution to the third objection, he says: "It is not impossible that in the knowledge of God, which exists as one and the same, a multitude of things that can be known should be retained. For the philosophers prove that God knows Himself, and besides that, other changeable things." And a little later: "Knowledge in God is actual, while ours is potential and depends on the object, which must not be admitted in God. Indeed, the human intellect cannot be informed regarding the mode of God's knowledge." and elsewhere: "God's knowledge is neither universal nor particular, for we measure the quality of His knowledge by His power, not by our own knowledge."

But so that we may explain this difficulty a little more easily, we must first set forth the divisions of things as they are made by their causes, so that we may weigh—since God knows all—of which things He is the author and of which He is the permitter. There are, in the universe, four efficient causes: **Nature**, **Art**, **Fortune**, and **Divine Providence**. The first and the last are the same...

<summary>Postel describes the "Great Chain of Being," placing humanity as the goal of nature with the unique purpose of contemplating God. He then argues for Divine Providence by citing Plato and Averroes to show that the material world requires a constant Divine intellect to maintain its existence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Postel’s defense of Divine Providence. Having established man as the pinnacle of creation on the previous page, he now addresses the philosophical problem of why an all-knowing God allows evil, suffering, and physical deformity to exist.</meta>

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.

...since nature itself possesses neither will nor motion on its own. Just as things exist from nature, they show by their perpetual order that they have God as their author and protector in every detail. Whatever things happen by chance and outside the divine judgment—with God himself permitting it—God knows those things too. Similarly, those things done by us, whether good or bad, which I place within the category of human art and industry. Therefore, nothing can be placed within his ignorance. 

But Alexander <note>Likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, a 2nd-century philosopher who argued that God's providence only extends to species, not to individuals/particulars.</note> and those who, due to the perceived inconsistency, wish to strip God of the knowledge of particulars, will object: "If they make God know all things," they say, "they speak impiously, because he would see so many impious deeds and ignore them." A fine inference! If a prince's servant manages affairs poorly while the prince knows—and yet that prince is driven to vengeance by anger <note>original: "bilis", literally "bile" or "choler"</note>, a passion which God lacks—would he not immediately take up arms against that servant and his kin for all his crimes? Is there not always freedom of choice <note>original: "libertas arbitrij"</note> in that servant, so that he can repent and become better after his errors? Is it not just as metals are often purer after the rust they had from the mines is caught and wiped away? 

Furthermore, since everyone overflows and is pressed by vices—both from the disease of matter and of habit—who would not rather hope for the final act of life <note>original: "catastrophen". Postel uses the language of theater to describe the end of one's life.</note>, so that he who persists in acting unjustly that far cannot be excused? Would these things not be more praiseworthy than vengeance in a good and upright man? How much more should this be approved in God, who is of the highest gentleness and kindness? He cannot be impious or unjust because he sees, knows, and permits these things. For there will be a place for giving an account, which you must undergo whether you believe it or not; there you will know God not as unjust, but as most just. 

But this objection comes from those who think God is unjust because they judge that the minds of men die after fate <note>meaning after death</note>, and they wonder why God has not exacted the punishments for their impiety. That he sees things made by himself and nature is no obstacle, even though to our rashness some things in them seem evil; yet it is certain that nothing in them is evil that cannot be compensated for many times over by utility. In the first place, I know for certain they will point out many human bodies that are defective from birth—such as in their limbs, or even those lacking the use of intellect. They will assert that this is unjust, that no utility is gained from it, and that great misery is inflicted on the one having those defects; if God knows this, they say, he is unjust. 

But if God shows his power in one or another person to show how he could have formed even you, if he had willed, and even the whole race, what injustice does there seem to be to you? Especially since nothing of eternal happiness is lost for that person, even if they have an unfit body. To others, by comparison with their own happiness, countless utility is added. Indeed, it is the highest equity to be "unjust" in this way. 

Come now, is a head of a household <note>original: "paterfamilias"</note> unjust if, out of many servants of equal merit, he lowers some to lowly tasks and raises others according to his own judgment? And uses one out of many as an example for the others? Not at all, because he is permitted by his own right to allow what seems evil in appearance, as often as a greater utility flows from it to the whole flock. But we deny that this is just because we are ignorant; also because we remember evils but forget God’s benefits, whether we have gained anything from the use, form, deformity, or nature of creatures. 

This cause has led many to deny that providence either exists or cares for human affairs. Idle men, and those unskilled in the nature of things! They do not notice that there is no reason to believe that no law or right is implanted in human minds by nature, or that there are no laws among men, just because unjust judges overturn rights or crafty men pervert the law with law. For he would be plainly foolish who would conclude thus. Divine providence does not exact punishments in this world; it wishes to give deserved ones when there is no longer a place for repentance. Otherwise, since all things were made for the sake of man, if he were to be nothing after this life whether he acts well or ill after so many hardships—and since even the lowest things have their ends—would the most excellent thing, which is second in order after God, lack an end? It cannot be. Things that happen by chance, since they come from the necessity of matter, are not evil. Properly speaking, therefore, that which is evil is done by the will, for the violation of which one must pay—

->punishments<-

He maintains that true justice is deferred to the afterlife, where the soul’s eternal state outweighs temporal hardships.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument for Divine Providence. Having previously established that God’s presence is required for the order of nature, he now refutes the idea that God is ignorant of individual affairs (particulars) or that he is the source of evil. He relies heavily on Aristotelian teleology—the idea that everything moves toward a purpose—to show that a creator must remain intimately involved with his creation until its completion.</meta>

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...punishments are necessary; hence wickedness is furthest from God, since that which they call "iniquity" is actually the most distinguished property of the entire divinity. Not only does God himself preside over this moderation of individual things, but he also sends "separated substances" <note>This refers to spiritual beings, such as angels or intelligences, who exist without physical bodies.</note> that are good to stand by. However, he permits evil ones to be present among men, kingdoms, and places frequently; these the ancients called Genii <note>Spirits or "guardian" entities, both helpful and harmful.</note>. I will treat these immediately after adding a few authorities from the philosophers to prove my point. Aristotle, in his second book of *Natural Things*, or *Lessons on Physics* <note>original: "Naturalis auscultationis," the standard Latin title for Aristotle's Physics.</note>, says this:

> In those things in which there is some end <term>finis: the ultimate purpose or goal of a thing</term>, what comes before and after is done for the sake of that end. Therefore, as a thing is born to be, so it is made; and as it is usually made, so it is always made, unless something stands in the way. But it is made for the sake of something; therefore, that which it is born to be is also for the sake of this end. If a house were among the things produced by nature, it would be made exactly as it is now made by art. But if things which belong to nature were produced not only by nature but also by art, they would be produced in the same way they are naturally born to be. For one is the cause of the other, and art carries out all those things which nature cannot, yet it imitates nature. If, therefore, things made by art are for the sake of a certain end, it is certainly established that natural things are also made for the sake of a certain end.

And a little later:

> As art is sometimes frustrated in its end, so also is nature by the defect of matter <term>materia: the raw substance of the universe which receives form</term>, or rather, nature sometimes (though rarely) does not achieve its end, etc.

From these I infer that an efficient cause is required for created or artificial things for as long as they are receiving their completion. Even all the parts of things which ought to be present for the completion of any thing must necessarily be known and adapted by the acting cause until the finished work arises; otherwise, nothing would be completed. Therefore, as long as the construction of any work lasts, the artistic cause must be present, knowing, and completing the work. Since the world is perpetually in motion and in action, and is not completed until the last man of the world has been born, has lived, and has recognized God, it is most certain from what has been conceded that God knows even particular things. For if he were to leave this work even once (which cannot happen), it would remain imperfect, with the parts that lead to completion not yet applied to it. Since, therefore, its parts pass away every moment, they have need of healing through perpetual restoration and innovation (as the philosophers say); but this cannot be done without knowledge of all the parts. 

But if so many errors and imperfections occur, how can it be that this most wise judge, knowing all things, does not heal those imperfections? The cause is this: He indeed created matter to be a follower of forms <note>In Aristotelian thought, "form" gives shape, purpose, and identity to "matter."</note>, as I have already said, but in such a way that it always carries the evidence of itself. For if he generated it as perfect as the form (as he certainly could have), he would have made it unsuitable for subjects, and would have made the species created from it eternal. From this, all future things would have been both eternal and unique, like the forms themselves. Or, if by the creator's will, other things not subject to corruption had finally been produced in the course of time, all the elements would have been solid bodies endowed with life and body, piled up together without mutual use or order; and once those were completed, God would have been powerless to create further—all of which are unworthy of the creator. 

It was necessary, therefore, to have left imperfection in matter until the world is purified. That imperfection of matter, through the slowness or speed of motion and its own nature, causes it not always to be disposed by the forms—not by any fault or ignorance of the form or the creator, but by the flux of matter and the concurrence of external causes which, since they are placed in chance, cannot be numbered. From the preceding, therefore, we hold that God knows even particulars, tolerating and permitting evils, but not being their author. Nor is there one God as the cause of good and another of evil, as some fools have babbled, whom Aristotle hisses away <note>original: "exibilat", literally to hiss off a stage.</note> in the 3rd and 12th books of his *Metaphysics*. Furthermore, what we classify as evil is not evil unless it proceeds from human judgment. For a man to die who will eventually die anyway, or for houses to be burned which were eventually going to ruin and perish...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s discussion on why God allows seemingly bad things to happen and transitions into Chapter VII, which introduces "separated substances"—what we might call angels or spirits—as part of the cosmic order.</meta>

->WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK I.<-

...that fortunes gathered over a long time should perish and be scattered, or that they will not exist in the future, or that they will perpetually change masters—we mistakenly judge all these things to be among "evils." But he who has committed murder willfully and intentionally, who has set fire to homes, who has snatched away, violated, or plundered, and other similar things: he truly has sinned most gravely and committed evil. He has fallen away from the benefit of the Creator, and unless he repents, he will suffer eternal punishments. 

Therefore, nothing prevents these things from being known and tolerated by God, as if by turning a blind eye. For otherwise, as we have already said, through the deceits of men, God would hardly be worshipped by anyone in the world. For man is of such a depraved will that if he were to pay the penalty to God every time he sinned, the human race would have died out long ago. A ruler prefers to wait for reform rather than to rage against his own people. 

Nonetheless, God also permits the most heavy punishments to be inflicted upon men—by the work of demons who procure such things—starting with ignorance of oneself and of God, and finally through diseases of the body, the devastation of kingdoms, the plundering of provinces, plagues, famines, and wars. No one should doubt that all these things are born from the merits <note>In this context, "merits" refers to the consequences earned by human actions, specifically sins.</note> of men. For God permits these things to happen so that we may return to the path of innocence; for this is usually done only by those who are afflicted and divinely inspired, rather than by those who are fortunate.

### ON SEPARATED SUBSTANCES, OR
### *demons, or Genii. CHAPTER VII.*

In no matter has there been greater dispute, greater obscurity, or less agreement of opinions than when a discussion about demons or "separated substances" <note>Postel uses this term to describe spiritual beings like angels or spirits that exist independently of physical bodies.</note> has arisen among the philosophers. For on one hand, our ignorance of unknown things tends to pull us one way, while on the other, various observed effects pull us another. Therefore, this part must be touched upon and treated more diligently, precisely because it is more difficult. 

In the first place, I will set down the reasons; in the following order, I will rely on the authority of learned men; then I will persuade by the universal consensus of all nations. Finally, I will come to the effects and experiences, which are innumerable. If we are indeed able to grasp anything regarding these higher substances, it will surely be far more pleasant than the greatest knowledge of inferior things, as Aristotle says. For he says in the second book of *On the Heavens and the Earth*: "When we reach certain celestial things by demonstration, it happens that we rejoice exceedingly." Even if these reasons fall less under the perception of the senses, they will nonetheless be usefully received as being further proven. Just as many things are proposed to be believed by the unlearned, and even by great men, concerning God and other things that do no harm—and which it helps much to believe—proven by the simple authority and consensus of men.

<margin>From reason.</margin>
1. Just as up to this point we have found the truth from the contemplation of all nature and the comparison of causes and things with one another, so also it seems we must act here. From the motion of the heavens, Aristotle demonstrates it thus: "Every motion that is in itself unfailing comes from a mover who is moved neither by himself nor by accident" <term>per accidens: a philosophical term meaning something that happens incidentally or as a side effect, rather than as an essential property</term>. But there are many different motions in the heaven. Therefore, it is necessary that many movers be present for them. A body does not move unless moved by something else; this is proven by the very nature of motion. However, an incorporeal mover joined to a body is moved "by accident" by the motion of the body, as is evident regarding the soul. But in the celestial motions, it is necessary that there be movers who are free of both body and motion. Truly, those celestial motions are from some intellect; from which it is established that there are "separated substances," at least equal in number to the heavens.

<margin>From the harmony and order of the world.</margin>
2. A superior nature, in its lowest part, touches the highest part of the inferior. But a nature endowed with intellect is superior to a corporeal one, and it is that which gives completion to all corporeal things in man. Therefore, just as a body endowed with intellect is the highest among bodies, so it is necessary that the soul joined to it be the lowest in the genus of "intelligences"; and this soul itself is free from destruction. Therefore, from the order of things, there are also other substances above it, even of many orders and powers.

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument for the existence of "separated substances" (angels or pure intellects) by using the logic of hierarchy and the perfection of the universe. He argues that just as the physical world is filled with life, the heavens must also be populated by spiritual beings who can praise the Creator.</meta>

->ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-

3 If a composite thing results from any two parts, just as a difference of perfection is found in one of the simple parts, so it is in the other. Hence, there is something that is "first" and less in need of the rest: this is evident in the logic of physical bodies. For the **foundation of bodies** does not need others, but rather the reverse; thus, by analogy, a **separated substance** <note>A "separated substance" refers to a being that exists without a physical body, such as an angel or a pure intellect.</note> is also found. These differ, however, by comparison, even though they agree in their degrees. For in divine matters, the further things are distant from the "first" [God], the more they need Him for their perfection. In corporeal things, the opposite occurs. For **matter and form** subsist in a certain contrary way. It is indeed possible for the substance of insensible things to exist without life, sense, or intellect; and life can exist without sense, and sense without intellect—but not the other way around. So here, that which is most excellent—**man**—cannot subsist without the lower things. But our mind, which is already in the **fourth degree** and which by this reasoning ought to be more perfect than other separated substances, is (that is, to assign it among equal substances) far inferior and especially in need of the "first." However, in the reverse order, all things agree. For just as nothing is created without the "being" of matter, nor can it reach the summit; so also without God, the most excellent and infinite among all forms, there is no place for any substances. But just as the second degree of matter is more worthy than the first, so the second intellect is inferior in nobility to the first. And again, just as things endowed with sense are more noble than the first and second degrees, so the third things from God are less worthy than the second. And likewise, as the highest things here are most worthy, so there the third things from God (which are fourth in order) are lesser. Therefore, the perfection of lower things is not by reason of the body, but by reason of their approach to the highest; likewise, the cause of lesser nobility for others is their approach to matter and lower things. From this it follows that in the middle there is a **connection of both**, so that in the human body itself there is a most excellent form: the **mind**, descended from that **fifth nature** <note>original: "quinta illa natura"; Aristotle proposed a "fifth element" or quintessence, distinct from earth, water, air, and fire, which composed the celestial bodies.</note>, as Aristotle says, which is able to act, reason, and gather thoughts by itself—something denied to other living creatures consisting of the same elements. For if reason were from this [common] nature, it would be necessary for the brute animals to use it too, which is seen in no case. But these matters are better discussed where we treat the **immortality of souls**. Therefore, as there is a degree here, so there must also be one there. Consequently, between the mind and God, there are **separated substances**. If there were no intellects in that so bright and transparent matter and capacity of heaven (since all things consist of life and the praise and honor of God), it would certainly be absurd to have procreated so many kinds of animals in this filthy matter for the sake of one man—a praiser of God (if he is wise)—while in the most magnificent part of the world there was nothing but a desert. That would be just as if someone, seeking praise from his works and wealth, wanted those which are most magnificent to be entirely destitute of an inhabitant, while wanting the deformed ones to be entirely filled with a frequent inhabitant. Since the end of all things is in God—namely, that He may be acknowledged, praised, and loved (even though He does not need these things except by His will, for He lacks nothing else)—it is certain that He has left no place in the world empty of a praiser. From this the proposition is clear: namely, that there are most excellent **spirits** in the most excellent part of the world, where they assiduously praise God. Furthermore:

5 Whether there be one intellect or many, I do not wish to argue against **Averroes** <note>original: "Abenrois"; a 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose views on the "unity of the intellect"—the idea that all humans share one single capacity for thought—were highly controversial in the Renaissance.</note> here; I shall do that in its proper place concerning the immortality of souls. It is enough that by the consensus of all philosophers, the intellect survives after death; it is indeed separated from the body not by its substance, but by accident, and it survives. But that which exists "by itself" is prior to that which exists "by accident." Therefore, besides the human intellect, there are also other **separated substances**, subsisting by themselves. Thus the creation of **demons** <note>In this context, "demons" (dæmonum) refers to spiritual beings or intermediate spirits in the celestial hierarchy, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note>, which exists by itself, was made before the mind which is joined to the body itself. Thus the assumption is proven.

6 Furthermore, a **substance** can exist without quantity, but not the other way around. Moreover, substance is prior to all the most general categories in time, reason, and knowledge.

He concludes that the heavens must be inhabited by spiritual beings (separated substances) because it would be illogical for God to fill the "filthy" earth with life while leaving the "noble" celestial spheres empty of anyone to praise Him.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Postel’s philosophical defense of "separated substances"—beings like angels or pure intellects that exist without physical bodies. # BOOK I BY GUILLAUME POSTEL #

But no corporeal substance exists without quantity. Therefore, there can be certain things in the category of substance that are devoid of a body. Furthermore, everything possible is found in the nature of things; otherwise, the universe would be imperfect. Moreover, in eternal things, "to be" and "to be possible" do not differ. Whence it is established from that possibility that there are substances even besides God and the soul. For He is the highest of such things, and our soul is the lowest. It is necessary, therefore, that there be middle substances which are possible, so that they may exist. I could deal with this using even more reasons, but these will satisfy those seeking the truth in order to learn; for those seeking only to argue, neither these nor any other reasons will ever be enough. Now, I must rely on authority.

<margin>7</margin> Since I am about to confirm these things by authority, I could certainly bring forward the philosophers of all nations in my favor with a single word—those by whose judgment posterity has stood—unless a few stubborn ones were removed from the number. These, so they might differ from the rest, denied that there was any judgment within themselves. Among the Latins, if you except Pliny and Lucretius, no one will fail to subscribe to this. Among the Greeks, it is no wonder there were more, since the "pestilence of the world" <note>Postel likely refers here to the spread of skepticism or atheism originating from Greek schools.</note> flowed from there. They had Pyrrho of Elis, Sextus Empiricus, Lucian, Arcesilaus (though he seemed more modest, because he did not assert that the things he was ignorant of were false, but judged that assent should be withheld from things), Democritus, and their followers. For there was no kind of opinion or deed so foolish that it lacked an advocate or witness among them. They wished to fight against the sense of the entire world regarding the opinion on **separated substances** <note>Spiritual beings existing independently of matter, such as angels.</note>. I judge them unworthy of refutation because they recoiled from the opinion of everyone else. It is certainly not surprising that those who said nothing is perceived by our senses—and that all those things we touch were created falsely and uselessly, and that the whole world was a series of phantoms rather than substance—also refused to cast their vote for these substances. They were not men, but shams of men; or at the very least, they were forced to be not ignorant of this one thing: that they did not even know themselves. 

Let us see what moved others to introduce an opinion different from the consensus of the world. The abuse of all religions—namely, the **greed of the priests**—is the reason why people have less faith in things held sacred. Therefore, many used to call the gods "unknowing givers of wealth" <note>original: ἀγνῶς πλουτοδότας (*agnōs ploutodotas*)</note>, because those most innocent gods usually provided a very rich profit to the sacrificers. Therefore, when that pretense was seen almost everywhere, and they saw that everything teemed with deceptions and nothing of the truth lay beneath, they believed nothing. This very thing makes some people strangers to our own most holy persuasion; if they see the truth in one matter a hundred times, but feel that a falsehood has crept in once, they will immediately abolish, for the sake of that one sense, whatever faith they held before. It is established that this proceeds from the fact that they wish for things to be as they believe, and they judge with prejudice. This is how those Greeks and Latins felt about religions, deceptions, and demons: because those gods seemed to respond more frequently with slanted and obscure answers, as if uttered from "un-wisdom" <note>original: ἀσοφίᾳ (*asophia*)</note>. 

Thus, partly ignorance of things, partly pretense, and partly a lust for thinking and perceiving differently, caused them to claim that no separated substances exist. But let us dismiss those "followers of Democritus" and pass on to the most certain judgments. Let the **Prince of Philosophers** <note>A traditional title for Aristotle.</note> himself come forward, who says in Book 12 of his *Metaphysics* <note>original: τῶν κατὰ τὰ φυσικὰ (*tōn kata ta physika*)</note>, while investigating substances, that substance in the universe is divided two ways: into the **sensible-corruptible** and the **sensible-eternal**, and a third, **immobile** substance. The second cannot be understood except as separated substances. Because a heavenly body—insofar as it is a body and consists of matter and form—it is impossible for it to be eternal in the way we have already demonstrated. When he calls them "gods" more than once in his *Ethics*, it cannot be understood except as separated substances. Furthermore, by the authority of the same man already added before, it was clear that there are **intelligences** <note>In Aristotelian thought, "Intelligences" are the spiritual beings that move the celestial spheres.</note> that are the movers of the spheres. But it is most clear from what he said—that all things are in a certain way "three"—that there are separated substances. For after God, the first and unmoved cause remaining in Himself, who is the most simple **unity and trinity**, it is necessary that there also be these same...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD #

...harmony, there are three orders of separated substances <note>Separated substances: beings like angels or pure intellects that exist apart from physical matter.</note>, and these are themselves tripartite in nature. Since this does not contradict reason and follows the natural order of things, it must certainly be believed and accepted as proven, especially since it is held through revelation and inspiration rather than mere proof. Through the administration of these orders, the High God is accustomed to governing these lower realms. 

But I shall move on to Plato. After he spoke concerning the divinity of the heavens and the stars in the *Timaeus*:

> To speak of other daimons <note>original: *dæmonibus*. In Platonic thought, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note> and to recount their origin is a task beyond our strength. We must believe those who came before us regarding them. For since they claimed to be the offspring of the gods, it is certain they knew their own progenitors, whom they passed down to posterity. It is indeed most absurd to deny the children of the gods credit concerning their own parents, even if they speak without any demonstration—whether true or likely—as if one must simply obey the law of their words.

By this decree, he orders that what was handed down regarding religion by the ancestors long ago be ratified. And again, when he introduces the highest of the gods addressing the lower gods (that is, the daimons):

> Whatever is born, he says, is likewise corruptible. Therefore, since you were born, you are not immortal by your own nature. Nevertheless, since my power is immense and superior to corruption, I do not wish you to be held by the laws of death, etc.

Through these words, we have three of the greatest authorities: Pythagoras, Plato, and Cicero. An infinite crowd of the most learned men followed them: Plotinus, Iamblichus, Hermes, Amelius, Maximus Tyrius, Porphyry, Epictetus, Chalcidius, and Proclus. All of these asserted both that separated substances exist and that they are distinguished into good and evil kinds. 

By a certain succession of teaching, Pherecydes received this from the Syrians and Chaldeans, Pythagoras from him, Plato from Pythagoras, Cicero from Plato, and posterity from them. It would be nothing other than a burden to the reader to bring forward what Orpheus, Homer, Hesiod, and Empedocles wrote about them; or from the Latins—Virgil, Catullus, Valerius, Ovid, and Seneca—who would have to be examined almost in their entirety. Truly, it is necessary to bring forward one or two other passages from Plato. In the fifth book of the *Laws*, he affirms that when we are advanced toward the highest happiness, each person is helped by a daimon who presides over them, as if meeting a guide. In the *Apology of Socrates*, he proves that daimons are everywhere. In the *Cratylus*, he places them in a threefold genus: heroes made from men, daimons, and gods—all of which are separated substances. 

I could certainly bring forward many things from Proclus now, but because he plucked and claimed for himself all that our own Dionysius the Areopagite <note>Dionysius the Areopagite: A figure mentioned in the Book of Acts, but also the name attributed to a highly influential 5th-century Christian mystic. Postel claims the Pagan philosopher Proclus plagiarized him.</note> handed down, I shall skip them. For our own traditions are sufficiently proven to us. But before I come to the other authorities, I wish to bring forward what Plutarch—a man most skilled in both Latin and Greek learning—handed down, because his words do much for our cause and even confirm what we have in writing from the Sacred Scriptures. Concerning the "loss of the oracles," he writes thus:

> Concerning the death of these (he means the daimons), I heard a speech from a man who was neither imprudent nor vain: Aemilianus the rhetorician, whom many of you have heard. His father was Epitherses, my fellow citizen and my teacher in grammar. He related that when he was once sailing to Italy, he boarded a ship laden with various merchandise and a large crowd of people. As evening was falling one day, when the ship was near the Echinades islands, the wind died down and the ship was carried near the island of Paxi. While many were still awake and not a few were still drinking—supper not yet being finished—a voice was heard from the island of Paxi, calling "Thamus" once and then again, so that they wondered.

Philippus (whom Plutarch introduces in this passage) also had certain witnesses of these events, which he had heard from Aemilianus. 

Furthermore, Demetrius says (he is also introduced by Plutarch, and was a native of Britain) that of these islands which are around Britain, many are deserted and scattered (they call them the Orcades <note>The Orkney Islands</note>); some of these they named after daimons <note>Spirits or semi-divine beings in Greek thought.</note> and Heroes. ### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD ###

...harmonies of three orders of separated substances <term>separated substances: a philosophical term for beings existing without physical bodies, such as angels, demons, or celestial intelligences</term>, and these are also themselves tripartite. Since nothing in this contradicts reason and it follows the natural order of things, it must certainly be believed and accepted as proven, especially since it is held by revelation and inspiration rather than by mere demonstration. By the administration of these orders, the supreme God is accustomed to moderating these lower realms. 

But I shall pass on to Plato. After he spoke of the divinity of the heavens and the stars in the *Timaeus*, he said: "To speak of other daemons <note>original: *dæmonibus*. In the Platonic sense, these are intermediary spirits between gods and men, not necessarily 'demons' in the modern evil sense.</note> and to recount their origin is a task beyond our strength; we must believe what has been handed down by the ancients. For since they were descended from the gods, it is certain that they knew their own progenitors, whom they passed down to their descendants. It is certainly most absurd to deny the children of the gods faith regarding their own parents, even if they speak without any proof, whether true or probable, as if their words were a law to be obeyed." By this decree, he commands that what was long ago handed down by the ancestors concerning religion be ratified. 

And again, when he introduces the supreme God addressing the lower gods—that is, the daemons—he says: "Whatever has been born is likewise corruptible. Therefore, since you have been born, you are not indeed immortal by your own nature. Nevertheless, since my power is immense and superior to corruption, I do not wish you to be held by the laws of death," etc. In these words, we have three of the greatest authorities—Pythagoras, Plato, and Cicero—who were followed by an infinite crowd of most learned men: Plotinus, Iamblichus, Hermes, Amelius, Maximus of Tyre, Porphyry, Epictetus, Chalcidius, and Proclus. All of these asserted both that separated substances exist and that they are distinguished into good and evil kinds. 

By a certain succession of teaching, Pherecydes received this from the Syrians and Chaldeans; from him, Plato received it; from Plato, Cicero; and from them, posterity. It would be nothing other than a burden to the reader to bring forward what Orpheus, Homer, Hesiod, and Empedocles wrote of them, or from the Latins, Virgil, Catullus, Valerius, Ovid, and Seneca; they would have to be examined almost in their entirety. Truly, one or two other passages of Plato ought to be brought forward. In the fifth book of the *Laws*, he affirms that when we are advancing toward supreme happiness, each person is helped by a daemon who presides over them, as if by someone meeting them on the way. In the *Apology of Socrates*, he proves that daemons are everywhere. In the *Cratylus*, he places them in a three-fold kind: heroes made from men, daemons, and gods—all of which are separated substances. 

I could certainly bring forward many things from Proclus now, but because our own Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-6th century Christian theologian and mystic who combined Neoplatonic philosophy with Christian theology; Postel suggests Proclus actually took his ideas from Dionysius.</note> handed down these same things (though Proclus plucked them and ascribed them to himself), I shall refrain. For our own sources are sufficiently proven to us. But before I come to the other authorities, I wish to bring forward what Plutarch—a man most skilled in both Latin and Greek learning—handed down, because his words greatly serve our purpose and even confirm what we have in writing from the sacred scriptures. 

Concerning the "lost oracles," he writes: "Concerning the death of these (he means the daemons), I heard the account of a man who was neither unwise nor vain: the rhetorician Aemilianus, whom many of you have heard. His father was Epitherses, my fellow citizen and my teacher in grammar. He used to relate that once, when he was sailing to Italy, he boarded a ship laden with various merchandise and a great multitude of people. Toward evening one day, when they were near the Echinades islands, the wind died down and the ship was carried near the island of Paxos. While many were still awake and not a few were still drinking—the dinner not yet being finished—a voice was heard from the island of Paxos, calling out 'Thamus!' once and then again, so that they wondered. Now, Thamus was the Egyptian pilot of the ship, and he was unknown by that name even to many of the passengers. When the voice called a first and second time, he remained silent; but at the third call, he responded to the one calling. Then, raising its voice, the caller said: 'When you are near Palodes (a place not far from Corcyra), announce that Great Pan is dead' <note>original: *Pan magnus mortuus est*.</note>." 

Upon hearing this, Epitherses said they were driven into a stupor by great wonder, and they began to debate in their minds whether they should do as commanded or care no more about it. But Thamus decided that he must act accordingly.

...most perfect; however, they do not have this perfection from themselves, but receive it from the Highest. These are the words of Damascius <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 458–538 AD), the last head of the School of Athens.</note>, which do not differ much from the opinion of our Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, thought by Postel to be the convert of St. Paul, though now known as "Pseudo-Dionysius," a 5th-century Christian Neoplatonist.</note>. But indeed, Proclus <note>Another major Neoplatonist (412–485 AD) whose work deeply influenced medieval philosophy.</note> took so much from this source that he transcribed many things word for word, even while the works of Dionysius were still hidden. He did not want to credit them to their true author because he knew Dionysius was an initiate of Christ, to whom Proclus was hostile; he easily thought that Dionysius's works would perish, as the Christian republic was not yet firmly established. Lest these things be recognized, following the pagan custom to bolster their impious religions, he always calls "gods" those whom we call "angels." He even asserts three triads of them, so that there is absolutely no difference except in name, attempting to turn truth into a lie. Moreover, in place of our vocabulary, and so that his thefts would not be obvious, he used simple numbers. Thus, the first three orders for him are *intelligible, intelligible and intellectual, and purely intellectual* <note>original Greek: "νοητοὶ, νοητοὶ καὶ νοεροὶ, νοεροὶ μόνον"</note>. These terms hardly have a suitable Latin expression, unless you say "endowed with mind," "comprehending with mind," and "comprehended by mind"—which still cannot fully express the matter. For although no other genus follows these lower ones, they are so powerful in intellect that nothing at all is hidden from them, except for the first being, **Yahweh** <note>original Hebrew: יהוה</note>, whom they indeed know, but do not fully comprehend. They are arranged in these three triads. In the first order are those whose names that impious man <note>Proclus</note> wished to avoid: Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones, who purify, illuminate, and perfect all lower things. In the second are Dominations, Virtues, and Powers; having been purified, enlightened, and perfected by the highest order, they likewise provide for the lower ones. For the Principalities, Archangels, and Angels are only purified, enlightened,

<margin>Dionysius assigns this office especially to the angels, in *The Celestial Hierarchy*.</margin>
and perfected. From these orders, Providence wished for individual angels to be present to individual humans as counselors of the divinity, so that the soul placed within the body might more easily overcome the stubbornness of matter. Furthermore, they prove that there are various kinds of evil beings opposed to these. Plato writes of it, religion accepts it, and reason dictates it. For insofar as they are intelligences, it is certain they possess free will; hence they are called by Plato, the Pythagoreans, and all writers of ancient theology *kakodaimones* <note>original Greek: κακοδαίμονες</note>, that is, "evil demons." This is because they abused that choice and cannot return into favor with the First Cause, because they lack the divine favor and help from which they fell by their own will. These beings oppose individual angels, and each acts at least around individual humans, leading them away from the truth and forcing them to abuse true happiness in their own fashion; many examples of this will be made clear. Almost all who were Platonists, or men of a better school of thought, chose to call the good angels "gods," but the bad ones more frequently "demonic" <note>original Greek: δαιμονίους</note>, as Plato himself did first. For in the fifth book of the *Republic*, while he is advising on religion, he says that the common people themselves ought to be taught the difference—who among those departing this life are "demonic" and who are "divine" <note>original Greek: δαιμονίοι, τίνες θεῖοι</note>. Through these terms, he explains two kinds of men departing from life: namely, the good and the bad. But in this he erred: he posited that the souls of the wicked become demons. Psellus <note>Michael Psellus (1017–1078), a Byzantine monk and scholar who wrote "On the Operation of Demons."</note> easily reveals the mind of Plato in his book *On Demons*. He says that a certain Chaldean considers some demons good and some bad; but our pious discourse asserts that all are evil, because they sinned by choice and exchanged goodness for wickedness. The reason the Chaldeans thought some were good was that they used the labor of evil demons for futile and vain things, since they could not have compelled the good ones. These phantoms, as Hesiod says, *clothed in mist, roam over all the earth* <note>original Greek: ἠέρα ἑσσάμενοι πᾶσαν φοιτῶσιν ἐπ᾽ αἶαν</note>; they are seen wherever on earth they wish. Therefore Hermes, or Mercurius Trismegistus <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic writings are attributed.</note>, asserts that there are no good demons. Plato sometimes calls them good, sometimes bad. He calls them good more frequently, but bad in the third book of the *Republic*, where he says they are *the authors of sorcery and deception* <note>original Greek: γοητείας καὶ ἀπάτης αἰτίος</note>, which must be categorized as evil. And Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) and student of Plotinus.</note>, in his books *On Abstinence*, says the evil ones are contrary to the good, and are the authors of sorcery <note>original Greek: γοητείας</note> and of evil lusts...

...inventors of all things. For they wish to be seen as gods: and the power presiding over them (which we call Satan, that is, the adversary) seems like God to them. Although he errs gravely in this—since they sin in their judgment—nevertheless, in his assertions, he wrote things consistent with our own beliefs. This should be held as an even greater authority because it rises up against us, and he would hardly wish to concede even what is most fair to us. Indeed, testimony from an adversary is by far the strongest. Therefore, since those airy pests were cast down from the heavenly region, the world is stirred up and leans toward ruin. 

Moreover, that they exist and act in the air is established even by the "Philosopher of Truth" <note>Postel refers to Aristotle (384–322 BC), often called simply "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance texts.</note> in his books on *Metaphysics*, saying that these four bodies are substance, as well as the animals that arise in them—namely, demons—and their parts. Likewise, in the first book *On the Soul*, he says: "Someone might ask for what reason the soul that is in the air is more immortal and better than that which is in living beings?" Explaining this, Simplicius <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> says: "It is much more excellent if a race of demons is supposed to exist, which sometimes creeps into the body itself when it is subject to passions." This must be understood not as creeping in to provide the soul's form, but to torment and infect a body that is already animated. This happens so frequently that nothing is more common, as is evident from experience. 

Indeed, some were led by the reasoning that they were seen in the air, and sometimes in one place—often staying for many centuries—until finally they would vanish and take themselves elsewhere to destroy and drive men mad. The ancients thought they were mortal. Hesiod <note>An early Greek poet (c. 700 BC).</note> himself testifies to this when he says that the nymph-goddesses live ten times the life of a Phoenix, a span extending to 9,720 years. Antiquity seemed to say the same thing when it called them *Hamadryads* <note>original Greek: "νύμφας ἁμαδρυάδας"</note>, that is, Nymphs equal in age to the oak tree. These things are found to be false because those substances—whether pure or depraved—are of the simplest essence and cannot be corrupted as far as their essence is concerned. For they suffer no contrary force. 

What then was the cause for antiquity to hold such varied opinions about them, agreeing on nothing less than those "gods" who were made from demons? It was the cunning of a scoundrel <note>Postel refers here to the Devil.</note>, drawing clouds over the minds of mortals so they would be held in perpetual error. So that nothing might be firm or stable, he moved from one place to another, and with new crimes he lured new men to himself, until he turned everyone away from the knowledge of the "First Cause" <note>A philosophical term for God as the creator.</note>. He thrust himself into the place of God in the statues of things, animals, and criminal men, until the one Truth (which alone could do this in a world initiated into true sacred rites) blunted his efforts. Because of those changes, some thought they did not exist because they had not seen them; to others, they seemed to have died when they left a place; to some, this one was true and another false. Nowhere has lying been more frequent than under the influence of the "author of lies." For what wonder is it that many felt so variously about the most inconstant thing of all, when truth is called into doubt by many, no faith is given to the senses, the testimony of others is like a dream, and many hold the authority of the wise as equal to that of fools and children? They are moved by no consensus of the world, and some wish their own judgment of things to be preferred over the whole universe. If they hallucinate about the most certain things, what wonder that they are deceived in things doubtful and obscure? 

But although those driven headlong by stubbornness cannot be conquered by any arguments, I shall nevertheless bring forward the consensus of all nations regarding this nature of substances. If they refuse to stand by the judgment of divine men and those skilled in all things, let them at least receive those things which our ancestors, taught by experience, believed.

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...of the most perfect things, they do not possess that perfection from themselves, but receive it from the Highest. These are the views of Damascius <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>, which do not differ much from the opinion of our Dionysius <note>Postel refers to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian whose "Celestial Hierarchy" was highly influential.</note>. Indeed, Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist.</note> took everything from this source to such an extent that he transcribed many things word for word, at a time when the works of Dionysius were still hidden. He did not want to credit the author because he knew him to be initiated into Christ, to whom Proclus was hostile; he thought it would be easy for Dionysius's works to perish, as the Christian state was not yet firmly established. To prevent them from becoming known, following the pagan custom and to bolster their own impious religions, he always calls "gods" those whom we call "angels." He asserts three triads of them, so that there is absolutely no difference except in name alone, as he strives to turn truth into a lie. In place of our terms, so that his thefts would not be exposed, he used simple numbers. Thus, the first three orders for him are the "intelligible," the "intelligible and intellectual," and the "intellectual only" <note>original Greek: νοητοὶ, νοητοὶ καὶ νοεροὶ, νοεροὶ μόνον</note>. These terms hardly have a suitable Latin expression, unless you say: "those endowed with mind," "those comprehending with the mind," and "those comprehended by the mind"—yet even these cannot fully express the matter. For although no lower genus follows these inferior ones, they are so powerful in intellect that nothing in all of creation escapes them, except for the First Being, **YHWH** <note>The Hebrew Tetragrammaton, the personal name of God.</note>, whom they indeed know but do not fully comprehend.

<margin>
Dionysius assigns this duty chiefly to the angels in his book *On the Celestial Hierarchy*.
</margin>

They are arranged into these three triads. In the first order are those whose names that impious man <note>Proclus.</note> wished to avoid: **Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones**, who purify, illuminate, and perfect all things below them. In the second are **Dominions, Virtues, and Powers**; having been purified, enlightened, and perfected by the highest order, they likewise provide for the lower ones. For the **Principalities, Archangels, and Angels** are only purified, illuminated, and perfected. From these orders, Providence willed that individual advisors of the Divinity be present for individual humans, so that the soul placed within the body might more easily overcome the stubbornness of matter.

These same authors prove that there are also various kinds of evil beings opposed to these. Plato writes of it, religion accepts it, and reason dictates it. For insofar as they are intelligences, it is certain that they possess free will. Hence they are called by Plato, the Pythagoreans, and all the writers of ancient theology <term>kakodaimones</term> <note>original: κακοδαίμονες; meaning "evil spirits" or "evil demons"</note>; because they abused that choice, they cannot return to favor with the First Cause, because they lack the divine favor and help from which they fell by their own will. These beings oppose individual angels, and they act at least against individual men, leading them away from the truth and forcing them to abuse true happiness in their own fashion; many examples of this will be made clear.

Almost all who were Platonists or men of a better school of thought wished to call the good angels "gods," but more frequently called the evil ones "demons" <note>original: δαίμονας</note>; Plato himself was the first to do this. For in the fifth book of the *Republic*, while advising on religion, he says that the common people should be taught the difference: which among those departing this life are "demons" and which are "divine" <note>original: τίνες θεῖοι, qui diuini, qui dæmonij</note>. Through these two words, he explains the two kinds of men departing this life—the good and the bad. But in this he erred: he posited that the souls of the wicked become demons. Psellus, in his book *On Demons*, will easily clarify Plato’s mind. And a certain Chaldean, he says, considers some demons to be good and some to be evil; however, our pious discourse asserts that all are evil, because they sinned by their own choice and exchanged goodness for wickedness. The reason the Chaldeans thought they were all good was that they used the works of evil demons for futile and vain things, as they could not have compelled the good ones. 

These "specters," as Hesiod says, "clothed in air, wander over all the earth" <note>original Greek: ἠέρα ἑσσάμενοι πᾶσαν φοιτῶσιν ἐπ’ αἶαν</note>. Therefore, Hermes—or Mercurius Trismegistus—asserts that there are no good demons. Plato calls them sometimes good, sometimes evil. Good more frequently, but evil in the third book of the *Republic*, where he says they are "the authors of sorcery and deception" <note>original Greek: γοητείας καὶ ἀπάτης αἰτίους</note>, things which must be classified as evil. And Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and critic of Christianity.</note>, in his books *On Abstinence*, says the evil ones are contrary to the good, and are the authors of sorcery <note>original: γοήτας</note> and of evil desires...

...inventors of [falsities]. For they wish to be seen as gods; and the power that presides over them—which we call Satan, meaning "the adversary"—seems to them to be God. Even though he errs gravely in this, because they sin in their judgment, he nonetheless wrote things that agree with our own scriptures. This should be held as an even greater authority because it rises up against us, and he is hardly willing to grant us what is most fair. Indeed, testimony from an adversary is by far the strongest. Therefore, those airy plagues having been cast down from the celestial region, the world is agitated and leans toward ruin. That they exist and act in the air is established even by the "Philosopher of Truth" <note>Postel refers to Aristotle.</note> in his books on *Metaphysics*, where he wrote that those four bodies are substance, as well as the living beings produced in them—namely, animals and demons <note>original: "dæmonia"</note>—and their parts. Likewise, in the first book of *On the Soul*, he says: "One might ask for what reason the soul which is in the air is more immortal and better than that which is in living beings?" Explaining this, Simplicius <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> says: "It is much more excellent if the race of demons is supposed to exist, which itself sometimes creeps into a body subject to passions." This must be understood as "creeping in" not to provide form <note>In Aristotelian terms, the soul is the "form" that gives life to the body; Postel argues demons don't give life, they just invade it.</note>, but to twist and infect a body that is already alive. This happens so frequently that nothing is more common, as is evident from experience.

<margin>
On this subject, Plutarch [wrote] much in his book *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*.
</margin>
Indeed, some were led by the reasoning that because they were seen in the air, sometimes in one place, and often lingered for many centuries, but eventually vanished and betook themselves elsewhere to destroy and drive other men mad, the ancients thought they were mortal. Hesiod himself testifies to this when he says that the goddess-nymphs complete ten times the life of a phoenix, a span which would extend to 9,720 years. Antiquity seems to have been saying the same thing when it called them <term>hamadryad nymphs</term> <note>original Greek: νύμφας ἀμαδρυάδας; nymphs whose lives were tied to specific trees.</note>, that is, Nymphs equal in age to an oak. Because these false beings are of a lowly nature, they cannot be corrupted in terms of their essence, for they suffer nothing contrary to it. What, then, was the reason that antiquity felt so variously about them, such that they agreed on nothing less than on those "gods" who were made out of demons? It was the craftiness of that scoundrel <note>Referring to Satan.</note>, drawing clouds over the minds of mortals so that they might be held in perpetual error. So that nothing would be firm or stable, he moved from one place to another, alluring new men to himself with new atrocities, until he turned all away from the knowledge of the First Cause. He thrust himself into the place of God in the statues of things, animals, and wicked men, until the one Truth—which alone was capable of this in a world initiated into the true sacred mysteries—blunted his efforts. Because of those changes, some thought they did not exist because they had not seen them; to others, they seemed to have died when they left a place; to some, one was true and another false. Thus, nowhere has a lie been more frequent than under the influence of the Author of Lies. For what wonder is it that many felt such varied things about the most inconstant of all matters, when the truth is called into doubt by many, no faith is given to the senses, the testimony of others is treated like a dream, and many hold the authority of the wise in the same regard as that of fools and children? They are moved by no consensus of the world, and some wish their own judgment of things to be preferred over the whole universe. If they hallucinate regarding the most certain things, what wonder is it that they are deceived in things doubtful and obscure? But although those whom persistence drives sideways cannot be conquered by any arguments, I shall nevertheless bring forward the consensus of all nations regarding this nature of substances. Thus, those who refuse to stand by the judgment of divine men and those clearly skilled in all things may at least receive those things which our ancestors, taught by experience, believed.

[...corrup]tion, or fear of vice, or from doubt, it is necessary that before a law is established, there must exist in the nature of things that which is sinned against, that which sins, and that which is doubted. Therefore, these filthy acts were known in all affairs; evil deeds <note>original: "maleficia," often specifically referring to harmful magic or sorcery</note> were known; and it was established that such crimes were not rooted in human virtue. For otherwise, something very similar would have been seen throughout all of human nature. It was certain that these powers were summoned by the will of worthless men, by which harm was brought upon other people. Hence that provision in the first chapters of the Roman laws: *If anyone shall have enchanted the crops, or harmed them, let there be a penalty.* <note>Postel refers to the Law of the Twelve Tables, the ancient foundation of Roman law.</note> This very law was held as valid even many centuries later and confirmed by other laws; it would not have been done otherwise, unless the things had truly existed. I do not wish to touch upon how civil law treats these matters, lest I be too wordy; those things are open for all to see. In religious and sacred law, how frequent is the mention and prohibition of these things? Since laws do not belong to just one or two people, it is established that they are set down and approved by the consensus of all—both in all states, and especially in a popular and democratic state, where nothing was held as valid without the vote of the whole community. It is necessary, therefore, that there were and are separate substances <note>A technical term in Scholastic philosophy for beings without physical bodies, such as angels or demons.</note> and evildoers, by whose work worthless men undermined the Republic with unusual crimes. From that vice (since it was placed in the will of men to commit or neglect it) laws were born, which would both prohibit evil deeds and establish punishments for those daring to perpetrate such crimes. Indeed, of all the opinions held regarding things, nothing is so exactly weighed as a law, which is usually established not by a private citizen, nor by a single authority, but is weighed by the highest and wisest magistrate. I am referring to those laws in which there is no dealing with the confirmation of a single person's authority, nor with begging or the trading of money—laws where princes set rules for themselves by their own authority and compel even unwilling citizens to obey their decrees—but rather those matters in which a remedy is sought for the diseases that have arisen in the Republic. For the decrees of all administrations agree on this. To this is added that poets especially, historians, philosophers, and in short every kind of discipline-handler, have made mention in their writings of deceptions, enchantments, theurgy, magic, geomancy, hydromancy, pyromancy, aeromancy, fortune-telling <note>Postel lists various "manties" or divinations: geomancy (earth), hydromancy (water), pyromancy (fire), and aeromancy (air).</note>, and the demons from which all these things proceed. Surely this could never have happened unless the things existed for which names were invented and accepted by usage.

<margin>By the consensus of the common people and nations.</margin>

9 For since our notions depend on the object, it is necessary that the things themselves and the notion of them exist before the words. And yet, there is no language, whether barbarous or more eloquent, that does not have these names for demons and evildoers derived from the things themselves. From this it is established by the common consensus of all that the things themselves exist about which these words survive, and that separate substances gave origin to these things. They are, therefore, in the nature of things. It must not be omitted that in any religion—whether Mosaic, Christian, Muhammadan, or Indian—that type of man, so ruinous to others, is even now daily sought out for death and punished. In this matter, it could not happen that men bound by the most diverse human laws would agree, unless it were made known to all by nature, and they certainly recognized it to be a real thing.
