It is established that crimes have been admitted; witnesses agree; suspicion is firm; they acknowledge their offenses; they all agree in describing the mysteries. What more? It seems most certain because it is so. They are mostly unrefined and rustic people who endure these things. The demon seeks them out and more easily imposes upon their lack of sophistication. ### 55

Let us prove it to our own eyes. Thus, I begin first with the affairs of the Romans. Where effects are seen, even if the cause is hidden from us, it is necessary that we place a cause before the effects themselves. For nothing procreates itself. Does not that which presents itself to everyone’s eyes and moves by its own will necessarily exist? Is it not written in the Roman annals that during the consulship of Lucius Scipio and Caius Norbanus <note>83 BCE, during the Roman civil wars.</note>, between Capua and the Volturno river, a massive sound of standards and a horrendous clashing of arms was heard? And lest these be thought errors of hearing, opposing battle lines clashing were even presented to people's eyes for several days. Nor was that enough; so that the miracle would not lack the testimony of the senses of hearing and sight, or be held as uncertain, the sense of touch was added. For to those considering the miracle from within, footprints of men and horses appeared; and what could provide proof even to the incredulous, not only the grass but even the shrubs were trampled. All these things were deservedly shown by the demons whom the Romans worshipped; since they could not turn away the calamity they had begun, they were able to foretell it, and they fulfilled it among impious men. For a hundred thousand men were lost at that time in the civil war and the proscriptions of Sylla and Marius.

But perhaps those things, seen only once, do not prove that there are separate substances <note>term: "separate substances" (substantiae separatae) refers to beings that exist without material bodies, such as angels or demons.</note>. It must be confirmed by other examples. In the Antonine War, the same appearance was seen in Rome for a long time. When Pompey was killed in Egypt, the same clamor and crash so terrified the people of Antioch that they twice ran to arms at night. What could have been the cause of that roaring which seemed to be carried from the center of the earth into the sky during the consulship of Marcus Antonius and Aulus Posthumus? Are not your gods, O Romans (I address you, while excepting the good), even today the same? For it is established that in Italy there are and always have been many men similar to the "divine" <note>original: "δἰω" (diō), likely a Greek-inflected reference to the nickname given to the philosopher.</note> Pomponazzi <note>Pietro Pomponazzi (1462–1525), a philosopher who famously argued that the immortality of the soul could not be proven by reason, which Postel views as a dangerous heresy.</note>, who argued that there are no separate substances, and by perverting the sayings of philosophers, tried to persuade the Pope—who was greedy for novelty—of the mortality of souls. 

O Rome, how you are never without monsters! What of the serpents that glided into so many places and immediately vanished? Are they not illusions and images most like to foul demons? What of that fire, the harbinger of calamities, which was often seen to burn up the earth and sky, and to be carried from the west to the east and back again? Are these things done by natural and elemental labor? Certainly, if they proceeded from there, they would be fixed and firm like other things. 

There are innumerable things of this kind in the annals. I do not wish to touch upon the impostures of your false religion. For religions were introduced so craftily by you that after human labor was added to them, nothing certain could be held. However, the history of the Mother of the Gods from Pessinus <note>The goddess Cybele, whose sacred stone was brought to Rome in 204 BCE.</note> and the serpent of Aesculapius <note>The god of healing, brought to Rome in the form of a serpent to end a plague.</note> seems to contain actual events, which certainly could not have happened without the work of a demon. A swan could not be captured by human hands (though it could be seen by everyone) even when a large circle of people surrounded and watched it in the temple of Minerva. Thus, although the stories of Numa’s Egeria, the Proculus of Romulus, and other tricks were wisely devised to hold the minds of the foolish multitude, not all things in religions were similar. A demon spoke frequently in statues, temples, and animals; it even sometimes brought destruction so that it might be worshipped. For two whole days in the closed temple of Juno, an illusionist imitated the voice of an infant, so that the minds of the unrefined might be inflamed to worship. Why should I recall the injury inflicted on the Latin man <note>A reference to Titus Latinius, whom Jupiter allegedly punished for failing to report a dream about the Roman Games.</note> because he had not immediately revealed to the senate the procession of games usually held in the Circus Maximus? What does the foul nature of a demon not fabricate? Indeed, it commits crimes, and finally, when it seems to cure the very things it committed, it mocks and agitates the minds of men. If anyone wants more, let him read Julius Obsequens on prodigies, or Valerius Maximus on religion; he will see marvelous experiments regarding separate substances, of which, although their form is not seen, it is certainly established from their effects that they exist. Nor...

### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

For those phenomena occur either by human skill or by nature. For while natural events are fixed and usually happen in a single way, these others are illusions and mockeries <note>original: "praestigiae et ludibria"</note> proceeding from separate powers <note>The author refers to "separate powers" as spirits or demons existing apart from the physical body.</note>. All those natural things are grounded in universal experience, which is why they have earned our belief. In the past, these spiritual manifestations were seen; now, however, they are partly hidden or have vanished from these regions. It is well established by the preaching of the Word of God, which we have through Christ and in Christ, that many specters have disappeared. Truly, it remains a fact that in sparsely inhabited and mountainous places where Gospel preachers are rare, nothing is more common than sorcerers and evildoers <term>maleficis: practitioners of harmful magic or "maleficium"</term>, from whom innumerable disasters, calamities, and diseases proceed.

<margin>
Sometimes demons and their attendants also play together.
</margin>

When these people are caught, they cannot deny it; many admit their crimes of their own accord, and by withdrawing themselves from such a foul power, they end their lives through punishment without regret. If anyone does not agree with me, let them read what Giovanni Francesco Pico <note>original: "Ioannes Franciscus Picus"</note>, the Count of Concordia, wrote about these substances and their effects—based both on what he diligently observed himself and whatever he had read in written records. He did this to try to persuade many stubborn men who, hanging onto their bodily senses like cattle, otherwise give little credit to such opinions; he also sought to show how hard he had worked to uncover that obscurity of nature. Whoever reads that book which he titled *On Witches* <note>original: "de Strigibus"</note> will undoubtedly be satisfied in a wonderful way. I do not wish to bring forward the craft and the dire dangers of all those vanities which it is known once flourished in Toledo <note>Toledo, Spain, was famously associated with schools of magic and the occult in medieval lore.</note>, since they are very well known and originated from the plague of the Moors. Every day, people infected with that stain are caught around the slopes of the Pyrenees mountains and are usually given over to the avenging flames. Who in France has not heard of the "Gap Incident" <note>original: "Vapinense facinus," likely referring to a well-known contemporary report of demonic devastation in the region of Gap in the French Alps.</note>? The mountains driven upward and forward, the vineyards moved from their places, the meadows, the trees—in short, the entire surface of the soil—testify to and prove the crime of unspeakable spirits. This became known in the most famous courts; the wretched owners of the lands, now beggars, point it out. Nothing is more recent than that miracle, and nothing more certain. I do not wish to bring into the open how many substances of this kind are removed from possessed bodies every year by the command of the Lord, both in many other places and especially at the Column in Rome <note>Likely referring to the Column of the Flagellation in the Basilica of Saint Praxedes, a site associated with exorcisms and relics.</note>. If one goes to the sacred house of Philip the Sicilian, the same thing will clearly be seen. But these are our matters, and they ought not to be believed by the ungodly, even if they were seen a thousand times.

11 Now let us come to foreign nations which lack the light of the Gospel. In no part of the world is there not the greatest familiarity of certain people with those spirits. In many places, foul figures with airy bodies present themselves to everyone's sight of their own accord. What is more common in India than enchanters? No ship sets sail without a man skilled in magic; so that if a loss must be made, or has been made by anyone else, as soon as he is asked, he points out the place in the waters and recovers the things through divers. The people who live in America at nearly the 50th degree of latitude—among whom Magellan lived familiarly for almost six months while he was circumnavigating the globe—see specters of horrendous demons and call them "Setebos." A barbarian giant captured by Magellan himself revealed their horrendous appearance by signs and painting when he could not do so with words, on this occasion: while they were waiting for a more favorable breeze, they were busy trying to instill the principles of religion into that giant. For nature acts by a continuous, uninterrupted motion; those spirits act by both <note>presumably meaning both continuous and sudden motion</note> because they move by their own will.

Now, who could enumerate what happens in the northern regions? In Iceland—which antiquity seems to have been ignorant of—the effects of this "separate power" <note>A philosophical term for a spirit existing independently of a physical body.</note> are so great that no one is able to recount them all. Near the mountains that burn with perpetual fires in the manner of Mount Etna, specters offer themselves so frequently that nothing is more familiar; nor, until they vanish, would you believe they were specters. In the northern part of the island, there is a kind of ice from which miserable groans are heard; if you should try to carry away even a small piece of it from there, you would waste your effort. For it eludes the senses once you touch it. Huge rocks, torn from the mountains with violent force—which no human strength could move—are seen being carried through the air and driven from place to place. By what forces this is done cannot be grasped, unless by the intellect. These things agree with what Demetrius the Briton said in Plutarch's writings concerning the islands nearest to Britain. Ziegler <note>Jacob Ziegler, a German geographer.</note>, a man of singular knowledge in all things and absolute mastery of mathematics, records this; the authors are the Gothic brothers Johannes and Olaus <note>Johannes and Olaus Magnus, Swedish archbishops and historians.</note>, expelled from their own borders—the former being the most distinguished Archbishop of Uppsala, the latter driven from his ample possessions.

Truly, who could list the things done by impure substances in that part of the world closest to the Pole? Sometimes for two days, sometimes three, or even for a month, a specter offers itself like a servant; you would not recognize it for what it is until it disappears. Indeed, the familiarity with some of them is so great that they obey the nods of many people. Scarcely any of the Lapps <note>The Sámi people of northern Scandinavia.</note> are not powerful in magic songs, so much so that they can stop and sink ships if they choose. The authors are Ziegler and the Goths already named, to whom is added the testimony of Stella and the ambassadors of the Muscovites.

Wherever, therefore, the power of the Gospel has not been perceived, there these pests reign, and they come forth more frequently from caves and dens, just as antiquity seems to have believed. Hence it was said that the power of the oracles (which they knew had truly existed in many places) proceeded from the earth itself. This is still evident today in many places, and especially in the gold mines where one must go very deep into the earth. Johannes Agricola <note>Likely Georgius Agricola, the "father of mineralogy," though Postel writes "Ioan."</note>, a man most worthy of trust, narrates in his book *On Metals* that the mines of Bohemia, which are the most famous in all Germany, have frequent miracles of demons, and that their nature is varied. For in some mines there are malicious spirits who frequently suffocate and kill men; in others, they are even accustomed to prepare the works of various kinds. Thus, when those whose job it is to follow the vein have left the spot, they not infrequently find more dug out on a holiday night than they could have excavated in a whole week. Concerning these various kinds of spirits, see the letter of Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius, a famous abbot and occult scholar.</note>, the greatest investigator of magic, to the Emperor Maximilian. Regarding those things which happen near Sicily, if I were to bring forward anything by speaking of the underworld, I would render myself liable to the laughter of the impious; therefore, I let it pass. For it is well enough established that there are "separate substances" <note>spirits</note> in the nature of things, which is evident everywhere in houses and families. See what Alexander ab Alexandro <note>A Neapolitan jurist and author of *Genialium Dierum*.</note> writes...

### ON THE NATURE OF DEMONS AND ANGELS,
#### *and on magi and prophets, and the difference between them.* CHAPTER VIII.

**From** the preceding demonstration, philosophers are compelled to admit that those natures which we call **separate substances** <note>A philosophical term for beings existing without physical bodies, such as angels or spirits.</note>—some call them demons, others gods, and some call them angels—not only exist in the nature of things, but also differ significantly in kind. Pythagoras called the evil ones *subterranean* <note>original: καταχθονίους (*katachthonious*)</note> and the good ones *gods* <note>original: θεούς (*theous*)</note>, performing sacred rites to both: to the latter so they might be of benefit, and to the former so they might not do harm. The Latins also called the evil ones *veioves* <note>A Roman term for "adverse gods" or deities that could cause harm if not appeased.</note>, as if they were "adverse gods," and by another Greek name they were usually called *averters* <note>original: αποτροπαίους (*apotropaious*), referring to spirits that turn away evil.</note>. For the time being, I do not wish to descend into that arena to discuss the gods in general who were born from human merit; since these often exist by opinion and deception rather than the nature of things, they should be rejected in their proper place. We must discuss those who truly exist in the nature of things. Moreover, although among the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, who focused on physical and logical observation.</note> no distinction is handed down between these natures (which they thought were most simple), they are not therefore lacking in difference just because they did not write about them. For many things were hidden from them which posterity has most clearly known and proved, as was handed down in the preceding chapter.

That nature must be considered from its very origin. Just as our mind is endowed with the **freedom of choice** <note>original: "arbitrij libertate"</note>, so that it may act in either direction by deliberation and not by necessity; so it must be believed of those substances which are of a higher grade and devoid of body. For otherwise, the most excellent gifts of essence and thought would be lacking in the most perfect natures, which is not to be admitted. For nothing above this elemental mass is oppressed by servitude; all things are free. Therefore, it is certain that they can both use and abuse their power and liberty. That some have abused it, and abuse it daily, is shown by the laws that prohibit commerce with them as evil beings. Therefore, some are altogether evil and destructive, as has been demonstrated.

But since all things were created as the best by God, and if any are evil, they are so because of their own liberty or from the corruption and flux of matter, it is clear that they fell by their own choice from the prescription of divine goodness, and perverted their excellent nature through change. Since philosophy cannot grasp those reasons, yet the facts clearly appear to exist in the nature of things, it is necessary that it reach out its hand to religion. For in matters which are seen to exist by their effect, when the human eye cannot reach their nature through reason, one must acquiesce to **divine revelation**, which does not conflict with the nature of things.

Therefore, after all the most excellent things (as was possible through the condition of things) were established by the **first mover** <note>The philosophical term for God as the ultimate cause of motion in the universe.</note>, and since in those natures which cannot admit bodily sins into themselves—which were the most excellent—there appears a blatant wickedness harmful to man, it is necessary that they turned away from their beginning and nobility by some crime, and admitted into themselves the greatest vice, than which there is none greater. Thence (as is the nature of misery and envy), they strive to make men most like themselves and lost.

But what was said from the beginning must be repeated here from a higher principle. It is conceded by all philosophers worthy of the name that this entire temple of nature, which pertains to the parts subject to the senses, was established for some cause and is preserved in being; and man, truly, for the sake of God. Since the highest happiness is in knowledge, after this darkness, it is rightly believed that **eternal life** is to know God. For otherwise man (even if he enjoyed the most abundant use of these things) would be most unhappy if he lacked his purpose after so many exhausted labors. And God would be insufficiently wise, having wished to prepare so many and such great things for the sake of an eternal nothingness. He would surely be far inferior to spiders, which so diligently craft webs for the hunting of flies, if He had prepared such great things for the sake of a laborious life (and one more afflicted the better it is), yet wished it to be endowed only with present miseries. He would be not only unjust, but inept.

He concludes that human life must have a higher purpose in knowing God, or else the Creator would be less purposeful than a common spider.</summary>

<meta>catchword: soul</meta>

It does not align with human sentiment to suggest that God is unjust, unwise, or evil; much less does it align with the divine nature. Therefore, He created this entire universe—encompassed both by the perception of the eyes and the understanding of the mind—for His own sake, and for the sake of His own recognition and honor. Yet, since God Himself lacks nothing, is abundantly happy, the arbiter of the universe, and is so absolute that He cannot become greater or happier by the addition of our industry, what could we possibly believe man and his mind might offer Him? What could He take pleasure in that lies within our power? This is a harsh and difficult question, but one that must be resolved through the practical experience of this life. The appetite placed by nature in every individual, and that which is expected by everyone from human works according to necessity and utility, is **glory, honor, and renown**. For we see this naturally in every class of men—and all the more so in those who are more powerful and less in need of material things—that they are seized by a great greed for praise and glory, and they seek honors most earnestly. This does not actually add to their perfection, but it represents the loyalty of the men subject to them. By these "stings of glory," men are incited to take up virtue (which is otherwise difficult), so that, urged on by those little sparks, they may eventually undergo labors for the sake of virtue of their own accord, and return the prize of true praise to God. For our own glory is fragile and fleeting; quite often, when we busy ourselves with ascribing it to ourselves, we undergo infamy in its place. 

That honor ought to be referred back to its original causes—and yet those causes are not "needy" simply because they wish glory to be preserved for them—is manifest in us, who are composed of this fleeting matter. How much more, then, since we can honor, deserve, or know Him by no other means, must we ascribe all things to God, and refer the received use of both ourselves and external things back to Him? **Honor and the knowledge of God**, therefore, is the end of life. For wretched mortality can prove itself to God in no other way than when it places itself in the position of a son, and other men in the position of brothers, and acknowledges God as the Parent, whom it should love, praise, celebrate, cherish, and adore for these gifts. Since it is certain that solid honor is owed to God alone, the parent of all things, in exchange for the use of this life—and since He can be acknowledged by no other gift from us than when we fear Him as the most powerful, love Him supremely as the supreme good, cherish Him as a parent, and adore Him as the King of all kings—we must certainly acknowledge ourselves as guilty of ingratitude and violated trust if we do not return these things to Him. 

What punishment, then, shall we judge ourselves worthy of, when we not only neglect to acknowledge Him, but even busy ourselves with ascribing entirely to ourselves that one thing which we owe to Him? Would not any prince deservedly sentence to the ultimate punishment one who, despising the prince, claimed the ornaments of majesty for himself? For it is by that one thing above all others that sacred majesty is held. This is also evident by the logic of analogy. Since holy Providence wishes no return from a creature except for honor, love, and fear, it follows that even the **separate substances** <note>A term for angels or spirits who exist without physical bodies.</note>—who behold all things without the aid of a body and marvel at them in the Creator—were brought forth for this same duty of praise and honor, and were able to do so freely and not by compulsion. Therefore, in that one thing alone can they fail their Creator: if they attempt to ascribe to themselves that which they most especially owe. For since they are simple intelligences, lacking the aid of a body, they cannot trespass so gravely in any matter as when they proudly ascribe to themselves what is owed to God. 

That the demons committed this very act must be admitted by reason and held by religion. For when a great multitude of them saw the gifts given to them and that they had been endowed with freedom, they wished to ascribe their perfection to themselves; thus they fell from their rank and were cast down from the celestial region into the midst of these elements, becoming wicked demons. There, they are very frequently seen through their effects. For they mingle with lightnings, they are wrapped in the winds, they vex the seas, they besiege men, they bring infamy to houses, and they enchant, harm, and destroy crops either by themselves or through the instruments of wicked men. They oppose the efforts of men striving toward piety for this reason: so that there might not be...

These thoughts do not occur to the human sense—even one that is unfair, unwise, or evil—that God could be anything but good; much less so to the divine sense. Therefore, He created this entire universe, understood as much by the sight of the eyes as by the intellect, for His own sake, and for the sake of His own recognition and honor. But since God Himself lacks nothing, is abundantly happy, the judge of the universe, and cannot be made more perfect, greater, or happier by the addition of our hard work, what can we believe man and his mind can offer Him—something by which He might be captured or delighted—that is placed within our power? This is a harsh and difficult question, but one that must be resolved by the practical experience of this life.

The desire placed by nature in every individual, which is expected by all from human works according to necessity and utility, is glory, honor, and renown. For we see this naturally in every kind of person—and all the more so in those who are more powerful and less in need of material things—that they are captured by the greatest greed for praise and glory, and they seek honors above all else. This does not, in fact, add perfection to them, but it represents the loyalty <note>Original: "fidem." In this context, it refers to the bond of trust or submission between a subject and a superior.</note> of the people who are beholden to them. By these "stings of glory" they are incited toward virtue, which is otherwise difficult to embrace, so that, spurred on by those little fires, they may finally undergo labors for the sake of virtue of their own accord, and return the reward of true praise to God. This is necessary because our own glory is fragile and fleeting, and not infrequently, when we busy ourselves with claiming it for ourselves, we undergo infamy in its place. 

Therefore, it is manifest in us—who are composed of this fleeting matter—that honor ought to be referred back to its original causes; yet those causes are not "needy" simply because they wish glory to be reserved for them. How much more, then, since we can honor, deserve well of, or know Him by no other means, must we attribute everything to God, and refer back to Him the usage we have received of both ourselves and external things? Therefore, the honor and knowledge of God is the **end of life** <note>The "ultimate purpose" or "final cause" in Aristotelian terms.</note>. For miserable mortality can prove itself to God in no other way than while it places itself in the position of a child, and other men in the position of brothers, and recognizes God as the Parent, whom it should love, praise, celebrate, worship, and adore for these gifts. 

Since it is clear that solid honor is owed to God alone, the parent of all things, for the use of this life, and since He can be acknowledged by us by no other gift than when we fear Him as the most powerful, love Him supremely as the highest good, worship Him as a parent, and adore Him as the King of Kings, we must certainly recognize ourselves as rightly guilty of ingratitude and violated faith if we do not return these things to Him. What great punishment, then, shall we judge ourselves worthy of when we not only neglect to recognize Him, but busy ourselves with attributing to ourselves the one thing we owe to Him? Would not any prince rightly sentence to the ultimate punishment a man who, despising the prince, claimed the ornaments of majesty for himself—especially since majesty is held sacred primarily for that one reason?

This is also evident from the principle of **analogy** <note>Original: "analogię ratione." Postel is arguing that what is true for human kings and subjects is even more true for God and his creation.</note>. Since holy providence wishes for nothing to be paid back to it by any gift of the creature except honor, love, and fear, it follows that even the **separate substances** <term>Separate substances<note>Angels and demons; beings that exist without physical bodies.</note></term>—who behold all things without the aid of a body and admire them in the Creator—were brought forth for this same duty of praise and honor, and are able to do so freely and not by compulsion. Therefore, in that one thing alone can they fail their Creator: if they attempt to attribute to themselves that which they most especially owe. For since they are simple intelligences, lacking the assistance of a body, they cannot trespass so gravely in any other matter as when they proudly attribute to themselves what is owed to God. 

That the demons committed this very act must be admitted by reason and held by religion. For when a great multitude of them saw the gifts given to them and that they had been gifted with freedom, wishing to attribute their perfection to themselves, they fell from their rank. They were driven out from the celestial region into these elements <note>The "elements" here refers to the sublunary or earthly realm (earth, water, air, fire) where humans live.</note> and became wicked demons; here they are most frequently seen through their effects. For they mingle with lightning, are wrapped in the winds, harass the seas, beset men, bring infamy to houses, and—either by themselves or through the instruments of malicious people—they enchant, harm, and destroy crops. They oppose the efforts of men striving toward piety for this reason: so that men may not possess the...

<summary>Postel argues that the purpose of human and angelic life is to return honor and glory to God. He explains the fall of demons as a result of their prideful attempt to claim this divine honor for themselves, leading to their exile in the earthly realm where they now cause natural and spiritual harm.</summary>

## ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...a more fortunate soul, which is able to approach heaven, from which the others are eternally exiled and cast down. Therefore, those spirits <note>Original: "daemones." In the Renaissance, this term often referred to spirits generally, not just "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note> who were created by God as a single kind have been divided into two parts: into <term>εὐδαίμονας</term> <gloss>good spirits</gloss> and <term>κακοδαίμονας</term> <gloss>evil spirits</gloss>, whom we call good and bad angels. It is necessary to confess these things based on what is conceded (since we see them by their effects) and to investigate their nature by the same reasoning. We see from the writings of Proclus, Iamblichus, Hermes <note>Postel refers to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure thought to be a contemporary of Moses and a source of ancient wisdom.</note>, and others, that there are indeed two kinds, and that the good are distinguished by a three-times-triple difference. For there are nine orders of angels, or of gods (as Proclus and Porphyry <note>Neoplatonic philosophers who organized spiritual hierarchies.</note> call them), or if we prefer, of good spirits. They teach that the first orders receive the light of the intellect from nowhere else but God; the second receive it from these and pour it into others; while the lower orders only receive it. 

We must judge the same for their opposites, since they are found to have fallen from all those orders through their own pride, having denied God His honors. Furthermore, they are as much worse here as they were once of a more excellent condition. The mages <note>Scholars of ancient esoteric wisdom.</note> themselves admit this, binding individual types with specific names and sacred rites. There are, therefore, nine orders of evil demons (if "order" can exist in such ruined things), just as there are of angels. This very fact did not escape Virgil in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*, when he says: *And nine times the interflowing Styx hems them in.* <note>Aeneid 6.439. Postel interprets Virgil’s description of the underworld river Styx as a reference to nine ranks of demonic opposition.</note> For he says that nine orders of envy or hatred—that is, of demons—stand in the way of those who have departed from life without the Emperor’s command, preventing them from escaping. For he who commits suicide, since he could not commit a more monstrous crime, is rightly believed to be possessed by the entire cohort. 

Although it has been sufficiently proven by demonstration that there are diverse kinds of demons—because their effects fall under the senses—concerning the good ones (whom they call gods, heroes, or spirits), let it be agreed among everyone. To confirm the recognition of the evil ones, I shall bring forward a most ancient witness, Hermes Trismegistus, who flourished shortly after Moses and was regarded as a god. His words from the ninth dialogue of the *Pymander* are as follows:

> The Mind conceives all notions—good ones indeed, whenever seed is poured in from God; but the contrary, when seeds are cast into the soul by certain demons. Truly, no part of the lower world is devoid of the presence of evil demons. Finally, a demon, creeping into a human being, scatters the seeds of his own operation; the mind, splashed with these adulterous seeds and made pregnant, gives birth to adulteries, lusts, homicides, parricides, sacrileges, thefts, impiety, the overthrows of cities, provinces, and kingdoms, plagues of men, and all other evils. These are the works of a wicked kind, snatching the spirits, heroes, demons, and souls subjected to them either more sublimely toward heavenly things or more deeply toward plagues, according to their nature.

From this it is clear that demons, although they surpass our souls in intelligence, are nevertheless of two kinds. For it is certain that some bind us to lordship over matter, while others pull us upward, snatching us toward heavenly things more sublimely, or more deeply toward the lower, according to the nature of their appetite and our own. Therefore, those who make the noble nature of the soul cling to flowing and falling things (since its origin, nature, and end are heavenly, implanted in it by the divine nature) cannot be anything but wicked and depraved. This is because the study of all laws, all attempts at religion, the prescriptions of philosophers, our natural inclination, the innate love of knowing the truth within us, and the natural thought of God all call us upward and summon us away from earthly things. Therefore, those who wrote about magic and sacrifices handed down the distinct orders of the lower powers, just as they did the higher. For this reason, our Paul rightly called them the "princes and rulers of this darkness," and the "powers of the world," with whom we have a struggle; they can be conquered by no other power than the "shield of faith." <note>A reference to Ephesians 6:12-16.</note> Just as the highest order of angels, who are called Cherubim, Seraphim, and Thrones, contemplate the inaccessible light and receive from it their purification,

He highlights that evil spirits fell from these same orders due to pride and now influence human vice.</summary>

### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I, PAGE 61

...[perfection], light, and the completion of all good, happiness, virtue, and knowledge: so it is necessary that those who fell from that kind by their own choice must dwell in the greatest darkness, wickedness, unhappiness, vice, and ignorance of themselves. For a thing becomes so much worse as it has changed into the opposite from a more sublime nature. This same comparison finally claims its place even in the second and third ranks. Since, indeed, every natural thing consists in action, it is necessary that these <term>separated substances</term> <note>Postel uses this term to refer to spirits—beings that exist without physical bodies.</note> act upon certain subjects, and thus they act upon mortal souls, either directly or indirectly, according to whether their lot is good or unjust. Those who are moved by the good spirits, with the power of the unjust ones driven away, are in a happy state and are useful to the commonwealth. They recognize God everywhere and are masters of themselves. The opposite happens to those possessed by the impure company of demons. For they do all things for their own ruin, the overthrow of their brothers, for the destruction of public utility, and to the disgrace of God.

<margin>These things are also in the book of the Shepherd, or "Concerning the Two Ways." <note>Refers to the *Shepherd of Hermas*, a popular early Christian text that describes two angels accompanying every person.</note></margin>
But these things are common to the whole human race: to have two different companions for the entire duration of life, by which the freedom of our soul is incited. For no one will strive unless he has competed legitimately. It happens indeed, by a similarity of life, that more than one spirit from the two orders may be present to a person. From this, many are powerful in divination, because the commerce of separated substances intimately works its way into the soul, so that by observing their movements, the soul may reveal those things which are above human capacity. Yet one must not descend into the opinion of Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher who wrote extensively on the nature of the soul and demons.</note>, who teaches that a body of this kind, by whose command admirable virtues are performed, no longer lives and acts from its own soul, but has life from a "divine particle" approaching it. For it is impossible for a man to be truly <term>informed</term> <gloss>given his essential form or life-force</gloss> by a demon. Hence no mage could ever truly raise the dead. A spirit often offers itself as a specter; otherwise, it clings to the soul and there reveals the future. Thus, in hope of our familiarity and of gaining our company, they perpetrate deeds surpassing human strength—good ones, if the inspiration was good: or conversely, if evil. In this they differ: those who approach by divine movement, and not merely by permission, can do all things, because they adhere to the First Cause <note>God.</note>. The evil ones can do only those things which serve for show, but not for the use or restoration of nature, except when they have first harmed or faked it. For those things which they commit, provided they have not taken life, they are able to restore; but life, whether taken away by them or lost by other means, they are never able to return.

<margin>Prophets and Sibyls.</margin>
Those who are divinely inspired, or who have surpassed the human condition through angelic company, are called **prophets** if they are men; if women, they are **Sibyls**. Those possessed or led by more wicked demons, if they have summoned them voluntarily, are usually called mages and sorcerers. If they suffer them unwillingly, they are called <term>energoumenoi</term> <note>From the Greek word for those "worked upon" or possessed by an outside force.</note> by our people for this reason: because the demon carries out his works in them as if using them as instruments. Therefore, when a demon is admitted into an unwilling person, it is accustomed to violently distress both the body and soul. This kind is frequently seen, and is expelled by exorcists by the power of the cross and the name of Christ.

<margin>The exorcists in the primitive Church were different from certain scoundrels today.</margin>
The first kind, using a spirit <note>Original: "daemone"</note> familiarly because of their innocence of life, is not in vice, because such a person never commands evil angels except to ensure they do no harm, and then only in the name of the most high God. For an angel does not obey another angel, except by the command and power of God. Therefore, prophets and divinely inspired men, in the name of God and through the ministry of angels, command the dire powers and force them to do what is commanded; they use the work of the good spirits to cure both bodies and souls—not at all for mere tricks, except when public utility demands it for the sake of the unfaithful, so that at last, even unwillingly, they are forced to believe these things have proceeded from God.

<margin>Josephus calls upon Jesus. <note>Likely a reference to the historian Flavius Josephus and his mentions of exorcism or the "Testimonium Flavianum."</note></margin>
Therefore, men have familiarity with separated substances either willing and knowing, or unwilling and ignorant. Those who are ignorant and unwilling, forced by the good spirits, break out into words not premeditated by themselves; some do this constantly, others occasionally, for the benefit of mortals. Such was the case with Saul while persecuting David, with Caiaphas speaking of Christ, and with that man who foretold the destruction of Jerusalem many years before, when he could not be moved from his cries even by torments. I would believe that the Sibyls suffered as willing but ignorant...

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I, PAGE 64

Ragged, filthy, needy, despised, alone, and most poor, you are able to cast down the power and majesty of laws with a single act. This is not, it is not a human power; behold, it is God! Thus you differ from ruined men—and even more so because in you dwells the whole fullness of divinity. While sustaining the form of a servant, you demonstrate both the office of a prophet and the majesty of God. Satan knew this after he saw the effects of it, and he used his own ministers to become **apes of divine works** <note>original: "simiæ diuinorũ operum"; this refers to the common medieval idea that the Devil mimics God's miracles with cheap tricks to deceive humanity.</note>, eventually preparing vengeance for that wicked nation. These same impious men (as Egypt has never lacked the deceits of demons) stood against Moses, the prophet of God, and rose up with false powers against the true ones. But at last, the inferior were conquered by the better, and they yielded to the divine will, acknowledging that there is a power of God greater than demons. For Satan does not conquer himself; it would be contrary to nature for anything natural to rise up against itself. From these outcomes, it is clear which demons are evil and which are good: from this, men who use <term>separated powers</term> <note>Spiritual forces or beings that exist apart from physical matter.</note> that exceed human effort can be distinguished. 

A wicked man and a demon, while playing tricks on the eyes with **illusions** <note>original: "præstigijs"; refers to magical deceptions or "sleight of hand" rather than true miracles.</note>, drive men mad with empty terrors, promise false and fleeting things, pursue vices, and persuade others toward virtue through the cunning of deception: he approves of virtue in word alone, but condemns it by his deeds. By God’s permission, he sends evils and plagues because of our crimes, or as a test. He wishes to be seen as a god, rejoices to be celebrated by the words of all, seeks to be praised, desires and snatches at empires, and subverts human affairs so that he may finally satisfy his own greed. But if this is not permitted, he seeks fame and immortality through his illusions. While **Simon the Samaritan** <note>Also known as Simon Magus, a practitioner of magic mentioned in the Book of Acts who later legends say tried to prove his divinity by flying in Rome.</note>, the "god" of Nero—a lid worthy of its pot—strove to seek the heavens, he was cast down by divine power through the prayers of Peter and Paul, and shortly after resigned his unhappy soul to its owner. 

<margin>
The Ecclesiastical Histories report this concerning Peter.
</margin>

All Rome is witness, Hegesippus is witness, Tertullian is witness, and Nero is witness: who for this reason did away with Peter and Paul. While Simon desired to procure eternal fame for himself, he achieved eternal death along with eternal infamy. What shall I say of **Apollonius**? <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker often compared to Jesus by pagan writers.</note> He preferred to lay hands on himself rather than fail to beg for a reputation of divinity. I say nothing of the others. For the most unhappy catastrophes closed the final act of their story. 

Between the good and the bad, there has arisen a certain clever, shifty kind of men. Such was the kind that gave origin to false religions, feigning and lying about divine conversations, and meanwhile devising tyrannies and violent empires. I will not speak of this now, but rather when I treat the origins of all religions. We are forced to recognize the distinction between separated powers from their effects—both in themselves and especially when men use their works. For the evil ones prepare and bring ruin both to themselves and to the spectators who believe them to be divine. The good ones, by their effect, direct both bodies and souls: then, they seek out, provide, and execute what they do for the safety of both. There is a need for minds to be most holy if they are to either command the evil spirits or be familiar with the good ones. For **wisdom does not enter into a malevolent soul** <note>A reference to the biblical Book of Wisdom 1:4.</note>, nor does any familiarity with divine spirits. Those who are willingly occupied by evil spirits seem to be upright in words and signs, and they fake virtue as much as they can. For they do not wish to betray themselves immediately, before they have enticed men under the pretext of honesty and extorted their faith. Thus, they conquer by forcing themselves upon others more frequently, and once men are conquered, they abuse them to their own destruction and the destruction of others. 

Through good powers, Divine Providence does not indeed create, but seems to rule these lower things—even if, by infinite virtue, it provides for everything, however small. By the command of God, the good spirits exhort us toward virtue and toward common and private utility by inspiring us; the evil ones, by His permission (so that they may exercise us), discourage us with false inspirations. When we pay too little diligent faith to good exhortations, angels show us the divine will through men, and confirm it with signs. For no prophet was ever certain without a sign or a sure prediction of the truth. Whence **Muhammad** <note>original: "Muhamedes"; Postel, though a scholar of Arabic, often polemicized against Islam as a "false religion."</note> is not a prophet, as he lacked both.

<summary>Postel distinguishes between genuine divine miracles and demonic illusions, citing the historical failures of Simon Magus and Apollonius of Tyana. He argues that true prophets are confirmed by beneficial signs and the promotion of virtue, whereas false religions and figures like Muhammad lack these divine proofs.</summary>

...and established by many of the greatest [powers]. Against these very ones—I mean humans and angels, and the commands of God—they oppose themselves by their own will as unjust powers, and they use the instruments of wicked men. From this, innumerable evils gush forth, while the causes themselves remain hidden. For the more pious someone is, the more ardently the demons press against him, lest he make progress, and they pervert him either by a poorly weighed opinion of the truth, or they drive him away by harms to the soul or body, both from all good things and especially from true piety toward God, knowledge of self, and love of neighbor. No mortal who has ever attempted to descend into himself can deny this. For there is no one who is not moved toward virtue itself by a certain natural motion, and who does not feel within himself the love of truth (which consists in the knowledge of one's self and of God). However, although we have **free will** <note>original: "liberum arbitrium"</note>, we can never execute those desires in such a way that we are not either entirely deprived of the very wish, or find many things lacking in it for a perfect completion. Therefore, a few things must be said by me regarding the nature of man.

### ON THE NATURE OF MAN. CHAPTER IX.

Even if now a huge multitude of people seems scattered across the whole world, and an innumerable number has inhabited the world from the first man down to our own memory, yet no man can deny that all have flowed from one single beginning, and being born of one parent, gradually passed into various regions. For the philosopher **Averroes** <note>original: "Abē reis"; referring to the 12th-century Andalusian polymath Ibn Rushd, whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to Renaissance philosophy.</note> testifies that they are of one origin, and says that the whole generation depends on the first man. Thus they name the lineage from the father anywhere among the nations, not from the mother, for those who are referred to a certain lineage. For if they were not from the same first parent and one beginning, without a doubt one of two absurdities would follow: either that God was superfluous, or that there are multiple kinds of men. For if He created more individuals of the same **form** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the essential nature or "blueprint" of a thing that makes it what it is.</note> beyond the manner later accustomed by nature, He expended superfluous effort, since it could happen otherwise by the order of nature. But if there are different forms, those would be seen; yet neither is to be admitted. For there is one form, namely humanity itself, with which all are endowed, nor have more been seen. God, indeed, never wished to lead what nature could do outside its limits. For it was enough to have created a man and a woman for natural propagation, and having instilled the appetite for procreation, to have left the care of posterity to them, as with the other living creatures. For just as in all other things procreated from seed and accustomed to being procreated, **unity necessarily preceded every number**, so also it must be confessed in the human race. Before every number, there is unity. For that reason, all are held by the same laws of nature; the same force of reason drives them, the same appetite incites them, the same goal urges them: by which it is most clear that they are held by the same nature and composition of both soul and body, and are always connected by the same **matter and form** <note>The two basic components of any being in Scholastic thought: "matter" is the physical substance, and "form" is the organizing principle.</note>. For it does not happen that figures and qualities ascribed to forms are commonly formed by another form. For a confusion of all species would occur, and the order of things would be overturned. 

But someone will object that heads are lacking to the **Blemmyes** <note>A legendary race of headless people described by ancient and medieval writers, said to have their faces on their chests.</note>, that some have a dog's head, others a pig's snout, some are "goat-women" and **satyrs**, others are **thong-feet** <note>original: "imantopodas"; a mythical race with long, strap-like legs.</note> or **crooked-feet** <note>original: "loripedes"</note>, and that kind of being. Since they seem to have human sense but a dissimilar figure, into what kind do you think they should be referred? You will learn by experience itself (I grant also that there are fabulous things, which I do not think are true, such as those handed down about the **Centaurs**). If they speak, if they gather thoughts, if they reason, if they remember, if they are held by a sense of religion, do not doubt that they are to be inscribed among men: otherwise it is established that they are an unknown genus of living creatures. Truly it can happen that the most perfect form and figure with which we have been endowed by the Creator is changed; and while lost men take the risk of that form through excessive license through various species, they procreate various monsters, which then go off into a lost kind and a dissimilar figure. Also by the work of unspeakable demons, seed being cut off from elsewhere and placed...

->DE ORBIS CONCORDIA<-

...in a natural place, and with proportionate heat, that certain types take their beginning is not alien to their nature. Furthermore, that nature itself can be altered by art, as far as shape is concerned, is supported by the most famous author Hippocrates in his books *On Airs, Waters, and Places*, speaking of the **Macrocephali** <note>literally "long-heads," a group Hippocrates claimed shaped their infants' skulls</note>. For such an opinion had prevailed among them—that it was noble to be born with an elongated head—that by the care of midwives and physicians, the soft heads of newborn infants were shaped into an oblong form, until nature, imitating art, began to produce such children as had previously been shaped by hand. A truly incredible thing, had it not been known by the whole world and written about by such an eminent man. 

That there are some of a cubit’s height <note>about 18 inches</note>, therefore called <term>Pygmies</term>, with swine-like snouts, heads sunk into their chests, narrow mouths, and prominent or hooked noses, or entirely flat-faced—all this could have been caused by art turning nature upside down. Just as by modern industry it has been achieved that fruits are born without seeds, though with a grace far inferior to natural ones. For they smell more of water than the nature of fruit. Therefore, variety of shape does nothing to change the essence, as long as the nature of the form remains in things and the innate power of reason flourishes. 

This human of ours seems to have been composed with the best constitution, whether you look at the gifts of the mind or the body, and so happily equipped to distinguish things to be avoided from things to be sought: as one whom divine power had shaped with a sacrosanct breath and adorned with judgment and the prudence of choosing; lest, while he wished to pursue those things which do not pertain to the end proposed for him, he should be the author of his own ruin. For alone out of so many natures of living beings, he is a sharer in reason and thought; by this alone he surpasses the beasts and is joined to God; through this he conjectures, argues, refutes, and concludes. Unless <term>philautia</term> <note>original: "φιλαυτία"; meaning excessive self-love or narcissism</note>, self-love, and ignorance, contempt for the First Cause, one’s own rashness and thoughtlessness—and added to these, the depravity of customs and the variety of opinions taking their origin from those first principles—had begun to twist and bend him in every direction, all humans would be as similar to one another in both reason and mind as each is to himself. 

From this it has happened that all good men, when they knew that man was born for the sake of man, were called gods to one another; whereas, on the contrary, one equipped with human opinions and worldly prudence is commonly said to be **a wolf to his fellow man** <note>original: "homo homini lupus," a proverb suggesting humans can be predatory toward one another</note>. Since, therefore, among other kinds of living creatures, no species rages against its own kind—all live uprightly within their own genus—as that famous man says: "only for man do the most evils come from man." 

Thus we see that what was most excellent by the gifts of nature has become the most ruinous of all. Nor does he bring destruction only to others, but also (which is itself against nature) he rejoices in his own miseries, of which he wishes to appear—and in truth exists as—the daily smith and craftsman. For it happens to him from the use of natural things that, just as he was nobler by condition from the Creator, so he has been made worse by the depravity of his own will. The more delicate the body of a thing was, the more its putrefaction corrupts the air. The finest vinegar comes from a similar wine without art; a fall in high places is fouler and greater than in a slender fortune. The foulest smells come from the most delicate foods. 

O miserable man, who have cast yourself down of your own accord, and seek yourself outside for so long, and become worse by the day. Therefore, hinting at these things, antiquity established several ages of man, according to the ratio of metals, which were especially hostile to a corrupted posterity. For the first was called the **Golden Age** and the second the **Silver Age**, though both are now lacking. Hence Homer says, "they themselves perished by their own recklessness," <note>original: "οἳ δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ ταῖς ἀταθαλíαισιν ὄλοντο"</note> and elsewhere, "Few children, indeed, are like their father; the majority are worse, and few are better than their father" <note>original: "παῦροι γάρ τοι παῖδες ὅμοιοι πατρὶ πέλονται, οἱ πλείονες κακíους παῦροι δ’έ τε πατρὸς ἀρεíους"</note>. Humans, he says, are the craftsmen of their own fortune. And few children are like their parents; more are worse, few are better. But if the newborn take something of contagion and temperament from their parents, as they certainly do (for it is the way of nature that the noble are born of the noble, and the fearful of the fearful), let no one wonder that humans have long since reached such a point of wickedness that nothing more can be added to it. Plato confirms these opinions in his *Alcibiades*, even citing those verses of Homer:

<meta>Continuity: Following the discussion of physical diversity among humans (like the Macrocephali and Pygmies), Postel now moves from the physical body to the internal state of the human soul. In vain, he says, do mortals placed in the midst of evils accuse the gods, when they are caught in their own miseries and even undergo evils worse than death of their own accord. From this, it is clear that some have entirely cast off their own nature and put on a contrary one, so much so that they do not even feel their own unhappiness. Others, though they feel it and attempt to look deep into themselves, acknowledge the disease but cannot heal themselves. Glory drags them one way, pleasure drives them off course, opinion besieges them on all sides, and invincible necessity presses upon them. By all these things, reason is toppled from the citadel of the mind and, against its own judgment, **yields the palm to the victors** <note>original: "porrigit uictoribus herbam" – a classical idiom meaning to admit defeat, literally "to reach out the grass" as a sign of surrender</note>. Since this stupor or depravity of nature dwells in every single mortal, and all agree in it, it must be that—just as they received right reason and the most perfect judgment from the Author in the first man—this noble gift was likewise endangered in that same man. For as all plants agree in having "living roots" <note>original: "viviradicibus," referring to cuttings or roots that propagate a plant's nature</note> that indicate disease, so, unless light from heaven shines anew, all agree in evil; thus, acknowledging themselves, they do what they do not wish. Others, even if they are swept away by depraved habit, still judge that they are acting badly, yet do not cease. But in this they differ: while both wander astray, the latter sins willingly, the former unwillingly. The **reins of human choice** <term>liberum arbitrium</term> <note>Postel uses the metaphor of a charioteer to describe the faculty of "free will" or "human choice"</note>, which was the one most excellent thing in man, are so poorly managed that they cannot be restored to wholeness except by Him who was the first Author. 

If indeed someone should say that this inclination toward the bad side and toward vanity is provided for the sake of virtue—which is placed upon a steep and difficult path—he would be saying something, but very little of the matter. For since it is pure liberty, there ought to be no reason to incline more toward one side than the other. This we see ourselves, when we choose one of two goods without any resistance, or when we avoid a greater evil. For in those cases there is no compulsion, nor any vehement inclination that urges us on because of a vain opinion, a bit of minor glory, or pleasures that undermine us. From this it is clear that we are all depraved, originating from a single source, and are hard-pressed by the power of demons. 

But how can it be that this plague with which we are infected reigns in all people and creeps further day by day, given that our soul is not "passed down" <note>original: "ex traduce" – referring to Traducianism, the theory that souls are generated by parents like plant cuttings, which Postel here rejects in favor of the soul being created directly by God</note> but "creeps into" our bodies from heaven? For from the soul, the power of choice is usually born, by which we are incited to noble deeds and flee their opposites. Truly, nothing can be solved more easily than this question. Let us assume a certain common principle upon which both sides agree. Neither nature nor art performs anything without an instrument so disposed that it is most fit for its functions; nature demonstrates this through certain laws. Nothing grows without the action of heat upon a moisture that is either radical <note>the innate, vital moisture of a living being</note> or accidental. These are, therefore, the instruments without which nature can do nothing. If these are out of proportion and depraved, excessive moisture will kill and cause rot; vehement heat will burn and consume the moisture. If they are less than is proper, it is necessary that everything suffers from wasting away. This, however, is not to be attributed to the impotence of nature, but to a flaw in the matter and the instrument. For if the seed is worthless or faulty, even a well-disposed instrument will not act upon it. Just as an axe fit for splitting wood will not act upon stones or metals, so it will not act upon those woods 
<margin>† which have turned into the nature of stone.</margin>
which have petrified, nor upon those that are faded and poorly solid. For it cannot split heaps of hay, wool, cotton, and the like, which are not bound together because of their softness. Three things, therefore, must be weighed in every action (so that nothing exists without the image and mystery of the **Trinity**): the Agent, the Instrument, and the Patient <note>the "Patient" is the object that receives the action</note>. The latter two must be disposed proportionally to the power of the agent. For if a most prudent prince lacks a soldier, he achieves nothing; if he has one unfit for carrying out affairs, the result is the same; if he has the best leader and soldier, but victory cannot be had because of the highest mountains, the strength and fortification of the place, or anything else, what, I ask, can he effect? Does he not therefore seem imperfect? The same logic applies to the blacksmith, the axe, and the material. For

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

No one, therefore, is imperfect simply because they cannot act with the blunt edge of a tool, or because they cannot cut a material that is harder than the tool itself. Thus, it happens that the very objection which seemed to work against us actually confirms our position most strongly. For since the **soul** <note>original: "animus"</note> is of celestial origin—or is at least carved from the **fifth element** <note>original: "quinto elemento" – also known as the 'quintessence' or ether, the celestial substance ancient philosophers believed made up the heavens, distinct from the four earthly elements</note> which has no contrary—it must be most perfect. Moreover, whatever is most perfect and celestial is equally present in everyone. 

From this, it is clear that the vice and the unfitness for receiving the soul's actions reside in our physical matter and our **lineage** <note>original: "traduce" – a reference to 'traducianism,' the theological idea that the soul or its corruption is passed down from parents to children like a physical trait</note>. This is no ordinary defect, as it almost forces us to act against the goal set before us (unless a divine power is present to restore us); meanwhile, other living creatures seem to avoid what is harmful and choose what is desirable more prudently than man himself. What animal anywhere has ever taken its own life through imprudence or vice? They set a limit to their nature out of necessity, not out of pleasure. 

But, good God, how many men has gluttony killed? How many has drunkenness consumed? How many has the use of lust made to live in a state of constant death? How many has the greed for possession cast into immense labors and dangers? How many has the desire for revenge and the irrational fulfillment of the will thrown into disgrace and a criminal death? What more can be said? Man fights with himself at every moment and seems to begrudge himself the happiness of living, while he arms himself with every skill for his own destruction. Therefore, our progeny is most wretchedly affected, following so poorly those things that would benefit it, and so unskilled regarding the future that while it thinks it is choosing a certain end, it invites its own ruin by those very choices. 

This is why many who look deep into themselves have been driven from life by a weariness of living, while others have been led to despair by the repentance of failed efforts. This is through no fault of that most noble **intellect** or the reason placed within us, but rather the stubbornness of the depraved human mass. For this reason, some judged that it was best not to be born at all, or to be abolished as quickly as possible—erring only in this one vice: they were ignorant of the purpose for which God had created man.

It also follows from our first principles that the intellect is not only unable to act upon depraved matter, but also upon that which is disturbed or not yet properly arranged. For suppose there is a skilled craftsman and an excellent tool, and the underlying material is not unfit to receive the action: if the proper position and resistance are lacking, the craftsman certainly cannot act. Just as a blacksmith would be unable to shape glowing iron in the air without an **anvil**, and as long as this is the case, he cannot work according to his art; so too with our body. Since it is nourished by the **vegetative or nutritive life** and moved by the **sensitive life** <note>Postel follows the Aristotelian hierarchy of souls: the vegetative (growth), the sensitive (senses/movement), and the intellective (reason)</note>, if anything in the nutrition is done wrongly, the senses must also act wrongly; and if the first does not act at all, the second lacks a place to act. 

Thus, if the vital and sensitive parts within us are perverted, or not yet fully developed, the intellect will not act at all, or it will act only slightly and imperfectly. This is why the action of the soul does not seem clear in children, the elderly, the delirious, or the foolish—not because the soul is absent or imperfect in itself, but because the instruments are damaged. For since we consist of a vital, sensitive, and intellective soul, the second does not act without the arrangement of the first, and the third does not act without the activity of these two. In the same proportion that the lower functions are made imperfect, the faculty of the higher one to act is diminished. 

We see this very thing in various subjects. For some children, by their excellent physical constitution, are immediately wiser than old men. If the intellect came to us only through habit and experience, as the **atheists** <note>original: "ἄθεοι" (atheoi) – those who live without God or deny divine providence</note> wish, it would be impossible for such a noble gift to exist in a child who lacks experience of things. Certainly, it cannot be denied that our life becomes more obedient to the intellect through use, and is, as it were, tamed and domesticated by reason itself. It is just as if a blade, through constant use, acted more readily upon the material, and the material itself, having been cut more frequently, immediately admitted the sword from every side without a great effort by the one wielding it. Thus we see that the elderly, through constant experience of things, are for the most part wiser than others. This is not because the intellect or reason increases within them, as the common people say, but because the vital and animal lives have been made more fit and more obedient to the mind’s 

**movements.** <note>catchword: motibus</note>

He uses the analogy of a blacksmith and an anvil to show how the mind's higher functions depend on a well-ordered physical and sensory foundation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument regarding the soul’s interaction with the physical body. In the previous page, he used the analogy of a craftsman hindered by poor tools. Here, he addresses the physician Galen's materialistic objections to the immortality of the soul, arguing that the soul's perceived failings are due to the body's "depraved" state rather than a flaw in the soul itself.</meta>

->GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.<-

...movements. Therefore, when the blood perishes in animals, life perishes and the soul departs, because the instrument of life has collapsed. And this is what can be answered to **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD) was a prominent Greek physician whose views dominated Western medical science for over a thousand years. He often linked mental states directly to physical health.</note> when he questions **Plato** and all those who wish to persuade us of the immortality of souls: why is it that when the blood flows away, the man dies? Certainly, if Galen had wished to investigate the nature of the mind <note>original: "animi"</note> and the soul <note>original: "animae"</note> as deeply and diligently as he examined the parts of the body, he would have undoubtedly seen that in his elementary matter there are no parts which have the power of judging, deliberating, and thinking about the end of things, and in short, of gathering and knowing all things, even those that are absent. He would have subscribed to **Aristotle** and antiquity rather than trying to devise something new and denying that reason exists within himself. 

For if the reason and intellect within us are assumed to come from the elements, it must be either by reason of matter or by reason of **temperament** <term>temperament: the balance of the four bodily humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) which ancient medicine believed determined a person's physical and mental state</term>. If it were from matter, then even the parts of the elements—rocks and metals—would also understand. If it were from temperament, then the more a brute beast approached the human condition, the more it would possess reason. But this is seen in none of them. Therefore, both premises are false. It is established, then, that the intellect comes from elsewhere and enters into all men from heaven. 

But Galen will object again, citing Aristotle (if he is indeed the author of that clumsy book *On Physiognomy* <note>original: "περὶ φυσιογνωμονίας" – a Greek treatise on how physical features reflect character, attributed to Aristotle in the Renaissance but now considered pseudo-Aristotelian</note>): the character of the soul follows the temperament of the body. Fair enough. The sensitive soul itself is affected by the passions of the body (as is clear in the books *On the Soul*) and as long as it is affected by its own disturbed order, it judges poorly or is affected in some other way. A drunkard, with his brain filled with fumes, becomes either cheerful or gloomy according to the nature of his temperament and the circumstance. I admit it. But what happens to him is not unlike lamps: which are nourished when oil is applied moderately, but when it is too much or withdrawn, the light vanishes. An ape suffers the same as a man. Therefore, it is not the mind or reason itself that is affected, but in a composite and depraved body, it performs its duty poorly—even according to Aristotle. 

However, that there is something in us above those things which proceed from temperament is most clearly proven by the fact that we judge against the senses of nature, even in the midst of passions. If this were not done by a different nature, it could not happen at all from the one that is entirely affected. For it is established by its own nature that a single sphere is moved by a single motion, and cannot be carried in different directions by a single action. Thus, no action of a single agent can take place unless the actor is focused on that thing. And yet, to be angry and to judge that one ought not to be angry are different things, which happen at one and the same moment. Therefore, they come from two principles that share nothing in common. For this reason, precepts against anger and the movements of the sensitive soul are given to us; which to this day would have been done in vain by wise and learned men and by laws. For if we consisted only of that soul common to the beasts, we could not be healed by precepts. 

Whence it is necessary to confess that immortal souls, always consistent with themselves, act within us, and the imperfection of the action does not stem from the soul. And it is established that the human race is altogether depraved, and that there is therefore no fault of dullness or slowness or imperfection in the soul itself. Although this is widely evident from what was said above, even the most unskilled—let alone philosophers—will grasp it by considering the end and goal of man.

## ON THE GOAL OF MAN IN THIS LIFE,
## *and how far it stands from the rule of duty.* CHAPTER X.

Not without reason did antiquity wish to celebrate the phrase "Know Thyself" <note>original: "τὸ γνῶθι σαυτὸν" – the famous Greek aphorism inscribed on the Temple of Apollo at Delphi</note> and to heap it with every kind of praise. For from the knowledge of oneself proceeds the entire rule of duty: just as from ignorance and neglect flows unhappiness and a heap of false opinions. But whoever said that, said it indeed: but he neither taught nor provided the means by which we might achieve it. Whence, although everyone has had it in their mouth, in actual effect and the practice of life, either no one or certainly very few—and those most happy—have possessed it...
