<meta>This page transitions from a critique of Galen’s materialism to a foundational philosophical definition of humanity. Postel moves from discussing the physical instruments of the soul to the Aristotelian "four causes" that define human existence, setting the stage for his argument on human purpose and divine accountability.</meta>

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...except for those whom providence has shaped and renewed again. For since to know truly and by demonstration is to know through the cause, unless one has known the causes of oneself, no one could ever descend into themselves so as to weigh for what end they were truly made. Or if perhaps some were able to know, no one was ever able or took enough pains to perform it, without always being many parasangs <note>A parasang is an ancient Persian unit of distance, roughly 3.5 miles; Postel uses it here to mean "leagues" or "a great distance."</note> distant from the true goal. Therefore, let us begin to know man from the causes themselves, and let us attempt to seek ourselves through these reasonings, not outside of them. We must propose here matters that are quite common, yet without which there is no place for greater things, and from which one may arrive at a great knowledge and demonstration of present nature. 

Of man, as of all other natural things, there are four causes: the original, two joined causes, and that which is toward the end. It has already been made clear in the preceding parts that all things were created by God the author, all things are ruled by Him, and preserved in being. Therefore, **Providence** is the **efficient cause** <term>efficient cause: the primary source of change or rest; the "agent" that brings something into being</term> of man. He has the joined causes in common with other composite things: **matter** and **form**; the former in common with other bodily things, the latter distinct and suited to the species. Now there remains the fourth, the most excellent of all, and without which the others would be in vain. For art and nature are accustomed to do all things for the sake of the **final cause** <term>final cause: the "end" or purpose for which a thing exists or is done</term>. 

Since in the whole nature of things nothing is more excellent than God, it is established that God is the end of man. But if some impious person denies this to me, I shall compel him either to admit it or to cast off human judgment. It is established that for things of different conditions, their ends are also different: those of more excellent things are more excellent, and those of lower things are lower. But in the lower world, nothing is more excellent than man. Therefore, nothing more excellent than his end can be given. Since truly nothing is greater than God, it is established that He is the end of man: so that He is the beginning and the end of all things, the efficient cause and the final cause—just as man himself is the primary cause and final goal of his own actions. The comparison differs in this: that God Himself is the goal in His own nature; but man—that is, man's utilities, which serve to preserve life for himself and his kind—are, or ought to be, the goal of his own works. 

Now from these things we can circumscribe a certain notion of man by definition. **Man is the most excellent animal of the whole world, endowed with intellect, soul, and body, made for the sake of God.** 

These things having been established, we must see by what means he may best prove himself to that final cause, or in what things, by exercising himself, he can perform those actions which are not useless toward that goal. For any craftsman, while he strives toward the end of his work, is usually extremely attentive to those things which lead to it. First, so that he may do all those things that look toward the end. Second, that he may not do useless things. Third, that he may not commit anything that fights against the utility and beauty <note>original: "decorem"</note> of the work. For he would deservedly be condemned for unskillfulness, and should return the expenses to the master and compensate for the loss of time, who would be so insane as not only to not act usefully and honorably toward the fixed goal, but would waste labor, time, and resources—not only uselessly, but in a way that is costly to himself, the master, and the object. To himself, shameful, useless, and harmful; to the master, unjust; to the object, which ought to have been a cause of duration, destructive. 

So man, placed in this life, endowed with soul and body, must, by attending to the goal, diligently take care lest he sin against his goal in those ways. By knowing and re-knowing himself, he must see that he does not wish some counterfeit work to be approved as legitimate before God. Let him consider how gravely he commits a fault when he is not satisfied with having wasted his effort and done no good, or having produced a useless and unjust work, but has thought the Lord so mindless and negligent <note>original: "supinum"</note> that He either would not see those things, or seeing them, would not disapprove and would neglect them. This deed is no less than the crime of treason <note>original: "violatae maiestatis scelere" — specifically the crime of lèse-majesté or offending the dignity of a sovereign.</note>. For he thinks there is no Lord who proclaims and believes Him to be mindless, foolish, and destitute of reason and judgment, or an approver of evil works. For he who is bound by no laws of justice or injustice can be no one in a republic, either because he does not understand...

### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I

...or because it is not grasped, or is restrained. For to fools and the mentally impaired, right and wrong are the same, because they grasp the reason for neither. To tyrants and the spreaders of injustice, it pleases them to observe no distinction between these things. He, therefore, who sins against God of his own will is deservedly called guilty of <term>lese-majesty</term> <note>original: "reus maiestatis"; here meaning high treason against the divine sovereign</note>.

But we must persist in the comparison of the craftsman acting toward a target <note>original: "scopus"; Postel uses the image of an archer's mark or a craftsman's goal to define human purpose</note>. For a greater light will shine from this upon our discussion. Every craftsman needs a body, a strong instrument, and material before he begins any work. In the same way, man has those three things by which he may work toward an end, granted to him by God in this temple of nature; and as often as he abuses them, so often does he despise and mock the Master who gave him this charge. 

Those three instruments granted to man for action are: first, man himself, given to himself by God, consisting of such excellence that he cannot be equated to or valued against this whole lower world. For in vain would this massive structure encompassed by the heavens have been made for man's sake, unless the human "end product" were more excellent than the work of the universe itself. Man is the end-goal of the material world, while God is the target for man. 

The second thing, which should properly be called the "instrument," consists of the goods of the soul, the body, and fortune, by which man acts upon the material—that is, upon his fellow man. In the meantime, he must take care that while he uses the instrument awkwardly—the handle, for example, or any other part of the tool—he does not imprudently cause himself harm without achieving a greater benefit. 

Therefore, all these things must necessarily be referred back to God, the giver and creditor of all these things, as if to a target. As often as we stray from Him by our own will, so often do we commit a most serious offense. This is easily seen by a single reason: if someone proceeds to such a level of impiety against a father that he not only despises and mocks him, but also rises up against his dignity and abandons his prescribed duty, is he not deservedly condemned for ingratitude and disinherited from his father's estate? If an earthly father, who is merely an instrument for propagating the body, deservedly takes such heavy punishment from an ungrateful, unjust, and ruined son for the sole reason that the son despised, provoked, or harmed him, how much punishment do we think is deserved by almost all men? For they neglect God—the author of the body, the soul, and all goods—and sin at every single moment against His precept, which was planted in their souls so that there would be no room for ignorance or excuse. 

Indeed, we ought to love God above all things as a parent, and love our fellow man as a brother (and as a son of God) just as we love ourselves, preserving ourselves in the highest innocence as children of God. Yet we neglect this so much that not only do we not love God above all things, but we prefer a harlot, money, the most vain opinion, glory, and pleasure to Him. We cancel out His precepts with our words or deeds as if they were counterfeit, and we even attempt to cast Him down from His throne. 

As for the one we ought to have held in love as a brother, and whom we should have cherished and bound to us through kindness in the manner of a father, we instead strip him of his possessions, his body, and his reputation; we busy ourselves with harming him by whatever art we can. In all this kind of duty, nature had prescribed that we should most especially prove ourselves to God. 

What shall I say of ourselves? How many crimes does a man commit against himself? The soul—given by God, akin to the divine, and capable of virtue—we immerse into a bottomless pit and whirlpool of all crimes. We establish the body as a slave to all pleasures. The very things and the instrument with which we ought to have provided for both our brother and ourselves equally, we instead abuse to the ruin of both. And meanwhile man—if it pleases the gods! <note>A classical idiom used here ironically to mean "Heaven help us"</note>—

claims he can be just without God, the renewer of this corruption. O blasphemy! This is "human justice": to pile up wealth by any craft, to care not for what is enough, but only that no other be richer than you. What else do you see in the "most holy" man (as far as human laws allow) except that he is judged "the best" simply because he abstains from evil? But that is just as if someone well-skilled in a craft, whose industry ought to be building houses for the whole neighborhood, were called the "best craftsman" simply because he had done nothing bad to anyone with his tools. ### ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

# BOOK I

To what end a strong and fit body? To what end the power of the mind? For what purpose, finally, were all these things granted to man? Should a man be considered among good citizens if, while living in the city, he daily gathered a great heap of tools into his house and spoke most excellently about the work itself, while in the meantime, for lack of craftsmen, the materials were neglected and perished, damaged by wind and rain? He would not only be a bad citizen but most unworthy of dwelling in that city. 

And yet, we are not ashamed to gather wealth from everywhere as if we were to live forever; we heap up and bury immense weights of gold and silver, stolen from the countless poor—either by our ancestors or recently by ourselves—who are worn out by hunger, thirst, cold, and labor. We all judge these things to be unjust, yet no one corrects them. Is it not a sign of a most depraved and utterly rotten nature to judge what you condemn, yet not correct it? 

If you sin against yourself alone, you do an intolerable injury to the Father, the most worthy author of nature, and you destroy yourself. If you commit a wrong against a brother—that is, another human being—undeservedly, you deny yourself as a son, him as a brother, and God as Father. But who does not treat it as a joke to not only commit these things daily, but to encourage as many as possible to do the same? To arm our own people with cunning, and to draw those below us by example and our equals by companionship into crime—that is indeed considered a "work of virtue" <note>Postel uses heavy irony here to describe how society has inverted morality.</note>.

<margin>Against the followers of Pelagius.</margin> <note>original: "Contra Pelagiastros"; referring to the Pelagian heresy, which taught that humans could achieve goodness through their own will without divine grace.</note> And our "petty philosophers" <note>original: "philosophastri"</note>, having spoken of virtue, dare to affirm that human nature has no stain in itself; they think virtue is just words, as they think a sacred grove is just wood. Without a doubt, since even the most perfect man judges himself to have sinned against himself, his brother, and God, and neither strives to nor can correct it, it follows that human perfection does not depend on man and cannot be restored by him. 

For it is established—alas, it is more than enough established—that this <term>feculent mass</term> <note>original: "massa feculenta"; a theological term describing humanity as a mass of dregs or corruption due to original sin</note> is entirely depraved, since although it recognizes judgment and guilt, no one provides an absolute remedy. Whoever, therefore, looks into himself and considers the target <note>original: "scopus"; the intended goal or mark of human life</note> for which he was established by God, cannot help but cry out to divine providence and confess his own impiety, because he sins so gravely against it daily; and he feels nothing in himself (even if he exerts all his strength) except his own condemnation, unless God helps him. 

Those, however, who are driven by the power of God are entirely different from the worldly; they strive to turn all things to the glory of God, they commit nothing unworthy of the children of God, and they spend all their effort and wealth on others rather than themselves. They willingly weaken the body with fasting, vigils, and labors; they adorn their minds with virtues, laugh at the splendor of worldly things, and embrace insults. They show utter contempt <note>original: "oppedunt"; literally "to fart at," a vulgar expression of total disdain</note> for the power of "fortune" (a hollow word) over them; they undergo death voluntarily for the sake of reverence and to avoid vice. 

When many most famous philosophers saw the followers of Jesus Christ to be of this kind, marvelling at the present divinity and the transformation of the men, they voluntarily joined their fellowship. For they said it was impossible that those who sought death with cheerfulness could be evil or criminals.

<margin>Contempt for death.</margin> For although there may be great constancy in a person throughout their whole life, whether toward vice or virtue, there is no soul so great and lofty that it cannot be weakened and broken by the terror of conscience—unless it is one entirely conscious of no guilt, or if some human failing has occurred, it knows for certain that providence is merciful toward it. 

But some impious person might object here: "That God is unjust, who permits this plague to reign in nature, and has placed that law in souls which no one is able to observe." Watch your tongue! <note>original: "Bona verba"; a Latin idiom used to stop someone from saying something offensive or unlucky.</note> Is a father or a friend unjust because he gives things that I can use for both good and evil, simply because I abuse them? Is He unjust, who bestows so many and such great benefits upon us that the world itself—and all who were, are, or will be—are unequal to acknowledging the benefit, even the smallest, which has been granted to a single person by God? Because of the magnitude of the obligation, it is entirely impossible to satisfy it. That which is supreme goodness is here called "injustice." To this is added the fault of our first parent <note>Adam</note> and our own, by which we daily provoke the God who ought to be worshipped by us. God gave what is best, [leaving it] to our use and judgment...

<summary>Postel argues that human nature is fundamentally corrupted by sin ("the feculent mass") and unable to achieve its divine purpose through will alone. He defends God's justice against claims that He is unfair, pointing instead to human abuse of free will and the transformative power of divine grace seen in the early Christian martyrs.</summary>

by free will. We lose it in such a way that we do not even feel that we have perished. There is no injustice in God; it lies within us and in the "mass" of nature <note>Latin: *massa*; a reference to the Augustinian concept of *massa peccati*, the "lump of sin" into which all humanity has fallen.</note>. Returning, then, to our plan, we must acknowledge that the material substance of us all is nearly lost through descent <term>Traducianism (ex traduce): the theological theory that the soul and its corruption are transmitted from parents to children through natural generation</term> from the first man. Although our soul is always present and capable of action, it is unwilling to yield its stubbornness any further. Thus, for the correction of that material—so that it may act well and look toward its intended goal—there is need of a distinguished physician, one who is no less than the Creator himself.

### ON THE NECESSITY OF THE PRESENCE OF GOD INCORPORATED
->among men.  C H A P T E R  X I .<-

God, the almighty and all-knowing, to whom future things are just as well known as the present and the past, most clearly perceived before He created man what course of life he would take—both in general and in specific details. Yet, even though He knew that man would perish, partly through his own doing and partly through the craft of the devil, He did not wish to abandon his creation. For it would have been a sign of fear, weakness, small-mindedness, and folly to delay for that reason, since He was just as able to heal man as He was to create him. 

Therefore, since the most wise God made all things perceived by the senses for the sake of man, and man for the sake of his own salvation and happiness, for the benefit of other men, and for His own honor, He necessarily judged that the corruption inherent in things because of their material nature would also affect him. This corruption, I say, is not ordinary, nor similar to that in other things. For the more excellent He fashioned man than other living creatures, the more serious He foresaw his fall would be. Indeed, a transgression is more serious the more prudent and great the person who commits it. This is why brute animals do not sin, because they do not choose; the downfall of a king is greater and more conspicuous than that of a private citizen. 

We have already addressed why He did not create man absolutely free from sin, and so good that he was unable to sin. For it was not permitted by the nature of matter, nor possible through free will. Indeed, unless the nature of matter experienced "accidental" <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that is not essential to a thing's nature, such as a person being sick or a chair being painted red.</note> corruption within itself, it would be just like an incorruptible form, and would not have left room for the variety of forms we see. Moreover, since the nature of the Good is blessed in every respect, it cannot be anything but free. For he who does good against his will—besides being a slave—is just as if he were not doing it at all. No opportunity for merit (which arises from freedom) can exist for someone who acts well whether they want to or not. 

Thus, there was no way God could have created man with a better lot, as far as this present life is concerned. If He created him—as has been established—and knew that he would become unjust and evil through the depravity of his nature (which is most true), it was necessary that even from the eternal constitution of the world (I mean the "uncreated" world, conceived from eternity in the divine mind through the Wisdom of the Son), He had already pre-planned a remedy for this ruin. This remedy would be that, when man seemed to have reached the peak of wickedness, He would then send His Son for our restoration. 

Since, therefore, this depravity was all the greater because the men whom it affected were greater and closer to God, an intolerable plague invaded everyone shortly after the world’s creation—save for a few who, with great difficulty, preserved the knowledge of themselves and of God. Many demons spread their works into the gatherings of these few men (for both of these natures <note>Meaning humans and demons.</note> had fallen through free will, as we have seen) and both used their will for evil. Therefore, even while the knowledge of God the Creator was still fresh, and while they had recently enjoyed angelic visions because of their innocent lives, God did not use mere warnings for these wretched men. Instead, having ordered the element of water to return to its natural order (from which it had receded by His command), He wiped everyone out in a flood of waters, save for a very few. This was done not by some new plan or change of heart, as the philosophers suggest, but by eternal deliberation. And lest the trivialities of the Greeks should seem sterile...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...invented nothing of their own, nor ascribed anything to their own region, they even bring in a great fire <note>original: "conflagrationem"; likely referring to the Greek myth of the world ending in fire (Ekpyrosis) or the myth of Phaëton.</note> sought from other sacred sources to accompany the flood; but they lie with little wisdom. For the control of the sun was never permitted to that ruined man Phaëton, much less to any good man, that he might set the orb of the earth ablaze because of human errors. Furthermore, if there had been such a fire, men could not possibly remember it, since no living animal can be rescued from fire; yet we can meet the dangers of water with ships, provided we have forewarning. This is the divine order of things. 

When destruction began to spread once more (for among those who escaped the peril of the flood, there was one who was not quite upright, though saved for his father’s sake <note>A reference to Ham, the son of Noah, often depicted in early modern theology as the progenitor of "corrupt" lineages.</note>), God the Blessed began to deal more mildly with the offspring produced by that race, and He no longer sought to destroy them. For lightning bolts would not have been enough if He had wished to pursue the sins of every person. Furthermore, those holy men who survived the flood had received by hand from their ancestors knowledge of the ancient condition of things, as much as divine goodness had revealed to the first parents of the human race, either by Himself or through an angelic vision <note>original: "spectro"; here meaning a manifestation or appearance.</note>. These things were entrusted to a few good men—namely, those who possessed the wisdom to become better through them and who sought to lead and benefit others. 

Yet, human ferocity could not be turned away from its own destruction by those laws. For the multitude and the pride of this world are of such a nature that if you share sacred things with them, they are neglected and become cheap through common use; but if you reveal nothing, they immediately begin to be carried headlong into vices as outlaws. Therefore, there is a frequent need for repeated miracles, or rare and new wonders, so that you may draw the multitude wherever you wish. Satan, understanding this while God wished to be held in honor, left no stone unturned so that he might offer himself in place of God, deceiving people under any appearance of good. 

Therefore, God sent certain angels throughout the whole world and revealed what was to be expected concerning a future remedy, and what was to be done in future times (as far as it is permitted for man to know). Thus, He divinely inspired the **Sibyls** <note>The Sibyls were legendary prophetesses of the ancient world. Christian writers like Postel believed they were divinely inspired to predict the coming of Christ to the pagans.</note>, women who were moved by God at various times and in various provinces. While they warned everyone, they especially urged the heathens, who were captured by false religions, to acknowledge the one God and the coming change of kingdoms and false religion. Their verses were most religiously collected and preserved, both by many others and especially by the Romans, in whose libraries they remained until the time of Constantine. 

But these things were of little benefit to ruined men, who were as if deafened at the **Cataracts** <note>original: "Catadupas"; a reference to the waterfalls of the Nile. Ancient geographers claimed the roar was so loud that the local people were born deaf; Postel uses it as a metaphor for spiritual deafness.</note>. Few were skilled in these matters; and those who opposed the efforts of demons and removed false persuasions were gifted with hemlock <note>A reference to the execution of Socrates, who was forced to drink hemlock for challenging the traditional gods of Athens.</note>. Thus, vice creeps in easily but can hardly ever be torn out. 

Divine Providence, therefore, wishing to leave nothing untried that pertained to the salvation of men, saw the entire world laboring under a most heavy disease. He did not wish to reshape the whole body at once—a mass foul and laboring under its own weight—because the people could not all come together in one place on earth to hear the prescriptions of God, and they were prone to lose things that were only rarely impressed upon them. Instead, He chose a nation which He had determined from eternity. Through the ministry of both angels and men, He would use writing to repeat the prescriptions for living which He had initially willed to be naturally implanted in the minds of all. Thus, for those whom conscience did not move, the written words would refresh their memory of that which had perished within them. 

He therefore chose **Abraham** from the Chaldean race to be the one to whom He would give the beginnings of the holy law. By the command of God, Abraham chose to go into exile from the unspeakable Babylonian people, lest the contagion of a wicked religion bring a stain upon the fledgling faith. His progeny, imbued with holy precepts, remained there for four hundred years, eventually settling in Egypt. At that time, **Moses** was sent; he rescued an immense number of people—who had been contaminated by participating in Egyptian religion and oppressed by a most heavy tyranny—into the jurisdiction of God. God wished this to be accomplished in one nation, not in many, so that by the example of these men at least, foreign nations might see that it is far happier to live under the empire of God than under that of demons. If He had wished to give it to other peoples (for the slanders of the impious must always be satisfied), He would have given either the same law or a different one. If the first, He would have done so in vain, since it could be propagated and handed down from the first; if...

...to all provinces the same Law, it would have been superfluous, and the freedom of choice in receiving what was accepted from others would be removed, and for that reason, one would believe without merit. For it would have been necessary to use wonders and signs throughout the whole world to compel belief. Furthermore, there would have been no difference between truth and falsehood, since by necessity there must be a conflict between the true and the false until the very end of the world. If, however, He had given a different truth, He would no longer be God. For only one truth underlies the nature of things. Therefore, nothing better could have been done than what was done. Moses, therefore, relying on divine power, terrified the Egyptians with wonders, attracted his own people, and led them to that place where he set forth the divine law and confirmed it with miracles.

But God prescribed such a law there as a skilled teacher <note>term: "pædagogus"; in the ancient world, this was a tutor or guardian who supervised a child's conduct and led them to school.</note> is accustomed to do for children arriving at the "bitter roots" of doctrine. For if, when a child arrives, the teacher immediately threw against him whatever habits he had from home—whether perverse or unsuited to discipline—he would undoubtedly not be inviting the child to schooling, <margin>Nevertheless, He thus most wisely consulted the unrefined, so that in the shadows of ceremonies the whole business of Christ and the formation of character was designed.</margin> but would rather frighten him away as if from a torture chamber; nor could he imbue a stubborn nature with any principles of discipline. Thus God the Blessed, acting as if He were looking the other way, even connected His law to many of their unnecessary works and vices, and set down as law what He permitted to their tender age, which was as yet unsuited to grasping divine things. Such are all the kinds of sacrifices, vengeance, divorce, and many similar things. For it is better to have a "half-evil" man than to leave him altogether lost.

Since there is a need for sacred ceremonies in every religion, both for the sake of all who are imperfect and for the sake of providing a sign, it is manifest that sacred days and rites must be established in certain places: not for the sake of God, who is everywhere and always present, but for our sake. Since we consist of body and soul, we find it necessary to explain those things which are in the soul by some sign of the body. For although deep meditation is more excellent than spoken prayer, the words of prayers must nevertheless be brought forth by the mouth and accompanied by signs. 

Therefore, in order to lead their worship—which had been undermined by the idolatry of the Egyptians—back to divine honor, He commanded that all those things which used to be sacrificed to Egyptian idols should be sacrificed to Him. This was not for the sake of the "savor" of the meat (for as the Royal Prophet <note>King David, in Psalm 50:10-13.</note> says in the person of God: *All living things are mine. If I were hungry, I would not ask you; I do not feed on flesh or blood*), but so that He might turn a bad form of worship into a good one. The same is the reason for divorce. The injuries they were frequently accustomed to receiving in Egypt made them more prone to vengeance. For patience, when wounded too often, turns into fury. The commanded "thefts" of Egyptian vessels were justified by the fact that justice had not been granted to the afflicted people themselves; such actions are even permitted when, if ordinary justice is denied, one can obtain what is theirs without public riot. For if the laws do not help a Republic or a single assembly, it can justly obtain its own from another by any skill. God permitted this to them as compensation for the <margin>Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century Church Father who wrote against heresies.</note> argues excellently concerning the right by which God ordered the Egyptians to be plundered.</note> injuries they had received, so that they would not be delayed by the occasion of seeking or demanding what was theirs. 

The unleavened bread was nothing other than a way to ensure the beginning of the divine benefit was not forgotten. Therefore, there is no reason for the impious to say that God was the author of evil, or that He changed His mind. For it was not an evil thing to obtain what was one's own; nor was it a change of mind to permit those things and set them down as if for a law, without which He could not otherwise have offered the best and holiest precepts and persuaded them while still preserving their freedom. For God does not wish to bring force upon the will, except perhaps to a certain private individual, so that from there they might pass into acting freely out of habit. He wishes the proverb to hold true: *Break rather than correct those things which have hardened into depravity*; He does not wish for people to be lost. 

Although the Israelites were almost compelled by wonders and signs to receive the sacred law, we can nevertheless judge from ourselves what sort of people we would have been if we had stood in their place. We judge the vices of others easily, while we applaud our own. If those who saw God present and were daily stirred by miracles were such as they were, what of the rest? How great was the impiety in the whole world, if even among the pious there was sin? So reluctantly does man rest in God. We have been spectators of that kind, but we are far inferior to the actors themselves. Furthermore, that Law, although it was bitter, nevertheless seems not unlike a teacher’s rod. For it reveals vices by the punishments it inflicts; yet it cannot substitute virtue in their place.

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

Thus the Law given to Moses pointed out vice, and by pointing it out, increased it; yet it could never remove it. For it beat the people frequently, but did not reform them. But let us consider this: if those who possessed two laws—both the law of nature and the restored Law of Moses—were still wicked men, what should we judge of those who lived without any law at all? The holy prophets, sent by God, succeeded Moses. Observing that the Law was being entirely perverted and neglected, they rebuked these evil men. They gradually tried to diminish the people's confidence in mere ceremonies, teaching that salvation did not reside in rituals, but in charity, piety, and self-knowledge. They taught that while ceremonies were signs not to be neglected—provided their internal power was present—if that power were missing, God was being mocked rather than worshipped. It eventually happened that those living under the Law became the worst of all men. Indeed, they were worse than the lawless nations because they abused the best of laws as a cloak and "color" <note>original: "colorem"; here meaning a deceptive outward appearance or excuse</note> for their crimes, overturning holy prescriptions with their own human traditions. Therefore, when there was no longer any room for true piety except among a very few, and when humanity was perishing by its own hand throughout the world, ambition, glory, pride, and the other plagues of the earth reached their peak. At that moment, when there was no more room for minor remedies because divine and natural precepts had been trampled underfoot, the greatest of evils required the greatest of remedies. It was necessary for God himself to come—not as a ghost—but clothed in a human body. For God’s threats, human efforts, and even the arts of the angels had become obsolete. From the humility and faith of Abraham—who as a youth was able to see Noah <note>Postel refers to traditional biblical chronology where the lives of Noah and Abraham overlap, suggesting a direct link to the world before the Flood.</note>—the people who had been granted the Law gradually fell away. Though frequently called back to the path of truth by the prophets, worn down by captivities and wars, and corrected often, they had slid into such vice that nothing could be added to their wickedness. This nation sinned against God all the more gravely, and the hope for repentance seemed smaller, because beyond the crimes reigning everywhere among the Jews, their impious magistrates established "sacred" rules that both contradicted holy scripture and paved a wide path to wickedness. The laws of God had taught that God must be loved above all things, and that parents should be honored and helped with resources. However, through the greed of the scribes and Pharisees, the words of the divine law were circumvented by fraud; they decreed instead that no one was bound to support his parents—not even a father—provided he had bound his resources to the temple with an annual gift. <note>Postel is referencing the "Corban" practice criticized by Jesus in the Gospels, where religious donations were used as a legal loophole to avoid family obligations.</note> God’s law sought the hearts of men, but the synagogue burdened its people only with ceremonies, and the heaviest ones at that. In short, gold—as Isaiah had already said six hundred years before that age—had been turned entirely into dross. Now, if we consider human affairs among foreign nations more diligently: the Romans, who originated from shepherds and bandits, had reached such a size that, because of what they had snatched from the whole world through plunder, slaughter, violence, and injustice, they were now beginning petty civil wars at home. They were laboring under their own massive weight, degenerating from an aristocratic tyranny into a monarchy. The entire world, lying subject to their empire, suffered damage from these pestilential men—not only in their bodies and after the plundering of their property, but in their very souls. The affairs of Greece, once most flourishing, had either perished entirely or had degenerated from virtue into vice. For those crafty minds devised and taught the Romans the arts of pleasure and luxury, by which wealth poorly gained might be even more poorly squandered. The disciplines that had once been the greatest good for Republics now brought only ruin and the annoyance of learning without any fruit. Pythagoras, Plato, and Aristotle lay buried and forgotten; instead, the Epicureans, the followers of Arcesilaus, the Pyrrhonists, <note>term: "Arcesilani and Pirrhonici"; these refer to schools of philosophical Skepticism that Postel believed undermined certain truth.</note> sophists, gluttons <note>original: "gastrimargi"; a Greek-derived term for those enslaved to their stomachs.</note>, and similar plagues were thriving. You would have judged that whatever excellent things God had given to men had all been turned toward human destruction rather than benefit. Therefore, people thought there was no God, because He seemed to see these things and yet endure them. Satan moved about in a most vast dominion over affairs. The poor man languished under oppressions, while the rich man, amid his ill-gotten gains, devised every possible crime. And meanwhile, that hollow splendor of unhappy men swept the innocent into sin. For even if one did not sin through violence and injustice, the very abuse of things and the terrible example (which almost all courtiers always...

(follows) the magistrate left a plague behind him everywhere; so much so that in no part of the world was there any peace, until Augustus, having finished off his allies and rivals, brought a long-lasting peace to Rome, under whom the Creator wished to send salvation to the world. Just as the Emperor had brought some rest to the weary bodies of men, so eternal Wisdom would come to provide eternal happiness for minds acknowledging the truth. For God, like a most devoted father, did not want the one for whose sake He created all things—and who was created for His own sake—to be merely exposed like a wild beast after being raised, and to be thereafter not at all concerned for such a noble nature. Instead, like a most wise physician, He wanted to proceed gradually from the smallest remedies to greater ones, so as to leave no room for excuse. 

For if Jesus Christ, the <term>Angel of Great Counsel</term> <note>original: "magni consilij angelus"; a title for the Messiah derived from the Septuagint translation of Isaiah 9:6</note>, had come immediately at the first instance of wickedness, mortals could have said that there was no need for such a great remedy for their reformation; they might have claimed that if some angel or prophet had come, they would have been ready to repent. Your Creator tested everything, O man, in order to lead you back to the way of truth. The works of the prophets and legislators were always a certain "accession" <note>an approach or progressive addition</note> made toward God. 

But since all men are children of God, it must be admitted that they are a care to the Father. For since it is known that God has care for particular things, even the smallest, how much more for human beings? Otherwise, He would be similar to one who took care that stones, cement, lime, gypsum, bricks, beams, rafters, and so on, were preserved, transported, and raised into a structure, but then ultimately seemed to neglect the finished work itself and hold it as nothing; no greater madness than this could ever exist. Therefore, such a thing falls neither upon God nor upon a prudent man. 

Man is something greater than the lower world; therefore he is a care to God above all things, even more than the world itself. For that heavenly mind is deservedly to be preferred to all these material things. Indeed, man has need of two things to return into favor with himself and with God. For it is necessary both to innovate <note>renew or restore</note> nature, and to have the faculty of using that nature once it is innovated. For if you wish a captive to serve you, it will be necessary both to free him and to watch over him, lest he fall back into the same dangers. Neither an angel nor a man can perform this work in a whole human being; hence it remains that it must be the work of God, if it is to be repaired in anyone. 

And if it were demonstrated that these defects of nature were repaired in <note>original: "C millies centenis hominum milibus"; Postel uses this large figure to represent an immense, perhaps infinite, multitude of people</note> hundreds of millions of men, it will be established that it was the work of God. It is appropriate in divine matters that effects seem to receive their demonstration from what follows after. For instance, if someone wants to create the most certain faith for himself that the divine prophets—Moses, David, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the rest—were truly divine, he will not call them divine simply because they predicted Christ; rather, it is from the advent of Christ, about whom they all predicted and who bears witness to them, that they will most deserve the belief in their divinity. 

So also Christ himself, although he clearly testified to his divinity through every kind of miracle, yet gave much greater <unclear>uui</unclear> <note>likely "vim," meaning force or power</note> strength to faith in his members—the Apostles and martyrs—who in his name alone performed all the miracles that can fall within human perception. But we are called to greater miracles: how the Son of God received this stain of nature into Himself without stain. This must be sought by a higher method. 

God, the Best and Greatest, unless He were <term>triune and one</term> <note>Postel is explaining the Trinity as a logical necessity for the act of creation</note>, could not have brought things into being. For the Mind was endowed with Wisdom, and led by Will and Love toward the creation of the universe; without these qualities of the most simple Being, nothing could have been brought into existence. In His Wisdom, therefore, or (as is better) through Wisdom in the Holy Spirit, He established all things—He from whom, through whom, and in whom all things exist. For He could not have produced anything while being ignorant or unwilling. That Wisdom of the Father is called the Son, the Word, the Beginning, and by many other names. Just as the eternal God created all things through Wisdom—that is, the Son—so He wished them to be restored through the same. And just as we are blind in the works of creation, so in the mystery of restoration—which is far more sublime in our estimation—we must entirely dismiss our senses and place our faith in divine words. # ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

### Book I

78

We see that we can comprehend by no human skill the distinction of those properties which are within the soul—namely, <term>intelligence</term>, <term>reasoning</term>, and <term>memory</term>—even though we certainly grasp by arguments that they exist. How much less, then, can we capture that eternal and infinite nature and supernatural Cause? We know within ourselves that the soul which is in us does not require a physical place, nor is it moved locally, except accidentally when the body moves. Yet we see that in the blink of an eye it can penetrate, traverse, and contemplate the entire world, and bring back to us highly perfected notions of things. From this it is clear that spirits, once released from the company and prison of the body, traverse this entire matter of the sensible world immediately, far more perfectly and freely than we do. For our spirit is frequently called away from the contemplation of great things by these coarse senses of the body. Hence it happens that in dreams, when the soul seems more released from the body, revelations, divinations, and many forewarnings of events occur.

Of how much power, then, must we consider that infinite Divinity to be—to doubt whose power is to overturn the truth of all things? The Wisdom of God willed to lower itself into an immaculate Virgin—who by an eternal privilege was immune from the <term>original stain</term> <note>original: "labe originali"; referring to Original Sin</note> of other men—by the command of the Father and the guidance of the Holy Spirit. So the order of things demanded. For it was fitting for God to fulfill all possible modes of generation. The first was without seed and without a "vessel" <note>the womb</note> suited for generation <note>referring to the creation of Adam from the earth</note>. The second is common to all nature, from seed cast by a propagator and placed within a vessel suited for generation. The third, as if mixed from both, is closest to the act of creation: it is from a vessel, yet without seed sought from elsewhere. It was necessary for Christ to be born in this way. For just as it was most excellent and admirable to have created the first man by command alone, outside the vessels of nature, with clay brought into a <term>temperament of flesh</term> <note>original: "carnis temperamentum"; the physical balance of the human body</note> (which we must believe because we see it was done), so also it was most worthy of the Creator to make the first restoration similar to the creation. In this way, the generation of the Restorer would be akin partly to nature and partly to the work of the Divinity, just as the God-Man possessed a unique and peculiar nature. For it was fitting for the Restorer to differ from those being restored in his generation and principle, just as he did in his nature; and he ought not only to be distinguished by his body and origin, but he also needed to accommodate himself to us.

For God could have visited us with a body brought from elsewhere (just as <term>apparitions</term> <note>original: "spectra"; spiritual manifestations or phantoms</note> have often been seen); he could also have used the common mode of birth, or a partial one. If he had done the first, mortal persistence and impiety would not have believed that he had a true body. Many heretics have given proof of this, having dared to assert that he did not have a true body, but a <term>phantasmic</term> one <note>a reference to Docetism, an early Christian heresy claiming Christ only appeared to be human</note>. If, however, he had been born in the common and vulgar way, he would never have been received—seeing as he was hardly accepted even when born of a virgin and made famous by the clearest signs and miracles. Thus, a middle way had to be chosen for the Mediator, for many reasons. First, so that he would not wish to redeem us without our own flesh and the physical temperament he received; which he would have done if he had taken flesh from elsewhere. Second, so that he might indeed take on flesh, but would not receive into himself the stain of a depraved nature, which he had come to wipe away from pious men and those who would believe in him. Third, so that the God-Man might be born by a generation different from others, yet most worthy of Him. Fourth, so that he might participate in the extremes of both, just as he joined two extremes in one subject: for as God, he descended into the Virgin without seed by the guidance of the Holy Spirit; but as man, he willed to take from her a body like our own. Fifth, so that the highest dignity of the Divinity might correspond to a similar dignity in lower things; namely, that he who was God and immune from all stain might take flesh from a most innocent and pure Virgin, in a mortal body as close to the Divinity as is permitted. For although the common mode of generating was instituted by God in nature so that nature might be continued and propagated through it, nevertheless the act of conception and the <term>venereal act</term> <note>sexual intercourse</note> cannot be free from the stain of sin. All religions, even the false ones that mimic the true, have naturally recognized this, since they require virgins for sacrosanct supplications and in the highest...

...they wished these things to be celebrated only during times of great crisis. For otherwise, they would not have been so eager to appease the wrath of the divine power with girls and virgins rather than with married women. Hence the Romans—as they were superstitious in a wonderful way—whenever a <term>hermaphrodite</term> <note>original: "androgynos"</note> was found anywhere in their domain, or whenever anything else had terrified the city, would kill the hermaphrodite and then purify the city with twenty-seven virgins singing. This was also done at times of the greatest danger by thirty boys <term>having both parents living</term> <note>original: "patrimis & matrimis"; a Roman ritual requirement that a child's father and mother both be alive for the child to be ritually pure.</note> and as many virgins. Because of this, they would kill corrupted Vestal Virgins by burying them alive—an unheard-of punishment. Certainly, unless virginity were something familiar and related to divinity, they would have at some time preferred selected men and women who might excel even the virgins themselves in piety. They knew naturally what David religiously says: *And in sins did my mother conceive me in her womb* <note>original: "Et in peccatís cōcepit me in conceptíone mater mea"; Psalm 51:5.</note>.

Therefore, just as nothing is greater than God, and nothing besides Him could restore the corrupted nature of men, so too, in order to take on our body and join it to divinity, nothing more noble or more related to God could offer itself than a virginal body. <margin>Isaiah 7</margin> The holy prophet had predicted that it would happen that a virgin would conceive and give birth. The <term>Temple of Peace</term> <note>A reference to a medieval legend that the Roman Temple of Peace would stand until a virgin gave birth; it was said to have collapsed on the night of Christ's nativity.</note> at Rome, which was said to be eternal, then collapsed when the virgin gave birth. However, so that such a great mystery of the divine incarnation might be hidden from Satan and the wicked rulers of the Jewish Republic, Christ willed to be born under the shadow of marriage, lest the demon stir up more enemies against the nascent Truth; and lest, when the virgin appeared pregnant outside the laws of marriage, she might be branded with the mark of disgrace by the law of her fathers, and finally that which was most excellent might become a source of shame for her and her parents.

In addition to these things, Christ, taking upon himself and around himself all the <term>sacraments</term> <note>Here meaning "sacred rites" or "mysteries."</note> of the Old Law, willed to become all things to all men, and to prove that the law to which he submitted himself had been given by God as its author.

Therefore, from a virgin, he willed to take a form similar to ours and connect it to the divine—a form which was indeed animated, adorned with divinity, and endowed with a <term>double will</term> <note>Postel refers to the orthodox doctrine that Christ possessed both a human and a divine will.</note>. Into this composite being (having pitied human nature), he took upon himself whatever afflictions were owed to us, opened the truth of God within it, cured all kinds of diseases as a testimony of his divinity, raised the dead, put demons to flight, and for our salvation willingly underwent death. He rose again in the same body and ascended into heaven with it, so that through the affliction and purification of our assumed flesh, as many as believed that this salvation was prepared for them and were initiated into his sacred mysteries—totally overcoming the stubbornness of the flesh—might be able to reach the place where he first carried a body like ours. For he willed to die for the salvation of us all in such a way as to show that true professors [of faith] are never without their own trials; and that one must persist all the more ardently in offering the Truth to a blinding world, the more certain and present the proposed reward is.

If anyone should ask why he willed it so and not otherwise: that person would be asking the same thing as why he fashioned us no differently. To such a person, it must be answered with absolute authority: because he so willed it.

The whole <term>corrupt mass</term> <note>original: "massa corrupta"; a term used in Augustinian theology to describe humanity's state after the Fall.</note> could not be restored in any other way than by being joined to God. From his blood and water, he left us a <term>holy cleansing</term> <note>original: "sacrosanctum lustrum"; referring to the ritual purification of Baptism.</note> by which we are cleansed from every stain of nature and preserved from the assaults of Satan, so long as we demonstrate in our deeds what we promise in words: innocence, charity, and faith. We give this faith to God, adorned with praise, fear, and love, binding our neighbor to us through charity in every kind of duty, and commending ourselves before God as if we were newborn infants in our innocence.

Although Jesus Christ, the son of God and of the Virgin Mary, sufficiently showed his divinity in his miracles themselves, while he performed all things by his own word (for he said to the blind, "See," and they saw; to the dead, "Rise," and they rose; to the lame, "Walk," and they were made straight; to the lepers, "Be cleansed," and they were cleansed; to the demons, "Go out," and they were forced to depart; in short, he did everything in his own name, as he was indeed God), nevertheless, the Gospel was confirmed most of all by his power when all these same things were done by his disciples and by holy men in his name...

...it is so, that more than twenty thousand people have risen up in various regions <note>Postel likely refers to the rapid spread of the early Church and the miracles associated with the Apostles.</note>) there would be no languor, no infirmity, wherever even the least of the Apostles and saints of Jesus Christ might be. Moses, Elijah, Elisha, and as many as performed miracles, did them in the name of God. Only Jesus Christ did them in his own name, since he could rightly do so. For he himself with the Father and the Holy Spirit was, is, and shall be one God, one substance. For that assumption of flesh in no way hindered the incomprehensible God from being entirely where he was in the body, and in the administration of all nature. For he cannot be hindered who is not contained by any place, and yet holds all things. 

<margin>The example of the sun especially pleased the theologians.</margin> 

I cannot wonder enough at such blindness in men, that they dare to bring these things into question, when we see very familiar examples in the smallest things, and how very many things are entirely in one place, and yet entirely in all and diverse places. Who would not admire the nature of scents, which, though they come from a single source <note>original: "scaturigine," literally a spring or fountainhead</note>, are nonetheless represented equally to the nostrils of all? The same is to be judged of sounds regarding ears, and likewise of the images of things striking the eyes of all: of the rays of light stretched into all parts of power, of the same image seen in innumerable mirrors. All these things show that while a thing is in one place, it is not moved away from another. How much less could that omnipotent God, penetrating all things, be entirely circumscribed by a place? These things surpass local motion, nor should they be bound by the laws of bodies. 

But if we see these things in objects that proceed from a body, how much greater must we think that cause to be which is devoid of a body, by whose nod the stars shine, the heavens are moved, the elements remain constant, living things live, sensible things feel, and rational things excel in intellect? Will not he who makes things be born (as the prophet inspired by divine power says <note>A reference to Isaiah 66:9: "Shall I who cause delivery not give birth?"</note>) be able to generate? He who made things exist out of nothing, will he not be able to make something out of something? Just as he made the first man outside the <term>vessels of nature</term> <note>Postel uses this term to refer to the womb and the standard biological reproductive process.</note>, which did not yet exist, could he not only make him be born thus, but also in many other ways? For it is the same to God to be born from seed or without seed. For as for our wanting to impose a law on him from the common use and sense of things, what else is it, I ask, than wanting to constrain infinite power within a finite place or limit? It was not necessary for divine power to be moved from its place (although it is understood to act more nobly in the heavenly region) in order to raise the form of our body to itself and join it to divinity. 

Come, let us draw examples of such power from things subject to the senses. Who, being unskilled in natural matters, would admit that fire is truly mixed with the earth in every natural compound, and especially in that endowed with life, because this never falls under the senses? <note>Postel refers to the Aristotelian and alchemical theory that "elemental fire" is a hidden constituent of all living matter, providing vital heat.</note> Yet nothing is more proven or more manifest to a philosopher. But fire is a body, yet it does not fall under the senses. The Virgin was made pregnant by the work of the Holy Spirit, and in the natural way completed the time of carrying in her womb. Christ was born as God-Man. Like other men, he drank, ate, and suffered other physical needs; lest, while the works of divinity were seen in him and the sufferings of the body were hidden, he should be said not to have been a man, but only God. Besides the necessary cause for his coming among men, which we brought up above, this cause can also be brought forward:

### FROM NATURAL DESIRE.

Nature or God has given no false desire for things to any kind of living creature. For although men (who alone are able to sin in this corporeal world) pursue many false things, they are not false insofar as they are in the use of things; but the falsehood proceeds from a depraved motion of choosing. For there is something in individual things to be desired which is desirable in itself and which has the form of good. But the reasoning of laws, things, place, time, and persons, being little observed, causes us (while we pursue the appearance of good) to choose things that are diametrically opposed. All men are held by a longing for divinity; in seeking this, they err in that they wish to attain it before the time (that is, in this life), without sufficiently balancing their vow with its end. # THE BOOKS OF GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.

Whatever exists in this lower life is subject to flux, ruin, oblivion, and corruption; but divinity is eternal. Therefore, divinity can indeed be possessed, but not in these earthly realms. Since we are all held by that desire for the divine, it is certain both that divinity exists and that it can be joined to man by divine favor, and man to it. Otherwise nature, which is accustomed to doing nothing in vain, would trick us with a false hope. Since man cannot attain that divinity by himself, nor receive it from the angels, it remains that he must receive this from God. For although in soul—either in hope or in reality—man could seek heaven again through the gift and direction of the Creator, he could never be perfected in the flesh so as to be able to do this by himself. 

It was necessary, therefore, by the gift of the Creator, for our flesh to be joined to God, so that it might fully attain what nature gave us the instinct to desire. For the soul alone is not "man," nor is the body alone, but both together. Therefore God, the Son of God, was made man for that reason, at the time when it seemed good to divine providence. For just as nature did not grant the best possible state to a creature immediately, but rather a creature receives its fulfillment especially when it has become more mature, so God did not wish in the beginning either to bring the absolute remedy for himself or to restore the way to divinity for man, which had perished in Adam.

->FROM THE IMMENSE GOODNESS OF GOD.<-

God, the best and greatest <note>original: "optimus maximus," a title traditionally used for Jupiter but here applied to the Christian God</note>, out of his immense and highest goodness, was altogether bound to perform his highest and most apparent work—one greater than which cannot be given or even imagined. He had to do it in such a way (since he made all things for his own glory and honor) that it would be manifest and clear to man. This work must be either uncreated, or created, or consisting of both. He produced the uncreated Son from eternity; but he produced created matter and form, either separately or together, when it pleased him to found the world, which had been preserved from eternity in his mind. 

There remained a third thing, the greatest and most noble of all: the God-man <note>original: "homo deus"</note>, God before the ages, and man in time. In him, God made both extremes one; in him, the most absolute perfection was joined to the greatest imperfection. Just as the sluggish and inert earth is quickened into life by a fiery force hidden in compound things, so also our heaviness and weight might be liberated by God the best and greatest and drawn into heaven. 

For before he placed the finishing touch <note>term: "colophonem" (original Greek: κολοφών). Historically, this refers to the final stroke or the crowning completion of a work.</note> on mortal things (which find their completion in man), he willed the whole of human nature to pass through individual ages—progressing from small beginnings to greater things—after the manner of a single human life. He willed for the prodigal adolescence and youth of humanity, rushing into every crime by its own lust, to cool down and experience the danger of error, until it reached a consistent age. This is the age in which one must especially come to one's senses and think about the future and about death. Then the supreme governor himself, pitying our errors, willed to be present; not in that form invisible to man in which he always exists, but in that which would be clothed in our body. In this form, although divinity (which cannot be seen by eyes) remained unseen, yet he might testify by his works that the fullness of divinity dwelt within him. Thus, he made our weak and corrupt nature truly happy, as it was now able to be joined to God. Grace be to you, Jesus Christ, who took upon yourself the stain of those who acknowledge you, made them sons of God and your brothers, and established them as co-heirs of the kingdom of God.

The most perfect figure, and the one most similar to God, is the circle, as I taught in the first chapter. For divine power is so sprinkled through all things that it is everywhere in the manner of a center, whose arches <note>original: "absides," referring to the segments of a circle or the orbits of planets</note> are extended equally into infinity. Therefore, because equality is sprinkled in every direction—as if from a center to the circumference—it agrees with the circle through its power, but in the way the infinite relates to the finite. Any circle also agrees with the archetype in its form. # ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

Just as a circle is defined or formed by its properties, so too we cannot conceive of a divine image unless we perceive in God an infinite power from which all things flow, a comprehension or knowledge <note>original: "verbum," referring to the Logos or the Word</note> through which all things exist, and a love or will <note>original: "benevolentiam," or benevolence</note> proceeding from both, in which all things were established and flourish. Just as we see the logic of total unity within the trinity fitting together perfectly in all things, it is necessary that it does not falter in the manner of its composing and finishing. For although God is without beginning, like a circle already completed, they correspond most truly in this: for a total completion, the lowest must be joined to the highest, and the ends to the ends. The highest end is God, the lowest is man; the two extremes are God the beginning and man the end. 

To complete this unity, so that man might achieve salvation, it was necessary for God to be joined to man and become one; this was accomplished in the nature of Jesus Christ. For just as in all things contemplation <note>original: "θεωρία" (theoria), meaning deep thought or speculation</note> precedes action <note>original: "πρᾶξις" (praxis), meaning practice or deed</note> regardless of time, so from eternity the most holy Trinity—through power, will, and wisdom—drew the first lines of the universe after eternal thought in the act of creation. Finally, in the "re-creation," coming to the nearest point, it truly joined the end to the beginning when it worked the salvation of the universe through the God-man <note>original: "θεάνθρωπον" (theanthrōpon)</note>. 

Thus Jesus, assuming human flesh for a twofold reason, wished to make man, in a sense, God. This occasion was twofold: the fitting <note>original: "decorum"</note> and the useful <note>original: "utile"</note>, from which the just <note>original: "iustum"</note> arises. For where these are separated, truth perishes and justice is driven away. It was fitting for the sake of universal harmony that God be joined to man; it was useful for man—lost by his own choice and unable to rise by himself—to be helped. The "fitting" refers entirely to the one acting (God); the "useful" refers entirely to the one receiving (man). From these two, the "just" was born as a mixture of both, by which rewards are given to the good and to those who follow their Restorer as much as they can, while evils are given to the wicked; and otherwise, praise is given to the Creator. 

Since no part of duty should lack the honorable, the fitting, the good, the useful, or the just, it is impossible for all men to know this naturally unless it was instilled by a single common principle. Likewise, it was neither right nor possible that in the union of God and man—the beginning and the end—these three necessary things should not concur for our salvation. To preserve the harmonic order of the universe and fulfill God's truth, it had to happen this way. For God is truthful; He established the ends for all things below man so truly that no living creature could be ignorant of them or bypass them (unless through man's negligence). He also preordained an end for man—this small world <note>The "microcosm," a common Renaissance idea that the human being is a miniature version of the entire universe</note>—who is far superior to material things, so that he might become far higher and happier than himself and greater than all material reality. Man could not reach this end without that honorable, useful, and necessary connection, permitted by the true God and required by needy man.

### FURTHERMORE, FROM THE WELL-BEING OF MAN, OR HIS LIBERATION.

We have taught above that man was created at his best by God, but he brought evil upon himself by his own choice, and in that evil he takes delight. He is therefore oppressed by his own depraved nature. We have also seen that he is attacked by depraved angels <note>i.e., demons</note> and made a slave to them in sin. For since they fell from their own goodness, it is certain they changed their nature into its opposite. Instead of angelic perfections—which consist of pursuing, praising, and thanking God and men for God's sake out of charity—it is clear they took up the opposites: blaspheming the Creator and venting their envy upon man. Thus man is clearly oppressed by a double tyranny. 

Added to this was the yoke of the Mosaic Law, given to those meant to be restrained in rebellion or stirred to virtue through small physical rewards; it oppressed the older people of God with a heavy servitude. Therefore, since depraved man could not rise by himself, and much less drive away a dark power far stronger than himself, it was necessary for the Author of both to come in a different way than at the beginning. He had to purge that nature in Himself which had conceived the stain of sin, so that He might bring the power of faith against the perverse enemy, and that the same Author of the law might lead the soul to the truth which...

<summary>Postel argues that the Incarnation of Christ (the "God-man") was philosophically necessary to complete the "circle" of the universe, joining the highest (God) to the lowest (man). He explains that Christ's coming was "fitting" for divine harmony, "useful" for man's salvation, and "just" in its rewards, ultimately liberating humanity from the tyranny of internal corruption, demons, and the heavy yoke of the old Law.</summary>

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.

...before, they were joined and given to the body. Since the root of all evils arose in human flesh from neglecting divine providence, the other two <note>likely referring to the soul and the intellect discussed on the previous page</note> would not have had power over man if he had followed the logic of the divine command. Because of sin, the power of the demon weighs upon man, and the Law was given for that reason. Thus, it could not have happened otherwise than by joining that diseased flesh to God, so that the freedom given in our original condition might be restored within us. Therefore, Christ is the **God-man** <note>original Greek: θεάνθρωπος (theanthropos)</note>.

## FURTHER, FROM THE SUBSTITUTION OF THE ANGELIC NATURE OR
## the laudatory nature of the Creator.

<margin>He follows the opinion of theologians who believe man was created so that the number of lost angels might be replaced.</margin>
**O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!** The judgments of God are a **great deep** <note>Postel quotes Romans 11:33 and Psalm 36:6</note>. Since God created all things for His own praise, and did so for the sake of creatures endowed with intellect or reason—so that they might be perpetually happy in praising Him—He placed angels (who excel in intellect) and men (who excel in reason) under the power of their own counsel, as the Wise Man says. He did this so that if they persisted in His praise, they would enjoy granted happiness forever; but if they withdrew from their duty, He would lose nothing, while they would accumulate eternal misery and torments for themselves. For it is fair that for an offense against infinite majesty, infinite torments should be imposed, since God is supremely just. Whether they sinned or not was the same to Him regarding the order of the universe, though not regarding the fault itself. For as much as was lost of the angelic nature, that many praising souls had to be substituted. Adam with his posterity could have been immortal if he had not abused his freedom. And the demon could have remained in his angelic order, praising God, as he had been created good. Man sinned; the demon was cast down. God's goodness wished to provide for man for a double reason: because the impulses of the flesh (though not as fragile then as now) and also the craftiness of the demon had tempted him toward defection.

Thus, so that the will of God might be fulfilled while keeping free will intact, and so that the place from which the evil angels fell might be refilled and lost salvation restored to man, it was necessary for that corrupted flesh—all but abandoned by free will due to immense desires—to be restored anew, and to be joined and united to the Creator. Just as nothing creates itself, so nothing can recreate or restore itself. There was a need, therefore, for a Creator who, having assumed and joined human nature to Himself, would wash away the vice of man within Himself. He did this so that as many as would swear by His words and obey them in all things as far as they are able, could not only return to the condition of the first man (as if by the **right of return** <note>original: "postliminio," a legal term for the restoration of rights to someone returning from exile or captivity</note>), but, becoming superior and sharers in angelic virtue, they might fill that place with blessed souls, and finally even bring a solid and corporeal human nature there. Thus, God's original plan achieves its end by God Himself becoming man. For otherwise, salvation could not be returned to man through man, nor would it have been possible to provide for everyone except through the creative wisdom of God. Therefore, the fall of the angels was repaired by Christ, the God-man, and a dignity and happiness greater than that at creation was restored to our nature, which had utterly collapsed. I could derive the same argument again from the purpose of man, had I not touched enough on both. For I have, as they say, **"whitewashed both walls with the same bucket"** <note>A Latin proverb, "Eadem fidelia duos parietes dealbare," meaning to achieve two goals with a single effort or proof</note>. For so that the purpose of divine grace and predestination might be brought to effect, it was necessary for man—for whose sake the world was made—to be saved and reach his end by following either free choice, inspiration, the law, or grace; and likewise, conversely, for those who did otherwise to be damned without any just complaint. So that God might restore the lost elect who wished to obey, He Himself came to the aid of the good and to offer counsel to the evil, so that by His help they might also repent, or else be most justly assigned to the worst punishments. Therefore (which should be terrifying to us), no punishments of divine vengeance are so immense as those imposed on any damned person as they are on evil and faithless Christians. Indeed, eternal punishments are owed to all those who...

He emphasizes that while God's justice is infinite, His grace provides a path for the "elect" to surpass even the angels through Christ.</summary>
