# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...in this life they contravened the divine law, and died without charity <note>In a theological sense, "charity" (caritas) refers to selfless, divine love rather than just giving to the poor.</note> and true piety toward God. Because they neglected the innumerable benefits bestowed upon them by God, they not only failed to give thanks to the Giver, but even abused those gifts to His dishonor and to the destruction of themselves and other men. But for Christians—who, besides the blessings of creation, also neglect the far greater blessings of **restoration** <note>Postel uses "restoration" (instauratio) to refer to the redemption of humanity through Christ.</note>, and have ignored, mocked, or even (as some do now) attacked the God-man with insults and reproaches—neither pen can write, nor tongue express, nor mind conceive how great the torments are that are prepared for them.

### AN ARGUMENT FROM DIVINE JUSTICE.

<margin>
He follows the opinion of those theologians who say that Christ did not satisfy for the sins of men so fully that nothing is also required of us.
</margin>
That man was created for the sake of something which easily surpasses the world in value is proven by the fact that the lower and visible world was made for his sake. Truly, the **end** <note>The "end" (finis) refers to the ultimate purpose or goal of a thing.</note> must be far more excellent than those things which exist for the sake of that end. Otherwise (as I frequently emphasize, and not without cause), the Author of such a massive undertaking would be unwise and aimless if He had made man without any purpose, since all other causes act for an end more excellent than themselves. For there is nothing here that is—I will not say blessed in every part—but rather, nothing that is not utterly miserable. Therefore, man cannot and should not have been made for the sake of misery (even though the world of fools places misery in what they call "supreme happiness," since the best things here contain more affliction than joy), but rather for the sake of some greater happiness than can be felt, seen, heard, or thought of in the whole world. And yet, this sort of happiness is eternal and immense. It remains, therefore, that man was made by the eternal and immense God for the sake of eternal and immense happiness, and that he can and must attain it. 

But since in the first man—who of his own will fell away from such a great goal—all posterity was deprived of its end because of sin, and could not rise back to innocence by its own power, it was nevertheless impossible for God to be cheated of His own design. For how could a man who had destroyed himself satisfy a most just and infinite God, whom he had offended infinitely, since man is a finite creature? By no means could he have justly expiated a crime committed against God's infinite goodness, even if he killed every single man a hundred thousand times over with the harshest torments—unless He who was also infinite paid the penalty on behalf of all, and led lost man back to the appointed goal. 

It was necessary, therefore, for the Creator, the Wisdom of God, and the Word, to be joined to our body: so that He, who alone was able, knew how, and was willing, might satisfy the offended and most just Divinity by undergoing a death heaped with unheard-of torments and insults. He did this especially to provide for those who would busy themselves with imitating Him to the best of their ability. For although the fruit and the payment of the death of Jesus Christ is offered to all, and many (through the supreme mercy of God) are translated immediately from death to life and from sin to **justification** <note>The process by which a person is made righteous in the eyes of God.</note> by God’s hidden judgment, nevertheless, unless one has cooperated with Christ through good works and has filled up "those things which are lacking in the suffering of Christ" in his own flesh (as Paul says in Colossians 1), by wailing, mourning, fasting, giving alms, repenting, and confessing, and performing other works of piety toward God, oneself, and one's neighbor—then undoubtedly, Christ is so far from benefiting that person (if they have had the use of reason since their baptism) that He instead stands as a vehement obstacle, condemning and gravely accusing them. 

For it is most just that, just as the God-man Jesus Christ died for each and every person for the sake of preserving justice and for an infinite expiation, so too everyone called into the freedom of the cross should imitate their Leader with good works, if they desire to be His soldier. From this it is clear that they are not merely heretics, but impious, who subtract our works from our salvation. For although we cannot wash away infinite guilt, nor absolutely merit the kingdom of heaven by "worthines" (<term>condigno</term>) <note>The term "merit of condignity" refers to a work that deserves a reward out of justice, rather than just out of God's generosity.</note>, it is nevertheless most equitable that God should not be unmindful of our obedience in doing good and fleeing evil...

<summary>Postel argues that because human sin is an infinite offense against an infinite God, only a God-man (Christ) could provide satisfaction. However, he insists that individuals must "cooperate" with this salvation through pious works like fasting and almsgiving to truly benefit from Christ's sacrifice.</summary>

<margin>

</margin>
...the habit of our good work; and it is so necessary that it is impossible for an adult to attain salvation without their own effort.

### FROM THE POWER OF GOD.

Although the all-knowing God foreknew that man would abuse his free choice, He nevertheless did not cease from his salvation, so that He might show in his **restoration** <note>original: "instauratione". Postel uses this term to describe the renewal or "setting right" of the world through Christ.</note> an omnipotence no less than that of creation. For He is able to restore lost man once again, just as He was able to create him. In no other thing, therefore, could man see God's power more openly than in the fact that He hid that power—which was equal to creating the world—beneath the lowliest and most rejected of men. Truly, it belongs to one more powerful to have led anything through to the end than merely to have ordered it toward an end. From this, innumerable myriads of the holy followers <note>original: "sectarum". While "sects" often has a negative connotation today, here it refers to the various branches or groups of the faithful following Jesus.</note> of Jesus have performed such stupendous miracles after Him, by relating them back to Him, that that immense power shone forth almost more in them than in their Master: which is a sign of His inexhaustible power and infinite grace.

### FROM WISDOM.

It likewise belongs to the Wisest Being to come to the aid of collapsed things no differently than if they had remained eternal. Since man is to be saved and led to infinite happiness, this cannot be done except through the highest and omnipotent wisdom, which knew how to purge vices and strengthen shattered parts just as it once joined them in their first nature. This, the one God-man Jesus was able, willing, and obligated to provide.

### FROM CHARITY.

<margin>
Faith in Christ makes one blessed, which is practiced through the sacred mysteries.
</margin>
**Charity** <note>original: "Charitas". In this context, it refers to the divine, selfless love of God for humanity.</note>, mercy, and love for the human condition had to join the highest things to the lowest in the same way, so that man might achieve his goal. For otherwise, the author of charity would have seemed quite alienated from humanity if He—who alone was able—had not raised up a nature so collapsed, lying in misery, and entirely perishing. But He who was able did indeed raise it up and cleanse it; and daily He joins it to Himself through the most holy sacraments, so that once health has been received, one may strive to follow the examples of His goodness (from which whatever is good has flowed) through those sacraments by which He heals our fragility and through his own diligent work.

### FROM THE CONSIDERATION OF THE GRAVITY
### of the Offense.

<margin>
It is said of all: he who despises you, despises me.
</margin>
Just as he who is greatest and most knowledgeable sins most gravely, so a subject sins all the more according to the greater authority against which he commits the act. For one ought to be punished more severely for an offense against a king than against a duke; against the Supreme Pontiff than against a priest; against the highest judge than against a lowly judge <note>original: "pedaneum". This refers to a judge of lower rank who typically handles minor or local cases.</note>. Thus the offense is estimated according to the quality of the person offended or harmed. Since God acts for the sake of an **end** <note>The "end" (finis) is the ultimate purpose or goal of a creation.</note>, He made man the most excellent of living creatures for the sake of the most excellent happiness. And since God is infinite, an infinite punishment is owed for a sin committed against Him; for indeed He is no less just than He is merciful. But unless God had given man that for which he was made, human nature would not have reached its goal. Therefore, it was necessary both that predestination be preserved and that justice and mercy be fulfilled. However, it is impossible for man to satisfy an infinite offense by his own strength. Nevertheless, it was necessary for human nature to pay the penalties worthy of the crime. Thus it happened that infinite wisdom, truth, and mercy assumed human flesh in the name of all, and took on all of corrupt nature, so that He might pay an infinite penalty in an infinite subject <note>In theology, the "subject" here is the person of Christ; because Christ is infinite God, his suffering has infinite value to pay the infinite debt of sin.</note>, which was owed to the infinite gravity of the crime. Therefore, it was absolutely necessary that the infinite God be incarnated and take upon Himself the debts of all men, paying them so completely that He forgives everything for one who comes to baptism and undergoes penance; yet for one living longer under the holy law, it is necessary to cooperate. For "he will not be crowned unless he has competed lawfully" <note>A reference to 2 Timothy 2:5, emphasizing that salvation requires following the "rules" of the Christian life.</note>.

# FROM THE CONTEMPLATION OF THOSE
### things which are done by free will.

It is impossible for things done by different people—who agree neither in language, education, nor customs—to coincide in every detail in the same way, unless the principle upon which they all depend gave that consistency to all of them. Therefore, it follows that since these things happen among temporary <note>original: "momentaneos". Postel refers to the fleeting, short-lived nature of human life compared to the eternal.</note> men in such a way that they could not be better, even the Prime Mover acts by these same laws in the reason of the universe. For whatever proceeds from our free will is first conceived and stirred in the mind; finally (as I have already taught above), it comes into a certain unfolding, appearing as a <term>ground plan</term> <note>original Greek: ἰχνογραφίαν (ichnographian). An architectural term for a floor plan or sketch.</note> or an <term>elevation drawing</term> <note>original Greek: ὀρθογραφίαν (orthographian). An architectural term for a vertical projection or finished plan.</note>, and at last rises into a physical work; finally, it offers use and a purpose. Truly, it is fitting that in the thinking mind there should be power, knowledge, and a will or eagerness for doing the thing, even before one comes to the <term>diagram</term> <note>original Greek: διάγραμμα (diagramma). A schematic or outline.</note>. In the same way, Divine Providence, which made all things in the most excellent manner, acted thus in the completion of the universe. For, weighing all future things in His mind from eternity, holding and knowing all things in Himself as if present—being powerful, knowing, and willing—He created all things in time when it seemed right. As if by an unfolding of His power preserved in His mind, He drew the lines of creation for the sake of the happiness of free man. By gradually polishing this work through talent, cultivation, and laws—both divine and human—and by carving the rough material, He finally rendered the work complete when Wisdom herself revealed herself. From the "elevation drawing," He constructed the building once the foundations were laid—that is, with man absolved from guilt. Furthermore, this most noble building is completed daily by the work of the Holy Spirit, until we come to the finishing of this state of corruption, and man finally attains his end after corruption; man, for whose sake all things exist, just as he exists for the sake of God. But as the work of creation is attributed to the Father, so restoration or redemption is attributed to the Son (or Wisdom); however, the "building up," which is in charity, is usually attributed to the Holy Spirit. Finally, the "end" or purpose belongs properly to the entire Trinity, just as the eternal mind was an inseparable Trinity and Unity from the beginning. In a similar way (although thought, unfolding, and work—and power, wisdom, and eagerness, love, or will—cannot and should not be confused or separated, as these things are stirred in the mind before they are done by us), we say that the work belongs to power, the thing devised and sketched in the mind belongs to the unfolding of wisdom, and the actual effect belongs to the will. But because we are temporary beings, we cannot individually increase a thing for so long that we coincide with the works of the Holy Spirit. Yet in the beginning and the end, in the thought (which brings great pleasure) and in the use and the end, all three properties are established as one, enjoying their own happiness in the divine manner. In the first place, God the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit—or Power, through Wisdom, in the will or love of helping—revealed the traces of Himself in the creation of the world. But a much greater faith had to be established, and was established, when the Wisdom of God, the Word or the Son, showed Himself under the garment of our flesh and placed the <term>final touch</term> <note>original: "colophonem". A term for the finishing stroke or crowning achievement of a work.</note> upon the "small world" <note>original: "paruo mundo". A reference to the "microcosm," a common Renaissance idea that the human being is a miniature version of the entire universe.</note>, its matter being entirely purified. Indeed, redemption is a greater work in terms of its effect than creation. Since, therefore, this is most worthy of God, necessary for man, consistent with natural harmony, handed down by prophets and holy men, believed as sacred dogma, and in every way agreeable to reason, it must be held—even at the risk of one's life—that Jesus Christ is God-Man, necessarily incarnated for our salvation and the salvation of all believers.

Since in God "to be able" and "to be" are exactly the same, and since He can do whatever things are most absolute and perfect; and since nothing can be greater or more noble than to unite the lowest things with the highest; it was necessary for God Himself to join human nature to Himself (not separately, but united) before it could receive its perfect completion. For just as it is not enough for a happy composition to have two middle elements sharing...

communicating in one quality, namely air and water, unless the bond of the extremes also be added (I say of earth and fire)—the former for the physical mass, the latter for life and balance: so for the well-being of man it was not enough to consist of body and soul, unless there were added to this bodily mass, mixed from the soil, the nature of fire and of the most simple God, so that this most absolute composite might reform the rest and lead them toward the most perfect happiness of life.

## FROM THE NATURE OF THE GOOD.

It is a matter most certain by the consensus not only of philosophy, but of the whole world: the more common a good is, the more divine it is. By which proverb or sentiment, it appears that God communicates Himself most especially in whatever ways are possible. Truly, He can communicate Himself in four ways: by presence, by power, by union of essence, and by union of person. He is present everywhere. The force of His power, moreover, is seen diffused and scattered even into the smallest things. For nothing lacks a miracle, or a thing to be admired however hidden it may be, which does not itself come from matter. Union occurs in the [Divine] Persons essentially. There remains the fourth communication: which ought not to happen with the good angels, for they have not sinned; nor with the evil ones, because they cannot repent; nor with beings lower than man, which lack all sin and do not require duration <note>Postel argues that animals/plants do not need the specific "duration" or eternal restoration that fallen humanity requires.</note>. It is necessary, therefore, that the union of the Divine Person happen with man, so that He might lead him back to happiness. Therefore, it was necessary for Christ to become the <term>God-Man</term> <note>original Greek: θεάνθρωπον (theanthrōpon). This term emphasizes the union of two natures, divine and human, in one person.</note>. Otherwise, God would have begrudged us one of His ways of communicating; a thing which must not be admitted. By these reasons, it was altogether necessary that at some time God should be seen joined to man. Even if this were not necessary, nor predicted by angels, Sibylls, prophets, and even by demons forced to confess it, nevertheless Christ showed enough in Himself that God was joined to human fragility in Him. For the resurrection of Christ alone is seen—and truly is—as much greater than creation as eternity is more excellent than corruption. For we are born to die; but He lives, never to die. But since the followers of Muhammad <note>original: "Muhamedicí".</note> disagree with us concerning His death, even though they do so against the consensus of the whole world, I judge they must be persuaded by those external testimonies, lest they say we have forged these things.

## ON THE DEATH OF JESUS CHRIST THE SON OF GOD
### and of Mary, external testimonies. CHAPTER 12.

**S**ince it is certain that everything we hope for and have from Christ depends upon the death of Jesus Christ, we would believe the rest in vain unless we preach and believe that He took our infirmities upon His own body and fixed them to the cross. To believe other things about Him not only does not help, but is even vehemently harmful. Therefore, when Muhammad—not entirely ignorant of either our religion or the Jewish religion—perceived this goal we had set, he wished to attribute all other things to Him, even greater things than have been handed down to us in writing, yet he takes away His divinity and His death, upon which the hinge of our salvation turns. He did not do this because he thought what he wrote was true, but so that by removing Christ's merit and purpose, he might seize a prophetic tyranny for himself; these things will be exposed more widely in their proper place in his life. In this place, I will deal with him briefly. If you do not wish to believe the Gospel, O follower of Muhammad, I shall produce other most certain witnesses, most different from us and entirely opposed. From the pagans: Pilate, who had judged Jesus; Abgarus <note>King Abgar V of Edessa, who in legend corresponded with Jesus.</note>, who had not yet believed in Him; Tiberius, Hadrian, the Roman Senate, the reproaches of all the Gentiles, Phlegon, Lucian, Pliny, Plutarch, and others. From the Jews: both all of them in general, and six hundred places in those books with which they have tried to provoke Him, and from the Talmud. Pilate himself, after he had seen that He had risen, then wrote this letter concerning Him to Tiberius Caesar.

Pontius Pilate to Tiberius Caesar, greetings. Recently it happened (which I myself later proved) that the Jews brought a cruel punishment upon themselves and their nation. For when it had been promised to their fathers that God would send them a holy man who would be called their king...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument regarding the unique status of humanity. Having previously discussed the necessity of a mediator between God and the physical world, he now explores the original state of Man (Adam) as a "microcosm" and the historical evidence for human longevity, which he uses to prove the superior physical and spiritual condition of early humanity before it was further corrupted by sin.</meta>

->ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-

...none more excellent, none more free. For, being established at the very peak of the whole of visible nature—which the Greeks therefore called the <term>microcosm<note>Greek: *mikrokosmos*, meaning "little world." This is the philosophical idea that a human being is a miniature summary of the entire universe, containing both material and spiritual elements.</note></term>—as a sort of compendium of the highest and lowest created natures, it was necessary that whatever qualities were most supreme should be implanted within him by the Creator. Indeed, it must be admitted that he possessed the highest freedom in all of nature, than which nothing can truly be greater. We still see great traces of this freedom in those who, by divine inspiration, have looked deep within themselves, though in others we see only faint glimmers. For everything drives into slavery the man who does not depend upon God and himself, but is instead agitated by the whims of fortune and by things placed at the mercy of recklessness and chance. Such a man is actually so far from being free (as all philosophers admit) that he carries about him the foulest masters, infinite in number, from whose tyranny human effort cannot be rescued; so far, indeed, are we removed from that distinguished condition of the first man. 

Placed in that excellent constitution, the most happy Adam (as far as is possible on earth) was able to die by his own power or to be eternal by the favor of God. God did not wish to give him this favor of immortality under such a condition that he would be forced to accept it, lest by imposing that necessity He should take away his free will. For it was placed within him to follow divine prescriptions, either by obeying commands or by not committing forbidden acts. Indeed, unless it were placed within your own liberty to do either of the two, you could not be truly free. Therefore, since he was free and could act against the law of prescribed reason by sinning, he was capable of being both mortal and non-mortal. 

Truly, it must be believed out of God's immense goodness that man received from his Maker a certain law by which he—who had not yet sinned—would not be coerced, but rather directed, since he was capable of straying. It is more certain than certainty itself that God gave him everything pertaining to human happiness. If he kept these prescriptions, he would be happy and eternal; if he broke them, he would eventually pass away, oppressed by innumerable calamities in life. 

Furthermore, that man once possessed a more majestic body than he does now, and a life that was almost immortal by its own nature, is argued by the fact that even after the corruption of the fall, men lived nearly a thousand years before the Flood. This is established not only by our own sacred writings—that is, the divine letters handed down by Moses—but also by the testimony of outsiders. Valerius Maximus, citing Xenophon, reports that a king of the Latins lived 800 years, and his father 600; to these he adds Dandon, who lived 500 years, and Litorius Epius, who lived 300. Berosus and Hellanicus <note>Ancient historians often cited by early modern scholars to provide "pagan" corroboration for Biblical accounts.</note> write that there were many men of very long life before the Flood. 

<margin>
Josephus mentions these in his *Antiquities*.
</margin>

The lives, deeds, and arts of these earlier people are attested to by two columns that survived the Flood, which were still seen in the land of Syria fifteen hundred years ago. One was made of brick and the other of bronze, so that they might withstand the injuries of the heavens and the elements <note>This refers to a legend recorded by the historian Josephus, claiming the descendants of Seth erected pillars to preserve astronomical knowledge from fire and flood.</note>. Who has not read that the lives of the famous peoples—the Seres, the Macrobii, the Ethiopians, and the Pandorans—were three times longer than ours? 

Moreover, so that it might be less surprising that the Almighty God gave this to the first man and his descendants, even human art has advanced toward this goal. Who before our age, not so long ago, has not heard it reported and read that a certain John lived 300 years (whom they therefore call "John of the Times")? <note>Johannes de Temporibus was a legendary figure said to have been a guard for Charlemagne and to have lived for over 361 years.</note> Truly, that lifespan, increased through frugality and moderation, is much more wonderful than the ancient one; for in the ancient age, men did not suffer from many corruptions, if you compare both to our own time. 

Lest public evidence be lacking (though which Pope it was does not occur to me now), there are certain decrees preserved in Rome by which a certain German man wished to testify to posterity that by a certain chance he had lived 500 years. He reports of himself: that having once been captured by pirates, he was sold to a certain petty king in Arabia. Many years later, when the ruler of another territory greeted this king through ambassadors, he sent him a gift of a certain medicine by which, as he said, life could be prolonged for many years. Since the king did not wish to try the danger of it on himself (as all things are suspect to tyrants), he ordered the captive German to try it. Thus it happened that after five hundred years, or a little less, he went to Rome and wished this to be publicly signified by a papal diploma. There is also a noblewoman in England (whom they say is from Tormeriaco <note>Likely a reference to a specific localized legend or a misspelling of a French or English estate name.</note>), who, while intent on hunting, happened by chance upon an alabaster jar full of ointment; having anointed himself with it, a countryman lived 300 years in good health...

He provides historical and legendary evidence, ranging from biblical patriarchs to a 500-year-old German captive, to prove that human life was once much longer and more robust.</summary>

...he remained unharmed, except for laboring under the pain of the soles of his feet (which he had not anointed). There are many such instances; if we marvel at human art in these things, what must we judge concerning the power of Nature and of God? Lucian left a record in his writing *On the Long-Lived* <note>original: *de Macrobijs*. Lucian of Samosata was a 2nd-century satirist; his work *Macrobii* lists people famous for their longevity.</note> that many people lived to nearly two hundred years. Truly, however, there is no example so memorable as that of Artephius the mage <note>A legendary figure in medieval alchemy and occultism, often claimed to have lived for centuries by using an "elixir of life."</note> (about whom Roger Bacon <note>The 13th-century English philosopher and scientist who explored the boundaries of medicine and alchemy.</note> wrote), who, while wandering the world and studying his art, wrote about it and used the art of healing to reach the age of one thousand and twenty-five years—a claim he left behind in his writings on magical experiments. Yet no one can exceed the boundaries of time in which our first parent <note>Adam</note> lived, except with the greatest difficulty. From this it is clear: if Adam lived so long (namely 930 years) even after his nature was corrupted, what might he have been able to achieve with the help of God?

To return to the matter at hand, such was the condition of the first man: he had the **ability to die** and the **ability not to die** <note>original: *posse mori & posse non mori*. This is a standard Augustinian theological distinction regarding human nature before the Fall.</note>. But after nature was corrupted—which infected us all—the condition became the **ability to die** and the **inability not to die**. In nature restored by Christ, however, there is the **ability not to die** and the **inability to die**; this is a result of grace, not of nature. Therefore, since Christ, being God-man, took on our flesh and established himself as a guarantor <note>original: *uadem*. A legal term for someone who provides security or bail for another.</note> for man toward God the Father, he took upon himself the aforementioned conditions of the flesh. For if you look to his divinity, which had joined itself to a body, he was able by its power not to die. If you look to our necessity and his own immense goodness, it was altogether necessary for him to die. Finally, that same flesh, having been raised, confirmed the third state <note>The state of immortality/glorification.</note>.

And likewise: he shared with the first innocent man an immunity from sin; he shared with the corrupted man the punishment and other defects; and from the third condition (which belongs to those who have taken his name) he shared the fullness of grace. This grace is indeed greatest in the saints, yet it does not yet seem to be fully completed. The fourth state is that of the blessed and of divinity: the **inability to sin** and the **inability to cease from the contemplation of God**. For the very humanity of Christ the God is held in admiration of the divinity joined to it. Thus it is also established that he had, and has, two wills. His human will felt our calamities and fled from death; his divine will was the complete opposite. For "he was offered because he himself willed it." <note>A reference to Isaiah 53:7 in the Vulgate translation.</note> Therefore, his death for us was so necessary—in order that he might pay the penalties owed by us in his own body—that otherwise his coming would have been entirely in vain. For it would have been rightly impossible for any human or angelic power to satisfy God for our sins. From his fullness, therefore, we have all received; otherwise, his presence would not have helped us, unless he had restored the original purification into the nature of our flesh, which was cleansed in his name.

But if he purged us in the baptism that is performed in his blood, why did he not entirely restore our original freedom? And why does a person who has been "dipped" <note>A reference to baptism, from the Greek *baptizo*, to dip or immerse.</note> still produce another child with the stubbornness of the "seed" <note>Referring to the transmission of original sin through biological generation.</note>? There is a very familiar example in human affairs. If you graft <note>original: *insitę*. Postel uses the analogy of botanical grafting (*insitio*) to explain why the children of Christians are still born with original sin.</note> a noble scion or bud onto an ignoble and wild trunk, it causes the fruit to differ from the trunk and to follow the nature of the graft, as if the previous nature were dead and abolished. Thus, those fruits do not reflect the first nature, but the added nature, as long as they are in use. However, if the seeds from even the best fruit are then committed to the best earth, they do not produce a tree similar to the grafted scion, but return entirely to the original [wild] nature. So it is in a Christian man. If he is baptized and produces fruits worthy of repentance, he is accepted by God, and those fruits are good. But if his offspring is not washed in holy baptism, undoubtedly whatever he produces is "wild," depending on the vice of the first nature.

There is another far more excellent reason why it was necessary for Christ to suffer for man (and not merely to act as a prophet and then be snatched away into heaven for fear of death, as Muhammad <note>original: *Muhamedes*. Postel is refuting the Islamic view that Jesus was not crucified but was taken up to heaven by God.</note> wishes to persuade us), and to pay whatever cause of sin was owed. We shall persist in our example of the "guarantor." Since man was miserably lost and—like a person with dropsy <note>original: *hydropis*. Dropsy, or edema, was often used in literature as a metaphor for an insatiable, self-destructive desire or greed.</note>—indulging himself toward his own destruction, no human satisfaction (for God is so just) nor even the works of all mortals could reconcile him to God; instead, all would have perished most miserably. Therefore, the thing to which man was most especially liable was death. There is no more grievous punishment in this life than death, and it is twofold: of both the body and the soul. Concerning which I shall speak...

<page-num>92</page-num>
<header>ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD</header>

When the immortality of souls is discussed, it will appear to those who rightly estimate the human condition that man’s obligation toward God is so great that it exceeds the powers of the entire world. For even if there were a hundred worlds equal to this one, inhabited by countless men, they could not justly repay the benefit bestowed upon a single man alone. Who could contemplate the vastness of the sky and the world? This was prepared for the benefit of man. Who could count all those things born from these elements? They are under human dominion. Who could conceive in his mind the gifts of the body—sense, movement, life, sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch—or the use of things which he employs for utility and necessity? Who would not marvel and be utterly stunned if he were to look more closely at the gifts of the mind? And could man repay these things? Scarcely.

But if, having neglected these gifts, he should even act against them, what punishment do you judge him worthy of? What son would not be marked with the brand of an ungrateful mind—one upon whom a father had bestowed the smallest part of similar benefits—if he did not acknowledge, praise, and exalt the giver? Of how great a punishment would he be worthy if he even brought war against his own father and, at last, destroyed himself willingly and knowingly? From these things especially, it can be seen how indebted man is to divine providence, and how guilty he is on every side; so that nothing more lenient could be owed to him for his merits than death, proscription, and perpetual exile from that father against whom he had committed such wicked things—he who wished to destroy himself, kill all his brothers, and drive his father from his own seat, and did so as far as he was able.

Therefore, that one Son of God of ours, who is infinite and greater than the world in infinite ways, when he took up the name of man, had to pay that greatest debt. He therefore underwent death—and not a common death, but one unheard of, heaped with every kind of punishment—after which he wished to impart eternal salvation to those believing in him. For having been raised and having entered heaven, he opened heaven to us who are grafted into his trunk <note>Postel uses the metaphor of "grafting" (as in gardening) to describe the spiritual union between Christ and the believer.</note>, so that we might produce new fruits of a new life in certain hope. The same demonstration follows from the reason of his supreme goodness. For it is characteristic of that goodness to be widely open, and to employ supreme mercy and inexplicable charity. But no one can have greater charity than when he lays down his life for his friends. Therefore, Christ died for us, the just for the unjust.

If you had any knowledge of antiquity or faith in the Old Testament (which Muhammad <note>original: *Muhamedes*</note> nevertheless urged should be consulted in doubtful matters in many places), you would apply yourselves to these things, and in countless places, you would recognize both that the coming Christ was God among men and that he would suffer the extremes from his own people. Therefore, dearest brothers, whoever does not believe in the death and divinity of Christ is condemned, if he has heard of it. Alas, by the lust of one man and the desire for ruling, you have perished; you are condemned because you are outside the way of salvation. Countless thousands of men have perished by the false persuasion of one man. Your princes, the heirs of a wicked man, keep you in those shadows by the work of crafty men, lest you come to the light of true knowledge. How can it be that any of you believe in the resurrection—though it is written often in the Quran <note>original: *Alcorano*</note>—when no one among you has provided proof of it?

We, however, have besides the faith handed down to us, also a leader who had to suffer death so that he might create faith in that resurrection. <margin>Great authors record that both the Blessed Virgin and John "fell asleep" <note>original: *obdormivisse*. A theological term for death, particularly used for the Virgin Mary's "Dormition."</note>.</margin> We also have Mary and John the Evangelist, who, like Enoch and Elijah, sought heaven in the body <note>Postel refers to the tradition that Mary and John were "assumed" or taken into heaven body and soul, similar to the biblical figures Enoch and Elijah.</note>. Therefore, it is familiar for us to hope for the resurrection, but for you, it is a mockery. For if anyone weighs the life of many, and especially of your magistrates, nothing is more greedy than they, and nothing is more cruel than the soldier. From this, it appears that they believe in nothing after this life, except in words only. For otherwise, they would put a limit on their pillaging.

### WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK I.
### 93

Through doubt and negligence, posterity gradually falls away from the understanding and belief in things once proven. There is a need for a certain diligence in demonstrating and repeating these truths, whether this is achieved through human, divine, or a mixture of powers. Indeed, oblivion occurs for many reasons, but most especially because of the constant fluctuations of worldly affairs and the negligence of our ancestors. Humanity itself, daily joining and changing the forms of diverse matter, nourishes those brought into life and consumes those who have been raised; thus, it weakens their opinions and sciences, even though the remedy of literature <note>Postel refers to "literarum," meaning written records or scholarship, as a cure for historical forgetting.</note> may provide a cure for this. When a province is overturned by war, sacred beliefs perish, and evil and new ones creep in; they spread more widely and easily the more absurd they are and the further they are alienated from reason. Thus it happens that things received from fathers or ancestors are scattered among a few if they are good, but if they are evil, they spread to everyone. For both by the vice of our depraved nature and by sluggishness, as well as by the work of suggesting demons, falsehood itself rules almost the entire lower world. Truth has always resided with the very few. And because the smaller part always follows the larger and worse part, truth has no place; or if it does have a place, because no one can truly fight against reason, it is praised in words but banished in deeds.

But let us deal with an example: What greater or truer persuasion could ever be held concerning a divine man than that which was held concerning Moses, when he enticed his people to himself with wonders and miracles, and forced a tyrant <note>A reference to the Pharaoh of Egypt.</note> to lose a great part of his empire? This matter was carried out in a gathering of six hundred thousand men capable of bearing arms. <note>The biblical figure from Exodus 12:37, implying a total population of millions including women and children.</note> Nevertheless, a few months later, after so many wonders, after the present light of divinity (even while it was still present!), they began to doubt whether they could be saved by God when they were hemmed in by the sea and the army of Pharaoh. 

He confirmed the preceding events by divinely opening the Red Sea, and with them having crossed between walls of water, the enemies were killed to a man, suffocated by the water returning to its place. A few days after the crossing of the sea and these first miracles, because of a slight thirst, everyone doubted the power of God. He wished this power to be represented not by providing water naturally from wells, but from a place plainly sterile. From an entirely rocky mountain, He provided such an abundance that so much could not be had from a very great river. 

Not long afterward, when they suffered any scarcity, they asserted that God was not powerful enough to give them food; the manna sent from heaven persuaded them of the contrary. Finally, they began to complain about their side-dishes. Moses brought it about that there was such an abundance of meat <note>The quails mentioned in Exodus 16 and Numbers 11.</note> sent from heaven that it was equally sufficient for all, both the lowly and the rich. For God is no "respecter of persons." <note>original: "acceptator personarum." A theological term meaning God does not show favoritism based on social status.</note> Yet God gave His gifts in such a way that, meanwhile, a great multitude died a present death to persuade the rest that one must neither doubt divine power nor detract from His greatness. 

Now, with the multitude satisfied in all things, but having forgotten the Creator, they demanded an Egyptian god <note>The Golden Calf, often associated with the Egyptian bull-gods Apis or Mnevis.</note> be made for them. For this, there was need for a great punishment, so that no one would dare to mutter against God anymore. But as we seek adversity by our own "Mars" <note>A classical idiom meaning "by our own efforts" or "by our own warfare."</note> in prosperous times, and perish willingly, factious men began to pour out against Moses what they did not dare vomit against God. Since they did not dare to say what they revolved in their minds out of fear of death—namely, "Who appointed God over us?" <note>The Latin text reads "Quis constituit Deum super nos?" though this likely refers to the rebels questioning the divine hierarchy or Moses's specific appointment by God.</note>—they rose up against the most pious leader and the public order. They said there was no reason why he should be obeyed, for there were many in that gathering who could provide what Moses provided; therefore, it was also permitted for them, or at least for part of the multitude, to preside over sacred matters. 

Moses, whose speech a little earlier had softened the anger of the Creator, perceived this; he permitted them to act according to their own lust, since it seemed so to them. He ordered them to separate themselves as if they were "holier" than the gathering of all others, to take up incense and censers for themselves, and to kindle sacred fires; thus, God would show whether that arrangement pleased Him. The factious men withdrew, gathered together, and burned incense. It is marvelous to tell, and horrible in the doing: the earth, gaping open, consumed them alive. <note>The story of the rebellion of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram from Numbers 16.</note> See what posterity does. ...can be said of a man by God, even when miracles are openly performed by a leader, his own generation scarcely believes; the very nation that lives with him daily disparages him. Yet after his death, most brilliant signs followed, providing faith to the successors of Moses. Therefore, as I was saying at the start of this chapter, that first knowledge was by far the greatest and most certain, so that it might be known what kind of man Moses was. Truly, when those future events which he had predicted are seen to have come to pass, then finally that conviction is confirmed and, as it were, renewed. 

The leader who succeeded him <note>Joshua, the successor to Moses</note>, having called upon God, did the same in the bed of the Jordan as Moses had done at the sea. An innumerable multitude crossed the dry riverbed; he placed a heap of stones in the middle as a sign of the event. Yet these things are not enough. There was a need for signs that would be open not only to the chosen people but would reveal themselves to the entire world. The sun was stopped while Joshua pursued the enemies of the faith with the people of God, making that day much longer than others. The Persian is a witness, who left this recorded in his celestial journals <note>Postel refers to ancient Persian astronomical or historical records.</note>; lying Greece is a witness, falsely ascribing this miracle to Phaëton <note>In Greek myth, Phaëthon was the son of the Sun-god who lost control of the solar chariot, causing a global catastrophe.</note>. How much less strange it would have been to have believed so, when he was ignorant of all things, and to have ascribed divine power to a known scoundrel <note>Referring to the mythological Phaëthon</note>, had that unrefined opinion not had its own witnesses even among men of a more learned age; for there was no lie so impudent in Greece that it lacked both faith and a witness. That halting of the sun, which occurred and was seen with the agreement of the whole world, was thought to be a conflagration. But the author was worthy of Greek cruelty, to whom poetry gave its support. 

There was also the highest admiration throughout the whole world for the backward movement of the sun performed under Hezekiah <note>King Hezekiah of Judah, for whom the sun's shadow moved backward ten steps as a sign of healing (2 Kings 20).</note>, commended in the literary monuments among the Persians; this perhaps gave the origin for another "conflagration" among the Greeks. Is it any wonder that the timelines do not agree? The more refined letters among the Greeks had nothing certain six hundred years before Christ. For even if Homer was somewhat earlier in age, living around the time of Solomon, he nevertheless has no history to which you could deservedly grant your trust. Herodotus <note>Often called the "Father of History," though Postel here doubts his accuracy.</note>, four hundred years later than him, scarcely earns trust even in Greece. For deeds long since performed in other kingdoms, brought only by report—and gaining strength by the length of the journey—only then finally arrived there when they had grown old elsewhere. The Latins, truly, had only recently accepted the use of the alphabet. 

But not to wander too far, through the innumerable deeds performed by the divine will of his successors, Moses earned the weightiest credibility—right up until He came whom he himself had predicted would come, about whom the holy prophets had foretold in countless oracles. Then Moses ceased to be celebrated, a new light having dawned with the birth of Jesus Christ, the God-man. Even if He had earned great enough authority and faith—for there was no miracle of His (unless He willed otherwise) that was not performed in the sight of at least a thousand men, and in various places and regions—nevertheless He began to have by far the greatest authority when, by the invocation of His name alone, or even by the sign of the cross alone, all His disciples miraculously performed all those same wonders which He himself performed in His own name—and if the occasion arose, even greater ones. Therefore, they did not demonstrate the divinity of their Teacher through predictions of the future or prophecies in the manner of the ancients (for after the divine remedy, none remains, nor after the truth can anything alien slip into its place that is not false), but by the presence of divinity, they showed that nothing is difficult or impossible for God. They healed every kind of disease; they restored life and soul to dead bodies even when they had been kept for a long time, preserving them for many years afterward. They cast out demons from the body. In short, nothing was difficult for them; they could do all things in Him who strengthened them: Jesus Christ. 

Although Muhammad <note>original: "Muhamedes"</note> wished to diminish this through the whole tenor of his persuasion, he was nevertheless forced to admit it in more than one place—either so that by mixing some truth with falsehoods, he might entice through those flatteries the simple Christians who had themselves seen and read of the miracles. For he says that men dressed in white garments (by whom he means the Apostles) performed miracles; and he proposes a parable about them in the Sura of Jesus <note>original: "Sora iessu." Postel likely refers to Sura 19 (Maryam) or references to the disciples (al-Hawāriyyūn) in the Quran.</note>. ...is said to return to God. Come now, oh true lovers of truth, let us weigh everything more diligently and compare the opinions of the world with the works of the faithful who believe in Christ, and let us see men who are truly transformed. This world of ours (I mean this dregs of humanity that depends on the whim of fortune), what crimes does it not commit? What fraud does it not devise? What tragedies does it not stir up? What law is so holy and inviolable that it does not pervert for the sake of acquiring wealth, favor, or a little bit of glory? A man rushes into a thousand dangers while he thinks he is securing peace for himself by right or by wrong; and while he seeks reasons for a longer life, he perpetually has death as a companion, carries it, and summons it. 

However, a man once truly devoted to Christ—both in his soul and through outward signs—in order to commit nothing unworthy of divine goodness and to present himself to men in a way that leads to their salvation, first denies himself, strips off his own lust, and takes no care for his own body. Whatever he has, he desires it to be provided for others, not himself; he covets no one’s property; he bestows his own on everyone; he prays for his enemies, nurtures them with kindness, and breaks their resolve through patience, preferring to suffer death rather than to commit a crime. In short, he denies himself and all his possessions rather than act against what is right and just. Although many pagans <note>Postel uses "ethnici" to refer to non-Christian classical authors like the Greeks and Romans.</note> left this sentiment in writing, none of them ever confirmed it with their deeds. Aristotle left it written down, and Plato approved of it: that it is better to die than to act against virtue. Horace <note>A Roman lyric poet of the 1st century BCE.</note> depicted the good man as one "who fears disgrace more than death" <note>original: "peius leto flagitium timet"</note>. Truly, those are merely words; these are deeds. Whom can you show me from the world who preferred to die rather than commit a crime? Yet they all confessed it was better to do so. Therefore, every one of them acted against their own conscience and condemned themselves. They were so depraved under Satan and nature that they saw in the knowledge of the good only their own judgment, not a remedy. 

To a Christian or a truly pious man, however, it seems so hard to commit an unjust deed that hundreds of thousands of millions have perished for the sake of asserting the truth and repudiating the false; they were most ready for death out of fear of sin. And so that a greater power of divinity might be seen, even infants rushed into death spontaneously and persistently, lest they eventually perish through sin—those who were entirely ignorant of sin, having been driven toward happiness by the Holy Spirit even before the age of discretion. When the princes of the world saw this, driven by the furies of Satan, they knew they would inflict a more grievous punishment on girls and virgins if they gave them "to a pimp rather than to a lion" <note>original: "lenoni, quàm leoni"</note>, as Tertullian <note>A prolific early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) known as the father of Latin theology.</note> says. For no wild beasts dared to touch those holy bodies unless the one being offered was willing. That constancy, clinging to the souls of Christians against the judgment of the entire world, proves that God alone has truly transformed the minds of those men and shows a present reward for the future life. For how else could it be that they were so entirely different from the minds of other men and the corrupt senses of public opinion? Especially since they were composed of the same elements and soul as the rest? How, I say, could this happen unless that transformation proceeded from God as its author? For He alone knows how to alter the nature He composed. Nor is there any reason for tyrants and executioners to say there is such power in magic. For the least of Christians could defeat every kind of magician with the sign of the cross.

Furthermore, as Tertullian says in truly golden words: "Nature has drenched every evil with either fear or shame. Criminals, after all, long to hide, avoid appearing in public, tremble when caught, and deny their crimes when accused; they do not confess easily or always even to an enemy. Certainly, when condemned they mourn, they turn the impulses of an evil mind against themselves, and they blame fate or the stars. They do not want the crime to be their own, because they recognize it as evil. But what is similar to this in Christians? No one is ashamed, no one repents, unless they regret not having been a Christian sooner. If one is marked out, he glories in it; if he is accused, he does not defend himself. When questioned, he confesses even voluntarily; when condemned, he gives thanks. What kind of evil is this, which has no fear of the martial evil? No shame? No evasion, no repentance, no lamentation? What kind of evil is this, in which the accused rejoices, whose accusation is a prayer, and whose punishment is happiness?" Thus far Tertullian.

...it is possible for man) through God, while the miracles of the leader were manifest, that same generation hardly believed; indeed, that nation which dealt with him daily disparaged him. But after his death, much more brilliant signs following the faith were shown to the successors of **Moses**. Therefore, as I was saying from the beginning of the chapter, that first knowledge was by far the greatest and most certain, so that the character of Moses might be known. But when those future things which he had foretold are seen to have come to pass, then at last that persuasion is confirmed and, as it were, renewed.

The leader succeeding him <note>Joshua, who led the Israelites into Canaan after Moses.</note> did the same in the bed of the **Jordan**, having implored God, as Moses had done in the sea. A countless multitude crossed the bare bed of the river with dry feet, and placed a heap [of stones] in the middle as a sign of the event. But these things were not enough. There was a need for signs that would not only be open to the chosen people but would also manifest themselves to the entire world. The sun was stopped while **Joshua** pursued the enemies of the faith with the people of God, and it made that day much longer than all others. The **Persian** is a witness to this, having left it written in his celestial diaries; **lying Greece** <note>original: "Græcia mendax" — a common Roman-era literary trope regarding the Greek tendency to turn history into mythology.</note> is also a witness, though it falsely ascribes this miracle to **Phaethon** <note>In Greek myth, Phaethon lost control of the sun-chariot, nearly scorching the earth; Postel argues this myth is a corrupted memory of Joshua’s Miracle.</note>. How much less wonderful would it have been to believe such a thing—since they were then ignorant of all matters and ascribed divine power to a scoundrel known to them—if that unrefined opinion had not had its witnesses even among the men of a more learned age? Indeed, there was no lie in Greece so shameless that it lacked credit and a witness. That standing still of the sun, which was seen and agreed upon by the whole world, was thought to be a great conflagration. But the author of that tale was worthy of Greek cruelty, and poetry gave its support to his version.

There was also the greatest wonder throughout the whole world when the sun retreated under **Hezekiah** <note>Referring to the sign given to King Hezekiah in 2 Kings 20, where the shadow moved backward.</note>, a fact commended in the literary monuments of the Persians. This perhaps gave origin to another "conflagration" story among the Greeks. Is it any wonder that the timelines do not agree? Liberal studies <note>original: "Líteræ humaníores"</note> among the Greeks possessed nothing certain until six hundred years before Christ. For **Homer**, although he was slightly earlier in age (living around the time of **Solomon**), nevertheless records no history to which you might deservedly give credit. **Herodotus**, coming four hundred years after him, hardly deserves credit even in Greece. For events that had happened long ago in other kingdoms reached them only by rumor, gaining "strength" from the length of the journey, arriving there only when they had already grown old elsewhere. Indeed, the **Latins** had only received the use of the alphabet a short time before.

But lest I wander too far: from the countless deeds performed by his successors at the divine nod, Moses earned the weightiest credit—until He came whom Moses himself had predicted would come, and about whom the holy prophets had foretold in countless oracles. Then Moses ceased to be the primary focus as a new light arose: **Jesus Christ**, born as God-man. Although He had already earned great authority and faith—for there was no miracle of His (unless He willed otherwise) that was not done in the sight of at least a thousand men in various places and regions—He began to have far greater authority when, by the invocation of His name alone or even the sign of the cross, all His disciples miraculously performed everything He Himself had done in His own name—and if the occasion arose, even far greater things.

Thus, they did not demonstrate the divinity of their Teacher through predictions of the future or prophecies in the manner of the ancients (for after the Divine Remedy, nothing else remains; nor after the Truth can anything foreign take its place without being false), but by the presence of divinity, they showed that nothing is arduous or impossible for God. They healed every kind of disease; they restored life and soul to dead bodies even after they had been kept for a long time; and they drove demons from the body. In short, nothing was difficult for them: they could do all things in Him who strengthened them, **Jesus Christ**.

Although **Muhammad** <note>original: "Muhamedes"</note> wished to diminish this through the whole tenor of his persuasion, he was nevertheless forced to confess it in more than one place—either to mix some truth with his falsehoods or to entice simple Christians, who had seen and read of the miracles, with such flatteries. For he says that men clothed in white garments (by whom he means the **Apostles**) performed miracles; and concerning them, he proposes a parable in the **Surah of Jesus** <note>original: "Sora íeſſu" — Postel likely refers to the parts of the Quran (Surahs) that discuss Jesus (Isa) and his disciples, such as Surah Al-Ma'idah.</note>. But there is no need for that confirmer, except so that the unhappy Muham[medans]...

# GUILLAUME POSTEL BOOK I
## ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
### 95
f 1

...be said to return to God. Come then, O true lovers of truth, let us weigh everything more diligently and compare the opinions of the world with the works of those who faithfully believe in Christ, and let us see men truly transformed. This world of ours (I mean this rabble of humanity that depends on the whims of fortune), what crimes does it not commit? What frauds does it not devise? What tragedies does it not incite? What law is so sacred and inviolable that the world will not pervert it for the sake of acquiring wealth, favor, or a little bit of glory? A man rushes into a thousand dangers while he thinks he is securing peace for himself—whether by right or by wrong—and while he seeks the means for a longer life, he constantly has death as his companion, carries it with him, and summons it. 

But a man who is truly and from the heart devoted to Christ through signs, so that he commits nothing unworthy of divine goodness, offers himself to others as a means by which they might obtain salvation. First, he practices <term>self-denial (abnegatio)</term> <note>Postel uses the term 'abnegat' to describe the total surrender of the self to God's will.</note>, strips off his own lusts, and takes no selfish care for his own body. Whatever he possesses, he desires it to be used for others rather than himself; he covets no one else’s property, but bestows his own upon everyone. He prays for his enemies, nurtures them with kindness, and breaks their hostility with patience; he would rather accept death than commit a crime. In short, he denies himself and all his possessions rather than act against law and equity. 

Although many pagan writers left this sentiment in their books, none of them confirmed it by their deeds. **Aristotle** <note>The famous Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE).</note> left it in writing and **Plato** <note>The student of Socrates (c. 427–347 BCE).</note> approved of it: that it is better to die than to act against virtue. **Horace** <note>A leading Roman lyric poet during the time of Augustus.</note> painted the "good man" as one who fears disgrace more than death. But those were merely words; these [the Christians] are the deeds. Whom from the secular world can you show me who preferred to die rather than commit a crime? Yet they all confessed it was better to do so. Therefore, every one of them acted against their own conscience and condemned themselves. They were so suppressed under Satan and a depraved nature that in their knowledge of the "good," they saw only their own judgment, not a remedy. 

To a Christian or a truly pious person, however, committing an unjust or wicked deed seems so harsh that hundreds of thousands have perished for the sake of asserting the truth and repudiating falsehood. They were most prepared for death out of fear of sin. And so that the greater power of divinity might be seen, even infants rushed headlong into death of their own accord and with persistence, lest they should eventually perish through sin—they who were entirely ignorant of sin, driven toward happiness by the Holy Spirit even before the age of discretion.

When the princes of the world saw this, driven by the furies of Satan, they realized they could inflict a more grievous punishment on girls and virgins if they gave them to a **pimp** rather than to a **lion**, as **Tertullian** <note>An early Christian author (c. 155–220 CE) from Carthage.</note> says. For no wild beasts could have truly argued that God alone had transformed their minds, as the judgment of the Christians remained fixed against the opinion of the whole world, displaying the present reward of a future life. For how else could it happen that they were so entirely different from the minds of other men and the corrupted sense of popular opinions? Especially since they were composed of the same physical elements and soul as the rest. How, I ask, could this happen unless that transformation proceeded from God the Author? For He alone knows how to alter the nature He composed. Nor should the tyrants and executioners say there is such great power in magic; for the least of the Christians could defeat every kind of magician with the sign of the cross.

<margin>In the *Apology*, chapter 1.</margin>
Furthermore, as **Tertullian** says in truly golden words:
> Nature has imbued every evil with either fear or shame. Finally, evildoers long to remain hidden; they avoid appearing; they tremble when caught; they deny when accused; even when tortured, they do not easily or always confess. Certainly, when condemned, they mourn; they turn the impulses of an evil mind against themselves; they blame fate or the stars. They do not want the deed to be theirs, because they recognize it as evil. But what is there similar to this for Christians? No one is ashamed, no one repents, unless it is that they were not Christians sooner. If one is marked out, he glories; if he is accused, he does not defend himself. When questioned, he confesses even of his own accord; when condemned, he gives thanks. What kind of evil is this, which does not have the fear, shame, evasion, repentance, or lamentation associated with a crime? What kind of evil is this, for which the defendant rejoices, whose accusation is a wish, and whose punishment is happiness?

These are the words of Tertullian.

## 96

<margin>
The pious who today believe the **Gospel** in **Germany** and in other regions do not despise true **miracles**, such as those performed by the **apostles** in the name of **Christ**, and such as **God** often performed in the memories of the **martyrs**, to testify to their sanctity and true religion.
</margin>

When I consider these things, I cannot help but be moved by indignation that certain pestilential men—incendiaries of the world, plagues, far worse than **Muhammad** himself, worse than tyrants, and even worse than **Satan** himself—have dared to attribute divine miracles to the devil, even though they were performed through the invocation of the name of **Christ** and **God**. O unheard-of plague! O poison from which the ruin of the whole world proceeds! O plague worse than the **Antichrist** himself! It was not enough to have overturned sacred and public orders, to have cast fire into the midst of **Christianity**, to have trampled the most holy sacraments underfoot, to have torn the **Gospel** apart, and to have overturned the decrees of the apostles; they must also say that he was a most foul demon, he under whom **Hell** trembled, and whom **Satan** himself with his followers was forced a thousand times to confess as **God**. For what else is it, I ask, to trample **Christ** underfoot, to call him a demon, and to deny that he is **God**, than to assert that while his holy name is invoked, while prayers are offered to his holy **martyrs** so that they might implore healing, an evil demon is working miracles? 

But he rightly does not believe the saints can do anything, who believes their souls are mortal, or at least that they do not exist in the nature of things until the judgment. For that is what the "sleep" <note>Postel refers to 'psychopannychism' or 'soul sleep,' the belief that the soul sleeps between death and the final judgment, a doctrine held by some radical reformers.</note> means to those who falsely boast today that they are so imbued with the **Gospel**. These are the nurseries of a most reckless man, an overthrower of the divine order. From this source have arisen **Anabaptists**, <term>Catabaptists</term> <note>original: "Catabaptistę". A derogatory term for Anabaptists, literally meaning 'those who baptize against' or 'drowners'.</note>, and apostate **Jews** from **Christ**. For as many as this opinion has shaped here, they are now almost all either impious, or while speaking frequently of the **Gospel**, they differ not at all in their lives from **Epicureans** <note>Followers of Epicurus, here used as a slur for those perceived as living only for physical pleasure and denying divine providence.</note> and from men living by their own laws. But regarding these, I shall speak in another place. We must return to the propagation of the **Gospel**.

<margin>
But these same people attribute lying signs to the operation of the **devil**. Such things as were done among the pagans, and today are done among the **Turks**. The kind of things **Paul** attributes to the **Antichrist**, and **Augustine** in the 20th book of *The City of God*.
</margin>

How many rhetoricians, even those supreme in eloquence, could have persuaded people by the most absolute art of speaking of that which the rough fishermen, ignorant of all letters, persuaded them: that a man affixed to a cross was **God**? And this among the most refined listeners, adorned with every kind of literature, while both letters and worldly fortunes were flourishing and brought to their peak? Truly it was not a human work to have not only conquered dejected, wealthy, prudent, refined, and polished men, but even to have drawn so many into their own opinion that they themselves underwent death spontaneously and of their own accord for the name of **Jesus**. The more the matter was foreign to human sense, the more lively it was. The ignorance of the men would have been more easily persuaded by rhetorical deception <note>original: "fuco rhetorico", literally 'rhetorical rouge' or 'fake coloring'.</note>. But those works and that life full of **God** created the greatest faith by far. Nothing was done in secret. 

While the most celebrated empire of the whole world was flourishing—so much so that nothing could be added to it, and it was already laboring under its own weight—when the disciplines refined by the **Greeks** had now reached their summit among the **Latins**, in short, when nature, art, and fortune seemed to have contended for power, **God** willed to save those who believe through the "folly of preaching" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 1:21.</note>. The knowledge of all doctrines yielded the palm <note>original: "herbam porrexit", a Latin idiom meaning to concede defeat or give up.</note> to rustic simplicity, the recklessness of fortune gradually gave way to nakedness, and all care of the body to neglect. Hence the conflict was all the more grave: while **Satan** exercised dominion in his own followers, the truth remained victorious through patience. 

O, if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths, so that I could at least paint these things <term>in a mere sketch</term> <note>original: "ichnographicè", from the Greek for a ground-plan or floor-map.</note>. **Satan** yielded unwillingly, the empire of the world yielded, and false religion—the more crowded it was with human efforts, the more falsely it was sunk—yielded the power of the world to **Christ** through humility and patience. This was not the power joined to the recklessness of fortune, but that which resisted the truth. Princes learned, just as the commoners did, that they differed not at all in condition from other men; that they owed everything to **God**, and to men as their brothers. "The wolf dwelt with the lamb" <note>A reference to Isaiah 11:6, symbolizing peace under Christ.</note>; the greatest tyrant, driven by the virtue of the **Gospel**, ceased to exercise tyranny over the lambs and began to hold all subjects in the place of a brother. In short, **Christ** made all things one among his own. If today there are no such **Christians**, it is the fault of men and of the times, not of the faith. For men have perverted all things, yet **God** never ceased to reveal himself to the world through the preachers of the **Gospel** with **miracles**, until they were open to all. To some, miracles still live; and today...

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK I.

where, in a part of the world recently opened to us, access to the **Gospel** is established, it is customary for it to occur through miracles and following signs in the name of **Jesus Christ**. By all these things, the truth of the **Gospel** is most greatly confirmed, as well as the divinity of **Christ** and his presence with his own followers; for unless he were **God** and had truly suffered, this could not happen. But if the power of **Jesus Christ** was admirable in that alteration of the souls and opinions of his people—and especially in the constancy of the **martyrs** and the performing of miracles—it was by far greatest in the tradition of the **Gospel**, which must be discussed briefly.

### ON THE CERTAIN FAITH AND AUTHORITY
### of the Gospel. CHAPTER XV.

<margin>Luke, in Acts 1 <note>The author likely refers to the prologue of the Gospel of Luke (Luke 1:1), which mentions many previous attempts to write the history of Christ.</note>, indicates that many tried to weave together the Gospel history, but did not succeed.</margin>
Since **Christ** lived in such poverty of all things that he did not possess even as much ground for the rest of his body as wild beasts have in their dens <note>A reference to Matthew 8:20: "Foxes have holes... but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head."</note>, and in such simplicity and gentleness that he yielded nothing to the most innocent children, and finally in such wisdom and prudence that he could be overcome by no one: how did it happen that his persuasion was received within thirty years? The Jewish magistrates, because of his lack of means and his neglect of status, considered him entirely unworthy of their company; yet, on the other hand, those unskilled in worldly matters, moved by his miracles and teaching—because these things never contradict the deep senses of the soul—judged him to be either **God** or the greatest of the prophets. How could this happen without any force, without the deception of human wisdom, in those very places where he lived his life, unless the very things he had done and taught were impressed upon people exactly as they were, and confirmed by the miracles of those preaching them? How could it be that things which seemed so diverse in a man merged into one in such a way that the same meanings resulted from his doctrine, and were approved by everyone as the things he had done and taught in his life (except for the unspeakable magistrate resisting for the sake of retaining human power)? The **Gospel** is a divine work. For immediately after his death, it was written and preached by **Matthew**; whom **Luke** followed shortly after, a man most skilled in human affairs; not much later **Mark** followed, the disciple of **Peter**; to all of whom **John** added the finishing touch <note>original: "colophonem," literally a finishing stroke or ornamental ending to a book.</note>. Not only did these men write, but up to fourteen others had recorded in writing what they had seen, and others explained more broadly what had been omitted. All these things were preached not only to foreign nations, but first in those places where he had lived. There, although many **Hebrew** magistrates opposed his divinity, nevertheless, because things had happened just as they were written and reported, no one was ever able to deny anything; this is an argument of indubitable faith. For if those men—who were entirely devoid of human authority and even hated because they neglected worldly splendor or glory—had been found to have read, written, or recited anything false, who would not have immediately accused them of lying? Who would not have hissed them off the stage? But so far was **Christ** from wanting to embrace human protection at the beginning of his religion, that even if any were offered, he would not have approved it. His most holy **Church**, in which he reigns present, when it saw such a multitude of **Gospel** writers, decreed that the number should be immediately reduced to four, which it uses now—both for the sake of removing human persuasion and because the holy prophet had foretold that four living creatures, to which they correspond in likeness, would be sufficient for praising the **Creator**. **Ezekiel**, in his first chapter, while painting the image of divinity in spiritual veils, intended that significance. Moreover, that he wanted [human] reasoning removed from the conviction of the **Gospel** appears most clearly in the works of **Clement** <note>Clement of Rome, traditionally the fourth Pope and author of several early Christian writings.</note>, the disciple of **Peter** and companion of the **apostles**, and even the supreme pontiff after **Peter**. For when the **Church** saw that he had written many things about **Peter** (whose *Acts* his work also promises), and had confirmed them with human reasons, and had pierced the **Gentiles** with the highest eloquence and their own persuasions, it did not want that book among the sacred and canonical
