...no one among the learned was considered truly educated who was not thoroughly versed in the knowledge of Greek literature; and this had been the case since the times of Alexander the Great. For who would not marvel that, only a few years after him, seventy-two elders could be summoned from the single senate of Jerusalem and brought to King Ptolemy for the translation of the Law? <note>original: "septuaginta duos senes... pro legis interpretatione." This refers to the creation of the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, which Postel uses to prove Jewish literacy in Greek.</note> Was not Aristobulus most eloquent? Philo, among the Jews, could even be compared to Plato. Josephus, that most famous historian, sufficiently revealed how great the knowledge of the humanities was among the Jews, as he yielded nothing to the Greeks in eloquence and refinement. The Jews, therefore, were not ignorant of human affairs. 

Why then did they not all come to Christ? Wealth, public office, glory, honor, "smoke," and the "popular breeze" <note>original: "fumus, aura popularis." These are idiomatic terms for fleeting vanity and public acclaim.</note>—all of which had to be either abandoned or deemed as worthless—stood in the way. Lest this itself seem a marvel regarding the Jews, it occurs in every nation and province. For as many as are either occupied in the courts of princes or perform the duties of magistrates (if you except a few), they are so far from being willing to suffer even the slightest loss for the sake of the truth, that they hold nothing sacred or holy, provided they can benefit themselves or their own, and acquire the "smoke" of honors. This is the disease of the world. 

From his very eloquence you will see that Luke was most skilled in the Greek tongue. Furthermore, from his professional practice, it is certain that he necessarily read philosophy diligently; otherwise, he could not have been a physician. I do not speak of Paul, who came to us by compulsion <note>A reference to Paul's dramatic conversion on the road to Damascus.</note> after many injuries inflicted upon our people. From their writings, Paul, Dionysius the Areopagite, Ignatius, and Hierotheus seem to be supreme Platonists. Why should I mention Aquila, Apollos, and Timothy, of Jewish descent? The more learned they were, the more quickly they flocked to our side. What was more learned than Hegesippus? What was greater than the younger Philo? They strove to prove our faith by their lives and writings: Meletius, Justin, Quadratus, Aristides, Melito, Theophilus, Modestus, Tatian, Musanus, Bardesanes, Apollinaris, Miltiades, Apollonius, and countless others, both Greek and Latin, no less eloquent than wise. All of these wrote on behalf of our religion to the Roman emperors against false persuasions: they did not only wish to approve of our teachings and live by their rule, but departing from the families, familiarity, friendship, and fortunes of emperors, they even dared to attack with writings those emperors most hostile to us, to uncover for them the vanity of false persuasion, to suggest our own, and finally to die for asserting it. 

If anyone wishes to satisfy himself regarding the erudition that was in Clement, let him read his *Recognitions* <note>An early Christian prose romance formerly attributed to Pope Clement I.</note> (as Rufinus translated them, although I think the translator departed significantly from the majesty of the author); he will see nonetheless that the whole world of academic disciplines was most familiar to him. The works of Justin are extant; the same may be judged of them. Who would not marvel that a Roman senator would voluntarily prefer the Cross to the *trabea*? <note>The *trabea* was a ceremonial robe worn by high-ranking Roman officials and senators; here it symbolizes worldly power vs. religious devotion.</note> Let Tertullian be read. Cyril, Lactantius, Victorinus, Arnobius, Origen, and Basil are all extant; all of whom were engaged for a very long time among the pagans. He who reads these will see that they knew nothing of Aristotle or Plato that they had not considered far more diligently; and yet they preferred the doctrine and cross of Christ to vain opinions and reasonings. I do not wish to linger longer on these. 

I could fill as much paper with the names of men most celebrated in every kind of literature as I could smear with my own writings: men who, having disregarded the vanity of human philosophy, so embraced divine philosophy that they wished for it to be confirmed by the most bitter death and by unheard-of and innumerable torments. If someone should object that they were neither great men nor enriched with great honors and fortunes: I care nothing for the condition they were in, whether of slender or splendid fortune, it matters not. We see the poor seeking riches and wealth with all their might, by which they try to cast off the laws of necessity; we see the rich moving every stone so that an addition may be made from wherever it may be obtained. What sort of people they were before (as I said) does not matter. It is certain that they preferred splendid things of hope and fortune, which not even enemies dared to hope for. <meta>This page continues Postel’s argument regarding the nature of divine law versus human law. Having established that early Christians were often highly educated people who sacrificed worldly status for truth, Postel now addresses why the Gospel's demands seem so difficult or contrary to human nature.</meta>

### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.
### 101

Why would that Creator establish laws so abhorrent to our senses? Since they ought to be of use to humans, not to angels or some perfect nature? The reason is evident: so that while we see that those things which proceed from Him can only be most just, we might also recognize ourselves in them. We feel ourselves to be so depraved and pulled away from the laws of nature that nothing is more bitter to us than sacred sweetness, nothing more turbulent than peace, and we think nothing worse, more profane, more unjust, or more shameful than what is good, holy, just, and honorable. This is done especially so that we might confess—even when we have done all that is placed within our power—that we are **unprofitable servants** <note>original: "inutiles servos." A reference to Luke 17:10, emphasizing that human effort alone cannot earn divine favor.</note>. By feeling ourselves powerless to fulfill those precepts, we may ascribe even those things which were done by us with His help to God as their author. For He gave us to ourselves, He gives us life within ourselves, He supplies the instruments by which we may act well, and He offers the material in which we can exercise our abilities.

The Divine and Evangelical Law differs far from human laws in many other ways, but most significantly in its beginning and its end. For human laws remove—or rather, they busily try to remove—vices from the Republic only after they have emerged. But God, the best and greatest, meets even the **tinder** <note>original: "fomiti." Postel uses the theological concept of *fomes peccati*, the "kindling" or inclination toward sin that remains in human nature.</note> and the root of sin. For example, regarding homicide, human law will say: "He who knowingly and willingly kills a man shall be punished with death." But the divine law says: **If anyone says to his brother "raca," he shall be liable to judgment.** <note>original: "racca." An Aramaic term of contempt meaning "empty-headed" or "worthless," used by Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount.</note> **Love your enemies.** Why such a deep-rooted beginning? Because if hatred, rivalry, complaints, anger, contentions, and **self-love** <term>philautia: a Greek term for excessive or blind self-love</term> did not precede it, there would have been no place for the actual deed. Remedies must be applied at the head. Where there is perpetual love, there can never be malice, or a wound, or death.

How then does the same God seem at odds with Himself? For in the Old Testament He said only, **You shall not kill, You shall not commit adultery,** etc. But in the New, as if greater prudence had been added to Him, He says: **Whoever hates his brother is a murderer** (1 John 3), and, **Whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.** What do these things mean? He wished to treat the Israelite people (as we have already said) in the manner of a wise tutor. Therefore, because of the **hardness of their hearts** <note>original: "duritiam cordis." A common biblical theme explaining why Mosaic law permitted certain things, like divorce, that the Gospel later restricted.</note>, He gave them those laws which were indeed divine, but not much harsher than civil ones. This was so that through the law, which brings nothing to perfection, they might eventually come to the Evangelical law as "half-evil" rather than "entirely evil." The Gospel itself requires a person not just to be good in outward signs, but also most pure in the interior mind. For whoever is such a person, since he lives within himself, can commit absolutely none of the more serious crimes. For that reason, the Law of the Gospel is rightly called **Grace**. The other is called by the name of **Law** because, like the laws God gave to other nations by natural impulse, it established a man as "civilly good." The prophets, understanding this many years before Christ, busied themselves with reducing all legal matters to the purity of the heart. Therefore, the Gospel alone testifies that its author is the searcher of hearts, pulling up the origins and "tinder" of crimes by the roots. Truly, those laws—which the world does not approve of, or if it does, confirms only in word—must be weighed one by one to see how great their utility would be in this life if they were kept.

---

### ON THE MORE DIFFICULT PRECEPTS 
#### OF THE GOSPEL. CHAPTER XVI.

For many reasons, the laws of Christ seem unbearable to ruined men; but for no greater reason than that they suffer from innumerable vices of the mind and body. Whoever burns with bile, and is accustomed to irritate it frequently and make it sharper at the slightest occasion, judges it impossible not to take revenge. He who rushes headlong into lust and seeks "tinder" on all sides to incite his passion cannot bear this precept: **He who looks at a woman to lust after her,** etc. If anyone is held by the pursuit of glory and "smoke," you could never persuade him that he who is least and most abject should be the greatest of all, the most dear to God, and the closest.

He argues that these difficult commands are intended to show humans their own depravity and their total dependence on God's grace.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument regarding the psychological and spiritual resistance humans feel toward divine law. Having previously noted that human laws only address vices after they manifest, Postel now explores how personal vices—specifically greed, ambition, and the desire for revenge—distort our judgment and lead to the creation of false laws, using the example of Muhammad as a foil to Christ.</meta>

### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
### 101

For it would seem that whoever advocated for these things <note>referring to the selfless demands of the Gospel mentioned on the previous page</note> intended to trample upon the splendor of empires, magistrates, and all high dignities. One who suffers from **greed** <note>original: "auaricia." In Postel's time, greed was seen not just as a love of money, but a fundamental spiritual sickness.</note> will never be able to persuade himself that it is better to give than to receive; that everything should be bestowed generously (even upon an enemy), and that ultimately no reward should be demanded for a kindness. So it is in all other matters: as each person is inclined by their passions, so they judge against those things which do not serve their own **lusts** <note>original: "libidini." Here meaning any unchecked desire or passion, not exclusively sexual.</note>. 

But who is not driven off course by the heat of glory? Whom does **ambition** <note>original: "ambitio."</note> not twist and kill? To whom is pleasure not a familiar disease? Whom does the madness of **revenge** <note>original: "uindictæ."</note> not drive insane? Over whom does anger not exercise its tyranny? From whom does the thirst for "having" not demand a penalty? Nor does a man suffer the dominion of just one or two masters; rather, these are the vices of nature: if any one of them once creeps in and occupies the whole man, it immediately summons all the others like **satraps** <note>original: "satrapas." A term for provincial governors in the ancient Persian Empire, used here to mean the subordinate "officers" of a tyrant vice.</note> and ministers of tyranny. O wretched man, you who suffer these things for one fault—that you are ignorant of your own self.

It would indeed be more tolerable if each person perished by their own vices and perished only for themselves. But the more a person is pressured by those vices, the more they struggle to pour them into others. Thus, what once appeared to be a vice in that individual now becomes "praiseworthy" through the fellowship of everyone committing the same act, because he has many associates and colleagues in his opinion—as if a man burns any less simply because he burns with many others. Thence vice rushes into the name of virtue and occupies its throne; from this point on, the names of virtue are indeed splendidly proclaimed, praised, and extolled in this mortal life, but in practice, vice is what is exercised.

Under the pretext of the holy laws of the **Gospel** <note>original: "Euangelij."</note> (because they seemed too difficult for men ruined in mind and body), **Muhammad** <note>original: "Muhamedes." Postel, a scholar of Arabic, often engaged in fierce polemics against Islam, viewing it as a distortion of the "natural law" he sought to restore.</note> introduced his own persuasion, fighting diametrically against **Christ** <note>original: "Christum."</note>. No mortal was ever more deceptive, more stirred to revenge, or more ruined by the filth of all vices than he. For he used to boast that in one hour he had satisfied fifteen of his wives and handmaids. Furthermore, those he held as his closest friends, if they offended him by even a nod, he would kill while they slept in their beds. Therefore, he said his law was a "middle ground" between the Old and New Testaments, and he decorated it with "noble deeds" of this kind. It was not enough for him to perish so that he might rule; but because vices were criticized in him, lest they seem like vices, he issued laws daily so that the same things were permitted to everyone as were permitted to himself. 

The **revenge** <note>original: "uindictam."</note> which he exercised most willingly, he wanted confirmed by law: thus he asserts that a man is condemned who does not immediately repay an injury with an injury. So, throughout his entire law, in order to protect his own vices, he established laws favorable to his own crimes—as will be evident in the study of his life and doctrine. 

Princes, courtiers, and men placed at the very peak of worldly affairs do almost the same thing everywhere. Although they do not pass formal laws permitting the license of crimes, yet while they serve as the example, their consciences make them fear to prohibit in others what they themselves commit. Thus it happens that from the very source where justice should flow to humanity, a stain and a plague instead crawls into everyone, for this one reason: that they do not obey the most holy laws of Christ. 

If, for example, while they are pursuing revenge, they were to propose this to themselves: first, that they act against the law of God; second, that it is necessary to bring a stain upon nature; that whoever seeks revenge is pressed by infinite fires; that he who thirsts for a neighbor's blood must perish himself, or the other must, or both; that he will involve his family and parents along with his adversaries; and that he can be defeated with great shame or "win" without any true **glory** <note>original: "gloria."</note>, killing a man and destroying nature itself, which was the cause of life and endurance. 

Anyone who weighed all these things—would they not consider it far better to flee so many evils and conquer an opponent with patience, rather than undergo so many dangers for the sake of a trivial "opinion" of honor? Especially since after the crime is committed, he will only gain envy from the many, disgrace from the good, and a false "glory" from a very few—and those fawning flatterers and enemies hiding under the name of friendship. I am silent about the eternal repentance for the deed, the eternal **Furies** <note>original: "Erinnyes." In Greek mythology, these are the female deities of vengeance who hounded those who committed crimes against natural order.</note>, and the neglect of God. For all these things must seem trivial to a man who, for the sake of a flimsy reputation, rushes headlong into death.

...destroys. "But," someone says, "if I suffer an injury with impunity, I will only invite more wickedness from a dishonest man through my **patience** <note>original: "patientia." Here meaning endurance or long-suffering in the face of provocation.</note>." It can be restrained by **laws** <note>original: "legibus."</note>: approach a judge. But because you share a part in the crime, and perhaps you even provoked the one you now wish dead, you prefer to decide by your own will rather than by what is just and good. If, by inflicting a reciprocal injury on another, you could recover your health or the things you say perished because of him, that would indeed be deserved. If he took your foot, and his was useful to you while yours was lost, you might want to obtain it from him; and so it is in similar cases. That would at least be something. 

But since you gain nothing else from **revenge** <note>original: "uindicta."</note> except that you hurl a reproach back at him, it is a wonder why you are so insane. You cry out that he is a worthless and shameful man because he caused harm to a human being. But do you not see that when you desire to inflict harm upon him, you take those same crimes upon yourself? For you are causing harm to a human being. "But he did it first," you say. He will say the same of you afterward. Therefore, because of revenge, there will be an eternal **hell** <note>original: "infernus." Used here to describe a state of perpetual misery or spiritual ruin.</note>, both in this life and the next. 

Vengeance belongs to God alone. He who carries it out in his own name denies God, whom he does not believe to be just or capable of returning rewards according to merits. However, to carry it out in a public capacity, or for the sake of the afflicted and the needy who require help—that vengeance, if it cannot be settled otherwise, is most just. Yet no one cares for this kind of justice; everyone pursues the former kind. 

Someone will say: "It is given by nature to all living creatures to protect themselves and their own." Indeed, it is established by nature for all animals that lack law to kill and pursue their enemies. But for a human, whom **reason** <note>original: "ratio."</note> commands, who governs himself by judgment, and who looks within himself after the first impulses—for him, laws have been laid down, judges established, and a path for the repayment of injury lies open. He must not rage against his own kind as oxen, horses, or lions do. For civil laws prohibit this in vain if we must act simply because something is rooted in our nature. Those impulses must be moderated by reason; otherwise, one must necessarily rush into all other dangers and deny that God exists by pursuing personal revenge. 

We wish to snatch everything away from God and ascribe it to ourselves. It is no different than if there were many brothers in one family born of the same father, and one, having received an injury from another, wanted to repay it himself, taking away the authority and judgment belonging to the father to keep for himself—even though it is well known by the common proverb: *Everyone is blind in his own cause.* 

But this opinion has grown strong: "If I do not take revenge, I am not **noble** <note>original: "nobilis." Postel is critiquing the aristocratic "code of honor" where refusing a duel or a fight was seen as a loss of status.</note>, I am not brave, I will not be considered a good and spirited soldier." If acting like a soldier means killing a brother or a companion; if it is "noble" to prove in yourself what you condemn in another, then so be it. Why are you a slave to the eyes and judgments of others? What is fame and the judgment of others to you, provided you feel you have done nothing unworthy of yourself? You cannot be changed by another’s judgment. Be good: let them judge you as evil as much as they like, you will not be the worse for it. If it is otherwise, take care to amend what they disapprove of. If they see a deserter in war, or one who is soft and remiss toward the enemy, or one who rejects commands, then there would be a rightful reason for concern regarding fame and honor. 

But "smoke and fame" change nothing in the reality of things. That opinion twists us because we hold and believe in neither God as a father nor man as a brother. From here comes the root of all evils: **hatred** <note>original: "odium."</note>. Nothing is more holy or true than that saying of John: *He who hates his brother is a murderer.* <note>Referencing 1 John 3:15.</note> It is now clear enough how much this wretched mortality would benefit by subscribing to the divine precept of pardoning injury, and in how many calamities those who think, speak, and act to the contrary are involved. A perpetual fire burns their hearts, and a continuous fear congeals their blood. For he who wishes to be held as formidable by another must also be touched by dread. 

How much happier is he who breaks anger with a soft response, conquers hardship with patience, makes a friend out of an enemy through kindness, accepts peace in place of war, and, to put it in a word, attempts to reconcile his brother to himself through every kind of duty? There is also a difference in these laws from the civil and **Mosaic** <note>original: "Mosaica." Referring to the Law of Moses.</note> view. For political laws forbid a man from pursuing injuries by his own will after the first impulses of the mind. But whether he loves or hates...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

As they are unable to do so, they neither prescribe nor care for it. **Israelite law** <note>original: "Iſraëlítica." Referring to the Mosaic Law of the Old Testament.</note> permits one to hold an enemy in hatred, and commands it for the same reason we mentioned above. However, the **precept of Christ**, which commands his followers to live together like angels in the highest bond of peace, establishes not only that injuries must be forgiven and vengeance left to God, but also that the greatest friendship must be maintained with an adversary. One must overcome them with such kindness that, whether they wish it or not, they look inward at themselves and confess they were most unjust for repaying good with evil. **If your enemy is hungry**, says **Paul**, **feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink. For by doing so, you will heap coals of fire upon his head.** <note>A quote from Romans 12:20, citing Proverbs 25:21–22.</note> By this speech, he understands that the fire of **charity** <note>original: "charitatis." A selfless, divine love for others.</note> will necessarily fall upon him in such a way that he begins to see himself for who he truly is. Christ is not satisfied if we depend on outward signs, whether in avoiding vice or in conferring a benefit. He demands the **powers of the soul**; if these are lacking, the labor is in vain. We must love and do good from the soul; we must withdraw from evil from the soul. 

He who strives to win over an enemy with kindness seems most like **God**. For while humans are accustomed to provoke God at every moment and turning point of time—striving to do so, blaspheming, neglecting Him, some denying Him by deeds and others even by words—He nevertheless confers benefits upon everyone equally. Therefore, he who wishes to prove himself most truly a son of such a Father must do exactly the same toward all his brothers, both toward everyone in general and especially toward those of the **household of faith**. For a son ought not to be in a better condition than his father. The Father not only does not punish, but heaps the greatest gifts upon them, and often the greater the gifts, the worse the people are; so that, at the very least, bound by those gifts, they might either acknowledge so great a Giver or deservedly perish as ungrateful. 

Conversely, because His own people are already His, He brings them back to Himself through **afflictions**, lest, uplifted by prosperity, they become like the wicked. These people ought to give everything to their brothers because they know God as their common father; the others, however, hoard the things God has given because they act as if they were emancipated, outside the brotherly fellowship. He who loves God the Father above all things, and his neighbor as himself, will undoubtedly take no account of parents or possessions, provided he is joined to the Author of all things. **This is eternal life: that they may know You, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent.** <note>A quote from John 17:3.</note> For this to happen, one must leave all things to possess You. 

The **philosophers** <note>Postel refers specifically to the Greek intellectual tradition.</note> tasted these sentiments in some way, but in such a way that they taught them only in words and not in deeds, as I said before. No one was ever willing to suffer even the smallest loss for the sake of observing a precept of **Plato** or **Aristotle**, because they denied by their lives the laws they laid down. Plato certainly wished to move toward brotherhood in his **community of goods**, but because he did not know how to distinguish what ought to be common and what private, he established a **brothel** <note>original: "lupanar." Postel is critiquing Plato's *Republic*, which proposed a community of wives and children, which Postel views as immoral.</note> rather than a Republic. 

But at this point the world will object: since laziness and the impulse to inflict injury are innate in the majority of men, if we endure everything and give everything away, we open the doors to idleness and voluntarily invite injury upon ourselves. Oh, if only those who object to such things had at one time seen, in the most uncultivated and deserted places of **Egypt**, more than three hundred thousand men whom no law could prescribe anything! <note>Postel is referring to the Desert Fathers and the massive monastic communities of late antiquity in Egypt.</note> Everyone was most wealthy, even though they all lived by profit and the labor of their hands. Riches flowed there from the whole world, where none grew; in the cities, there were as many **communal houses** <note>original: "κoινóβια" (koinobia). These were monasteries where monks lived together in community rather than as hermits.</note> as there were homes. Why should I mention the life of the **Apostles**, and the innumerable multitude following them everywhere in the world? 

It was often seen, by the diligence and example of a single good bishop, that while a famine was distressing the whole world, no one in his jurisdiction felt it at all, due to the greatest charity. It was not that the crops there were more

plentiful than elsewhere, but that they were less private. Each person was eager to put his own goods into the common pool; there was equal abundance for all, and no penury. He who had spent his own first received from others, and in the meantime nothing was lost to the **treasury** <note>original: "fiſco." Referring to the public or state funds.</note>. For **Satan** is accustomed to object this against the perfection of the **Gospel**: if there are not some who are very wealthy, it will not be possible...

He cites the early Egyptian monks and Apostles as proof that a society based on shared goods and manual labor can eliminate poverty and survive famine better than private ownership.</summary>

### ON THE DIFFERENCE IN ORIGIN BETWEEN THE PERSUASION OF Christ, and false religions. CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>The sharing of property. But because of the pursuit of "mine" and "thine," human affairs do not allow it. Therefore the church rejects the dogma of the **Apostolics** or **Apotactics**. See **Epiphanius**. <note>Postel refers to the *Apotactici*, an early Christian sect mentioned by the church father Epiphanius of Salamis, who believed that renouncing all property was necessary for salvation—a view the mainstream Church rejected as an extreme heresy.</note></margin>
Although these matters have been treated extensively, it nevertheless seemed appropriate to touch upon this in a few words here for a greater confirmation of the **divinity of Christ**: by what arts the plagues of wicked scoundrels thrust themselves upon the ignorance of men, and in what way Christ revealed himself to the world in such a short time. However, to weigh these things, we must look at the conditions of human affairs so that we may discern what is according to **nature** and what is against it. No student of philosophy can deny that everything created has within itself a certain hidden cause for **self-preservation**. From this, it appears that individual things, as far as their nature allows, desire a certain duration and—if it were possible—**immortality**, and they seek out all the supports by which they might achieve this. Those things which lack both sense and life, but consist of a simple essence, are nevertheless usually bound by such a link that they are only dissolved with difficulty. For that which does not fight with sense or will, resists through the hardness and persistence of its body; thus we see that those things which tend toward the preservation of things are most in accordance with nature. For if the **Creator** wished that care to rest upon all things, it is most certain that they also most desire to endure. 

Hence, although all corruptible things cannot avoid corruption, they nevertheless fear it most. Therefore, whatever things bring about corruption are most repugnant to nature and resist the will of the Creator—especially those things which tend toward the destruction of men, and particularly if that stain proceeds from a certain choice and deliberation. For things that do not act of their own accord, but spread a common danger or destructive action to their neighbors—such as the corruptions of the air, waters, and other things which bring a stain upon human bodies from the imperfection of nature—these act without the will of the Creator, but not against it, as He permits them; they do not deserve indignation. Likewise, the harms caused by wild beasts and all living creatures are without fault, since the desire to inflict injury is absent. Therefore, only that destruction which proceeds from **evil demons** and **men** is condemned, and it is rightly said to be armed against **God** and **nature**. 

Consequently, it is certain that all **wars** ever undertaken (except for two causes) are against God and nature, because they bring destruction to human nature and a stain upon the things prepared for its safety, contrary to the order of the whole. Those **two causes**, however, must be proven by the example of our own nature. For since nature has granted that all living things—but especially man—should protect themselves and their property, and since whatever things cause harm and bring destruction are either **internal** or **external**, war against both types of enemies is just. Things that are lower than man never labor under internal discord, because they never fight with themselves; for they lack judgment and reason. Man, furthermore, carries an enemy at home, or has an external one. Since he labors under a thousand monsters of vice as if by a domestic sedition, he must first take care to drive that filth from his home and restrain it, before...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument from Chapter XVII regarding the rarity of true followers of the Gospel and the spiritual nature of the Christian life, transitioning into a discussion of the specific sacraments or "mysteries" established by Christ.</meta>

Indeed, good men are rare, scarcely as many as the gates of **Thebes** or the mouths of the fertile **Nile**. <note>original: "Rari quippe boni, uix totidem quot Thebarũ portæ, aut dítis hostía Nili." Postel is quoting the Roman satirist Juvenal (Satire XIII) to emphasize the scarcity of truly virtuous people.</note> Nor should all those who today bear his name be considered among his true followers. For he demands the soul, not external things, except insofar as what is carried in the heart is revealed through signs. Just as in the beginning of all things, God created the highest of powers in the **Wisdom of the Son** without the aid of material things, and gave them to man not by any merits of his own but as a supreme gift; so too did the Son of God, **Jesus Christ**, wish to fulfill the renewal of man without the support of any external power. This was done so that human ability could attribute nothing to itself in this matter, but rather might marvel at it eternally, more than it can comprehend. For just as we know by nature that man is born, made by God, and propagated—because it has happened so—yet we do not grasp *how* it happens; so too we know that men, divinely driven by the man-God Jesus Christ through contempt for the world, conquer its pride and arrogance. Yet how this is actually done, we cannot grasp. For to undergo evils willingly, against the common opinion of mortals—those things which are here called "good"—and to despise everything except God and virtue, that certainly does not come from man. This is the power of the **Gospel**, the difference between truth and lies, and a firm and constant rest even amidst torments.

## ON THE EXCELLENCE OF THE MYSTERIES
### established by Jesus Christ, by which his divinity is also most clearly revealed.
#### CHAPTER XVIII.

In order to establish a certain faith in his power among mortals, Christ, having been raised in body and soul into heaven, promised gifts and, as it were, <term>treasures</term> <note>original: "κειμήλια" (keimelia). These are "heirlooms" or "stored treasures," referring here to the spiritual gifts and sacraments bequeathed to the Church.</note> to all his followers, so that after ten days he provided them. With these gifts, not only were the disciples themselves adorned, but they also rendered those to whom they wished to bestow them just as endowed with the same faculty as those who had first received them. This is the **grace of the Holy Spirit**, which taught various languages, granted power over all kinds of diseases of both mind and body, exhibited the **sacred orders** by whose succession the sacred mysteries would be handed down here, and confirmed the faith already accepted. By those sacred mysteries, we perceive that although Jesus dwells bodily in heaven, he nevertheless moves among us in such a way that he is never absent. For just as it is not enough for the nature of God to have produced all living and breathing things by his favor unless he preserves and cares for what was produced until they reach the end of their life—otherwise it would be better not to have produced them than not to preserve them—so also it was not enough for Jesus Christ to have sent out his disciples well-formed and armed and prepared on all sides against the arts of the **devil**, unless he refreshed, strengthened, and vitalized their strength daily with **heavenly nourishment**. For such is the weakness of our nature that we would immediately fall away from the most excellent things unless we were continually helped by divine power. Those imbued with these sacred mysteries, who received from Jesus the power to bestow them upon others, are divided into three ranks: **Bishops**, **priests**, and **ministers**.

<margin>See Dionysius on the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, also on the Celestial Hierarchy.</margin> <note>Postel refers to the writings of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite (5th-6th century), whose works on the "hierarchies" of angels and the church were central to medieval and Renaissance theology.</note>

These men bestow the sacred gifts upon all those of lower dignity. The **Pontiff** <note>Here referring to the Bishop or High Priest within the hierarchy.</note> holds the place closest to God and perfects the priest and the ministers, while the priest perfects those below him. Such great power has always been seen in that highest order—even if the man himself does not live up to the dignity—that all separate powers yield to him, and divine things assent when he performs the duties of his order. For demons are very frequently cast out from possessed bodies by men who do not lead a sufficiently praiseworthy life; from which it is clear that this is done not by the man, but by the present divinity. The sacred order of pontiffs and priests receives those coming to Christ with the **holy washing** (Baptism); the pontiff alone imposes hands and confirms the faith received (Confirmation). He imposes **penance** on those who have fallen and confess their errors;

...a few, receiving the **Eucharist** in their hand and applying little faith, would find embers, coals, or stones closed in their hand. For not a few, as a proof of their faith, what appeared to others as bread was to them flesh. Finally, those about to die are anointed, and those who are to live together are bound by a **sacrament** <note>referring to Marriage</note>: so that our whole life, through the frequent remedies of Christ, might daily return into grace with Him, provided that repentance is the companion of our past life. And what you might wonder at even more: the princes of many nations, from the time they received Christ (even though they received their anointing for the administration of a kingdom, not for holy orders), are celebrated for unheard-of miracles. This is not through pagan arts, like the **Marsi** and **Psylli** <note>Ancient tribes famous in antiquity for their supposed immunity to snake venom and power over serpents</note> against serpents, but they achieve it through their dignity. The **Kings of France** cure countless thousands of men of the **scrofula** disease <note>original: "scrophularum morbo" - a form of tuberculosis affecting the lymph nodes, traditionally called the "King's Evil" because it was believed the royal touch could cure it</note> by a single touch and by invoking the name of Christ. The **Kings of Britain** were accustomed to heal those with the **falling sickness** <note>original: "morbo commitiali" - epilepsy</note> even when absent, by giving rings. The **Roman Emperor** has an equal privilege, which I understand many others were accustomed to use. From this it is clear that what Christ, the Truth itself, said is most true: *I am with you even until the end of the age.* For in reality, this is confirmed even today.

## THAT NO ONE HAS ATTAINED, OR CAN
### attain happiness, except by observing the precept of the Gospel.
### CHAPTER XIX.

<margin>
The gift of Christ’s healing is bestowed upon everyone.
<note>original: "Charisma sanationis Christi est cuicunq; collatum"</note>
</margin>
Since the discussion is about happiness—not that which is usually perceived through bodily pleasures, nor that which is customarily sought from fortuitous things placed outside our power, nor that which strives for glory and the catching of popular favor, nor that which **Epicurus** places in the absence of pain—I think it must be understood: since none of these can be pure. True and divine happiness, however, is necessarily free from evil and misfortune. For if you measure happiness by the use of the body, you cannot achieve it: because all things that affect the senses of the body are tempered with the greatest troubles. For besides the trouble of seeking them, they become cheap through constant use, turn into disgust, and harm our desires; since the capacity to enjoy is outrun by the will. Suppose you have placed your highest good in **Venusian matters** <note>sexual pleasures</note>: if the capacity is there, the body is weakened, strength is overturned, nature is worn out, and pleasure turns bitter. If the opportunity is lacking, you burn entirely, you itch all over, for that one vice—because you have received a dire tyrant into your friendship. Gorge yourself with delicacies of all kinds: what else do you do but hasten diseases? If you are drenched in perfumes, unless you change them daily, they do not affect the senses; they become cheap through constant use; everything desired for too long wears out. Therefore, that cannot be happiness. 

Now, if you regard those things which are not within you as happiness, what else are you doing but killing yourself with a perpetual vow of desire? For those things help you, as **Horace** says, *as painted pictures help the bleary-eyed, or warm wraps help the gout*. <note>Postel is quoting Horace's Epistles (1.2.52-53) to argue that external riches cannot comfort a mind troubled by desire or fear.</note> For whether you desire or fear, what does it matter to the case? If, whatever you see, be it better or worse than your hope, you become numb with eyes, soul, and body fixed? It is necessary that you do and suffer many things you do not want, and few things that please you, if you must hang upon the necessity of fortune. "But," one says, "glory feeds me." Truly a remarkable reward for immense labors: a tiny rumor coming from a few peasants or ignorant men! Unless you live up to it, it is a disgrace; if you earn the votes of many, you acquire envy, not praise. How many do you see more famous for their crimes and outrages than for their virtues? How often do worthy deeds follow? For it is placed outside ourselves, what others might judge of us. If they are well-disposed, you do not need their praises; but if they are ill-disposed, they will belittle your deeds with slanders or bury them in silence. If they are unknown, what is their opinion to you? Since they cannot report you, they will praise the deeds but will not know the author. Suppose you could earn praise from everyone; what does it contribute? Do you feed on it while absent—

<meta>This page continues Postel’s philosophical inquiry into the nature of true happiness, contrasting the fleeting nature of worldly fame with the enduring stability of a soul aligned with God. It builds upon the previous discussion of miracles and divine authority by rooting the Christian life in the exercise of free will and the pursuit of immortality.</meta>

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

<meta>catchword: Concerning</meta>

...[you might ask yourself], what are you doing? Suppose it helps you: how long will fame last, when even the turning of a single year buries the most brilliant deeds? Meanwhile, consider at what great cost you pursue it. You must abandon yourself entirely and be utterly stripped of your holy freedom. You must be clothed in another's wish, not your own; you must serve the eyes, ears, and palates of others, and experience the servitude of all for the sake of the highest vanity.

Come now, whoever seeks true pleasure, set before yourself Osiris, Alexander, Caesar, Xerxes, Hannibal, and whatever greater monster <note>In this context, "monstrum" refers to an extraordinary or portentous figure, often one of unnatural scale or power.</note> this mortality has produced: how does fame help them now? Where is their posterity? Where are their brilliant deeds? And meanwhile, so that they might claim for themselves glory, fame, and honor—which belong to God alone—what did they not suffer? What disaster did they not bring upon the world? You cannot be greater than they were, and yet now they are nothing.

If you propose "indolence" <note>original: "indolentiam" — here meaning a state of being free from pain or disturbance, similar to the Stoic "apatheia."</note> for yourself in this life, you will never be able to achieve it. However, although these names for happiness are false, there must be something true in the nature of things, of which these others are but imitations <note>original: "simiae" — literally "monkeys" or "apes," often used to describe things that mimic the real thing poorly.</note> and dreams. Since the nature of the soul remains to us (for whatever things are thought to be "good" must belong either to the soul, the body, or to fortune), it is necessary to place true happiness in the soul.

Therefore, happiness is the action of a soul acting freely—namely, the contemplation of its God and of nature, and a disdain for "great things" and for those things subject to the whims of fortune. Whoever, therefore, is oppressed by any desire placed outside our own judgment <note>original: "arbitrium" — our capacity for choice or free will.</note> and outside what is just and honorable, cannot be happy. Certainly, there can be no free will unless it possesses a capacity corresponding to its wish. For whoever wants what he cannot do is oppressed; he who is oppressed is a slave.

What, then, should be done? If the wish should not exceed the capacity, must we become sluggish? Should we hope for nothing? We must not be sluggish. We should hope for those things which are placed within our own power. Thus, every effort should proceed from us in such a way that, in external matters, a completely contrary outcome is expected. If a matter turns out prosperously, let the unexpected results be more pleasant; let adverse things, having been foreseen long before, not weigh us down. Let us be like our [Saint] Paul, *as if having everything, yet possessing nothing* <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 6:10.</note>, or vice versa.

Since, therefore, no action can be performed without a goal, and a certain goal cannot be sought from uncertain things, it is necessary that the end be set elsewhere. For the "final cause" <note>The "finis" or purpose for which something is done.</note> drives whatever acts by deliberation. Therefore, God, one’s neighbor, and the actor himself are the end and goal of human action. For a truly free man does everything either for the sake of divine honor, or for the benefit and salvation of his neighbor, or for the sake of preserving his own innocence. Furthermore, he is accustomed to always follow what reason persuades and never to assent to lusts.

In truth, whoever lives this way (if any man ever could), if divine inspiration grants this to anyone, he is a Christian. For whoever knew the Wisdom of the Father <note>A traditional title for Christ as the "Logos" or Divine Reason.</note> before He came among men, and had glorified Him as God, was saved by His mercy—as must still be held and hoped for those who have not yet heard of Christ. But he who knows Him, however justly he may live, unless he believes he will attain salvation through Him, is utterly lost; for those who act well out of a love for justice also ascribe their righteousness to God, without whom they can do nothing. 

It cannot be, therefore, that one who depends on human affairs is ever happy. For he who is deprived of his wish does not act happily. But it only happens that one is deprived of God if he wills it. Therefore, whatever we do, if we do it for His praise and honor as a common Father, it is certain that we act happily, not expecting the vain and fleeting rewards of great labors, but those which are most certain and immortal. All these things we hope to attain in the wisdom of God—Jesus Christ, God and man—and we believe it more certain than certainty itself. For since nothing in these dregs of mortality <note>original: "fece mortalitatis" — a phrase suggesting the corruptible, sediment-like nature of the physical world compared to the divine.</note> is worthy of virtue (than which nothing is greater), virtue can be granted no other reward for its merits than God and immortality. Therefore, we must now discuss the immortality of souls.

<summary>Postel argues that true happiness cannot be found in worldly fame or external fortune, but only in the soul's free alignment with God and the pursuit of virtue. He concludes that because earthly rewards are insufficient for true virtue, the soul must be immortal to receive its proper reward in God.</summary>

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I, ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS,

<meta>catchword: professor.</meta>

### Proofs. CHAPTER XX.

<margin>1st Argument from the Purpose.</margin>That all things are led by a desire for the Good, that there are various kinds of goods, and that there exists in the nature of things a certain supreme and entirely blessed state in which the peak of happiness is placed—this is proven both by the consensus of all philosophers and true religion, and is confirmed throughout this entire work. Since every agent <note>An "agent" in this philosophical context is any being or force that performs an action.</note> (chance excepted), whether natural or artificial, acts for the sake of an end <note>original: "finis" — often translated as "end," "goal," or "purpose." Postel uses the Aristotelian idea that everything is made for a specific purpose.</note>, it is manifest that the Supreme Agent—than whom none more excellent can be given—also acts for the sake of the most excellent end. Therefore, although there are various acts and intermediate or lower ends established by Him, it is clear that they all strive toward the Supreme End and become, as it were, appendages to it; even if they are not present within the supreme end itself, it is enough that they preceded the work as instruments. The goal of the First Agent and supreme happiness are clearly the same thing. For the "Supreme Good" of any action is first in the mind. And since it is the final cause, it must also be the first in the soul. Yet that which was first in the mind of the Creator was the purpose, and that purpose was immortal and most like Himself: from which it is established that the Supreme Good is immortality. Moreover, since whatever things exist in this lower world, subject to the senses, are prepared for the use of man as if for their best purpose, it is necessary that man—as the most excellent part of the lower world—attain a purpose worthy of himself and most excellent, both in this life and the future: here, virtue, than which nothing is better; there, immortality, than which nothing greater can be given. We see, indeed, that some men partly attain the penultimate end; but as for the ultimate end, since men do not yet attain the Supreme Good in the body, it must be reached by immortal souls. Therefore, it is necessary to posit and believe in the immortal nature of souls. Otherwise, nothing would have been made for the sake of a purpose, unless that which is most excellent also had a purpose. But some godless person—the philosopher Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and Epicurean who argued that the soul dies with the body.</note>—will object: "Virtue itself is the end, bringing its own reward to itself." Hey you, hey you, pay attention! You are supplying me with the very weapons with which I shall pierce you. Virtue consists in action. You must admit that, or you will become a stone. I grant it. But every action is a kind of movement. Every movement, however, naturally tends toward rest, as if toward its purpose. Therefore, since virtue never rests [in this life], it cannot be its own purpose or reward. From which it follows (against you and that lost Satan who introduced this idea to remove God as the final purpose from the minds of men) that an eternal and supreme end is necessarily owed to the action of virtue: namely, Good and Rest. For you will not deny that the supreme cause of the supreme end must come to be, or else you strip off your humanity. Nothing is prior to virtue. Therefore, nothing greater than its reward can be imagined. And just as no one has yet carried the full circle of all virtues within themselves in the body due to the magnitude of the matter, so too has no one been able to grasp its reward in the soul due to its excellence. Truly, I shall not depart from this place before I reveal the arts of the foul demon, which he uses in bewitching men—even those of the greatest reputation. These effects will betray their author. When that plague, most excellent in intellect <note>Referring to Satan as a fallen, yet highly intelligent, being.</note>, perceived that the study, love, and admiration of virtue had been implanted in the souls of individual men by divine providence, and noticed he could not uproot such a seedbed from the Creator's soil, he approached from elsewhere and crept into the citadel through tunnels. He offered a fraud covered in the mask of honesty and a poisoned cake smeared with honey: he began to praise virtue, to extol it to the heavens, and to rattle on about nothing else. He affirmed it to be so great that it should truly be believed to be the Supreme Good. Thus, while he praises the skill of the archer, he removes the target <note>original: "album" — the white bullseye of a target.</note>. Meanwhile, the man—due to the scoundrel’s captured goodwill and insinuation—does not notice that he achieves nothing by beating the air. For it happens that he who has aimed at nothing else but shooting throughout his whole life’s course is, on the last day of his life, just as unskilled in that art as he was on the first.

<summary>Postel argues that because all actions must have a goal (a "final cause"), and virtue in this life is a constant "movement" without rest, there must be an immortal state of rest (the Supreme Good) waiting for the soul. He critiques Lucretius and the "deceptions of Satan" for suggesting that virtue is its own reward, arguing this is a trick to distract humanity from their true target: God and immortality.</summary>

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
<page-num>114</page-num>

<margin>From the nature of the human mind.</margin>
3. The nature of the soul, the intellect, the reason, or the human mind (for it is well-established that a philosopher should not argue over words so long as the subjects themselves are understood) would reveal its own immortality from its very substance, even if it were not proven by any other means. I believe no one relying on the sense of reason—except for *Pomponazzi* <note>Pietro Pomponazzi (1462–1525) was a controversial Italian philosopher who argued that the immortality of the soul could not be proven by Aristotelian reason, only by faith. Postel strongly opposes him here.</note> and his followers—doubts that there is a certain power in human nature that other types of living creatures lack. Thus, it is certain that this can be argued by many proofs drawn both from authority and from reason. Truly, I shall place the authorities of the prince of philosophers, *Aristotle*, in the first position, both to assert the truth and to refute and expose the vanity and impiety of man. Thus it is written in the first book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de Anima"</note>: "The intellect, however, seems to be a certain substance, and it is not corrupted." <note>Aristotle, *De Anima* 408b. Postel is using this to show that the mind is a distinct 'thing' that doesn't break down like physical matter.</note> For it would be corrupted most of all by the decay of old age. The philosopher leaves us to conclude that since the intellect is most vigorous when the body is wasting away, it must be of a different nature than the body. He adds a little later: "Understanding and contemplation are indeed sometimes dulled when something else inside the body is corrupted (as in illness or drunkenness), but the intellect itself is free from passions <note>original: "expers passionum" — in this context, 'passions' refers to being acted upon or changed by external physical forces.</note>." Gathering thoughts, loving, and hating are not its own affections, but belong to that which possesses the intellect—that is, the animated body—insofar as it possesses it. Therefore, when this body or composite thing is corrupted, it neither remembers nor loves. For those things and their like did not belong to the intellect itself, but to the whole composite. But the mind or intellect is something more divine and free from passions; therefore, it is not moved. In that passage, he argues against the definition of *Plato*, who defines the soul as moving itself. For if it were moved, it would suffer change. It clearly appears, according to Aristotle’s own opinion, that our immortal intellect, soul, or mind is of a different nature from bodies, and is immortal. However, because it is not moved, it differs from the soul that gives form to the body. For to be moved happens only by accident. Furthermore, we feel within ourselves that the intellect is not moved into action [locally], since at any instant we can revolve the notions and reasons of things in our mind. It is no different than how rays of light act instantly across the whole area of their power without local motion, just as the eye perceives the images of things in an instant. These three things are most real, yet they are not bodies. Indeed, in the second book of the same treatise, the same Philosopher, after partitioning the nature of living things into the nutritive, sensitive, intellective, and motive faculties, adds: "Concerning the mind and the contemplative faculty, it is not yet clear. For it seems to be another genus of soul, which alone is separated, just as the eternal is from the corruptible." There, all the interpreters agree—even *Averroes* <note>original: "Aben reis" — Postel’s Latinization of Ibn Rushd (Averroes), the influential medieval Islamic philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note>—that this nature of the soul is superior, more noble, and entirely immortal. And yet that "good man," if it please the gods, *Pomponazzi*, in order to pervert that opinion which was cutting his throat, reads it as a question, wishing to anticipate the mind of the author. O Italy, do you even nourish such monsters of men, who are not satisfied with being impious themselves unless they also offer their poison to everyone else? With this ruinous influence, they penetrate the courts of princes and there promise impunity for crimes, where their works are preached daily. A little later at the end of the fourth chapter of the same book, as the Latin commentators note, he says: "Wherever there is reasoning, there must also be all the lower faculties, but not vice versa. Regarding the intellect or contemplative mind, however, it is a different case." From these words, *Averroes* and the other interpreters infer that it is a more divine genus, and not at all subject to the corruption of matter. There are many other authorities in *Aristotle*. But these are sufficient. *Plato*, *Cicero*, and men of a better school of thought <note>original: "melioris hæreseos" — Here, 'heresy' is used in its older Greek sense of 'school of thought' or 'sect' rather than purely religious error.</note> wished to persuade us of nothing other than that souls are immortal. In this they disagree: for some posit them as being entirely free from passions, as *Aristotle* and *Averroes* seem to want; others say they will have an aptitude for the bodies in which they lived and a memory of things done in them: which are the beliefs of *Plato* and ourselves, and these are most true. Otherwise, many absurdities would follow: that souls are a part of God; that there is only one soul for everyone; or that there is neither justice nor injustice.

<summary>Postel uses Aristotle’s *De Anima* and the commentary of Averroes to argue that the human intellect is a divine, immortal substance distinct from the physical body. He vehemently attacks Pietro Pomponazzi for suggesting that the soul’s immortality cannot be proven by reason, viewing such skepticism as a moral poison.</summary>

[...that the soul continues] to exist; and that in the future, there are neither punishments nor rewards. All these ideas clash with the reason and the goodness of the Creator. It is enough to have turned the arguments regarding nature, which were sought from Aristotle, against such impious people. However, the true quality of the soul must be sought from another source. For Aristotle said that the soul was not fully understood by him, except for the fact that it *exists*, and that it is unlike lower things. <note>original: "inferioribus dissimilis." Postel is arguing that while Aristotle proved the soul exists, he didn't fully explain its "divine" quality, which Postel intends to do here.</note>

<margin>From the nature of its substance.</margin>
4. Regarding the nature of its fundamental essence, or substance, the argument can be made this way: Whatever things share the same principles and have all their matter in common must also function the same way in their combined form. For example: all things produced from the four elements <note>The "four elements" refer to earth, water, air, and fire, which medieval and Renaissance thinkers believed made up all physical matter.</note> have their existence, their life, and their senses in common according to their types. Those that share the first quality, share all the first; likewise with the second, and so on for the third and fourth. For it is certain that the things in which they agree have risen from the same principles. But since in man there is the faculty of contemplating, gathering information, and remembering, it must be held as "more certain than certain" <note>original: "certò certius"</note> that this power depends on something other than the physical elements. If that power were in the nature of the elements or in the musical harmony of the body’s composition, then surely it would be seen in lower creatures, proportional to their level, or at least by some slight sign. Yet there is no such thing in lower animals. Therefore, the intellect does not come from lower matter. It remains, then, that it comes from the highest source. But above the moon, all things are eternal; therefore, the mind is also immortal. <note>In the Aristotelian world-view, the "sublunary" world (everything below the moon) was subject to decay, while the "celestial" world (above the moon) was eternal. Postel is placing the human mind in that eternal category.</note> I had already gathered these points against Galen. <note>Galen (129–c. 216 AD) was a Greek physician whose writings often suggested the "soul" was merely a result of the body's physical temperament.</note> Aristotle, so that he would not have to say that souls were born from the divine—which would make it seem like God performs the "labor" of creating every single day—did not trace them all the way to heaven. Instead, he taught that they glide down into lower things from a "fifth element," which they call *entelechy*. <note>term: <gloss>entelechia</gloss> (entelechy). For Aristotle, this was the "actualization" or the form that makes a body alive. Postel identifies it here as a "fifth element" or quintessence to explain its non-physical origin.</note> It is enough that I have obtained this much from him. For Aristotle barely admitted the existence of spiritual things and separate substances, except insofar as he knew them through the senses of the body. Certainly, the mind must be held to have a supreme origin. And since that origin is eternal from its latter part, the minds must also be immortal.

<margin>From the equity and justice of God.</margin>
5. Since supreme equity and justice are necessarily admitted to exist in God (for if He were not just and good, He would not be God), He must also have a subject over which He exercises that power. For it is necessary both to possess justice and to use it. Otherwise, it is useless if it is never in action. Now, justice is spoken of in respect to error and sin. If there were no sinning, nothing would be judged. But only those beings that possess free choice commit sins. For those things that do not act against the judgment of reason or sense do not sin. Therefore, only the demon and the human can commit a sin. For only God, the demon, and the human possess free choice. The demon sinned once so that he might be damned; but humans sin daily. Therefore, it is a work of the most just nature both to be punished and to be gifted with a reward. But when our bodies have rotted away here among us, no punishment can be inflicted upon them. It remains, therefore, that the soul stands as a survivor, in which God may exercise the action of His justice. For if men did not suffer punishment and reward, God would undoubtedly be wicked <note>original: "nepharius"</note>, as He would be giving such impunity for crimes to the impious, to robbers, tyrants, assassins, and those infected with every stain of wickedness; and in the course of this present life, He would cherish them with such prosperity that they would be all the happier the more destructive they were to nature. This reasoning—that God seems to them to be either non-existent or to neglect human affairs—certainly pushes many people into crime with loose reins. But at this point, one must conclude either that the world made itself without an author, or that the soul is immortal. But it is clear that God is the author of the world. Therefore, He takes vengeance on the impious. For if the soul is mortal, God does not exist. For whoever proposes an unjust God, removes Him entirely. If He punishes, some petty philosopher might say, then He is moved by emotions. I will argue by comparison, showing how it can happen even in a man that he takes punishment, yet is not "moved" by passion. Imagine a master of a house presiding over a huge family, who has spoken his laws thus: "whoever moves himself from such or such a place, unless he repents, let him perish." Could not all who are in that assembly, in the presence of the master, commit a fault and plunge themselves into ruin and the abyss, even without any change in the master himself? For it is so established by eternal law, and there is no need for a repeated decree.

### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

How much easier are these things regarding the highest good? For whoever exempts himself from divine laws binds himself to the perverse power of demons. For those demons are the torturers of those whom they entice to themselves with flatteries. Indeed, God had created them neither evil, nor for this purpose initially, lest any injustice be done to anyone. Yet He knew it would come to pass that there would be no shortage of mockers and scoundrels <note>original: "sannæ & nebulones." These terms describe those who mock divine order or live worthlessly.</note>, by whose labor the wicked spirits of men would pay their penalties. Just as now among men—even if no injustice is committed by God—there are never lacking those who, having been corrupted, bring destruction to others; this happens not by God’s procurement or incitement, but by His permission. For He placed man, as the Wise Man <note>Likely a reference to the Book of Sirach or Solomon in the Bible.</note> says, in the hand of his own counsel, and He does not wish any force to be applied to our free will. For he who does good unwillingly, and does not develop the habit of acting from the soul, is just as bad as a worthless person. Therefore, God exacts punishment from the wicked, yet He is not moved by passions because of it. There are also souls upon whom justice is exercised, and these are immortal. For otherwise God, who is "pure act" <note>term: <term>Pure Act</term> (Actus Purus) — A philosophical concept describing God as complete and perfected, with no unrealized potential.</note>, would act in potentiality only according to justice—which is not to be conceded.

<margin>From the reasoning of the nature of the universe.</margin>
6. The Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> says: "that because of which each thing is such, is itself more such." <note>A reference to Aristotle's *Posterior Analytics*, suggesting that if a cause makes something have a quality, the cause must possess that quality even more strongly.</note> Whether the world is assumed to be eternal or temporary, since it was made for the sake of man, God, the most wise author of both, ought to give the greatest duration—indeed, eternity—to man, for whose sake the world is either eternal or of the greatest duration. For since the world and the things within it have their duration for the sake of man, it is necessary that man be "most such"—that is, most durable. However, the greatest durability is eternity. It is necessary, therefore, both that the souls of men be eternal, and also that they eventually receive back their bodies, so that the complete man, enduring forever in eternal happiness, may make use of an eternal and purified world. Therefore, the soul is eternal, specifically so that the end <note>The "end" here means the ultimate purpose or goal.</note> would not be inferior to those things which exist for the sake of that end, and so that the one for whose sake all things are "more such" would not himself be "less such."

<margin>From the wisdom of God.</margin>
7. The eternity of souls is proved in a similar way by this reasoning. For a wise person ordains a good thing toward a good, and the best toward the best. God ordained all the good things of the world toward a good—that is, toward the purpose of man. But the best thing—that is, man, the most excellent part of the corruptible world—He established for the best: namely, for eternal happiness, than which nothing better can be imagined. Therefore, it follows that souls are eternal, so that by enduring forever they may attain the best end. For otherwise God would be accused of the greatest imprudence for making that which is most excellent so vanishingly brief that man would be the most degraded and miserable of all living creatures.

<margin>From the omnipotence, goodness, and will of God.</margin>
8. The omnipotent goodness of God wills that those things which are most excellent should have the greatest participation in the highest good. For just as a good is more divine the more common <note>Meaning "widely shared" or "universal."</note> it is, so He who is endowed with the highest good holds nothing more primary than to communicate His good as greatly as possible to capable natures. Princes, magnates, and the wealthy show off their masks <note>original: "laruas." Here used to mean false fronts or empty displays of status.</note> not by sharing, but by hunting for glory and "smoke" from the admiration of fools. God, however, communicates not masks, but Himself, most powerfully and eternally to human minds capable of the highest good. Therefore, after this life filled with miseries, He preserves eternal souls for Himself for eternal rewards, whether they be good or evil. Furthermore, He does not wish other things inferior to man to be capable of the highest good, since they have their end in the fact that they assist man by his use of them. But in eternity, when the soul shall rule over bodies, their use will not be necessary once corruption has ceased.

<margin>From the nature of sin.</margin>
9. We have said in previous sections, when we were treating the necessity of the divine incarnation, that a sin is considered more grave the greater the person is against whom it is committed. This is clear enough. Hence, so that man might attain the end for which he was created (and which he had lost by his own will), it was necessary for an infinite redeemer, greater than the world—the God-man <note>original: "Θεάνθρωπον" (Theanthropon). A Greek term for Christ as both God and Man.</note>—to satisfy the infinite sins of all and the infinite penalty of even a single sin. Truly, since this miserable mortality heaps sins upon sins daily, it also heaps up an infinite offense...

<summary>Postel argues for the immortality of the soul based on the purpose of the universe, the wisdom of God, and the requirements of divine justice. He contends that since the world was created for man, man's existence must be more enduring than the world itself, necessitating an eternal soul.</summary>

### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I

...offense <note>The text begins mid-word, completing "offensam" from the previous page.</note> can be washed away by no one except through the death of Christ and faith in His mercy, it is necessary, by the laws of divine justice, that the wicked be afflicted with eternal punishments. Conversely, it is necessary that those whom God has pitied, and who have striven to earn His favor through good works and to prove themselves to Him, be blessed with eternal joys. This is so that the benefit performed for the sake of an infinite God might result in a joy that is both most just and granted by the highest goodness. This cannot occur if the souls of men—who were able to act well or ill through their own free will—do not survive. Therefore, it follows necessarily, both for the sake of God and the sin committed against Him, as well as on account of His most severe justice, that the soul must be immortal for either punishment or reward. Indeed, the wicked are justly punished, while infinite goodness comes to the aid of the good. Since His justice and mercy are eternal, the soul in which He acts by punishing or blessing must also be eternal in the future.

<margin>From the properties of the divine nature.</margin>
10 I think no one is so insane or impious that they could deny that eternity exists in God. Truly, whatever things are most perfect, since they exist in God in the most perfect way, are also co-eternal with the divinity. Therefore, not only are the primary attributes of the Persons—namely power, wisdom, love, will, or charity—destined to exist in God after the purified matter of this world has passed away, but also mercy and truth. Neither Plato, nor Aristotle, nor their followers would deny that God holds compassion within Himself without any imperfect emotion. Since, therefore, those two properties are eternal, it is necessary that they act eternally upon some subject created from matter; for they cannot exist in vain. Therefore, it is necessary that the souls of men survive for some time, not only because of the scales of divine equity (as I taught before), but also that they endure forever. And not only those souls, but the whole human being, in whom both mercy and truth—or justice—may act. Therefore, etc.

<margin>From the perfection of the universe.</margin>
11 The entire mass of nature consists of a certain harmonic and concordant perfection, as I said especially in the chapter on the Trinity. For all things consist of matter, form, and the composite of both. Therefore, whatever is found to have extremes must also necessarily have a middle part participating in both. Since it is established that there are "separate substances" <note>A philosophical term for purely spiritual beings, like angels or demons, who exist without physical bodies.</note> which are eternal (though they are created) because they do not contain within themselves their own opposite or this fleeting and corruptible matter, it is necessary that there be a middle nature, partly eternal by nature and partly corruptible. This is the human nature, which agrees with the demons <note>In this context, Postel uses "demons" in the classical sense of "daimons" or spirits, referring to the shared immortality of the soul.</note> in the immortality of souls, and with the beasts in the body. Therefore, the most beautiful part of man, namely the soul, is immortal.

<margin>From the perfection of the soul.</margin>
12 Mortality or corruption happens through movement and the power of the heavens <note>Refers to the celestial spheres and stars, which in medieval science were thought to govern the change and decay of physical matter on Earth.</note> acting by the command of the Creator. Therefore, the heavens only corrupt those things upon which they can act. For a lower thing does not act upon a nobler thing. And yet the heavens, though they possess only "being" or (if they prefer) even "living" in a sense, nonetheless differ greatly from the nobility of the soul, which is above sense and life. Hence, the soul cannot be subject to the actions of the heavens. Therefore, it has been said by the astronomers: *The wise man shall rule the stars* <note>original: "Sapiens dominabitur astris." This was a common maxim suggesting that while the stars influence the physical body, the rational soul remains free.</note>. Since, therefore, the soul neither has an opposite in its composition nor can be dissolved by the heavens, it must be eternal. These points are from St. Jeremiah and Thomas Aquinas.

<margin>From the nature of its action.</margin>
13 Whatever is received into something is received according to the mode of that in which it exists. For example, the forms of things in the possible intellect <note>term: <term>Possible Intellect</term> (intellectus possibilis) — The capacity of the human mind to receive and process information, acting like a blank slate that can become all things through knowledge.</note> are entirely intelligible, just as the intellect is immaterial. Since they are immaterial in act, they must be incorruptible; therefore, the intellect is as well. But since that "possible intellect" is a part of our soul, it is necessary that the soul be immortal at least to that extent. For the agent intellect <note>term: <term>Agent Intellect</term> (intellectus agens) — The active power of the mind that "shines a light" on sensory experiences to turn them into universal, abstract concepts.</note> is the light of the soul.

<margin>From the mode of acting.</margin>
14 Nothing can be corrupted by that in which its perfection consists. Just as the perfection of fire is to act vehemently with heat or light, it follows that it cannot be corrupted by the action of heat and light. Likewise, since the perfection of the soul in this life is its... from the body in...
