# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD
<meta>catchword: of the universe,</meta>

...withdrawal into contemplation (for it is perfected the more it considers immaterial things furthest from the body through the sciences), it is necessary that when it is separated by death, it be far more unencumbered for contemplating and knowing, and thus immortal. For in life, the companionship of the body seems to stand in its way.

<margin>From a comparison of power.</margin>
15 Everyone admits that the efficient cause is more noble than its effect. But the possible intellect <note>intellectus possibilis: a Scholastic term for the mind's capacity to receive and process information, acting as the "matter" of thought</note> makes things intelligible in actuality—things which are by nature immaterial and eternal. Therefore, it follows that since the intellect is more noble than these, it must be immortal. For insofar as they are intelligible, they are eternal; but even more so, the intellect itself, in which they reside as if in a subject, must be immortal.

<margin>From the consideration of the soul's matter.</margin>
16 Although some may wish to claim, and it may be granted to them, that our soul consists of matter and form because of the intellect and will, it does not follow that it is not incorruptible. For corruption <note>the process of decay or breaking apart</note> does not occur where no "contrary" element is found in the composition. For generations and corruptions arise from contraries acting upon contraries <note>An Aristotelian principle: things only break down if they are made of opposing elements like hot and cold</note>. Therefore, the heavens are not naturally corrupted, because they lack matter subject to corruption. In the soul, however, the notions of all things are conceived without contrariety, since by its own knowledge it makes them into a unified branch of learning. Thus it follows that souls, surviving death, always flourish.

<margin>From the difference between the soul and lower things.</margin>
17 The proper action or operation of a thing follows its own nature. Furthermore, the soul's proper action is to understand and to will—something it shares with angels and blessed substances that are entirely devoid of bodies. It acts more in accordance with its nature the more it is removed from the body. For this reason, divinations, forewarnings, and prophecies occur either through dreams, ecstasy, or the movement of the mind. Since "to understand" is of an eternal nature, souls must be most especially of such a nature, and they thrive in understanding all the more when they are more detached from bodily things. Hence it happens that no mortal fails to admire by nature those who exercise virtues furthest removed from the use of the body. For life is more perfect the more it is lived according to the intellect and the less according to the body. It is therefore clearly established that the nature of souls is eternal; it has nothing in common with these lower things and uses its functions more intensely the more it is withdrawn through knowledge from the nature of lower and material things. You might attribute these ideas to Thomas <note>original: "Thomae" – refers to St. Thomas Aquinas</note> and Jeremiah the Sicilian <note>original: "Hieremiae Siculo" – likely a reference to a medieval or contemporary commentator</note>.

<margin>From the supreme desire of the human soul.</margin>
18 It has already been demonstrated above that all people are naturally held by a desire for immortality and permanence. This could not happen at all unless the soul were able to achieve it—either by its own effort, the effort of another, or partly both, in whatever way. For nature does not typically excite motions in a species unless it is also possible for the attainment to follow. Since man undergoes even the most difficult things for the sake of that end—as if for rest and the highest good—it is clear that he looks toward immortality. Otherwise, it would follow that nature does something in vain, which must not be admitted. For if anyone should say that this desire arises in some from deception, smoke, and the opinions of "great men," and that the lowest people are not held by this expectation, the opposite will be clearly established when put to the test. For common people make almost every kind of vow and bind themselves with every kind of religious practice so that they might enter into a kinship with God, even though they are pressed by very few intellectual opinions. The great men differ greatly from them; for through images, noise, pride, pomp, and rare deeds, they try to seize immortality in this life and cast God down from His heaven. Those who almost never attain it deservedly use force, so that at least they might seem to have wanted it. But the lowest rely on hope and humility. Truly, all tend toward the same goal: while the former march on a royal path, the proud seek shortcuts through the twists and rugged places of the way. Therefore, the soul is immortal, so that it may attain through the grace of Christ what nature taught it to desire. Truly, these points are more than enough. For whatever could be added would be more of a burden than a benefit. Thus, from the justice of divine providence, from the nature of the soul, from the ends of things, from the reward of virtue, from the nature of action, from natural motion, from the reason of the universe...

<summary>Postel provides several philosophical proofs for the immortality of the soul, arguing that because the intellect can process eternal truths and lacks physical "contraries" that cause decay, it must survive the body. He concludes that the universal human longing for eternity, found in both peasants and kings, proves that such a state must exist through Christ.</summary>

## ON THE RESURRECTION. CHAPTER XXI.

Divine goodness was not satisfied with merely giving essence to things themselves, unless it also conferred well-being, and that than which a better state cannot be given according to the nature of that species. This can be seen in all nature below man. For all living creatures, which were created for the use of man, because they attain their end and highest happiness in him, therefore have the culmination of their happiness here in this life. This is most evident from the fact that no sign could ever be taken from any living creature that it was held by any desire other than for the present life. From which it follows, since they have lived and brought utility to man, they have attained their end and highest good through all things. For if nature had otherwise given them a certain movement and appetite for greater things, if anything further had been lacking to them, she <note>Postel personifies Nature here as a creative force</note> did not do so. Therefore, their well-being consists of life and sensation. 

But if we begin from the wonder of the smallest of all living creatures, who would not be stunned, and rather be deprived of sense, than grasp that power by which the creature is constrained and brought from matter to form <note>Aristotelian concepts: "matter" is the raw potential, while "form" is the specific identity or "soul" of the creature</note>? Who would not see providence present in all things? All things have care for themselves and their posterity. They know what they must flee and what they must seek for the preservation of life. 

In short, they are pressed by no troubles. For it is certain they are affected by the sense of sadness and pleasure, but they do not think about being affected, nor do they know it. They certainly suffer all things, with pain equal to human feelings; but truly, it is not an evil for them, because they do not understand it to be an evil. For although they flee harmful things, they do this spontaneously and by the guidance of their nature, not by thought and intellect. Otherwise, they would have gathered themselves together and risen up in arms against the men who use and abuse their labor. 

And so they are slaughtered and killed in the midst of herds, with no knowledge of another's or their own misfortune. For they are not affected by the sense of things past, except as long as the object or its action is fresh. For they have memory, as we said, but not reminiscence <note>original: "reminiscentiam" - a technical distinction where memory is a passive storage of images, while reminiscence is the active, intellectual effort to recall them</note>, nor are they driven by any judgment of the future, except when the object is imminent. 

In all these things, the Creator willed that there be a much more certain and acute sense of discernment in animals, and it appears far more perfect than in man. For the more careless of the future or more forgetful of the past God willed to make them, the more sagacious He made them for present things, so that they might be moved most sharply by present objects. Therefore a dog, who when the enemy is absent no longer thinks he has an enemy (though an animal must have many enemies, attacking almost all living things), if an adversary approaches the arena, he is so powerful in smell that he immediately gives it away with a bark and looks out for himself with strength or flight. 

And so they perceive things from the object, but they do not recognize them, nor do they weigh their nature. Since they suffer all bodily calamities, yet they do not judge themselves to be suffering. Therefore, they come very close to the "indolence" <note>original: "indolentiam" - here referring to the Epicurean concept of *aponia*, or the total absence of pain and mental disturbance</note> of Epicurus. Nor are they therefore devoid of their own happiness and highest good. They are therefore in their own end and goal when they have lived, because they lived for man if he was able to use them. For if man abuses them, nothing lives or profits him, since he perishes more—just as a person with dropsy <note>a condition of swelling or excess fluid</note> perishes from drinking, a plethoric person <note>someone with an unhealthy excess of blood or "humors"</note> from food, a learned show-off from arrogance, or a madman from a sword—with the things themselves having no vice in them. Now if anyone should look at with what great industry the Creator covered and armed those creatures against enemies and all dangers, who would not fail in wonder? He clothed them all with the toughest skin, some with hair, some with bristles, fleeces, or shaggy coats.

<summary>Postel argues that while animals possess acute senses and memory, they lack the intellectual capacity to suffer "evil" or contemplate the future, fulfilling their purpose entirely within this life. This contrasts with humans, whose capacity for judgment necessitates a divine afterlife and resurrection.</summary>
<keywords>resurrection, divine justice, animal instinct, memory vs reminiscence, providence, Epicurus, teleology, Scholastic philosophy</keywords>

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
<note>original: "DE ORBIS CONCORDIA"</note>

Scales were given to fish, and feathers and plumage to birds. He granted shells to snails, and to trees He sometimes attributed even a fourfold layer of bark. Yet to man, who was intended to rule over all other living creatures, He conferred nothing other than a total nakedness of all things and an extreme weakness. Who would deny that those creatures have achieved an excellent end in this life, when they are happier than the man set over them in at least one respect: they are not burdened by opinions <note>Postel uses "opinions" here to mean the anxieties, doubts, and existential dread that come with human consciousness</note>? Certainly, if no other life were to follow, man, the prince of all living beings, would become the most miserable of all. I do not see what could be thought of as more absurd than this. For if those creatures were made for the sake of an end, then man, for whose sake they exist, must also attain an end. Since they possess a state of "being best" <note>original: "optimum esse," a technical term for the perfection of a thing's nature</note> while they live for the benefit of man, it remains certain that man must also achieve a certain "best" state arising from the nature of the Creator. For otherwise, the intended end <note>man</note> would be in a more unjust condition than the things made to serve that end, which is against all reason and the order of things.

2 Furthermore, as we have seen, the better a person is in this life, the more unhappy they are. Therefore, man does not possess his highest good <term>Summum Bonum; the ultimate goal or supreme happiness of human existence</term> here. For we have seen that he seeks to attain this through the soul itself, which is by far the most excellent part of man. However, since the well-being of a thing does not consist of only one part, but of the whole, it is necessary that the body itself—the solid human being, which has never yet possessed true well-being—be raised up, joined to the soul, and gifted with immortality. Therefore, at some time, there will be a future resurrection. This same point is evident from divine justice.

3 For since it is necessary, given that justice stands, for souls to be immortal so they may receive the rewards of their choices—whether kept well or poorly—and since they did not act well or otherwise alone, but only with the body’s consent and the execution of the work: so it is also entirely necessary that bodies will one day be present for the souls, and that the human being be remade, so that he may also receive the things proper to the body. For as has already been said, the soul is not the human being, nor is the body the human being, but the body joined to the soul together composes the human being. There is a need, therefore, for the body to be awakened from the dust, and for a resurrection of the solid human being to eventually occur. Otherwise, one would have to admit to an injustice in God, which is a spiritual crime even to think.

<margin>He conceived this opinion from discussions concerning the glorified body.</margin>
4 The logic of order also persuades us of the same. For it is characteristic of God’s wisdom to make all things most orderly. Now, form <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "form" is the soul or the organizing principle, while "matter" is the physical body</note> is ordered toward matter, just as matter is toward form. Furthermore, it has already been shown above that man was born for a happiness far greater than the human mind can conceive. Moreover, since it is clear that the nature of souls is eternal, it follows necessarily—for the sake of preserving order in the universe—that the form ordered toward matter, and vice-versa, should be united once more according to their suitability to share the price of their common work. Thus, that very same body which was once joined to the soul, and to that very soul which gave it life, may feel the rewards for its merits through a vital bond. Indeed, we must especially shun the impiety (for it should not even be called a heresy) of those who affirm that the body to be raised will not be the same one that exists now, but a new one, not subject to corruption or deformity. By this axiom, God is denied, for such an injustice is ascribed to Him—that He would reward what did not labor—even if He were said to be so powerless that He could not perfectly restore a now-imperfect body in every detail during the resurrection. For if you take away the rewards for merits, you deny God. If you give them, but not to the one who merited them, you do the same. Since actions belong to the individuals <note>original: "suppositorum," referring to the whole person as a legal/moral entity</note> and not just a part, rewards belong to the whole and not just a part; to the same thing, not to something different. It remains, therefore, to conclude that for the sake of order and divine decree, our same soul, recreated again after its sleep, and that very same body which exists now, reduced to the highest perfection and the fullness of the age of Christ <note>A common medieval theological belief that the resurrected would appear in the prime of life, approximately thirty-three years old</note>, shall be joined together again for rewards, good or bad, and live forever.

5 To be "best" is immortality; to be "worst" is mortality. God either does not wish to confer immortality upon man as the highest good, or He is not able. (For

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument for the physical resurrection of the human body. He transitions from philosophical proofs based on the justice of God to addressing specific logical objections regarding the nature of animal immortality and the problem of cannibalism.</meta>

### BOOK I OF GUILLAUME POSTEL

(As was demonstrated above, man, being endowed with virtue, is worthy of the most excellent reward.) God cannot but will the most perfect things; yet dissolution <note>The breaking apart of the body at death</note> is a state of greater imperfection than restoration. Therefore, He wills all things to be most perfect. That He is able to do this, just as He wills it, should be doubted by no one. For just as He brought the parts—known only to Himself before they were joined—into the original composition of the person, so too can He gather those parts even after they have been scattered. If we were to deny this power in God, He would appear more powerless than many human craftsmen, who are able to restore many things by reassembling the parts of a composition. They differ in this: for God, the basic elements cannot perish, whereas for the human craftsman, corruption <note>The decay or loss of materials</note> is an obstacle. Since, therefore, He both wills it and is able to do it, and is Himself the most excellent Being, it is necessary for man to be an eternal, solid whole, and for the body to be raised and united once again with the soul. Therefore, the resurrection of the dead man shall come to pass.

However, we must here encounter two slanders of the impious. For if God wills all things to be most excellent and immortal, then they will say: "Therefore an immortal ox will be better than a mortal one; thus the ox shall also rise again." I respond: God indeed wills all things which are made for an end and for the sake of God, for He is the beginning and the end. Therefore, whatever things contribute to that end are necessary. But when the necessity ceases, the things themselves must cease. In this life, for the sake of human needs and uses, all animals were necessary to man; but since man, once raised, will not be subject to physical necessity, he will have no need for the other animals. For then man will neither drink nor eat, nor will he procreate. Indeed, all change of matter will cease. Since God and nature do nothing in vain, and since there will then be no need for those animals, they will no longer exist in the nature of things. But man—the commander of lower things, created for the purpose of praising, knowing, and loving God because of the world He created—will be the only one from the lower order of things who is necessary, being abundantly happy in the knowledge of God without any need for corruptible things.

<margin>Methodius also beautifully solves this objection in his *Sermon on the Resurrection* found in the works of Epiphanius.</margin>
The other objection is this: It is impossible, if there is to be a resurrection, for all men to rise. For countless people have become the "supper of Thyestes" and the "banquets of Tantalus" <note>Postel refers to Greek myths of cannibalism to illustrate the problem of one human body being consumed by another</note>. Everywhere on earth there have been cannibals <note>original: "anthropophagi"</note>; they exist even today in many parts of the world. The Scythians <note>An ancient nomadic people</note> used to hold banquets where they gave their own bodies as food to those mourning them. All those who were devoured have become parts of those who ate them; therefore, the former will lack the matter that the others now possess. For if those who were devoured are to be made whole, the devourers will be left imperfect, and vice versa. These are the arguments of the adversaries, to which I respond with a few words.

The nature of our daily food teaches us that only a very tiny portion of what is taken in is actually joined to the nourished body, so much so that after many months, hardly any addition can be seen. Since we cast off the largest and most corporeal part as waste and excrement, the part that remains in the body appears to be the smallest; because of this, if the body has already reached its full growth, it is certain that as much of its "own substance" flows away as is added. This is something that neither philosophers nor physicians will deny. For it is established that nature requires drink and food because of the <term>fluor substantiæ</term> <note>original: "flow of substance." The theory that the body's material is in a constant state of flux, losing and replacing atoms</note>, as they say, using a truly appropriate term. Indeed, our body, being "confluent and perspirable" everywhere—as Hippocrates <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine"</note> says—continually loses something through its actions, which must be restored by food. Therefore, one body does not truly enter into the permanent essence of another body; rather, something very thin and compatible with the parts is added, exactly in the amount that was lost elsewhere, and nothing more.

Bodies are also whole in themselves without the addition of food, and can naturally endure for many days in this way, especially for those accustomed to it. Indeed, many examples are seen of men who have lived for many years without any use of food or drink and without the rejection of waste. Charles de Bovelles <note>A French humanist scholar and mathematician</note> mentions in his letters a certain man who lived for twelve years in perfect health without food or drink, even though the ancients wrote that the seventh day of fasting is fatal to a man. A little while ago there was a Scotsman in Rome, and afterwards in France and Syria, who...

### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

27. ...On that day he took very little food, not so much out of religious devotion as out of habit. The Holy Fathers testify that many have lived for eight days on the reception of the Eucharist alone. But modern impiety disapproves of such things. I shall pass over in silence the man who was seen to live for many years without food and without drink <note>original Greek: ἄσιτος & ἄποτος (asitos and apotos)</note> during the time of Pope Nicholas V, an account written by Poggio Bracciolini <note>A famous Italian humanist and historian (1380–1459)</note> in those same days. Furthermore, the fame of the girl living an "angelic life" for two years now without food on the outskirts of Heidelberg is known to everyone. From these examples, it is clear that very little food actually reaches the body itself; indeed, it can lead a life even without food. Physicians would not admit this unless they held it to be a proven fact. Therefore, that very slight loss of the moist parts <note>Postel refers to the "humors," the fluids ancient and medieval doctors believed governed health</note> cannot be missed by the whole; rather, it makes the body more fit. For a body that suffers nothing, such a great abundance of humors will not be as necessary as it is now. For now, because of dangers, nature "stores up" a treasury of these fluids—and to such an extent that, not infrequently, fevers are ignited within it when that treasury becomes putrefied. Truly, since the condition of the body is destined to be entirely free of flaw, it will easily be able to overflow with life.

Jesus Christ, our leader, was the example of the resurrection. By His example, we hope for the future age and proportion <note>The "perfect age" (often thought to be 33) and physical stature of the resurrected</note> of all people. Truly, since those matters are placed within His judgment, I do not dare to say anything further about them. I hold it sufficient that nothing stands in the way of resurrected bodies even if they were devoured by those who are likewise to be resurrected. For just as much of them perished as arrived from elsewhere <note>Postel argues that because the body's matter is constantly being replaced through metabolism, the specific "atoms" or parts are not unique to one person over a lifetime</note>. And if a little more was added (as in youths), it is so thin that it escapes the senses, and he who rises can easily do without it without any imperfection. 

To respond briefly to the objections by summarizing: God wills the resurrection of man as necessary for his happiness and for the sake of divine praise; however, He does not will the resurrection of those things made for the sake of man <note>i.e., animals and plants</note>, since they would then be superfluous. He is also able to reform the parts, gathered from everywhere, just as He created them, and nothing shall hinder Him. Therefore, by reason—namely the well-being of man, which he does not attain in this life—and furthermore by the argument of divine goodness and equity, and because He begrudges no one the most excellent things, there shall be a future resurrection of human bodies.

6. Whatever things are sought for the sake of the body in this life usually bring disgust, nausea, satiety, forgetfulness, and neglect as soon as they arrive. Virtues alone are the true goods of the soul; the more they are possessed, the more they are desired, and the less they satisfy <note>In the sense of "satiate" or "make one bored"</note>. Thus, these two conditions are entirely contrary to one another, just like the things for which they were intended. From this it follows that the summit of all virtues is celestial and immortal, and it is possible to obtain it. For God would not bait the wretched soul with such a thing unless it were to eventually attain something eternal and greater than these fleeting matters. Therefore, the soul has a true goal in heaven and with God in absolute virtue (if it follows virtue; or punishment, if it follows vice), where it cannot receive rewards alone. For the whole man is not merely a soul. Therefore, there shall be a resurrection of the body, because it followed the movements of the soul. The whole man shall receive the reward, not just a part.

7. Different ends exist for all different things. For the same ends cannot belong to different things. Since man differs greatly from all other things and living creatures, he ought to have a different goal. Therefore, his goal cannot be bodily pleasure, in which he has the beasts as companions; nor can it be the mere absence of pain, for then stones would be happier than he. From this it follows that there is something greater than these things, in which the soul ought not be the only participant, since man does not consist of the soul alone. Therefore, it is necessary for bodies to be raised, so that the "solid" <note>Complete or substantial</note> man may become a participant in a "solid" joy of immortality. All the arguments which were deduced from divine properties in the chapter on the necessity of the Incarnate God and on the immortality of souls can be applied here. For whatever things prove the immortality of souls, the same...

# ON THE TRANSFORMATION OF MATTER
->necessarily in the future.<-
### CHAPTER XXII.

It is most clearly evident in all things, and established by the judgment and authority of all philosophers, that God wishes to preserve the same order—and one similar to Himself in every part—throughout all of nature. In the total use of things, the end <note>The "end" or *finis* refers to the final purpose or goal for which something exists</note> differs from that which tends toward that end. Furthermore, there can be no doubt that the end is by far the most excellent part of both nature and art. Unless it were true that those things which are the goal are better than the things used to reach that goal, then all things would be done in vain, and nothing would act according to order and deliberation. For it would be plainly foolish and entirely lacking in mind to consume an action in vain and report nothing from it except the action itself and spontaneous labor—or if anything more were gained, it would be something worse, or plainly equal and similar. Since all these things are utterly absurd, they contradict the order of things, common sense, and authority. Therefore, one action cannot be the cause of a nearly identical action or movement.

It follows, then, as the Philosopher <note>Postel refers to Aristotle, who was known simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance scholarship</note> left written and as our senses teach us, that all movement occurs for the sake of rest. Since, however, all things here are in some way in motion, it is certain and necessary that a state of rest will one day come for all things. Aristotle does not hesitate to concede this regarding the elements; indeed, he affirms it. Movement, therefore, will one day stand still in rest and eternal peace, without any motion. For when these fleeting things perish, or cease to act and suffer, there will be no need for the celestial motion which is the cause of the generation, corruption, and alteration of these things.

But since matter can never be entirely exterminated by its own nature, and since it is necessary for a future rest to eventually arrive, it is necessary for that matter to be changed. For as long as it remains as it is now, it must be liable to "passions" <note>term: "passions" (passiones). In 16th-century philosophy, this refers to the capacity of matter to be acted upon or changed by external forces, leading to decay</note>. If actions and movement are to cease, as is necessary, it follows that matter will also be immune to corruption and will become very similar to an incorruptible form; this is what holy men and divinely inspired people have affirmed through oracles.

However, we cannot know what the future "best state" of that matter will be—that which survives the universal conflagration—because we entirely lack an example of it. Yet, when we consider the diverse kinds and perfections of gemstones, and how they are naturally held in high price by all people even though their true power remains hidden, it may come to mind that there will be a certain affinity between the mass of the elements and these gems. Not that the elements will be exactly like them, but (as a single diamond serves as proof) they will yield to no power. For the "goat's blood" will then be missing, even if matter becomes adamantine <note>original: "hircinus sanguis." Ancient and medieval lore held that the diamond—the hardest substance—could only be broken or softened by the blood of a goat</note>. Who would not admire pyropes, carbuncles, hyacinths, pomegranate-stones, and small garnets? <note>Postel lists various red and precious stones: the "pyrope" and "carbuncle" were names for deep red garnets or rubies; "hyacinth" often referred to a yellow or orange zircon</note> What mind would not be turned to stupor by that transparent greenness of the emerald? Who can grasp the clarity and solidity of the diamond? And yet, although these are the highest things we possess, they seem to be scarcely a shadow and a dream of the things to come. For just as nothing more perfect and incomprehensible than God Himself and the First Cause can be given, so nothing is more incomprehensible than His highest effect and effort. He wished to scatter small fragments and rudiments of this in nature—not so that they might adorn the mistresses of princes, or...

...might excite immortal desires in us: but that they might carry us away into the admiration and contemplation of future things. Who does not see how far we have wandered from this goal? But because nothing can be perfect unless the dross, the slag, and all the refuse are consumed, fire—which is the tester of even the most perfect things—will offer its service to the Creator and will purify everything. Nature seems to approach this task gradually. Gold, well-refined <note>original: "excoctum," meaning cooked out or thoroughly melted to remove impurities</note> by fire, represents certain images of the most perfect earths, just as the diamond represents the most perfect waters. For these two cannot be simply dissolved by fire unless you add chemical agents <note>original: "pharmaca"</note>. Therefore, just as these small fragments require the work of a purifying and testing fire for their well-being, so too does the entire universe have need of a purgation.

There are, therefore, three times of the Creator corresponding to His power, which are in some way similar to our own times established under motion. For among us, there is the past, the present, and the future. The past is infinite with respect to the "now" <note>original: "instans," the present moment</note>, and it can never be used again. The present seems to be within our power, but in truth, we can do nothing in it before it has already passed away. In the future alone is happiness. With God, there was eternity without matter. The present and the "now," with respect to the past, is something insensible; it is the duration of the world, with matter subject to birth and decay <note>original: "generationi & corruptioni," the Aristotelian cycle of coming-to-be and passing away</note>. The eternal future will be characterized by the true enjoyment of matter brought to perfection and immunity from decay. All our actions provide evidence for this. For all effects have a past time in the mind, a present time in the work, and a future time in the enjoyment. Since these very things exist in us and are most excellent, it is clear that we have them from the example of the Divinity. For nature has an analogy both with itself and with art.

Furthermore, the end <note>The "end" or *finis* refers to the final goal or purpose</note> of all arts is rest; therefore, it is also the end of created nature. God—who is most happy in Himself and to whom no matter or creation could bring any perfection—established all these lower things for the sake of man, and man for the sake of divine honor and contemplation (in which lies the highest happiness). He did this so that, out of this corruption and constant labor, where the best men are tested and refined as if by torments, He might finally lead them into that happiness which is eternal and most like God. May He deign to lead us there by His mercy. Having drawn these arguments from the storehouse of reason, it seemed right to hand down those decrees which Truth itself, God in God the Son, opened to the world, and which He wished to be believed by His own authority without the use of logic—so that the impiety now rising and reigning in the whole world might be countered. To make this clear, I subjoin the decrees supported by authority to these demonstrations.

### CHAPTER XXIII.

It is handed down and believed by authority that God, existing from eternity, is Three and One. For He has Power, Wisdom, and Will, which we call "Persons" or the attributes of the Persons. The first, generating Wisdom from Himself from eternity, we call the Father; the latter, the Son. The Will, proceeding from Power and Wisdom, we name the Holy Spirit. By Him, through Him, and in Him the world was created, consisting of both corporeal substance and that which is devoid of body—which we call the visible and the invisible. By "invisible" we understand the separate substances <note>A philosophical term for angels and spirits who exist without physical bodies</note>, both the good who are confirmed in goodness, and those who have become depraved by their own will and bring destruction upon men. We believe all visible things were made for the sake of man, but man for the sake of God and himself: so that by glorifying God, he might be immortal. ## THE SECOND BOOK OF GUILLAUME POSTEL OF BARENTON.

->PREFACE TO THE SECOND BOOK ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD, and an exhortation to truly pious men, that they may prepare themselves to engage through letters and reason with the foul rabble of the Mahometans <note>original: "Mahumedicorum," referring to Muslims</note>, and assist in the duties of princes.<-

**H**ow great a stain the unrestrained desire for ruling has brought upon the world to this day; how great a loss among mortals the laziness and luxury of many have introduced; and how great a plague arises daily from the empty contention of the many who neglect and overturn their own affairs at home while seeking the affairs of others that are hardly beneficial—all this, I judge, is known to anyone who possesses experience of the world or is well-versed in the records of history. For when empires either arise or are expanded through long preservation for the sake of profit and lust rather than the welfare of the people, it happens not infrequently—even if the occasions seem most just at first glance—that wars bring no less misery to the victors than to the vanquished, leaving behind an equal sense of unhappiness for both peoples. But with Divine Providence so permitting on account of human wickedness increasing with age—because man preferred to be ruled by another’s will rather than his own, and to follow another man as leader rather than reason—the world has never not been worn down by wars. This is the punishment for neglected duty. This is the pledge of eternal punishment for the wicked and for those who depend only upon this "mask" <note>original: "larua," implying the deceptive or superficial appearance of worldly life</note> of human affairs; but for the pious, it is a sign of the favor of God, who calls His own back to Himself through calamities. Therefore, God the Best and Greatest is almost always accustomed to compensate for the loss of external things and the damage received in wars, either with a certain festive peace, or with laws and a better cultivation of souls. For new empires are accustomed to be refreshed by the cycle of peace and to bring about the forgetting of certain corrupt things; they render those who were previously puffed up by success and exercised tyranny over others equal to the rest, or even inferior to the lowest, and they bring new...

...they introduce the principles of both things and opinions: so that however much more unhealthily a war offers itself to those whom it oppresses, it may bring a far happier condition of things to the survivors. Furthermore, the worship, customs, beliefs, literature, and laws of the victors are often accustomed to leave to the vanquished a utility far greater than what they possessed before their defeat. Thus it happened that although the Romans and Greeks—whose empires were the most widely extended and renowned next to the peoples of the East—claimed victory over the whole world known to us, carried off spoils, and not infrequently used their victory most cruelly; nevertheless, they left behind everywhere the seeds <note>original: "seminaria"</note> and practice of laws and customs more closely related to nature, as compensation for the loss sustained. 

Certainly, other types of changes, such as those which occurred at the hands of the **Scythians** <note>Ancient nomadic peoples of Central Eurasia, often used in this period as a archetype for "barbarian" invaders</note> and barbarians, more frequently and almost utterly uprooted whatever ornament both literature and morals these two nations <note>the Greeks and Romans</note> had contributed. Therefore, the incursions of the Barbarians are most hostile to nature, and are, as it were, entirely armed for its destruction. Yet, they possess at least this much less evil: that as much as they bring a more immediate slaughter to human bodies, they bring much less harm to minds. For placing the goods of the body at the highest level of happiness, they bring neither many nor perverse laws; but rather, once things are settled and they have caught their breath from war, when they consider the happiness and leisure that the conquered people used to enjoy under their own laws, they embrace those laws. 

This is shown by the many incursions of the **Scythians** and **Goths** into both Asia and Europe; the assaults of the **Huns**, **Heruli**, **Alans**, **Saxons**, **Normans**, **Vandals**, and **Lombards**; and their permanent settlements everywhere in Europe. For all of them accepted the laws of the vanquished, both because of their utility and because of their own ignorance of literature and disciplines. Other empires, therefore, have this quality: they either bring laws and culture to the vanquished in place of plunder and victory, or they inflict a stain only upon the bodies, but do not likewise thrust the blindness of some foul superstition upon the minds.

However, the **Arabic filth** <note>original: "Arabica colluuies." Postel uses highly polemical language typical of 16th-century Christian views on Islamic expansion.</note> has brought such a foul slaughter to both bodies and minds almost throughout the entire world, that whatever plagues it ever experienced before ought to be considered happiness, if evaluated by a just comparison of things. For besides the fact that an impious persuasion suggests it—that nothing is more excellent, and no way to happiness more direct, than if one slays as many mortals as possible in the name of a disagreeing dogma—the miserably deceived nation, captured by a darkness greater than that of the **Cimmerians** <note>A mythical people said to live in perpetual mist and darkness; a metaphor for total ignorance</note>, nourishes, fosters, protects, and cherishes a perpetual nursery of robbers even among its own people under the name of "soldiers of God." 

Since, therefore, God created man (for whose sake all other things exist) for the sake of duration, the laws, empires, and all kinds of magistrates should primarily hold the rationale of preserving his life for as long as possible. Therefore, those holding the reins of power should seek out, accumulate, and preserve all supports of both body and mind from every side. But this one law of a treacherous tyrant <note>referring to Muhammad</note>, with the **Furies** <note>Deities of vengeance in Greek mythology</note> as its authors, rising up and armed, has brought such slaughter to mortals and such ruin to all things except for pleasure and vice—attacking the majesty of God, the safety of human nature, the health of minds and bodies, and public peace—that it truly can and should be called the "devastation of the world." For it never permits its own people to enjoy peace, nor outsiders to enjoy quiet. 

**Egypt** once had twenty thousand cities; now it has barely ten municipalities and six cities. More than ten thousand cities once adorned both parts of **Asia** <note>Asia Minor and Greater Asia</note>; now barely two hundred remain. All is a wasteland, overgrown with briars and thorns because of the **Nomads** <note>referring here to the Saracens or Turks</note> enrolled as soldiers for their religion. By what great follies he ensnared the minds of those devoted to him will become clear through the whole course of this book, especially in the examination of the **Alcoran** <note>The Quran</note>. Finally, when I have revealed how crudely he felt regarding God, demons, and natural things, I shall show in a few words what great calamities they are subject to who live anywhere on earth under the **Muhamedan** empire. Since, therefore, it is established by the decrees of all that wars and changes of things have been introduced by the permission of Providence for the punishment of crimes: it is certainly necessary that...

## WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK II

...which are most bitter, are nonetheless prepared for the sake of avenging the most heinous crimes. Nor do I dwell at all upon what many say—that there are certain fixed periods of history, joined to the recklessness of fortune and the lust of wicked men, from which wars are accustomed to arise. For if they admit that the world has a cause and is ruled by providence (for otherwise I do not deal with those who believe in blind Fortune), they will never be able to deny, since He has a singular care for creating and preserving individuals, that He has a far greater concern for the preservation of a multitude, whether in a city, a province, or in any kingdom whatsoever. For unless He restrained this mass with eternal commands, everything would continually burn with wars. To return to the matter, therefore: the greater the offenses, the greater the punishments God allows to be inflicted—not only upon those who committed the offenses, but also upon their descendants and their close associates—so that by the punishments inflicted, they might learn either not to commit similar crimes or to expiate those already committed.

With what crimes the peoples formerly alienated from the law of God most provoked Him—since there was no vice by which those destitute of divine law did not most foully suffer—I could not easily say. For they were rushing daily into mutual slaughter. But I will provide proof for my statement from the sacred scriptures by running through a few examples. On account of the depraved sons Hophni and Phinehas, who were not corrected by their father <note>Eli the High Priest; see 1 Samuel 4</note>, the entire army of the people of God was slaughtered by the Philistines. For a crime is considered more grievous in proportion to the status of the one who sins. The expiation for David’s sin implies this as well. The Babylonian Captivity avenged the fact that God had long since been forsaken even by the priests and princes in order to worship Baal. 

But because no more monstrous crime could ever be committed than the killing of Jesus Christ, the God-man, by his own people: so too, no slaughter was ever made so memorable as that under **Titus** and **Hadrian** in the land of Judea, in which, in two expeditions, sixty hundred-thousand men <note>original: "sexagefies centena hominũ milia" — i.e., 6,000,000. Postel uses hyperbole common in his era to emphasize the scale of the tragedy.</note> were slaughtered to a man. Indeed, the remnants of the Jewish people have been in captivity everywhere in the world since that time, according to the prediction of Christ. Many innocent people are killed daily through slanders; but for the God-man to have been killed by his own priests—those who claimed to be the preservers of His law—is a crime more monstrous than any punishment. 

Yet what is holier than a faithful and perfect Christian, to whom all nature is subject through the virtue of piety in the name of Jesus? Certainly nothing. Therefore, he who sins under such a holy law sins more gravely than any other mortal. "For the servant who knows the master's will and does not do it, shall be beaten with many blows" <note>A reference to Luke 12:47</note>. Antiquity did not remain silent about the fact that the most savage persecutions arose against the Christians because many, already initiated into the sacred mysteries, were behaving with little holiness, and others even impiously, under the sacrosanct title of innocence. 

Thus, to come to the point, I am led by conjecture to believe that on account of the monstrous crimes of false Christians, this **plague of the law of Muhammad** was sent into the world, so that those who impiously abused the most holy law might feel God as an avenger in a perpetually raging plague. And lest posterity should further contend and sin in luxury and glory, the administration of temporal affairs was permitted to this rising tyranny. Jerusalem, in which were the first patriarchs of our holy religion, came first into the power of the enemy without any difficulty. Not long after, Alexandria and Antioch were taken away; even though previously the Christians had held the power of the magistracy there peacefully for over three hundred years. Indeed, the common people there had given their names to Christ six hundred years before. 

Unless a certain monstrosity of crimes and an abuse of the things that had come from piety—a nation once most dear to God being intent on luxury and gluttony—had driven the favor of God away from the Christian world, it could not have happened that a naked barbarism, destitute of all things and powerful only in multitude, could have reported a victory over those peoples who, even without arms, were formidable throughout the whole world. The Emperor **Heraclius** <note>Byzantine Emperor, r. 610–641 AD</note>, most unworthy of the name, was competing in luxury and inert idleness with the most abandoned men when this faction in Arabia began to arise. The Roman Pontiff was not satisfied to neglect the regions of the Eastern religion (though holding the first place among the patriarchs in councils), unless he also ambitiously sought that name of "Pope"...

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

...hatred of which such great fires are ignited, he sought it so that he who was supreme and desired to be so might be called as if by <term>antonomasia</term> <note>original: *ἀντωνομασίαν*; the rhetorical device of substituting a title or epithet for a proper name, such as calling the Pope "the Holy Father"</note>. Indeed, all priests before him were called by this name, as can be seen from the letters of Jerome, Augustine, and other Latin authors, and likewise from the common word for sacred dignity in the Greek church. For they call priests *Papas*. Perhaps such an august name came from heaven, from Jupiter Papa, who was worshiped by the Bithynians <note>An ancient people of Asia Minor</note> with pure hands and without any cultic ritual according to an ancient erroneous rite. I do not labor much over where the name flowed from. Phocas <note>Byzantine Emperor, r. 602–610</note> granted its use to Boniface IV.

But it is helpful to examine the cause of this disease a little more broadly, so that at least after it has consumed all the limbs of the Christian body so deeply through the neglect, malevolence, or ignorance of the physicians of that time, we may look out for ourselves and, according to the proverb, "become wise like the Phrygians" <note>A classical proverb referring to those who only learn the truth after a disaster has already happened</note> even if late, and be helped by another’s danger. To make the beginning of such great calamity more clearly visible, I will first pursue the condition of the affairs of the Empire, and then the affairs of the sacred magistrates. 

Pope Gregory was a man of remarkable piety and learning, such that even now he holds the fourth place among the sacred doctors because of his writings. His pontificate fell during the times of Emperor Maurice, who confirmed Gregory in the papal seat under the most unfavorable conditions of the times, despite Gregory's reluctance and even his secret refusal of such a great burden and honor in letters. Perhaps the Emperor saw him as a man devoted to the solitary life, suitable for someone to whom he could commit the cares of such great business and the dangers of the looming Lombard wars, and whom he could laugh at and pursue with insults at his whim. In other respects, however, he is said to have held Christian piety faithfully enough. 

And so, having been in power for a long time, he alienated the minds of the Italian people on two accounts: because he provoked that most holy man [Gregory] by harassing and mocking him even with public insults, and because Gregory took up—no less diligently than any soldier or general—the care that the Emperor neglected, and he held not a few cities in loyalty to the Empire, though not without risk to his own life. The soldiers, moved by hatred against the Emperor for these reasons, created a common soldier [Phocas] as Emperor. Warned by an oracle, Maurice attempted to flee by night; he was captured at Chalcedon, brought back to the city of New Rome <note>Constantinople</note>, and beheaded. It is believed that this faction was stirred up by Heraclianus, a man of great authority in that city, so that he might give the Empire to a friendly soldier who had no confidence in his lineage, which he could later hand over to his son Heraclius after Phocas was removed. For such is the nature of ambition: that under the guise of piety, it rushes into frauds as if through tunnels, and exposes those whom it pretends to wish well to dangers and envy. 

After the patricians and men of the opposing faction were removed, as is customary in military coups, Phocas held the Empire for about eight years. During that time, the entire East was in turmoil; the Persians not only revolted from the Empire but broke into Roman territory and even to the borders of Asia Minor, threatening Africa and Egypt. The primary care of military affairs was given to Heraclianus and Priscus, his son-in-law. They were met from Africa and Egypt, and the hostile onset was sustained rather than driven back; meanwhile, various factions arose from the sacred order in Constantinople.

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK II

...troops, as if about to encounter an enemy, once the matter had first been excellently arranged for betrayal, <margin>...most steadfastly rejected it as a mark of the Antichrist: but to Boniface III.</margin> selected leaders were sent ahead partly into Greece: Priscus the son-in-law, and Heraclius the son. Their goal was that, once Phocas <note>The Emperor Phocas, r. 602–610, often depicted as a tyrant in Byzantine history</note> was captured at an opportune moment, upon the arrival of Heraclius the elder with his forces, they might immediately behead him. Thus, by the same arts with which he had gained the empire, he lost it. 

<margin>So it could thus be read: Gregory the Roman.</margin> Therefore, Heraclius was hailed as Emperor by the soldiers, who had already been bribed by his father's distributions. At the beginning of his reign, a great weight of war loomed. For at that time, it was not a matter of acting to expand the empire, but of thinking how to ward off the enemy from the home hearths. That war had already arisen during the times of Maurice <note>Emperor Maurice, r. 582–602, whose murder by Phocas sparked the war with Persia</note>, and it is the primary occasion of today's calamity. Having broken the enemies in several battles, the Emperor completely dissolved into idleness and luxury, until finally the <margin>...truly the Roman bishops with the Italian party, etc.</margin> enemy—who did not merely rush into the nearest borders of Greece—subjugated all Egypt and Africa. He raged with such power that he denied peace to Heraclius, even though it was for sale at any price. 

On one side, this most insolent enemy pressed hard; on the other was the shame of our religion: the wood upon which Christ hung <note>The "True Cross," a primary relic of Christendom</note>, which had been kept in the hands of the enemies for ten years since the fall of Jerusalem. But the nobles pressed most vehemently, begging, imploring, and adding threats to their prayers, saying that if he did not act, both the nobles and the soldiers would seek a leader for themselves who would help in such a crisis of affairs. Compelled and stirred up, not so much by a sense of duty or fear as by the desire that no mark of infamy should graze him—for the great, the more contaminated their lives are, the more they tend to put on a show of virtue and flee the mark of disgrace—he undertook the task and took up the war, having prepared a massive army. 

Chosroes <note>Khosrow II, the Sassanid King of Persia</note>, terrified by this movement beyond expectation, abandoned his insolence and fled. Leaving the place near Azotus where he had decided to fight, he retreated in fear to his own lands across the Euphrates, consuming the crops with fire wherever he traveled so that he might strip his adversary of the ability to follow. Heraclius did not press on sluggishly (as rare and unusual things burn brightly); he overturned everything, devastated the land, invaded Mesopotamia, and dislodged and routed the general Salbaras <note>Shahrbaraz, a famous Persian general</note> who held defenses at the Saron river. He was succeeded by another named Says <note>Sain Vahmanzadegan</note> with the full strength of the army. 

With him, a doubtful and day-long battle was joined, until toward evening, as victory was leaning toward the Persians, God the Best and Greatest willed to help His own. For suddenly such a crashing of the air arose, with such a horrific noise, such a dark cloud of hail and rain lashing the faces of the Persians, that the Persians, stunned by the heavens, were almost brought to total slaughter. When Chosroes repaired his strength, the attempt was no more successful. Heraclius had hired for that expedition the forces of certain Arabs already infesting that part of the world in the name of Muhammad. This event, it seems to me, was a great step toward those things which followed afterward. 

Heraclius, as victor, brought back twenty-seven military standards of the enemy along with the Life-giving Cross. But Syrochius <note>Kavad II, also known as Siroes</note>, the eldest of Chosroes' sons, because he had been passed over by his father (who had made the younger son Medarses a partner in the remaining empire), entered into a treaty with Heraclius and removed both his father and brother to seize the kingdom. Scarcely surviving his father by a year, he left the reins of power to his son Adheser. After him, Hormisdas was appointed. Engaging with him, the armies of Muhammad took away both his empire and his life, and forced upon the common people the ravings of their persuasion, to be believed under penalty of death. 

This was the end of Persian affairs. Heraclius, celebrating a triumph, returned the sign of our redemption to Jerusalem. He restored the patriarch Zacharias—who had been an exiled companion of the Wood for all fourteen years—to his see, and after holding the customary supplications, he departed from Aelia <note>original: *Aelia*; the Roman name for Jerusalem, *Aelia Capitolina*</note>. However, as if no enemy remained in the whole world, once he had settled the pay for the Arabian soldiers (whose help he had needed), he disbanded the Roman army far from home and left it plundering and wandering in Syria; from which no small dregs [of soldiers joined] Muhammad, the prince of all robbers...

...joined himself to Muhammad (as is likely). The Emperor himself immediately returned to his former way of life, and added to his previous pleasures this: that he hung entirely upon magical deceptions. Indeed, he followed and fostered the Monothelite heresy <note>The Monothelite heresy taught that Christ had two natures but only one shared "will." It was a controversial attempt to reconcile orthodox Christianity with Monophysitism.</note> at the persuasion of Pyrrhus and Cyrus, <margin>One was from Alexandria. Therefore it could be read thus: the Bishops of Constantinople and Alexandria.</margin> the bishops of Constantinople, though he had once persecuted it. He gave a clear proof of his lust in that he took his niece as his wife <note>Heraclius married Martina, the daughter of his sister Maria, in 623 AD, an act considered incestuous and scandalous by the Church.</note>. 

But as misfortune drags misfortune along, with the public treasury squandered on luxury, the foreign soldiers could not be paid according to their agreement. Irritated by this, and even insulted by the treasurers, the Arab soldiers took up arms against the empire. In a few years, by devastating Syria and Egypt, they captured and plundered the most famous cities of western Syria: Damascus, Antioch, and Aelia Capitolina, which is Jerusalem; and through fear of death, they persuaded many to accept their false belief. Such were the beginnings of these pestilential affairs. 

The Emperor had been warned by an oracle, when consulting diviners, to beware of a circumcised people, for a great evil threatened the empire from them. But he, interpreting the oracle as referring to the Jews—whom he thought were the only circumcised ones—forced them all to baptism throughout the whole empire by power. But the matter tended elsewhere: namely toward the followers of Muhammad, who also observe circumcision. That occasion, along with the recovery of the Cross <note>Heraclius famously returned the "True Cross" to Jerusalem in 630 AD after it had been captured by the Persians.</note>, was the reason why he, who deceived the world with a false appearance, was thought to be the best of men. He even dealt with neighboring princes via letters, urging them likewise to force the Jews into the faith of Jesus Christ. That age was entirely full of disease. No region in the whole habitable world lacked its own upheaval. 

Italy was so agitated by the Goths, Lombards, and Arians <note>Arianism was a Christian sect that denied the full divinity of Christ; it was the dominant faith of many Germanic tribes.</note> that almost no city lacked factions. Almost everywhere there were two bishops: one Catholic, the other Arian. Sisebut, the king of the Visigoths in Spain, stripped the Romans of all their garrisons. In Gaul (though I do not know if it happened before or from that time), Theodebert was eliminated by his brothers Chlothar and Theoderic. Those men were—as their names indicate—more akin to the ferocity of the Goths than to the well-known humanity of the Gauls. 

I certainly think this beginning of misfortune flowed from the Emperor's foul alliance with the enemy of Christ, and it first fell back upon the head of the empire itself. For no one ever gave their trust to the Muhammadan dregs without immediately paying the penalty to that same people. Let the ill-omened dealings of Heraclius serve as the primary historical proof. In the second place, let them be compared among themselves: shortly after the Persian Empire was seized, the Turks—at that time an ignoble people living near the Caspian Sea—were summoned by Muhammad <note>Postel likely refers here to a Persian ruler or a later Islamic leader using the name, or perhaps the broader "Muhammadan" forces.</note>, prince of Persia, against Ishmael, the Caliph of Babylon. When they arrived, having immediately defeated the enemy and stripped the very part of the kingdom from those who had summoned them, they seized the empire and have held it almost to this day. 

An alliance was also entered into with the administrators of Egypt, and the same thing happened: it was ruled there until the Circassians, who are also called Mamluks <note>The Mamluks were a class of warrior-slaves who eventually overthrew their Ayyubid masters to rule Egypt.</note>, came to dominate their masters, having also been brought in from elsewhere for pay. Roderic, king of the Goths in Spain, by raping a young woman—the daughter of Julian, the Roman governor in Mauritania—caused the father, overcome by grief, to call upon the innumerable dregs of that nefarious nation in friendship, granting them the power to cross into Spain to avenge the crime committed against his daughter. As a result, once the king was finished, within three years almost all of Spain fell into their power; from there they could never be dislodged until the time of Emperor Frederick III <note>Frederick III (r. 1452–1493). Postel is referencing the completion of the Reconquista in 1492.</note>. Julian truly paid the penalty for his imprudence to that treacherous nation, losing his life along with the province. 

I do not wish to mention at what great cost they were invited into Italy during the time of the conflict between Frederick Barbarossa and Pope Alexander III. Certainly, no one has ever experienced either the help or favor of that nation except to their own great misfortune. Let the Emperor of Trebizond, finished off by his ally, bear witness. Let the Egyptian Sultans, [frequently] by their servants...

...were very frequently cut down. I return to my purpose: namely, what the condition of things was in the Church of Christ when the destructive dogma of the Quran <note>original: "Alcorani"</note> grew strong. We have seen the contention that arose <note>original: "oborta," the catchword from the previous page</note> concerning the primacy in the time of Phocas <note>Byzantine Emperor (r. 602–610) who recognized the primacy of the Roman See.</note> between the Eastern and Western Church, but for a far different reason. For John <note>John IV "the Faster," Patriarch of Constantinople, who claimed the title "Ecumenical Patriarch."</note> had long been contending for authority and the vindication of a title; on the contrary, Saint Gregory, when he was in that see which was established as the first by the consent of the whole Church, said that such an ambitious title should be recognized by no mortal. As a sign of this, he was the first to take up the name of humility: **Servant of the servants of God** <note>original: "Servus servorum Dei," a title still used by Popes today.</note>.

When this dispute had arisen long ago, and already from the times of Maurice and Gregory, Phocas (as I said) acted for the sake of entering into a friendship with Boniface IV. He brought it about that the **Pantheon** <note>original: "πάνθεον," meaning "temple of all gods."</note>—that is, the temple of all the gods constructed in Rome during the time of the false religion, a work of Marcus Agrippa—should be dedicated to the memory of the Virgin Mother and the other saints. Furthermore, he decreed that the Roman pontiff should use the title of "Pope" and that the Roman authority should be primary over all churches. Although the Church had held this until that day by the consensus of all the faithful, nevertheless, because no one had filed a suit regarding that matter, the power or decrees of the Emperor had not yet been used for it. Therefore, that which the most holy pontiff had studied to defend with the greatest zeal—lest he or another should seize it—was immediately dragged elsewhere after his death,

<margin>Gregory the Great.</margin>
differently than he intended. For between him and Boniface III, the see was occupied for only two years by two men. The first of these was Sabinian, a wicked man and most unjust toward Gregory, who sat for seventeen months; the other was Boniface III, who sat for seven. Sabinian was a factious man who, having stirred up infamy against the holy pontiff out of extreme envy of his integrity, had obtained the papacy by capturing the people's favor through evil arts. Since he could not exercise his hatred against the body of that most holy man, he wished to abolish his works by a wicked edict, and he ordained that no one should keep them in their home. Indeed, he agitated the people against Gregory for one thing only: that he had cast down various statues of the ancients and ornaments of the city. This was completely false, for he had removed nothing other than idols and the remnants of old superstition. When, however, he was warned by the people during an extreme scarcity of grain that he should imitate the holy man in almsgiving, he added slanders to slanders, saying that Gregory had consumed the entire treasury of the church so that nothing could be distributed.

There was, in truth, in the Lateran Basilica a very great force of gold to be converted to pious uses. For when Severinus, twenty-nine years later, was created pontiff by the people and clergy according to custom, and was to be confirmed by the Exarch <note>The Byzantine governor of Italy, based in Ravenna.</note> of Ravenna in the name of Heraclius, the Exarch Isaac—in order to win favor with the Emperor who was in need of money (as pleasure-seekers always are) and to look out for himself—said he would not otherwise approve the votes of the people unless the power of the Lateran treasury was given to him in the name of the Emperor. The Pope, otherwise a good man, agreed under compulsion; the sacred money was partly sent to the Emperor, partly given to the soldiers, and partly went to Isaac. The holy pontiff <gloss>Gregory</gloss> had fled the proud title; the other <gloss>Boniface III</gloss> seized it. Gregory had collected money from piety to be converted to pious uses; his wicked successor, sparing it in a time of extreme scarcity so that he might one day devour it, left that same money for the one who would follow shortly after, to be the price of a sacred office. Then the entire state of the Eastern Church began to totter with factions. The Bishop of Constantinople took the name of Patriarch on his own authority, from which a plague arose.

<margin>Of Nestorius</margin>
...that had arisen, there were immediately as many opinions as there were heads. For there were many Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who denied the full divinity of Christ.</note>, and not a few imbued with the error of Nestorius <note>Nestorius taught that Christ existed as two persons—one human and one divine—rather than one person with two natures.</note>. The faction of the Monothelites <note>A 7th-century heresy claiming Christ had two natures but only one will.</note> had even occupied the citadel of the Empire. This causes me to readily agree with the opinion of those who claim that Muhammad was aided by a certain monk named Sergius <note>A common medieval Christian legend that a heretical monk helped Muhammad write the Quran.</note>; that is, he wished to persuade him that there were no other "good Christians" in the whole Quran except those who, after the manner of Nestorius, did not acknowledge the full divinity in Christ. Thus, even today, there are many Christians in the Eastern regions, but they are nearly all related to that dogma. When Geber <note>original: "Geberus." Likely Jabir ibn Aflah, a 12th-century astronomer, though Postel treats him here as a historian of customs.</note>, in his *Almagest*, records the calendars of famous peoples, he describes the festivals of the Nestorians and the Jacobites <note>Members of the Syriac Orthodox Church.</note>, both of whom favored Muhammad. They have many customs unknown or unusual to the Roman Church, such as the Feast of the Baptism of Christ, the Appearance of the Cross in the sky, the Feast of the Crown, of the Ears of Grain, of the Grapes, and things of this sort. 

These things paved the way for impious persuasion, while we either snored, devoted to luxury, or brought evil upon our own heads by provoking others through hatred; we preferred for both sides to perish rather than to set aside ambition and preserve the "bond of peace in union" according to the precept of Paul. We have now been paying the penalty for that crime for nearly 950 years. From this, I am easily led to believe that no less a crime was committed by us than by them, which has turned the mercy of Divine Goodness away from the prosperity of the Christian state since that time, so that our dross might be smelted to the quick—just as it is being smelted in the Eastern and Greek Church. For "our gold," as the prophet said, "has been turned into dross." 

Certainly, if we wish to weigh the facts themselves according to the standard of their own principles, there is no condition today among the ranks of Christians—however holy it may appear in outward show—in which the most "perfect" person of this age even approaches the perfection of those who were once considered barely honest. Suppose there are some: their number will certainly be so small that you could scarcely find as many as there are gates of Thebes or mouths of the wealthy Nile. What else is the monastic order today (if you except those who have joined of their own accord at a mature age) than a refuge for the disinherited? 

Certainly, unless God had left us a seed, we would be like Sodom, and not unlike Gomorrah. Among the four orders of Mendicants <note>The Franciscans, Dominicans, Carmelites, and Augustinians.</note>, there have always been many men of singular learning, whose labor compensated for the curiosity and negligence of many others. From this it clearly appears that although those men are human and struggle with their own imperfections, the "poverty of things" in monasticism is most excellent. For if you look at those who gave their names to Benedict, Bernard, and others for the sake of a stricter profession, through nearly ninety different distinctions, you would undoubtedly scarcely find one in a hundred in any century who practiced anything worthy of a man, beyond <term>οἰκονομίαν</term> <note>original: "oikonomia," referring here to the management of household affairs or material administration rather than spiritual labor.</note>. For if they have lived only according to the common standard of the vulgar crowd, they think that is truly most excellent. 

But, good God, how much this way of life differs from the condition of that ancient age! I do not wish to run through every single order. For everywhere so many things offer themselves that are unworthy of their duty, that I judge it better to cover them in silence than to stir them up. To this day, the Great and Good God has indulged us, perhaps so that we might repent and leave behind this more-than-Sybaritic <note>Sybaris was an ancient Greek city famous for its extreme luxury and decadence.</note> luxury. Now "the axe is laid to the root." The same fate hangs over us that befell the entire East. 

Come then, dearest brothers! Since the princes are not permitted, through their own preoccupations, to turn this plague away from the lands, let us run to meet it. Let us oppose ourselves for the name of Jesus Christ; let us sharpen the swords of reason against the impious nation, ready to strike at the first opportunity. Are we not ashamed that only a single corner of dominion in Europe is left to Christ? What account of our laziness are we going to give to God, that no one opposes himself to such a great calamity? Certainly, many martyrs, most famous for miracles after death, teach us that this cause is most pleasing to Christ. For many daily opposing themselves...
