...those <note>original: "tes", the end of a word like "resistentes" (those resisting) from the previous page</note> resisting perverse dogma, God grants healing after death to those who approach their graves in the name of Christ. Do we think Christ will fail His own people? He is the one who caused the tongues of African bishops, which had been cut out by the Arians <note>The Arians were a heretical sect that denied the full divinity of Christ; the Vandals, who were Arians, persecuted North African Catholics in the 5th century.</note>, to grow back so they could continue to proclaim the truth. Why is it that this foolish and futile opinion is held by many as if it were a most sacred decree: that the "time of martyrs" has passed? As if an opportunity to prove oneself to Christ, even at the risk of one's life, were ever lacking! If the ungodly and those far from the primary knowledge of the faith were missing, there would still be no shortage of heretics, the impious crimes of princes, or the wickedness of evil tyrants. Even if both the ungodly and heretics were gone, there will never be a lack of affairs in this world through which a soul, relying on God, might exercise itself and become a witness for Him. I do not wish to bring up examples of the earliest martyrs when countless myriads already speak for themselves. The rebuke of Herod brought death to John the Baptist. A bold reprimand of the Emperor Valens <note>An Arian Emperor (reigned 364–378) who clashed with orthodox bishops.</note> would have brought death along with exile to Basil the Great, had Providence allowed it. How many times did John Chrysostom oppose the Empress Eudoxia, who was infected with the Arian heresy, at the risk of his life? He suffered exile twice for that reason. Thomas of Canterbury <note>Thomas Becket (1118–1170), the Archbishop of Canterbury murdered in his cathedral after conflicts with King Henry II.</note>, slain for the preservation of the Church’s liberty, later shone with miracles. All these examples show that in nothing ought we more to prove ourselves to God than in persuading others of the truth and asserting it.

There was never a more fertile harvest promised to Christians from the death of Christ than there is now. For what difference does it make whether a man has never known the truth, or has forgotten it? The whole world is in greater darkness now than when Christ sent the workers into the vineyard. Certainly, just as no superstitious plague has ever been more monstrous anywhere among the nations than the <term>Muhametana</term> <note>Mohammedan (Islamic)</note> faith, so nothing can be done in the name of the Savior that is more pleasing than to oppose it with all one's strength. Angelus of Sicily, gloriously preaching Christ to the Moors, finished his life by the sword after long imprisonments. Likewise, five <term>Franciſcani</term> <note>Franciscan</note> martyrs—Berard and his companions—were beheaded in Mauritania <note>Specifically Morocco, in the year 1220.</note> for that reason, becoming glorious through miracles immediately after their deaths. Anthony, who is called "of Padua" from the place of his burial, had attempted this same risk in his youth; but with the business unfinished, he was forced to return because of his ignorance of the language.

The <term>Arabica</term> <note>Arabic</note> language alone is what is needed, beyond the capacity for engaging with the enemies of Christ, for it opens the way for someone about to travel through almost the entire world. For no language, as far as the memory of literature records, has ever occupied so much of the earth: the two Mauritanias, Numidia, Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Arabia, Syria, Asia Minor, Armenia, Mesopotamia, Assyria, Persia, Parthia, Aria, Gedrosia, and the greater part of India embrace it for the sake of that ruinous dogma. The <term>Clementina</term> <note>The "Clementine Constitutions," specifically referring to a decree from the Council of Vienne (1311) that mandated the teaching of Hebrew, Arabic, and Chaldean in major universities.</note> had ordered concerning teachers that the primary Universities ought to have two doctors of that language, so that every age might have men fit for uprooting that persuasion from the minds of people. This has not yet been done.

I have now laid for you, as far as my meager ability allowed, the foundations of that learning by printing a grammar. I possess a vast supply of books in this language, considering their rarity. But that which can best make you ready and equipped in every part is the refutation of that insane dogma. I have indeed undertaken that work—not like those before me who attempted the same task using a Latin version, or (to speak more accurately) a Latin *inversion* <note>original: "inuerſione." Postel is making a pun: the previous translations were so bad they were "inversions" or "perversions" of the original Quran.</note> of the <term>Alcorani</term> <note>Quran (Alcoran)</note>, but from the Arabic manuscripts themselves. Come then, O most dear brothers, especially you who profess a contempt for the world: help me, both with your labor and your prayers. Follow a leader, even if he is not skilled enough. Even the greatest geniuses began from a basic apprenticeship. From these beginnings of proving ourselves to Christ, we shall proceed to greater things. Thus it will happen that the zeal of Princes will be stirred in that direction and lean toward this care. A small flame has not rarely stirred up the greatest fires. Why do we have such a great love for life, which must be relinquished even against our will? How...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...uld <note>original: "rat", the end of a word like "curaret" or "superaret" from the previous page</note> more surely do so by committing that life to Christ, in whose presence to have died is to have lived. We have seen four or five expeditions against the **followers of Muhammad** <note>original: "Muhamedicos"</note> undertaken boldly at the persuasion of one or two men; certainly, if these had been equipped with arguments as fit for overturning their dogma as they were with arms, the **Arabic plague** <note>original: "Arabica lues"; Postel uses this term to describe the spread of Islamic influence as a spiritual contagion.</note> would have been utterly destroyed. Arms are accustomed to go first in dangerous times. Let letters go before; let piety and faith provide the armor. Otherwise, if we employ the same sloth that has endured to this day, we shall undoubtedly, against our will, undergo the yoke of a foul slavery of both minds and bodies. If you will not [exercise] while healthy, as <term>Horace</term> <note>Quintus Horatius Flaccus, Roman lyric poet. Postel cites his *Epistles* 1.2.34.</note> says, you will run when you are dropsical <note>A medical term for edema or swelling; the metaphor suggests that if one does not take preventative action when healthy, they will be forced into much more difficult labor once the disease of "slavish" subjection takes hold.</note>. The world, afflicted under that pestilence, mourns: and that condition of affairs which it refused to preserve when it was free—as it ought to have—it now experiences against its will. The **Greek church** abused its wealth for luxury: now that wealth goes to the soldier, and provides the strength to oppress that very church. 

Thus God has ordained that, after He has waited a long time for us to repent, He drags those who are unwilling. The very things we use for destruction, luxury, and pride, He transfers to others, so that we may receive affliction from them instead of pleasure. That monstrous tyrant <term>Mehmed II</term> <note>original: "Muhamedes", referring to the Ottoman Sultan who conquered Constantinople in 1453.</note>, who captured <term>Constantinople</term>, is said to have spoken when he saw the heaps of wealth and the books of accounts with which the patriarchate overflowed in its decoration and pomp:

> O impious men, this shall recoil upon your own heads; you, by abusing such vast wealth against the prescription of your own law, have accelerated your ruin. I shall see to it that posterity pays the penalty for your sin.

To the soldier afflicting the Christian cause, this money shall go. Nor was there any delay before he ordered that wealth to be gathered into a single treasury, from which it was permitted to take only for military expeditions against the enemies of the Muhammadan religion, and for the use of the poor, pilgrims, and impoverished men who are engaged in the study of literature. Toward this purpose, sixty thousand gold pieces are spent annually in the name of alms. Once, this treasury was exhausted by <term>Sultan Selim I</term>, the father of the reigning <term>Suleiman</term>, contrary to the decree of his grandfather, when he was hurrying to the Persian war at <term>Chaldiran</term> <note>The Battle of Chaldiran in 1514, where the Ottomans defeated the Safavid Persians.</note>. Thus the patriarch accumulated eternal disaster for his descendants. 

Indeed, the lower orders of that church were no more fortunate. For whatever was owed to the churches, whether by tithes or other revenue, all of it went to the soldier. So it is no wonder that those Princes abound with an eternal and numerous military. For another is immediately substituted in the place of one who has died, not unlike the curates here. Unless we provide a remedy in time, the same fate looms over us. It is true that among the victors, each nation is usually left the free practice of its own religion, albeit in the greatest poverty; but the emperor’s edict daily leads away the youth from Christian parents throughout the entire empire to be enrolled in the military after a few years of training. And finally—which is the worst of all—the youth swears by the words of the **Quran** <note>original: "Alcorani"</note>, having denied Christ. 

And do these things not move us? When various religious orders arose among us with a certain fervor, at first the highest piety flourished in them, and they turned away the wrath of the divinity from raging against other mortals with their holy prayers. But gradually, as that "good strife" (as <term>Hesiod</term> <note>Ancient Greek poet who distinguished between "bad" strife (war) and "good" strife (competition that leads to hard work).</note> calls it) grew cold, they returned to the old pursuits common to mortals, and began to differ from the rest by little more than their outward dress. For this reason, in various ways, one part of the church approved only a single order, because it saw that everything becomes corrupted with time; another part substituted new orders for the corrupted ones. Among the Greeks and in almost the entire East, only the order of the <term>Basilians</term> <note>Monks following the Rule of St. Basil the Great.</note> is found. The <term>Benedictines</term> succeeded the followers of <term>Augustine</term>. Truly, the zeal of those good men tended toward this: that they might restore that Apostolic way of life which had become famous through men of remarkable holiness in many other places, but especially in the deserts of **Egypt and Syria**, for nearly three hundred years...

... <note>original: "rat"</note> that it should be embraced by as many as possible; and it did not succeed unsuccessfully. For the most brilliant lights of the world have taught that this institution was pleasing to Christ. From the flock of **Benedict** <note>St. Benedict of Nursia, the father of Western monasticism.</note>, **Berno** arose, who gave origin to the **Cluniacs**; **Bruno** to the **Carthusians**; **Stephen Harding** <note>original: "Ardingus"</note> to the **Cistercians**; **Norbert** to the **Premonstratensians**; **Stephen** to the **Grandmontines**; **John Gualbert** <note>original: "Galbertus"</note> to the **Vallombrosians**; **Bernard** to the **monks of Clairvaux**; and **Romuald** to the **Camaldolese**, and so on. All of these, in truth, wished to differ from the ancient rite and fellowship of living for no other reason than that they saw the holy institutions were poorly preserved amidst abundant wealth. Therefore, striving toward the narrow path, they fled from corrupted associations. 

Truly, because integrity can scarcely be preserved in the midst of riches, there finally arose **four orders** <note>The Mendicant Orders (Franciscans, Dominicans, Carmelites, and Augustinians), who took vows of extreme poverty.</note> destitute of both private and communal wealth, than whom none were better except for those first ones closest to the Apostles. For although they are men, just like the rest, they did not have the plagues arising from their own wealth, as those authors—**Elijah** and **Augustine**, though absent and long since departed from this present life, and **Francis** and **Dominic**, being present—instituted. 

But to what end is this? So that it may be clear, since there is such a great harvest in the whole circle of the earth and so few workers, that there are many who have promised their labor with a cheerful mind to the Father for cultivating the vineyard; yet the vineyard is not only not cultivated by them, but is so neglected that it should not even be called a vineyard. Now the **Gospel of Christ** <note>original: "Christi euangelium"</note> begins to spread in the **New World** <note>The Americas.</note>. **Peter Martyr** <note>Peter Martyr d'Anghiera, an Italian-born historian of Spain’s explorations.</note> writes that many monasteries for instruction in the <term>catechism</term> <note>Basic religious instruction often given before baptism.</note> have already been introduced there by the **Franciscans** and **Dominicans**. As long as there was a great ignorance of letters, almost no parish priests skilled in sacred literature, and a great scarcity of books, your labor, Brothers, was more necessary. 

But now, since laziness and an excessive multitude of those living off the expense of others is given as a reproach to you, and is even thrown in your teeth by children, wash away that stain! Conceive again the spirits of the ancient fathers; dare something. Followers will never be lacking. The more cruel the **followers of Muhammad** <note>original: "Muhametani"</note> are toward those who even dare to mutter against the deception of the **Quran** <note>original: "Alcorani"</note>, the more one must hope that Christ will be present to aid His own. There shall finally be **one fold and one shepherd** <note>A reference to John 10:16, a central theme in Postel's vision of global religious unity.</note>. 

If, however, we hesitate any longer, there is a danger lest this small corner of the world, in which the empire of Jesus still flourishes, should perish through our own sluggishness. We must not delay in the manner of heretics and the impious. For they say that the **followers of Muhammad** should not be resisted, as they are sent by God to avenge our iniquities. Others say that Christ’s empire should be left to Him, so that He Himself may protect it. God is not accustomed to do anything without human choice when it can be done by it. It is necessary for those who are His, if they wish to enjoy His happiness, to strive with the full effort of both body and mind so that His doctrine may lie open as widely as possible. 

If once the dogmas of that perverse teaching begin to be torn up in one place, that whole mass will collapse with no trouble. Provided that princes perceive that their empires can be retained under the doctrine of Christ, they will easily yield, and we shall report a victory than which none has ever been or will be more memorable. May God grant it. 

For since the use of that persuasion <note>Islam</note> and language <note>Arabic</note> lies open so widely—extending from the **Pillars of Hercules** <note>The Strait of Gibraltar.</note> through Africa to the 180th degree along the <term>tropic</term> <note>Postel is describing the vast geographical reach of the Arabic-speaking world across the Southern hemisphere as understood in 16th-century geography.</note>—if once those who use it and hold great authority among their people can be conquered by our reasons, they will gird themselves for the work and, together with us, busily hand down the doctrine of Christ to others. It is not as difficult to join battle with them as is commonly believed. For they will never be able to withstand our reasons. Therefore they immediately resort to punishments if anyone says even a single word against the Quran or its decrees. Those who offer themselves will possess their souls in patience. They will be conquered by miracles. Christ will be present, if once we undertake to join battle armed with faith.

But enough of these matters. Therefore, taking heart against that destruction and meditating upon its ruin among you, take your start from the life of the false prophet.

# EXPOSITION AND REFUTATION OF THE MUHAMMADAN PERSUASION.
## The Life of Muhammad, the Lawgiver of the Arabs.
### CHAPTER I.

Since many and varied details present themselves regarding the arts by which Muhammad was raised to the height of power, I have decided to describe his life in the manner of **Suetonius** in his *Lives of the Caesars*. I will use certain arguments and "topics" so that the facts may be more easily understood and held in memory. In this way, related matters can be collected more easily, allowing the reader to explain things that are otherwise unpleasant to read or hear without any boredom.

Therefore, I shall first set forth his lineage, the arts in which he was educated, his natural disposition and character, which supporters he used to promote his "sacred" ideas, and which he used to acquire power; also, with whom he contracted alliances, how many wives he took, and finally, by which expeditions he acquired that power which he left to his **Kuraish** <note>original: "Coraisinis"</note> descendants; and lastly, by what fate he died and where he was buried. Then, using the same method, I will examine the Quran, reducing its contents to "commonplaces": what he wished to treat, what he took from the Old Testament, what from the New, what errors were admitted in them, and what things are unique to him. Finally, I will discuss which authors are used by those who have sworn by his words, following the Quran. In the last place, I shall speak of the succession of power. But now, I begin the work.

# WILLIAM POSTEL’S BOOK II

...by what supports he who is being described was able to use, whether for the path of virtue or vice, so that we may recognize him. Thus, we may discern what he owes to his ancestors and what he achieved through his own efforts. It is recorded that Muhammad <note>original: "Muhamedes"</note> had ancestors who were citizens of the Arabian city of Mecca, from an undistinguished family. They were called the Quraysh <note>original: "Choreissos"</note>, a people devoted to carrying merchandise from Persia, Syria, and Egypt into Arabia. He was born to a father named Abdullah ibn Abd al-Muttalib <note>original: "Hebdalla mutalibo"</note>, a man who was (as they would have it) wealthy and opulent, and a mother named Aminah <note>original: "Imina"</note>. They were pagans <note>original: "ethnicis"</note> and citizens of Mecca, as some writers have left in their records. According to others, he was born in Yathrib <note>original: "Ietriba"</note>, which some call Iefraba. The more common opinion among them is that he arose from Mecca. 

However, he is described as being descended from those whose efforts the later Caliphs <note>original: "Chaliphę"</note> utilized in handing down their persuasion. For Yathrib is called *Medina alnabi*, which is to say, "The City of the Prophet," because he was born and buried there. Others, however, assert it was only called so because of his residence and burial. This obscurity concerning his origins arises because he had seven men in the closest intimacy who were accomplices in the entire ten-year fable <note>Postel uses "fable" (fabula) to express his view of the Islamic tradition as a fabrication.</note>; others opposed these men out of envy and wrote certain chronicles of his life that were entirely different from their view. 

These first seven are: Asserus son of Amerus, and another of the same name, the son of Chetirus, Umar <note>original: "Homarus"</note>, Humeranus, Eleanfarus, Aeonus, and Napheas. Theirs is the more common and primary opinion. For they are even said to be participants in the law of the Quran <note>original: "Alcorani"</note> and were admitted into fellowship by the prophet. Yet, when they were frequently questioned about this law, they affirmed they knew nothing. They were opposed by more recent figures instructed by the subsequent Caliphs: Abozeidus, Ibnabdallaus, Muhammad son of Ezra, Alphalus son of Jafar, Abohumarus son of Zeidus, and countless others, in order to give greater authority to the smaller city in which he was buried. 

Nor was it enough for them to have defected from the first witnesses; they even devised two genealogies with invented names. One goes from Adam through Ishmael, with a certain "light" passing from men to women <note>This refers to the *Nur Muhammad* (Light of Muhammad), a traditional Islamic concept of a prophetic light passed through his ancestors.</note> all the way to his father. The other goes backward from Muhammad to Adam. And lest they seem to have told too few lies, they used the testimony of a single maidservant, Halimah <note>original: "Halimæ"</note> (she had raised the orphan), claiming that his mother gave birth without pain, and they devised many other things worthy of such authors. 

Wherever he may have been born, it is agreed by everyone’s calculation that he was posthumous <note>His father died before his birth.</note>. It is recorded that his mother died two years, or as others prefer, four years after his birth. Having been taken into the guardianship of his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib <note>original: "Abdemutalibi"</note>, and under the care of Halimah, a poor woman from the province of Venizat, he was raised in quite meager circumstances, as can be seen from many sources. For he himself confesses this about himself in the Quran, saying: 

> You were poor, and you were enriched; you were an orphan, and you were taken in. <note>A translation of Surah Ad-Duha (93:6-8).</note>

Furthermore, he had the domestic care of camels in the house of one of his kinsmen until, being already grown according to the custom of his ancestors, he began to drive pack-camels—on which all merchandise is usually carried in those regions—back and forth from Arabia into neighboring regions. All of these things cannot be arguments for a noble or powerful family, if we look at things as they are usually judged among us. I say this so that, having carefully weighed the man's origin, we may see where he first made his step toward power. It may be, however, that his father’s wealth was so narrow that it was hardly sufficient for him and his brothers, of whom he was the twelfth. If it were relevant to the matter, I would publish their names. But it is of no help to know anything else about them, except that it is well known they were his most bitter enemies because of his imposture—with the exception of two, who defected from the worship of idols to his foolish trifles. Furthermore, he killed the rest. So great in the man was the [love] of his kin...

# ON THE INHABITANTS OF MECCA, AND what opportunities for his faction Muhammad <note>original: "Muhamedes"</note> had.
# CHAPTER III.

<margin>This is Kedar <note>original: "Cedar"</note>, son of Ishmael, whom others call Qaydar <note>original: "Caidrum"</note>.</margin>
Although it may not seem to fit the argument to discuss a location when one ought to be speaking about a man's life, nevertheless, because the consideration of both place and time contributes greatly to the understanding of the events themselves, I believe I must speak—before I proceed further—about the condition of the men who inhabited Mecca <note>original: "Mechæ"</note> at the time Muhammad was born. Mecca is a marketplace situated in the western part of Arabia Felix <note>term: "Arabia Felix" (Happy Arabia); a classical name for the fertile southern region of the Arabian Peninsula</note>, about a hundred miles distant from the shores of the Arabian Gulf, which we are accustomed to calling the Red Sea in sacred writings. Whatever spices exist in the region of Sheba <note>original: "Sabæa"</note> are usually brought there due to the frequent trade of all nations. It was a people of quite corrupt morals, who placed nothing among the "goods" of life except the pleasures of the body. As often happens in such places, due to the constant presence of diverse visitors who change daily, various types of sacred rites were held; thus every nation might find even their own ancestral gods, from wherever on earth, in that great and busy marketplace.

The greater part of the people living there when Muhammad was striving for new things served idols, which were called Al-Lat and Al-Uzza <note>original: "Ellet & Aluza"</note> (some wish these to be Pallas and Venus). The Jews observed the Mosaic temples. Certain Jacobite and Nestorian Christians <note>These were specific Eastern Christian sects that Postel identifies as being present in Arabia</note> had their own rites. But by far the largest part of the pagans were accustomed to gather for the sake of sacred rites at a certain temple located in the middle of the city. Those who have written of Muhammad's affairs—wishing to trace the authority of their religion back to the highest principles—claim that this temple, where the tower called the Qibla <note>original: "Alquibla"; here referring to the Kaaba or its orientation</note> is, had already been built from the time of Ishmael, and that the sacred rite was instituted by Abraham, Ishmael, and Kedar <note>original: "Cahidaro"</note> his son. Wishing to provide proof for this, they add that Kedar, so that the idol <note>Postel uses "idol" here to refer to the Black Stone or the site itself from his polemical perspective</note> would not be ignored, placed a marble stone in that part of the tower opposite it, so that someone who could not enter the temple due to their business might at least worship upon seeing the sign. Meanwhile, those "good" historians do not notice that while they seek the antiquity of a prophetic lineage, they actually establish the leaders of that lineage as the authors of idolatry; especially since elsewhere these liars, being poorly mindful of their story, say in the *Hazear* <note>likely referring to a collection of Hadith or history</note> that he was born of a most just and religious people. And he himself confesses that he was in manifest error and cherished idols; and it is written in the Sunnah <note>original: "Suna"</note> that he worshipped the stone: thus does the lie agree with itself. Lest the ancestral rite be entirely abolished, they still worship that stone today in memory of their fathers. They say, indeed, that in that city or nearby, Abraham wished to sacrifice his son; and therefore they observe many ceremonies during the pilgrimages that take place over four months, as if they were instituted by Abraham in that very place. Among these, none is more frequent than the killing of many sheep, in memory of that ram which Abraham had sacrificed in place of his son. But more of these things in their proper place. Now we must come to his upbringing.

They tell six hundred such absurd, ridiculous, and old wives' tales that it is shameful to read them. But from these, let others who find pleasure in such things learn the rest. ...species, clouds, winds, and angels. The birds wanted to nourish him with fruits because they could easily collect many of them. Thus the whole faith of the Quran <note>original: "Alcorani"</note>, or at least of the book *Haffear* <note>original: "Haffear"; likely a reference to a specific biography or collection of traditions</note>, which is of equal authority, depends on the report of Halima. 

But, O sensible readers, listen to this miracle with an open mind, and learn all things from this one instance. When he had reached about five years of age after being born, he went to the folds of the shepherds one day and reported that he had been seized by an angel (having devised this when he was already forty years old, and employing Halima as a witness); he claimed he was led apart from the others and disemboweled with a razor by that same angel. The angel, having extracted the heart from the body, cut it in half, and from it cut away a certain small black piece, and immediately replaced the heart and made him healthy again. The angel told the prophet that this small piece, by which the devil tempts men, had been taken away from him. You have it, you see it; judge for yourselves about him. 

I find nothing further handed down until his 15th year of age, at which time he was assigned to the care of camels. Meanwhile, his poverty of fortune, or the rudeness of his entire nation, is proven by the fact that he knew neither letters nor how to swim <note>original: "nec literas nec nare"; a classical idiom for being completely uneducated</note>. However, I would easily believe that through constant conversation with boys trained in various cultures, he heard certain trifles about individual religions; and finally, when he had grown up, he recalled those things to memory and applied them to his own craft. For the Jews, who were numerous, could have sought to capture the boy, so that they might then especially make one proselyte twice as bad as themselves. Concerning his soul and the form of his body, since nothing has been handed down, I can judge nothing except from the effects. For I find nothing written except by those chroniclers of the Caliphs <note>original: "Chaliphorum"</note>, who make him more beautiful than angels. That he was of a strong body is proven by his lustfulness, for he would enter twelve women in a single hour; and he himself said that he had the strength of forty men in his loins. He was certainly of a mind most desirous of vengeance. Truly, I have nothing certain about him up to his 25th year, nor what he did.

### BY WHAT BEGINNING HE TRANSITIONED TO A MORE 
### SPLENDID FORTUNE. CHAPTER V.

Having been given, as was said, in the fifteenth year of his age to the care of camels in the household of one of his relatives, he traveled back and forth for the sake of trade, and observed the various rites of men as the opportunity of the place allowed. For that place was at an equal distance from Babylonian Assyria, Egypt, and from the most famous city of the entire East (as long as things were prosperous), Jerusalem. Imbued with that resourcefulness <note>original Greek: "πολυτροπία" (polytropia); meaning versatility or wilyness</note> and craftiness, he already began to meditate on greatness. This addition of luck came to him: that on account of his bodily strength, Khadija <note>original: "Hadeiaga"</note>, a rich and very powerful woman who had married his kinsman (whose affairs Muhammad was managing), was seized by love for him, and she used him in a secret habit as often as it was permitted. Thus it happened that, after the wretched husband was removed—not without suspicion of poison—the slave married his mistress as his wife and obtained ample resources. Such is the power of female lust. Not long after Khadija began to live familiarly with her new husband Muhammad, she perceived that the man was violently seized by the falling sickness <term>morbus comitialis</term> <note>epilepsy; called the "assembly sickness" because its occurrence was considered an omen to dissolve public assemblies</note>. This he had previously cautiously concealed, and she had been ignorant of it. Khadija then began to repent of the deed; yet there was no place for divorce on this most just occasion, before that scoundrel published a law for any occasion...

He claimed it had been revealed to him by the **angel Gabriel** that this passion had so troubled him because he was not attending to the office of **prophecy** to which he had been appointed by God. 

Thus he began to weave a certain marvelous tale: he would seclude himself from human company for the whole day, and not rarely at night; every day he would go into a **cave** <note>original: "specum"</note> not far from the city for many hours. There, as he said, he practiced fasts, endured divine conversations, and felt frequent ecstasies. He continued this until he drew not only the woman into an opinion of his holiness, but also many powerful men into his way of thinking—as they were ignorant of all things, especially divine matters, and were almost all **fools** <term>original: "suphehę"; likely a Latinization of the Arabic *sufahā’*, meaning "fools" or "unthinking people"</term>, as he calls them—that is, stupid and unrefined. 

The woman, although she was almost brought around to his view, nevertheless knew the man "inside and out" <note>original: "intus et in cute"</note>, and could hardly persuade herself that there was not some fraud underlying this prophecy. For she frequently objected that an angel did not seem "good" who would torture a man even to the point of spasms and apoplexy, and to foaming at the mouth and sweating of the entire body; surely he could persuade him of divine things at less cost. Furthermore, she argued that if he were truly a prophet and a friend of God and the angels, he could obtain from them the favor of not appearing at such inconvenient hours: so that they might cease to seize him during sleep, at the table, while eating, or in the middle of **sexual intercourse** <note>original: "in ipso coitu"</note> and similar occupations. 

But when she saw the matter proceed as far as madness, she said it was the work of the **devil** and not of God, which made him feel quite poorly. However, with trifles and with responses supposedly given by God during his spasms, he eluded the woman’s objections as best he could rather than truly answering them. I believe he had heard—or perhaps had seen in many places where oracular priestesses remained—those seized by fury giving divine responses. He knew this was an ancient type of imposture; he knew many were mocked by those tricks. By these means, he enticed the minds of the Jews and terrified the idol-worshippers and citizens of Mecca, so that a good part of them favored him.

### BY WHICH SUPPORTERS HE GATHERED
### power. CHAPTER VI.

**A** great multitude of Jews, who seek their Messiah everywhere on earth, were living in Mecca. When they saw that this man said things consistent with their own law, and was affected in a way beyond the custom of other men—thinking nothing of madness or disease was underneath it—they joined themselves to the man. They began to approve his decrees all the more easily because he established ceremonies almost at the discretion of the Rabbis. For he agreed with them on frequent washings <note>ritual ablutions, or wudu</note>. For a long time, he even prayed toward the temple in Jerusalem, which looks toward the north from that region. This continued until the Jews sensed they were being deceived and recognized the schemes of a man aspiring to tyranny, who was otherwise clearly insane and raving. For his disease progressed to the point that he barely enjoyed a lucid interval once every many days. Wanting to excuse this defect, the authors of the book *Al-Shifa* <note>original: "Assiffai," referring to the famous biography by Qadi Ayyad</note> say that the prophet so weakened himself with fasting and vigils that his senses failed him, and he was rendered thunderstruck by God, so that he believed he constantly heard a voice calling him, yet when he turned, he saw no one. Frequently telling this same thing to his wife Khadija <note>original: "Hadisæ"</note>, she judged these to be the tricks not of an angel, but of a foul demon, and her husband to be plainly foolish and out of his mind. From this, he was seized with such grief that he wanted to throw himself headlong out of a window, preferring to die rather than be seen as a fool. Yet such an "excellent prophecy" mocked the woman, for he said that Gabriel was immediately present and said to him: "O Muhammad, God greets you, and through me He wishes it to be known to you that you shall be the prophet and the most perfect of all creatures." These things are in their books, by which the wretched people do not see that their own authors cut each other's throats <note>contradict one another</note>. For how could he be a prophet destined from eternity, gifted with light, born circumcised, visited by angels, disemboweled <note>referring to the story of the opening and cleansing of Muhammad's chest</note>, and suffer similar things, who before the fortieth year of his life had not received word from an angel that he would be a prophet? That book completely destroys the credibility of the chronicle *Al-Fasri* <note>original: "Alfear"</note>, which they especially approve. But I return to the Jews. They, thinking he would be the Messiah, joined the man: they established sacred rites, and even [formed] an affinity with...

On the 13th of the month of Ramadham <note>Ramadan</note>, Moadus <note>Likely Mu'adh ibn Jabal, a prominent companion of Muhammad</note> was therefore placed in charge of the city in the prophet's name, to ensure that the recently established sacred rites were observed. Meanwhile, while he besieged the neighboring city of Cambichum <note>Possibly a Latinization of Khaybar or Ta'if</note>, lest any uprising arise in Mecca, he sent Vbecharum <note>Abu Bakr, Muhammad’s father-in-law and the first Caliph</note>—whom we have mentioned—there and entrusted him with the care of the republic, so that among other things he should take care that no one be admitted into it except those who had been initiated. Those who wished to receive the law were admitted on that condition. He also took care that the prophet’s treasury was supplied, so that there would be enough for expeditions. Matters were confirmed for him in this manner. Great ease was also added to his affairs. For when he traveled through the countryside, villages, and estates, he was so hostile regarding the law that those who did not pay tribute or give their names to his persuasion were endangered in both their fortunes and their bodies; but those who believed and joined him enjoyed immunity (except for what went to the treasury). By these tricks, it happened that a great multitude of men came to him daily. Fear urged some; others feigned repentance; and countless others, the most lawless of men, joined him for the sake of plundering and harassing their neighbors. Thus, in a very short time, a great army coalesced, and the dregs of society increased to such an immense degree that not infrequently in the Quran <note>original: "Alcorano"</note> he complains that there are more than is proper, and that they come for the sake of living rather than for fighting. Thus, neither under him nor without him was anything safe. By these arts, by these allies, and in this manner he prepared his power; but we must speak briefly of his followers whose learning he used. The authors of the chronicle *Assear* <note>original: "Assear"; referring to the Sira, the traditional biographies of the Prophet</note> mention two Christian men who lived in his vicinity, hiring out their labor to a certain sword-maker; it is believed that Muhammad used their company when he was writing the *Assuar mechiet* <note>original: "Assuar mechiet"; referring to the "Meccan Surahs" or chapters of the Quran</note>, that is, the chapters of the Quran written in Mecca. Not once in the Quran does he excuse this crime: [claiming] that he had no teacher; [claiming] that it is so elegantly composed that in the whole world nothing similar could be written except by God. How many Jews he had [among his followers] has already been made clear enough. Certain men of our own, close to those centuries, have left it written that a certain fugitive <margin>of Nestorius</margin> monk named Sergius <note>A reference to the monk Bahira or Sergius, a figure in Christian polemics alleged to have taught Muhammad</note>—corrupted by the vice of Nestorius <note>Nestorianism, a Christological doctrine labeled as heresy by the Byzantine church</note>—betook himself there when he was being prosecuted in Constantinople for violating our religion. They say he made the man a semi-Christian and, at the persuasion of the Jews, induced him to delete many things written against Christ. I more willingly grant credit to this narrative because those Christians who write these things were of the highest authority and lived almost at the same times, and they wrote to similar learned men; hence, it is not to be believed that they raised false objections. Nevertheless, their histories do not mention him, as far as I have read, nor does any work of a refined man...

### WITH WHOM HE JOINED IN AFFINITY
### CHAPTER VII

So great was the deceit of this impostor that he seems to have desired to obtain nothing from his friends sooner than women, if any appeared to be of a more elegant form. The first was she who has already been written of, whom they call Hadeia <note>Khadija, Muhammad's first wife</note>, the witness of the whole fable: through whose wealth he acquired power. Besides her, when he reached the height of his affairs, he married fifteen other wives, or at minimum eleven, and as many concubines as he wished: whom he boasted of entering in a single hour. He claimed that no bull could enter more cows in one day than he, by "prophetic virtue," could work upon women. Regarding his intemperate lust, there is no clearer example than when he took Assam <note>Aisha</note>, the daughter of Vbecharus <note>Abu Bakr, the first Caliph</note>, when she was eight years old; having accepted her as his betrothed, and respecting neither the laws of nature nor the tender age of the infant, as soon as he saw the beauty of the girl, he loosed the girdle of Venus <note>A classical idiom for deflowering or consummating a marriage</note>, in a "prophetic" manner indeed. But while I wish to touch upon his vices, I am drawn in so many different directions that I do not know where to begin, so overwhelmed am I by the mass of them. Therefore, the end of his life must be concluded. Finally, the crimes of this wicked man must be treated through certain places and arguments.

With Vbecharus <note>Abu Bakr</note> appointed as governor of Mecca, as we have said, Muhammad conquered neighboring regions with a formidable army and ordered them to obey his laws, and he forced incursions of his power as far as Persia, Syria, and Egypt. He also relied on the power of the petty rulers of Armenia, who wasted the neighboring borders as far as Coele-Syria with their raids. But by far the greatest opportunity given to him to increase his power seems to me to have arisen from the error and sluggishness of our own people. For I am easily led to believe that, on account of the monstrous crimes often committed by many of ours under the pretext of piety, that plague undermined all minds, and as a punishment for crimes, with God's permission, was raised up by Satan. Thus I am easily persuaded that he did not lack impious soldiers who would defect from our side. The wound was then fresh; the Church, barely breathing after the Arians, Nestorians, Eunomians, Ebionites, Pelagians, Donatists <note>These were various Christian sects deemed heretical by the central Church</note>, and six hundred such monsters had been scarcely driven away, had only just caught its first breath in the hope of a cure. Scarcely were any legitimate leaders confirmed in the outlying regions when, before the scar had even closed, this plague arose: into which whatever destruction and error had ever been devised flowed, as if into the Augean stable <note>original: "Augiæ stabulum"; a mythological reference to a stable of extreme filth</note> and a sewer. To this—as if Satan had not done enough to undermine minds—the sluggishness of the Emperor Heraclius brought the greatest loss of all fortunes. For meanwhile, while he hunts all day, plays the harlot all night, plays at dice, and tests the art of Apicius <note>original: "Apitij artis"; a reference to the Roman gourmet Apicius, implying gluttony and decadent luxury</note>, he effeminates the whole mass of the empire by his example, grants the soldiers a vacation from their duties, and squanders the treasury among harlots, adulterers, flatterers, and triflers. To put it briefly, while he carried all his counsels in one head, about 600 years from the passion of Christ...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
# DE ORBIS CONCORDIA

...[In that] year, Khosrow <note>original: "Chofroes"; Khosrow II (r. 590–628), the last great king of the Sassanid Empire</note>, King of the Persians, attacked Syria, Egypt, Africa, and the other provinces of the Empire that were left without protection. He was victorious, proceeding from Babylon all the way to the Mauretanias <note>Modern-day Morocco and Algeria</note> with no one resisting him. His son attacked Thrace from the north. Yet the Emperor <note>Heraclius (r. 610–641)</note> was not stirred from his lethargy until the nobles threatened that, unless he showed himself a man, they would seek a leader elsewhere. They warned that the Empire was finished unless help arrived within a few days; that they should not wait at home for a "peace for sale," which the barbarian would not even agree to sell at Carthage, far from his own home. Added to this was a great reproach to the Christian name: with Jerusalem overturned, the most holy Cross of Jesus Christ <note>The True Cross, captured by the Persians in 614 CE</note> had fallen into the hands of the enemy. They warned that God would be the avenger of their sluggishness if they were not roused to extinguish the fire consuming the world. They argued that great empires are permitted by God so that we might conquer the proud and help the oppressed.

Moved by these words, the Emperor gathered the largest army he could, destroyed the forces of Khosrow’s son, and, relying on this recent victory, approached the very heart of the barbarian empire. Crossing Mesopotamia, he sought Chaldea. Struck by this unexpected movement, the barbarian abandoned Africa and returned home at the fastest possible pace; he who a little while ago was thinking of imposing laws upon the world was now forced to worry for his own altars and hearths. As he returned, Heraclius met him with a massive force, prostrated the enemy, recovered the Cross, and dictated terms to the vanquished, who obeyed. Thus Heraclius, triumphing with the sacred gift, sought Jerusalem, and having restored the Temple, he replaced the sign of our redemption.

When these things were finished, now exhausted—as if he had circled the entire world and no enemy remained in the whole earth—he sent his soldiers into the middle of Syria, far from home. These men, reduced to the utmost poverty by a lack of resources, were forced to harass those they had come to protect. A soldier driven to despair looks not for whom he may benefit, but whom he may harm. To desperate men, the most wicked and audacious person is the most esteemed leader. It seems to me that Muhammad <note>original: "Muhamedes"</note> acquired such great power by being aided by these wandering soldiers. For it would not have been possible, without the help of veteran and trained soldiers, for naked Arabs to conquer I know not how many well-fortified cities in Syria, Persia, and Egypt. Greater ease was added to this because, upon hearing the rumor of the Emperor's army, everything was full of trepidation. Strengths were broken, affairs were afflicted, and the Roman magistrates were removed. Khosrow had been unable to substitute his own men for them, and the Emperor, given over to sloth and idleness, did not care to restore them. All these things, it seems to me, gave Muhammad a great opportunity to plot his revolution.

However the matter stands, he gained possession of Arabia and its borders. Moreover, to make his soldiers more spirited, there was frequent reading of the Quran <note>original: "Alcorani"</note>. Pilgrimage was also frequently performed. Indeed, he wrote three chapters in the Quran concerning military law: that he who is killed in the war of God shall be entirely happy. He claimed that the dead wish to return to life only so that they might die again in battle. All things belong to the faithful soldiers and the prophet. Others who refuse to believe are either to be killed, driven into slavery, or at the very least, their property is to be plundered.

Three times he set out on a journey, approaching the temple of Mecca with an army, performing those sacred rites which were customary among his ancestors. For as he was a turncoat <note>original: "uerfipellis"; literally "one who changes skins," implying a deceptive or shifting character</note>, he borrowed certain ceremonies from the Jews as long as he could retain their support. Yet, so that he might also keep the Gentiles <note>In this context, the local polytheistic or pagan tribes</note> through their ceremonies, he took care to perform the same rites in the name of God around the tower of the <term>Qibla</term> <note>original: "Alquibla"; the direction of prayer, though Postel here describes it as a physical structure or tower</note> that used to be done in honor of idols. Furthermore, from the time he became an exile—either because he did not dare, out of a consciousness of his misdeeds (and indeed he rightly ought to have feared ambushes), or because he did not want to live in Mecca among a people aware of his crimes and madness—he went to the city of <term>Yathrib</term> <note>original: "Iefrab"; the pre-Islamic name for Medina</note>. This city had been destroyed a little before by the incursions of robbers and was inhabited by a few Jews. He remained there when he was at home, having violently ejected from his possession (even before the conquest of Mecca) an orphan, the son of a certain blacksmith,

GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK II.

...[of the] son, whose house, estates, and courtyard he occupied. Having established his seat there, he saw to it that a **Mosque** <note>original: "Mesgedam"</note> was built, in which the **Quran** <note>original: "Alcoranum"</note> would be read. He died in that same city at the age of sixty-three, seized so violently by his **falling sickness** <note>original: "fontico morbo"; a term used historically for epilepsy, which Postel and his contemporaries often interpreted as a sign of demonic possession or a physical ailment the Prophet allegedly disguised as divine ecstasy</note> that, with his muscles contracted, all his limbs seemed to represent a circular shape, especially his fingers. From this, certain prominent interpreters of his signs even concluded that it was permitted for his followers to engage in perverse crimes. For this reason, those among them who are insane, or who most closely resemble the Prophet, and who act like animals, are believed to be most holy.

That he was also driven by a demon—besides the fact that this was an accusation leveled against him two hundred times, as he never fails to repeat in the Quran—was also demonstrated by the catastrophe of his life's end. For if he had devised his deceptions entirely by human craft and prudence, he never would have predicted that he would rise again on the third day; instead, he would have taken care to vanish immediately in the manner of the ancient gods. However, by his own command, he was exposed under the open sky for three days in expectation of his resurrection, until the stench drove everyone away. His corpse was cast out of the city during a riot, and the common people, having been deceived, all returned to their former rites, until they were brought back by the hereditary soldier whom they call the **Soldier of God**, and were forced to pay tribute. 

For **Abu Bakr** <note>original: "Vbecharus"</note>, who succeeded him, said that he had left a great sum of money in his will for the soldiers who would confirm the religion. Today, all of Arabia, Syria, and the whole of Africa are afflicted by this plague of bandits, so that no one can ever travel there safely unless they are in a **caravan** <note>original: "carauana"</note>, as they call it—that is, in such a large company that they cannot be terrified by attackers. For it is permitted for any thief or desperate man to call himself a "soldier of God" and to fall upon the property of all. Every year, the most powerful Prince of the Turks is forced to give wages to sixty thousand of these men, lest they harass the settlers or infect the cultivated provinces. 

The Prophet's corpse, cast out from the city, was eventually buried and preserved by his kinsmen **Ali** <note>original: "Haly"</note>, **Zayd** <note>original: "Zeid"</note>, and several others. They placed it in a certain crypt in the Mosque of **Yathrib** <note>original: "Iezrab"; the ancient name for Medina</note>, not in the temple of Mecca as is commonly reported. Therefore, every year, when one goes to Mecca for the sake of pilgrimage, one must first go to **Medina al-Nabi** <note>original: "Medina Alnabi"; the City of the Prophet</note>, that is, to the city of the prophet Yathrib, where the body is kept. Finally, in memory of the sacrifice of **Abraham**, they go to Mecca, where they also fulfill their vows in two places: in the city at the tower of the **Qibla** <note>original: "Alquibla"; the direction of prayer</note>, and on a certain mountain nearby, where they throw stones behind them, by which they are convinced the devil is put to flight. I shall recount his expeditions when I speak of the origin of the empire.

## ON THE MIRACLES OF MUHAMMAD. CHAPTER VIII.

Prudent men and philosophers, when they consider by what logic men grant their assent to absurd things placed outside the laws of reason, are accustomed to first investigate by what deed they were persuaded. They can be satisfied by many reasons. First, after Muhammad had converted his publicly hidden illness into a reputation for sanctity, he did not try to join to himself men skilled in affairs, but rather **sedentary workers** <note>original: "sellularios"; low-status urban artisans</note> in the cities, and the unrefined and stupid in the fields—all of whom he laughed at even while capturing them with his nonsense. He calls them **fools** <note>original: "Supheha"; from the Arabic *sufaha*</note> and **nomads** <note>original: "Ahrab"; from the Arabic *a'rab*</note>, unrefined and rustic folk, whom he nevertheless used first for conducting ambushes for plunder and then for waging just wars. By their effort, he despoiled parents of their fortunes because they would not subscribe to his absurd follies. He crushed, plundered, and despoiled the dissenting Jews and subdued his enemies. 

The second reason is the ineptitude and supine ignorance of all things among the common people, who for the most part receive and approve whatever is said without any discussion—and all the more so the more absurd they are. From this, one may gather the absurdity of these follies. For even the rustics themselves laughed at him as a poet—that is, a mere writer of rhythms—or an impostor, or one possessed by a demon...

### ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

...naming him with such titles: they greatly disguised his gullibility, an accusation thrown at them a hundred times, and he claimed the sickness was in their own souls. But the reason they truly followed the man was that, besides the reasons I brought up earlier, he also promised he would make them exempt from the **imperial treasury** <note>original: "fisco"; referring to the state tax system of the Byzantine or Persian empires</note>. For since they were being crushed by the will of petty rulers—and there are no people who do not necessarily have to give something to the treasury—the miserable wretches thought that freedom and immunity would immediately arrive from heaven. Therefore, even when he was pressing them the most, he always had this on his lips: "Follow the prophet; follow those who ask no reward from you, and who are gracious." Led on by that expectation, they all revolted from their own princes or republics, driven by both fear and hope.

There was also another, more urgent reason. Since there is no nation in the whole world more soft, more effeminate, or more inclined toward lust, he wished to applaud the vices of all. For when he was confronted with the plurality of wives—which was not granted by the law of his fatherland, where at one time one wife had twelve husbands—he said it was permitted for a prophet to take as many as he wished. And for that reason, he said God had decreed that private citizens might have four, or as many as they could nourish and rule, who could be divorced and taken back according to certain laws. 

Furthermore, when he was confronted with the fact that the Law of his fatherland forbade illicit intercourse with handmaids and female slaves, he sanctioned it as if by divine law, so that it might likewise be permitted to anyone. For he claimed that the slaves themselves are a man's money, and therefore the handmaids are like **arable soil** <note>A common polemical trope in 16th-century Christian descriptions of Islamic law, suggesting a purely utilitarian or carnal view of women</note>. If anyone had committed any most disgraceful vice, provided he were a **Muslim** <note>original: "Musulman"</note> and were washed, he would be clean; and he claimed God is favorable to the "faithful" (for so he calls his own in the **Arabic** <note>original: "Arabica"</note> tongue, whom we call **Saracens** <note>original: "Saracenos"</note>, a name unknown in their own writings). 

He did indeed institute a **Lent** <note>original: "Quadragesimam"; Postel uses the Christian term for a forty-day fast to describe Ramadan</note>. But lest it be too heavy, and as if God were the God of the day and not of the night, he wanted the nighttime gluttony to compensate all the way until dawn. In short, whatever was pleasing to lust, the belly, or the private parts, he wanted to permit to everyone as if God were the author of it. It is no wonder that men devoted to luxury were enticed by these opportunities. 

Yet, to this was added the far greatest cunning and craftiness of the scoundrel. When he called himself a prophet, his followers would object: "All the holy prophets were most famous for clear miracles; you, therefore, produce some specimen of divine familiarity, show some miracle, and we will follow you." If he was pressed, he would say that he was not God, that miracles belonged to God alone, and that he was only a forewarner and a preacher. There were others who said both. He would reply that God did not want him to perform miracles because they had been rejected and slandered in the case of previous prophets; or, lest they believe he was God and worship him, he ought to do nothing else than remind them of miracles and the **Book of God** (for so he calls natural and artificial things) and speak words about the **Day of Judgment**, and about **Paradise**, and **Hell**. 

Furthermore, whenever he dealt with Paradise, he suited himself to the character of the listener. For he asserted in six hundred places that his followers would experience all the pleasures of the body. But when he saw that, nevertheless, there were many whom he could not satisfy with these tricks and trifles regarding miracles unless he produced something unusual, he also professed to have performed many miracles by his words. From among their number, O wise reader—as God loves you—weigh these things. For he said that he had done so much; and if he had done it, judge how worthy they would be of a divine man.

The first I have already recited: when he was five years old, he was disemboweled by **Gabriel**, and his heart having been torn out, a small black particle was dragged away (by which men are tempted), and then the heart was replaced. He saw it, felt it, and told his nurse; she believed it and recited it to great men, who wrote it down. See whether a man can judge this to be happening to himself, even if it were happening; and if it were done, weigh the effect and the witness of the miracle. How was he not tempted by the devil afterward, when he was occupied by him his whole life—a plunderer, a 
**robber** <note>original: "latro"; this is the catchword for the next page</note>

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK II

...robber, fratricide, seditious person, impostor, treacherous, deceitful, etc. Hear another one, reader, and hold back your laughter, if you can. For I cannot. When he was wandering alone one day (for all these things happened while he was alone and present) and wanted to relieve himself—pardon the expression, but the words match the deeds here—the heat of the sun was burning his head. He ordered the trees he saw to provide shade while he purged his body. Immediately, they were uprooted and came running to him, providing shade for the "prophetic evacuation," and once he was done, they returned to their places. Is this not a great miracle, worthy of such a prophet? Indeed it is. And lest you think I have made this up, it is written in the books of the **Sunnah** <note>original: "Suneh"; refers to the body of traditional social and legal custom and practice of the Islamic community, often used to interpret the Quran</note>, which has almost more authority than the **Quran** <note>original: "Alcoranũ"</note>, as are the things that follow. 

The third is not dissimilar. When he was sixteen years old and given to **Khadija** <note>original: "Hadegæ"; Muhammad’s first wife and employer</note> to care for camels, he says that when he was alone and his head was burning intensely from the sun, a cloud appeared at his command. It walked with him all day long, protecting him from the sun's harm. Judge for yourself this "arbitrary movement" of clouds. 

I come to the fourth. When he was in a cave to escape the reputation of being ill <note>Polemicists like Postel often claimed Muhammad's revelations were actually symptoms of epilepsy</note>, Gabriel came to him and brought that law, which was issued piece by piece over twenty-three years and has almost perished, as we shall see. 

In the fifth miracle, rocks, mountains, trees, and birds would speak to him as he returned from the cave after hearing Gabriel. Through this trickery, he even wanted to avoid the appearance of madness when he perceived himself being called from every side. This was also presented to Khadija. 

The sixth is entirely memorable. When a certain **Abu Jahl** <note>Postel uses "Bugellinus," likely a corruption of Abu Jahl, a prominent opponent and relative of Muhammad</note>, his relative, continually refused those trifles he preached, he finally said: "If you perform the miracle I am thinking of, O Muhammad, I will become a **Muslim** <note>original: "Mussulman"</note>." To which he replied, "I will do it, just speak." The other said, "Make the moon descend from heaven and be divided into two equal parts; let half enter through your sleeves, the right into the right and the left into the left, and finally let it emerge whole from your chest and return to heaven." Having been asked, he did it: the moon was split, entered his sleeves, and returned from his chest solid. Yet the man would not believe, but said it was manifest sorcery. There you have a miracle. The moon—the twenty-seventh part of the earth, serving the whole world—without anyone noticing except two men, enters a man's sleeves. These things are clearly worthy of both the author and the believers. 

Listen patiently, kind reader: I will add two more. When he was traveling alone one day, there was a tree trunk in the middle of the path, and the prophet had to turn aside a little. To prevent this, the trunk split down the middle, giving way to the passing prophet, and then immediately closed back up of its own accord. Another: When he was outlawed, on the night he had to leave, a palm trunk in the middle of his house, which had been watered, wept at the prophet’s departure. The Muslims who were called all saw this. When his adversaries were waiting in ambush to catch him in a certain place, he put ash on the heads of the horses so that he would not be seen, and was thus invisible to the enemies. He told these stories about things done to him and by him. 

But why do we suffer a lack of miracles, when all the verses of the Quran are called **Ayat** <note>original: "Aiet"; meaning signs or miracles</note>? Did not Gabriel assist for a full twenty-three years, giving pieces of the law? Was it not a great miracle when his primary wives caught him in adultery, even after he had sworn oaths of fidelity ten times, and Gabriel brought a law that permitted the prophet to do whatever he pleased? And that the prophet should not depend on women, for he would have others from elsewhere if these would not stay? What is more notable than the miracle by which God gave the prophet the wife of **Zaid** <note>original: "Zeidi"; referring to Zaynab bint Jahsh, the former wife of Muhammad's adopted son Zaid ibn Harithah</note>, his servant, and announced that he should divorce her, since no one should have a wife who pleased the prophet? Are these not truly divine miracles? 

Wake up, O miserable ones, wake up, and finally recognize the imposture committed against you. The remaining miracles will be noted as we run through the individual **Surahs** <note>original: "Asuar"; the chapters of the Quran</note>...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
### Page 150

...and the psalms of the Quran. But lest it escape my memory—for I had almost forgotten it—I wish to add the most famous of all miracles, since many such things present themselves in the Quran.

In chapter or **Surah 16** <note>original: "Capite uel ſora 16"; in modern numbering, the Surah "The Children of Israel" is Surah 17</note> of the Quran, which is called **Banu Israel** <note>original: "benu Iſraël"</note>, that is, the *Children of Israel*, it is written: <note>Postel provides a phonetic Latin transliteration of the Arabic from Surah 17:1</note> *Sobhan illedí aſraí bihebdihí leilan mín elmeſgedí ilharaní, illaí meſgedí elacza*, etc. That is: **Praise be to Him who transported His servant by night from the Haram temple** (that is, of Mecca) **to the Aqsa temple** (that is, the holy place of Jerusalem). On this passage the commentators agree—and the **Hashiyah** <note>original: "Haſſear"; likely referring to marginal commentaries or glosses</note> and the **Sunnah** <note>original: "Suneh"</note> support this—that it refers to a certain great and immense miracle. Listen then to a narrative worthy of Apollo <note>A classical reference used here ironically to mean a tall tale or a grand prophecy</note>.

One night, while he was sleeping deeply at about the third hour before dawn, he was awakened by a great knocking and rose from the house of his wife **Hafsa** <note>original: "Haſſe"</note> in **Medina** <note>original: "Almedina"</note>, which is also called **Yathrib** <note>original: "Ieſrab"</note>. Immediately, opening the door, he sees **Gabriel** in the public street with seventy very white wings, and with a very white animal called **al-Buraq** <note>original: "Alborach"</note>, who said to him: "Come, Muhammad, I will show you the secrets of heaven; mount al-Buraq." But al-Buraq, having the form of a donkey, said: "I will never allow him to mount me." Gabriel said: "Permit it. Muhammad is the greatest of creatures, and he will make you the happiest of animals, for you shall be the first to enter Paradise."

Having taken him up, he carries him to Jerusalem. On the journey, there were two women who called to Muhammad; the angel forbade him to answer them. For it would have happened that if he had answered the first, all Muslims would have been Jews, for she was the one who had spread the Law of the Jews; if he had answered the second, they would have been Christians. In the Temple, all the prophets met him, asking that he pray for them, which he did in the **Mihrab** <note>original: "Machrib"; Postel likely confuses the term for a prayer niche with "Maghrib" (the West/sunset prayer), but defines it here as the "Holy of Holies"</note>, that is, the Holy of Holies. Finally, upon leaving the Temple, a ladder was offered from the gate of the Temple up to the highest heaven. They climbed it, and from there the prophet reported these things.

In the first heaven, made of silver, from which the stars hang by golden chains, was **Adam**, who commended himself to Muhammad's prayers. There were all kinds of living creatures there, with angels praying for the earthly animals. There was a rooster there, larger than the whole world, who, when he crows, makes the earthly ones crow. In the second, made of gold, was **Noah**. In the third was **Abraham**; its material was precious stone. In the fourth, made of emerald, was **Moses**; then **Yahya** <note>original: "Iachie"</note>, that is, John the Baptist. All of them prayed to Muhammad to intercede for them before God. In the seventh, he found **Christ**, whom Muhammad asked to pray for him.

Thus Muhammad approached God, within the distance of a **bow-shot** <note>original: "iactum baliſtæ"; a reference to the Quranic "two bows' length" (53:9)</note>, as he says in a certain Surah called **al-Najm** <note>original: "Negium"</note>, that is, *The Star*; and he asserts that he has feigned nothing, even though everyone laughed at him. There he spoke with God familiarly and obtained certain gifts, which I will add immediately. This is the gist of the matter and the major points. For if I wished to recount how many absurdities are there, and the angels, who have 700,000,000 heads, and follow similar details minutely, a truly massive book of nonsense would be made from it. And he found those who believed these things! Indeed, he confirmed that vision with privileges granted to him by God, which I add here:

1. That he should be the first of all men.
2. That he should be the most honored of all the sons of Adam.
3. That he should be called the universal redeemer.
4. That he should know all languages, though he barely knew one.
5. That all the spoils of war or his prey should belong to him.

The force of this "miracle" alienated not a few from the sect. Now I must move on from miracles to other things. For I consider it enough to have pointed these out, so that it might be known with what stupid judgment he thrust those things forward, and how crude were those who received them. Truly, the stupidest of all are those who wished for them to be committed to writing. There are six hundred similar things in the **Sunnah**. The book on the teaching of the prophet, on chronicles, and the **Mashhad** <note>original: "maſhod"; likely referring to traditional accounts or testimonies</note>, and in short, seven hundred approved books are teeming with these absurdities.

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK II, 151

## ON THE CEREMONIES INSTITUTED BY MUHAMMAD. CHAPTER IX.

Even if these matters seem to have little weight in refuting falsehood and seem to contribute little to our purpose, they nevertheless seem worth touching upon for many reasons. For the common people and country folk are very easily captured by those ceremonies which are external, and like larger apes, they are more easily led to that which they understand less. I shall therefore touch upon these practices, not as extensively as they exist—for that would be an endless task—but insofar as they are common to all, and insofar as Muhammad wished to differ from us, even though he took the examples for all these things from our traditions.

It seems to me that I can fittingly begin with marriage, since that is the beginning of a human being. In this, Muhammad wished to agree with neither the Jews nor the Christians. For neither of those marry without the blessing of a priest. He, however, assigns or divorces a wife by the authority of a **Cadi** <note>original: "Cadhi"</note>, that is, a judge. Everyone marries, except for certain holy men and those dedicated to religion; yet even they, if they wish, can leap back from their profession.

Once a boy is born, he is raised by his mother or a nurse, according to their fortune and the man's self-restraint. For they are not accustomed to have relations with pregnant women. Because of this, the interpreters of the law say that many wives are permitted. In the 14th year of his age, just like **Ishmael** <note>original: "Ismaëlis"</note>, the boy is circumcised, so that they do not coincide with the Jews on the eighth day. In other respects, they say a person is purified and saved by daily washings—even if overtaken by death—so that they do not coincide with the Christians in having only one baptism.

Indeed, almost everything among them consists of these washings <note>original: "ablutionibus"</note>. For before the daily prayers, the dirty limbs, face, hands, and arms, along with the legs, are washed. For the Friday prayer, the whole body is washed. After passing urine, flatulence, semen, or excrement, one must wash. For this reason, both women and men are frequently in the baths, and especially on Friday.

In prayer, the **Muslim** <note>original: "Mussulmanus"</note> differs from the Jew. For those who follow the Mosaic law pray once a day for the most part, and twice on a solemn day. Christians pray seven times; the Muslims pray five times: before dawn, at noon, at the third hour after noon, at the evening hour, and at the first watch of the night.

The sacred day of the week for the Jew is the Sabbath; for the Christian, the first day, which they call the Lord's Day; for the Muslim, it is Friday. In their greater fast, they have a period like **Septuagesima** <note>A pre-Lenten season in the Christian calendar</note>, while the Christians have **Lent** <note>original: "quadragesimam"</note> as a lesser fast; the Muslims observe thirty days <note>This refers to the month of Ramadan</note>. Once a day, Christians and Jews take food, and at a single hour; the Muslim grants the whole night to his belly after the fast.

Christians pray toward the East because of Jerusalem; Jews pray toward the West for a certain reason; Muslims pray toward the South because of **Mecca**. For from **Yathrib** <note>original: "Ieſrab"</note>, which is **Medina, the City of the Prophet** <note>original: "Medinat alnabi"</note>, Mecca is toward the south.

The Christians have a solar year, the Hebrews a mixed one, and the Moors <note>Postel uses "Mauri" to refer to Muslims generally</note> a lunar one. Hence their "Passover" <note>This refers to the Eid festivals</note> occurs at any time of the year. On that day, they forgive one another with a kiss of the hands; Christians do so with a word and communion, and Jews with unleavened bread.

The Christians are carried out for burial feet-first; the other two head-first. The corpse of a Jew sits <note>This likely refers to a contemporary belief or specific burial rite where the body was positioned upright or propped up</note>; the Muslim corpse lies in a spacious place, while the Christian is in a narrow one. The Jew prays for the deceased; the Muslim prays and eats with the poor; the Christian prays and distributes alms.

For pilgrimages, the four months immediately before and after the **Bayram** <note>original: "behiram"</note>, that is, the "Passover" or feast, are designated. For the Jews, the Passover recalls the crossing of the Red Sea; for the Christian, the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ, the God-man; among the Arabs, it marks the origin of the Law. Thus, while he took the greatest care not to agree with other religions, he enticed those **ignorant ones** <note>original: "supheha," likely from the Arabic *sufaha* meaning fools or the simple-minded</note> and the unskilled, who were the beginning of the great multitude. But now we must come to the Law and their prescriptions, so that we may see by what authorities and by what requests these things are supported.
