# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

## ON THE QURAN, THE SUNNAH, AND OTHER books of the Muslims, and their approval.
### CHAPTER X.

We have already sufficiently shown how, for the sake of deceiving his wife Khadija <note>original: "Hadegæ"</note> and because of the "falling sickness" <note>A common medieval reference to epilepsy, which critics of the era claimed Muhammad used as a cover for his revelations.</note>, Muhammad used to enter a cave and report his dreams as divine responses. It is accepted among them that he received the entire law in a single night—although he contradicts himself elsewhere, saying he received it bit by bit. If, however, he received it in Mecca <note>original: "Mechæ"</note>, as is written and accepted, then part of it must (by their own logic) be false. For a large part was written in Medina, as is clear from the titles of the chapters, especially those pertaining to plunder, theft, and the laws of war. Therefore, the whole work is not divine if it was received in Mecca. 

If, however, that famous Gabriel gave it to him on that "happy day" in Yathrib <note>original: "Iezrab"; the pre-Islamic name for Medina</note> (for many are uncertain where it is said to have been given), then by far the largest part is not from him, for it was written in Mecca. Therefore, it was not given by Gabriel. But if it is said to have been given in small pieces and scraps, then it contains a frequent lie within itself: that it was received in a single night or day. 

But however the matter may be, it was not published while he was alive, lest its truth be questioned. Rather, after the pamphlets were received by a scribe and committed to memory by certain people, he would hide them away in various small chests, sometimes in holes in the walls, or elsewhere; it was from these places that the law was collected and fashioned when it was repeated. 

He used to promulgate two kinds of precepts and laws: either general laws or privileges. He granted privileges only to himself, and laws to everyone else. But before I proceed from this point, I wish to touch upon certain laws granted specifically to him, so that the rest may be judged by these. It was ordained that all Muslims <note>original: "Mussulmanos"</note> must be content with four wives at most, except for the Prophet. For him, it was permitted to take as many as he pleased. I shall indicate those places by examining the Quran <note>original: "Alcoranum"</note> from which these meanings are drawn.

Secondly: although all Muslims have it permitted by law that wives who have been left or divorced may be allowed to marry anyone else, and the women themselves may choose other husbands for themselves, he did not wish this to be permitted for his own wives. This was so that—since by prophetic authority he could treat them well or poorly at his whim—those who had come from great parents and wealthy backgrounds with a huge dowry could not leave the Prophet. Thus, he even willed that they should not take other husbands even after his death.

<margin>Surah 143 <note>Postel uses an older numbering system for the chapters of the Quran.</note></margin> The third privilege concerns the fact that while Moors <note>A term Postel uses here generally for Muslims.</note> must, by law, distribute both the use of their property and their physical presence equally among three or four wives (or however many they have), otherwise the wives may seek a trial before a judge and a bill of divorce—from which an innumerable harvest of lawsuits arises among the Muslims—that law did not prescribe such things for the Prophet. This was because he loved and enriched whichever wives he wished, and left those he did not. 

For he was vehemently infatuated with that girl I mentioned before, who was taken at eight years of age, the daughter of Abu Bakr <note>original: "Vbechari"</note> (who reigned after him), named Aisha <note>original: "Axam"</note>, and also with Hafsa <note>original: "Haiezan"</note>, the daughter of Umar <note>original: "Homari"</note>. For although he had thirteen wives besides them, he slept with these two more frequently. Whereupon the others complained vehemently. He therefore restrained them with his usual oracle <note>meaning a divine revelation</note>, which nevertheless became suspect even to the women. For they used to say that God was exceedingly obedient to the Prophet, since He would immediately give him laws to suit his pleasures. The law stated that the Prophet should not care about the words and objections of women, and that he was allowed to do whatever he wished with them. 

But they especially marveled at the indulgence of his God when, after broken oaths, frequent perjuries, and the man being caught in adultery with a Jewish woman given to him as a gift by Baheira, king of the Jacobites <note>Likely a reference to Maria the Copt; "Baheira" usually refers to a monk in Islamic tradition, but Postel identifies him here as a king.</note>, God even spoke familiarly with the Prophet. For since he could not keep faith with his wives due to the elegance of the Jewish woman and his impatience of love, he published that somewhat obscure law a few days later: that...

### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK II.

The aforementioned wives were greatly amazed at these things and were struck dumb. Thus from this arose the **fourth privilege**: that the Prophet could take women given to him as legitimate wives without a dowry contract <note>original: "dotali instrumento"</note> or the presence of a judge.

**Fifthly**, while it is permitted for no one to have another man’s wife, he claimed that he was not bound by this law. For he asserted that no one should keep wives who pleased the Prophet. Therefore, under the guise of law, he forced husbands—through oracles, prayers, threats, or even beatings—to give a bill of divorce to their wives, whom he then married immediately. These are the laws the Prophet chose to use for himself. Although there are countless similar examples, one may judge the lawmaker from these.

Upon the death of Muhammad <note>original: "Muhamede"</note>, power was first seized to restrain the masses by Abu Bakr <note>original: "Vbecharus"</note>, Umar <note>original: "Homarus"</note>, and his kinsman Ali <note>original: "Halys"</note>—all of whom were fathers-in-law <note>Postel incorrectly identifies Ali as a father-in-law; he was actually Muhammad's son-in-law.</note> of the Prophet—who eventually began to turn against one another. However, by the force of the testament, persuasion, and military strength, Abu Bakr proved superior and took control of affairs. Second in line was Umar, who was also intent on holding the masses together. Third was Uthman <note>original: "Odmanus"</note>; when he saw that the people could not be kept in their duty by arms alone, he decided to take the law—which until then lay hidden and was only preached from hearsay and memory by some (so much so that there seemed to be as many laws as there were men)—and compile it from oral reports and writings into a single volume, from which alone authority should be sought.

Therefore, first in Mecca <note>original: "Mechæ"</note> and finally in Medina <note>original: "Medinat alnabi," meaning "City of the Prophet"</note>, he began to open the Prophet’s writings and, through his scribes, set about reducing those various fragments into one, just as they presented themselves. The prophecies, which were themselves torn and mangled—partly from pamphlets gnawed by mice, and partly obliterated by the passage of time, having been placed at various times in small chests or in holes in the walls—were gathered. They were made into chapters <note>original: "capita"</note> with various names, but connected in such a way that there is no sequence of "before" or "after"; rather, they fit together only because nothing truly follows from what precedes it, even if the order were changed. Indeed, nothing in the whole work is logically connected.

Furthermore, because many fragments were pulled from holes in walls, it has turned into a religious custom: whenever Muslims find Arabic writing at home, on the road, or anywhere else, they place it back into holes in walls as if it were a fragment of the holy law; once placed, they kiss it so that their law does not perish. Those fragments found in the house and chests of Aisha <note>original: "Axæ"</note> (for she, as I said, was the chief of the women and the one he trusted with everything) were arranged into *Surahs* <note>original: "Sorat"</note> or *Assuar* <note>original: "Assuar," meaning chapters</note>. Those collected in Medina are called *Madaniyat* <note>original: "Mediniet"</note>, and those collected in Mecca are called *Makkiyat* <note>original: "Mechiet"</note>: that is, chapters, songs, psalms, or prophecies written in those places. The whole work, which was then much larger than it is today, is called the **Quran** <note>original: "Alcoranum"</note>, which means "collection" or "reading." 

Because it is divided into various chapters, it is also called by another name, **Al-Furqan** <note>original: "Alphurcan," meaning "The Criterion" between right and wrong</note>. The *Surahs*, or chapters, are called "songs" or "psalms" because they were usually read and chanted. Individual verses are called **Ayat** <note>original: "Aiet"</note>, which means "miracles." And because in those verses almost everything contradicts and "slaughters" one another, their later generations called some **Muhkamat** <note>original: "Muhquemat," meaning decisive or clear</note>, which are the judging verses whose sentence must stand; others they call **Ghair Muhkamat** <note>original: "Gair muhquemat"</note>, meaning non-judging. 

They are, moreover, of two kinds: some are called **Nasikh** <note>original: "Naceh," meaning abrogating</note>, which are positive; others are **Mansukh** <note>original: "Mansoh"</note>, which revoke the former. This was done (not at that time, but by the cunning of later men) by the Caliphs <note>original: "Chaliphis"</note> and the Jurists <note>original: "Alphachijs," from the Arabic *al-fuqaha*</note> so that their faith would not utterly perish. When the law was fresh, and it ought to have been held as most certain and constant, there was absolutely no one who agreed with anyone else regarding it. Uthman first took care to call a council of the "parents" <note>likely referring to the *Sahaba* or Companions</note> and any survivors of those seven men whom the Prophet had held in such familiarity that he said the law had been entrusted even to those seven. All of them claimed they had nothing certain; or if some did have something, each claimed his own was best and true, and the others false. Others affirmed the exact opposite. Furthermore, as is common in new developments...

### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

There were many others who also claimed the entire prophecy for themselves, so that they might captivate the people and seize the wealth of the party. Uthman <note>original: "Odmani"</note> held greater authority once the others were suppressed. Yet even that law could not satisfy everyone. For more than two hundred versions of the Quran <note>original: "Alcorana"</note> were written that were entirely different, with each man having his own book, since they saw that the successors themselves held power by virtue of it. Certain people, following the twelve successors of Muhammad, removed many things from that edition of Uthman, such that they took away more than two hundred sentences from the first chapter and substituted I know not how many others. Many people, led by this example, began to do the same, so that prophetic faith was utterly vanishing.

Moved by this situation, the Babylonian Caliph <note>The "Babylonian Caliph" refers to the Caliph of Baghdad, though Postel notes the seat of power shifted from Arabia to this region.</note> (for there the first seats of power were fixed after Arabia), acting as the arbiter of the law—for those first successors joined both powers to themselves, the sacred and the profane—called a council at Damascus. Some call him Marwan <note>original: "Merbam"</note> the son of Elhassem, others Abu Bakr <note>original: "Abobecharum"</note>. He decreed that whoever was a learned follower of that religion should come to the council and bring as many copies of the books treating the law as they possessed. He spent a great deal of money on this matter, buying up all the collected books and enclosing them in one place. Along with those books, he gathered six men who were highly skilled in that persuasion: Muslim, Bukhari <note>original: "Buheirū"</note>, Abu Dawud <note>original: "Buhorū"</note>, An-Nasa'i <note>original: "Annecenū"</note>, At-Tirmidhi <note>original: "Atermundū"</note>, and Daud <note>Postel is listing the traditional authors of the six canonical Hadith collections, known as the *Kutub al-Sittah*.</note>.

The task was committed to them to gather from that entire mass of books a treatment of the law, its origin, and its progress into six volumes, such that each man individually completed the whole work. This work precedes the Quran in authority and is of greater trust in doubtful matters. Therefore it is called the *Sunnah* <note>original: "Suneh"</note>, that is, the "law," like a second law <note>original: "δευτέρωσις" (deuterosis); a term Postel borrows from Jewish tradition to describe the Mishnah or oral law.</note>. Those opinions which those six men collected both from the Qurans and from their interpreters, they fortified with four authorities. For if anything was reported by the disciples of Muhammad and by Aisha <note>original: "axa"</note>, his more beloved wife who was privy to his stories, it is held in the first place as most true, and judgment is rendered according to it. In the second place is the sole authority of the other wives, and it is called a "weaker testimony." In the third place is placed the report of the doctors who lived at that time. In the last place is the authority of doctors who were indeed of lower rank, but who had lived since the time of the prophet.

When the work was finished, the remaining books from which they had made their selections—amounting to the loads of two hundred camels—were sunk in the nearby river. It was prohibited for anyone to use any books other than the *Sunnah* and the Quran. Thus, all writers are accustomed to cite from that book in this way: "Such a person, from such a person, from such a person, from such a person; this man had it from that one, and that one from Aisha <note>original: "Assa"</note>, or from the prophet, or from any other of his household." This is their faith.

But immediately after the council, which was called a hundred years or thereabouts after the death of the prophet, that manifold opinion of the six authors birthed even greater doubts; until, a few years later, the care of the matter was committed to four primary men, that they might collect the institutes of religion into "common places," and each one individually treated all the matters. The first of these was called Malik <note>original: "Melichus"</note>, whose decrees the desert Arabs, Egyptians, Africans, and Spanish <note>Referring to the Moors of Al-Andalus.</note> approve. The name of the second was Al-Shafi'i <note>original: "Saphihius"</note>, whom the people of Baghdad and Mecca follow. Ibn Hanbal <note>original: "Hannibal"</note> is heard in Persia, Assyria, and Armenia. Abu Hanifa <note>original: "Abahaniphā"</note> is followed by the Syrians and Alexandrians. Thus, there have arisen among the Muhammadans not seventy "nations" or sects, as they call them, but as many as there are provinces obeying these trifles. From both books of the doctors and the *Sunnah* there emerged one work which is called *Anwar* <note>original: "Anuar"</note>, that is, "The Flowers," where someone tries to collect something that stands certain for himself out of all of them. There is also an innumerable multitude of other books, so that there are 700 volumes whose sayings command faith. But in the first rank of authority is the *Chronicle of Hassiar* <note>Likely the *Sira* or life of the prophet by Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham.</note>, the book *Ariscele*, the book *Mashool*, and the *Chronicle of the Kings*. From these, the deeds, doctrine, and character of the prophet can be sought, from which these things have been gathered. Furthermore, there are certain interpreters of the Quran approved by everyone...

THE BOOKS OF GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK II.

Buhatias, Butzemamin, Mahinud of Mecca, and I know not how many others, divide the Quran itself into various chapters according to the custom and use of different regions. For in Africa, Egypt, and Spain it is divided one way, and in Arabia another. In some versions there are *Asuar* <note>original: "Asuar," the Arabic term for chapters or Surahs</note>, that is, 211 chapters, contained in four books. In the first of these there are 5; in the second, 12; the third has 19. The rest are in the fourth, namely 85; for the final chapters consist of only two or three verses. Others claim there are 112, as I have in my African manuscript. In the Asian one, there seem to be three fewer. But these details are of no consequence. We must weigh what it contains: namely, what is its own, what is taken from us, what is against us, and what is against itself.

## WHAT THE SCOPE AND SUMMARY 
## Of the Quran is. CHAPTER XI.

In the beginning, his retreat into a cave seems—as we have already said—to have made Muhammad very favorable toward the Jews, until they fell away from him; then indeed he began to act against them. Similarly, he seems to have been well-disposed toward Christians; and indeed he would have been, had he known any others besides the Nestorians <note>A branch of Christianity that emphasized the distinction between the human and divine natures of Jesus; Postel suggests Muhammad’s denial of Christ's divinity stems from this specific influence.</note>. He could not immediately find a middle path until, having compared the power of both peoples, he decided upon this course. For if he had imitated the Jews entirely, the glory would be ascribed to Moses; if he had joined the Christians, Christ would have utterly displaced him as a mere man. But so as not to seem lacking in ancient authority, he said that he followed and taught the "Law of Abraham." As he says in the Sura of Jonah <note>original: "Ionus"</note>: "This Quran was not fashioned without God, but rests upon certain authority between the Old and the New Testament." While he seems to teach the worship of one God and condemn idols throughout the whole work, he rises in direct opposition to Christ, against whom Muhammad seems to have written the Quran. However, as often as he names him (except in two or three places), he attributes all the highest things to him, except for divinity and death. Yet in almost every section he says that he [Jesus] is not God, and that he created nothing, and does not help now, along with six hundred other blasphemies. 

The summary and substance of that book is as follows: That there is only one God, creator of heaven and earth and all that is in them. That he created man from mud, then from cartilage, then from flesh, and finally breathed his spirit into him. That he created angels and demons: the former from heaven, the latter from fire. That the devil was unwilling to worship Adam when commanded, and was therefore condemned. That he sent many prophets to predict the calamities that came to those who did not believe. That he [Muhammad] is also a prophet who must be believed, lest the unbelieving perish; and those who called him a liar will feel the punishment. That there is a Hell prepared for unbelievers: a voice will come from heaven with a shout, with a trumpet, and with a drum; the dead will rise and receive their own bodies back. The wicked in hell will swallow poison, sulfur, and the fruits of the Zaqqum tree <note>original: "Zaconi"</note>, <margin>† For food; unless perhaps it signifies the place of the damned.</margin> and that dwelling is evil. 

God is wise, just, good, and honored; he will do injury to no one and will repay each person. The good who gave alms and performed *assala* <note>original: "assala," referring to the Salat, the five daily prayers of Islam</note> <margin>* that is, prayers.</margin> and did good, and paid tithes, will be in paradises where there are rivers of milk, honey, and wine, and all kinds of fruit. There are cupbearers <note>original: "catamyti oenochoi," Greek terms for young male servants</note> adorned in many-colored garments, who will give a certain powder of salvation. And there will be most beautiful women with large blue eyes, who for fifty years will engage in a single act of love, and always remain virgins. Pillows are placed there, where the saved may sit together and speak with one another and with the angels. You will find each of these sentiments at least six hundred times in the Quran. And while he hammers these points home in almost every section, he stuffs everything with blasphemies and follies against the teachings of Moses and Jesus Christ. For the occasion...

-># THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD<-

There were many others who also claimed the entire prophecy for themselves, so as to capture the people and take possession of the faction's wealth. The authority of Othman <note>original: "Odmani"; the third Caliph, Uthman ibn Affan, credited with standardizing the Quranic text</note> was greater once the others were suppressed. Yet even that law could not satisfy everyone. For more than two hundred entirely different versions of the Quran were written, with everyone having his own book, since they saw that the successors themselves held power by virtue of possessing them. Some people, after the twelve successors of Muhammad, removed many things from Othman’s edition itself, so that they took away more than two hundred sentences from the first chapter and substituted I know not how many others. Led by this example, many began to do the same, so that prophetic faith clearly began to vanish.

Because of this, the Caliph of Babylon <note>Postel likely refers to the Abbasid Caliph in Baghdad, which was often associated with ancient Babylon in early modern European thought.</note>—for the first seats of power were fixed there after Arabia—acting as the arbiter of the law (for those first successors joined both sacred and profane power to themselves) called a council at Damascus. Some call him Merbam, son of Elhassem; others call him Abu Bakr <note>original: "Abobecharum"</note>. He decreed that whoever was a learned follower of that religion should come to the council and bring as many copies of the books treating the law as they had. He spent enormous sums on this matter, buying up all the collected books and locking them in one place. Together with those books, he gathered six men highly skilled in that persuasion: Muslim, Bukhari <note>original: "Buheirum"</note>, Buhorus, Annecenus, Atermundus, and Daud <note>These names refer to the authors of the "Six Books," the primary collections of Hadith (traditions) in Sunni Islam, including Sahih Muslim and Sahih al-Bukhari.</note>.

The task was entrusted to them to collect from that entire mass of books a treatment of the law, its origin, and progress into six volumes, such that each individual would complete the entire work. This work precedes the Quran in authority and carries greater weight in doubtful matters. Therefore it is called the *Suneh* <note>original: "Suneh," referring to the Sunnah, the body of traditional social and legal custom</note>, that is, the "Law," like a <term>repetition of the law<note>original: "deutérōsis," a Greek term used by Christian scholars to compare Islamic or Jewish oral traditions to the "second law" or Mishnah.</note></term>. Those rulings which these six men collected both from the Qurans and from their interpreters were fortified by four levels of authority. For if anything was reported by the disciples of Muhammad, or by his favorite wife Aisha <note>original: "Axa"</note>—who was privy to the stories—that is placed first as if most true, and judgment is made according to it. In the second place is the sole authority of the other wives, which is called a weaker testimony. In the third place is set the report of the scholars who lived at that time. Finally, the lower authority belongs to scholars who lived after the time of the prophet. 

When the work was finished, the remaining books from which they had selected—amounting to two hundred camel-loads—were sunk in the nearby river; and it was forbidden for anyone to use any books other than the *Suneh* and the Quran. Thus all writers are accustomed to cite from that book in this way: "So-and-so, from so-and-so, from so-and-so... who had it from Aisha, or from the prophet, or from any other of his inner circle." This is their faith.

But immediately after the council, which was called about a hundred years after the prophet's death, that manifold opinion of the six authors gave birth to greater doubts; until a few years later, the care of the matter was committed to four primary men, that they might collect the religious institutes from those works into "Common Places" <note>Thematic arrangements of law and theology.</note>, and each one would also treat everything individually. The first of these was called Malik <note>original: "Melichus," founder of the Maliki school of law</note>, whose decrees the desert Arabs, Egyptians, Africans, and Spaniards approve. The second was named Al-Shafi'i <note>original: "Saphihius"</note>, whom the people of Baghdad and Mecca follow. Ahmad ibn Hanbal <note>original: "Hannibal"</note> is heard in Persia, Assyria, and Armenia. They follow Abu Hanifa <note>original: "Abahaniphā"</note> in Syria and Alexandria. Thus, among the Muhammadans, there have arisen not just seventy nations or "sects," as they call them, but as many as there are provinces obeying these trifles.

From both the books of the scholars and the *Suneh* there emerged one work which they call *Anwar* <note>Arabic for "The Lights" or "The Flowers"</note>, that is, "The Flowers," where a certain man tries to collect something consistent for himself from all of them. There is also an innumerable multitude of other books, such that the sayings of those who establish faith fill 700 volumes. But in the first rank of authority is the *Chronicle of Siyar* <note>original: "Hassiar," likely the Sira or biography of the Prophet</note>, the *Book of Risala* <note>original: "Ariscele"</note>, the *Book of Mashool*, and the *Chronicles of the Kings*. From these, the deeds, doctrine, and character of the prophet can be sought, from which these things have been gathered. There are, furthermore, certain interpreters of the Quran approved by everyone...

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK II.

Buhatias, Butzemamin, Mahinud of Mecca, and many others, divide the Quran itself into various chapters, according to the reason and custom of different regions. For it is divided one way in Africa, Egypt, and Spain, and another way in Arabia. In some versions, there are **Asuar** <term>original: "Asuar"; chapters, now commonly known as surahs</term>, which is to say 211 chapters, contained in four books. In the first of these there are 5; in the second, 12; the third has 19. The rest are in the fourth, namely 85; for the final chapters are some of only two or three verses. Others want there to be 112, as I have in my African copy. In the Asiatic copy, there appear to be three fewer. But these matters are of no importance. It is the content that must be weighed: what is its own, what is from us, what is against us, and what is against itself.

->WHAT IS THE SCOPE AND SUMMARY<-
->of the Quran. CHAPTER XI.<-

In the beginning, during his retreat into the cave, it seems that Muhammad greatly favored the Jews, as we have already said, until they broke away; then, indeed, he began to act against them. Similarly, he seemed well-disposed toward Christians; and in truth, he would have been, if he had known any others than the **Nestorians** <note>A Christian sect that emphasized the separation between Christ's human and divine natures, often viewed as heretical by Postel's contemporaries</note>. Nor could he immediately find a middle way until, having compared the power of both peoples, he established his position. For if he had entirely imitated the Jews, the glory would be credited to Moses; if he had joined the Christians, Christ would have entirely displaced him. But lest he seem to lack ancient authority, he said that he followed and taught the law of **Abraham**. Regarding this, he says in the chapter of **Jonah** <note>original: "Ionus"; referring to Surah 10, Yunus</note>: "This Quran was not made without God, but rests upon certain authority, between the Old and the New Testament" <note>original: "Non fuit istud Alcoranum abſq; Deo effectum, sed authoritate certa nititur, inter uetus & nouum Testamentum"</note>. Thus, while he seems to teach the worship of one God and condemn idols throughout the whole work, he rises up diametrically against Christ, against whom Muhammad seems to have written the Quran. However, as often as he names him (except in two or three places), he attributes all highest things to him, except for divinity and death. Yet in almost every sentence, he says he is not God, and created nothing, and does not help now, and adds six hundred blasphemies. Therefore, the compendium and summary of that book is of this sort:

That God is only one, the creator of heaven and earth, and of all things that are in them. That he created man from mud, then from cartilage, then from flesh, and then breathed of his spirit into him. That he created angels and demons: the former from heaven, the latter from fire; that the devil was unwilling to worship Adam when commanded, and for that reason was damned. That he sent many prophets who foretold calamities that came to those who did not believe. Also, that he himself is a prophet who must be believed lest the unbelievers perish, and those who called him a liar will feel the punishment. That there is a hell prepared for the unbelievers; a voice coming from heaven with a shout, with a trumpet, with a drum, and the dead shall rise again and receive the proper things of the body. The wicked in hell shall devour poison, sulfur, and the fruits of the **Zaqqum tree** <term>original: "Zaconi"; a cursed tree in Islamic hell described as having fruit like the heads of devils</term>; that dwelling place is evil. 
<margin>For food. Unless perhaps it signifies the place of the damned.</margin>
That God is wise, just, good, and honored, and will do injury to no one; he will reward each one. Those who gave alms and performed **assala** <margin>* that is, prayers.</margin> <term>original: "assala"; the ritual prayers or Salah</term> and did good, and paid tithes, shall be in paradises in which there are rivers of milk, honey, and wine, and all kinds of fruits. There are **cupbearers** <note>original: "catamyti œnochoi"; Postel uses a term often associated with young male companions to describe the immortal youths (ghilman) who serve in the Islamic Paradise</note> adorned in many-colored garments, who will give a certain powder to the saved. And there will be most beautiful women with large, blue eyes, who for fifty years will be in one act of love, and always remain virgins. Cushions are placed there where the saved may sit together and speak with one another and with the angels. You will find each of these sentiments at least six hundred times in the Quran. And meanwhile, while he instills these things in almost every sentence, he inserts all manner of blasphemies and silliness against the teachings of Moses and Jesus Christ. On the occasion...

Indeed, regarding the just accusation of idolatry against the people of Mecca, he <note>Referring to Muhammad</note> almost never fails to repeat: "And they have taken gods besides God, and there is no god but God, and they give God a partner," <note>original: "Et susceperunt præter Deum, deos, & non est deus præter Deum, & participem faciunt Deo." This refers to the Islamic concept of Shirk (associating partners with God)</note> by which he means they worship idols. He claims that God placed an obstacle before the eyes of many so they cannot see Him, and that they are all in manifest error. By all these statements, he targets Christ and his followers, as well as **Al-Lat** and **Al-Uzza** <note>original: "Ellet, atquę Aluza"; these were pre-Islamic Arabian goddesses</note> and their worshippers in Mecca. He did this with such cunning that if some people turned the accusations back on him, he could say he meant others, and vice versa. I would gather more examples here, were it not my intention to examine everything as I go through the Quran.

# WHAT HE TOOK FROM THE OLD AND NEW
# TESTAMENTS. CHAPTER XII.

<margin>That is, Eber, from Genesis.</margin> God creates the world, sometimes in six days, sometimes in eight; then Adam, and so on. He touches upon the story of Noah twenty times to instill terror. He mentions Eber, whom he calls **Hud** <note>A prophet in the Quran often identified with the biblical Eber</note>. He refers to Abraham and Lot very frequently. He recounts the punishment of Sodom and Gomorrah, saying that it rained marble <note>Postel uses "marmore" to describe the "stones of baked clay" mentioned in the Quranic account of Sodom</note> upon them. Touching upon something of Jacob and the children of Israel, he recites the entire story of Joseph. He frequently mentions the approach of Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh, the leading of the children of Israel out of Egypt, and David and Solomon; the Psalms, Job, Jonah, and Elijah are cited once. Indeed, he adorns everything with so many fables—like decorative emblems or mosaic work—that it would be an infinite task to touch on them all. Those will be dealt with during the detailed examination. I must also briefly touch upon what he takes from the New Testament. He relates the story of **Yahya** <term>original: "Iachiæ"; the Arabic name for John the Baptist</term>, that is, John the son of Zechariah, in his own fashion, as he had learned it from storytellers. He mentions Joachim, Mary and her salutation <note>The Annunciation</note>, the birth of Christ, his education and miracles, and the Gospel in many places, and the Apostles in one or two. More than once he mentions the priests and their sluggishness; but truly, he treats everything with the same level of honesty as mentioned above. Therefore, the history must be recounted from the beginning, not as it stands for us, but as it has been corrupted by that **shifty creature** <note>original: "stellione"; literally a spotted lizard, but used here as a term for a deceitful person or scoundrel</note> and enriched with dreams. These are the things he infected from the Old Testament.

<margin>Corruptions in the Old Testament.</margin> He claims the Demon, who was created good, was created evil by God; and thus he denies God when he makes Him the author of evil. When he commands that Adam be worshipped by angels and demons, what else does he do but attribute the very beginning of impiety and idolatry to God? When he says the devil was created from fire, does he not also make him mortal, as one consisting of elements, whereas separate substances <note>i.e., spiritual beings</note> should be eternal? But why be surprised? He makes the same devil a listener, witness, and preacher of the Quran, and finally even a **Muslim** <term>original: "Musulmanum"</term>. He attaches a thousand fables to Noah’s ark; and in the book of his doctrine, dung, a mouse, a pig, an elephant, and six hundred other absurdities are added to this story. He makes Abraham an idolater, and the son of Lazarus; this is because he misunderstood the Gospel parable of Lazarus and the rich man, where Lazarus called Abraham not "son," but "father." Furthermore, he relates a thousand fables and dialogues between him and his parents. He treats almost nothing from that history with integrity, except the vision of the three angels. All these will be noted more extensively in their proper place. In the story of Joseph, he adds a dialogue and the violence of his mistress <note>Potiphar's wife</note>, and a dispute decided by a garment torn from the back—supposedly a sign that the woman was the aggressor. Regarding Moses and the Magi, what does he not devise? What does he not invent concerning the boy and the fish? Now let the demons of Solomon come forward, let the speaking animals appear, the **hoopoe** <note>original: "upupa"; a bird that acts as a messenger in the Quranic story of Solomon</note> sent as an envoy, and the Queen of Sheba called by it, the faith preached by a hoopoe, and so on. I do not see what could be written that is more foul, foolish, or "pleasant" <note>Postel is being sarcastic here</note>. But for now, I am satisfied to have pointed these out as if with a finger, since nothing can escape us as we run through the text. <margin>Depravations in the Gospel</margin> These are the things admitted in the New Testament, etc. Concerning Zechariah the father of John...

[In the story of] John, he says that he was mute only during the nights. <note>Postel refers to the Quranic account of Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, who is told he will not speak to people for three nights (Surah 19:10). Postel views this as a corruption of the biblical account where Zechariah is mute until the child's birth.</note> Concerning Mary, he claims that she gave birth at the foot of a palm tree; that, being pregnant by the Holy Spirit, she fled her home; that she was received with insults by her parents; and that she was the sister of Aaron, even though she lived 1,506 years after him. <note>This is a common historical critique by Christian authors of the Quranic verse (19:28) addressing Mary as "Sister of Aaron," which they argued confused the mother of Jesus with Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron.</note> He also claims that Christ, as soon as he was born, spoke to her and told her to shake the palm tree and speak to no one. These are the more notable instances of errors against us.

Against himself, however, he contradicts himself in nine thousand places. For he claims the law was given to him in a single day, yet elsewhere says it took twenty-three years; he persuades others that he is the prophet of God, yet then says he does not know what will become of himself. He claims to be a prophet from birth, yet elsewhere says he was a poor man and an idolater; and that Abraham was the first **Saracen** <note>A term used by medieval Europeans for Muslims</note>, yet later says it was granted to him by God to be the first of the Saracens. In the chapter *Al-Mu’min* <note>original: "Elmumin"; The Believer, Surah 40</note> and elsewhere, he says he does not wish to compel anyone to believe; yet elsewhere he sees to it that those who do not believe him are killed and plundered. He says he seeks nothing from anyone, yet he demands tithes from the faithful and spoils from others. He claims his law is a middle path between the Old and New Testaments, yet elsewhere says it is the law of Abraham. He says God is one and has no partner; yet everywhere he joins himself in partnership with Him when he says, "Believe and obey God and His Apostle." While he says God alone is one, he then joins the Spirit to Him.

To summarize in a single word: nothing is so established by him that its opposite does not also find a place. Elsewhere he forbids wine; yet elsewhere he allows that recently pressed wine may be drunk even to the point of drunkenness—an idea which originates from his disease. <note>Postel refers to the common European belief of the time that Muhammad suffered from epilepsy, and that his dietary laws or "revelations" were linked to his physical condition.</note> For he prohibited to others what he himself either dared not drink or could not tolerate because of his illness. Now I come to the matter at hand. I will run through the whole Quran, noting certain passages; finally, I will relate what damage that nation suffers as a result.

## AN EXAMINATION OF THE QURAN CHAPTER BY CHAPTER, OR
### *The Surahs.* CHAPTER XIII.
<note>original: "Asuar, excussio." Postel uses "Aswar" for "Suwar," the plural of Surah (chapter).</note>

Imitating the custom of many who wrote on this hodgepodge of trifles before me, I would have attempted to gather the more notable lapses of the man in specific categories, were it not that I decided for two main reasons to run through everything in order. For as many as have written against this man have busied themselves with collecting errors of the same kind. Among these, the first place is held by **Ricoldo** <note>Ricoldo da Monte di Croce (c. 1243–1320), a Dominican missionary whose polemic against Islam was widely read</note>, who wrote in Latin, and whose book **Demetrius Cydonius** translated into Greek; and **Juan Andrés the Moor** <note>Ioannes Andreas Maurus, a former Muslim jurist from Valencia who converted to Christianity and wrote a famous refutation of Islam in 1487</note>, who was finally led to our faith by the Divine Spirit, both of whom were skilled in the Arabic language. But the most skilled of all in the law, the traditions, and the language—in which he had been instructed by his ancestors—was **Al-Faqih** <note>original: "Alphachius"; likely referring to the legal title of Juan Andrés or a specific jurist</note>, that is, the supreme interpreter and priest. Truly no one wrote more learnedly than he. **Dionysius the Carthusian** and **Cardinal Cusanus** <note>Nicholas of Cusa</note> also wrote, but they were unskilled in that language. Hence they cannot truly press the point as the two aforementioned authors did. Many others have touched upon it here and there and wished to condemn those absurdities in snippets, whence I see that no room is left for me to collect those instances. The second reason is that since the Quran is a kind of solid lie and a continuous imposture, it cannot be gathered in specific places other than by itself as a whole.

-> *Al-Fatiha*, that is, the opening of the book. <-
<note>original: "Phatehet elchitabi, id est ingressio libri"</note>

This is the common prayer of the Muslims and the beginning of the Quran, which consists of seven "miracles," that is, verses. In this I wish to show the reader what an <term>Ayah</term> <note>original: "Aiet"; The Arabic word "Ayah" means both "sign/miracle" and "verse."</note> is, so that he may understand what follows. I place the <term>Ayahs</term> themselves with numbers. **1. In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate.** He used to say this preamble always after being seized by his illness and ecstasy.

In the chapter *The Believers* <note>original: "Elmumin", referring to Surah Al-Mu'minun.</note> and elsewhere, he says he does not wish to compel anyone to believe; yet in other places, he sees to it that those who do not believe him are killed and plundered. He claims to ask nothing from anyone, yet he seeks tithes from the faithful and spoils from others. He says his law is a middle path between the Old and New Testaments, but elsewhere says it is the Law of Abraham. He says God is one and has no partner; yet he everywhere joins himself into a partnership with Him when he says, "Believe and obey God and His Apostle." While he says God alone is one, he later joins the Spirit to Him. To summarize in a single word, nothing is so firmly established by him that its opposite does not also find a place. In one place he forbids wine, yet in another he allows that which is recently pressed to be drunk even unto drunkenness; this has its origin in his disease <note>Postel, following a common medieval and Renaissance trope, attributes Muhammad’s revelations to the "falling sickness" or epilepsy.</note>. For he prohibited for others what he either did not dare to drink or could not endure because of his illness. Now, however, I come to the matter at hand. I shall run through the whole Quran, noting certain passages; finally, I shall relate what harms that nation suffers because of it.

### THE QURAN BY ITS INDIVIDUAL CHAPTERS OR
### Asuar <note>original: "Asuar", from the Arabic 'suwar', the plural of Surah or chapter.</note>, an examination. CHAPTER XIII.

Imitating the custom of many who wrote upon this patchwork of nonsense before me, I would have attempted to cover the more notable lapses of the man in a few specific places, had I not decided for two primary reasons to run through the whole work. For as many as have written against this man have busied themselves with collecting errors of the same kind into specific categories. Among these, the first place is held by Riccoldo <note>Riccoldo da Monte di Croce (c. 1243–1320), a Dominican missionary whose polemic against Islam was highly influential.</note>, who wrote in Latin, and whose book Demetrius Cydonius translated into Greek; and Juan Andrés the Moor <note>original: "Ioannes Andreas Maurus", a former imam from Xàtiva who converted to Christianity in 1487 and wrote a famous polemic.</note>, who was finally led to our faith by the Divine Spirit—both of whom were skilled in the Arabic language. But the most skilled of all in the law, the traditions, and the language in which he had been instructed from his ancestors, was the Al-Faqih <note>original: "Alphachius", from the Arabic 'al-faqīh', meaning a legal or theological scholar.</note>, that is, the supreme interpreter and curate, than whom surely no one has written more learnedly. Dionysius the Carthusian and Cardinal Cusanus <note>Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464), author of "Cribratio Alkorani" (Sifting the Quran).</note> also wrote, as did many others, but they were unskilled in that language. Thus they cannot truly press the point as the two aforementioned authors can. Very many others have touched upon the subject sporadically and wished to rebuke those follies bit by bit, so I see there is no room left for me to simply collect specific topics. The other reason is that, since the Quran is a kind of solid lie and a continuous imposture, it cannot be categorized by any other means than by its own sequence.

->The Opening of the Book <note>original: "Phatet elchitabi", i.e., Al-Fatiha.</note><-

This is the common prayer of the Muslims and the beginning of the Quran, which consists of seven "miracles," that is, verses. In this, I wish to show the reader what an *Ayat* <note>original: "Aiet", the Arabic term for a verse of the Quran.</note> is, so that he may understand what follows. I mark the verses themselves with numbers. **1. In the name of God, the merciful, the propitious.** He used to say this prologue always upon recovering from his disease and ecstasy.

arising. From which it resulted that [this prayer] is placed before the beginnings of all chapters of the Quran, and by religious philosophers at the beginning of their works. But pay attention to the "miracles" <note>original: "miraculis". Postel is referring to the *Ayat* (verses) of the Quran, which literally translates to "signs" or "miracles." He uses the term mockingly here.</note> themselves. First: **Praise to God, the Lord of the ages, that is, the merciful and propitious.** Second: **To the king of the day of judgment.** Third: **Lo, let us serve, and lo, we shall be helped.** Fourth: **Direct us [into] the straight point.** <note>original: "punctum rectum". This is Postel's translation of the Arabic *Sirat al-mustaqim*, usually translated as "the straight path."</note> Fifth: (a great pause) **The point of those in whom you are well pleased.** Sixth: **Without anger against them, and they shall not go astray.** Seventh: **You have the miracles: you see the meanings.** Thus he holds the entire Quran, so that whether the meaning is complete or incomplete, they call it a "miracle": I see nothing more absurd than this. 

This prayer is common to them, as the Lord’s Prayer is to us; and it is recited by some even to the point of "battology" <note>A term for Greek meaning "vain repetition" or "babbling."</note>, such that they repeat the same thing, or two or three words, a hundred times, saying: *Alhamdu lilla, hamdu lilla, hamda lilla* <note>original: "Alhamdu lilla" (Praise be to God).</note> and its other words in the same manner. And this is done in the public prayer by the *taalima* <note>original: "taalima", likely from the Arabic *ta'lim* (instruction).</note>, that is, the minor priest <note>original: "sacrificulus". A diminutive, somewhat disparaging term for a cleric or Imam.</note>, on behalf of those who pray negligently (as they say), so that by this repetition he may make up for their errors. Some [pray] in the middle of a field so assiduously that they collapse exhausted; others by whirling the body around <note>A likely reference to the "Whirling Dervishes" or Sufi practices of *dhikr* (remembrance).</note> so that they become entirely outside themselves, and finally (by inviting Muhammad) they pour out some trifles and obscurities, so that idolatry and fanatical responses seem to have been revived in them. Thus Satan never fails to intrude himself. These things are usually repeated in fixed numbers for the "task," when they pray five times in a natural day. But enough of that. It seems to have nothing against us, but whoever is skilled in Arabic will see that where he calls it the "point" and "the straight point," the Quran is understood. For *tzirat elmustequim* <note>original: "tzirat elmustequim", i.e., *Sirat al-mustaqim* (the straight path).</note>, that is, the straight point, is for them synonymous with the Quran. They therefore ask to be directed toward destruction, since they pray with a vow to be directed into the "straight point" of the Quran, which is woven together with lies.

->Surah al-Baqarah, that is, the Song of the Cow, the first chapter of 285 miracles.<- <note>Postel refers to the second chapter of the Quran, *Al-Baqarah*. He counts it as the first major chapter after the opening Fatiha.</note>

I shall weigh everything a little more precisely at the beginning of the first book, and in this chapter especially the first part, so that in other places it will not be necessary to linger so much, but
> ...all things should be briefly indicated and compared with these. He says, therefore: **This book, in which there is no blemish or doubt, is a direction for those who fear, who believe in the hidden or latent (God) and pour out prayers, and bestow from that which they have, and who believe in that which has been distilled upon you from heaven, and what was distilled from heaven upon those who were before you, because in the future life they shall be innocent; they are in the direction of their God, and prospering.** There are six *Aiet* <note>original: "Aiet", i.e., *Ayat* (verses).</note>.

There is not a single word there that is not vain or superfluous. And yet, Muhammadan, after you approve of these things, it is necessary that you also do them. As for what he first says—that there is no blemish, doubt, or stain in this book—it is false. For it contains nine thousand lies, and innumerable conflicting things, than which nothing is more foul, as will be made clear and is already known. Hence, it cannot be a "direction for those who fear." For all feared you, O Muhammad, as a tyrannical prophet; yet they were not directed by you, but destroyed. Rather, you wanted the ignorant, enticed by these words and seized by the fear of God, to fear you. For you say later that you ought to be feared, and you join yourself to God in that fear. Christians believed in the "hidden God" before you; they prayed and gave more alms than your followers. Among the Jews, however lost they may be, there is still no beggar; therefore you add nothing to them. 

Truly, no one could believe in that which you say was sent into you from heaven, since you performed no signs, you labored most foully under every vice, and you drove people by force. Indeed, all the prophets were famous for the innocence of their lives, for miracles, and for certain predictions of future events. However, it is certain that one ought to believe in that which was sent from heaven before you, and it is established through you. Since God is one and true, He is not changed. What the Truth has once delivered must remain settled. But those who were sent before you, since they are from God, if you contradict them, your words are false. And in almost all things you are contrary or different. Therefore you are not from God. But if you ought to be accepted, others must also be, so that good may be done. Therefore, O Muhammadan, the Gospel...

### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK II.

...and the Law of Moses, so that you might receive the news as good, true, and sent from heaven. You must either believe those are entirely from God, or say that the Quran contains a lie right from the doorstep. Therefore, our things <note>Meaning Christian and Jewish scriptures.</note> are from God, while yours were invented by the authorship of a demon; nor do our things need the testimony of an impostor. Here certainly, as often elsewhere, he said one thing and thought another: while he draws everyone to himself, he seems to approve of everyone's opinions so that he may capture unrefined listeners, gradually instilling his own ideas and overturning those that are best and already accepted. It had been confirmed through many centuries and miracles that the first laws were sent from heaven; but desiring to be sponsored by their authority, you insert your own things into them, and that very frequently. "Such a one was a Prophet, and sent by God, such and such a person, this one and that one also predicted thus, and it happened so, therefore Muhammad is a prophet." It is just as if someone were to conclude: the garment is white, the undershirt is white, the tunic is white, therefore the hat is also white, because they agree in covering the body. Before all others they believed in the future life—indeed, you learned it from them, since you were an idolater by law and parentage, as you yourself admit. There follows:

Do you see how, after he seemed to rightfully attack those idolaters, he then accuses the others who were of honest faith (suppose they were good Jews or Nestorian Christians <note>The Church of the East, a branch of Christianity that was widespread in Asia and the Middle East during this period.</note>, for a choice must be made among many evils) and tries to pull them entirely over to his own opinion? He says all believe wrongly who do not believe him. He proceeds to be impious toward God when he says He adds evils to our evils. Wherefore you warn in vain, if God is the author of evil. I proceed to the rest, and in these few points I wish to show the ignorance of the Latin translator: and I will show how rashly the ancient versions are trusted for the purpose of refuting them. Meanwhile, I do not wish to omit that his tyranny is widely apparent in the words that follow. For unless he had already used violence against them, they would never have professed one thing with their mouths and another in their hearts for a matter so vain and futile. Men were being miserably killed, and harassed by slaughters and robberies, and they feigned [belief] so that they would not suffer worse. He called this a "disease of the heart," that they brought forth one thing with their mouths when driven by fear, while they were being pulled elsewhere by the judgment of their conscience. He says later:

<margin>“</margin>> the *Supheha*," that is, the simple and unrefined. Are they not unrefined? And therefore they do not understand.

What do these things mean? "Believe as the men" (for thus he says *elnass* <note>original: "elnass", the Arabic *al-nas*, meaning "the people."</note>, meaning cultured and civilized men). ...and with power, desiring now to emerge. Let us compare, using this art of teaching, the condition of this law. When Moses led out the people of God, he did not say, "Believe because that nobleman believes, or because this man believes," but rather, "Because God wills it so." Regarding this matter, he said: "If you doubt, I am prepared to show that God acts with me through unheard-of miracles." And he proved it with signs. So did Elias, and so did Jesus Christ. All heretics, however, creep in by another way, since they seek glory for themselves and not for God. They raise certain inconveniences. They point out the vices of men placed in high dignities <note>Postel is likely referring to corrupt church or state officials of his own time to draw a parallel.</note>; from there, they persuade the unlearned multitude that those vices belong not to the men, but to the very office itself. Therefore, they say the offices are evil and must not be tolerated. Meanwhile, the wretched common people—incapable of discerning the difference between the office and the office-holder—and having been enticed, follow these impostors who are greedy for new things. Or, if they insist most strongly, if their novelty is not disapproved by someone’s judgment, they claim it is approved by great men whose judgment is sincere; by inventing a large fellowship of believers, they gather crowds and rise up against all other "impious" (as they call them) men for the sake of persuasion. Meanwhile, they invade the wealth and fortunes of better and more steadfast men. In this way, heretics have dragged countless people to their destruction; in this way, they have incited factions within Commonwealths. Thus did Muhammad persuade the Meccans <note>original: "Mechenses"</note> by focusing on the inconveniences of false religion and the authority of the magnates.

But a certain <term>Al-Faqih<note>original: "Alphachius." A term for a Muslim jurist or scholar of religious law.</note></term> will object: "Did he not most justly oppose the most vain worship of idols?" If someone exchanges bad things for the worst things, it is a most foolish work. Indeed, there is nothing more displeasing to God than the worship of idols. To worship the one God, however, holds nothing evil. If God is worshiped well, nothing is more excellent. If he is worshiped poorly, and the greatest vices are covered under that name, it is far better to be ignorant of Him and be led by natural law <note>The "precept of nature" refers to the innate moral sense Postel believed all humans possessed even without revelation.</note> than to blaspheme Him once known and "worship" Him with crimes. For as our Evangelist Jesus Christ says: *The servant who knows the will of his master and does not do it, shall receive many lashes; but he who does not know and does not do it, shall receive fewer.* <note>Postel is quoting Luke 12:47-48 from the Latin Vulgate.</note> For two reasons, it would have been better for the Meccans to remain idolaters than to become what they are now. First, because if any among those who were ignorant of the true God had been a very good person by the guidance of nature—even if he had not heard of Christ—he could have been saved; whereas no Muslim can, or ever could be saved, unless he returns to his senses toward Christ. The second reason is also clear: for if you preach Christ to idolaters, they easily believe and embrace the true faith; but Muslims even persecute and kill Christians. Therefore, Muhammad taught poorly and from an evil beginning, since the faith of even the rustic pagans was less evil. For pagans easily believe the Gospel; and if they perished, they would have perished alone. But all of Africa and the greatest part of Asia has perished under the plague of Muhammad. Furthermore:

> ” Those who believed are captured; they say, "We believe." And when they return to their demons <note>A polemical translation of the Quranic "Shayatin" (devils/satans), usually referring to the leaders of the opposition in Mecca.</note>, they say, "We are with you; surely we were only mocking." These are they who thought that darkness was guidance, and no respite shall remain for them, nor shall they be guided. Their example is like the example of one who once prepared a light, and there is no splendor around him; God withdrew their light, and left them in darkness, so that they may not see. Deaf,

dumb, and blind (the people), yet they do not return to their senses. In this same passage, he acts by terrifying them, and proceeds to take away the judgment of truth from the men themselves, and to establish God as the author of wickedness. If God takes away the light, who can believe? Therefore, it must be that the followers believed in the light of the devil, they who are "Muslims" without the light of God. For if they are deaf, blind, dumb, and have no judgment to recognize the light, it follows that they are led into persuasion from elsewhere, and not from God, who took away the light so they might not see: therefore, they are led by the devil, which is the truth. It follows: *But when darkness, thunder, and lightning shall proceed (distill) from heaven, they will put their fingers in their ears because of the crash of the tremor of death, and God will destroy the impious. ,, When you become ungodly toward God, then you will be made dead, and He will give you life; finally, He will make you die, and later He will give you life, and then at last you will return to Him. <note>A paraphrase of Quran 2:28.</note>
These are mere scarecrows to prevent anyone from defecting from his law. It follows:
,, It is He who created for you whatever is in the whole earth; then He ascended to the heavens and leveled them as seven heavens, and He is wise in every thing. <note>A paraphrase of Quran 2:29.</note>
Here he makes God move with local motion and makes Him finite, and thus even corruptible; he also inverts the order of things. For things higher in dignity preceded in creation, except for man, who is the end-goal of the lower matter included in the world. For this reason, Moses said, *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth*: <note>original: *In principio creauit Deus cælum et terram*. Quoted from Genesis 1:1.</note> the heaven and celestial things as causes in the first place, and elementary things as effects in the second. Not that by successive motion those were first and these later, but that in the intellectual disposition, He created them together as they were thus known—things which could not have been grasped by us otherwise unless they had been written so. Then he says:
,, And when He said to the angels, "I am placing a prefect <note>term: *præfectum* (prefect/deputy). In the Quran, this is the *Khalifa* (Caliph/Vicegerent), referring to Adam's role on earth.</note> on the earth," they said, "Will You place in it one who will corrupt it and shed blood? But we will praise You with Your renown and we will sanctify You." He said, "I know what you do not know."
,, And He taught Adam all the names, and their breadth or accidents, above the angels. And He said, "Call upon them"—that is, celebrate Me in heaven—"if you are truthful." And they said, "We praise You, nor do we have knowledge except what You have taught us, for You are the wise judge." <note>Postel's translation of Quran 2:30-32.</note>
All these are dreams written nowhere else, tending toward the goal of eluding with fabulous dreams that which the sacrosanct Trinity had said (making God speak, since otherwise we cannot express the concepts of the divine mind): *Let us make man in our image and likeness.* <note>Quoting Genesis 1:26.</note> Furthermore, the word <term>Pheseda</term> <note>original: *Pheseda*. A Latinization of the Arabic *fasād*, meaning corruption, mischief, or decay.</note> which he used for "corruption" does not only signify that necessary natural corruption which is the opposite of generation, but is everywhere understood as the corruption of sin. In this sense, if he accepts God as the author of evil, he does as we saw above and denies that He is God. Indeed, he manifestly constitutes the angels and God as evil, since they wish for a man who is produced as a murderer. Even <term>Abenreis</term> <note>Postel likely refers here to Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the famous Andalusian philosopher. He is arguing that even a "pagan" philosopher like Averroes is less impious than Muhammad.</note> is distant from such impiety. O prophet of Satan and instrument of the devil! For God created nothing evil. It follows:
,, He said, "Hey Adam, call them by their names." And when he called them by their names, He said, "Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you hide?"
You see how he joins together things that are disjointed and abrupt, since he does not say *what* Adam is calling. This is a mutilated emblem taken from the imposition of names upon animals and things. <note>Postel is comparing the Quranic account to Genesis 2:19-20, where Adam names the animals.</note> He adds:
,, And when we said to the angels, "Adore Adam," they adored him, except for the devil, who was proud and was among the impious.
Consider, O stout-hearted reader: to the Muhammadans, God is the author of evil, unjust, a murderer (for he who is the cause is at fault), and an idolater—for the blessed God wishes to be worshiped above all...

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK II.

...[all things], God now commands the angels of Muhammad to worship a man—a mortal, a sinner, and a shedder of blood. <note>Postel is reacting to Quran 2:34, where God commands the angels to prostrate before Adam. In Christian theology, worship is reserved for God alone, hence Postel’s outrage.</note> O madness and impiety, wicked even to think! And Satan seduced them both from it and led them out from there." The Holy Scripture says: "Do not eat"; this book says: "Do not approach."

The Scripture says that the wife gave her assent to the tempter; here, he takes away free will from man when he says Satan *made* them do it, rather than they having done it by consenting. "And we said: 'Go out, having become enemies to one another, and you shall have labor and affliction on the earth for a time.'

You see how, while he mixes everything with falsehoods, he is serving his own interests. For *huda* <note>original: *huda*, Arabic for "guidance"</note>, that is, "direction," is usually used to refer to the Quran. And here he says it was promised to Adam. I am not unaware that it is sometimes understood as other forms of guidance; but if you ask a Moor what he first understands by that word, he will say *mustequím elzírat* <note>original: *mustequím elzírat*, a Latinization of the Arabic *as-sirat al-mustaqim*, meaning "the straight path"</note>, that is, the "right covenant." Consequently: "And those who acted impiously and called our miracles

> false, they are companions of the fire, and in it they shall sit and remain." He says these things for his own benefit, so that those who resist him and reject his impiety and nonsense may appear impious. "O children of Israel, remember my benefit which I bestowed upon you, and keep my covenant by keeping your own covenant, and persist. And believe in that which has been sent down from heaven as most certain, regarding that which is with you—that is, your law—and be not the first impious ones against it, and do not dispute about our miracles, not even the smallest bit, but fear."

In this place, he sufficiently reveals his cunning when he says this is a confirmation of the Old Testament. From there, to a people waiting and eager for new things, he wished to thrust himself forward in the place of the Messiah. For having captured them, he thought it would be easy to use them as a step toward capturing the rest. But if he confirms the Quran, the Law of Moses ought not to contradict it—which it does in many ways. Yet he terrifies them so they do not investigate the doctrine, lest the deceit expose itself. "Do not mix the truth with falsehood. Cover and hide

> the truth, and you shall be wise."

In this place, he openly betrays himself while he persuades them to conceal the truth—which he himself certainly did, thrusting forward all manner of falsehoods. This passage needs no refutation. Then: "Be vigilant in prayers according to our custom, pay

> tithes, obey with your parents, speak to men with innocence, purify your souls, and read the book, if by any means you may understand. Help one another with patience and prayer, for that is greatness, except for the perverse."

All these things are taken from Moses and Christ, except for the reading and the *Hazala* <note>likely referring to *Salat*, the formal Islamic prayer</note> according to the custom of Muhammad. It follows:

Fear the final day; a soul shall not be rewarded for a soul in any way. And you shall not receive mercy from it, and you shall not receive justice from it, and they themselves shall not be helped."

This scoundrel <note>original: *nebulo*</note> here applauds the Jews and rises up against Jesus Christ. For that is his habit: what he does not dare pour out against one, he says against another. Truly, I have followed the order of the continuous discourse enough; now I pursue the more notable passages. "And when

This is most false. For everywhere in the Quran *Teuriet* <note>original: *Tawrat*, the Torah</note> signifies the Law of Moses; *Alphurcan* <note>original: *Al-Furqan*, meaning "the Criterion," usually another name for the Quran</note> and *Alcoran* are the same thing. # ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

-> BOOK II <-

For before Muhammad, that word or title of the <term>Quran</term> <note>original: *Alcoranus*</note> and the <term>Distinction</term> <note>original: *Alphurcanus*, referring to *Al-Furqan*, a name for the Quran meaning the "criterion" between right and wrong</note> was unheard of, yet Moses had preceded the times of Muhammad by two thousand 120 years. And:
> "When we said to Moses: 'Strike the rock with your staff,' and twelve springs flowed from it." <note>A reference to Quran 2:60.</note>

He added this number here from his own mind, so that he might seem to the Jews to possess something more through prophetic revelation than Moses did, and thus draw that fickle nation to himself. As for what follows:
> "And when you said: 'O Moses, we can no longer endure a single food. Therefore call upon your Lord for us, that He may produce for us from what the earth produces: of its beans, cucumbers, greens, lentils, and onions.' He said: 'Do you wish to exchange what is good for what is evil and uncertain? Go away to Egypt, and your request will be granted to you.'" <note>A paraphrase of Quran 2:61.</note>

All these things were added for the sake of gaining the trust of the Jews. From these details, it is clear that the author is a liar, since he claims these are nothing but the "scriptures of the ancients"; and eventually, led by repentance a hundred times over, he denies the same because his cunning was exposed. But listen to the goal of this scoundrel:
> "But those who believe and are guided, whether Christians or <note>Postel uses *apostatae* (apostates) here, likely referring to the Sabians mentioned in Quran 2:62</note> apostates: whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does good, they have their reward with their Lord, nor is there fear for them, nor shall they be confounded."

This axiom reveals the author's true character. All nations were professing their own religions as good and saying there was no need for a better one, and therefore they were unwilling to receive the new Muhammadan religion. He persuades them that salvation is found everywhere, so that when they think all religions are equal, being so coerced and pressed by his persistence and tyranny, they might not delay in crossing over to his own prescriptions. That is his intention. 

Truly, I would wish to ask all the followers of Muhammad: since all laws are good for those who do good, would not an idolater—if he uses the natural law well, does good, and believes in a judgment (for even an idolater seeks or knows a God)—be equally on the path of salvation as one who received a law from Heaven? If the Jews and Christians grant this, then God gave those laws in vain, since good and evil people are found everywhere, and "good" pagans would be saved just as "good" Christians and Jews. See where this proposition leads. Therefore, the law of Muhammad does not make a man any better than a good idolater—indeed, it makes him far worse, which the devil, the author of this prescription, was forced to say through the mouth of this prophet. 

But suppose that the <term>Mussrechine</term> <note>original: *Mushrikin*, meaning polytheists or those who "associate" others with God</note>, that is, the idolaters, are worse. If there is salvation in all laws, then why, in the chapters titled <term>Elemphaal</term> <note>Sura 8: *Al-Anfal*, The Spoils</note>, and <term>Catel</term> <note>A reference to *Al-Qital*, or Fighting/Killing, often associated with Sura 47</note>, and <term>Muhamed</term>, and <term>Theubet</term> <note>Sura 9: *At-Tawba*, Repentance</note>—which concern the spoils of war, the slaughter by Muhammad, and conversion—why do you turn your weapons against everyone? Why do you kill the Jews, who are wretchedly afflicted throughout the world? Why do you not spare the Christians, the most innocent race of men? Why do you order them to be killed without distinction? Are you not the most unjust of all mortals? For besides the fact that you treat the law of God as no better than the law of idols, you also overturn our law, which you have confessed (and are forced to confess) is divine, and you destroy its followers. 

This was Muhammad’s strategy: to pave a way for the devil and to deny God. For he who equates an idol and the laws by which it is worshipped with God and divine things, what else is he doing but denying God? There is indeed (as we also admit) salvation for certain individuals within various laws, but only if they have not heard of the true God or His son Jesus Christ. However, after receiving knowledge of the truth, if anyone does not believe, no salvation remains for them at all, no matter how many good works they perform. 

Let those who find this opinion pleasing listen with an open mind. Let us suppose some man was brought up with the greatest innocence, lived most blamelessly with others, and possessed the most excellent condition of both soul and body (for without these, the functions of the intellect cannot be performed properly); let us say he never stole or possessed another’s property, but freely gave what he had to the needy, and healed all kinds of diseases of both mind and body...
