Yet, like a robber, you do not ask for it, you simply take it; and elsewhere you speak against this very point. Arabia was peaceful and happy before you, but you have placed it in perpetual unrest. In this persuasive section, he has made use of a rhetorical device <note>original: 'occupatione rhetorica', or preterition, where a speaker emphasizes something by claiming they will not mention it.</note> by which rhetoricians say exactly what they claim they do not wish to say. While he was receiving from everyone, he said he wanted nothing and sought nothing, so that they might follow him. 

When, however, he was argued against for bringing forward many things contrary to divine law, he immediately devised an answer: <margin>“</margin> "And they do not truly attribute to God His power when they say: He does not send down anything from heaven upon men. Say: Who sent the book with which Moses came into the light and as a guidance for men, which you have arranged into scrolls, from which you hide many things <margin>“</margin> and conceal many others?" <note>Refers to Quran 6:91.</note> It is not enough to say this; it would be necessary to demonstrate it. Since this concerns the deeds of men, if it is established, it is not enough to have said it; it must be proved at least by conjectures. Since Muhammad cannot do this, it follows that he lies impudently. For not even one "jot" or "tittle" <note>A reference to Matthew 5:18.</note> of the law has perished; it was so diligently preserved that every single sentence, period, and letter was numbered. 

Muhammad was refuted by the sacred scriptures. Since he could not say they were false or corrupted, he devised another excuse: that the entire scripture is not contained in what is currently held. But nothing of that letter has perished. To be sure, the interpretation was handed down to the wise, and not all things are permitted to everyone; but the whole of it has always been intact, and he could not produce a single omitted passage. 

Regarding what he says a little later against Christ—that God Himself does not have a son since He had no wife—no one ever believed a son was born from the Father in divine matters in the way we are born here. For God is an incorporeal Mind, generating from Himself eternal Wisdom, by which all things were produced into being, preserved, and restored; without this Son, nothing at all would subsist. In the Son—that is, in His Wisdom and Word—He created the world; in the same Son clothed in our flesh, He reformed that same world in man, who is the compendium of the whole. Therefore, He does not generate by a female and a companion, as you suppose, you most impudent **anthropomorphite** <term>ἀνθρωπομορφίτα</term> <note>original: 'anthropomorphite', one who attributes human form or physical characteristics to God.</note>! Rather, He produces all things in His own image and gives them life by His own finger—that is, the Holy Spirit. 

I am forced to repeat these things frequently for this reason: that this is the primary aim of this scoundrel, who is most cunning in earthly matters but most ignorant in divine ones. It is necessary to hear the remarkable judgment of this beast in divine matters, to see the genius he possesses. He says: <margin>“</margin> "O hosts of demons and men, did there not come to you prophets from <margin>“</margin> among yourselves, telling you of miracles and announcing your day to you? They said: We are witnesses against ourselves. And the present life seduced them, and they confessed against themselves <margin>“</margin> that they were impious." <note>Refers to Quran 6:130.</note> 

The most wicked race of demons—turned and intent upon the destruction of men, unconvertible—has [according to him] performed the embassy of God! Whence, according to Muhammad, it must be said that there are good demons, and that they have Republics and embassies, and turn themselves to good, and enjoy present delights. For this reason, he says elsewhere that they have been made **Muslims** <note>original: 'Mussulmanos'. Postel is critiquing the Quranic concept of the Jinn who convert to Islam.</note>. And meanwhile, he makes them all ignorant of themselves, since without an envoy from their own kind sent to them, they would not know they were impious. This is Muhammadan theology. Take heed, you miserable and blind Muslims!

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
## Page 190

Since <term>separated substances</term><note>A philosophical term for beings without physical bodies, such as angels or demons.</note> are endowed with the most lively intellect, comprehending everything except God, how can it be that they are ignorant of their own condition, that they are held by present delights, or that they could compose an order worthy of a Republic? Especially since their corruption creeps through all of nature. As for his <note>Muhammad's.</note> disapproval of the decrees of the Jews, he does so unjustly, since he brings forth no authority against the Holy Authority. Furthermore, that he introduced his law because of various sects introduced by heretics is more certain than certainty itself. For he took the sons of Satan, proscribed from the holy religion, into his fellowship; he thought them the greatest because they favored him, and therefore throughout his whole work he claimed they "believed well." Finally, he repeats that he was commanded to be the "first <term>Saracen</term>" <note>original: 'Sarracenus'; a medieval term for Muslims.</note> or Muslim. However one takes it, it is a lie, as has already been demonstrated.

->Surah Al-A'raf, Meccan, Verse 205<- <note>Postel refers here to Surah 7, Al-A'raf. While he notes the final verse of the chapter, his commentary covers the themes of the entire Surah.</note>

> Immediately from the very threshold, he repeats the error already refuted: that God told the angels to adore Adam, and Satan said to Him, "I will not adore him." And God said, "What prevented you from adoring Adam when I commanded you?" He said, "I am better than he, because You created me from fire, but him from clay." God said, "Depart from it (Paradise) and do not be proud within it." He said, "I will wait until the day of judgment."

There are in these words as many errors as there are periods. God is made the author of evil and idolatry by commanding angels to adore a man, even though He keeps honor and glory for Himself alone. He says the demon was damned because he did not adore a man, whereas it was because he did not honor God as God. He says he was created from fire—yet no separated substances consist of fire, for they would then be corruptible in the manner of matter. Finally, he says they shall be saved <note>Presumably referring to the respite given to Satan until Judgment Day.</note>, all of which fights against that very nature. Lastly, he says that God corrupted Satan; thus he makes God the author of evils, or rather, the author of nothing. Where the Holy Scripture <note>The Bible (Genesis 3:5).</note> placed the phrase, "you shall be as gods," he said "as angels," which is different. Finally, regarding what he says—"their private parts were revealed"—they could not be revealed if they had not been covered. But Holy Scripture has: *And the eyes of their knowledge were opened, and they saw that they were naked.* Thus, he always wished to add, subtract, or change things in the sacred texts. 

While he objects with the "old wives' tales" of the <term>Thamud</term>, the <term>Ad</term>, <term>Hud</term>, the she-camel, <term>Shuaib</term> of Midian, and the like, these are merely the dreams of the old women of Arabia, which nurses have long been accustomed to sing to babbling infants before his time. To the objections that he was a fool and out of his mind, he cannot satisfy them in a way that would keep people from believing it to be true. But meanwhile, I had forgotten to mention regarding the she-camel, according to the interpreters, that she was two miles in body length. 

It shames me to report how many fables he attaches to the history of Moses concerning the departure from Egypt; he did this to entice the Jews, saying that he possessed certain things which they themselves did not have in their Law. He has Moses threatened with the cross by those whom he had conquered, though they had no legal right under Pharaoh. He makes Moses call himself the "first of believers"—thus neither Abraham nor Muhammad was the first. The golden calf "lowed," and Moses grabbed Aaron by the hair. He says God made the children of Israel go astray, yet God was calling them back to Himself and to justice. He says fish came of their own accord to the shore by the sea on the Sabbath day when they worshipped; and when they did not worship, they did not come. Yet, on the Sabbath it would not have been permitted to gather manna, so how much less to catch and cook fish? He says twelve springs gushed forth where there was only one. In short, almost everything is full of lying fabrications; because they can be refuted by the sacred text, I leave them be.

This is the beginning of the law of plunder and the prescription of slaughters. So that nothing might be holy before his followers, he encourages them as much as he can. He asserts they are damned if they ever turn their backs, and that all goods belong to God and to whomsoever He wishes to give them. Indeed, this chapter...

# G. V. L. POSTEL, BOOK II.

is called "The Spoils" <note>original: "Quæstus"; referring to Surah 8, Al-Anfal ("The Spoils of War")</note>, because it was written against the citizens of Mecca who had driven him from the city due to sedition: it claims that all gains are good as long as a fifth part is yielded to the prophet. These are the "prophetic" laws. Moses saved his own people; Muhammad destroyed his citizens, despoiled them, killed them, and put them to flight. Christ willed that all things be brought together for the use and charity of men as if they were brothers; the Arab prophet willed his own people to be enriched by the spoils of others. In truth, he inculcates nothing else in this chapter but tyranny and blood: he kills, leads away captives, and converts, such that no tyrant in the whole world could have written laws more suited to absolute power. Therefore, one may call Muhammad a soldier and a pirate <note>original: "prædonem"; also meaning a robber or plunderer</note>, but not a prophet. Indeed, he is so far from being a prophet that nothing more alien to God and nature was ever born. The following Surah <note>original: "Sorat"</note> is of the same sort, which is called "Conversion" <note>original: "Conuersio"; referring to Surah 9, At-Tawbah ("Repentance" or "Conversion")</note>: and for that reason, it was also written in Medina, where he lived as an exile. Furthermore, he wants everyone to be received, provided they pay tithes—except for those upon whom he wished to take vengeance. From this, he shows what kind of prophecy his was and at what target it aimed. Finally, he commands something against nature: that they should kill their fathers, brothers, and other parents if they refuse to believe. Then he teaches that one must "spend in the way" <note>original: "expendendum esse in uia"; a reference to the Quranic phrase 'fi sabilillah', which Postel interprets here as financing raids</note>, which is to say, to blockade the roads. For he considers this a most just source of income. He held the Quraysh <note>original: "Choraisios"</note>, his own kinsmen, as enemies, and in four or five attacks, he attempted to intercept them with their merchandise and camels, but he was repulsed. Whereas before he used to say, "Follow those who ask no reward from you and are rightly guided," now he says, "Pay and spend whether you wish to or not, because you are unjust." Indeed, he so insisted upon plunder that he himself said they would flee into caves if they could, to avoid suffering what he imposed upon them. However, after he had tormented them remarkably, he saw that almost all those he had bound by oath were failing him; therefore he threatened them with destruction, as in the times of Noah, Hud <note>original: "Had"</note>, and Thamud <note>original: "Thamuz"</note>, so that he might retain them by any artifice. If he could not do so by force, he would attempt it by the fear of God. Truly, besides Zayd <note>original: "Zeidum"</note>, Abu Bakr <note>original: "Vbecharum"</note>, Umar <note>original: "Humarum"</note>, and Amr <note>original: "Ahmerum"</note>, they were almost all peasants who followed him partly out of fear and partly out of hope for plunder. Moreover, so that he might have the best pretext for killing his brothers, he said that Abraham did not spare his father, and preferred to leave his paternal goods and believe in God rather than plot anything against his father. Abraham did indeed leave his parent and kindred in Chaldea, but he never wished to act cruelly against nature under the pretext of religion; he left everything he could rightfully seek so that he might obey God. But this prophet did not fear to remove nine brothers from his midst—a man born for the destruction of nature. Whoever weighs these two chapters more diligently will see that laws more suited to a faction could not be set down by any most bloodthirsty tyrant in the whole world. For there is nothing in them without blood, even though he makes God the author of such impiety. In this, he seems very similar to the ancient impostors who faked conversations with the gods because of the ignorance and fear of men, and gave laws suited to their own faction. This might have been tolerable in him if he had given anything by which nature might be helped—as did Solon, Lycurgus, Zamolxis, or Charondas <note>Ancient legendary lawgivers of Greece and surrounding regions</note>. But he overturned many well-established things and wrote more to the destruction of nature and reason. Let us come to other matters.

### Surah Yunus, that is, Jonah. The Ninth Chapter, Meccan. <note>In the 12th-century Latin translation used by Postel, the numbering of the Surahs differs from the modern standard; here he identifies Jonah as the 9th Surah, whereas it is modernly the 10th.</note>

Now that the slaughter in Mecca has been carried out, vengeance taken upon enemies, and citizens killed, he seems to have written this cautionary work; for in it, he opens his design more clearly than before, which he would not have done unless matters were settled. On account of this, he was asked by the assembled company to produce the Quran <note>original: "Alcoranum"</note>, which he refused to do. But from the beginning of the chapter, something must be noted:
> Are these miracles of the Wise Book not a wonder to men, that we have revealed to a man from among themselves, and that he should forewarn men...

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD
<meta>catchword: scendam</meta>

> ...and preach to those who have believed, that they POSSESS the firstfruits of truth with their Lord. The Chaphiri <note>original: "Chaphiri"; referring to the Arabic *Kafirun*, meaning disbelievers or infidels</note> said: this is an evident incantation. For your Lord is God, who created the heavens and the earth in six days: then he was raised above the throne, where he disposes the command; nor is there any redeemer <note>likely a translation of the Arabic *shafi'* or intercessor</note>, except after his command. These are his words.

All these things must be weighed more precisely. Consider with what judgment he attributes prudence, wisdom, and justice (for he grants the Quran <note>original: "Alcoranum"</note> these and similar titles in many places) to a book written in quaternions <note>folded sheets of paper</note> and small booklets, when these are qualities that can only exist in a soul, and flow from there into action. Inanimate things, such as a book, cannot act, neither simply nor by deliberation. How could men find him admirable when, contrary to the law of nature and the common condition of things known even to the most unlearned, he described nothing and published no sign? A prophet was never considered admirable simply because he was chosen from among men; rather, it was because he excelled other men through divine works. Yet men wondered that this "prophet" was a man from among themselves—that is, similar to them, a worshiper of idols in his youth, luxurious, frequently seized in mind <note>a reference to Muhammad’s reported seizures, which critics interpreted as madness or demonic possession</note>, a disturber of all things, bloodthirsty, bringing no miracle worthy of a man of God or profitable for the use of men: and moreover, one who would not allow his words to be weighed by anyone. They were right to wonder. For God would be most unjust if he sent such prophets to restore nature. If men had already believed, they had no need of a prophet. But if he says "those who were believing," how can they be the "firstfruits of truth," when Abraham existed two thousand and more years before him? When Moses and the sons of Israel were chosen and proven by God? And when he himself admits that Abraham, Moses, Christ, and the prophets were messengers of the truth? This, therefore, is a shameless lie and a contradiction. Who ever told you that it was a "manifest incantation" <note>an accusation of sorcery</note> when you performed no miracle? You are merely repeating the objection raised by the Jews against Christ so that you might seem to have something in common with him.

If, however, you did perform any miracle in the presence of certain people, it was that of "bringing the moon down from heaven." For all other things were never done with any witness, except for the watering of the palm trunk. If you brought the moon down from heaven, which mortal perceived it, since the whole world would have lacked it as long as it was in your sleeves? <note>Referring to the story of Muhammad splitting the moon and hiding the pieces in his sleeves</note>. Suppose Bugellinus <note>likely a contemporary reference or a name used to denote a specific witness or "fool"</note> saw it: how did the rest of those who lacked it not notice, since even tiny eclipses <note>original: "eclipses unciales"; literally "eclipses of an inch"</note> are preserved in the records of the nations? How large were your sleeves, that they could contain the twenty-seventh part of the earth? These are trifles and the ravings of old women, just as in the past sorceresses and poisoners used to play with the minds of men through delusions. They promised the same things as you. For this reason, Circe, Medea, and Calypso were infamous—poisoners celebrated in both Greek and Latin literature. If the Arabs called you great for this reason, they did so rightly, because you were playing with delusions. 

The miracles that God displayed in the heavens in the name of his people are entrusted to the literature of all nations. The Persians recorded the standing still of the sun under Joshua, and its backward movement under Hezekiah. The Greeks thought there would be future conflagrations because of this, and they committed it to writing—fabulously, yes, but hinting at this truth. What shall I say of the eclipse of both luminaries at the death of Christ? Phlegon <note>a 2nd-century Greek historian</note>, living in Rome, mentions it; the Chaldeans noted it in their annals; the Egyptians saw it. In Heliopolis, Dionysius and Apollophanes <note>Christian converts said to have witnessed the darkness of the Crucifixion in Egypt</note> debated it. Those are truly miracles: yours, however, are either trifles or delusions. 

Afterward, in your usual manner, you make God a being who needs a place and is finite, since you claim that after the matter was arranged, he sought the heaven, and was moved from place to place like a man—comprehending nothing truly worthy of God in your whole work. You do not realize that you deny God when you make him finite and moved by location. But you will object to me, I know, that it is written in the sacred scriptures that God...

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK II.
<sig>r</sig>
<meta>catchword: Muhamed (Muha-)</meta>

... [I will] descend and see if they have completed their iniquity in deed <note>original: "scendam & uidebo, si iniquitatem opere cõpleuerint"; a reference to Genesis 18:21</note>: and that our Christ descended from heaven, and many other places where the divine words seem to attribute local motion to God. When we treat of God or His power in sacred matters, we accommodate ourselves to the sense and capacity of the reader, so that we seem to place many passions or actions in God: because the effects seen in these lower things are such as men would perform when moved by similar affections. Therefore, we understand those effects from the result, not from any motion or agitation of the **immobile God**, yet never casting God down from His own heaven. For although His force and power are seen everywhere and represent themselves in His traces, nevertheless we affirm His majesty to be chiefly in the superior heavens.

But you, who affirm that the *herss* <note>original: "herss"; the Arabic *Arsh*, meaning the Throne of God</note>—that is, the seat or throne—is the proper place of His majesty, make Him move from His place when you contend that He is below His *herss*. Thus we differ greatly: we acknowledge His power everywhere, but His majesty to be above all matter; you desire His majesty to be thrust down from heaven into these lower things along with His power, and to have performed manual works. Furthermore, as often as we read that a phantom of God was represented, we contend that these were the ministries of angels, which God willed to be carried out as if by the service of a body. As for the idea that God "disposed" things only after He had returned on high, having finished what was to be done here: that is false. For before the constitution of the world, all things were clear, foreseen, and ordered by the Divinity; these He finally brought into being when it seemed good to Him, and as it [still] seems good. He therefore disposed nothing once the world was created, for that would imply a new will in Him, which is repugnant to His nature.

It follows: **"And there is no redeemer except after His command."** <note>original: "Nec est ullus redemptor nisi post pręceptum eius"; likely quoting Sura 10:3</note> These things were written for the sake of the grace and redemption of Christ, since it was both believed and seen that the remission of sins was held through Him. For whoever are baptized in Christ, and the martyrs, have so shown themselves to have obtained remission from Christ that nothing was so arduous—with the sole exception of creation—that they could not do it in the name of Christ and God; and yet all those things are ascribed to God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. This plague of a man <note>referring to Muhammad</note> was not ashamed to wish to take from Christ the Redeemer what he, a most impure man, attempted to ascribe to himself from a forged revelation. For he says that God—whom he had approached within the distance of a bow-shot—in the highest heaven, even above Christ, gave to him that he should be <term>Muhamed Mustapha</term> <note>original: "Muhamed Mustapha"; Muhammad the Chosen</note>, that is, redeemer and sanctifier. For <term>saphia</term> <note>Arabic *safiya*</note> is to act holy; whence <term>sophi</term> <note>Sufi</note> means holy, and <term>estephaia</term> <note>Istifa</note> to sanctify. From this comes the participle or active verbal noun, <term>Mustaphai</term>, that is, the sanctifier. 

Impious and ruined man, you wished to seize for yourself the title of God and to detract from God; you did not grant it to Christ, who is both Man and God. Let the fair reader see how many errors and blasphemies are in three or four verses of this law, and let him judge the faithfulness of the whole work by them. For if it were permitted to examine it thus, there would appear as many errors as words where he wished to defect from us—which he did by design. Now I pluck out certain things bit by bit. 

**"And when our miracles are read to them, those who do not hope for our encounter said: Bring a Quran <note>original: "Alcoranum"</note> without this, or change it. Say: it is not permitted for me to change it by the judgment of my soul, because I follow nothing except what is revealed to me, because I fear the Lord if I should offend Him."** <note>A paraphrase of Quran 10:15</note> He calls the miracles of God and nature "his own" throughout the whole work, which is impious and a claim to participate with God. Furthermore, he enunciates all the acts of God indefinitely without changing the person or the manner of speaking after he has spoken of himself. But it is a common thing, and in individual verses of the <term>Quran</term>, he tacitly admits (which he cannot deny) that there are many lies, things contrary to the sacred [scriptures], and impious things; yet, lest he should seem to change his dreams, he says it is forbidden for him to change anything in it. If nothing is to be changed in the <term>Quran</term>, how could God be so foolish and unskilled?

### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
<page-num>194</page-num>

Muhammad indeed acts the wise man. For if his law was revealed with God as its author, and yet it clashes with divine law in six hundred <note>Postel uses "six hundred" as a common Latin idiom meaning "countless" or "innumerable."</note> places—since it cannot be that God is false, wicked, or a liar—it follows that Muhammad is treacherous, impious, and an impostor. Thus, he recognizes what is false, but out of fear of losing his power, he refuses to change it; that is the reason for his "revelation" and the aim of his law. If he had published it [plainly], he could have been refuted by even the least of men, since he would be found contrary to himself in every individual <term>verse <note>original: "A iet"; from the Arabic *Ayat*, meaning a sign or verse of the Quran</note></term>. Say, then:
> » Does any of your likenesses or partners direct you toward the truth?
> » Say, God directs toward the truth. Is not He who directs toward the truth more worthy
> » to be the leader than one who does not direct unless he himself is directed? And what is the matter with you, that you 
> » judge thus? Many of them follow nothing but opinion. But opinion detracts
> » nothing from the truth, for God is wise in what they do. And let it not be that
> » this Quran is a fiction without God. But it defines that which was in hand 
> » before it, and distinguishes the book in which there is no blemish, from the Lord of the ages. Do they
> » say, "He forged it"? Say: Come with a chapter <note>original: "capite"; Postel is translating the Arabic *Sura* as the Latin *caput* (chapter).</note> similar to this, and invoke whom you 
> » can besides God, if you are truthful; indeed, they have called false that which they did not com-
> » prehend with knowledge. And by no means has its interpretation come to them. <note>This blockquote is Postel's translation of Surah 10 (Yunus), verses 35–39.</note>

In this passage, while he pretends to speak against the Meccans, he also rises up against those whom he has approved in countless other places. For he wishes to turn away the foolish common folk so that, having abandoned the prescription of the holy laws, they might follow him. It had already been proven by many miracles that what preceded him was from God; therefore, he says that "direction" belongs to God, so that those who came before him might seem to have lacked it. He certainly could have followed them if he had wished, but he preferred to deny God and follow his own lust. To be sure, it is God who directs toward the truth, but He uses men as His instruments, and He bestows greater gifts upon one than another; hence, those whom He sent previously are not false. Because you contradict all of them, you must be the liar. Who are those who follow nothing but opinion? Certainly not the followers of either Law [Jewish or Christian], for both posit God, though one explains Him more fully. Before the Messiah had come in the flesh, the mystery of the Trinity was not known to the common people, but only to the wise. But after Christ arrived, those mysteries were made clear, without which the world can neither be built nor restored, much less saved. Therefore, those things are not matters of "opinion," but yours are, and most false at that. For what is more subject to opinion, or more foreign to the truth, than that a man should be a prophet who brought about the destruction of nature, who performed no signs, who contradicted all good men, and who has nothing in common with anyone (except our own people) but heresies and damned opinions? A man who thirsts for the blood of all, flies upon their fortunes, and kills his own citizens and brothers. 

To this we add: since God gave all the prophets before him, by whom a depraved nature could be directed and illuminated, how could it be that He gave this prophet to the world after the greatest of all, Jesus Christ? A prophet who would lead men back from a written law and a law of grace to a natural and corrupt state? Would it not be a clearly delirious Providence that would undertake such great works to form man, and send the greatest of prophets—than whom no greater can be given—only to finally revoke everything back to the state from which He had led it? See how absurd these things are, and full of mere opinion. He had heard that "opinions are pushed out by opinions" in false religions; therefore, he said that the truth was like opinions, so that wretched men, blind in divine matters, might prefer his opinion. For such men, at the persuasion of a demon, falsehood is usually more acceptable than truth. Furthermore, since many objected to him that the Quran was a fiction—as it seemed to be, and was—he says that nothing similar could be forged without God. I would subscribe to this sentiment, were I not afraid of pinning impiety upon God. For if all extremes of things were attributed to God, He would undoubtedly seem to be the author of the Quran. However, just as when we speak of the highest truth, we [attribute it] to God...

...we attribute to God: so here we must attribute the highest lie and ineptitudes, which agree with no kind of learning, to its highest author, who since he cannot be God, must be the worst of all demons. And because they said this fiction was not the law of Abraham, nor of Moses, nor of Christ, since it went against all of them, he [Muhammad] devised this (which I brought up before): that it was a distinction and confirmation between those things which were in [their] hands—that is, the New and Old Testament—so that he might always find some means of elusion. But how can it be that there is a middle ground between two extremes, which departs from the ends of both? It cannot be. Therefore he would have spoken better if he called it a contradiction against both Testaments, since in six hundred <note>Postel uses "six hundred" as a common Latin idiom meaning "countless" or "innumerable."</note> places it sins against the aim of both laws. 

But I proceed to other matters; I have already satisfied the denial of the divinity of Christ and that God has a son, which he repeats here and three hundred times elsewhere in the Quran. When however he was urged to admit that the laws were otherwise good and proceeded from God, then he said: <margin>„</margin> "I have my labor for myself, you have your labor for yourselves; I am innocent of what you do, and you of what I do." <margin>„</margin> He does this for the sake of retaining everyone in his power. He makes Moses impious when he says he prayed to God against Pharaoh, whom he was striving to convert so that at least he might leave the people whom he [Moses] had come to lead. For although God had hardened the heart of Pharaoh—that is, had left him in pure natural [faculties] and depraved opinions and desires—nevertheless His Apostle [Moses] ought never to commit the act of interceding with God for a man's destruction, for that would be against His majesty. 

As for what he calls the people of Jonah, that Ninevite people to whom he was sent is far different from the region in which Jonah was born; for he was a Syrian, from Phoenicia. Nineveh, however, is in Assyria. But to have been ignorant of that is nothing. <margin>„</margin> When Muhammad says, "Will you not compel men until they believe? and it is not placed in the power of man to believe except by the command of God," <margin>„</margin> he is impious and nefarious, who has compelled [them] by force, slaughters, plunderings, captivities, and blood, when God had not yet granted that they should believe, even if the law had been good. Therefore religion was not to be introduced by the sword, since God did not yet wish them to believe—He who can make all peoples come together. But in this place he was satiated with the blood of citizens, and had given place to vengeance in the two preceding chapters; fury, sated with blood, rages less.

-> Sura Hud 10 <note>This refers to the 11th chapter of the Quran in modern numbering.</note>. Meccan. <-

Repeating that the creation was made in six days, immediately, so that he might differ from Moses, he admitted an error; for where Moses has, "And the spirit of the Lord was carried over the waters," he put, "And his *hers* <note>original: "hers"; Postel's transliteration of the Arabic *Arsh*, meaning 'Throne'</note>, that is, his throne, was over the waters." Although the greatest divine force is seen in the nature of water—and so great that all things seem to be born from it—nevertheless the true seat of divinity was never attached to a corruptible element. The supreme power of God, creating all things through wisdom, effects all things in His spirit as if by the finger of God, showing the greatest strengths of His power in the waters. 

Nor was it enough to have admitted an error in the change, but he also added another: that God placed His throne over the waters to prove who among us was of better operation. He makes God needy of place and proximity so that He may know our crimes and deeds; whereas He fills heaven and earth, filling all things and being unplaceable, and only to be known privatively <note>A theological term (apophasis) meaning God is understood by what He is not, rather than by positive definitions.</note>. He acknowledges a little later how he gathered power from rustics and commoners who had joined themselves for the sake of plunder; and yet they, although unskilled, laughed at his trifles, whence he threatens them with the punishment of fire. He adds a little later, in his usual way, to the history of Noah, that one of his sons refused to follow his father and sought a mountain and perished; which must therefore be called false because it is not in the sacred [scriptures].

->Al-Hijr, 15. Meccan.<-

" We never destroyed any city unless it had a known book: nor 
" will a people anticipate its term, nor delay it. They said, 'Hey you 
" upon whom the memory has come, you are possessed by a demon; why

He says there is no city that does not have its own law and memory: therefore he was fruitlessly thrusting his own "memory" upon those who already had one. For he calls the Quran *dhikr* <note>original: "dilzicri"</note>, that is, "endowed with memory," meaning it is full of the recollection of created things. But that is most false—that everyone has a just knowledge of the law of nature. For some are so depraved that they rise up against its prescriptions despite their conscience, such as the Maneaters <note>original: "Anthropophagi"</note>, Cannibals, and as many peoples as plot the ruin of nature—like Muhammad, who approves of promiscuous intercourse and unions with beasts, and persuaded his own followers to perverted lust. Therefore, not all cities or peoples have a "book" in the sense he means. For all have it only as far as knowledge is concerned, but few for the sake of moral correction—and those only the best Christians. I say the "best," because not everyone who has given their name to Christ is immediately a Christian. Therefore, only those gifted with the divine spirit through Christ have the law by which they recognize sins and flee from them; other mortals merely know of them. 

As for what you say—that no peoples or cities hasten or delay their own misfortunes and historical periods—you entirely take away free will <term>arbitrium liberum</term> from men. A republic of men would then be nothing more than a herd of oxen or sheep. Laws, corrections, and counsels are in vain if human efforts achieve nothing in this life. It has resulted from this that those among the followers of this law <note>meaning Islam</note> who claim the highest sanctity—ranking just after the beasts—do not move from their spot when rain, hail, or storms arrive. Instead, they say it is "fate" <note>original: "fatum"</note>, and that it must be endured because God sent it. If we have no power of choice, let us go and rush into pleasures and crimes like beasts, for we cannot do otherwise. See where this doctrine leads. A gathering of many men is far superior to one or two; therefore, it can meet evils and prolong its own existence by any remedy. 

But not everyone knows where these ideas lead. When circumstances in Mecca changed, he wanted to soothe the minds of the survivors with these words: that it was not his fault, his own choice had not sinned, but God had sent an end to things so that no one could escape. This is true insofar as you consider the event itself, but false regarding its timing. God indeed predestines all things by inclination, not by necessity; by necessity of nature, not by a fixed time. And if He did this through all circumstances, "Who are you, O man, to answer back to God?" <note>A reference to Romans 9:20.</note> God certainly never imposes a necessity for evil, otherwise He would be evil; but sometimes He sends what seems to be evil to someone, specifically when a great good follows from that event. You therefore wrongly take away the place of human prudence, Muhammad, for the sake of covering up your crime. 

That they said you were "seized by a demon" was no lie. For the sake of hiding the "falling sickness" <note>A historical term for epilepsy, which medieval critics often claimed Muhammad suffered from.</note> from your wife Khadija <note>original: "Hadegian"</note>, you feigned being a prophet, and Satan began to twist you against your will, when you perceived everything addressing and calling out to you. This is evident in many other places, but especially in the final chapters of the Quran, in which you defend yourself with God against *waswas* <note>original: "uisnas"</note>, that is, against the disturbance of the mind sent by a demon. Therefore, it is no wonder that these lies are so poorly connected, since two ruined authors devised them: a man with a disturbed mind, and the demon inhabiting him. 

But how do you dare, you ruined scoundrel, to say that the laws of the ancients have vanished? "Now," he says, "the law of the ancients (or the first ones) has vanished." How can it be that a law vanished whose worshippers were the most numerous in the whole world? The world was occupied by Jews and Christians, except for a few idolaters, when this plague flowed from you into it...

Therefore, the law could not have perished. Suppose there are very few people who perish under the prescription of any law whatsoever; as long as they exist, the law flourishes. But if even a worshiper is lacking, do you not think laws still exist for that reason, since they depend on an eternal and immutable divine authority? As long as a prince remains, and as long as the foundation of any republic exists, laws are also ready to be observed. Since, therefore, the good laws that were published and promulgated before you come from God, the eternal author, not one jot <note>original: "unus apex"; a reference to Matthew 5:18, often translated as "one iota" or "one tittle."</note> of them can perish until they are fulfilled. Therefore, you falsely said they had perished. I pass over the repetition of idolatry—of which he makes God the author—and the creation of the demon from fire, and the fables mixed with sacred histories, so that I am not forced to repeat the same things so frequently and dwell on them any longer. I previously noted the marble stones—from which this chapter <note>original: "sora," referring to a Sura of the Quran.</note> gets its title—with which God rained upon Gomorrah and the other submerged cities.

<note>Postel refers to Sura 16, "The Bee" (An-Nahl), though his source numbers it as 15.</note>

Hear the usual blasphemies. He has already confessed in countless places that laws were given by God before him, and yet he now says the devil is their patron. How can it be that Satan, God’s adversary, is a patron under the law of God? For the Jews indeed, a demon has been their patron from the time they rejected and killed Christ, who was promised to them in countless places. On account of his death, through two Roman invasions shortly after the death of Christ, sixty times a hundred thousand men <note>six million</note> were destroyed. When they wished, under the authority of Emperor Julian the Apostate, to restore the Temple *Elmihrab* <note>original: "Elmihrab," likely Postel's transliteration of "Al-Mihrab," meaning the sanctuary or prayer niche, here referring to the Temple in Jerusalem.</note>—that is, the Holy Place of Jerusalem—divine power caused an earthquake to arise from the site of the foundations, and globes of fire and flames consumed the builders, once and again, until they stopped. These things were written by secular authors and those foreign to us; we did not invent them. From this, it is certain that the one religion of Jesus Christ is true, over which Satan has no patronage; rather, he has it over the impious liar Muhammad. I think you remember that in two places previously he prohibited wine—not indeed, as I thought, because of the wine itself, but because of the vice of drunkenness. Now one may see that, led by regret, he praises and approves of drunkenness. An outstanding law! It forbids carrying a sword, yet permits and commands the killing of a man; when nevertheless it is the intention of a true legislator not only to prohibit the acts themselves, but especially the instruments by which a vice can be committed. He says:

> And from the fruits of the palms, and from the clusters of grapes, he has granted that you take from them intoxication and good wealth; in this is a miracle, etc.
<note>Postel is translating Quran 16:67.</note>

India <note>In the 16th century, "India" was often a generic term for distant Eastern or tropical lands.</note> abounds in no other wine than palm wine, which strongly intoxicates, just as does the wine of pears, apples, serviceberries, or even ale. For all those, when drunk in large quantities, attack the brain, which Muhammad approves. When he was driven by his followers to change something, he did it under compulsion, lest they all defect. And he says:

> And when we changed one miracle in place of another miracle <note>Postel uses "miraculum" for the Arabic "ayah," which can mean both "miracle" and "verse."</note>, and God is wiser in what He sent, they said: "Surely you invent these things." But many of them do not understand. Say: "The Holy Spirit sent it from your Lord, so that those who believed might be confirmed," in which is a message and guidance for the Muslims. And therefore I understand, because they will say: "Truly a man teaches him the common language in which they agree, and this is clear Arabic."
<note>Postel is translating Quran 16:101-103, addressing the concept of abrogation (naskh) where later verses replace earlier ones.</note>

While he tries to satisfy these objections, he betrays himself. There would have been no need for change if he had received it from God. And yet he changed it; hence he attributed it to the Holy Spirit, as if the Spirit changes things more easily. He says that those who object do not understand whenever he cannot satisfy their objections. That he was making it up was known even to the "bleary-eyed and the barbers" <note>original: "lippis & tonsoribus," a Latin idiom from Horace meaning "it is common knowledge known even to the lowliest people."</note>; for even the peasants objected to it. How could he confirm the believers when he contradicted everyone? Concerning those who taught him in the common tongue, it is certain; for regarding those guards <note>original: "spatarijs," possibly referring to the *spatharii* or imperial guards, or perhaps a specific group mentioned in Postel's sources.</note>, the authors

What the word *agemij* <note>original: "agemij"; referring to 'Ajam, an Arabic term for non-Arabs or foreigners, particularly Persians.</note> means in this place, I do not quite grasp. For Muhammad did not wish to be bound by any rules, neither of reason nor of eloquence; yet they claim he is most eloquent because he wrote almost rhythmically, though even that was without any laws. A little later, when he calls this law the "law of Abraham," it is clear how falsely he asserts that.

->*Sura of the Children of Israel, 16. Meccan.*<-
<note>Postel refers to Sura 17, "Al-Isra" (The Night Journey), often titled "The Children of Israel." In his source, it is numbered as 16.</note>

From the very beginning, he sets forth that foolish vision and the riding of Borachus <note>original: "Borachi"; refers to Buraq, the celestial steed of the Prophet.</note>, and says that God stayed through the night with his servant. Indeed, the commentators pour out so many foolishnesses and blasphemies against God, and such ignorance in matters, that no patience could listen to it. [They claim] holy men are separated by heavens; animals of every kind, larger than the whole world, are in the heavens; there are gates in the heavens made of tangible matter; God is finite; the name of Muhammad is written in all places alongside the name of God; all angels and prophets adore Muhammad. They even claim the holy and blessed pray to this sink of crimes to pray for them before God, as if the blessed in heaven lacked something. From there he reports great privileges, all of which I have noted before. Yet he did not dare—even though he had climbed to the highest heaven—not to confess that Christ was greater than himself, and he begged Christ to ask God on his behalf. These are the foolishnesses. Now, if the various levels between the heavens were added from the commentators, who would not burst with laughter upon hearing them? All these things are worthy of their authors and those who believe them.

But perhaps the followers of Muhammad might wish to rebuke me because I said that Muhammad gathered strength and assumed ferocity through the factions of the Jews (while he was believed to be the Messiah, or the one who would lead them back to Jerusalem). Let them hear the meaning of this passage, which the ignorant read and admire; those with a little knowledge grasp it but neglect it, and the truly learned laugh at it. He says:

> We gave the book to Moses, and we placed it as a direction for the children of Israel, so that you should not take any protector besides me. The generations of those whom we carried with Noah, the glorious servant; and we told the children of Israel in the book, that they would be corrupted on the earth twice and be exalted with great exaltation. And when these promises arrived, we sent against them our most cruel servants, and they tracked through the recesses of the dwellings, and the promise was made and fulfilled. Finally, we shall return the turn to you over them. We shall endow you with money and children, and we shall make you a great multitude. If you do well, you do well for yourselves; and you shall enter the temple, just as they entered it the first time, and you shall destroy those who exalt themselves with destruction. Perhaps your Lord will have mercy on you, and perhaps your promise is our promise: and we shall place Gehenna <note>Hell</note> as a barrier for the ungodly. Because this Quran directs the leaders for the people.

Even if that sentiment sufficiently reveals its author, nevertheless, because of that prophetic phrasing that is not accessible to everyone, I judge that it must be explained a little more broadly. He says it was written in the law of Moses that the Jews would be dispersed twice (for he understands that by *tupsidune* <note>original: "tupsidune"; likely a phonetic rendering of the Arabic *tufsidunna*, meaning "you will cause corruption," from Sura 17:4.</note>, that is, "they would be corrupted") and twice gathered—a thing which I have never read, nor do I remember seeing. But the Jews were easily going to grant this to a new Messiah, provided he had shown himself a man in restoring them rather than in plundering them.

They indeed endured several captivities: many under the Judges, one under Saul, and another under the rule of the Greeks. However, two are more famous: the captivity under Nebuchadnezzar and the one under Titus. <note>Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed the First Temple in 586 BCE; the Roman Emperor Titus destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE.</note> Muhammad, therefore, wished to make promises to those eager for revolution, whose characters he knew were prone to forming factions. He suggested that if they were willing to follow him and vent their rage with every kind of cruelty upon anyone they encountered, they would not lack a leader. For once the inner chambers of others' houses were broken open, everything would become their plunder. If they were willing to follow a leader in this matter and "do well"—by which he means to fight manfully and pillage—they would acquire for themselves great wealth and an abundance of children. Truly, this man—a self-styled prophet endowed with extreme cruelty—assumed an extraordinary title for himself so that he might capture the attention of those he addressed with such praise. Indeed, they shall never have any leader except the Antichrist, who, in the manner of Muhammad, will join together wealth and crimes of every kind under the pretext of divine authority. Such a man was each "Son of the Lie" <note>original: "Barcoziba"; referring to Simon bar Kokhba, leader of the Jewish revolt (132–136 CE). His name was punningly changed by critics from Bar Kokhba (Son of a Star) to Bar Koziba (Son of a Lie).</note> and that future leader at sea, called "another Moses" in Crete. <note>A reference to a 5th-century Jewish claimant in Crete who promised to lead followers across the sea to Israel on foot; many drowned.</note> Such a man was Muhammad.

There was also a man, shortly before these present years, who solicited Christians to join Judaism and wished to be called the "King of Tabor." <note>This likely refers to Solomon Molcho (c. 1500–1532), a Jewish mystic who, along with David Reubeni, met with world leaders. Tabor refers to Mount Tabor.</note> When he was asked what he thought of the Messiah, he answered ambiguously: <term>שלוח הוא</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Shaluach hu," meaning "He is the sent one" or "He is the messenger."</note> "perhaps you will see," asserting this of himself in the Hebrew fashion. I understand that this wicked man was sentenced to the flames by Charles of Austria, the fifth Emperor of this name, because in Spain he wished to draw many people (who were not averse to various persuasions) toward Judaism. <note>Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, oversaw the trial of Solomon Molcho, who was burned at the stake in 1532.</note> Muhammad, in this same place, also sought to capture followers with an ambiguous word: "Perhaps," he said, "your promise is our promise; perhaps God will have mercy on you and lead you back to your sacred rites, as in the past." With these ambiguous responses, he mocked that miserable nation for a decade, until his follies were exposed to the others by Ben Salone, and they gradually began to fall away. Thus, he discusses nothing more frequently than the "perfidy of the defecting Jews."

We must not neglect the title of this "prophet," since he approved of that name for himself and held it as a place of honor—a title we usually grant to impious, wicked, and nefarious tyrants. And yet (God help us!) he is a "prophet" who turns this divine virtue not against the enemies of his state, nor toward the preservation of sacred things, nor toward the care of parents, but toward the slaughter of kinsmen, the subversion of religion, and the upheaval of all things. Under such a leader, the citizens could have achieved vast dominions, and he himself could have performed great services if he had been of sound health. But since he suffered from diseases of both mind and body and was marked by the suspicion of sorcery, he plotted the ruin of his own citizens; no one would have wished to obey him without a religious fiction. From these things, his character is sufficiently known. 

However, it was not enough for him to have favored the Jews unless, to gratify them, he also attacked Christians and blasphemed against Christ. He says that God does not have female angels; that is certain. He says there are not two gods; we also constantly affirm and believe this. "Therefore, Christ is not God"—that does not follow. "God does not beget in our human manner, therefore He does not beget at all"—it is impossible for the Eternal One *not* to beget a Son from eternity, which is to say, His Word and Wisdom. Nor are there two gods because of this, because the whole divinity is in the Father, the whole in the Son, and the whole in the Holy Spirit. For to repeat an example often used for those unskilled in divine matters: the conception of any thing (for example, a house to be built) exists entirely in the mind; the same is entirely in the word and explanation; and the same is entirely in the physical building. And yet, there are not three "buildings," but one house. Thus, the most powerful God must know what is to be done and must will it before His immense power creates anything. Unless He perpetually begat the Son—just as any thing has its own duration or "offspring"—nothing would exist in the world. No form could be attached to matter unless Power bound the forms of matter, Wisdom fitted them to their proper shape, and Will preserved them in existence for a long time. But that bloody scoundrel did not grasp these things, for he cared for nothing of God except for words, his belly,

...and he proved his glory through shameful things. To the Jews seeking miracles, he says that God did not grant him miracles for this reason: that when He sent them in the past, they rejected them under a false pretext. An extraordinary evasion, and his usual trick! <note>Postel refers to the Islamic view that since earlier peoples rejected the miracles of prophets like Moses and Jesus, Muhammad was not given public signs of that nature.</note> For that matter, if some did not believe Moses at first sight before it was known whether he came from God, did no one believe him? Six hundred thousand men with their families eventually believed, for whom he organized and handed over a most peaceful republic. If the Jews did not obey Christ, who was God-in-man, was there for that reason no Christian nation? Within a hundred years of his death, without any force or bloodshed—except that of the martyrs—Christ was accepted. If, therefore, you were bringing miracles, it would not have been necessary to kill, plunder, and drive away your own citizens and brothers. If not immediately, you would have triumphed eventually like the others. 

However, I accept what he grants when he confesses that he possessed no miracles. Therefore, the "trees of defecation" <note>original: "arbores cacationis"; likely a polemical mockery of Islamic descriptions of Paradise or dietary laws</note> and the "splitting of the moon," and so on—these miracles are fables and dreams. After he has brought forward many trifles, as he does in his whole work, he says: 
> If all demons and men wished to compose a similar Quran <note>original: "Alcoranum"</note>, they could not. 
This is something I believe and concede to the man, for it seems impossible to rational animals to compose anything similar, since it is outside of reason, method, and anything other than a repetition of <term>battology</term> <note>battology: The practice of repeating words or phrases excessively to the point of being meaningless.</note>. For if it were according to God and the order of nature, and the method of the disciplines, there would be some art of imitation, as we see in the other sciences. Here, truly, there is neither order, nor light, nor any greater trace of reason than if an old woman were to repeatedly heap up mentions of the heaven and earth, man, ship, ox, milk, fruit, food, and beasts, and everywhere joined the name of God the Creator (whose name not even idolaters are ignorant of). In considering this matter, there is no peasant who is not superior to this lawgiver. Therefore, he asserts that nothing similar can be composed by anyone who might deservedly bear the name of a man. 

But hear the man’s extraordinary doctrine. 
> They will ask you, he says, about the spirit. Say: the spirit is by the command of the creator Lord, and you have but little knowledge. 
A definition worthy of such a teacher! It is as if someone were to ask, "What is a sword?" and the teacher should answer, "It is that which the one who needs it commanded to be made." By Muhammad’s definition, a dog is a spirit, and a stone is a spirit, since all things are by the command of the creator. How much better he would have distinguished it if he had said first: the Spirit of God is His efficacy in lower things, in which all things are preserved and consist; but the spirit of nature is that by which all things are animated by the command of the Creator. For if it were worth the effort to say anything based on this definition of the prophet, I would say he binds God to matter and creates himself daily. This is not the only such instance; all his sayings are similar, whence I truly think Muhammad is refuted by no one better than by himself. 

Indeed, he makes angels corporeal and subject to wounds and death, when he says: 
> They said, God sent a man as an apostle. Say: if angels remained safely on earth, we would also send angels from heaven as apostles. 
An extraordinary judgment from the man! Are substances devoid of body—except insofar as they take on a deceptive body of air—subject to the injuries of men? O good lawgiver, so well-skilled in nature (with which he was supposedly so familiar), a plain rustic <note>Postel uses "rusticum" to imply Muhammad was uneducated and lacked philosophical training.</note> who believes spirits are violable—or if he does not believe it, he writes falsely. When the tributes given to him did not seem large enough, and the Jews excused themselves on account of their poverty, he said: 
> If you possessed the treasures of my Lord’s mercy, even then you would hold them back for fear of expenses, because man is greedy.

Otherwise, regarding what he says about God giving Moses nine miracles, God actually exhibited ten before Pharaoh, and innumerable others besides.

-> Surah Al-Kahf <note>original: "Sora Elchahaph"</note>, that is, The Cave. 17. Meccan. <-

Although in this whole chapter he rises up against the divinity of Christ (as he never fails to do), he nevertheless takes from us the history of the Seven Sleepers <note>The "Seven Sleepers of Ephesus," a legend of Christian youths who hid in a cave to escape Roman persecution and awoke centuries later; the story appears in Surah 18 of the Quran.</note>, which is very widely known.

# WILLIAM POSTEL’S BOOK II
<page-num>203</page-num>

...the divinity of Jesus is evident, so that he might prove the resurrection of the dead. I will explain this story to them. 

When the Emperor Decius <note>Trajan Decius, Roman Emperor from 249 to 251 AD, known for his systematic persecution of Christians.</note> was stirring up a persecution against the Christians, there were in Ephesus seven young men, the sons of the wealthiest and most prominent citizens, who, along with many others, had given their names to Christ. Therefore, when Decius wished to be present at the execution—like a torturer thirsting for the human and innocent blood of his subjects—he took many lives through martyrdom. To these youths, however, on account of the nobility of their parents (as he said) and the consideration of their age, he granted a few months to see if they would recoil from Christ and perform sacrifices to the idols; or if they persisted, their parents should have no doubt that they would perish by unheard-of tortures as soon as he returned. When the impious emperor departed, the youths began to consider together by what arts they might deliver themselves from the power of the tyrant. Having taken some money from their parents, while they deliberated and consulted either about flight or voluntary exile, they agreed to hide in a certain cave very near to Ephesus, at the edge of Mount Mycale, for as long as it took for the fury of the wicked prince to cease. Thus, for many months, they sang praises to God. One of them, however, at fixed hours and in turns, sought the necessities of life from the city so that they might sustain their existence. 

When the emperor returned, he sought the youths for the punishment of their souls or bodies; he ordered their parents to be seized in their name, and immediately threatened them with tortures unless they produced their children—for his mind was greedy for blood. They were betrayed, the place was approached, but the youths did not come out. See what madness and the agitation of a demon can do in a man: he ordered them to be enclosed alive in the cave, and his commands were immediately obeyed. However, a certain Theodorus, a pious man who had concealed his true persuasion, inscribed their deeds, the events that transpired, and the names of their parents, along with the time and the name of the persecutor, upon leaden plates <note>original: "laminæ plumbeæ"</note>. He placed these upon the structure by which the cave was being closed in such a way that no one would notice; yet, if it were destroyed, they would be revealed. 

Thus, for a total of 181 years, they remained enclosed in the cave until the times of Theodosius <note>Theodosius II, Eastern Roman Emperor (r. 408–450 AD). During his reign, the story of the Seven Sleepers was "rediscovered."</note>. By chance, it happened that a certain citizen wished to construct a building in the nearby area and was debating how to more conveniently transport materials. The workmen said there was a certain mass not far off, like a wall, and that stone could be taken from there. He heard this, tore it down, and carried the materials away; he saw the cave but sought nothing else. Once the air was let in, the seven youths, as if awakened from sleep and being famished, sent their companion out for his usual duties. He went out, suspecting nothing of the situation, and approached Ephesus. Immediately, the new face of all things terrified the youth; he doubted whether he was dreaming or awake. Neglecting all else, one thing especially stunned him: he saw the sign of the cross—which the impious emperor had been persecuting "yesterday" (as he thought)—placed above the gates of the city. Approaching the individual gates, he found the same thing. He asked with great fear whether that city was Ephesus; they said it was. 

Meanwhile, as if he had become outside of himself, he went to the market to buy bread and side-dishes for the others and himself. No one recognized the coin he offered. Indeed, they said they would turn him in unless he gave them a share of the treasure he had found. He denied having found anything and, leaving the coin behind, wished to flee lest he be betrayed. He was captured and brought before the magistrate. He was asked where he was from; he said he was a citizen, the son of such-and-such a citizen. He brought no less wonder to everyone than he felt himself; seeing all the citizens, he recognized none of them. He referred everything to "yesterday"—even the emperor, who it was well known had died 180 years before. He said he had six companions in the cave and had come to buy food for them. Once the sacred magistrate was brought in, the miracle was recognized. The Bishop, approaching the place with almost the whole city, found everything consistent with what the youth was saying, except for the time. Indeed, entering the threshold of the cave and bringing a light, he saw the leaden tablet left by Theodorus, which bore witness to the blockage and the time. The whole circle of citizens was brought in; whoever wished spoke to the youths, and there arose a very great and palpable faith in the resurrection. Immediately, however, the Bishop and the magistrate wrote to Theodosius, who was staying in Constantinople, and summoned him to the sight of the miracle. He came, and saw with...

# THE DIVINITY OF JESUS AND THE RESURRECTION
<page-num>203</page-num>

...the divinity of Jesus is evident, so that he might prove the resurrection of the dead. I explain this story to them <note>The "them" refers to the followers of Muhammad, whom Postel is addressing in this polemic</note>. 

During the reign of Emperor Decius <note>reigned 249–251 AD; a Roman emperor known for instigating the first empire-wide persecution of Christians</note>, while he was stirring up persecution against the Christians, there were seven young men in Ephesus. They were the sons of the wealthiest and most prominent citizens, and along with many others, they had dedicated their names to Christ. Now, when Decius wished to be present at the executions—like a torturer thirsting for the human and innocent blood of his subjects—he consumed many through martyrdom. However, for these young men, on account of the nobility of their parents (as he said) and in consideration of their youth, he granted a few months' reprieve so that they might shrink back from Christ and perform sacrifices to idols. If they persisted, he warned that upon his immediate return, they would perish by unheard-of tortures. He told the parents not to doubt this. 

When the impious emperor departed, the young men began to deliberate together on what means they might use to deliver themselves from the tyrant’s power. Having taken some money from their parents, and while they were consulting about either flight or voluntary exile, they agreed to hide in a certain cave very near to Ephesus, at the edge of Mount Mycale <note>A mountain on the western coast of Ionia in Central Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey)</note>. There they would remain hidden for as long as it took for the fury of the heavenly prince to cease. Thus, for many months, they sang praises to God. One of them, however, at fixed hours and in turns, would seek out the necessary provisions from the city so that they might sustain their lives. 

When the emperor returned, he sought the young men for punishment or death. He ordered their parents to be seized in their name, and immediately threatened them with tortures unless they surrendered their children; for as his mind was greedy for blood, he was ready to inflict it. They were betrayed. The location was approached, but the youths did not come out. 

See what madness and the agitation of a demon can do in a man: He ordered them to be walled up alive in the cave, and his commands were immediately obeyed. However, a certain man named Theodore, a pious man who had hidden his true convictions, inscribed their deeds, their history, and the names of their parents—along with the date and the name of the persecutor—on lead plates <note>original: "laminæ plumbeæ"</note>. He placed these within the structure by which the cave was being closed in such a way that no one would notice; yet, if it were ever torn down, they would be revealed. 

Thus, for a total of 181 years, they remained enclosed in the cave until the time of Theodosius <note>Postel likely refers to Theodosius II, who reigned 408–450 AD</note>. By a stroke of fortune, it happened that a certain citizen wished to construct a building in that nearby location. While he was considering how to more conveniently transport materials, his workmen mentioned that not far away there was a certain mass, like a wall, from which stone could be taken. He heard this, tore it down, and carried the stone away. He saw the cave but sought nothing else. 

Once air was admitted, the seven young men—as if awakened from sleep and feeling famished—sent their companion out for his usual duties. He went out, suspecting nothing of what had happened, and approached Ephesus. Immediately, the new appearance of all things terrified the youth. He doubted whether he was asleep or awake; but neglecting all else, one thing especially stunned him: he saw the sign of the cross <note>original: "signum crucis"</note> placed above the city gates—a sign which the impious emperor had been persecuting only yesterday (as he thought). Approaching each gate, he encountered the same thing. He asked with great fear whether this city was Ephesus; they said it was. 

Meanwhile, as if he were outside of himself, he went to the market to buy bread and side-dishes for the others and himself. No one recognized the coinage he offered. Indeed, they said they would turn him in unless he gave them a portion of the treasure he had found; he denied having found anything. Leaving the money behind, he tried to flee so as not to be betrayed. He was captured and brought before a magistrate. He was asked where he was from; he said he was a citizen, the son of a citizen of such-a-name. This brought no less wonder to the officials than he felt within himself; seeing all the citizens, he recognized no one. He referred everything back to "yesterday"—even the emperor, who it was well known had died 180 years prior. 

He said he had six companions in the cave and had come to buy food for them. Once the sacred magistrate was brought in, the miracle was recognized. The Bishop, along with almost the entire city, went to the location and found everything consistent with what the youth had said, except for the matter of time. Entering the threshold of the cave with a light, he saw the lead tablet left by Theodore, which provided proof of the walling-up and the date. A whole circle of citizens was admitted, and whoever wished spoke to the young men. This became a most great and palpable proof of the resurrection. Immediately, the Bishop and the magistrate wrote to Theodosius, who was then in Constantinople, and summoned him to witness the miracle. He came and saw with...

...to the whole clergy, he addresses them, encourages them, and immediately the young men die. When the Emperor <note>Theodosius II, who reigned during the discovery of the Sleepers</note> wished to build a massive temple for them in that place and adorn it with much gold, he was warned by the spirit of one of them in a dream not to do so. He was told he should consider it enough that the Creator had provided, through them, the most certain evidence of the faith in the resurrection, in order to refute the many heretics who were then doubting it. These are the main points of the history, which Muhammad does not handle with the purity of the sacred accounts; for he everywhere fabricates something of his own. For instance, he brings a dog <note>In the Quran (Sura 18), a dog named Qitmir is said to have guarded the entrance of the cave</note> along with them, so that we might believe in the resurrection of dogs along with him. For he places the bodies of certain animals in heaven along with his <term>Al-Buraq</term> <note>original: "Alborach"; the celestial steed that, according to Islamic tradition, carried Muhammad from Mecca to Jerusalem and through the heavens</note>. Those wretched people believe that God will gather the spirits of all animals together with the spirits of men at the resurrection; no blasphemy can be given that is more impious than this. 

Furthermore, those young men suffered these things for the sake of the crucified Jesus Christ, and they did not set up any "partner" with God, since he himself is that one same God, as well as Father and Spirit, as I have often taught. I do not wish to say anything of the paradises of Eden, except that in addition to the higher things, there come golden bracelets, and green garments of silk and fine linen, and reclining upon cushions in a good mansion, and so forth—so that, according to Muhammad, the life of the soul and the body is the same. Moreover, regarding the parable he proposes of the rich and the poor man, saying that the poor man without wealth enters paradise more easily than the rich man—who wished to despoil everyone and amass such great power—he did that, in my judgment, out of "charity": so that when he had stripped everyone of their possessions, they might seek paradise more expeditiously, while he himself might take up everyone’s burdens <note>Postel is being sarcastic here, suggesting Muhammad impoverished his followers for his own gain under the guise of helping them get to heaven</note>. 

I will not speak of God, Adam, and the devil. For I have often shown that he makes God the author of idolatry. Who could recount how many fables he attaches to Moses, concerning the boy and the fish? Those things are entirely foreign to the sacred scriptures and will refute themselves. Those fables and parables which he weaves into the history of Moses are allegorical, and are not sufficiently known to me. But they seem to deal with an orphan whom a father despoiled of his paternal estate and house in <term>Yathrib</term> <note>original: "Iezraba"; the ancient name for the city of Medina</note>, a crime than which none is more foul.

As for the claim that John <note>the Baptist</note> had a "book"—that is, the Law—it is false, for he was the herald of Christ.
