## GUILLAUME POSTEL’S BOOK II.

...I am the servant of God; God has given me a book and made me a prophet, and made me blessed. I fear because I have been made so, and he commanded me to perform prayers and give tithes as long as I remain alive, and to cherish my mother; and he did not make me headstrong or laborious. Peace be upon the day I was born, the day I shall die, and the day I shall remain alive. This is Jesus, son of Mary, the word of truth, about whom they doubt. God did not take a son; praise be to Him. <note>Postel is quoting from the Quran, Sura Maryam (19:30–35), which describes the infant Jesus speaking from the cradle.</note> He fabricated all those things for the sake of the final period of time. I have already demonstrated many times that it is impossible for God to create or restore anything except through the Son. Indeed, he creates all things in God the Son; he restores all things in the Son as the <term>God-man</term> <note>original: "θεανθρώπῳ" (theanthrōpō)</note>, which I proved at length in the previous book. But the individual lies offered by the prophet’s <term>Spatharii</term> <note>Postel often uses this term—originally referring to Byzantine guards—to describe those he believed influenced or edited Muhammad’s revelations</note> must be shaken out. When did Mary ever withdraw from her parents, since the Gospels never speak of it? That is already one lie. For she was carefully educated, partly in the temple and partly at home with her parents, until the coming of the Holy Spirit and until she was married to Joseph. The custom of veiling virgins had not yet arrived among the Jews, which is why this also was made up. He says the Holy Spirit was sent instead of an angel, so that he might seem to make him a creature—impiously indeed—though he arrived by an angel being sent. If he makes the Holy Spirit a messenger, no one can distinguish them. Furthermore, after she conceived, she did not withdraw from the house until they went to Bethlehem to register their names.

Where is that palm tree trunk? Pious Muslims, speaking to our people, say that this palm lived again and lasted until our own memory. We do not need lying miracles; we have it written otherwise, we receive it, and we believe it. The claims that she wished for death, and that the infant spoke to her, etc., are fabrications—granted to us, as it were, so that by believing them, we might deny God. Where was she commanded concerning prayers and tithes? These are all lies of the Spatharii and of a dreamer. Now, who does not see that the Spatharii imposed upon this prophet an error of 1,500 years? For Mary the mother of Christ is far removed from Mary the sister of Moses and Aaron; and this, if the gods please, is no small lie. <note>Postel identifies a famous chronological critique: the Quranic address to Mary as "Sister of Aaron," which Christian polemicists argued confused Mary with Miriam from the Book of Exodus.</note> May the man perish wretchedly with his trifles. As for the rest: he was not satisfied to say that demons are made of fire, and that they were created evil and stupid, but he must also claim they are mortal. For he says they will die on the day of judgment and finally live again; no lie is more false than this. For since they lack a body and can be nothing other than spirits, why would they die? Since they do not have corruptible matter that can be cut away. That would be done in vain, which never happens by God's authority.

### 19. Ta-Ha <note>original: "Theh."; likely referring to Sura 20 of the Quran.</note>

In reciting the history of Moses, he adds fabrications everywhere with his commentaries; at one moment he says Moses was raised by his sister, at another by Pharaoh's wife, whereas the sacred texts say he was raised by the daughter. He sets a date for the Passover so that the magicians might come against Moses, though there was no Passover yet, for it was instituted after the crossing of the Red Sea. Moses, as if holding the legal right of the province, says he will hang the magicians from a palm trunk after their hands have been cut off. Furthermore, he calls Aaron a "Samaritan"; for what reason, I do not know. <note>Postel is likely referring to the "Samiri" mentioned in Sura 20, who is associated with the Golden Calf.</note> Finally, Moses seizes him by the hair and beard. Moreover, he does not wish to publish the Quran until he completes it, which never happened before his death, as I have already said, lest he be proven false. Finally, he says the demon showed the Tree of Life to Adam, as if God had not shown it. As a punishment for impiety, he says God will raise the impious as blind. Lastly, since he snatched from everyone by right or wrong, he says he seeks no reward, so that he might cover his vices; he says things contrary to his deeds, etc.

### 20. The Prophets <note>original: "Prophetæ"; referring to Sura 21, Al-Anbiya.</note>

He heaps up ravings, weaving fables in his usual manner, so that he might elude those who said that a man similar to others, distinguished by no prophecy, had fabricated and dreamed these things. He concludes that others were prophets before him, and therefore he is one too. He claims the Quran and the <term>Criterion</term> <note>original: "Alphurcanū" (Al-Furqan)</note> were given to Moses and Abraham, which we have previously shown to be false. He fabricates fables about David and Solomon. He claims God taught judgment concerning the vineyard and the sheep, which things are clear by the account...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...[col]lations of the emperors <note>This likely refers to the transmission or collection of historical records.</note> he held these things. For nothing is intact. He wishes, I think, to speak of Nathan’s admonition and the proposition of the two men, one of whom had ninety-nine sheep, and from the one who had only one, he took it away, etc. <note>A reference to the parable in 2 Samuel 12 used by the prophet Nathan to rebuke King David for taking Bathsheba.</note> As for the vineyard, I do not know what he was dreaming of. That power over the winds and demons granted to Solomon, I do not recall in the sacred scriptures, much less the craft of a smith. <note>Postel is noting that the Quranic depiction of Solomon as a commander of winds and jinns (demons) does not appear in the Hebrew Bible.</note> He numbers Enoch, Job, and the others along with Ishmael, so that the impious might seem to be in pious company. 21. Elhegh <note>original: "Elhegh," referring to *Al-Hajj*, the Islamic pilgrimage.</note>. That is the pilgrimage, usually performed for four months in the year to Mecca, in memory of Abraham and his sacrifice. Therefore, he established certain things there conforming to idolatry, and he is, so to speak, similar everywhere. It has already been refuted that Abraham was ever in the "ancient house" <note>Referring to the Kaaba in Mecca.</note>; therefore, I do not linger. Muminine <note>original: "Muminine," from the Arabic *Mu’minin*, meaning "the believers."</note>, that is, the faithful. 22.

Because he had been caught in adultery by his wives with a young Jewish girl whom <term>Bahyras</term> <note>Bahira, a monk who in Christian polemic is often depicted as Muhammad’s secret mentor.</note> had given him, and he had committed perjury, having been bound under the name of God in faith to his wives: therefore he sets down a law here by which the same is permitted to all followers as to himself, lest the vice should be seen in him, since it would be permitted in all—as if a hundred thousand men sinning would be less of a sin than one man alone. For if it is an unjust thing to commit adultery and not to render the debt to a wife, which nature has taught, then beyond a doubt it could not become lawful by the law and promise of this prophet. I wish now to explain this deed a little more extensively, so that everyone may be able to weigh what is contained in that "Chapter of the Faithful" and look deeply into this "faithfulness." For this chapter, and the one following, will greatly reveal this prophet to us. I shall begin the matter more deeply, from the start.

When this prophet began to travel through the neighboring countryside and villages of Mecca for the sake of preaching—having already contracted alliances with great citizens and being accompanied by a large crowd—he won over and reconciled the neighboring minor rulers as best he could, either by love or by terror. Among the others was a certain man on the borders of Arabia named Bahyras, who presided over a flock of heretical <term>Jacobites</term> <note>A Monophysite Christian sect from the Middle East.</note>. Since he was otherwise hostile to the rest of the Christians, if any were nearby, he held nothing more important than that "like should be joined to like," so that, according to the proverb, "similar lips might have similar lettuce." <note>A Latin proverb meaning "like to like" or "a matching pair," often used derisively.</note> A heretic cherishes and embraces a heretic and the impious; all the lost souls and those accused of violating religion fled to Bahyras. Indeed, <term>Muhamedes</term> gathered to himself a dreg-heap of all the lost souls and those eager for revolution. Among the other gifts with which this prophet was endowed, Bahyras chose one most suitable for the man: although he was fifty years old, he chose a girl of elegant form, fifteen years of age, named <term>Marina</term> <note>Likely referring to Maria the Copt, though Postel identifies her as Jewish here.</note>, and gave her as a gift to Muhammad as a <note>original: "μνημόσυνον" (mnēmosynon), a memorial or token</note> of their alliance. Having received her, the master immediately began to fall desperately in love with her, although he had already taken as wives three or four very wealthy Jews and the daughters of the most famous citizens of Mecca, up to fifteen in number, as I have said. The girl tried for a long time to protect her modesty, but finally she succumbed to the prophet’s favors, partly by her master's command and partly by prayers and payment. But the matter did not turn out quite happily or "prophetically." For the two most noble and beloved wives he had, <term>Hassa</term> daughter of <term>Ubecharus</term> <note>Likely Aisha, daughter of Abu Bakr.</note>, and <term>Hafeza</term> daughter of <term>Humarus</term> <note>Hafsa, daughter of Umar.</note>, caught the man with the young girl and rebuked him sharply. They threatened that they would complain to their parents, petition the judges for a divorce, and defame him among all the believers. Terrified by these things, the prophet, as a suppliant with tears, prostrated himself at his wives' knees, swearing he would never commit such a thing in the future, and that he had been overcome by the violence of love. He invoked God, the law, and an angel as a sworn oath that if he ever committed such a thing again, he would fear no punishment. He was urged by a greater fear of them than of others, because he had obtained vast wealth from their dowries and the greatest favors from their parents; all of which he would lose if they left the man. The women, being not at all wicked, accepted his oaths.

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK II.

...they spared the man, yet in such a way that if he committed the act only once more afterward, he should hope for no mercy: they told him the man and the law were finished, and they would betray and ruin everything. For several days he commands his lust, held back by religion, or rather by the fear of the women; finally, committing the same crime, he is caught by them. They depart, defame him, and betray as much as they knew of the secret mysteries: that the man was an impostor, impure, driven by demons and furies, who feigned divine conversations, took everything good he had from other laws, and they left nothing of the scoundrel's arts unexposed. By these things he was brought almost to the point of despairing of everything, until, coming to his senses, in order to retain the minds of the multitude, he proposes this law, which is at the head of this Sura <note>Postel is referring to Sura 23, "Al-Mu'minun" (The Believers).</note>.

This is the law, this is the cause. Blessed are those who rush into crime and wickedness in the manner of the prophet, who not only frequent their wives but even slaves of any kind—for he writes indefinitely. Nor is there in the <term>original text</term> <note>original: "autographo"</note> of the law the word for "handmaid," but *eu ma melecheta aimanuchum* <note>Postel’s transliteration of the Arabic *aw ma malakat aymanukum*, usually translated as "or those whom your right hands possess," referring to captives or slaves.</note>, that is, or "what your faith has acquired"—that is, what the crowd of the faithful has seized, gained, or acquired under the pretext of faith, in which number are captives and male servants, no less than bondwomen and handmaids. Unless he had understood it thus, he could have used the word *amet* <note>original: "amet," referring to the Arabic *amah*, meaning a female slave.</note>, which signifies a handmaid. But he wished to establish a broad law, in which not only a recently admitted crime would be permitted, but—what is worst of all—it would be granted and made praiseworthy for everyone. 

O men captured in sense! Do the deceptive interpreters mock you so that you do not understand these things, written by the authority of an evil demon? That law confirms those which I brought forward earlier regarding pederasty. This law was prepared for this purpose: so that all things might be permitted under its name which are otherwise prohibited by divine, natural, and restored law. An excellent faith, and worthy of its author. How shameful this author is in his writing, I do not say: he uses his own words, and is everywhere accustomed to using foul and intentionally sought-after terms for the secret and reproductive nature in both men and women and beasts, and for the actions themselves. 

But it is no wonder: since, willing and seeing, he permitted the adulteries of even his own wives, from which one may detect an argument for a low mind, born only for frauds and impostures. Therefore, having captivated his followers with such a sweet and benevolent law, the prophets <note>Postel likely uses the plural here to imply Muhammad and his inner circle of collaborators.</note> not only pardoned what he had now made lawful by the authority of God, but even blamed the wives because they had rebuked in the prophet that which was so pleasant and good. The parents also, having calmed the women’s minds, persuaded the wives to return to the prophet’s house and to obey him in all things. For it had been revealed to him from heaven that what they had thought was a sin was not a sin. The wondering women said nothing else to their parents except that this prophet must be a very great friend of God, whom God loved so much that He complied with all his desires. 

Abu Bakr <note>original: "Vbecharus"</note> and Umar <note>original: "Homarus"</note>, and others privy to the story, imposed silence on the wives, not because they cared for Muhammad or his trifles, but because that matter seemed to pertain most to them. For when they gave the wealthiest and most beautiful virgins as wives to the mad and criminal <note>original: "fontico," likely a typo for *fontico* (source-like) or *fontico* as a derivative of *fons/fontis*, but in this polemical context, it often implies a "fount of evil."</note> prophet, it was done so that, having acquired that power, matters would come to them after the prophet's death. Therefore the scandal was more easily settled, with few understanding the tricks, and those especially pretending to believe, so that at last that rustic and plebeian crowd, when it saw that the great men were not moved by that scandal but saw them believing the revelations, might willingly acquiesce and not desert him. Indeed, he was very frequently reproached from that time even...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...by the unlearned, which he repeats throughout the chapter: That he sought nothing else but empire, and that he added nothing to divine precepts but commentaries and trifles, practicing an old trick; that a man possessed by demons <note>original: "dæmonijs agitatū"</note> could not enjoy any familiarity with God; and if he possessed anything good, it was from the ancient scriptures, not revelation. Moved by these arguments, he [Muhammad] says it was revealed to him by an oracle that he should leave everyone for a time in their foolishness. For he claims they do not consider that they might more quickly obtain wealth and children from his path—as if that were true, or as if those things were the reward of the good in this life. Truly, he held those who were superstitious, unlearned, and forgetful of past events—and who used no comparison of things—with ambiguous and uncertain promises, as if they would be happier under one tyrant than under another. The scoundrel <note>original: "nebulo"</note> knew that wretched men, pressed by calamities and frequent injury and plunder, are refreshed more by even a small breathing room than they were by great wealth before their afflictions. Therefore, new instances of happiness, however modest, seem equal to the most joyful things after times of adversity. I do not repeat here the blasphemies against Christ and God, which I have more than once refuted. I proceed to the rest.

->Elnor <note>An-Nur, "The Light." Though Postel labels this as chapter 23, it corresponds to Sura 24 in modern numbering.</note>, that is, the Light, 23, written at Medina.<-

Just as we saw such "faithfulness" in the head of the faithful, so we shall see such "light" in this smoke: for just as the man’s wickedness was clear in the preceding chapter, so it will reveal itself in this one and illuminate its author. He says:
> We sent the Sura <note>A chapter of the Quran.</note>, and we explained it, and we sent in it miracles of wisdom, if perhaps you might remember. Let the female fornicator and the male fornicator each be struck with 100 lashes: and do not take mercy on them in the law of God, if you believe in God and the last day, and let some of the faithful be present at their punishment; let the fornicator not contract [marriage], etc.

These things refer to the reason for the acts committed above: that God therefore permitted many wives, maidservants, and male favorites <note>original: "catamitos," though Postel’s interpretation of the Quranic text here is highly polemical and deviates from standard Islamic law.</note> so that they would not commit adultery; and if anyone did commit it, the punishments would be such as are described here. Yet before this law, there was a paternal custom and habit that a man should not know any woman other than his wife, not even a maidservant; for it would not have been a vice if it had already been permitted before. Truly, the law he established, he never kept. For Aisha <note>original: "Assa"</note>, the daughter of Abu Bakr <note>original: "Vbechari"</note>, whom he held most dear, was openly accustomed to many lovers. For this reason, he was warned by many that he should at least repudiate her, saying it was quite shameful for the primary woman of the prophet to act so publicly as a harlot. To them, he said nothing else but that she was his most beloved, and therefore he would not repudiate her. The lazy scoundrel placed no honor before his eyes, so long as he could seize tyranny. When he took her as a wife and deflowered her at eight years old (as I said), he "sold the empire," as Plautus says, and "possessed a dowry rather than a wife." And yet, the sacrosanct faith of the Quran and the exposition of prophetic deeds depend on the report of a public harlot, the wife and daughter of a tyrant, nor is anything more holy than that "faith." For her opinion is called *dhache tzahh* <note>original: "dhache tzahh," a corruption of "Hadith Sahih," meaning an authentic prophetic tradition.</note>, that is, "this is certain and complete." And she, who would not be admitted to testimony in secular judgments due to her infamy, brings authority to divine law. The crime of that harlot excited the greatest dissension among his successors, from which the faction of Ali <note>original: "Halí"</note> and Abu Bakr began, through which many myriads of men perished and thirty caliphs <note>original: "chaliphæ"</note> were subsequently destroyed.

But these things were not established for the sake of women, but for the sake of the prophet and his wives. For by whatever law a husband is not permitted to falsely accuse his wife of adultery without the proof of four witnesses, by that same law it was not permitted for the prophet's wives—who did not have four witnesses—to accuse him of adultery, as if...

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK II.

...since the law had already been established, everything points to this: although it is permitted to take legal action against slaves, so that if by chance one were caught with another woman, she could not be accused. And let him not be admitted, he says, as a witness, who has falsely accused. How much greater punishment was Hassa <note>Postel likely refers here to Hafsa or Aisha, Muhammad's wives. Aisha was the primary figure in the "Affair of the Slander" described in Sura 24.</note>, the restorer of the Quran, worthy of? If someone who falsely accuses of adultery is marked with such infamy, how much more worthy of punishment is the one who commits it? These things must be weighed.

> And meanwhile, if he repents and does good, he who was infamous, God is pious and merciful.

He says this so that no one pays a penalty:

> For who, when dragged to punishment, does not repent and do well, if he is believed?

Certainly any impious, unjust, and guilty person becomes pious, just, and innocent in words when pressed; and if pressured further, in deeds; therefore, if you remit the punishments to God, there will never be any.

> But if, he says, he cannot prove it except by himself, one witness is enough, provided that in four attestations he says: "By God, I am among the faithful." And fifthly, the curse of God be upon him if he is a liar. And they shall remit the punishment to her (the woman) if she testifies in turn four times that her husband is a liar, and fifthly that the wrath of God be upon her if her husband is truthful. And unless God were kind to you and His mercy, and certainly God is a wise turner <note>Referring to God turning toward man in repentance.</note>.

See how he makes a way for perjuries while he places the proof in an oath, since nothing is more common than an oath among the Muslims <note>original: "Mussulmanos"</note>, and meanwhile it goes to nothing while the woman denies the charges with contrary oaths, so that the judge's time is wasted in vain. But I come to other things which are relevant.

> Have you not heard the good opinion of believing men and women among themselves when they said, "This is a manifest fiction"? Did they not come to him with four witnesses? And because they did not come with witnesses, they are liars in the sight of God. And unless God, etc.

You see the mysteries betrayed; therefore he wants his wives and domestics to be held by the law now established, after they had opened up secrets. Nor does adultery trouble him so much—which had already begun to be made legitimate by the preceding law—as much as the fact that they had said the law was a fiction and a trick. For his followers rightly believed them, as if they were privy to the prophetic secret; hence he bears this most annoyingly, and would want them to have proven with four witnesses that it was a fiction, when it was already obvious even to the blind and the barbers <note>original: "lippis & tonsoribus"—a Latin idiom meaning "everyone knows it."</note>. For already it has been objected to him a hundred times, and he did not demand four witnesses: but to be betrayed by those of his own house is an argument for the truth, therefore four witnesses are needed. I continue.

> And when you were slandering with your tongues, and saying with your mouth that in which you had no knowledge, and thinking it a light thing which in the sight of God is great; rather, when you heard it, you ought to have said about it: "May it not happen to us that we speak of this, far be it, this is a great sin."

How can it be that this prophet so fears the tongues of his servants and friends (for so he calls the *believers*, both men and women <note>original: "muminīn & muminet", from Arabic mu'minin and mu'minat.</note>)? He wants to be so religiously worshipped and admired that it is not even permitted to speak of them? Truly he must be worse than bandits and any other lost souls, since all his household are a fear to him. How does it happen that if he is a prophet of God, he does not send down divine fire upon the seditious, like another Moses? Does he not devote them to destruction like Dathan and Abiram, or punish them with leprosy like the sister Miriam? Moses did not need to repeat so often, "I am a prophet of God," as if there were nothing else in his law. It was not necessary to iterate a thousand times: "They say you are making these things up, you are driven by a demon, insane, and other vices." Since no similar suspicion fell upon Moses and the prophets. Therefore, when so many types of wickedness were thrown at you by the voices of all, it was impossible for you to be innocent. For the voice of the people in exposing crimes is the voice of God. In none of the true prophets will you find that he asserted this about himself three or four times. They held it sufficient to have brought forth the divine message, whether the listeners believed or did not believe; but you wanted to join those Jews, or Christians, or heathens to yourself. Therefore, because of your crimes and vices, [it was] opened to all...

...[it] had so often to be invented, lied about, and excused. This is the true sense. Furthermore, it was no sin to speak of the law of Moses or of Christ; their teachings were set before everyone, and there was no sin in discussing them. But the interpreter Al-Bukhari <note>Original: "Buhatias." Likely a reference to Muhammad al-Bukhari, the famous collector of Hadith.</note> will say that he is not referring to the Law, but to the more secret matters of the prophet. I understand: it was not fitting for Aisha <note>Original: "Assam." It was not for her and Hafsa <note>Original: "Hafezæ." But great grief drew those things out of the women. They could have remained silent until the injury compelled them to blurt out what they knew. If you had not believed it, they would not have confirmed what even external peasants suspected, believed, and objected to. 

> God forbids you from returning to the like of this forever, if you are believers. <note>Quoting Sura 24:17.</note>

What he fears, and sees to be true, he forbids by God’s authority to be uttered: in this way, God was favorable to him. And likewise: 

> Indeed, those who desire that scandal should be publicized among those who believe shall have a great punishment in this world and in the next; and God knows what you do not understand. <note>Quoting Sura 24:19.</note>

Now forced, he calls it a "crime": but he says God is the avenger if anyone wishes to spread it. O good prophet, what punishment does he deserve who speaks the truth among the faithful? Do you wish to lie, then? Your power would have perished immediately if "holy simplicity" <note>An ironic term for the uncritical faith of the masses.</note> had known you as a criminal, an impostor, an adulterer, a guilty man, a maniac, and a madman. For you do not fear the others. It is strange that the God whom those faithful serve—who are conscious of your affairs—would wish to entrust anything to them that he would not want to share with others. O destructive plague! Did you not believe that these things could become known to posterity? God took care of those things, clearly, so that if He knew a man like Muhammad, He would speak out and immediately hurl lightning bolts at him or her. Meanwhile, as if doing something else, he interjects about alms <note>term: "eleemosyna" (alms/charity). These are the bandits by whom all Asia and Africa have been shaken, so that now one cannot pass safely except with a large escort—worthy of alms indeed! For they beg in such a way that if you do not give, they seize it themselves. I have sometimes seen on the shores of Asia that plague of men begging in such a way that no house, no hearth was safe from them if you did not give what they demanded. But to the point. 

> O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own until you have knocked and greeted the inhabitants with peace; this is good for you, if perhaps you take heed. And if you find no one in them, do not enter until permission is given to you. He still fears being caught in his crime; this is the reason for the law, a cause worthy of its author. As for his prescribing to which persons women should show their beauty—who would not laugh at such a meticulous legislator? The dictate of nature and reason has taught this in a far more honorable way than this law. What if they are ugly? They will be able to show themselves to no one. But "beauty" is a broad term. It can be shown in such a place that it is not even safe to show to a father or a son. Faith and honesty are needed in this matter, not law. 

Indeed, few know where the command that girls should not be forced into chastity leads. Since it was turned into a reproach and a mark of extreme lack of self-control for the prophet—that he loved Mariya so uncontrollably and had "tasted" Aisha in her eighth year of age—in order that it might not be a vice, he wants it to be permitted for girls of that age to seek husbands. This is the true sense. For those Suras <note>Original: "Asuar." A Latinization of the Arabic 'Suwar' (chapters).</note> are excuses and laws concerning the prophet's wives. ->**Al-Furqan 24**<- <note>Original: "Alphurcan." This refers to Sura 25, titled Al-Furqan (The Criterion). Postel’s numbering (24) likely reflects the Latin translation by Robert of Ketton or a specific manuscript tradition he was using.</note>

He begins immediately with blasphemies against God and Christ, claiming that God did not beget a son. Now, I have very frequently proven to this pestilence <note>Postel uses "pestis" (pestilence/plague) as a derogatory term for Islam or the Quranic doctrine.</note> that it is entirely impossible for anything in the whole nature of things to subsist, unless God from eternity created a son out of himself. Among all nations, it is agreed that there is one first infinite cause; however, no matter how powerful it may be, unless that same cause is also most wise and benevolent, it can create nothing at all. Nor is it enough to have used such wisdom in the first creation of things, unless that same wisdom—insofar as this life lasts, that is, generation and corruption—disposes, rules, and preserves in being whatever things exist in the nature of things. That wisdom we call the Son of God and the Word. In power is the whole divinity; in wisdom is the whole divinity; in benevolence is the whole divinity; yet there are not three divinities, but one divinity. Just as in the thought of a thing the whole thing exists, and in the word and explanation the whole thing exists, and in the completion of the work the whole thing exists; yet there are not three things, but one thing. For the sake of those men whom this plague has fascinated, I frequently repeat these things, so that they may cease from blasphemy against God and his Christ. Therefore, Christ, the son of Mary, is the wisdom of the Father, begotten from eternity. But when it seemed good to the divinity, that same Wisdom joined to itself our flesh from a virgin, and God was made man; against whom this lost scoundrel <note>Referring to Muhammad.</note> rose up for the sake of comparing his own power. But the truth of the Lord remains forever. Finally, he brings up the objections usually made against him: that [the Quran] is a fiction, and that others provided him with assistance—which is well known regarding the Jews. For they promoted him into their own persuasion when he was an idolater, and bound him to them by initiating him through marriages. For a Jewish woman would rather die than marry a man of a foreign persuasion even today. But he married not one, but four or five very wealthy ones. The teachers who armed him against Christ were Abdalla ben Salom <note>Abdullah ibn Salam, a companion of Muhammad and former rabbi.</note>, whom he used as a secretary, and whom he finally took care to have killed deceitfully while sleeping in his bed; the second was Nehabanus, son of Mahania; the third was Chabinanus, who were leaders of the synagogues. Countless others joined them and instructed the man for a decade, until, withdrawing from him, they left the impure man behind. He also used the labor of neighboring Christians, whom I have often called by the name of **Spatharians** <note>A term Postel uses elsewhere to refer to a specific sect or perhaps the "sword-bearers" (from Greek *spatharios*), here likely implying heretical Christian informants.</note>, from whom he drank in everything distorted and mangled. ...a certain Nestorian hermit, who told him many other things, but most importantly the story of the **Seven Sleepers** <note>original: "dormientiū"; a popular legend about a group of youths who hid in a cave to escape religious persecution and slept for centuries as a sign of the resurrection</note> to provide a manifest faith in the resurrection. Gabriel was there in Medina, just as the Jews were in Mecca. In those histories of the prophets which the Caliph Merbas <note>likely referring to a Caliph such as Marwan II, though the name is corrupted here</note> drowned in the river, it was also noted that shortly before the death of Muhammad, the Jews wished to elevate Ali—the nephew of this prophet and a very young man—as a prophet. While Ali was incautiously searching for a cave suitable for his faction, he found Muhammad in a cavern with the Nestorian monk. Thus, it became open what everyone had suspected: that he sought a teacher from somewhere other than an angelic spirit. Therefore, the scoundrel <term>nebulo</term> <note>a Latin term for a worthless person or rascal</note> feared in a marvelous way lest his tricks be uncovered. He busied himself with winning over the young man with great gifts; however, he could not prevent the matter from being betrayed. He countered this in this place and many others by bringing nothing but divine threats, saying that those who spoke such things were injurious. In this way, the deception <term>fucus</term> <note>literally "dye" or "paint," used here to mean a false pretense</note> revealed itself. Concerning **Sergius the Nestorian** <note>a figure frequently cited in medieval Christian polemics as a monk who supposedly assisted Muhammad in writing the Quran</note>, it was common knowledge to all. Indeed, all those things have been erased from their histories, nor can they be proven except by the commentaries of the **Sunnah** <note>original: "Suneh"; the body of traditional Islamic law and practice</note>. He proceeds to threaten those who said he was nothing but insane, or that he received what he dictated daily, evening and morning, from elsewhere. They argued that if he had an angel, the angel ought to see to it that he no longer lived off of others. Finally, as if he were a prophet, he says it is no wonder if he and the Quran are opposed, for all prophets had adversaries. But if someone is a prophet simply because they have adversaries, then thieves, murderers, plunderers, the impious, sorcerers, and other wicked men are among the prophets; for they all have the good, the laws, and the judges as hostile and infested enemies, since they plot their destruction. That Muhammad was a prophet in this way, no one denies, and he left this confirmed by many arguments. The rest are the usual repetitions.

### 25. The Chapter of Poetry. <note>referring to Sura 25, "Al-Furqan" (The Criterion), or possibly Sura 26, "Ash-Shu'ara" (The Poets)</note>

Since he mixes nothing but falsehoods with truths, adding many lies and "old wives' tales" of Arabia to the histories of the Old Testament, and recites his usual miracles and blasphemies (already refuted above), I shall write nothing further on this section.

### 26. The Chapter of the Ant. <note>Sura 27, "An-Naml"</note>

He patronizes himself and applauds his own vices when he depicts Moses seeking fire from a bush <margin>”</margin> and God calling him to Himself without fear. *For my messengers are none but those who have sinned; then if they are converted, God is merciful and pious.* For although he [Muhammad] was most defiled by every stain of vice, he nevertheless claimed God was favorable and familiar to him, and that vices did not stand in the way of piety and prophecy. Then he joins a lie to the sacred history, claiming that Moses came to Pharaoh with eight miracles; whereas he said nine before, and in both there is a lie, as there were ten. Then, fashioning a fable about Solomon, he says: *And Solomon succeeded David and said: "O men, we have been taught the speech of birds, and we have been given all things, for this is a distinguished benefit." And the cohorts of demons, men, and birds were summoned by Solomon, and they assembled until they came to the river of the ant.* The ant said: *“O ants, enter into your dwellings lest Solomon and his cohorts seize you, for they will not spare you.”* And a clamor was raised by their voices, and he [Solomon] said: *“Teach me so that I may praise You for Your benefit, with which You have benefited me and my father, so that I may do good,”* etc. Who can bear to hear such nonsense? But those things are nothing compared to the hoopoe bird <term>upupa</term>, and its conversation, embassy, and preaching. Let whoever wishes look at those absurdities with which he mocks God and men. Nothing more insane or delirious can be found; and yet this law is said to be from God and divine. I remain silent on the horrendous nonsense regarding the throne, the **Queen of Sheba**, and the servitude of demons: all of which...

That Moses was thrown into the sea is false. They were sending those to be killed into the river Nile, from where he was taken up and raised by the daughter of Pharaoh. ->28. The Spider.<-

There is nothing more worthy of its author in this chapter than the fact that he promises a future resurrection for all living things, so that not only animals but even inanimate creatures shall be eternal. If miracles are with God alone, and some prophets possessed them, then they were close to God. However, since you <note>Muhammad</note> have none, you are a stranger to God. Therefore, the miracles of the wolves, the Buraq, the tree trunks, the moon, and the heart <note>references to various Islamic miracles/traditions</note> were not true but false, because you are not God. I skip over several chapters here, very similar to the others, so that I may come to more noteworthy things at the 32nd **Sora** <note>Surah</note>, which opens to us many famous crimes of the prophet.

**Elagzab.** <note>Surah Al-Ahzab, "The Confederates"</note> First, it must be seen how, when he violently invaded the property and inheritances of others in **Medina** and expelled the Jews and other inhabitants, so that they were forced to seek help from their kinsmen, it is hinted at in these words:

By these words and those following, he claimed he had a right to their property because they would not submit to his persuasion. He expelled the wretched Jews and Christians living in **Iezrab** <note>Yathrib/Medina</note> from their homes on the pretext that there was a "disease in their hearts." Such was the "equity" of the prophet. Those wretched Jews were indeed persuading many followers to leave the prophet and return to their own affairs so they wouldn't be crushed by the mob. ...a certain Nestorian hermit <note>A reference to Bahira, the monk who, in Christian polemics, was often claimed to be the "real" source of Muhammad's knowledge</note>, who told him many other things, but especially the History of the Seven Sleepers <note>original: "historiam 7. dormientiũ"; referring to the Christian and Islamic legend of youths who hid in a cave to escape persecution and slept for centuries</note> to provide clear evidence for the resurrection. And just as the Jews were in Mecca, Gabriel was in Medina. In those histories of the prophets which the Caliph Marwan <note>original: "Merbas Chaliphas"; likely referring to Marwan II, the last Umayyad Caliph</note> submerged in the river, it was also noted that shortly before the death of Muhammad, the Jews wished to elevate **Halim**, the nephew of this prophet, to the status of a prophet. He was quite a young man, and while he was incautiously searching for a cave suitable for his faction, he found Muhammad in a cavern with the Nestorian monk. Thus, what everyone suspected became open: that he sought a teacher from elsewhere than from an angelic spirit. Therefore, the scoundrel <note>original: "nebulo"; Postel uses this to refer to Muhammad</note> feared in a wonderful way that his tricks would be exposed. He busied himself with winning over the young man with great gifts, yet he could not prevent the matter from being betrayed. He encounters this youth in this place and many others, asserting nothing other than divine threats and saying that those who spoke such things were injurious. Thus the deception revealed itself. Regarding **Sergius the Nestorian**, it was confessed by all. But all these things have been erased from their histories; they can only be proved by the <term>Sunnah</term> <note>original: "Suneh"; the body of traditional social and legal custom and practice of the Islamic community</note> commentaries. He proceeds to threaten those who said he was nothing but a madman, who daily, evening and morning, received from elsewhere the things he dictated. If he had an angel, that angel ought to see to it that he no longer lived off the ideas of others. Finally, as if he were a prophet, he says it is no wonder if he and the <term>Alcoran</term> are opposed, for all prophets had adversaries. But if someone is a prophet simply because he has adversaries, then thieves, murderers, robbers, the impious, sorcerers, and other wicked men are among the prophets; for they all have good men, laws, and judges as enemies and foes, since they plot their destruction. Thus, no one denies that Muhammad was a "prophet" <note>Postel is being sarcastic here, implying Muhammad is a "prophet" only in the sense that criminals have enemies</note>, and he left this confirmed by many arguments. The rest are his usual repetitions.

### 25. Sigra, Poësis. <note>original: "Sigra, poësis"; referring to Surah Ash-Shu'ara (The Poets)</note>

Since he mixes nothing but falsehoods with truths, adding many lies as well as the old wives' tales of Arabia to the histories of the Old Testament, and recites his usual miracles and blasphemies (already refuted above), I shall write nothing further on this section.

### 26. Formica. <note>original: "Formica"; referring to Surah An-Naml (The Ant)</note>

He protects himself and applauds his own vices when he makes Moses seek fire from a branch of a bush <note>the Burning Bush</note> and has God call Moses to Himself without fear. 

> For my messengers are none but those who have sinned; then if they are converted, God is merciful and pious. <note>A paraphrased translation of a Quranic verse (27:10-11) used by Postel to argue that Muhammad was justifying his own "vices"</note>

For although he was most defiled by every stain of vice, yet he claimed God was propitious and familiar to him, and that vices were no obstacle to piety and prophecy. Then he joins a lie to sacred history: that Moses came with eight miracles to Pharaoh—though he said earlier it was nine—and in both cases it is a lie, since there were ten <note>Postel is comparing the Quranic account of the "signs" of Moses with the ten plagues of Egypt in Exodus</note>. Then, inventing a fable about Solomon, he says:

> And Solomon succeeded David, and said: "O men, we have been taught the speech of birds, and we have been given all things, for this is a distinguished favor." And the hosts of demons, men, and birds were summoned by Solomon, and they assembled until they came to the Valley of the Ant. An ant said: "O ants, enter your dwellings lest Solomon and his hosts crush you without noticing." And a cry was raised by their voices, and he [Solomon] said: "Teach me that I may praise You for Your favor, with which You have favored me and my father, that I may do good," etc.

Who can bear to hear these absurdities? But these are nothing compared to the hoopoe <note>original: "upupa"; a bird that acts as a messenger for Solomon in the Quran</note>, and its conversation, its embassy, and its preaching. Let him who wishes look at those follies with which he mocks God and men. Nothing more mindless or delirious can be found—and yet they say this law is from God and is divine. I am silent regarding the horrendous absurdities about the throne, the Queen of Sheba, and the service of demons—all of which relate to a wo-

...terrors of petty trifles were brought forward. I wonder what audacity that pest <note>Referring to Muhammad</note> had, who judged men to be as stones and mushrooms—if indeed he judged anything at all. In this chapter, he wished to gratify the Jews and enrich their sacred rites; therefore, he promises them that he will reveal many things in this Quran about which they disagree. In truth, I believe that nothing could have been proposed to this man to which he would not have given an answer—a thing permitted only to fools and madmen.

->27.<-

That Moses was thrown into the sea is false. They used to send those to be killed into the river Nile, from whence he was taken up and raised by the daughter of Pharaoh. Here [it is said he was raised] by his wife, and previously by his sister; so much does this man’s work never lack a lie. What does he not falsely attach to sacred history? Concerning Pharaoh, Haman <note>In the Quran, Haman is an official of Pharaoh, whereas in the Bible, he is a minister of the Persian King Ahasuerus; Postel notes this as a chronological error</note>, and the key to the treasures which forty men could not move <note>A reference to the story of Korah (Qarun) and his immense wealth</note>. The history must be sought elsewhere, from the book *Hasſiar* <note>original: "libro Hasſiar"; referring to *Sefer HaYashar* or "The Book of Jasher," a Jewish midrashic text</note>, along with Alborach <note>The Buraq, the celestial steed of Muhammad’s night journey</note> and Gabriel. At the end of this chapter, he cuts the throats of his own chroniclers, who trace the light from Adam down to him and say the prophet was born circumcised. For if he were a prophet from birth, how is it that he did not know it for so long, such that until the 40th year of his age, he did not feel or know himself to be a prophet? Indeed, he himself confesses that at one time he did not think so. *Say,* he says, *my creator knows who is guided, and who is in manifest error. And you did not hope that the book would be delivered to you, except by the mercy of your Lord; therefore, do not be uplifted above the blasphemers.* <note>A translation of Quran 28:85-86</note> In this place, he pretends to spare the idolaters with whom he had been educated, imbued, and initiated. But he did not think it would happen that the later Caliphs would once make him so great; nor did they sufficiently notice what he confessed about himself.

->28. The Spider.<-

There is nothing in this chapter more worthy of the author than that he promises the future resurrection of all living things, so that not only animals but even inanimate creatures shall be eternal. For the word *chelec* <note>original: "chelec"; likely the Arabic *khalq*, meaning creation</note> is general to all created things. Concerning the brutes, this is written as an article of faith in the "Reasons of Faith" in the book *Tezchere elimam* <note>original: "Tezchere elimam"; likely referring to *Tadhkirat al-Imam* by Al-Qurtubi, a work on the afterlife</note>. If miracles are with God alone, and some prophets had them, they were close to God. Since, however, you have none, you are a stranger to God. Therefore, the miracles of the wolves, the Buraq, the tree trunks, the moon, and the heart were not true, but false, because you are not God. I skip over several chapters here, very similar to the others, so that I may come to more noteworthy things: to Surah 32 <note>Postel is likely referring to Surah 33, *Al-Ahzab*</note>, which reveals to us many famous deeds of the prophet.

**Al-Ahzab** <note>original: "Elagzab"; Surah 33, "The Confederates"</note>: First, it must be seen how, when he violently fell upon the property and inheritances of others in Medina and expelled the Jews and other inhabitants, so that they were forced to seek help from their tribesmen, it is hinted at in these words: *Remember when the double-hearted <note>The "hypocrites" or Munafiqun</note>, and those in whose hearts was a disease, said, "His Apostle promises nothing but losses and inconveniences"; and remember when certain citizens of Yathrib <note>original: "Ietribae"; the ancient name of Medina</note> said, "There is no place for you, go back." And some of them asked leave of the prophet, saying, "Our houses are ruinous," though they were not desolate, but they wished to flee...* <note>Translating Quran 33:12-13</note> By these words and the following, he said that he had a right to their things because they would not acquiesce to his persuasion. For when he had started this fable for ten years in Mecca with the Jews, and they had withdrawn from the open deceit, when he had to go into exile in the 50th year of his life or thereabouts, he expelled the wretched Jews and Christians living in **Yezrab** <note>Yathrib/Medina</note> from their homes, on the pretext that there was "disease in their hearts." Such was the "equity" of the prophet. The wretched Jews indeed persuaded many followers to leave the prophet and return to their own people, lest they be crushed by the crowd. When he sensed this, his prophetic "equity" raged more sharply. At first, it had been enough to punish...

...having stripped that city <note>original: "pillum," likely a printer's error for "oppidum" (town), referring to Medina</note> of all its fortunes, now nothing is enough for him. At first, it was enough for him to have occupied a place in which he might act for the sake of his own pleasure; now he wishes to establish a permanent seat. Indeed, he leaves the greatest proof of his cruelty, not only in many other places but in that very place shortly thereafter. And when we approach, you see them as if they were dead, tormented by fear; but when we depart, they sharpen their tongues to rebuke you.

What else would happen when a tyrant arrives? In his presence, all things are like the image of death, nor is it permitted to judge freely except when he has departed. But that "equity" of his must be confirmed. 
<margin>»</margin> "You shall kill some of them, others you shall lead away as captives, and you shall occupy their possessions, their goods, and the land which you had never entered, because God is powerful over all things." <note>A paraphrase of Surah 33:26-27, referring to the conquest of the Jewish Banu Qurayza tribe</note>
That is to say, Muhammad is a most cruel robber, who under the name of God commits every crime. But a cohort of women had to be lead along with the prophet, and they had to be governed by the terror of the divine power, so that all things might be permitted to the prophet both at home and abroad. 

But I had forgotten a most beautiful and truly "prophetic" passage, which although it is not in the African manuscript, is found in others: 
<margin>»</margin> "And if you do not recognize your fathers or your brothers in your faith and your wealth, it is not necessary for you to worry about that in which you sin; and therefore let your hearts not waver, since God is merciful and pious toward the prophet; those men are the faithful," etc. <note>This refers to the concept in Islam where the bond of faith (Ummah) supersedes biological kinship</note> 
This is so that it may be permitted for his followers to rage most "justly" against their parents, and to kill fathers and brothers; it is enough to use the name of faith as a pretext for ignorance. And God is favorable to the prophet, for whose sake these things are done. Since he had declared war on his brothers, and had already killed some, he wished that on account of this new faith, not even fathers should be recognized by their sons, but that fathers, brothers, relatives, and kinsmen should be put to death. Oh, how far these things are from Christian piety! 

I return to the women. 
<margin>»</margin> "O prophet, say to your wives: if they love this world and approach its splendor, I will give them life and many delights." 
This, and the following verse, pertains to those wealthy women who had left their men and were very rich citizens of Mecca; to them, therefore, he promises what he prohibits to others: so that it may be clearly said of him, "whatever pleases him is permitted." He adds terrors, saying they are worthy of a double punishment if they do not approach—for this is what it means "to sin" in this place—otherwise, there is a great reward from God if they obey. God spares the Messenger more if he kills parents than he spares other men. If the wives do not obey, they are worthy of a double punishment; a fine "equity" indeed.

I had said before (as I have been able to note quite often) that Muhammad makes God his partner. 
<margin>»</margin> "It is established," he says, "as a precept from God and from His prophet, that there may be no believer without a believer." <note>Likely referencing Surah 33:36</note> 
Does he not strive to make his own authority equal to the divine authority, while he wishes to be held as a partner and participant in the divine empire? How often does he insist: "Hear God and His prophet," "Obey God and His legate," "Those who do not believe in God and His legate," etc. Is this not participating in divine power? Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the rest of the prophets used to say, "Hear the word of God" only—not "of God and the prophet," like this scoundrel <note>original: "nebulo"</note>. For they sought no wealth, honor, or favor for themselves, as this false prophet does; and therefore they considered it enough to open the impulse of the divine spirit. Since he had nothing from God or from right judgment, except what was begged from elsewhere, he never fails to join himself to God, and he hammers it into the credulous crowd. Such is the nature of falsehood: it never fails to commend and thrust itself forward more ardently and frequently the less it approaches the truth. For while it frequently occupies minds with self-commendations, it removes and evades the opportunity for examination, lest it be recognized. But the continuous discourse in these several verses must be heard. 

<margin>»</margin> "Let there not be," he says, "a believer without a believer, since God and His prophet have established a precept, if their precept is good for you. And he who turns away from God and His prophet already errs in a manifest error." 
These things pertain to the same point as above: that he may share power with God. But concerning Zayd <note>original: "Zeido"; referring to Zayd ibn Harithah, Muhammad’s adopted son, and the controversy regarding Muhammad's marriage to Zayd's former wife, Zaynab</note>:

### WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK II.

> "And when you said to him upon whom God bestowed favor, and to whom you also bestowed favor: 'Keep your wife for yourself, and fear God,' and you hid within yourself what God was about to reveal, fearing men, though God is more worthy of fear. And when Zayd <note>Zayd ibn Harithah, Muhammad's adopted son</note> had completed his desire for her, We joined her to you in marriage. Let there be no scandal among the faithful concerning the wives of their servants <note>Referring here to adopted sons or dependents</note>, once they have fulfilled their desire for them; and let the command of the Lord be done. Let there be no scandal upon the prophet in that which God said. He possesses the power of the law; God was among those who passed away before, and the command of God is most powerful. Among those to whom the prophecy of God arrived, they all fear Him, and fear no one but God, and it is enough to find sufficiency with God. Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but he is the prophet of God, the seal of the prophets, and God is wise in every matter." <note>This is a Latin translation of Surah 33:37-40</note>

Oh, what great mysteries lie hidden here! Muhammad had kept Zayd as a servant in his home almost from boyhood; to ensure Zayd would be the first to be initiated as a Muslim <note>original: "Mussulman"</note>, he gave him his freedom, though not without vast promises. A few years later, after his followers had been enriched by plunder, and because Zayd managed the household affairs quite faithfully, Muhammad gave him his own kinswoman in marriage. Zayd lived with her for some years and loved her exceedingly. However, while the "prophetic race" was dwelling in Medina and Muhammad was beginning to exercise kingly power, he was seized by love for the wife of his most faithful servant and kinsman. 

And so, going to his house when the husband was not found, he said to the woman (as it is written in the book *Hassiar* <note>Likely referring to the *Sira*, or biographies of the Prophet</note>) that Zayd had chosen the best hinge for his door. He commanded the woman—who did not understand those words—to repeat them to her husband. When Zayd heard this, immediately (as one who had long known the man’s mind and knew how to interpret "prophetic" ambiguities), he said that the "hinge" meant the wife in the prophet’s saying, and the "door" was the house. This meant that because he had a wife of elegant beauty, he ought to leave her so that she might go to the prophet. For such was the man's character: unless you did his bidding immediately, he was accustomed to compel you with lashes and death. 

Both were dissolved in tears. Without delay, a "prophecy" arrived which commanded Zayd to divorce his wife. He had to obey at once; he left the house, and the next day she married the prophet, who already had twelve wives. This is the course of this "prophetic" history; this is its meaning. Truly, a great scandal arose concerning this matter: that he had been so unjust as to take another man’s wife, and so wicked as to marry a kinswoman—a thing he had forbidden to others by different laws. 

Now the text must be examined more closely. At the beginning, he reproaches the servant for the favors received from himself and from God—that is, from the plunder. For Zayd had led many attacks on the merchants who were besieging Mecca <note>original: "Mecha"</note> from all sides, and there he became wealthy. When Muhammad saw that everyone was deeply offended, he claimed that he had commanded Zayd to keep his wife, even though he had forced him to divorce her. 

And since Zayd did not dare to even open his mouth in the prophet's presence, but complained of the injury when he was away, Muhammad says to the man (who was silenced and approving the deed out of fear) that Zayd was hiding something within himself, but that God would reveal it. This meant that if the prophet heard anything more about the matter, the man was finished—he would die by the authority of "God." He adds that Zayd should not fear men, but God—that is, the fury and insane rage of the prophet. 

Then at last, he turns what he committed into a law: namely, that the same thing is permitted to anyone else regarding their household and subjects. That is to say, after they have forced their wretched subjects to divorce their wives so they can marry them immediately, they say that once "desire has been fulfilled," there is no scandal for the master, or for the one who compels the servant by fear of death to give up his wife. And because "God said it," it is done. Thus, from his crimes were born the laws by which the same was permitted to others. They took many wives because he had many; slave-girls and concubines are permitted to all without fault because that fault had been turned into a virtue for the prophet; catamites <note>A derogatory term for boys kept for sexual purposes; Postel is making a polemical accusation here</note> are made legitimate because they pleased the prophet. To enter into...

### ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD
### BOOK II.

...[By] that same law, it is permitted to plunder everything, to plot against the lives of all; every act is made lawful once the name of "faith" is brought forward. Because it was permitted to the prophet, it is considered honorable to marry the woman abandoned by a forced servant <note>Referring to Zayd ibn Harithah, who divorced his wife Zaynab so Muhammad could marry her</note>, simply because the prophet approved of it. Oh, blind men! How can you bear these impieties, let alone ascribe them to God and comment upon them so seriously? But I proceed.

"There is no scandal for the prophet in that which God commanded." <note>A paraphrase of Surah 33:38</note> But if God commands whatever is pleasing to him, then whatever pleases him is lawful; this is the law. The command of God among the ancients was indeed powerful—that is true—insofar as they were mighty in signs, miracles, wonders, and the foretelling of events. It did not consist in despoiling citizens of their fortunes, nor in slaughtering brothers and parents, nor in bringing back dreams and lies from caves, nor in invading the property of others with hostilty, nor in engaging with beasts, nor in oppressing servants, nor in committing all the sins and other crimes which I shudder to even mention. In these and similar things, you have made the "command of your God" most powerful. It is certain that you have a God who differs from the rest of the whole world. The God of nature sometimes allows adversity to befall a man; the God of Muhammad commands and approves whatever tends toward the ruin of nature.

But let us hear the status of this prophet: "To whom the prophecy arrives, all fear him, and he fears no one." <note>original: "Ad quem peruenit prophetia, eum timent omnes, neminem timet"</note> O, the patience of miserable men! Let the prophet rush into right or wrong, let him overturn the sacred and the profane, let him bring ruin to everyone—he fears nothing. What bloodthirsty tyrant could have devised a more convenient law for himself? For any impious crime committed, Muhammad fears no one, even though he has inflicted six hundred injuries; from this it is clear that he did not use laws, he who wished to be the lawmaker for everyone. For if he had any spark of humanity in him, he ought at least to have feared offending another man. Truly, he says he fears no one but God. But does not he who commits impious atrocities and claims to fear God lie? Does he not affirm by his very deeds that there is no God?

Yet God spares the prophet more than others, as was said before. A sin is usually considered more grievous the greater the person who commits it. Muhammad wants to be the greatest of all, and yet he wishes to sin in nothing, even while he transgresses against God, nature, and man. It is enough for him to "acquire with God." Plunderer, thief, robber, tyrant—as long as he takes it in the name of God, it all belongs to him. Such are the origins of your wealth, O Muslims <note>original: "Mussulmani"</note>.

What follows is a little more obscure: "Muhammad is not the father of any of your men." <note>Surah 33:40</note> He wished to suggest by this that kinship should not prevent him from marrying a relative. For as long as she was not the wife of his biological son, he could take her according to his law as a legitimate wife. Therefore, as he said before, "He is not the father of your men," because he takes your wives in marriage whenever it pleases him.

"He is truly the seal of the prophets," <note>original: "sigillum prophetarum"; a central Islamic concept (Khatam an-Nabiyyin) meaning the final prophet</note> that is, the completion, after whom there will be no other. There will be many like you as long as the world lasts, but none were truly meant to come for 600 years before you. For the end of the law and of prophecy was Christ Jesus, God and man; He was the "seal of the prophets." God would have acted in vain and foolishly if, after sending the highest remedy for all things, He had reserved for Himself another lesser one. Even by Muhammad's own admission, the greatest of the prophets was Jesus Christ. After the greatest remedy has been applied to human affairs, there can be no place for a lesser one. For if a column can barely bear its burden, how can that same burden be supported by a stake or a pole?

You are not the "seal," Muhammad, except perhaps the seal of evils. There are still those like you to come until the end of the world, until the most wicked and last of the antichrists arrives. You have paved the way for him by admitting every kind of pleasure and vice into religion. He will truly surpass you, for he will confirm his power with lying signs; his reign will be as much shorter as the violence with which it erupts is greater. But God is truly wise in all things, and powerful against you...

### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK II.

...to defer the final punishment until the day of judgment. As for the rest:

"Worship God morning and evening; it is He who prays for you, and His angels, so that He may lead you out of darkness into light." <note>A translation of Surah 33:41–43. Postel is using a Latin version of the Quran, likely the one edited by Theodor Bibliander, which contains translations that were often polemically charged or misunderstood.</note> It is certainly strange to wonder to whom God could pray, unless He prays to Himself. If we think of God as He is God, nothing could be more absurd. If the Spirit compelled you, even against your will—as it did Saul and Caiaphas <note>Biblical figures who spoke divine truths despite their personal opposition to God's will</note>—to utter this concerning Christ, against whom you write, I praise the Spirit, not you. For we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, both God and man, who is also the atonement for our sins. This same sentiment is repeated more than once, so that it may be understood. Certainly, you understand God as praying to Himself, and His angels also; for the conjunction "and" teaches this. Although I am ashamed of these absurdities, these privileges must also be added—privileges granted to himself by himself, against the rules laid down for others.

<margin>cc</margin>
> "O Prophet," he says, "We have granted you the power to dismiss your wives once you have given them their gift; and also your female servants, once you have given the gift from those things which God has bestowed upon you; and the daughters of your paternal uncle, and the daughters of your paternal aunt, and the daughters of your maternal uncle, and the daughters of your maternal aunt, who travel with you; and faithful women, if they have given themselves to the prophet, if the prophet wishes them to be joined to him, it is good for you, above the rest of the faithful. We already know what we have set forth among them concerning wives and female servants or slaves, so that there may be no offense toward you among any on that account: since God is pious and merciful. You shall join to yourself and embrace whomsoever you wish, and whomsoever you have desired from those you have released. Nor is this forbidden to you. Whatever is permitted, if you please their eyes, and they are not saddened, and if they all accept what you give them. It is not permitted for you to exchange wives—that is, to have parents or strangers along with your own. But if their beauty pleases you, besides the female servants, God is pious. O you who believe, do not enter the houses of the prophet unless it is permitted to you for eating, not looking at the vessels. But when you are called, enter; and when you have eaten, depart; and do not recount deeds or things done, since the prophet takes this badly, and is bashful before you, but God is not bashful before the truth." <note>This blockquote translates Postel's Latin version of Surah 33:50–53.</note>

The meaning here is abundant. The law he had placed upon others—that they should not divorce without just cause—he exempts himself from, both for many reasons and on account of parents. For that scoundrel was of such "charity" that he drove away all parents from himself, because he did not use them; he could also have any women he liked as wives without a dowry agreement. Furthermore, while he wanted others to be bound to treat their women with equal law, he himself approves, summons, repudiates, and treats as he pleases whichever women he wishes, wanting to be held by no law at all. If they receive gifts, if they smile, they are immediately the legitimate wives of the prophet. Nor should he suffer scandal for any reason, whatever he may commit, because "God is merciful and pious."

Furthermore, because he was committing crimes of all kinds at home—misusing whoever he wished, <term>catamites</term> <note>A term historically used to refer to younger male sexual partners; Postel uses it here as a polemical accusation against Muhammad’s household</note>, female servants, and wives, arranged according to various arrangements (which I cannot decently describe)—he did not want anyone to enter his house unless invited to the table. And when invited, he did not want them to look at the cups and the furniture, because the spoils of the Arabian world were to be seen in his possession. Moreover, he wanted things to be done there in silence, because on the occasion of the things the guests saw there, they were compelled to tell of the man's wicked deeds, which troubled him greatly. Therefore, he makes God the author and avenger of these laws. Judge these "prophetic" deeds, and evaluate their author. The ancients were very stupid in accepting the false religions of robbers and ruined men, but there has not been a more wicked or more foolish man since the world was founded. From this, it appears with how much blood he persuaded them, and how many thousands of men he killed to persuade them. But I wonder how he could terrify those who were members of his own household with such trifles. But indeed, everyone, even in his own house, obeyed...

...to defer the final punishment until the day of judgment. As for the rest:

"Worship God morning and evening; He it is who prays for you, and His angels, that He may lead you out of darkness into light." <note>Postel is quoting a Latin translation of Surah 33:41-43. If this is said of God insofar as He is God, nothing more foolish can be imagined. Although I am ashamed of such follies, I must also add those privileges granted to him, by himself, contrary to the rules he prescribed for others.

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD #

...carried out his bloody edicts. <note>The text likely completes a word like *ferebat* or *gerebat* (carried out) from the previous page.</note> Hear the decree: "If those in whose hearts is a disease do not cease from their behavior in the city, and if they continue to spread rumors in the city, they are cursed. Wherever they are found, seize them and kill them." <note>original: "Audite præscriptum... male-dicti sunt." A paraphrase of Surah 33:60-61.</note> Because women had a little while before revealed his tricks, and everything had been made public, he therefore threatened death if anyone so much as whispered. On that pretext, whomever he saw who was wealthy or living in fine houses, he would say there was a "disease in his heart." Unless they sought safety in flight and left their possessions behind, especially the Jews—whom he called the authors of fables and arsons—they were killed. And indeed, they were justly afflicted and despoiled of their goods there, for out of envy for Jesus Christ, they had paved the way for this pestilence to achieve tyranny. Thus, they were entirely oppressed by these and similar laws.

->33.<-

It is shameful to recount what is found in Chapter 33 <note>Postel refers to the chapters of the Quran, though his numbering often shifts between Surahs and his own thematic divisions.</note> concerning the demons of Solomon, and their works, and the winds. They are all similar to his stories of hoopoes, birds, and ants; certainly, if some most delirious old woman were to recite them in that manner, she could not keep infants and nursemaids listening. And yet, if it please the gods, these things are said to be from God! The interpreters of these trifles are not ashamed, but linger over them as if they were holiday entertainments. Finally, he silently babbles blasphemies against Christ and exhorts the lowly to believe by the example of the wealthy. But, as he says, the commoners often did not have the "knowledge" that the magnates had, because the latter were skilled in the fable which the poor were ignorant of, and they brought it forward. Therefore, he now calls each by its proper name: the poor he calls *mutzehiphune* <note>original: *mutzehiphune*; from the Arabic *mustadh'afin*, meaning the oppressed or weakened.</note>, that is, the afflicted and the weak; the wealthy he calls *mustecberine* <note>original: *mustecberine*; from the Arabic *mustakbirin*, meaning the proud or arrogant.</note>, that is, the proud and elated. For those among his magnates were men who shortly before had been proletarians, those counted only by their heads, cobblers, and craftsmen. By the company of such men, joined with some wealthy men from Mecca, he increased and prepared his power. However, a man who was recently poor and suddenly enriched can scarcely be held by any laws; thus, he is accustomed to be arrogant.

->34. Angels, or the creator.<-

"Praise be to God, the creator of heaven and earth," he says, "who made the angels messengers, endowed with two, three, or four wings; He adds to creation what He wills," etc. <note>A translation of Surah 35:1.</note> What nonsense he offers at the beginning, he who would say that angels were at some time "apostles" or "prophets." For the word *rossol* <note>original: *rossol*; Arabic *rasul*, meaning messenger or apostle.</note> signifies both. To what people, then, did they announce? What law did they give? We read that three angels visited Abraham, but they neither gave a law nor had such various wings. But these things tend elsewhere: because in the account of the journey and the riding of the *Alborac* <note>original: *Alborac*; referring to the Buraq, the winged steed of Muhammad's Night Journey.</note>, Gabriel is said to have had 70 wings, and he saw angels having infinite millions of wings, and being a hundred thousand times larger than the world. Thus, so that he might be seen to have "seen" angels, he proposed this mystery of wings. However, in the Sacred Scriptures, as often as the apparitions of angels have presented themselves to human senses, no mention is made of their wings. The "oarage of wings" is attributed to bodies only because one sees that nothing can be carried into the air without that effort; but for spirits devoid of bodies, no wings are necessary, except that we might accommodate divine things to the weakness of our senses, since in this body we can conceive of nothing except through examples and objects. All lower things fight against Christ. For by the suggestion of his Jewish informants, he intended nothing else in the whole Quran than to extinguish the glory of Christ the <term>God-man</term> <note>original Greek: θεανθρώπου (*theanthropos*); a theological term for the union of divine and human natures in Jesus.</note>. To do this with a greater pretext, he refers all natural things to God as their author, as if we denied that—namely, so that Christ might appear to have created nothing, when nevertheless without Him nothing was made, nor could be made. For God, though most powerful, created nothing without the Word and Wisdom; which Solomon so greatly celebrated in the Proverbs that I wonder at the Jews, so captured in mind, who read those things daily and never understand them. But concerning that same Word, or Wisdom...
