For while everyone recognizes a chance prediction, no one recognizes lies and ambiguities. Indeed, while the person seeking counsel is being deluded, they do not expose the lie, partly so they are not said to have been cheated, and partly because they hope for the future. He who thinks he has gained a benefit from it boasts of it to everyone. The people have become stunned, hardened, and calloused by these injuries to both soul and body; the skilled magistrate tolerates and ignores it, and in his desire to maintain power, he seems to approve of things that ought to be condemned. To one who rightly estimates the condition of human affairs, there was never a more unhappy state of lands in the whole world than where that wretched persuasion has imposed itself, and where a region suffers and nourishes this "soldier," a spontaneous wanderer "in the way of God" <note>original: "in uia Dei"</note>, without selection and without a leader. For it is enough for that crowd to profess the name of religion (which anyone may do), while they run riot through all things. Trade is ruined by these pests, who inflict injuries and unbearable expenses upon all provinces. For how few can wait until a cohort gathers, prepares, arms itself, and collects its baggage? A whole year passes you by in deliberation.

O most powerful ruler of the Eastern Empire <note>A direct address to the Ottoman Sultan</note>, has this crowd fascinated your eyes—you, a leading man skilled in affairs and the ruler of the most distinguished part of the world—or do you, even seeing and willing, approve of the losses of your people and yourself? The farmer is worn down by beggary, expense, plunder, and raids; the traveler by dangers, the merchant by costs, and the treasury by loss. If, after the manner of Christians, each man were content with his own wife, and if that entire pestilence were outlawed once and for all—so that no one, under penalty of death, would dare to be in those fellowships or to be enrolled and act in them—and if the privileges and immunities granted by princes were abolished, undoubtedly that breeding ground would vanish immediately.

Indeed, one should not be moved by the miracle that they say happened under Murad II <note>original: "Hamurate secundo," referring to the Ottoman Sultan who reigned 1421–1444 and 1446–1451</note>, a prince who loved truth and justice. For it is certain that it was done by the agency of a demon. The story, as it is told, goes like this: When the prince was considering the destruction of that unspeakable dregs of humanity because of their crimes—and while he wished to prefer the Imams <note>original: "Imamos," Islamic prayer leaders</note> and Teachers <note>original: "Taalimanos," likely from the Arabic 'ta'lim' for instruction, referring to the Ulema or scholars</note>, and others who perform the duty of teaching, as people whom the State <note>original: "Respublica"</note> neither can nor should do without—he wanted a decree to be promulgated by the judgment of the supreme court. On the night before the day the edict was to be issued, Prince Murad was roused from his bed and driven by a pressing urge of nature to a certain narrow place near his own house. There, as he went to sit, all the floorboards suddenly broke, and he was left hanging high up over a beam. Until, having called upon God, a certain man appeared in the dress and clothing of the primary sect of these scoundrels, freed the man, and placed him back in his bed.

Moved by this, the prince ordered at dawn that as many Dervishes <note>original: "Dermischler," a Latinization of the Turkish 'dervişler'</note> as were present in Constantinople should come to the court at a appointed hour, as he would give a public gift <note>original: "congiarium"</note> to all. They came; he bestowed the gift, meanwhile watching to see if he could recognize the one who had rescued him from danger. All passed by, but he was not there. An elder rose from the whole flock and said that the one who had been present and had helped him was not a single individual, but the common advocate for them all. He said the Sultan ought to weigh from this which were more useful: those who preach, or those who travel and pray. Thus they were not expelled, but were even preferred over those most useful men whom the State cannot do without, even in the falsest of religions. Who [could believe] this...

Yet whoever thinks they have gained some benefit from it never stops praising them. The people have become stunned, hardened, and calloused by these injuries to both soul and body; the skilled magistrate tolerates and ignores it, and in his desire to maintain his command, he seems to approve of things that should be condemned. To one who rightly judges the condition of human affairs, there has never been a more unhappy state of lands in the whole world than where this wretched persuasion has imposed itself, and where a region suffers and nourishes this "soldier wandering in the way of God" <note>referring to the dervishes</note> without selection and without a leader. For it is enough for that crowd to profess the name of religion (which is permitted to anyone), and then to run riot through everything. Commerce is hindered by these pests, who bring injuries and unbearable losses to all provinces. For how many people can wait until a cohort gathers itself, prepares, arms itself, and assembles its baggage? A whole year passes you by in mere deliberation.

O most powerful ruler of the Eastern empire <note>referring to the Ottoman Sultan</note>, has this crowd fascinated your eyes—you, a leading man skilled in affairs and the ruler of the most noble part of the world—or do you, seeing and willing, approve of your own losses and those of your people? The farmer is worn down by beggary, expense, robberies, and raids; the traveler by dangers, the merchant by costs, and the treasury by loss. If, according to the custom of Christians, each man were content with his own wife, and that whole pestilence were outlawed at once—so that no one would dare, under penalty of death, either to be in their company or to be enrolled and act among them—and if the privileges and immunities granted by princes were abolished, that seedbed would undoubtedly vanish immediately.

Indeed, one ought not be moved by the "miracle" which they say happened under Murad II <note>original: *Hamurate secundo*</note>, a prince who loved truth and justice. For it is well known that it was done by the author of demons. The story, as it is told, goes like this: When the prince was considering the destruction of this unspeakable dregs of humanity because of their crimes—even if some among them seemed good, he still wished to prefer the Imams <note>term: *Imamos*, Islamic prayer leaders</note> and the Teachers <note>term: *Taalímanos*, from *Ta'lim*, meaning those who provide religious instruction</note>, and others who perform the duty of teaching, as the Republic neither can nor should be without them—and he wished to promulgate a decree by the judgment of the supreme court, the following happened. On the night before the day the edict was to be issued, Prince Murad was roused from his bed and driven by a violent urge of nature to a certain narrow space <note>a latrine</note> near his own house. There, as he went to sit, all the floorboards suddenly broke, and he was left hanging high up over a beam. Once he had called upon God, a certain man appeared in the habit and clothing of the primary sect of these scoundrels, freed the man, and placed him back in his bed. Moved by this event, the prince ordered at dawn that all the Dervishes <note>original: *Dermischler*</note> (as they call them) present in Constantinople should come to the court at a set hour, and he would give them all a bounty. They came; he bestowed it, meanwhile looking to see if he could recognize the one who had rescued him from danger. All passed by, but the man was not there. An elder from the whole flock rose and said that the one who had been present and helped him was not a single man, but the collective representative of them all. He said the prince should weigh from this who were more useful: those who preach, or those who travel and pray. Thus they were not expelled, but were even preferred over those most useful men whom the Republic, even in the falsest religions, cannot do without. Who [could believe] this...

<summary>Postel critiques the dervishes as criminal impostors who manipulate the public and the Sultan through supposed magic and a faked miracle involving Murad II. He argues that their religious immunity destroys the economy and that they should be replaced by legitimate teachers and monogamous social structures.</summary>

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD #
<meta>catchword: because</meta>

...who would not know that this is a fabrication of the devil (if it is true, and not rather a dream)? For God never does evil, and he is so far from acting like a traveling trickster <note>original: *circulator*, a peddler of charms or a street performer</note> that he instead heals such things; for otherwise, he would be most unjust. Who else, with such unusual vehemence, stirred the gut of the prince so that he did not go to his usual private retreats, but instead called his bedchamber attendants who never sleep? Is this not the art of the demon, dragging man toward impiety and nourishing a wicked and ruined crowd of men? The demon frequently sends in evils which he himself cannot take away or cure; and if he does cure them after they have been allowed, he merely seems to have bestowed a benefit—much like a thief who, when he has not destroyed something he had the power to destroy, acts as if he has done a favor. Who will deny that those scoundrels excel in the magical arts, since they had so maddened Muhammad <gloss>the poet</gloss> <note>original Greek: *ποιήτῷ* (poietō). Postel uses this to mock Muhammad as a mere fabricator of stories rather than a prophet.</note> with their wicked songs that, led by these illusions, the prince—otherwise most prudent—trusted himself entirely to them? Seeing this, a prince of the Tartars <note>Likely a reference to the Mongol or Timurid leaders who clashed with early Ottoman power.</note> dealt with those ruined men, so that once admitted into the prince's bedchamber they might dispatch him and strike off his head; if they did so, he promised he would grant them the reins of power, provided the title of Emperor was preserved. Money was counted out for this purpose, and a day was set. And it would have been done, had they not been caught the day before and paid the penalty worthy of their crime; from then on, he vented his rage against their entire race in such a way that while he lived, no one of them was ever seen in the court without the risk of their life. The same thing nearly happened to Bayezid I <note>The fourth Ottoman Sultan, known as "The Thunderbolt."</note>. For a man on the road, seeking alms with a hidden sword, nearly cut him down while the generous prince was looking for something to give the scoundrel; the violence of the blow left his horse half-dead. Let a prince see what a nefarious religion dares against private citizens, if it does not even care for princes surrounded by their guards. But enough of these things. Now we must observe how inheritances are divided among the sons of the wealthy. It is clear enough what kind of friendship must exist between brothers conceived by different mothers, since there is so little charity even from fathers toward their sons. Is it any wonder that there is much less from parents and relatives? For they think those who are worthless to both father and brothers pertain nothing to themselves; thus it is no wonder that the Akinji, the Azaps, the Garip <note>Postel lists Ottoman military classes: *Acangios* (light cavalry/raiders), *aslaparos* (Azaps, or peasant infantry), and *caripos* (Garip, a rank of the Sultan's cavalry).</note>, and the rest of the common soldiers are of such utility to the princes that it is not rare for the front line to be trampled by those following them, or to be laid down in place of a bridge or pavement when the army must cross in great danger. Hence, the life of a man is not worth as much as a beast’s, as their law persuades them that "it is best to die in the way of God." The laws of the partition of a family <note>Postel refers to the Roman legal concept *herciscundae familiae*, the division of an estate among heirs.</note>, and what portions he who can obtain a share of the inheritance should leave to his brothers and parents, he writes in the blood of those brothers. For as far as it can be done, if there is a prince like Muhammad, he sees to it that everyone is removed from the midst so that he alone may preserve the inheritance. Now, in as few words as the argument requires, I shall bring down the histories of the Muslims <note>original: *Muffulmanorum*</note> from the expeditions of Muhammad to our own times, so that once the practice of this governance is known, the wretchedness of the law may become most evident. For just as the virtue of the law of Moses is known from the lives and deeds of those who reigned after him, and the law of Christ from the lives of Christians, so too from the Caliphs <note>original: *Chaliphis*</note> who gained power after Muhammad, it will be possible to judge whether he left behind happiness or misery.

# THE DEEDS OF THE PEOPLES WHO #
## gave their names to Muhammad. CAP. XX. ##

Just as no nation has ever brought greater slaughter upon the world, more savagely routed virtue, or introduced more criminal vices, so too has no nation ever acted with less care or concern for their own history. For unless religion is joined to their crimes, they keep hardly any monument of history worth reading.

...which was done not so much by a neglect of literature as by a constant change of tyrannies. For when the soldier is perpetually eager for new things, the prince looks out for himself, and the petty priests—alienated from courtly and military affairs—either hide away or are plundered, there can be no place for men of excellent character, instructed in the arts of both war and peace in every age, who alone can judge and write about deeds with incorruptibility and sincerity. Thus, they have no writers; and if they do have any, because they contain monstrous crimes, they do not hand them over or believe them even to their own people, except after fifty years of life have passed. They entrust them to those administrators of religion, already so practiced in prudence that they can cover those monstrous vices with silence. For it has happened that many, through the thorough reading of the Book of Kings or Caliphs <note>Postel refers to historical chronicles of Islamic rulers, likely the *Tarikh* literature.</note>, have recoiled from that impiety: which hints at nothing other than that a tyrannical power, acquired through the greatest crime, increased by even greater ones, and preserved by the greatest, is set up in place of the divine, and that virtue is made out of the most detestable vices. A copy of that book was not made available to me, though it does not matter much that those crimes be uncovered among the Latins, for they could not be of benefit, and could certainly infect them. It would be enough for those things to be made public to all in an Arabic edition, so that what is hidden from the common people—miserably deceived—may finally betray itself to them. All the books of the Old and New Testament are available to everyone; they do not fear a censor. If anything human happened to either the prophets or the princes, those holy men do not blush to confess they were liable to sins: since, if one or two improbable deeds are contained in them, there are in compensation innumerable good things by which readers can be incited to virtue. In Muhammadan matters, it is the opposite, as is evident from the concealment. For there is scarcely any image of virtue there, but many monstrous crimes.

But we must come to the expeditions of the prophet, so that these prophetic matters may be more easily assessed. In the books of *Hassiar* <note>original: *Hassiar*, likely referring to the *Sira* (biographies of the Prophet) or the *Siyar* (traditions regarding war and statecraft)</note> it is held that Muhammad waged eighteen wars, eleven against the Jews, the rest against the Meccans, the King of the Persians, the Romans, and neighboring cities. The power of the Jews, as we have said, increased for ten whole years as a "new Messiah" <note>Postel asserts that Muhammad initially drew support from Jewish communities who may have viewed him as a messianic figure.</note>, and he won for himself the wealth of many rich and influential men. From Mecca he had both sons-in-law and supporters: Abu Bakr, Umar, Ali, and many of lesser name; from other places in Arabia, Uthman, Talha, Zayd (another besides the servant), Abd al-Rahman, and many others, whose silence is no loss to history, men, or reputation. Relying on their wealth, families, and kinships, he subdued as many cities neighboring Mecca as possible. Whatever was within many miles around Mecca he claimed for himself, the owners having been drawn into his persuasion, until from such a great crowd—either of those fearing his power and cruelty, or those seeking plunder of their own accord—a great number coalesced. Then finally he established a royal seat in Yatrib <note>original: *Ietriba*, the pre-Islamic name for Medina</note>, having driven out the Jews, who, seeking help from neighbors, were broken in many battles or raids. Therefore, they say, he raged against them. Meanwhile, those good historians do not see that they contradict the prophet, who in innumerable places accuses the Jews of a violated treaty. On account of this, he not only permits but commands anyone to kill them with impunity, as if they were infidels and carrying a disease in their hearts—not without divine vengeance, so that they might pay the penalties of the tyrant they themselves had fostered. Indeed, the mind of that prophet was incited to begin new things by a certain astronomer, who predicted changes of religions and kingdoms (as that race of impostors is always talking nonsense about something unusual), whom Muhammad used as a leader and consultant for many years. # ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK II

<page-num>240</page-num>

He profited not a little when he lied to the ignorant people and put forward ambiguous dreams. Indeed, so that he might complete his apprenticeship in the art—that is, the art of plundering—Muhammad attacked his own kin. For when he had established his seat at Medina, he sent Hamza <note>Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, Muhammad's uncle.</note>, the son of Abdemelech, with thirty mules and several footmen, so that they might lie in wait in the forest of Homs (which was on the route from Mecca to Syria) to watch for a company of the **Quraish** <note>The original Latin *Coraissorum* refers to the Quraish, the powerful merchant tribe of Mecca to which Muhammad himself belonged.</note>, his own parents and kin, who were laden with merchandise. They were to slaughter the men, seize everything, and bring it to the prophet.

But the outcome was far contrary to his expectation. For Hamza fell upon a company of a hundred men, whose leader was Angelus <note>Possibly a reference to a specific commander or a misunderstanding of a name in the Arabic sources Postel consulted.</note>, a man more warlike than Hamza. The raiders fled and returned to the prophet scattered and empty-handed. They informed him that he had sent them there neither prophetically nor prudently; for God seemed to be sleeping on the prophet's behalf then. Nor did that **Gabriel** seem prudent enough, who had persuaded the prophet to invest his first efforts so unhappily.

Nevertheless, Muhammad did not wish to desist from his undertakings. Entrusting the care of marauding to other leaders, he sent a crowd twice as large to blockade the same road under the leader Heguida <note>Likely Ubaydah ibn al-Harith.</note>, whom a certain petty king named **Abo Zipharus** <note>Abu Sufyan, a leader of the Meccan Quraish and a long-time opponent of Muhammad.</note> heavily defeated and put to flight. Few messengers returned from that expedition. The Quraish, passing through in the meantime, frustrated a third expedition sent for the same purpose; therefore **Zeidus** <note>Zayd ibn Harithah, Muhammad’s adopted son and a prominent military commander.</note>, the third leader, returned home with the business entirely unfinished.

Never were other prophets so frequently deceived, because they attempted all things under the leadership of God. Therefore, when he saw that the business conducted through his captains did not succeed, he himself went to the place of ambush to plunder the wealth of his parents. One man, named Muhazamus, resisted him strongly and routed the crowd of robbers; neither the prophet’s angel nor his deputy was present. Again, as he was of a most hostile mind toward his kin and eager to divert their wealth, he proceeded to another place, which they called **Barathum** <note>Likely a reference to the Battle of Badr, though Postel characterizes the early stages as failures.</note>, where he was likewise broken by **Umar**, the son of Halaphi. When he persisted a third time, he did indeed encounter adversaries, but they were far superior in strength; thus, the first six expeditions perished miserably.

But in the meantime, neither he nor his followers suffered any loss of spirit. For they were accustomed to live "prophetically" anywhere in the world, by the law that unless you gave to them, they would take it themselves. Indeed, if anyone opposed their crimes and was an associate, he was killed by treachery. If he was an outsider, Muhammad promised a paradise of pleasure to whoever would kill him and anyone else who did not acquiesce to the prophet.

Finally, such a great crowd of desperate and plundering men flocked to him that he had the roads blockaded on all sides. Thus, a large cohort of his **Quraish** parents, along with their merchandise and many camels, were intercepted by twelve men under the leader Abdasta <note>Likely Abdullah ibn Jahsh, whose raid during a sacred month was a turning point in early Islamic history.</note>. By these riches, he was not a little increased, and he began from that point to be much more favored and formidable. Having thus collected great power, he was also significantly increased by the plundering of the inheritance of the **Jews**. For because they had first sworn to his words and then, except for a few, had defected from him, their defection was more useful to him than their treaty. From those in treaty with him, he received something in the name of tithes for a whole decade; but from those who "defected," under the pretext of neglected religion, he snatched their entire inheritances and fortunes. 

And as they are, and have always been since the death of Christ, hated by all—whether Heathen or Christian—so every nation, while obeying the "prophetic" command in despoiling the Jews, also delighted to vent its rage out of national hatred. This remains even now, in every land, a great and notable testimony to the wicked impiety of that race, since they are in a worse condition among the Heathens and **Muslims** <note>Original: *Muslimunos*.</note> than among Christians, and are everywhere destitute of any magistracy. Muhammad, therefore, having increased his wealth through booty driven from all over Arabia, enriched by the spoils of his parents, and stuffed with the money of the Jews, appeared a match for the most powerful; and his friendship began to be sought and courted by neighboring petty kings.

### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK II
<page-num>241</page-num>

to be compared to a divine gift. Therefore, accompanied by a great number of supporters, he broke the nobility of **Mecca** <note>original: Mechae</note> in a valley very close to the city, shortly before he took possession of the city itself—an event we mentioned regarding the **Quran** <note>original: Alcorano</note>. Once the city was captured, nothing stood in his way: neighboring cities either surrendered or began to pay tribute. In this way, he who shortly before had been a beggar was made a tyrant, becoming all the more formidable as he appeared more cruel everywhere. 

The petty rulers near **Arabia Petraea** <note>The northwestern part of the Arabian peninsula, formerly a Roman province.</note> and those pertaining to the Persian borders sought help from the King of the Persians, whose forces had shortly before been worn down by the Emperor **Heraclius** <note>Byzantine Emperor (r. 610–641) who fought an exhausting war with the Sassanid Persians.</note>. The King gave what assistance he could and entered the Arabias. There, with his soldiers broken and weary from the journey, acting in a weakened region and laboring under hunger and thirst, his army was shattered and put to flight. He returned home trembling with only a few men. I do not find it recorded in writing who that specific leader was. However, I suspect it was the son of **Chosroes** <note>Khosrow II; his son Kavad II (Siroes) murdered him and his brothers.</note>, who had been the author of his father’s and brothers' slaughter, for the timing suggests it. 

After this victory was won, the soldiers became more spirited. Persuaded by their religion, they boldly invaded **Persia, Chaldea, Syria, and Egypt**. Through these incursions, that power began to be formidable in all places. I believe that certain remnants of the army which Heraclius had left in Syria were overwhelmed, perhaps under the leadership of some who had defected to Muhammad. For in the Quran there is one chapter titled **"The Romans"** <note>original: Rom; referring to Surah Ar-Rum. In the 16th century, the Byzantine Greeks were still called Romans (Romaioi).</note>, that is, the Romans or Greeks (for today the Greeks are called *Romaei*, that is, Romans), and it begins: **"The Romans have been defeated"** <note>original: Victi sunt Romani</note>, though they do not say in what place.

Whatever the case may be, shortly after Muhammad's death, **Abu Bakr** <note>original: Vbecharus</note> had gathered sixty thousand cavalry, in addition to countless infantry. Muhammad left his power to Abu Bakr and **Umar** <note>original: Homaro</note>, but Abu Bakr, being the elder, took possession of it. He increased the dominion as far as the **Armenias**, leaving only the coasts of Syria and a few of the stronger fortified cities. For between Palestine and Mesopotamia, because of the limits of the Persian Empire and Kingdom, everything was subject to incursions; there, the stronger man had the greater right to things by force. 

There were also others raised from the lowest power to great and illustrious fortune by Muhammad. The most prominent of these were **Uthman** <note>original: Vxeitus; likely referring to Uthman ibn Affan, though Postel uses a different spelling later.</note>, **Ammar** <note>original: Achmarus; likely Ammar ibn Yasir.</note>, under whose leadership he had entered Mecca, **Abu Ubaidah** <note>original: Abubardas</note>, **Zayd** <note>original: Zeidus</note>, and **Ali the Elder** <note>original: Halis senior; Ali ibn Abi Talib, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law.</note>; for Muhammad’s grandson was still unfit for handling affairs. These men, along with those I named above, were able to give the reins of government to whomever they wished, a practice which lasted among the **Caliphs** <note>original: Chaliphas</note> down to our own times. 

But as things ill-gotten slip away badly, after Abu Bakr had reigned only two years—during which he undertook the dangers of suppressing the multitude defecting from that dire and nefarious religion—he was killed by his necessary associate and familiar, **Umar**. Umar increased the power for ten years and strove to retain the people partly through war and partly through religion. For when he saw that many, although they did not refuse his commands, nevertheless laughed at the Quran—and that there were as many opinions about it as there were men—he began to collect its fragments, summaries, and books from wherever he could into one volume. But while he reigned longer than his successor wished, he was cut down, and **Uthman** <note>original: Odmamanus</note> succeeded to his place. 

As affairs became slightly more settled, Uthman began to seek out from the household of the Prophet those things which had been preserved both in writing and by hearsay, and to gather them into one. The first authority (as I noted when speaking of the origin of the **Sunna** <note>The body of traditional social and legal custom and practice of the Islamic community.</note>) came from **Aisha** <note>original: Assa</note>, the daughter of Abu Bakr, that notorious harlot <note>Postel uses the derogatory "scorto" to reflect his polemical view of Muhammad's wife.</note>; for she was an accomplice to the whole fable. Therefore, in their legal resolutions, after various doubts, her opinion is upheld, and so on, in the order as it has been noted.

And so, it was under Uthman that the Quran first began to be published from that copy which was preserved at Mecca and Medina for some years afterward. But thereafter a great license arose for producing that book; for later, no one failed to pretend they had a truer and better edition—not for the sake of the book, which they all knew was most foolish, but so that by it they might retain the deluded common people. For by the reputation of the book, [the state was] born, increased, and con-

### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
<page-num>242</page-num>

the kingdom was preserved. But when he had reigned for twelve years, a faction was stirred up by **Ali** <note>original: Halis; Ali ibn Abi Talib, the cousin and son-in-law of Muhammad</note>, and he was slain by a mob rushing upon him. His corpse was cast out of the city (just as the prophets were) in a mockery of religion and the prophet. For the crowd—to whom **Ali** had revealed the "fable"—said they should see whether this new author of the **Quran** <note>original: Alcorani</note> would rise again on the third day like a prophet; for his corpse had been kept for three days until it reached an intolerable stench.

**Ali** reigned for fourteen years, though not without great difficulty and seditions; he held the empire all the more precariously because he had revealed the tricks of false persuasion to a portion of the soldiers. Indeed, he turned back to that remedy with a late and almost regretful repentance. There was another seed of dissension dating back to the prophet's time. For when **Ali** foresaw that **Abu Bakr** <note>original: Vbecharus; the first Caliph</note> would reign after **Muhammad**, and that therefore anything would be permitted to that harlot **Aisha** <note>original: Assae; Muhammad's wife and Abu Bakr's daughter</note>, because matters and favor depended on her power and influence, very grave enmities arose between them, which reigned for many centuries afterward. These showed themselves most powerfully under **Ali**. The followers of **Abu Bakr** were called **Quraish** <note>original: Choraiſsi; the leading tribe of Mecca</note>, although they hardly belonged to the prophet's kin. Those who followed **Ali's** faction took their name from him. 

The **Moors** <note>original: Mauri; a term used here for North African Muslims</note> say that this **Ali** penetrated into **Africa** as far as the province of **Cyrene**, where a temple was built in his memory, which they call **Kairouan** <note>original: Caroan; the Great Mosque of Kairouan in modern Tunisia</note>. People flock there on pilgrimage from all over Africa, just as they do to **Mecca** and **Medina**. From that place, it came to be that companies of merchants and pilgrims are called **Caroana** or **Caravans** <note>original: Carauana</note>, because there is such a great multitude of desperate men in Africa that one cannot safely travel anywhere by land unless in a very large crowd. However, I cannot descend to the opinion that, having left Egypt behind him, he crossed over from the **Arabias** that far. For the **Caliphs** <note>original: Chaliphæ</note> were not established in **Egypt** before the hundredth year after the death of **Muhammad**. Yet both could be true: that he took possession of Egypt long before he transferred and established the seat of the Caliph there. For in the one hundred and thirtieth year of the **Hijra** <note>original: Alhigerę; the 'Exile' or flight from Mecca, marking the start of the Islamic calendar</note>, the **Mauretanias** <note>North Africa</note> were already being shaken by the incursions of these plagues; and it was the thirty-sixth year from the expulsion or **ostracism** <note>original: ὀστρακισμῷ; Postel uses the Greek term for banishment to refer to the Hijra</note> when **Ali** was finished.

A little before the death of **Ali**, **Hashim** <note>original: Haſcemus</note> was created prince, not in the prophetic city of **Yathrib** <note>original: Ietriba; the older name for Medina</note>, but in **Aracha** <note>likely Raqqa</note>, from where he set out with a large force to besiege **Yathrib** and killed **Ali**, whom many nevertheless write was his father. After nine years had passed, leaving his life and position, he left the empire to **Muawiya** <note>original: Moalbio; Muawiya I, founder of the Umayyad Caliphate</note>. This man overran **Syria** and occupied **Damascus**; he was a most bitter enemy of the Christians, though otherwise, as they write, he conducted himself laudably among his own people. He was most fit for plunder under the prophet, which is why the prophet foretold dominion for him. 

When he was removed after the manner of the others, **Yazid** <note>original: Ieudus; Yazid I</note> received the kingdom. By the same end, thirty **Caliphs**, with none intervening, were slaughtered by factions and miserable slaughter, so that they might leave the "virtue" of their law to be judged by posterity. If they had left life by a natural death, or had met it honorably among enemies, it could be said that it is common for princes that "no tyrant goes to Pluto's halls by a bloodless death." <note>A paraphrase of Juvenal’s Satires 10.112-113: 'ad generum Cereris sine caede et vulnere pauci descendunt reges et sicca morte tyranni.'</note> But if we consider any most unhappy state, even one born from the most savage tyranny (as almost all empires are), and compare it with this one, without a doubt the most unhappy people will be considered supremely happy when compared to these. 

**Lycurgus** gave laws by pretending to have a dialogue with a deity, yet they brought safety to the Republic and ruin to no one. The laws of **Solon**, **Zaleucus**, **Zamolxis**, and **Charondas** <note>A list of semi-legendary ancient Greek and Scythian lawgivers</note> contributed the greatest health to the states that used them. This "delirious persuasion" <note>Postel’s derogatory term for Islamic law</note> brought plague to the fields, calamity to the fates, hardships to men, destruction to the world, dullness to minds, and finally brought to its own princes the kind of death its author deserved—yet no one noticed. The **Caesars** seized tyranny over the Republic, and of the first ones, perhaps fifteen died from the seditions of veteran soldiers. The rest from that time died either manfully in war, or at home among their own—

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK II.
<page-num>243</page-num>

...closed their days honorably. These were buried by their children, parents, subjects, citizens, and friends. Now, if we compare those judges and kings who succeeded **Moses**—none of whom failed to die or pass away most honorably throughout a full eight hundred years—with these others, it will then be seen how much divine law differs from a lying and demonic one. I do not even bring forward the piety, innocence, and charity of our own people to oppose them (for compared to those most unhappy men, our people seem the most blessed), since the distinction between them is wider than that between light and darkness. For the sake of persuading and asserting the truth, for avoiding vice, and for preserving true piety toward God, the followers of **Christ** for nearly three hundred years voluntarily suffered death filled with every kind of torture and punishment. For if they had only wished to say this one phrase, "I am not a Christian," or "Christ is not God," they would have been acquitted and advanced with great honors.

But some **Muslim** <note>original: Musfulmanus</note> will object to me: "Our soldier and the followers of the prophet also die courageously for the sake of preserving and urging their religion." He dies indeed, I know, and many voluntarily cast themselves into dangers so that they may meet death after killing someone among the enemy. Truly, how much these things they commit differ from true piety—and from a man believing that an account of his deeds must be rendered to God—can be weighed from their way of living. For the soldier honors the prophet with every kind of pleasure; even the especially pious sacrifice to their spirits and their dead with fine stews and a more refined gluttony. Indeed, to have killed a man, to have plundered another’s goods, to have brought a stain upon one's own body and soul—provided the pretext of religion is present—the soldier places his glory in that. And with this "Lerna of crimes" <note>A reference to the Hydra of Lerna; a massive collection of evils.</note>, thinking himself most dear to God, he voluntarily hastens to those paradises which the prophet promised, so that he may contemplate for himself in a future life those supreme and eternal pleasures which he cannot attain here. It is just as if a bull rushing toward **Venus** <note>Lust or sexual desire.</note>, while he attacks his rival with his horns, should perish in the very conflict of his pleasure. 

**Christian** martyrs, most famous for their miracles, shrink from no punishments so that they may worship God above all things, keep themselves worthy of God the Father, and cherish another man as a brother just like their own body and soul. Your men, while they are armed for the destruction of nature, rush headlong into death. 

Truly, this **Arabian power** was immediately cut into various parts in its hundredth year, and once factions had created leaders, some were dispersed to the east, others to the north, and others to the west. Once **Egypt** was occupied—liberated, as he pretended, from the **Roman** magistrate who held it—a **Caliph** <note>original: Chaliphos</note> was established in **Babylon** <note>Likely referring to Cairo/Fustat or the later Abbasid capital.</note>. Those who sought **Assyria** were called by the ancestral name *benchi*, that is, **lords** <note>original: benchi; likely a corruption of "Beg" or "Bey"</note>. In **Africa**, they wished to call them **Sultans**, **Sharifs** <note>original: Seraphos</note>, and **Mawlas** <note>original: Maulas</note>, that is, the powerful, the wealthy, and the protectors. The term common to all was **Emir** and **Emir al-mumin** <note>original: emír elmumin</note>, that is, **Commander**, and **Commander of the Faithful**. Some of our people call them *Miramomelimos* and falsely think these are proper names. For it was a distinguished title of a prince, and of the **African** one especially, which is evident even from coins. For they were inscribed thus, as I have found certain from very ancient money coined already eight hundred years ago: "**Joseph**, Commander of the Faithful, son of the Commander of the Faithful, son of the Commander of the Faithful," all the way back to the great-great-grandfathers. 

Once those regions were lost through the sluggishness of the most cowardly Emperor **Heraclius**, it was very easy for them to retain what they occupied with no one resisting. For **Constantine IV** <note>Byzantine Emperor, r. 668–685 AD</note>, the fourth of that name, was forced to confirm a peace with the petty king of **Damascus**. Far more things would have to be brought forward by me here if I wished to hand down their histories exactly. Truly, I consider it enough to note the main points, to weigh their outcomes, and to reveal how they took possession of affairs. They took possession treacherously within the hundredth year from the **Hijra** <note>original: Alhigera; the migration of Muhammad from Mecca to Medina in 622 AD</note> or "the exile," perhaps by an opportunity offered from the fact that, a little before, having refuted a foolish persuasion, the King and Queen of the **Persians** had received holy baptism and had come to **Constantinople** in the times of **Constantine IV**. They did not, however, hold power any longer in **Persia**...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
### Book II

The kingdom was preserved. But when he had reigned for twelve years, a faction was stirred up by **Ali** <note>original: Halis</note>, and he was slain by a mob rushing upon him; his corpse was cast outside the city (just as they did to the prophets) in mockery of religion and the prophet. Indeed, he was forced to return to these same remedies with a late and almost penitent regret. There was another seed of dissension dating back to the time of the prophet. For when **Ali** foresaw that **Abu Bakr** <note>original: Vbecharus</note> would reign after **Muhammad**, and therefore everything would be permitted to that harlot **Aisha** <note>original: Assæ</note>—his daughter and the wife of the prophet—since wealth and favor depended on her power, the gravest enmities arose between them. Those of **Abu Bakr's** party were called **Koreishites** <note>original: Choraisis</note>, although they hardly belonged to the prophetic lineage. Those who followed **Ali's** side took their name from him. 

The **Moors** <note>Postel uses this term generally for North African Muslims</note> say this **Ali** penetrated into Africa as far as the province of **Cyrene**, where a temple was constructed in his memory which they call **Kairouan** <note>original: Caroan</note>. However, I cannot bring myself to the opinion that, leaving Egypt behind him, he crossed over from Arabia that far. For the **Caliphs** <note>original: Chaliphæ</note> were not established in **Egypt** before the hundredth year after the death of **Muhammad**. Both things could be true, however: that he took possession of Egypt long before he transferred and established the seat of the Caliphate there. For in the one hundred and thirtieth year of the **Hijra** <note>original: Alhigerę; referring to the Islamic lunar calendar</note>—that is, the "exile"—**Mauritania** was already being weakened by the incursions of these plagues; and it was then the thirty-sixth year from the expulsion or <term>ostracism <note>original: ὀστρακισμῶ; a Greek term for political banishment</note></term> when **Ali** was killed.

Shortly before the death of **Ali**, **Hashem** <note>original: Hascemus; likely referring to a member of the Hashemite faction or a confusion with Muawiya's predecessors</note> was created prince, not in the prophetic city of **Yathrib** <note>original: Ietriba; modern Medina</note> but in **Raqqa** <note>original: Aracha</note>, from which he set out with a large force to besiege **Yathrib** and kill **Ali** (whom many, however, write was his father). After a period of twenty years, leaving life and station, he left the empire to **Muawiya** <note>original: Moalbio</note>. This man persuaded **Syria** and occupied **Damascus**; he was otherwise a most bitter enemy of the Christians, though as they write, he conducted himself laudably among his own people. He was most skilled at taking plunder under the prophet; therefore the prophet foretold dominion for him. When he was removed, after the manner of the others, **Yazid** <note>original: Ieudus</note> received the kingdom. In that same manner, thirty **Caliphs** were butchered by factions and miserable slaughter without interruption, leaving the "virtue" of their law to be judged by posterity. 

If they had left life by natural death or honorably seeking it among enemies, it could be said that this is common to princes—that no tyrant enters the halls of **Pluto** <note>the Roman god of the underworld</note> with a "dry death" <note>a bloodless or natural death</note>. But if we consider any most unhappy state, even one born from the cruelest tyranny (as almost all empires are), and compare it with this one, without doubt the most unhappy would be supremely happy when compared to these men. **Lycurgus** gave laws with a feigned conversation with a deity, yet they brought safety to the Republic and destruction to none. The laws of **Solon**, **Zaleucus**, **Zamolxis**, and **Charondas** brought the greatest health to the republics using them. But this mad persuasion brought a plague to the fields, calamity to the fates, hardships to men, ruin to the world, dullness to minds, and finally to its own princes the kind of death the author deserved—yet no one noticed. The **Caesars** seized tyranny over the Republic, and among the first of them, perhaps fifteen (excepting a few) were killed by the seditions of veteran soldiers. The rest from that time either died manfully in war or at home among their own...

Postel argues that the internal bloodshed of Islamic history proves the "madness" of the religion, contrasting it with the beneficial laws of ancient Greek and Roman legislators.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Postel’s polemical history of the early Islamic expansion, contrasting the ends of Biblical and Christian figures with the rise of the Caliphate. He transitions from the internal strife of the early Caliphs (like Ali, mentioned on the previous page) to the broader geopolitical spread of "Arabian power" and the titles adopted by its leaders.</meta>

-># WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK II<-

...closed their days honorably. These men died among their children, parents, subjects, citizens, and friends. Now, if we compare those judges and kings who succeeded Moses—none of whom failed to die or pass away most honorably over the course of eight hundred years—with these others, it will then be seen how much the divine law differs from a lying and demonic one. I do not even bring up the piety, innocence, and charity of our own people <note>the Christians</note> to oppose them—beside whom those most unhappy people seem most happy—since the distinction between them is wider than that between light and darkness. For the sake of persuading and asserting the truth, for avoiding vice, and for preserving true piety toward God, the followers of Christ for nearly three hundred years voluntarily suffered death filled with every kind of torture and punishment. For if they had only wished to say this one phrase: "I am not a Christian," or "Christ is not God," they would have been acquitted and advanced with great honors.

But some **Muslim** <note>original: Musfulmanus</note> will object to me: "Our soldier and the followers of the prophet also die courageously for the sake of preserving and advocating for our religion." Indeed they die, I know, and many voluntarily throw themselves into dangers so that they may meet death after killing some enemy. But how far these actions they commit differ from true piety—and from a man who believes that an account of his deeds must be rendered to God—can be weighed from their way of life. For the soldier honors the prophet with every kind of pleasure; even the very pious sacrifice to their **saints** <note>original: diuis; Postel uses a classical term for "divine beings" or "saints"</note> and their dead with fine stews and a more refined palate. To have killed a man, to have plundered the property of others, and to have brought a stain upon one's own body and soul—provided the pretext of religion is present—the soldier considers that a matter of glory. With this **sinkhole of crimes** <note>original: lerna scelerum; a reference to the Lernean Hydra's swamp, signifying a multi-faceted evil</note>, as one most dear to God, he hastens voluntarily to those paradises which the prophet promised, so that he may contemplate for himself in a future life those supreme and eternal pleasures which he cannot obtain here. This is exactly as if a bull rushing into **lust** <note>original: in Venerem; literally "into Venus"</note>, while he attacks a rival with his horns, should perish in the conflict of pleasure. 

Christian martyrs, most famous for miracles, refuse no punishments so that they may worship God above all else, preserve themselves as worthy of God the Father, and save their fellow man as they would their own body and soul. Your people, while they are armed for the destruction of nature, rush headlong into death. 

But this **Arabian power** was split into various parts immediately in its hundredth year; once factions were created and leaders chosen, some were dispersed to the East, others to the North, and others to the West. Once Egypt was occupied—and "liberated," as they pretended, from the Roman magistrate who was crushing it—a **Caliph** <note>original: Chaliphos</note> was established in **Babylon** <note>This likely refers to the "Babylon of Egypt" (Old Cairo) or the general region of Mesopotamia/Baghdad</note>. Those who sought Assyria were called by the native word *benchi* <note>possibly a corruption of "Bey" or "Bin"</note>, that is, "lords." In Africa, they chose to call them **Sultans**, **Sharifs** <note>original: Seraphos</note>, and **Mawlas** <note>original: Maulas</note>, that is, the powerful, the wealthy, and protectors. The title common to all was **Emir**, and **Amir al-Mu'minin** <note>original: emír elmumín</note>, that is, "leader," and "leader of the faithful." Some of our people call them *Miramomeli*, and falsely think these are proper names. For it was a distinguished title of a prince, and an African one especially, which is evident even from coins. For they were inscribed in such a way, as I have found on very ancient money coined eight hundred years ago: "Joseph, **Commander of the Faithful** <note>original: emír elmumín</note>, son of the Commander of the Faithful, son of the Commander of the Faithful," all the way back to the great-great-grandfathers. 

With those regions lost through the sluggishness of the most cowardly Emperor **Heraclius**, it was very easy for them to retain the occupied lands since no one resisted. For **Constantine IV**, the fourth of that name, was forced to confirm a peace with the petty ruler of **Damascus**. I would have many more things to bring forward here if I wished to relate their histories exactly. But I am satisfied with noting the main points, weighing their outcomes, and revealing how they took possession of things. They gained power within a hundred years from the **Hegira** <note>original: Alhigera; the flight of Muhammad from Mecca</note> or exile, perhaps because the opportunity was offered when, a little while before, having refuted a foolish persuasion, the King and Queen of the **Persians** had received holy baptism and had come to Constantinople in the times of Constantine IV. However, they did not hold power much longer in **Persia**...

->### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-

faith. For when the Scythian forces under the leader **Mucaletio benco**—that is, "lord"—had been defeated, a certain petty king **Mahmedes** <note>likely a reference to a regional Muhammad or Mahmud</note> and **Imraël**, king of Persia, and the **Mahmedes** contending with him for the empire, were expelled by a newcomer. They eventually turned their forces, along with the remnants of the Scythians wandering here and there in Asia, toward the West. After Lesser Asia and the Armenians were subdued, they even dared, under the leadership of **Suleiman**, to seek out and besiege Constantinople, and to win over Thrace and the neighboring provinces. But after three years had passed, they were driven from the siege by a plague and forced to return to their own seats. At that same time (as that plague, like a scourge of God, was vexing the world), they rushed into Sicily and Campania, and held Sicily for several years. In Africa, matters succeeded for them according to their wishes, except when **Abdemelichus** <note>Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, 646–705 AD</note>, the **emir elmumin** <note>original: emirus elmumin; from the Arabic "Amir al-Mu'minin," meaning Commander of the Faithful</note>, was broken by John, the master of soldiers acting under **Justinian II**. But due to the faction of **Leontius** and the patriarch **Gallinicus**, **Justinian** was deprived of his empire and his nose <note>Justinian II was nicknamed "Rhinotmetos" or "the Slit-Nosed" after this mutilation</note> and sent into exile; thus he could not pursue the happily begun matter, as the tyrant **Leontius** occupied the empire. But the injury inflicted upon that most excellent emperor did not go unavenged. For **Apsimarus**, elected emperor by the army, deprived **Leontius** of his nose and empire and committed him to perpetual prison. Thus the Moors and **Muslims** <note>original: Mussulmani</note> lost their most excellent adversary, **Justinian**. For ten years earlier, **Amurathus** had agreed with him that, with Africa and Libya restored, he would pay to the empire one thousand gold pieces, one slave, and one horse every day for a full decade on account of the other provinces he occupied. Therefore, the fire that was nearly extinguished under **Leontius**—who consumed the treasury among harlots and abused it to gain favor (as is the custom of tyrants)—revived and raged far more cruelly than before. For they progressed even to the borders of Mauritania. There, however, while the prefect **Julian** was acting in the name of the empire, a dire and foul opportunity presented itself from **Roderick**, the king of the Goths ruling Spain. For while the most beautiful daughter of **Julian** was staying with the king’s wife for the sake of cultivation of manners and character, the foul and shameful king forced himself upon the maiden. Some say he could not obtain from her father the right to take her as a wife, and therefore sinned out of the vehemence of love. However the matter stands, the father **Julian**, moved by the just grief of the injury to his daughter, summoned a massive force of the neighboring **Muslims** and provided them leadership into Spain against **Roderick**. They crossed the strait, invaded, plundered, killed **Roderick**, established a kingdom, and subjugated all of Spain within three years. Not long after, **Julian** was crushed by them. For such is their loyalty toward friends: they immediately remove from their midst those whose labor they have used. I do not see what could be judged more foreign to humanity than this. Indeed, this can sometimes be done justly by a prince if the one who helped had acquired a formidable power; but to rage against a helpless friend truly fights against the law of humanity. Not long after Spain was conquered, another opportunity arose for invading even the Gauls <note>France</note>. For **Eudo**, prince of Aquitaine, being unequal in strength to the kings of Gaul with whom he was waging war, invited into Gaul that lost scum, which immediately showed the man what kind of assistance he had summoned. For whatever cities there were from the ridge of the Pyrenees mountains to the borders of the Pictones and Turoni <note>Poitiers and Tours</note> were pillaged and overturned, so that no greater devastation was ever seen or heard of among any nations than that where the **Muslim** army proceeded. Whereupon **Eudo**, like a "Phrygian wise too late" <note>original: Phryx et fero sapiens; a Latin proverb for someone who only learns through disaster</note>, having settled a peace with **Charles Martel** who then held the scepters of the kingdom, killed three hundred and seventy-five thousand in one day with the strength of the Gallic and Aquitanian armies alongside **Martel**. The rest, who were living in Narbonne, Toulouse, Salses, and other places under the jurisdiction of **Eudo** because of a treaty they had entered, were proscribed. Thus was that scum driven out of Gaul in the tenth year from which it had been called. They occupied Spain from the year of Christ 730 until 1400 or thereabouts. Indeed, how much peace they have among their own, is shown by the fact that in that same place...

20. In twenty years, they finished off fifteen of their own princes; nor did the usual slaughter cease until a certain Alhatabus <note>likely Al-Ashraf Sayf ad-Din Inal or a similar 15th-century Sultan; Postel's spelling of Oriental names often reflects phonetic transcriptions of his era</note>, to ensure the same did not happen to him as it had to the others, removed three hundred nobles from the midst, and thus reigned for a longer time. But perhaps it turned out more fortunately for the others. One may judge by their primary power. The wealth of the **Saracens**, as they are called, was always most flourishing in Egypt; therefore, it is likely that the example of those below depends upon this primary power. I will, therefore, touch upon their affairs summarily and insofar as it pertains to the matter. Because (as I have already noted before) they fear that their crimes will be seen and known by posterity, they do not care to record them in writing, nor do they wish to publish what has been recorded. 

In Egypt, although the rule was varied and held by those entirely different from the **Caliph** <note>original: Chalipha</note>—that is, the high priest, upon whom the authority of the law depends—nevertheless, until another of equal power opposed him in Baghdad in Chaldea, the other provinces always wished the final decision in doubtful matters to depend upon his opinion. This was **not for the authority of the law, but for the sake of order**, even though his dignity always appeared greater and more sublime than the others, because the first successors of Muhammad exercised both sacred and profane authority, and they fixed their seat there before power became divided. Since I have been able to obtain nothing regarding sacred matters except through the memory and reports of more recent writings, I shall speak of the profane authority, which is called that of the **Sultans** and the **Mamluks**. 

For when this nation acquires new seats, it wishes to abolish all monuments of those who came before, not only among foreign nations but even among their own, so that they might appear to be the first ones brought forth into the world as rulers. Therefore, they even change proper names, so that you might not recognize your own people in their writings: they utter Saul as **Talut**, Goliath as **Jalut**, David as **Dawud**, Solomon as **Suleiman**, Job as **Ayyub**, Moses as **Musa**, Jesus as **Isa**, John as **Yahya**, and many other names in an inverted fashion. 

They do the same with the names of provinces and cities. Mesopotamia is called **Merdin** and **Chorassan**, Armenia is **Erminly**, Cilicia is **Caramanly**, Galatia is **Othmanty**, Asia is **Natolda** <note>Anatolia</note>, Greece is **Romly**, Mysia is called **Bogdan**, Constantinople is **Stambol**, Adrianople is **Ederne**, and Pera is **Calata**. And thus they hasten to abolish not only the things themselves but the memory of them handed down in literature, entirely neglecting the writings of others.

<margin>The affairs of the Mamluks.</margin>
The affairs of the Mamluks are as follows. When frequent incursions were made into Asia and Europe two hundred years ago by peoples subject to the North, a certain nation belonging to the regions of Lake Maeotis and the Black Sea—once called the **Cercetae** and now the **Circassians**—having created a leader from among themselves and left only that portion of their people at home for whom the land could provide, sought out the Armenias and came into the borders of northern Syria, where they began to be formidable. Since those soldiers had no fixed seats, they began to serve as mercenaries among their neighbors. From this, it happened that a great addition of that nation was made to the Sultan of Egypt, and those Circassians were like the "slaves of the prince," which is what the term implies. 

For **Mamluk** <term>original: Mamluch; meaning "one who is owned"</term> signifies a royal slave, a word derived from **Melich** <note>Malik</note>, that is, "king." Taking the opportunity, since that nation never failed in Egypt from their first hiring, they did away with the proper prince and elected one from among themselves to preside over everyone and rule by certain laws approved among them. The first in human memory was **Cahith bencus** <note>Al-Ashraf Qaitbay, reigned 1468–1496. Postel interprets "bencus" as "lord" or "bey."</note>, that is, Lord Cahith, who dictated laws to the Egyptians from the Circassian perspective. Before him, the Sultans had reigned for nearly four hundred years, not without the help of the Circassians. For from the time they made their first incursion into Asia, they were sold every year by the neighboring Tartars from the remnants of their people, especially by those who are Muslims. For the Circassians who live near the Cimmerian mountains have given their names to Christ and are initiated in the Greek rite. After Cahith bencus, who reigned for thirty-three years, a great faction arose. For two Mamluk leaders began to contend with one another for the empire; one was called **Campsous** <note>Qansuh al-Ghawri</note>, the other **Acbardinus**...

-> ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD <-

...was observed. **Kansuh**, whose name was Qansuh al-Ghawri <note>original: Campfonicam; likely referring to the Mamluk Sultan Al-Ashraf Qansuh al-Ghawri</note>, so that he might more easily turn the minds of everyone toward himself, with difficulty persuaded the dying **Qaitbay** <note>original: Caitho; Sultan Al-Ashraf Qaitbay, d. 1496</note> to command that his fifteen-year-old son should reign after him. The father barely complied with this, because he knew the customs of his people and clearly saw where things were heading. For he saw that it would happen that, once the son was killed, Kansuh would seize the tyranny for himself. Nor was he mistaken. For before the young man had completed two years in his reign—not without the blood of citizens and nobles—the fraud was uncovered while he attempted to remove them with a poisoned banquet; he was judged an enemy and killed. 

With open hostilities finally breaking out, **Azbak** <note>original: Acbardinus</note> and Kansuh clashed; Azbak was bound and ended his days shortly thereafter. **Kansuh** <note>original: Chamſaus</note> then reigned, and as a reward for his favor, he created **Tuman Bay** <note>original: Tomumbencum</note> as the *Emirchebir* <note>original: Emirchebir; from the Arabic 'Amir al-Kabir', meaning Great Prince</note>—that is, the Great Duke, or as you might say, the Prefect of the Palace and the Military—because he had cut down the youth Muhammad <note>the son of Qaitbay</note> for the sake of the nobles. 

Meanwhile, **Janbalat** <note>original: Iambellatus</note>, the emir of Damascus in Syria, did not approve of the election of Kansuh and prepared for war. Kansuh—though not without suspicion of what later occurred, but because he could do nothing else—gave Tuman Bay the task of breaking Janbalat’s forces. They set out, held a parley, came to an agreement, and Kansuh was betrayed and driven from his kingdom. He fled to the citadel of **Alexandria**, where he was besieged, captured, and thrown into prison, having not yet completed twenty months on the throne. Janbalat was created and crowned Sultan; but while he seized the property of everyone, he fell into the hatred of the **Circassians** <note>original: Cerceticorum; the ethnic group that formed the elite of the Egyptian Mamluk military</note>, was captured, and strangled. 

Tuman Bay, succeeding him, was no more humane, but in the beginning, he began to act more moderately. By assessing every house in **Cairo** <note>original: Alcahiri</note>, he demanded six months’ worth of their rent, and immediately another equal amount, and finally a rent of ten months. He proceeded to proscribe, kill, and plunder foreigners, Christians, and Jews, and he divided their assets in such a way that unless any merchant immediately paid as much as the tyrant valued his life, he would be slaughtered and his goods assigned to the tyrant. And because he did not spare even the leading men in these matters, he was besieged; he fled through tunnels from the palace until, on the fortieth day, he was found by the associates of Janbalat, betrayed, and killed. 

Such is the state of those men who live under the law of Muhammad. All things are similar to one another, since none of those princes believes that there is a God. Then, by the consensus of everyone—though very much against his will and fearing danger—**Kansuh al-Ghawri** <note>original: Chamzaus Chaurus</note> was elected, and he reigned for a longer time, until he died, trampled in the middle of Syria by **Sultan Selim** <note>Selim I, the Ottoman Sultan</note>, the father of Suleiman. That was the end. 

It is no wonder for one tyrant to follow another. But that a brother should rise against brothers—that indeed is usually a source of wonder to us who are ignorant of those plagues. For no petty king reigns without the blood of his brothers or kinsmen, as I have heard from many places among the barbarians themselves in Africa. **Muley Muhammad** <note>original: Maule Muhamedes; the Hafsid Sultan of Tunis</note>, who now commands in **Tunis**, and to whom the **Emperor Charles** <note>Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor</note> restored his empire after driving out **Hayreddin Barbarossa** <note>original: Hairadino Aenobarbo; the famous Ottoman corsair and admiral</note> (a Greek man and a pirate), began his reign with the blood of seventeen brothers and as many kinsmen. Indeed, this is not usually considered a vice; since even the Law, by which they seem to mock God, does not prohibit it. For Muhammad advised in the **Quran** <note>original: Alcorano</note> that in the "Way of God" no account should be held of son, or father, or brother, much less of others. Each man, while he strives for power, says that he is in the "Way of God." Therefore, all things are permitted to him, since nothing is considered a vice. 

What shall I say of the "Scourge of God," **Timur** <note>original: Demirly; from the Turkic 'Demir' meaning Iron</note>, whom we call **Tamerlane**? Was there ever a man more made of iron than that Muhammadan? He was well-named; when crowds of infants, virgins, and priests approached him after his edicts, he trampled them like mud. For he valued a human being no more than a stone or a fungus.

<margin>Turkish affairs.</margin>
The affairs of the **Turks** are perhaps better; let us see. The first who began to organize their affairs as they are held today was called **Osman** <note>original: Odmanus; Osman I, founder of the Ottoman dynasty</note>, who, having oppressed many neighboring leaders, made incursions into Asia Minor in the year 1329 after the Passion of Christ. From him, they are called **Ottomans** <note>original: Odmanni</note>. It is thus a little more than two hundred years...

...rebellion <note>original: -nis; completing 'rebellionis' or 'seditionis' from the previous page</note>, from which this empire emerged; and through the sluggishness, envy, and factionalism of the Greek emperors, it arrived at the power it now holds. Their eleventh emperor, **Suleiman** <note>Suleiman the Magnificent, r. 1520–1566</note>, now holds power—a man certainly (for that nation) of the greatest humanity and equity. **Orhan** <note>original: Orcanes; Orhan Ghazi, r. 1323–1362</note>, having conquered all of Asia Minor, even captured Bursa, the royal seat of the emperors in Asia. His son **Murad** <note>original: Hamurathes; Murad I, r. 1362–1389</note>, summoned into Europe by an imperial faction, after giving victory to his ally, summoned his own men, who occupied what had been acquired for his friends. That factionalism teaches what it brings to summon a more powerful enemy for help. While he was being incautious among his attendants, he was finished off <gloss>killed</gloss> by a servant with a dagger. While his son **Bayezid** <note>Bayezid I, known as "The Thunderbolt"</note> more attentively followed his father’s undertakings in Europe, the "Wrath of God," **Tamerlane** <note>Timur the Lame, the Central Asian conqueror</note>, arose in Asia. When Bayezid opposed him with unequal force, he was captured by him and, bound in golden chains, was paraded around in a cage as a spectacle until he ended his days in Syria from hardship. **Mehmed Çelebi** <note>original: Cyris celebris; likely Mehmed I Çelebi</note> meanwhile strengthened affairs in Europe as best he could, until Asia Minor was brought back under control by **Mehmed I**. His successor, **Murad II** <note>original: Hamurathes secundus</note>, added all of Thrace and the Peloponnese, along with many other provinces, to the empire. **Mehmed II** <note>Mehmed the Conqueror, who took the city in 1453</note> captured and plundered Constantinople, along with many other places; and after many most famous deeds, he handed the kingdom to his son **Bayezid**. He <note>Bayezid II</note>, born more for peace and the study of philosophy than for war, died after being removed by poison by his son **Selim**. Thus, through Selim, power came to Suleiman. This is the summary of events, this is the order.

This history has been written extensively by many, so I do not dwell on it, since it is not my purpose to speak of the origin or progress of events, nor of famous deeds. I run through briefly by what arts they obtained their empires. **Bayezid I**, so that he might reign more securely, did away with his brother Suleiman. **Orhan**, son of Mehmed Çelebi <note>original: Cyri celebe</note>, was oppressed by his uncle **Musa**; and Musa, in turn, by **Mehmed**, Orhan's brother. Another **Mehmed**, having killed his brother, enjoyed the empire more securely. But nothing is more famous than **Selim** <note>Selim I "The Grim"</note>, who, having killed his father and his brothers and relatives, would even have removed his own legitimate son (unless the most prudent mother of the now-reigning Suleiman had forewarned the youth), lest the same thing happen to him as he had done to his father. These are the "benefits" of the Law of Muhammad <note>Postel uses this term to refer to Islam and its legal-political framework</note>. Let the Muslims <note>original: Mussulmani</note> read the histories of the Christians, and they will see the difference between the laws of Christ and those of the devil. I say nothing of the wearing down of subjects; the world and the memory of letters <note>scholarship and literacy</note> have never been in such a state of desolation as they are under the law of Muhammad, and will be, unless resistance is made. 

The Romans once collected more taxes from Egypt alone than the King of the Turks now takes from all of Asia and his entire empire; and yet the affairs of the people were most flourishing, even after an annual exaction of fifteen million <note>units of currency, likely sesterces or ducats</note>, as we call them. Certainly double that was demanded from Asia and paid. Today, taxes are wrung from all common people down to their very skin and soul, and yet the total does not even reach a quarter of that great sum. Because of the foul exactions of princes who have no fear of God before their eyes, people in all of Africa—formerly the most excellent cultivated province of the world—as well as in Egypt and Arabia, prefer to become **Nomads** <note>original: Nomades</note> rather than remain as farmers subject to the lust and plunder of others. If I am making anything up, there are most abundant witnesses: both those who are worn down by countless exactions, and those who openly swoop down upon the fortunes of others. Therefore, the desolation of the world can be called the "Muhammadan Law" rather than the Law of God, who wishes to cherish all things and for them to live in peace, and to endure for a very long time by proving Himself to them.

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...was [conducted] <note>original: "-batur"; the end of a verb from the previous page, likely "gerebatur" or "trahebatur"</note>. **Campsous** <note>Qansuh al-Ghuri, r. 1501–1516</note>, whose name was Campsonica, in order to more easily turn the minds of everyone toward himself, with difficulty obtained from the dying **Caithus** <note>Qaitbay, r. 1468–1496</note> a decree that his fifteen-year-old son should reign after him. The father was reluctant to comply with this because he knew the customs of the nation and saw clearly where things were heading. For he saw that once the son was killed, Campsous would seize the tyranny for himself. Nor was he mistaken. For before the youth had spent two years in the kingdom—and not without the blood of citizens and nobles—the fraud was uncovered while Campsous attempted to remove them with a poisoned banquet. He was judged an enemy and killed. Finally, with hostilities in the open, **Acbardinus** and **Campsous** clashed; Acbardinus was defeated and closed his days <gloss>died</gloss> shortly thereafter. **Chamsaus** <note>likely Janbalat, though the names are fluid in 16th-century Latin transliteration</note> reigned and, as a reward for his favor, made **Tomumbencus** <note>Tuman bay I</note> the <term>Emir-chebir</term> <note>Arabic: *Amīr al-kabīr*, meaning "Great Commander" or "General-in-Chief"</note>, which is to say the Great Duke, as if you were to say the prefect of the guard and the military, because he had slaughtered the young **Muhamed** to please the nobles. 

Meanwhile, **Iambellatus** <note>Janbalat</note>, the emir of Damascus in Syria, did not approve of the election of Chamsaus and prepared for war. Chamsaus—though not without suspicion of what would later happen, but because he could not act otherwise—gave the task of breaking the forces of Iambellatus to Tomumbencus. He set out; they held a conference and came to an agreement. Chamsaus was betrayed, driven from the kingdom, and fled to the citadel of Alexandria, where he was besieged, captured, and thrown into prison before he had even completed twenty months on the throne. Iambellatus was created and crowned Sultan. But while he fell upon the property of everyone, he incurred the hatred of the <term>Cerceticorum</term> <note>Circassians, the ruling elite of the Mamluk Sultanate</note>, and was captured and strangled. 

Tomumbencus, succeeding him, was no more humane, but began to vent his rage more moderately at first. By assessing a tax on the head of every house in Cairo <note>original: "Alcahiri"</note>, he demanded six months’ worth of their rent, then immediately as much again, and finally ten months’ rent. He began to proscribe, kill, and plunder foreigners, Christians, and Jews, and to seize their resources in such a way that unless any merchant paid immediately whatever amount the tyrant demanded, he would be slaughtered and his goods assigned to the tyrant. And because in these matters he did not spare even the leading men, he was besieged and fled from the palace through tunnels, until on the fortieth day he was found by the associates of Iambellatus, betrayed, and killed. 

Such is the state of those men who live under the Law of Muhammad. All are similar to one another, because none of those princes believes that God exists. Then **Chamzaus Chaurus** <note>Qansuh al-Ghuri, here called by a variation of his name</note> was elected by the consent of all—though he was quite unwilling and feared the danger. He reigned for a longer time until he died, trampled in the middle of Syria by **Sultan Selim** <note>Selim I, r. 1512–1520</note>, the father of **Suleiman**. That was the end. 

It is no wonder for a tyrant to rage against a tyrant. But for a brother to rage against brothers—that is truly something to be wondered at by us, who are ignorant of such plagues. For no minor ruler, as I have heard from the barbarians themselves in many places in Africa, reigns without the blood of his brothers or kinsmen. **Mawlay Muhammad** <note>Muley Hassan, r. 1526–1543</note>, who now rules in Tunis, and to whom the **Emperor Charles** <note>Holy Roman Emperor Charles V</note> restored the empire after driving out **Hayreddin Barbarossa** <note>original: "Hairadino Aenobarbo"; the famous Ottoman privateer and admiral</note>, a Greek pirate—that man inaugurated his reign with the blood of seventeen brothers and as many kinsmen. Indeed, this is not usually considered a vice among them, because the Law—by which they seem to mock God—does not prohibit it. For Muhammad urged in the **Quran** <note>original: "Alcorano"</note> that in the "Way of God" <note>original: "in uia Dei"; referring to Jihad or religious struggle</note> no account should be held of a son, a father, or a brother, much less of others. Each one, while he strives for empire, says he is "in the Way of God"; therefore everything is permitted to him, since nothing is a vice. 

What shall I say of the "Scourge of God," **Demirly**, whom we call **Tamerlane**? Was there ever a man of iron more so than that Muhammadan? He was well-named <note>Demirly/Timur means "Iron" in Turkic languages</note>: when crowds of infants, virgins, and priests approached him after his edicts, he trampled them like mud. For he did not value a human being more than a stone or a mushroom. Perhaps the affairs of the Turks are better; we shall see.
