# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK II

...of years <note>original: "annis"</note>, from which this empire emerged; and through the sluggishness, envy, and factionalism of the Greek emperors, it arrived at the power it now holds. The eleventh of their emperors, **Suleiman** <note>Suleiman the Magnificent, r. 1520–1566</note>, now holds power—a man certainly of the highest humanity and equity (at least for that nation). **Orcanes** <note>Orhan, r. 1324–1362</note>, having conquered all of Asia Minor, also took Bursa, the royal seat of the emperors in Asia. His son **Hamurathes** <note>Murad I, r. 1362–1389</note>, summoned into Europe by a faction of the [Greek] Emperor, brought in his own men after a victory was given to the confederates; these men then occupied what had been acquired for their friends. That factionalism teaches us what it brings to call a more powerful enemy to one’s aid. While he was insufficiently cautious regarding his associates, he was finished off by a servant with a dagger. While his son **Bayazetes** <note>Bayezid I, r. 1389–1403</note> followed his father’s undertakings in Europe more intently, the wrath of God, **Tamerlanes** <note>Timur the Lame</note>, arose in Asia. When Bayazetes opposed him with unequal strength, he was captured by him and, bound with golden chains, was led about in a cage as a spectacle until he ended his days in Syria from the toil. Meanwhile, **Cyris** <note>Mehmed I, known as Çelebi</note>, a man of celebrated deeds, confirmed affairs in Europe as best he could, until Asia Minor was received back into power by the first **Muhamed** <note>Mehmed I</note>. The subsequent **Hamurathes II** <note>Murad II</note> added all of Thrace and the Peloponnese to the empire, along with many other provinces. **Mahmetes II** <note>Mehmed II, the Conqueror</note>, along with very many other places, captured and plundered Constantinople; after many most famous deeds, he handed the kingdom to his son **Baiazeto** <note>Bayezid II</note>. The latter, born more for peace and the study of philosophy than for war, died having been removed by poison by his son **Selimus** <note>Selim I</note>. Thus, through Selim, affairs came to Suleiman. This is the summary of events and their order.

This history has been written copiously by many; for that reason, I do not dwell upon it, since it is not my purpose to speak of the origin and progress of these matters or their famous deeds. I run through them in a few words to show by what arts <note>methods or schemes</note> they obtained their empires. Bayazetes I, so that he might reign more securely, finished off his brother **Soliman**. **Orcanes**, the son of Cyris the Noble <note>original: "Cyri celeby"</note>, was oppressed by his uncle **Moses**; Moses, however, was oppressed by **Muhamed**, the brother of Orcanes. The second Muhamed, having killed his brother, enjoyed the empire more securely. But nothing is more famous than Selim, who, having killed his father and his brothers and relatives, would even have removed his own legitimate son (unless the most prudent mother of the now-reigning Suleiman had forewarned the youth), lest the same fate should befall him as he had inflicted on his own father.

These are the "benefits" of the law of Muhammad. Let the Muslims <note>original: "Mussulmani"</note> read the histories of the Christians, and they will see what a difference there is between the laws of Christ and those of the devil. I say nothing of the wearing down of the subjects. The world, in the memory of literature, was never in such a state of desolation as it is under the law of Muhammad, and as it will be unless it is resisted. Formerly, the Romans received more taxes from Egypt alone than the King of the Turks <note>The Sultan</note> now takes from all of Asia and his entire empire; and yet the affairs of the peoples were most flourishing then, even after an annual extraction of fifteen million, as we call it. Certainly, double that was commanded and paid in Asia. Today, tax is exacted from all the common people down to the skin and soul, and yet the total does not reach even a fraction <note>original: "quadrantes"</note> of such a great number. Because of the foul exactions of princes who have nothing of God before their eyes, the inhabitants of all Africa—formerly the most distinguished cultivated province of the world—as well as in Egypt and Arabia, prefer to become Nomads <note>wandering tribes/Bedouins</note> rather than remain open to another's lust and plunder while they till the fields. If I am imagining anything, there are most wealthy witnesses, both those who are worn down by innumerable exactions and those who professedly swoop down upon the fortunes of others. Therefore, the desolation of the world can be called the "Muhammadan Law" rather than the Law of God, who wishes to nourish all things and for them to live in peace, and to endure for the longest time by proving itself to Him.

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

### THE FIRST ENCOUNTER WITH THE MUSLIMS <note>original: "Mussulmanis"</note> ALREADY
->translated into Arabic by the author, the title of which in Arabic is, *A compendium of all doctrines which are required for human excellence.* It contains, in truth, a summary proof of the Trinity, praises of Jesus Christ and the Gospel excerpted from the Quran <note>original: "Alcorano"</note>, and the primary errors of that persuasion.<-

In the name of God, the merciful and pious. <note>This opening phrase mirrors the Islamic "Basmala"</note> Praise be to God, the most powerful, wisest, and best King of the Ages, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things; and peace to those who are strengthened by Him, and to those seeking Him in truth: and may the clemency of God, and peace, and mercy be upon all men. Amen.

Before every thing, a cause or causes preceded it, since no thing creates itself. Therefore, before all things is the highest God, powerful over all. The high God created this orb and world for His own praise, for the utility of men, and for both together. These three are one end, or the final cause <term>final cause: "causa finalis," the ultimate purpose or goal for which a thing exists</term> of the world. Man was created for the praise of God, for his own innocence and purity, and for the love of neighbor. It is necessary that these three be present in every good work, as a single thing: because it is not possible for a good work to exist without these three.

Every thing is either from the hand of God, or from the wisdom and will of men, or from the power of fortune.

In the power of God immediately are all things, but especially eternity and essence, the heavens, the stars, change, motion, rest, the natural order, and the four natures—namely fire, air, water, and earth—and those things which are born from them. Man, however, with prudence and reason, finds the roots and principles of non-natural things, and through his handling, he explains them into science and art. From chance <note>original: "casu"</note>, however, are those things which happen that have no likeness to the work of God or of men: such as are fortuitous events and non-natural or non-divine accidents. And every thing which has no cause in nature—and in short, all the disturbances of this life and its unhappiness—he calls the work of fortune. But the aim and end of God is to lead man, with faith and certainty, into his own necessity, the utility of necessary things, and into the knowledge of himself and the recognition of God, so that faith may then be given to men; so that man may become holy with virtue and the love of the highest good, and so that after this life he may know the cause of all things in the highest God. The point at which man ought to aim, however, is to console other afflicted men pressed by necessity, to help the rich and the poor, to harm no one, and to live as the precepts of divine and human law command him: and to dwell in this world as if in an inn, as one for whom the world is a single city, if he be wise. Fortune has no goal, since it acts nothing by its own will.

In every work there is a likeness to its author. But since in every simple natural thing there is an image of the trinity, it is necessary that in God, who created all things, there be a trinity. For nothing can be the same in all things at once without it being in their creator. Therefore, in what follows it will be seen that it is not possible for us to understand the highest God without the trinity. We shall begin, therefore, from the definition of God. God is the first cause of all nature, moving all things, commanding all things, power, wisdom, and love, which acts in the universe just as the soul and the intellect act in the human body, stirring all motions as He wills. Man, however, carries out his works with will and judgment (unless he is compelled); his intellect penetrates into every thing except God. And therefore the Greeks call him a "microcosm" <note>original Greek: μικρόκοσμον</note>, that is, a "small world," because in him is the example of God and of lower matter. For man lives in matter with the plants, feels with the living creatures, and understands and gathers with the angels and spiritual substances, speak-

## THESE ARE EXCERPTS FROM CHAPTER III OF THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD.
->Demonstration of the trinity in the divine nature.<-

It cannot happen that anything is made without power. However, although God is powerful, He does nothing without wisdom. But after power and wisdom, it is necessary that love or desire, or will, be present. Therefore, God is powerful, wise, and benevolent toward all things before He creates them. Thus power, wisdom, and love are one God. Power is the first person or subsistence <term>subsistence: "subsistentia," a philosophical term for an individual existence or "person" within the unified nature of God</term>, and therefore it is that which Christians call God the Father. But because from that power, wisdom is generated from eternity—without which nothing would be created—they call it the Son of God and His Word. And because from both proceeds love and will toward the things to be created, they name it the Holy Spirit. 

And properly, the Father is powerful, the Son is wise, and the Holy Spirit is loving—one God. They are one thing in their essence: all power is in wisdom and love, all wisdom is in power and love, and all love is in wisdom and power. This is just as an inheritance is one single thing, whether it exists as a thought in the mind, as text in a legal book, or as the physical place itself. <note>Postel uses the example of a "haereditas" (inheritance) to show how one reality can exist in three different modes without being three different things.</note> For they do not speak of three gods, but of one God: powerful, wise, and benevolent. 

Just as in every labor or work there is thought, speech, and operation, and yet there are not three works but one work; so power, wisdom, and benevolence, since they are different things, are one God and not three. Since power, force, or strength are properties of the beginning—that is, the Father; wisdom, however, or science, or knowledge are properties of the middle—that is, the Son; while will or love toward things, for the sake of the end, is a property of the completion—that is, the Holy Spirit. Therefore, in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, just as there is only one divinity, so power, wisdom, and love are one. 

Just as in every work, thought is a property of the beginning, the word or explanation is the property of the bridge between thought and art, and the operation has the property of the end and completion—and yet in every work, the thought, explanation, and operation are one thing. In this way, Christians do not think, nor do they affirm, that there are three gods, but that God is one in trinity, and threefold in unity; unity in trinity, and trinity in unity in the One. Nor can the intellect grasp God without power, wisdom, and love.

God is the intellect and mind powerful over all beings. And therefore, since He understands all beings in His essence, it is necessary that He knows and understands Himself and His substance in Himself. For unless He knew His substance in Himself, He would not be omnipotent. Therefore, it is necessary that God be the understanding intellect <note>original: "intellectus intelligens"</note> and the understood mind <note>original: "mens intellecta"</note>. But because of the knowledge of Himself, He has love and joy, since without knowledge of one's own good no one rejoices, and every man rejoices with the knowledge of his own virtue. 

God, therefore, according to His knowledge, rejoices in Himself more than all men. For that reason, in God, the understanding intellect, the understood mind, and love or joy are one thing. The understanding mind is the Father, the understood mind is the Son, and joy is the Holy Spirit. The Father is in His Son, the Son is in His Father, and the Spirit or love is one thing in the Father and the Son: substance in substance, or thing in thing, person in person, having nothing prior or posterior except in the order of naming and understanding. In these persons, there is no confusion, nor is there separation.

Just as in the dominion of the world there is a trinity in unity in every power (for nothing happens without God, heaven, and matter), so in the administration of individual kingdoms it is fitting that there be a trinity in unity, since nevertheless the rule or administration is one, which has priests or pontiffs, and a king...

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD
### Book I, Chapter III (Continued)

...and judges, and this is a single power or force: spiritual power, corporal power, and a middle power. Priests are like the servants of the Most High God in spiritual matters, kings in corporal <note>meaning physical or worldly</note> matters, and judges in both, acting as the hands of both. However, this administration is one: for kings do not reign without the servants of God (or religion), nor do priests reign without a governing authority, nor do these two achieve anything without equity and judges. Therefore, there is one power in a trinity. Nor is it possible for power to exist for long without this trinity. These things are necessary for preserving peace, just as power, wisdom, and love are necessary for God. For this reason, in every good work, it is necessary that there be equity of the heart, as well as human—that is, civil or social—equity, and a judicial or coercive force; for equity is not that which thinks of evil, or does it, or resists the law. Therefore, since good in this world cannot be held or preserved without a trinity, it is necessary that God, the fountain of good—from whose goodness these goods are given to man—possesses the trinity within Himself most perfectly, a trinity whose image is never absent.

Likewise, in natural virtue <note>original: "virtute naturali," referring to the inherent power or properties of things</note> there is unity in trinity, and trinity in unity, as I have said: there is a superior virtue, an inferior virtue, and a middle one. The highest virtue is found in spiritual natures—first in the highest God, and secondly in the angels and the citizens of paradise. The middle virtue is in the heavens and the stars, and from both of these comes the third, the elemental virtue, in which every body acts and suffers. These, however, are one virtue, because nature is only one.

Similarly, in every natural body there is a trinity in unity, and vice versa. For in every body there is a constancy of power, a progress from that power, and a love or "choice" during the act of doing. As we see in fire, its force or power lies in its constancy to burn, and from that power proceeds its action or operation; it acts more readily on a thin, light, and dry body than on a dense, hard, and moist one. From this, we see that there is something in it resembling a choice. Yet these things are one single force. For without power a thing cannot act, nor does it act at all without the progress of the action, nor does it act except upon a body that is prepared and "chosen" for it. In the same way, pepper burns the tongue rather than the skin by acting perpetually; nor does it cease to act until it perishes, or until a body fit for feeling the action is no longer present. The same judgment must be made for other things. Just as in the sun there is the solar body (or its center), its light, and its virtue; and these three are one in the sun. And while it acts, these three are one from one sun.

Furthermore, in every body there is <term>matter and form: the two fundamental principles of any object in Aristotelian philosophy—matter is the "stuff" and form is the "essence" or "shape" that makes it what it is</term>, and the composite made from both. These three are one body, nor is it possible for any thing to be made from matter without this trinity in unity. Form gives "being" to the thing, matter carries and sustains it, and the composite possesses both; yet one is not the other.

In the dimension of every body there is a trinity in unity; before any quantity can be known, there is length, breadth, and depth, for without these no measure will be recognized. In motion there is time—in the past, the future, and the present—nor can any one of these be known without the others. In every operation there is an <term>agent, an instrument, and a patient: the doer (agent), the tool used (instrument), and the thing being acted upon (patient)</term>. Every work is made by an agent, matter, and operation. The whole, indeed, is in the power of the agent, the whole is in the matter, and the whole is in the work; yet they are not three separate works, but one. This is the image of God.

Similarly, in spiritual nature there is unity in trinity, whether it be a spirit without a body, a spirit endowed with a body, or a spirit in a middle condition. The first is in God, angels, and demons, for they do not have a body. The second is in the elements: in that which only exists, or that which exists and lives, or that which exists, lives, and feels. For all life endowed with matter exists in these three stages. For an inferior spirit is in every thing, and properly in living things that lack intellect. But the third and middle, which is sometimes in a body, some-

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK II.

What is outside is either the soul or the intellect of man, in which there is a trinity in unity, and vice versa. For in the soul of man, there is a collection of sensations, reasoning <note>original: "collectio," referring to the gathering of thoughts or logical synthesis</note>, and memory; nor can it happen that these are separated from one another, for the whole soul is present in sensation and apprehension, the whole in reasoning or thought, and the whole in memory. This is the image of the highest God. The entire spirit of lower nature consists in the faculty of loving, attracting, and preserving; it is only one in the whole, and one in any part, and that is the image of God. So it is in the natural, vital, and animal faculties <note>these refer to the three "spirits" of medieval physiology: the natural (liver), vital (heart), and animal (brain)</note>. So too in the souls of brute animals there is apprehension, imagination, and memory: these three are one soul, which cannot be conceived without them. In all cognition, there is opinion (or imagination), doubt, and truth. For first we have an opinion about unknown things; if they are in the middle, we doubt; finally, through proof, we come to the truth. The whole mind is in the one, and the whole is in each individual part. Life is either merely natural (or vegetative), or sensitive, or intellective along with the body; the second does not exist without the first, nor the third without the first two. Yet life is one: it proceeds from the heart, lungs, and brain, through the veins, arteries, and nerves, mutually composing one harmony. Without the first parts, there is no place for the second. This is the image of God, who preserves all things in a trinity.

Regarding the tradition of every doctrine that comes into practice, it is not possible for it to exist without logical contemplation and operation <note>action or work</note>, as I taught above. The whole matter exists in contemplation, the whole in reason (or rational expression), and the whole in the work. Thus, in all of nature, we see the exemplar and footprint of the Trinity which is in the highest God, since He is the all-powerful Author over all things, who gave us this world in which His image resides, so that we might know Him, and His goodness bestowed upon us, and that we might praise Him forever. Therefore, God begot from His own power the wisdom and knowledge of all things, through which He created all things in love. Therefore, before anything was created, God begot His Son, whom the prophets called the Word of God <note>original: "verbum Dei"</note>, using a metaphor that can be understood by us. Just as we speak after we have thought, so after the power of God, we understand His Son as the Word, as if He were the Son of the Mind. They also called Him Wisdom, because it follows immediately after Power. From both, indeed, proceeds the Holy Spirit in eternity: these three are one God—powerful, wise, loving, glorious, judge, and King of Kings—who gave His law to Adam, the first of men, and wrote it in his heart; but he did not keep it. Therefore, after grace was lost through disobedience, the natural law lasted for two thousand years. At last, God gave the written law nearly five hundred years after the promise to Abraham, and He entrusted it to His servant Moses to instruct the children of Israel, who were indeed a hard and stiff-necked <note>original: "ceruicosos," a biblical term for stubbornness</note> people under a semi-perfect law. But after men were able to recognize that there is no salvation for lost and sinful man except in God and through God, when it pleased God, He gave His Word through His Spirit to take on a human body; so that, because men were entirely evil and no longer believed in divine inspirations, they might see a single body in which the divinity resided. He took on flesh in the Virgin Mary through the Holy Spirit, with an angel announcing it, just as when one person makes a concept known to another through a word, and the other conceives it in the mind. For the mind does not conceive the physical word itself, but the concept it brings. In the same way, the Virgin did not conceive the Holy Spirit sent from God the Father, but by means of the Spirit, she conceived the Wisdom and Word of God, which indeed came for the direction of all men. That Word and Wisdom is Jesus Christ, the Son of God, born of the Father before all ages, conceived in time from a Virgin, and made man to bring light to other men—existing as one who is both God and man, who alone is able to restore all men, just as He created all in one in the beginning: to Him be praise in heaven and on earth forever. Now, indeed, we shall write His praises from the book of the Quran <note>original: "Alcorani." Postel often cited the Quran to find "hidden" Christian truths or points of agreement to aid in conversion efforts</note>.

Likewise, in natural virtue <note>original: "uirtute naturali," here meaning the inherent power or capacity within nature</note> there is a unity in trinity, and a trinity in unity, as I have said. There is a superior power, an inferior power, and an intermediate one. The highest power is in spiritual natures: first in God the Most High, and secondly in the angels and the citizens of paradise. The intermediate power is in the heavens and the stars. And from both of these comes the third, the elementary power, in which every body acts and suffers. Form gives being to the thing, matter carries and sustains it, and the composite possesses both; yet one is not the other.

In every operation, there is an agent, an instrument, and the patient <note>the "patient" is the object or person receiving the action</note>. Every work is made by an agent, matter, and the operation. # CONCERNING THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD, #

### PRAISES OF JESUS CHRIST, ###
->In the Quran, in Surah Al-Baqarah <note>original: "Sora Bacara"; the second chapter of the Quran. Postel refers to it as the "first chapter," likely because it is the first major book following the short opening prayer.</note>, that is, in the first chapter.<-

> God said, "And we gave Jesus the son of Mary wisdom, and we formed him from the Holy Spirit." <note>original: "spiritu sancto"</note> So says Muhammad. He who possesses the wisdom of God, and is begotten or formed from the Holy Spirit, must necessarily be God and the Son of God; for even if we were not to believe him to be God, he is nonetheless more sublime than all other men, greater than all prophets, and more worthy of belief.

->And a little after,<-

> God says, "And we have ordained these prophets among themselves; for God spoke to some of them, and raised some of them by degrees, and we gave Jesus the son of Mary wisdom, and we formed him from the Holy Spirit." Although Muhammad writes elsewhere that wisdom was given to the prophets, nevertheless no one could possess it in its fullness <note>original: "solidam"</note> except for him who was conceived from the Holy Spirit, who is God, and Light from Light. The others were participants, but in this one is solid wisdom and divinity.

->In Surah Al Imran <note>original: "Humram"</note>, that is, the Surah of Joachim <note>Postel identifies the "Imran" of the Quran with Joachim, the traditional name of the Virgin Mary's father in Christian tradition.</note>, which is the second.<-

> Hannah, the wife of Joachim, said concerning her daughter Mary: "I have called her Mary, and I defend her and her offspring from the ruinous demon." From this passage, it appears that those two <note>Mary and Jesus</note> did not sin, for to be defended by God from the devil is to be without sin.

->And afterwards,<-

> "O Mary," (says the angel) "behold, God announces to you his Word <note>The concept of the *Logos* or "Word" is central to Postel's argument that Jesus is the manifestation of God's intellect.</note> from himself, whose name is Christ Jesus, the son of Mary, toward whom the faces of the present and future world shall be turned; he is among those who are near [to God], and he shall speak to men in his cradle and in his swaddling bands, and he shall be a most excellent man." Thus says the Quran. The Word of God is the most high God himself, so called because just as we do not understand anything from another man without a word or explanation, so we do not conceive of God's power without his own explanation, Word, and Wisdom, which is also God. Therefore, God is not without his Word or Wisdom, yet there are not therefore two or three gods, but one God, who is not confined to a place, yet is in every place. For God is not a body, but is free from body and matter. We do not call Jesus "God" according to his body, but according to his divinity; for the power of God and his wisdom are one and the same thing. Just as our own word is the "son" of our thought, and there is nothing in the word except what was in the thought—whether true or false—for thought, word, and the thing itself are essentially one reality; this entire force was the thing, and it is in the thought, and it is entirely in the word, and entirely in itself.

->And a little after,<-

> And God taught him (Christ) the book, and wisdom, and the law, and the gospel, and appointed him as a prophet to the children of Israel. "I have now come to you," (Christ says in the same place) "with miracles from your Lord. I create for you figures of birds out of clay, and I breathe into them, and they become birds by the permission of God. I heal those with scabs and leprosy, and I bring the dead to life, by the command or permission of God." The title of Creator and Resurrector of the dead, performed without prayers, belongs properly to the Son of God. Regarding the creation of the birds, this is a miracle from the Savior's infancy <note>Postel is referencing stories from the Infancy Gospels (like the Gospel of Thomas) which are also reflected in Islamic tradition.</note>. Furthermore, when Jesus raised the dead, he raised them by a simple command, with no prayers poured out, so that he might show himself to be God, the judge of nature. The apostles, however, raised countless thousands in the name of Jesus and his cross. But miracles can only be done in the name of God. Since, therefore, every kind of miracle has been done in the name of Jesus through the sign of the cross, it follows that he is God. Moreover, since we do not find in the Gospel (except for when he groaned over Lazarus) that he invoked his Father to raise the dead, it is not surprising, because he himself...

and the Father are one God. Moreover, that he was something other than a man is clear from these arguments. He demonstrated this in the miracles performed in his name alone; his true disciples and imitators did the same and even greater things in his name. With no one praying for him, he rose again; he transformed his people and made them different from worldly people. For other men are either evil, or they wish for the good and do not do it, or they do it less and more imperfectly than they would wish. Only true Christians have surpassed in their works those good things that could ever be written by philosophers. They did not fear death, but rather desired it. They held the pleasures of the body in hatred, contrary to the common nature of men; from which it is established that they were transformed by his words and sacraments with divine power. For this cannot be done by man. For only God, who knows nature because he made it, can thus change and mend it; men and prophets can do nothing else but speak and forewarn: only God gives perfection. But you, O Muslims <note>original: "Mussulmani"</note>, say the Gospel is too perfect, and therefore you prefer the Quran to it. If Christ was the greatest of the prophets, then he gave the greatest law, and the most perfect, and therefore it is necessary for salvation. This is why there are so few even among us who are truly good, because few obey the Gospel.

## ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD. ##

He was conceived of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, performed miracles in his infancy and throughout his life, and raised the dead by his own power alone—without invoking God <note>Postel emphasizes that Jesus did not need to pray to God as an outside power because he possessed that power within himself as the Son of God.</note>—and gave power to his followers so that, in his name and by the sign of his cross, they might do the same as he did, and even greater things. He did this so that they might all despise the world and desire death for the sake of the truth: receiving harm from all, yet loving all and bestowing benefits upon them—qualities which cannot be given to men except by God. He is nearest to God through his humanity, the judge of all, traveling with the good, and able to kill all in the blink of an eye. How then are others preferred to him? How is his law abandoned for another, which considers the pleasure of the body—shared with the beasts—to be the highest good? He who does not go to God through him is damned. For since God confers all things upon us through his wisdom, and that is his way of bestowing benefits upon men, it is necessary that we return to him by that same path; otherwise, we shall not arrive there.

->Praise of the Gospel, in Surah Al-Baqarah. <note>original: "Sora Bacara"; the second chapter of the Quran.</note><-

And they said: "Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided." Say: "Rather, the law of Abraham is gentle, and he was not an idolater." Say: "We believe in God, and in that which was sent to us, and to Abraham and Ishmael, Isaac and Jacob, and to the tribes, and what was given to Moses and Jesus and the prophets from their Lord; we make no distinction between them." <note>This is a paraphrase of Quran 2:135-136.</note> But why should we not distinguish between the true and the false, between that which is from God and that which is not from God? Why did God give us intellect and free will, if not so that we might understand what is true and what is false? He who speaks falsehood fears to have his words examined; therefore, if it is possible to be judged, he does not permit it. But he who speaks the truth rejoices that everyone knows it and disputes over it, so that it may be better understood. If, therefore, all the prophets—Abraham, Moses, the tribes, David, Christ—agree with one another, they are true. Therefore, if anyone does not agree with them and differs, he cannot be true. Thus must the distinction be made. Two thousand three hundred years before Muhammad came, the Law of Moses was as it is now; and six hundred years before, the Gospel and the New Law (or Law of Grace) existed, as it is in the languages of all nations. In no place in either Testament is it written that Abraham was in Mecca, or that he sacrificed there, but rather the contrary. In no place is it written that anything of the Law was given to Ishmael, except for circumcision. For he was expelled from his father’s house, an exile and an idolater, who took an Egyptian wife devoted to the cult of idols. This is contrary to the Quran, which is founded upon the faithfulness of Ishmael and the sacrifice of Abraham. <note>Postel is challenging the Islamic tradition that Abraham and Ishmael built the Kaaba in Mecca and that Ishmael was the son intended for sacrifice.</note>

This is a vast difference; because of this, they are considered most holy who enter into beasts, she-asses, camels, etc., who could not be so judged by everyone unless the law approved the deed. <note>This is a common, though highly inaccurate, 16th-century polemical claim that the Quran permitted bestiality by misinterpreting verses about God providing livestock for human use.</note>

God lacks nothing, nor does He use any thing, since He is abundantly happy without corruptible things. For this reason, Jesus wished to possess nothing. He who desires nothing beyond necessity is the most perfect of men. Such was Christ, and such were his followers. <margin>An address to the Muslim princes.</margin>
Come then, O princes, keep the earthly power you have now acquired and secured, and receive the truth of Jesus Christ. Although he [Muhammad] sought that power through fictions, you will possess it justly if you swear by the words of Jesus Christ; all peoples will follow you. See to it that the Gospel is read in your provinces, and that it and the Quran are debated with reason, and you will see a victory without bloodshed. Let the Suras of the Quran be brought together with the chapters of the Gospel—as the *Al-Furqan* <term>Al-Furqan: "The Criterion," an Arabic title for the Quran implying a discernment between truth and falsehood.</term> often says—and if it [the Quran] wins, all will become Muslims. All Christians can read the Quran, and it is read everywhere; but no one among us can believe it, because it seems to us entirely written against God and nature. By debating both, the truth will emerge.

That the Gospel is most true, however, and to be preferred above every law, is clear for these reasons: The prophets and holy men, along with the Sibyls <note>The Sibyls were ancient prophetesses of the Greek and Roman world whom Renaissance scholars believed had foretold the coming of Christ to the pagans.</note>, predicted unanimously in various places concerning Jesus and his Gospel; yet no one predicted Muhammad. Our sacred books were received early on, discussed in freedom, in councils, and with the highest wisdom, without any force. The Quran, by contrast, was forced upon the unwilling through fear of death or the confiscation of goods. By teaching gently and suffering all things, the Apostles taught the law of Christ. Soldiers, robbers, and tyrants persuaded the unskilled and the rustic of your law by force—laws which many of you would discard daily if it were permitted. But due to the danger to your lives, it is not permitted. 

The truth of the Gospel does not seek out corners <note>original: "non quaerit angulos," a Latin idiom meaning it does not hide in secrecy or evade public scrutiny.</note>; it may be dealt with publicly and privately. Our law teaches that there is no happiness for the body in this life: it places everything in the love of God, charity for one's neighbor, and one's own innocence. It harms no one and helps whom it can. Yours [your law], through sexual and bodily pleasures shared with the beasts, promises and expects paradise itself in those same things. Furthermore, it invades the property of others by force in the name of religion, and thinks nothing holier than having killed a man, whereas in our law nothing is more hateful. 

To this, what was holier than Jesus Christ and his followers, who handed down the Gospels to us? They would have preferred to die rather than to lie. What did Muhammad have of holiness, knowing fifteen wives in one hour? A killer of citizens, a striker of brothers, a perjurer, a robber, and more wicked than other wicked men. By how many infinite miracles is the Gospel confirmed! But Muhammad was never seen to have performed a single miracle; and what he said he did is ridiculous. Furthermore, countless external witnesses, the best of men, gave their names to Jesus Christ and his followers; no one ever (except followers who were accomplices to the fable, and peoples captured by trifles) failed to call Muhammad the most cruel tyrant of all. To this, since God wants the salvation of men to happen through the Gospel, if he approved of things against it and against nature, he would not be God. He waits for you to repent, and uses you as torturers against our crimes <note>Postel views the Ottoman military successes as a "scourge of God" intended to punish Christians for their sins and bring them back to true faith.</note>. By these reasons, you can know how much truth differs from falsehood. Even if Muhammad had not been forced to attribute to Christ and the Gospel what he did, natural judgment suggests it ought to be preferred over all the doctrine of the world.

<header>GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK II.</header>

# THE HARMONY OF THE UNIVERSAL WORLD AND OF THINGS
*established in the quaternary <note>The "quaternary" refers to the number four, which Postel believes is the fundamental organizational pattern of the universe.</note>, from which the greatest light for knowing the Trinity arises.*

Just as we have recognized the image of God and of the most holy Trinity—the cause of all things—within the material parts of the world, so we shall recognize that the image of God is seen everywhere in the harmony of four things, which must necessarily be understood as existing within God.

1. As we saw in the beginning, there is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: one God. The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God—not three, but one. These are power, wisdom, benevolence, and divinity: abundance, the progression of acting, choice, and eternity—the end and cause of all things.

2. There is apprehension, consideration, and remembrance: one total mind, one in three and one in each part—the knowledge of all things and the method of knowing the First Cause through its effects.

3. In created nature, there is the spiritual, the celestial, the lowest world. There is the world in the angelic mind and care (as in the most perfect subject), the world in the power of the acting heavens, and the world in the lower nature. These are not three worlds, but one, in each and in all: the preservation and growth of all things by the hand of the Creator, and the happiness of matter.

4. In the "lesser world" <term>Microcosm: A common Renaissance concept that the human being is a "little world" reflecting the structure of the entire universe (the macrocosm).</term>, which is man, there exists for his perfection whatever is created in all of nature: to be, to live, and to feel (along with the lower beings), and to understand (along with the celestial substances). Although the nature of the intellect or mind is not intertwined with the corruptible internal parts in the manner of a harmony, yet it is never found here without them. Indeed, that perfection is preserved for the state of resurrected bodies. Then it will be true to say: the intellect *is*, the intellect *lives*, the intellect *feels*. This is true now, but the terms are not interchangeable <note>original: "non convertitur." In logic, Postel means that while the intellect currently exists, "existence" as a whole is not yet fully identical with the "intellect" until the resurrection.</note>. For after the resurrection, there will be no "being" that is not intertwined with the intellect. Likewise, nothing will be "life" or "sense" alone, for to be will be the intellect, and the intellect will be to be. Similarly, the life of the intellect and the intellect’s life, the sense of the intellect and vice versa. Through this, it is clear that while other living things have received their fulfillment, man currently lacks it. The "well-being" of man is currently imperfect, and the happiness of the Form <note>The "Form" refers to the soul or the defining essence of a human being.</note> thrust down into the lowest depths consists in this.

5. In all sentient living creatures there is a vital force, a natural force, and an animal force: one life in three, and only one in all, which constitutes the well-being of living creatures.

6. The natural faculties in any life—even the vegetative—and in each part of a living being consist of the attractive, digestive <note>original: "coctrice," from "coctio," meaning a "cooking" or ripening process which Galenic medicine used to describe digestion.</note>, retentive, and expulsive forces. And although the last one [expulsion] may not seem intertwined with the others, and Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the most influential physician of antiquity; his theories on the four bodily "faculties" dominated medicine until the Enlightenment.</note> does not teach it as such, nevertheless, to those who consider it deeply, it is present in all. For just as if by some discernment of the soul, nourishment is drawn from the earth or from wherever it is mixed (the useful with the useless), when the desired part is drawn in, the harmful part is repelled and pushed out. Once that useful part is "cooked" [digested], there is a need for purging; for otherwise it would not be "cooked" if it were already entirely perfect. While it is retained and assimilated, the same law applies, for these forces do not take place in isolation. This is the means of preserving life, implanted by God into the principles of things.

7. In the works of nature improved by cultivation, there is the seed, the plant, the grafting (or any other cultivation), and the fruit. For although these seem to exist through themselves, yet they exist in potential within one another; for the fruit is potentially in the seed, and actually in the wild or grafted plant. In the use of this fruit lies the happiness of the present life.

8. In the sharing of fruits, there is the origin, the progress, the perception, and the use—everywhere in potential. From the first comes the second, and from both comes the third.

9. Time is past, present, and future: the whole in each and in all. There has been no moment since the world was created that lacked a "past," without having the others within it in potential. For there is no "past" that was not once "present" and "future," but they do not reverse from the latter to the former. For since every "past" once held the "future" within itself in potential...

### THE HARMONY OF THE UNIVERSAL WORLD AND OF ALL THINGS
->set in the quaternary, from which the greatest light for knowing the Trinity arises.<-

Just as we have recognized the image of God and the sacrosanct Trinity—the cause of all things—within the material parts of the world, so we shall recognize that the image of the four things which must necessarily be understood in God is seen everywhere in harmony.

1. There is, as we saw in the beginning, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: one God. Father as God, Son as God, Holy Spirit as God; not three, but one. These correspond to power, wisdom, benevolence, and divinity; or abundance, the progress of acting, choice, and perpetuity—the end and cause of all things.

2. Apprehension, consideration, and remembrance; one whole mind, one in three, and one in each—the knowledge of all things and the method of knowing the first cause through its effects.

3. In created nature: the spiritual, the celestial, the lowest, and the world itself. The world exists in the angelic mind and care as in a most perfect subject; the world exists in the power of the acting heavens; and the world exists in lower nature. These are not three worlds, but one, present in each and in all—the preservation and growth <note>original: *uegetatio*; refers to the animating life-force</note> of all things, the hand of the creator, and the happiness of matter.

4. In the "lesser world," which is man <note>The "microcosm," a common Renaissance idea that the human being is a miniature version of the entire universe.</note>, there exists for his perfection everything that is created in all of nature: to be, to live, and to feel (shared with lower beings), and to understand (shared with higher substances). Although the nature of the intellect or mind is not intertwined with lower, corruptible things in the manner of a harmony, it is nevertheless never present here without them. That perfection is preserved for the state of the rising bodies <note>The Resurrection.</note>; then it will be true to say: the intellect *is*, the intellect *lives*, the intellect *feels*. While this is true now, the terms are not interchangeable <note>original: *non conuertitur*; a logical term meaning the subject and predicate cannot yet be swapped (e.g., currently, "to be" does not always mean "to understand," but it will in the future state).</note>. For after the resurrection, there will be no "being" that is not intertwined with the intellect; likewise nothing will be "life" or "sensation." For "being" will be "intellect" and "intellect" will be "being"; likewise life will be intellect, and sensation will be intellect, and vice versa. Through this, it is clear that while other living things have received their completion, man currently lacks it. The imperfect well-being of man, and the happiness of the "form" <note>The soul or organizing principle of the body.</note> thrust down into the lowest parts, consists in this.

5. In all sensing animals there is a vital force: the natural, the animal, and the one life in three—and only one in all—which is the well-being of living creatures.

6. The natural faculties in any life, even the vegetative, and in each part of a living thing, consist of the attractive, digestive <note>original: *coctrice*; literally "cooking," the historical term for the body’s heat-based digestion.</note>, retentive, and expulsive powers. Although the last one [the expulsive] might not seem intertwined with the others—and Galen <note>A famous Greek physician (c. 129–216 AD) whose medical theories were standard for centuries.</note> does not teach this—nevertheless, to those who consider deeply, it is present in all. For when nourishment is attracted from the earth (or anywhere it is mixed) by a certain discernment of the soul—the useful mixed with the useless—the desirable is drawn in while the harmful is repelled and pushed out. Once the useful part is "cooked" [digested], a purging is necessary; for it would not be digested at all if it were already entirely perfect. While it is retained and assimilated, the same law applies, for these functions do not occur in isolation. This is the means of preserving life, implanted by God into the principles of things.

7. In the works of nature improved by human care: the seed, the plant, the grafting (or any other cultivation), and the fruit. Although these seem to exist on their own, the fruit is in them in potential; for in the seed the fruit is "potential," but in the wild or grafted plant it is "in act" <note>A distinction from Aristotelian philosophy: "potentiality" is the capacity to become something, while "act" is its actual realization.</note>. In the use of this fruit lies the happiness of the present life.

8. In the sharing of fruits: origin, progress, perception, and use, everywhere in potential. From the first comes the second, and from both comes the third.

9. Past, present, and future time: the whole in each and in all. Nor has there been any moment since the world was created that lacked a "past" without also having the rest in potential within itself. For there is no "past" that was not once "present" and "future," though they do not convert from the latter. For since every "past" had the "future" potentially within itself...

& and present; yet no present possesses a past, and no future can be present or past. Therefore, there is a rest to come for it—I mean for time and motion—so that the two later things might correspond to harmony, when in actuality there will be one and all.

10. In the act of moving, there is the mover, the moved, the movement <note>original: *motio*; the process of moving</note>, and the motion itself. Motion is found entirely in the agent, entirely in the patient <note>The "patient" is the object being acted upon.</note> or moved thing, and entirely in the movement, since it is only one thing.

11. In all things, there is abundance or power, progression, the love of acting, and choice; a single property that is whole in each part and one in the whole.

12. In the world, there is generation, duration, corruption, and continuous action and passion <note>In this context, "passion" refers to the state of being acted upon by an external force.</note>. For it is the disposition of matter resting in its form.

13. In the dimensions of bodies, there is length, width, depth, and measure; the whole is in each dimension, and yet there is only one measure in all of them.

14. The certain disciplines are music, geometry, astronomy, and arithmetic. The last, which I have placed in the final position because of harmony, is so entwined with the others that they cannot exist without it. <note>These four subjects constituted the *Quadrivium*, the higher division of the liberal arts in medieval and Renaissance education.</note>

15. In nature, which has matter joined to form, there is form, matter, the composite, and essence. This essence is whole in all and whole in each, being only one.

16. In human works, there is the action, the matter, the work, and the use. This last, "use," exists primarily in potentiality; for before use can exist, those other three must have preceded it.

17. In the action of loving, there is the lover, the beloved, and love; a unique affection, whole in the lover, whole in the beloved, and whole in the love itself. I mean perfect and reciprocal love, such as the charity of the perfect and the holy.

18. Peace is sought and preserved by the priest, the prince, and the judge. For peace must be entirely in the sacred state, entirely in the military state, and entirely in the judicial state, since only one peace is required in the republic—a peace suitable for minds, bodies, and affairs. This is the good and the goal of human society.

19. The causes of things are the efficient, formal, material, and final causes. <note>Postel is citing Aristotle’s "Four Causes," which explain why a thing exists and what it is.</note> The final cause is first in potentiality; for if it were not first in the mind of the agent, he would not wish to join matter in vain. Thus, in every action, it is asked: for what purpose, to what end, and for what use? The end is whole in the efficient, the material, and the formal causes.

20. Innocence, sin, redemption, and the status of human nature; a perfect condition that differs even as it exists fully under any status. Innocence was in the highest man, the first created, for God created all things perfect. Sin began in that same man, for it infected everyone such that they delight in their own miseries; though they know the good, they are not accustomed to doing it unless aided by God. Because all are indeed in sin, and since God wishes (while still preserving free will) to make everyone blessed, this cannot be done through man alone. Therefore, God—through His Son, who is both God and man—saves the faithful, the pious, and the perfect, such as are true followers of Christ. Thus we say there was **innocent humanity**, supported by God, in Adam; then **sinning humanity**, turning away from God and using the "natural law" which provides only a darkened knowledge (such were the men who heard nothing of Moses or the Gospel); and finally **redeemed humanity**, such as has embraced Jesus Christ.

21. Whatever a great or powerful lord does, he does either by himself, or through a servant or friend, or through a son. By himself: those things done without a medium. God created human nature with its gifts of the soul. When man perished of his own accord, about two thousand years later He sent into the light for some—to which others could approach—Moses with the law, along with the promises to Abraham and his legitimate descendants. When this turned into abuse after fifteen hundred years, He sent the ultimate remedy after himself: Jesus the Son...

faithful friend and servant, both God and man, so that he who was the creator of nature, and the only one capable of doing so, might become its restorer by taking on a human body. For it would have been foolish to have sent a servant twice with the same power. This is the character of sacred administration, this harmony, consistent and constant with itself in all things; thus it was born to preserve justice and equity among men.

22. The written law of nature and of grace, or justice. In a corrupted nature, an imperfect law is transmitted; in the written law—which is the Law of Moses—it is more perfect; but in grace, it is most perfect, and nothing can be added to it. For these encompass everything whatsoever necessary for salvation. Whatever contradicts them cannot be from God; it follows that whatever has been introduced besides them—such as the Quran <note>original: *Alcoranum*</note> or the books of heretics—must be from the devil. Therefore, just as a person who naturally knows themselves but acts against their conscience and does not reform or repent is condemned by their own judgment and accusing conscience; so too, one who hears of the Gospel (which corrects our fallen nature) but refuses to believe in it is consigned to a curse. For just as one acting in the past could use the memory of the present and future, and one in the present uses only the present and future, and one in the future uses only the future—so under the ancient law of nature, both Moses and Christ could be expected. Under Moses, only Christ was expected; under Christ, only Christ is in use. It follows then that whoever hears of the Gospel from which Jesus comes and does not believe in it at all is beyond any hope of salvation, unless they repent.

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
## BOOK THREE.
### CONCERNING RELIGION AND THE LAW COMMON TO THE WHOLE
### *world, or the Method of Law.* CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'C' featuring a seated scholar or scribe at a desk with an open book, surrounded by decorative floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>While reading the Pandects <note>original: *Pandectas*; the *Digest*, a vast collection of Roman legal writings compiled under Emperor Justinian</note> of Roman law, I saw that many things were written in them whose use among foreign nations was either unknown or obsolete. Yet I observed that these nations enjoyed their own peace just as much as if they had submitted to Roman civil law in every detail. Since there is but one truth in all of nature, though opinions are countless, I began to reflect that the cause which allows all peoples to join together in a lawful and civil manner cannot be a trivial or light one. Instead, it must proceed from that most certain principle by which human affairs are born, progress, and endure; I judged that this principle is what serves as the basis of proof for all people of all nations. Therefore, retreating from those opinions of Roman law which are so confusedly organized—by which the world is usually overwhelmed rather than truly helped—I turned to the precepts of inner philosophy. I began to draw out principles approved by all peoples and the conclusions derived from them, so that I might consider in what matters the whole world agrees. Since the book I have prepared on this subject required guides and additions at home, this seemed the most suitable place for it: so that after the truth known to a few has been proven through philosophy, and after false beliefs have been refuted by a true guide, the commonality of the whole world might follow. Finally, I consider how it might be achieved—just as the world agrees on these principles—that it might also join to them those things without which absolute happiness cannot be attained. And because the process of birth and origin cannot be understood without considering corruption, I shall speak first of the corruption, restoration, and origin of law, taking my starting point from the contemplation of nature as a whole.

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

Human affairs labor under their own bulk when they reach that point where they can hardly accept further growth, or where they retain their acquired greatness (which often spreads wider than their strength or wisdom) only with extreme difficulty. This is proven above all by the industry of man, which has either devised or received from God all the laws, religions, empires, and magistracies known to this day. For although this mortal life is governed by things either devised by prudence or produced by nature—and indeed cannot lack either without falling into ruin or facing immediate collapse—nevertheless, if these things exceed their proper measure, they suffer the same fate as lamps. If lamps are deprived of oil, they cannot stand or provide light; yet, when oil flows in too copiously, it kills the flame just as surely as if it were lacking. It is certain that this happens not through a fault of the oil or the light, but because the proper measure (<term>modus</term> <note>Postel uses the Latin "modus" to signify moderation, limit, and rhythmic balance</note>) was not applied carefully according to the requirements of both. Therefore, anyone will easily judge that the fault lies in the way the measure of things is overstepped, as one examines the various parts of nature and art discovered by human wisdom.

This terrestrial globe, which the sun warms and recreates through its cycles, is filled with seeds by the winters; the springtime excites these seeds by embracing them in its lap as they are born; summer educates what has been born; and autumn renders them fit for use. If any one of these seasons exceeds its measure even slightly, it does not merely fail to increase what it usually supplies so benignly, but it also leaves great defects behind. For a greater force of cold, if it remains too long in the womb and moistens too abundantly, causes things to be cast out like abortions. Even for those well-born, a heat that is too burning or poorly timed takes away their moisture, so that they either never reach maturity or come forth empty and withered. What is more useful or necessary than rain? Yet, when it is copious and long-lasting, it does not nourish, but rather causes rot. Heat, without which nothing reaches maturity, burns the crops and kills the young plants if it lasts too long. Thus, if change and moderation are lacking in these things subject to corruption, then undoubtedly whatever usually helps becomes a detriment.

Now, if we turn our attention to the sun itself, the parent of nature—observing how it produces annual successions for the greatest health and preservation of all things—we will sense that nothing in nature can be born, grow, or live without its pleasant gaze. Conversely, if it were to shine steadily with its rays without the variety of the seasons, it would bring not health to the fields, but pestilence and fire.

It will be most evident that human inventions are related to these examples from the fact that if a virtue exceeds its measure, it must lose its name and degenerate into a vice: gentleness will produce a weakness of spirit (<term>abiectionem animi</term>), courage will produce audacity, and compliance will produce flattery. It would indeed have been a small matter, or at least far less troublesome, if only nature itself (to which we cannot give prescriptions) were so unlike itself, or if virtues—which belong to individuals and the few rather than to everyone—brought loss by exceeding their measure. But even that which is most excellent in this mortal life—laws, both divine and human—also feel this pestilence. This is a sickness that is more bitterly deplored the more it escapes our perception. For in other matters, a vice shows itself immediately and can be healed by remedies or by fleeing it; but here, the more things are added to other things, the deeper the wound penetrates and the wider the disease creeps. Thus, the labor required to purge that **Augean Stable** <note>original: *Augeae stabulum*. In Greek mythology, cleaning the stables of King Augeas—which had not been cleaned for thirty years—was an "impossible" task performed by Hercules. Postel uses it here to describe the overwhelming task of reforming corrupted laws.</note> is seen to require a greater effort.

If anyone doubts that this is the case, they can recognize it most clearly by this reasoning. Is it not true that the **Mosaic Law** <note>The Law of Moses, or the Torah</note>—by far the most celebrated for its reputation of holiness and miracles and given by God—almost collapsed under the weight of opinions? And did it not, through the variety of traditions, so affect those devoted to that persuasion that it became by far the most difficult thing to observe? Even when their affairs were still flourishing, the far greatest part of the Jews themselves so feared that heap of opinions that they never even wanted to approve those books which follow the Mosaic ones; others hissed at the commentaries and traditions as if they were a plague. Of this disease, as he is the physician, so too is he the most ample witness: Chri-

# BOOK III OF GUILLAUME POSTEL

(Chri)stus, who more than once reproached the magistrates, saying that the law of God, weakened by this mass of opinions, had departed from the minds of men. For it happens by I know not what fate, that when we think we have most provided for this mortal life, we add medicine upon medicine to a disease that spreads wider and rises up daily, so that we wander furthest from the path of healing. Whence, in place of the ancient and genuine, the spurious and the new creep in; in place of the true, the fabricated. And from this, laws protect not Justice itself, but themselves. But while each person fashions whatever they wish concerning the law, Justice is utterly overturned by law. I would not dare to fully disclose what human industry has fashioned from the most absolute religion of Christ through various interpretations; yet, as is "known to the bleary-eyed and the barbers" <note>original: "lippis & tonsoribus notum" — a classical Latin idiom meaning something is so obvious that everyone, even those in a barber shop, knows it</note>, no one would deny that in certain respects, that law which has flowed from its various interpretations down to our times stands far apart from the Gospel. And it does so more and more, the further it recedes from the beginning. 

Apostolic men, neither weakened nor enticed by any human desire, increased and illustrated the most holy precepts of Christ with canons and rules. The first councils followed—and they themselves, gathered not by apparent ambition or factions but by the breath of the Divine, judged that not a few things should be added. Posterity then condensed that mass of councils and interpreters—which was not entirely consistent with itself, but was adapted to the logic of times, places, persons, and things—and digested it into commonplaces in a **problematic manner** <note>original: προβληματικῶς (*problēmatikōs*) — meaning as a series of questions or debates</note>, so that men began not to assert truths, but to doubt those things as if they relied only on opinion. For things had already reached such a state that more things were decreed for the sake of specific persons than for the sake of the office itself. 

Indeed, once wealth arose, fraud began to creep in through tunnels and gradually immerse itself in sacred matters; so much so that the things established five hundred years ago can no longer even pretend to be acts of piety. For that faction of great wealth demands its own protection, and a far greater one than the sacred things which originally produced that wealth. 

Yet, those things established first by decrees, decretal letters, <term>paleae</term> <note>marginal additions or "chaff" added to early canon law collections</note>, and <term>extravagants</term> <note>papal decrees circulating outside the standard legal collections</note> could still have been tolerable, if a far greater plague had not crept into this harvest of opinion: an innumerable crowd of interpreters. While this crowd dreams its own dreams, it pleases itself with its own opinion, contradicts others, approves some, and disapproves others. Preferring to protect opinion rather than truth, it has brought matters to the point where, by that law which human industry and commentary have devised, it is most certain that nothing is certain. No law is so unjust that it cannot find "equity" for itself through these opinions. Thus, it has become a trap for patrons, judges, and crafty men rather than actual Law, where we rely on opinions rather than equity, and follow the foul streams rather than the original springs. 

Thus, without this dull mortality even noticing, it happens that the nature and use of things handled by human judgment degenerate. What once helped many now harms many—and all the more so for those who possess the greatest innocence. For what would wickedness not pervert once it has gained a handle for covering crimes with the appearance of piety? Thus it happens that **"the height of law is the height of injustice."** <note>original: "summum ius summa iniuria" — a legal maxim warning that strict adherence to the letter of the law can result in the greatest unfairness</note> 

That would indeed have been more tolerable if that variety of opinions had only pervaded the public administration of affairs. But it has sought the very foundation itself. Men have begun to debate divine matters from both sides—matters about which it is a sin to doubt—so that an equal opportunity is seen to be given to anyone to defend anything, if once a person prefers human reason to divine authority. I leave this for consideration. 

It shall be enough to have said that unless we return to the head and the principle itself—after exploding these opinions of doubting and depraving, however widely accepted they may be—it will come to pass that not only private affairs, but also public ones, will be most gravely endangered and will soon collapse. It is plainly superfluous to propose an example concerning accidental things or those pertaining to wealth, since the matter reveals itself well enough.

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
### BOOK III

...lest I should judge. Roman opulence, gathered from the spoils and plunder of the entire world, bears witness to this; all types of republics <note>original: "rerumpub." — an abbreviation for *rerum publicarum*</note> confirm it, having been weakened by excessive wealth and the factions of more powerful citizens. Indeed, it was not so much a wonder that wealth, which is usually tossed up and down by the whim of fortune, should have caused harm by its abundance; but that religions themselves—which are born, grow, and persist chiefly through authority and opinion (except for the one true one)—should have grown so much through human arts, or rather through supine negligence, that an immense heap of opinions has arisen from the license of private judgment, just as excessive light dulls the sharp edge of judgment. 

But in civil or public laws, where not authority but the highest prudence, reason, and equity ought to be the governing force, to suffer from that same disease is indeed something to be greatly wondered at and lamented. Such is the condition of human affairs: just as a lack of light takes away the sight of things, so a light clearer than is proper (if I should call it brightness and not rather most dangerous lightning flashes) when it shines around, brings a flaw not to the things themselves but to the sharpness of the eyes, and makes it so that we can no longer judge things incorruptly, since their condition seems equal or very similar. 

However, how vice crept into that fortress of truth must also be briefly related. I do not wish to start the origin from the "double egg" (as the poet says) <note>original: "gemino... ab ouo" — a reference to Horace’s *Ars Poetica*, meaning to start a story from the very beginning (like the birth of Helen of Troy from an egg), rather than jumping into the middle of the action</note>, but I will take up Roman law <term>ius Romanũ</term> already grown to a proper size and bring it forward. I will reveal by what means it grew into this mass under which it began to labor long ago, so that it may appear from there: the same thing happened even among other peoples inferior in prudence, if they used the same written law for a long time. 

For who among mortals ever possessed greater prudence than the Romans? Where was there a more majestic senate, a greater abundance of legal experts <term>iurisperitorum</term>, a more distinguished cultivation of all doctrines, or a people more fit and inclined to conduct affairs excellently—had they not contaminated such excellent things with slaughter, robbery, and finally such a great lust for power? But since their law is now weakened by the commentaries of interpreters and, through the constant use of transferring it, is as if stale <note>original: "uapidũ" — literally "vapid" or like wine that has lost its spirit</note>, what should be judged concerning the law of the Athenians, Carthaginians, or other peoples is obscure to no one. 

Even in the times of Cicero, when Roman affairs flourished most, there was already a great abundance of opinions in civil law, which demanded art rather than further growth; this is best evidenced by the fact that those who presided over giving legal responses did not take up the whole mass, which was now like something immense, but chose specific arguments in which they wished to excel and be occupied for their whole life. They could not master that whole doctrine contained in many volumes, so that even the unskilled saw the most serious men sometimes slip in the smallest matters. 

For it was permitted to any of the ancient legal experts to propose entire books on various parts of the law as a law, according to their wish; while this was necessary at the beginning of the Republic and was observed and established in almost all democracies and aristocracies, it soon caused an immense multitude of opinions to grow. Different people treated different things, and not rarely the same argument was treated by different authors, delivering various things not only contrary to others but to themselves, according to their own judgment (as we are frequently affected). 

When Justinian wished to free students of law from the trouble of running through all these, he took care to select from that great number of 60,000 volumes those things which the Republic was using at that time, according to the persuasion of Tribonian <note>Justinian was the Byzantine Emperor who codified Roman law; Tribonian was his chief jurist and the primary architect of the *Digest*</note>; he cut away what seemed either obsolete, or superfluous, or contradictory, as he says. If only this had been done as much in reality as it was by edict and assertion, so that a legal expert could be trained in at least five years! He decreed, indeed, lest the Republic fall back again into a crisis already known before, that those things he had approved should be sacrosanct and inviolable; and that no one should add to or diminish them in any way...

He highlights Emperor Justinian’s attempt to simplify 60,000 volumes of legal thought into a manageable system, though he suggests the effort was not entirely successful in stopping legal decay.</summary>

### WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK III

...anyone would dare to touch; would that posterity had taken care that this were done. For although many things perished from the labors of those greatest philosophers—things which were useful to the Republic—nevertheless, it would have gone happily for posterity if we had taken care to preserve those great things with as much reverence as that most sagacious emperor <note>Likely referring to Justinian I, who codified Roman Law to prevent confusion.</note> desired. But as a plague necessarily arises for every individual thing, lest this part of the Republic be lacking one, there arose six hundred years ago a new kind of interpreters, contaminated by every kind of barbarity and ignorance of philosophy. While they compare laws to laws, they pour out darkness over obscure matters and rely on opinion rather than truth. They have incited such a crowd of similar people that in no art or doctrine has there ever been a greater lust for writing, or greater ineptitude. A single law, a single premise, a simple voice—which of itself can rely only on one truth—began to be translated into six hundred understandings. Each man brought forward and thrust upon us whatever he thought, or rather dreamed, as the true meaning; he adapted the truth itself to the facts like a <term>Lesbian rule</term> <note>A "Lesbian rule" was a flexible leaden ruler used by ancient masons that could be bent to fit the shape of a stone; Postel uses it as a metaphor for "bending" the law to fit one's own desires.</note>, rather than adapting the facts to the truth and the rule.

From this, judgment began to be based on opinions rather than equity; from this, the counterfeit appeared to succeed the genuine, the false the true, and the doubtful the certain. Thus, in this most beautiful art, things began to be handed down with a far greater license for doubting and proving whatever one wishes than if they had fallen among the Stoics or the Academics <note>Two schools of Greek philosophy; the Academics were famous for their skepticism and the belief that nothing could be known for certain.</note>. Even a man of no small authority, **Baldus** <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400) was one of the most famous jurists of the Middle Ages. Humanists like Postel often criticized his complex, multi-layered legal commentaries.</note>, brought forth and left in writing ten various and entirely contrary opinions on the same matter, and reported them in his judgments, even though only a single truth lay beneath. So great a thing it is, forsooth, to recede from equity, to rely on opinions, and to drag authorities to the facts rather than the facts to authority. Indeed, nothing is written so diligently that it cannot be violated and dragged into perversity, and—by opinion and an affected sense of judging—be converted into a contrary or at least a different meaning. Thus, it becomes "the highest law" <note>original: "summum ius." Refers to the proverb *Summum ius, summa iniuria*—the rigors of the law can become the height of injustice.</note> such that it contains plainly no law at all, and brings a fuel for lawsuits rather than an end to them.

Thus, we see that nowhere among nations is there a greater crowd of litigants and of those who make a profit from the law; nowhere is there a more ample supply of lawsuits than where Roman law has been received. Truly, those wretched men, depraved by craftiness, are either enticed by the false promises of patrons and bloodsuckers to seek any kind of lawsuit, or are driven to cover up any execrable crime. I am silent regarding the royal laws and rights, the edicts of the courts, and the judgments of the highest senate—even these have increased immensely and fight with one another—or the civil laws, whether written or unwritten, which are customarily observed. Meanwhile, they torture this wretched mortality with these <term>Erinyes</term> <note>The Furies of Greek mythology, who tormented those who committed crimes.</note>, so that today, to slay and finish off this monster, not just one Hercules, nor any of the greatest power, prudence, or authority among mortals, but the highest divine force seems required. 

Although this cannot be cured by a few words or a single remedy, nevertheless, this plague—which has devoured the blood, the muscles, and finally even the spirit of the Republic—must not be entirely neglected. Just as when a body is wrongly affected and disposed in its constitution of health so that it either cannot recover by the work of doctors or can do so only with difficulty, yet the doctor must not neglect that work by which he may turn away the increase of the disease or preserve a poorly affected life for longer. He should even apply those remedies by which the disease might be removed in a similar or related condition, and leave nothing untried. For it frequently happens, beyond the hope of the doctor, that those medicines which he hoped would be least healthful may, by unexpected chance, fortune, or providence, bring health to desperate matters. 

In this same order is the art of medicine for bodies: it retains and conserves bodies in prosperous health as much as can be achieved by the benefit of the art, restores those that are affected, and looks out for those that have been restored. Philosophy is in exactly the same position regarding the conservation of the Republic, while it either puts to flight present vices, or heeds and provides for those that are imminent, or thinks about the future by comparison with the past, so that it may dispel the many miseries of this life. Thus, there can be no end to writing; one’s duty in these matters is not to write things that drag the mind into diverse opinions, but those things which are...
