# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
### BOOK III

...would suffer. In individual republics, there are certain occasions and matters adapted to the thing, the place, the person, the time, and the customs; for the sake of these, prudent men often depart from <term>natural law</term> <note>Natural law refers to a body of unchanging moral principles regarded as a basis for all human conduct.</note> and from the law approved by all learned peoples. Thus it has happened that the law of the Romans, although full of equity, never fits the Gauls, Germans, Athenians, or Carthaginians, or any other polities in every respect. Yet it is certain that there is something which all nations approve first: even those whose writings, names, and customs were once unknown to us. For there is that supreme reason for establishing law which was born in all ages before any law was written or any city was established at all. 

Indeed, in our time another world <note>A reference to the "New World" of the Americas, which was being explored during Postel's life.</note> has been opened, the vastness of Africa and Asia has been made known, and the monuments of literature—both our own and those of the Greeks and Barbarians—do not yet precisely encompass the memory of even a sixth part of the world. Nevertheless, it is certain that those peoples, because they survived, agreed upon certain elements of law by which they might ward off mutual injury; otherwise, they would have been a source of destruction to one another. (This is true if they received instruction from prudent or wise men, or did not lose what was once received; for even among them, there are those who live in herds like beasts, without a fixed place.) For no one can deny that as many cities or certain places inhabited by men as have endured for a long time, they have done so by the benefit of law. 

I will therefore endeavor, although it is an arduous task, to hand down and embrace those principles—partly from philosophy and partly from the histories of nations—which no nation (either one that has long flourished or one that listens to the reasoning of the prudent) would not vehemently approve, or will approve in the future. I will mostly accommodate myself to either Roman or Gallic law, where such law is of the kind that is expedient for all men of the entire world and departs furthest from personal passions. 

Our labor tends toward this goal: that whoever wishes to more diligently understand and weigh these very elements may be able to do so here. Let them do this diligently before they look more deeply into that immense heap of all opinions which usually grows as republics grow and endure. For it will happen to them as it happens to those skilled in reading: whatever has been written in the type of characters they have diligently learned, they immediately have at hand and are able to read. Thus, he who does this will have already achieved something: even if he does not grasp the words of a different tradition, or the customs and civil laws, he will nevertheless have "open doors" and be far better prepared for the matter than one ignorant of the elements themselves. For once the words and facts are applied, he will immediately grasp the meanings and will judge what is <term>equitable and good</term> <note>original: "æquum & bonum"</note> in any cause. 

In this matter, it is well known that those philosophers who traveled anywhere among the nations were most powerful and successful, and were held everywhere in great admiration and use; for from the highest memory of letters, they gave laws and prescriptions for living to those republics. But if anyone should object that we already have the elements of law more diligently handed down in the Imperial Institutes of the Romans, I will not deny that—indeed, the elements of Roman civil law are handed down more diligently than I myself could do. But Roman Law is only that in which many things are seen to be adapted to the use of that specific republic and joined to its opinions; therefore, they cannot apply to any other system than that of its own republic. 

But I am about to deliver those things which are suitable for everyone. Furthermore, it seemed best to imitate the first of the philosophers and those who were never accustomed to deliver anything without a method. For what would it help to deliver even those things which were perfect in every number in themselves, unless you observe and hand down with the greatest success the art by which they can be embraced and kept in the mind? But because nothing offers itself as more common or more fit for the knowledge of things—whether in religion or in reason—than the <term>ternary number</term> <note>Postel was fascinated by "ternaries" or groups of three (such as the Trinity), believing they reflected the fundamental structure of the universe.</note>, I have established its model whenever [the nature] of things...

...the condition will allow, to follow a threefold division everywhere, once the reality of the matter has been established. For we see—to begin from the highest grade of all things—that the power of the highest, middle, and lowest spheres brings about one and the same effect in these lower realms. That is to say: God, or the First Cause, established the various motions of the heavens and planets so that by their apparent labor, whatever is born naturally on the earth or in the sea might be born. Power is hidden in the first cause, manifest in the second, and partly hidden, partly manifest in the third. All disciplines are contained within the physical, the ethical, and the logical: they contemplate, they speak, and they act. All things consist of a beginning, a middle, and an end; of growth, stability, and decay; of matter, form, and the composite. Bodily things consist of length, width, and depth. Time consists of the past, the present, and the future. All actions consist of the agent, the patient, and the action, with either side participating. An artisan is made by nature, doctrine, and use; nature brings talent, doctrine brings knowledge, and use brings the fruit. The sun is luminous by its body, its ray, and its power. In short, there is almost nothing that the most Holy Trinity itself does not touch; whence by philosophers and the more prudent religions, that number <note>The number three.</note> has always been held as a symbol of sacred things, as the father of nature, or as most consistent and connected with it—or, to speak with the Greeks, *connatural* <note>original: *ὁμοφυής* (*homophuēs*)</note>. 

First, indeed, I shall hand down whether the origin and consistency of things—which others call <term>substance</term> <note>In philosophy, "substance" refers to what a thing truly is in its essence.</note>—exists or not; then, division will indicate how many types there are; by definition, it will be opened up as to what or of what sort it is; finally, it will be revealed for what use these things are prepared. Lastly, I shall declare how things act or are acted upon, and by what reasoning they are composed. For the *fact* <note>original: *ὅτι* (*hoti*)</note>, as I may say partly with Aristotle, the philosopher of truth, and the *reason why* <note>original: *δι’ ὅτι* (*di' hoti*)</note> must first be sought. First the "what," second the "wherefore," is to be sought. 

But since it seems to me that no one can well define a thing, from which the substance of things becomes known, unless he knows how manifold that is about which the discourse is proposed, I have seen fit to hand down also the division and effects for the sake of the unlearned. Although he who knows the *reason why* <note>original: *δι’ ὅτι* (*di' hoti*)</note>—that is, the primary and final causes—would also know the division. Indeed, I would have studied to hand down this art in books without chapters and in long-drawn-out disputations, after the manner of the leading men in philosophy, had I not been led by the reasons of the elements and of art, which are usually treated in fixed chapters, so that I might propose the things themselves with frequent and distinct arguments. 

For if the Pythagorean authors, the most celebrated of all philosophy in both parts of Greece, did not want books to exceed three cubes of the number six <note>Postel refers to a Pythagorean numerological preference for structural limits in writing.</note>—so that the memory of readers and listeners might be consulted—then I must rightly take care in this argument of ours that no single chapter be of too prolific a length. I do this not so much for the sake of Pythagorean dogma (which, however, even for its authority alone, does not seem to me to lack reason), as much as to satisfy the delicate readers or listeners of our century. For in this so great a crowd of authors and "scribblers," and in such an inconstant roll of the dice regarding judgments—which must necessarily be undergone—one sees almost nothing that is not extremely long-winded, unless it is already proven by antiquity, which might satisfy the palate of many. So prone are people to judge their own century, and to approve of foolish ancient things rather than to agree with the <term>moderns</term> <note>Postel uses the term *neotericis*, referring to contemporary scholars of the Renaissance.</note> in any matter. In this regard, those people seem to me to have deserved poorly of nature, who contend that she concentrated her powers in those first ages in such a way that she appears a stepmother to posterity, but a mother to antiquity. He who does not wish to run through whole books will at least be able to taste one or two chapters for the sake of approving or disapproving, even with the "tips of his lips," and bring a judgment concerning what he has touched. I shall certainly never be burdened to approve that judgment with him, provided that, having looked at the whole work, he judges not from a sickness of the mind, but from candor. For by this labor I desire others to be excited to treat greater things in the same argument, rather than being left behind me. For he who is devoted to posterity [seeks] utility, but not likewise glory...

...condition allows, I will follow a ternary division <note>A "ternary division" refers to the practice of dividing a subject into three parts, which Postel believes reflects the Holy Trinity.</note> everywhere, once the reality of the matter is established. For we see, to begin from the highest level of all things, that the power of the highest, middle, and lowest spheres produces one and the same effect in these lower realms: namely, that God—the first cause—has ordained through the various movements of the heavens and the planets that, by their apparent labor, whatever is naturally disposed to be born on land or sea, is indeed born. Power is hidden in the first cause, manifest in the second, and partly hidden and partly manifest in the third.

All academic disciplines exist within the physical, the ethical, and the logical: they contemplate, they speak, and they act. All things consist of a beginning, a middle, and an end; of growth, stability, and decay; of matter, form, and the composite whole. Physical bodies are defined by length, width, and depth. Time is divided into past, present, and future. All actions involve an agent <note>The person or thing performing the action.</note>, a patient <note>The person or thing receiving the action.</note>, and the action itself, or a participant in either. A craftsman exists through nature, training, and practice: the first brings talent, the second knowledge, and the third brings forth fruit. The sun is luminous through its body, its rays, and its power. 

In short, there is almost nothing that the holy Trinity itself does not touch. For this reason, among philosophers and the more prudent religions, that number—three—has always been held as a symbol of sacred things, as the father of nature, or as being most in harmony with or attached to it—or as I might say with the Greeks, *homophuēs* <note>original: ὁμοφυής, meaning "of the same nature" or "kindred."</note>.

First, I will address whether the origin and consistency of things (which others call "substance") exists or not; then, the division will indicate how many parts it has; by definition, I will reveal what it is and of what quality; finally, it will be shown for what use these things were prepared. Lastly, I will declare how things act, or are acted upon, or by what logic they are composed. For the "that it is" <note>original: τὸ γὰρ ὄτι</note> and the "why it is" <note>original: καὶ τὸ δι' ὄτι</note>, to speak partly with Aristotle, that philosopher of truth, must first be sought <note>Postel is citing Aristotle's *Posterior Analytics*, which distinguishes between knowing a fact (*to hoti*) and knowing the reason for the fact (*to dioti*).</note>. First the "what," and secondly the "wherefore," must be investigated.

But since it seems to me that no one can properly define the substance of things unless they know the manifold nature of the subject being discussed, I have seen fit to provide the division and the effects as well, for the sake of those who are less refined—even though whoever knows the "why" (that is, both the primary and final causes) would also know the division. Indeed, I would have preferred to deliver this art in books without chapters and in long-extended discussions, after the manner of the leading men of philosophy, had I not been led by the principles of the elements and certain chapters of the art to use specific methods, so that I might propose these matters through frequent and distinct arguments.

For if the Pythagorean authors, the most celebrated of all philosophy in both Greeces <note>Postel refers to "both Greeces": mainland Greece and *Magna Graecia* (the Greek colonies in Southern Italy and Sicily where Pythagoras lived).</note>, did not want books to exceed three cubes of the ternary number <note>The cube of three is 27 (3x3x3). Postel is likely referring to a Pythagorean preference for sections or books of this length.</note>—to consult the memory of readers and listeners—since that number encompasses the logic of the universe, I must likewise take care in this argument of ours that no single chapter be of excessive length. I do this not so much for the sake of Pythagorean dogma (which, however, does not seem to me to lack reason, even if only for its authority), but rather to satisfy the delicate readers or listeners of our current age.

For in this great crowd of authors and people eager to write, and in the inconsistent gamble of judgments which one must necessarily undergo, almost nothing is accepted unless it is extremely long-winded—unless you see something already approved by antiquity that satisfies the palates of many. It is all too easy to judge one's own century harshly, and to approve the foolish things of old simply because they are ancient, rather than to agree with modern thinkers in any matter. In this regard, those people seem to me to have treated nature poorly, contending that she poured all her strength into those first centuries, so that she appears a mother to antiquity but a stepmother to posterity.

He who does not wish to run through entire books may at least "taste" one or two chapters with the tip of his lips, for the sake of approving or disapproving, and bear judgment on what he has touched. I will never find it burdensome to agree with such a person, provided that, after viewing the whole work, he judges it not from a diseased mind, but with candor. For by this labor, I desire others to be excited to handle greater things in this same field, rather than being left behind me. For he who is devoted to posterity seeks utility, not glory...

<header>ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD</header>

Unless it follows of its own accord, it ought to follow reason. Therefore, to use the words of Crassus in Cicero <note>original: "ut Crassi uerbis apud Ciceronem utar"</note>, I shall say nothing recondite <note>Hidden or obscure</note>, nothing worthy of the expectation of great or more learned men, and nothing unheard of by the prudent or new. For the basic elements which I have now decided to treat are intended for those who are young either in age or in learning, and for those who are still practicing at the training-post <note>original: "ad palum," a metaphor for a soldier or gladiator practicing against a wooden stake before actual combat</note>, but do not yet claim the prize of virtue in the heat of battle or the gymnasium. For it is necessary that the way to greater things be paved with small beginnings. Indeed, the greatest matters have frequently emerged from the smallest occasion. Who can say whether our labor—since it was undertaken for the sake of helping the Commonwealth—might one day inspire leading men in their oratory to pass down more perfectly what we have attempted?

Certainly, my authority was Cicero, a man placed almost beyond the reach of human judgment, who promised a work on this subject. However, he was either prevented by death, or (as is perhaps more likely for men granted great authority and prudence) he was unwilling to provide it because he might have been forced to write many things for the sake of popularity—as he certainly often did—or for the utility of his own Republic, which would have been poorly consistent with natural law <term>Natural Law: the universal moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason</term>. These, indeed, are his words: "If," he says under the name of Scaevola <note>Quintus Mucius Scaevola, a famous Roman jurist and character in Cicero's dialogues</note>, "I am allowed to do what I have long been thinking of, or if someone else occupies the task while I am hindered, or finishes it after I am dead—namely, to first digest civil law <term>Civil Law (Ius civile): the specific laws of a particular city or state</term> into its various classes, which are very few; then to divide the members of those classes; and then to declare the unique force of each through definition—you will possess a perfect art of civil law, one that is more great and fruitful than it is difficult and obscure. And yet, meanwhile, while these things that are scattered are being gathered, one may be filled with this knowledge of civil law by plucking and collecting it from everywhere." And a little later: "For all these things are placed before our eyes, located in daily use, in the meetings of men and in the forum; nor are they contained in so many writings or great volumes. For the same things were first brought forth by many, and then written down even more often by the same authors with only a few words changed."

Thus far Cicero. He gave me the courage to dare, after I had begun to grasp the sense of the Pandects <note>The *Pandects* or *Digest* is a massive compilation of Roman legal opinions commissioned by Emperor Justinian</note> and had more diligently examined in person three Republics that are easily the leaders in our memory: the French, the Turkish <note>The Ottoman Empire</note>, and the Venetian. I have also weighed the religions of many nations. To these, I wished to add a more diligent investigation of the Republics of all the ancients, as many as have been passed down in the memory of our people, or the Greeks, or even the Barbarians, and how they were restored to keep the people in their duty—which anyone may easily see in my work *On the Magistrates of the Athenians*. Furthermore, I have not neglected the political institutions of Aristotle, Plato, and Xenophon. If anything herein is written with more care, I wish to attribute it to their antiquity and authority; yet I dare to assert that through our own thinking and refinement, some things have been made no worse. A fair reader, skilled in antiquity and the experience of things, will not deny this, provided he reads the facts themselves, led by reason.

### WHENCE LAW FLOWED FORTH AMONG MEN. CHAPTER III.

Since by their own nature humans alone of all living creatures became forgetful of themselves and of the providence of reason implanted in them from the beginning, they began to turn away from the law of nature as soon as they gathered together. They raged against their own kind far more cruelly than even those animals devoid of judgment and reasoning. At first, indeed, having experienced the greater strength of another and fearing both the punishment inflicted on them and the greater power of an attacker, many abstained from those by whom they were endangered. Yet they continued nonetheless to be troublesome to others whose strength they did not fear, and they undermined the species. This animal <note>Referring to man</note>, being exceptionally endowed with memory and capable of reason when it is reminded of it—and feeling mutual disadvantages quite often, not without danger—was led by those among them who possessed a sharper wit, to...

[The Republic would have] indeed fallen, and from that injury which leads to the ruin and loss of one’s own species, or like the example of wild beasts who spare their own kind and come together for the sake of preserving it, man indeed abstained for some time. But since man was brought forth by nature as destitute of all things, he is entirely stitched together from shrewdness, craftiness, fraud, and deceit on account of a necessity that is either a constant companion or something to be feared. Indeed, his character even from his very cradle <note>original: "ab incunabulis," literally "from the swaddling clothes," referring to the earliest stages of life</note> is inclined toward evil. Forgetful of both danger and utility, as well as any warning, he would immediately return to his natural disposition. For before laws were born, the first and only method of possessing—and of preserving things out of a fear of necessity—lay in occupation <note>The legal concept of "occupatio," or taking possession of something that belongs to no one</note>. For everyone had an equal right to things themselves and faced a similar necessity; from this, both necessity and lust and vengeance increased their savagery, and the scale of injury grew as they aged.

When wise men saw this and took pity, they realized they could not heal this disease only with warnings and examples, which would soon vanish. Instead, they judged that people should be restrained by some bond by which they would easily allow themselves to be captured. For equity <note>Fairness and justice that transcends the strict letter of the law</note> itself could easily be persuaded, even with thin eloquence, to those whom the same nature had produced with similar bodies, corresponding limbs, similar needs, and as if they were brothers. The coming together and nature of other living creatures also persuaded them; animals spare their own kind (unless for the sake of lust or want) as much as possible. Indeed, they are so eager for preservation that many are incited by sounds, like a war-trumpet <note>original: "claſſico," a Roman signal for battle</note>, to their own defense and the driving out of others.

The frequent experience of mutual inconveniences, constant fear, love for oneself and one's kind, the similarity of all people, and even the example of creatures destitute of reasoning, not only persuaded but compelled them to swear into a certain law. If anyone acted against this law, he would be restrained either by everyone else or by one authorized by the rest, and he would be afflicted by a punishment equal to the one he dared to inflict on another.

Therefore, this was the first shaping of the law: *Whatever someone has committed against another contrary to the good of nature, he himself should be forced to endure the same.* For man is not only skilled by nature in seeking bodily good, but all kinds of living creatures must be judged by that same skill. This first element, placed partly by nature and partly by human prudence, gave the first place to possessions and the first security and tranquility among men. This was the first principle of human gathering and confederation. 

But since men were still half-wild, with uncultivated minds and great ferocity, and since they were driven by constant necessity and a singular envy for the things they needed—added to a proclivity for inflicting injury—they soon forgot the law rooted in reason. They would return immediately to their [violent] character, and unless they yielded to the desires of those they attacked, they would rage with thefts, looting, and slaughter. Thus, as vices were born and grew, new remedies had to be established. 

Lest the laws established be endangered by ignorance, or sit idle, or be concealed by the savagery of certain men, it seemed fit to translate them into letters <note>Writing</note>, which were then-recent human inventions devised like all other things. When I say that all things were gradually devised by man, I believe this is so certain and proven to all that there is no need to bring forward many arguments to confirm it. From the highest memory of literature (without which one cannot know whether deeds actually happened or not), all things must be traced back. Ditches, the coverings of trees, and huts made from tree branches were the first beginnings of even the greatest buildings. Through constant cultivation, wild things were tamed by hand; the acorn nourished the first farmers. From shepherds, robbers, and farmers, citizens were born or made, as were magistrates, princes, and judges—all things were led forth from the lowest to the highest. Some people placed at the very summit of affairs were not ashamed to admit this; indeed, the most excellent nations held these origins in honor and preserved them for a long time. They kept a senatorial house covered with straw <note>A reference to the *Casa Romuli* (Hut of Romulus) on the Palatine Hill, which the Romans preserved as a sacred monument to their humble beginnings</note>...

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD
<page-num>272</page-num>

The most holy senate of the Areopagites <note>The high court of appeal in ancient Athens</note> wished for it to be preserved for many years in the Areopagus, so that the city might remember its origin. The same was done by the Romans regarding the house of Romulus, even with its thatched roof; it was preserved for many years for the sake of memory. What else did the times of Saturn and the Golden Age, ignorant of gold, wish to indicate? You might prove by similar reasoning that both languages and characters <note>Writing systems or alphabets</note> were devised—excepting the Hebrew ones, although some are persuaded otherwise on that matter. For while a son listens to his father, a neighbor to a neighbor, and a servant to a master, those endowed with memory began to express what they heard and to apply it to the use of conversation. From this, they began to invent "natural letters" to depict the feelings of the mind through natural signs. Hence the Hieroglyphic letters of the Egyptians and the Western Indians <note>Postel likely refers to the indigenous peoples of the Americas, known in his time as the "West Indies"</note>. 

As the world grew a little older, it devised many systems that have perished, as well as those that have endured down to us, according to the parts of the mouth and tongue, the openings of the breath, and semi-perfect characters—those of the Phoenicians, Chaldeans, Arabs, Indians, and Africans. For they had devised no vowel pronunciations. The Greeks, receiving these from the Phoenicians, enriched them with order, forms, vowels, and declensions, from which the Latins <note>The Romans</note> took them many centuries later. Thus, the journey began from small beginnings toward great achievements. Therefore, chiefly by the benefit of these letters, the memory of the ages, the opinions of the wise, and the principles of law <term>ius: the body of laws or justice</term> began to be handed down and preserved. From this, posterity was increased by the wealth of their ancestors; from this, the arts were refined. 

It seemed best, therefore, to those wise men (to return to the point from which I digressed)—those to whom we owe either our happiness, or the youth, cultivation, and duration of our intellect and Republic—to transfer into writing those precepts by which human fury is usually mitigated. They did this so that they might be preserved by the benefit of memory and the monument of letters, and be placed in a location that was sacrosanct. From there, they could be taken up by judges or those endowed with any other authority, and brought forth like living witnesses, both to restrain the deeds of the wicked and to settle disputes. For they would have been established in vain unless they were also diligently preserved and applied—like a medicine to a disease—with a vigorous magistrate acting as their protector and champion. From this came praise and certain rewards promised and bestowed upon good men, and punishments and disgrace upon the wicked. 

But mortality, always striving for the forbidden, since it always teems with a vast crowd of the wicked, saw that it was not safe to inflict injury on anyone because of those who held the highest authority in restraining crimes. They would rise up against those authorities so they might never be restrained; not infrequently, they would attack them of their own accord so they could creep into their positions. Others, more crafty, committed nothing openly out of fear of punishment, but were accustomed to perpetrating many dire deeds in secret. This disease also had to be cured. And since those who were in charge of the highest affairs did not have enough strength (being weak and still lacking guards) to repel the injuries inflicted by them, nor could they easily acquire a guard from the rest of the common people in such a state of poverty, they recognized that they needed a remedy greater than a human one to know the hidden thoughts, frauds, and crimes of men. 

Indeed, it was observed that man is easily captured by the wonder of unusual things and is not difficult to lead toward a probable and true opinion (though he not infrequently gives credit to false ones). It was also seen that man is not entirely averse to returning a favor—an image of which can be seen in dogs and many tamed animals. Therefore, they persuaded men that there is some Divinity <note>original: "numen"</note> above the nature of visible things, of whom a forgetfulness had long since begun to take hold of men; to Him, these so many and so varied benefits, which had arisen neither by chance nor from themselves, must be credited. They spoke of a God who sees and hears all things, even the hidden and obscure, who is the founder of the universe.

He concludes that because human laws cannot stop secret crimes, wise leaders introduced the concept of an all-seeing God to maintain moral order through divine authority.</summary>

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK III
<page-num>273</page-num>

<note>original: "statim"</note> it is believed across all nations that God is present everywhere and will take punishment from all the wicked and criminal. Nor should the wicked, or those who refuse to obey commands, think it will be to their advantage that He does not exact punishment **immediately**. There is another life for souls after this age, in which He exerts the powers of both punishment and reward. This belief easily kept both the good (who actually need no laws) and many of the more unrefined people in their duty. However, because wickedness is rarely restrained by any laws without the use of force, it was necessary to maintain order through the protection of judges, or kings, or leaders (which in ancient times were the same thing). But how this power was acquired will be discussed in its proper place.

Necessity, therefore, as the primary origin of all things, produced two fountains of law. The **first** arose from the necessity of nature and wisdom; it was established and approved by reason and the correct judgment of men. Its springs, like basic elements, are placed directly before our senses in the contemplation of the lower natural world, so that this reason—implanted in the minds of men by nature—can be restored even with modest persuasion. This is specifically **equity**, the living roots of which God seems to have mixed into the minds of everyone to be perceived.

The **second fountain** proceeds from religion and the admiration, fear, or love of a God approved within the state, even when the true God is unknown. By this means, either hidden crimes are brought to light while men, driven by oaths, confess about themselves; or fear is struck into those who stray, lest they lose the good they enjoy through His benefit; or they fear losing the happiness that is believed to be either promised or given by a divine power. Often, the fear that we might be abandoned—either in our present happiness or in that which follows death—terrifies us. When I speak of "religions," I mean only those that have already faded away or are believed to be false by our people—not our Christian religion, which, as Christ himself asserted, will never be in danger.

**Human law**, to make its definition clearer, is the knowledge of what is fair and unfair according to <term>arithmetic or geometric equality</term><note>Postel uses these Aristotelian terms to describe different types of justice: arithmetic equality treats everyone exactly the same (like a flat fine), while geometric equality is proportional, distributing rewards or punishments based on a person's merit or status.</note>, and the distribution, assignment, and preservation of things to each person according to their merits and accepted rights. I call it **arithmetic equality**, following the opinion of Aristotle, when things are weighed and assigned by a valuation of money (or something that stands in place of money). I call it **geometric**, when we consider and assign a solid thing for a solid thing, or any other proportional measure. For you will have judged in vain unless you have also assigned the award.

**Divine law**, however, is the establishment of the equity that must be observed by anyone, beginning precisely where the powers of human law fail. Its observation is usually driven by the fear or love of either the Supreme God or the gods accepted by the State.

-> ## ON THE REASONS AND ENDS OF ALL <-
-> ### PERSUASIONS. CHAPTER IV. <-

Before I speak of law as it is approved by human senses and falls within the scope of reason, I must discuss the religions of all nations from their origin. I do this because, without the fear of God (or gods) and religion, no one could be kept in their duty for long except through violence. Furthermore, since God and all heavenly things are both prior to and more worthy than man, it seemed right to discuss these first. For religions were introduced either before empires began, or alongside power, or to strengthen that power, or even for their own sake without any concern for authority. Not infrequently, a religion was devised solely for the sake of mortal pleasure, to preserve the memory of men for a longer time. The **end** (or purpose) of religion lies either in the happiness of the people practicing it, or in the utility of the person who established it, or in both; or in preserving the memory of someone for a long time, who [was thought to be] among the gods...

He then begins a comparative study of world religions as the foundational "persuasions" that stabilize human society.</summary>

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
<page-num>274</page-num>

...it is believed <note>The text continues from the previous page's thought on the soul's journey.</note> to enter immediately after death, and is believed to fly up into heaven in the manner of eagles. It seems necessary to speak here about the **primary cause**, which first creeps into the mind and is the chief occasion for establishing human affairs. For when anything is done by prudent men, it is well established that it happens for the sake of some necessity, pleasure, utility, happiness, or opinion. 

The first religions of mortals, after the knowledge of God was lost <note>Postel refers to the "fallen" state of humanity where the direct, original knowledge of the Creator was clouded.</note>, were indeed instituted for the sake of **utility** alone, as things following necessity, and they seem to have been approved by men for this reason. For they followed, most of all, those things which are according to nature. 

Indeed, since man and all other living creatures naturally seek what leads to their preservation and flee from what leads to their corruption, both fear and desire are present in everyone: a desire for good things, and a dread of evil things (which others have called "the sought" and "the avoided"). Therefore, it is likely that the **First Cause** (namely, the Most High God) was presented for worship—He toward whose knowledge our eyes grow dim and the mind falters—as the one who would supply existence, life, sense, and all the necessities of human life so abundantly; and who would send evils and the deprivation of things upon bad and negligent worshippers and those ignorant of Him. 

And so that sacred rites might last longer, they were strengthened by sacrifices, as if the divinity were "captured" or pleased by them. This was done so that those who presided over oracles, expiations, sacrifices, and—to use one word—the **preservation of persuasion** <note>Meaning the maintenance of religious belief among the public.</note>, might be able to live. Truly that fear, or that desire, since it is most according to nature, usefully held the people under the power of a divinity. This was the most useful end, the first, and the one most in accord with natural necessity. 

This is truly the **target** <note>original: "scopus"</note> and the first reason for religions—not only of the ancient ones but also of the more mature world (not yet depraved by mere opinion): that man be held to his duty by the fear of evil or the love of good. Both of these are believed to be given and sent by the power of a divinity received into religion. 

The **Hebrew religion**, divinely revealed to **Moses** and confirmed by countless miracles, was content at first to promise an abundance of things and a long life—accompanied by the testimony of divine miracles—to the people who were to reach a greater perfection through those elementary steps. For we are all easily captured by our senses regarding things that serve the duties of this life. Therefore, it was demonstrated to them by many signs that God is perpetually present; He would endow His worshippers with great rewards and avenge Himself upon the impious and wicked with the greatest misfortunes. 

But as there is a supreme inconstancy in all things, and the nature of men who use prosperous things according to their own whims is prone to all vices, the **Jews** soon forgot their own persuasion and began to follow diverse religions. From then on, the **Prophets**—a race of men divinely inspired—affirmed that all the precepts of the received religion must be kept, not only out of a desire for temporary happiness or fear of evils (which were most pressing through wars and captivities), but also for the sake of **eternal punishment** or reward, which God would exercise upon eternal souls. They taught that the **lower places** <note>original: "infera loca", referring to Hell or Hades.</note> awaited the impious, while places bright and full of pleasantness awaited the religious. 

However, when the **Greeks**—who during their travels had drunk from the Indians, Persians, Syrians, and Egyptians—approved of these methods of keeping peoples in their duty (and especially that persuasion regarding the underworld and the **Elysian Fields**), they filled heaven, the underworld, and the world with such fables (with which they intended to cloak religion). They increased these with such absurdities and follies abhorrent to common sense through their own talkativeness, that the fear of the gods vanished, and the underworld and Elysian Fields began to be laughed at even by the commoners. 

From here is the source of the world’s weakening; from here the ruins, which not only infected what was healthy but also cast unhealthy things upon the world. The ancient religion of the **Romans** was not dissimilar, as they had drawn it from the Egyptians, when they saw those things...

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK III
<page-num>279.</page-num>

...the hope of the **Elysian Fields** <note>original: "camporum Elisiorum"; the paradise of classical mythology where the virtuous dwell after death.</note> and the fears of the underworld were being treated as a joke, and the souls of the masses could no longer be held back by those religions (for they had grown accustomed to them, as happens with all things). Therefore, they established a certain punishment that could terrify both the highest and lowest classes. 

Since, from their ancestral religion, they held a supreme observance for burying—or to put it better, **embalming**—their own, and since it was considered a great disgrace to the whole lineage to have an unburied parent, it was decreed that immediately after death, anyone (except the prince) could be accused by anyone else. If the accuser could prove the case, the judge would condemn the deceased to remain unburied until satisfaction was made by the relatives. Otherwise, he remained unburied: a perpetual disgrace to his family line. 

While this invention did not effectively restrain the poorer people (who could obtain their rights from anyone without fear of being accused), it was formidable to the great men and those who are accustomed to oppressing the weak through tyranny. For "a living dog is better than a dead lion," as the **Wise Man** <note>A reference to King Solomon in the Bible; see Ecclesiastes 9:4.</note> says. Just as the common people are easily kept to their duty by laws or religions, those who are led by glory and reputation, and who strive to leave a glorious memory of their name to themselves and their descendants, fear this above all: that they might undergo some mark of **infamy** <note>Public disgrace or loss of reputation.</note> even many centuries later. Yet, they themselves commit almost all the popular injustices unless they are restrained. The end of this religion, therefore, was the fear of infamy. It compelled parents, kinsmen, and relatives to live by the prescription of the laws, lest after death they should have to pay a penalty in the deceased's name or be touched by shame.

But that "excellent" invention was not very firm. It relied on the superstitious and ridiculous burial and guarding of the dead body, which was immediately rejected. Once that practice was cast down, that fear collapsed. Hence the fable of the underworld was invented by the Greeks: that the shades of unburied bodies cannot be ferried across by **Charon** <note>The mythological ferryman who carries souls across the river Styx to the land of the dead.</note>. Although I have spoken of true and false religion in the first and second books, the summary of our comparison must be repeated here in a few words.

The one **Religion of Christ**, beyond the fact that it encompasses the highest points of all laws based on reason (which are satisfied with keeping a man in his duty so that he does no harm), also persuades and commands us—by the example of the Most High God, who is exceedingly beneficent toward all, even the ungrateful and lost—that we should pursue with kindness not only friends but also enemies, and that we should forgive their injuries. It does this through the fear of eternal **perdition** <note>Eternal loss or damnation.</note>, the desire for perpetual happiness, or, what is most excellent, it desires the deed to be done solely by the example of God and the **love of virtue**. No greater thing than this can be devised for the preservation of human nature. 

But men full of atheism, madness, and mere opinion bark against this precept. They say it cannot be fulfilled by anyone, and therefore it is established as a law in vain. Let us see first: if someone who is once evil is always evil; and if he commits a crime against you or another, does he do so against everyone? And if someone has erred once, is he always worthy of punishment? If this were true, since by the consensus of all nations no mortal is without sin (and that most frequently), **Jupiter** <note>Postel uses the name of the Roman king of the gods to refer to the Divine Ruler/God.</note> would kill everyone and hold the empire for himself alone. Divine providence would indeed be either unjust—having immediately exposed man to the necessity of all things from which the occasion for sinning flows—or foolish, having produced man for immediate slaughter, and while wishing to rule, would remove those whom He would rule. Therefore, He wisely tolerates the wicked so that they may return to a fruitful life, which is more wise than if He killed them immediately. It is no different than how laws more easily endure the "boiling over" vices of youth until they come to their senses in a more mature age. If er—

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
<page-num>178</page-num>

...they used these things to bend and warn more unrefined minds. Soft acting on soft becomes sluggish and limp. Hard crushes soft. If soft acts on hard, and can press steadily and shape the form, it can neither break through nor shatter it. Such was the prudence of **Orpheus** (or whoever was the **Pythagoras** <note>Postel suggests that the myths of Orpheus might actually be attributed to the philosopher Pythagoras, or that they shared the same civilizing mission.</note> who, under his name, brought the religions of **Greece** and **Thrace**, which were once barbaric in their wildness). For when he saw that those peoples, among whom he is said to have traveled abroad for a long time, were held by religions that were for the most part entirely false—yet were persuaded without difficulty through the work of wise men—he instilled his own teachings into them so effectively that he is said to have drawn not only men, but even animals and all plants after him with his lyre. 

Pythagoras was certainly always considered the chief author of persuasions among the Greeks; hence, the authority of that religious figure began to be held as the equivalent of reason. Anything, even the smallest detail, was admitted by the common people, since the founders themselves, still unrefined, did not sufficiently know the nature of the supreme deity, and were led by weak reasoning and examples. And therefore, their decrees were approved by everyone as religion, because the wise, after perceiving their practical use, strongly approved them, and the common people easily believed them. 

Religion began to be propagated by such examples. From there, one can recognize its transfer into all of **Greece**, and then among the **Romans**. Hence both necessary and false things arose everywhere among nations. Since man is inclined to give thanks and is an admirer of unusual things, nothing can be more easily persuaded to him than that there is some divine power <term>numen; a Latin term for a spiritual force or divine will that governs a place or person</term>, by whose beneficence he has obtained some gift useful for life, or possesses this so great abundance of all things; and that this power can either give more to his superiors or equals, or deprive those currently present of it, and inflict many calamities. 

For all those things placed in this temple of nature do not appear to be established by themselves (since they lack reason and desire on their own) nor by men; they were very easily believed to have a hidden cause, because almost all men without letters and great experience of things are ignorant of the obscurity of celestial matters, separate substances, and the whole of nature. 

Those who do not grasp God defend the decrees of their fathers "with their teeth" <note>original: "mordicus"; a Latin idiom meaning to hold onto something tenaciously or doggedly.</note>. Those who know by what reasoning things were introduced, even if they are wise, leave no stone unturned so that the opinion of the received religion is preserved most completely and holily; otherwise, they overturn both themselves and the whole **Republic** <note>original: "Rempub."; here referring to the state or the social order of the community.</note>, unless they introduce another before they remove the first. 

But on fixed days, with sacred rites, ceremonies, sacrifices, and games, things began to be retained—not so much to keep the commoners and plebeians in the duty of religion, as to frequently recall and preserve them in memory while the crowd, liable to forgetfulness, gathers frequently and hears those responses given by priests and the authors of religions, and recognizes those things instituted by reason for public utility. For where some divine power was believed to have answered, the people were far more obedient than if a man like them had been their author. For no reason should be sought for a response or an oracle, though it usually is from a man. 

Thus, a religion that was indeed useful, though little explored except by those who knew and explained the reasoning of the **First Cause**, was introduced; it was indeed useful as long as both the unlearned and the experts were busy preserving it. But it either grew old, or, having been gradually corrupted and neglected, it fell into disuse. However, when crafty men, captured by ambition and the love of accumulating things and glory, saw that the unrefined and ignorant multitude was so easily captured and held by any religions whatsoever, and that they were not difficult to bind by the persuasions of those who seemed to possess something not merely human, but unusually great, they were not satisfied to use the received persuasion and introduce that which was beneficial to the people; instead, they sought that which [benefited] themselves...

### WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK III.
<page-num>279</page-num>

...put him in charge of the rest, so that he could give laws to his fellow citizens, and from those very small beginnings, he could inaugurate those kingdoms that later became both great and long-lasting. Furthermore, they wanted this opinion of divinity to be believed either from their very cradles or from the habits of their entire lives. **Jupiter**, the son of **Saturn** (to begin at the head itself), was exposed <note>In antiquity, "exposure" was the practice of abandoning an infant in the wild to die; in mythology, the child's survival was proof of divine favor.</note> because of an oracle that was begged for and devised by his uncle. This was done so that he, as the heir, would not expel his father from the kingdom and seek—and achieve—the tyranny of **Crete**, unless he were killed or abandoned. Eventually, having been raised by a goat, and not without the care of a deity (as it was believed), he drew the hearts of the Cretans—who were very much like himself—to him by this miracle of his infancy. He expelled his father and his uncle **Titan** from their ancestral possession and joined the kingdom to this persuasion so thoroughly that he not only convinced mortals of his own divinity while he lived, but after death, he held and maintained nearly the first place among the gods.

Indeed, his father **Saturn**, under whom the "Golden Ages" were believed to have existed, was forced into exile from **Crete** by his lying son. He sought **Italy**, which he held in obedience—following his son's example—so successfully through the arts of religion that he was easily considered the first and highest of the "mortal gods." This was where that famous and holy (if it pleases the gods) deification <note>original: "ἀποθέωσις" (apotheosis)</note> took place. Then, by the license of the **Greeks**, the sky was filled with fables, which I truly believe the barbarians—or those whose writings have not reached us, or whose commentaries perished and were suppressed by the efforts of the Greeks themselves—had practiced before. For without example or teaching, they hardly ever devised anything great on their own—if, however, it was "great" to deceive the world and hunt for kingdoms under the pretext of religion. 

Hence, not only men, but goats, rams, lions, bulls, and bears—hence ships, javelins, lyres, and arrows—occupied the heavens by that same license. For **Hercules**, the illegitimate son of a father worthy of him, **Jupiter**, it served as a sign of his immediate divinity that he was cast before a serpent; which, after the son of **Amphitryon** <note>A reference to the mortal "father" of Hercules; Postel is highlighting the confusion of his lineage.</note> was killed, he—being less than two years old (if it is worthy of belief)—dispatched. This presence of divinity and his victory over the serpent gave him the kingdom of **Africa**, and the conquered **Spains**, **Gauls**, and **Britons**, all obeying not only his laws but his religions. Because of this belief in a deity protecting even his infant years, he was believed to have finished off so many monsters and conquered so many tyrants—unless, of course, we believe that the Greek license for lying attributed to one man what many actually performed. 

The history of the **Egyptian** [Hercules] is well-established; the Greek ones can be doubted. **Osiris** the Egyptian as well (for from there emerged whatever false persuasion exists), although the Greeks contend he was from **Argos** because of the man's remarkable prudence and that he ruled the kingdom of **Achaia**—it matters not where he was from. He was believed to be the son of **Jupiter** (for to be descended from the gods was always a great thing), and by that reputation of divinity, he not only conquered the more famous parts of **Asia**, **Africa**, and **Europe**, but shaped them with laws and customs. He taught agriculture and left such an opinion of himself among all people that he was regarded as a God, about whom more will be said shortly. 

For I return to the "exposed" children, who truly seem to have applied themselves all the more ardently to virtue the more they received a stain from the injury of their parents: either to wash away the stain of their parents, to confirm religions, or to take vengeance on those who saw to it that legitimate heirs were abandoned for the sake of plundering them. Indeed, besides **Cyrus** alone, perhaps they were all "sons of the people" <note>A polite term for illegitimate children or those of unknown parentage.</note>. **Semiramis**, born of an unchaste mother and therefore exposed, was raised by doves (which gave her her **Syrian** name), and this gave her the most famous kingdom of all Asia. It incited her to acquire and complete such vast wealth, victories, and buildings that she left behind a sense of admiration mixed with envy even for the **Caesars** and **Alexanders**. Thus our nurses...

...by **name**. Because of the titles of goats, she-wolves, birds, and dogs, antiquity easily believed that these were the actual animals, when in fact they only shared the same **name**. **Cyrus** would not have so easily added his grandfather's kingdom to his neighbor's if he had not, after being exposed <note>The practice of "exposure" involved leaving an unwanted infant in the wilderness; surviving such an ordeal was seen as proof of divine protection.</note>, persuaded his people (who were perhaps oppressed by excessive tyranny) of the belief that a deity was his companion. I do not wish to bring up **Romulus** here with his she-wolf. For it was fitting that one born of incest should be raised by a prostitute <note>original: "meretrice lupa"; in Latin, *lupa* (she-wolf) was a common slang term for a prostitute, and Postel is suggesting the "miracle" was actually a mundane, if scandalous, upbringing.</note> nicknamed "she-wolf."

From such a founder of shepherds, thieves, and robbers, first a kingdom was born, then a republic, and finally an empire, most highly adorned with all titles of prudence, power, injury, and pride: of which it is better to remain silent—whether in a positive or negative light—than to write too little. I will not bring up **Aegisthus** raised by a goat, **Pelias** by a mare, or **Paris** by a bear, when they were said to have been exposed. For this example has been borrowed from the **Divine Law** <note>The "Divine Law" refers to the Bible, specifically the story of Moses in the reeds.</note> by countless people, following the likeness of **Moses**.

For whoever imitated this, even if they were able to pull some people to their side, they did so to try and rule over them. Who would not believe that the opinion accepted by the cruder folk regarding **Jupiter Ammon** being the father of **Alexander [the Great]** granted him easier victories than if he had been considered the son of **Philip** from the start? Suppose they never thought about religion after hearing they were exposed or born of gods. That opinion certainly lifts their spirits and depresses and casts down those of the common people. 

For all things are not to be judged false immediately just because some of that kind have seemed false. Not infrequently, portents, miracles, omens, and deeds have been seen from uncertain causes—not without the command or will of the **Supreme Deity**—which were often precursors of great evils or changes, so that mortality [mankind] might look out for itself. For as it frequently happens that a wise physician, skilled in the temperament of bodies, predicts diseases more often so they can be avoided; likewise, that supremely beneficent **Deity**, to whom we must give thanks for whatever we obtain in this life, often signifies to these republics and gatherings of men those things of which most mortals are usually ignorant.

For we consider the age, growth, progress, and ends of individuals as things that pertain most to us, but we cannot, or do not usually, weigh the condition of the republic or universal affairs. And because knowing these things is of great importance (regarding the state of human affairs), therefore **God, the Best and Greatest** <note>original: "Deus opt. max."</note>, frequently helps such a multitude in danger, and finally takes on the duty of a father when human remedies are lacking. Histories teem with such miracles, so that if anyone were so impudent as to assert they are all false, he would deny reason within himself; yet no one but a fool fails to recognize that many things have also been fabricated by crafty men, especially where they are similar. 

But which are true and which are false, some God will have seen. Unusual things were also an augury of kingdoms and great affairs. For **Hiero**, the tyrant of **Sicily**, while he slept, bees gathered honey in his mouth; for **Midas**, ants piled up grains of wheat—these were great proofs of power later acquired and increased. The **King of the Persians, Sophis** <note>Postel refers to the Safavid Shahs of Persia, commonly called "The Sophi" in 16th-century Europe.</note>, father of the currently reigning brothers, hiding for a long time in the woods without any support for human life, nevertheless recovered his father’s kingdom, not without proof of divinity, even though he was already older. The same is said to have happened to **Habidis**, the king of the **Tartessians**, who lived for a long time with a doe. 

What of the fact that some, born through the work of incubi <note>In medieval and Renaissance belief, an incubus was a demon that took male form to father children with human women.</note>, were later great? **Ulam** in **Tartary**, the **Hungarians** <note>Postel likely refers to the legendary origin of the Huns/Hungarians from the mating of witches and spirits.</note> in **Germany**, **Merlin** in **Britain**. Who would not believe that those familiar spirits <note>original: "familiares illos genios"</note> gave courage to **Socrates**, **Girolamo Savonarola**, **Apollonius of Tyana**, and many others to reach the height of affairs, unless they had been oppressed or hindered? With his own demon <note>Used here in the classical sense of a *daimon* or a personal guiding spirit.</note>, **Pythagoras** [held] the tyranny of the **Thurians**...

->G V L. POSTELLI LIB. III.<-

[...] did not blush to affect the same greatness. It is clear enough what the cunning of those was, who introduced religions not for the common good or out of necessity, but primarily for their own profit—and not a few also for their own reputation. For **Romulus**, on account of the price of his blood <note>original: "sanguinis præcium"; likely referring to the deification of Romulus following his mysterious death, which the senator Proculus Julius claimed was an ascent to heaven to pacify a restless public.</note>, was seen as a god by **Proculus**. Nor should we only call "religion" that which is instilled by some fear or love of a divine power, but also that which a leader desires to be offered to and believed by the common people. Now we must speak of those who brought opinions about the gods into the world for the sake of the people and themselves. 

Prudence joined with justice was the reason why those endowed with these virtues were not only held in the highest admiration by all, but also easily persuaded everyone that everything about them should be believed. For wherever we see in any man the highest integrity joined with equity, and that he is held by no ambition that would force him to speak against his faith and the feelings of his mind, we undoubtedly receive all his words as if from an oracle, and we take care to preserve them no differently than if they were uttered by some divinity. For a good and prudent man holds that place among other men in which God is even above the wise, and he is, as it were, privy to the divine counsel, since he is highly skilled in divine and human reason. 

By this reputation for justice and prudence, many were voluntarily called and chosen by the people to handle the reins of government (I am speaking of the world as it was beginning to be civilized). Some offered themselves for this duty partly out of care for the people, and partly from a drive for glory and ambition. Some stabilized an empire already gained and refined it with religions and laws. Not a few, who were seized by a greater desire for glory, seemed satisfied to have simply established laws. However, since all of them saw clearly—and were not ignorant of how grateful people can be—that many who had given the foundations to laws and republics eventually perished through the injuries and sedition of the people; and furthermore, because they knew that the minds of men are prone to change and ingratitude, they persuaded the people that they had a relationship with a certain divinity, so that their authority would be greater and twofold <note>The "twofold authority" refers to the combination of earthly political power and the unassailable mandate of a god.</note>. They claimed that by the counsel and work of this divinity, they did, established, and consulted on whatever they were doing. Faith was given to them more easily because the outcomes usually seemed to follow for the benefit of the republic. 

**Numa Pompilius**, being quite knowledgeable in **Pythagorean** doctrine <note>Numa, the second king of Rome, was traditionally—though historically inaccurately—associated with the teachings of Pythagoras to explain his wisdom.</note>, when he was called to govern the city founded by **Romulus** under omens, and saw that it had perhaps made away with its author because the minds were moderated by little or no religion or fear of the gods, he wanted first and foremost to persuade the people that he followed the authority of a divinity—whom he called the nymph **Egeria**—in all things. This was so that if anything displeased the people, or if something did not turn out successfully despite being done prudently, he would not suffer the punishment as the sole author. Thus he both looked out for the people and retained that dignity and greatness worthy of a kingdom. I do not wish to mention here **Lycurgus**, **Solon**, **Charondas**, **Zamolxis**, and others who are remembered as authors or restorers of laws for the great benefit of their people and common glory. For they all made their constitutions stable and firm with a divine author and oracles. In the first place, it was necessary to begin with religion and the gods or guardian spirits <note>original: "geniorum"; in Roman belief, a *genius* was a tutelary spirit or divine spark within a person.</note> whom they claimed to have as familiars. 

But the arts and ingenuity of them all were easily surpassed by the one Arab, **Muhammad** <note>Postel, a linguist and diplomat, often analyzed Islam as a masterfully constructed political and religious system.</note>; I have described him in the previous sections. In my own judgment, just as men can never exist or be kept in their duty without the belief in religions, so too belief can hardly be increased or preserved without arms. For this reason, ancient kings held the role of priest-sacrificers, with both powers joined under the name of empire.

He previously argued that some leaders use religion for personal gain or reputation; here, he explores how the "body" of the state (secular power) and its "soul" (religious power) must work in tandem, while warning of the corruption that occurs when priests or rulers manipulate faith for their own ends.</meta>

->ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD, BOOK III.<-

The King of the African Indians <note>likely a reference to the Emperor of Ethiopia, often called Prester John in this era, who was thought to hold both spiritual and temporal authority</note> is accustomed to give answers regarding religion and to select the high priests to whom he gives instructions. King David, by the name of prophecy, was able to do more than he could by his kingly power. Each of these powers ought to be tempered by the other. He who possesses the resources without which neither power can stand must moderate the judgment of all things regarding external affairs. For no one is ignorant that one holds the place of the soul and the other is, as it were, the body of the Commonwealth; if these are separated and scattered, the state must necessarily collapse. For if either is positioned apart, it wastes away in idleness unless it is stirred by proper attention, or unless it puts a limit on its own desire by the bridle of the other.

The strongest proof of this is that all religions first perished in the very places where they were first established. And unless the diligence of princes restrained luxury, they were destroyed by those who acted as their guardians for too long according to their own will. In matters of the soul, however, sacred power should be absolute. But while the <term>mystae</term> <note>original: "mystæ"; priests or initiates into sacred mysteries</note> favor themselves more than is fair, or look to their own interests, they do not sufficiently weigh the utility of all, but naturally tend to care for their own—since their livelihood is derived from it. Although income exists, as it seems, for the longevity and preservation of the religious order, no one should consider it a miracle if it is consumed elsewhere. For they do not set a limit for themselves; rather, a fairer judge and the best arbiter of the Commonwealth ought to do so. But it will be said later by what means especially all persuasions have perished or are about to perish. Now I must briefly explain how various cults of things crept into the world.

### The Origin of ABSURD RELIGION and
### *Idolatry* <note>original Greek: εἰδωλολατρείας (eidōlolatreias)</note>. CHAPTER VI.

Since this temple of nature and the immensity of its benefits draws men into stupor and admiration, they desire that their gratitude be directed toward some unknown cause. But the man who is ignorant of whom he should thank (for blind mortality cannot conceive the form of divinity) offers both fear and gratitude to whatever thing is introduced and presented by priests and "prudent" men. The priests appointed to the preservation of that opinion then increase and confirm it through divinations, enigmas, difficulties, or craft. Therefore, it was enough for tyrants and those who once held the reins of affairs to restrain the minds of the people with even the falsest religious opinions.

Regarding the decrees and responses or the oracles of the gods, or of the priests teaching their worship, it was neither permitted nor customary for anyone to demand a reason. The "prudent" ones, who know the practical use of things and pretend to approve, serve as examples to the common folk who are ignorant of matters; they are the authors of ensuring the received opinion about the gods is preserved, while the prince compels both groups through fear for the sake of public peace. Led by that credulity of the commoners and the multitude in the past, when the world was "less nosy" <note>original: "parum nasutus"; meaning less discerning or less suspicious</note>, those crafty princes and scoundrels—who sought to make the memory of themselves last as long as possible through either rare or noble deeds, or through glory, opinion, benefit, or craft—wished to persuade the unskillful crowd that after death they would be immortal gods. They claimed they would depart to heaven, where they would have care over mortal affairs—provided that all mortals, but especially those they had benefited or whom they had ruled, would busy themselves in performing sacred rites for them with frequent sacrifices. That is, so that their memory might be preserved longer, they would support their priests. For without an annual human remembrance and a contribution <note>original: "stipe"; a small coin or donation given for religious purposes</note> established for memory, nothing lasts very long. For time obliterates all things, but these things more slowly. Hence comes <term>apotheosis</term> <note>the elevation of a human to divine status</note> and the eagles released from the funeral pyre <note>referring to the Roman imperial custom where an eagle was released from the pyre to represent the emperor's soul flying to the gods</note>.

### WILLIAM POSTEL’S BOOK III. ###

...those seeking heaven, as if by conveying their souls, practiced a fraud that became so well known to both the Romans and the later Greeks that even the most powerful among them—now among more civilized peoples—could not manage to creep into heaven. From this came the stain and the origin of evil; from this came all kinds of sacrifices and games; from this arose the various types of funerals that sought the heavens. From there, sacred rites were born, then increased and confirmed by lies. From this, he began to be considered a God to whom the name "man" was not even worthily applied, but who instead suited the description of a most monstrous beast. 

Hence Mars became a robber and destroyer of cities; hence Jupiter a pederast and a potter <note>original: "figulus"; Postel likely uses this to mock Jupiter as a mere "shaper" or craftsman of deceits</note>; hence Mercury an impostor and a fast-talker; Venus a prostitute; the Lemnian smith <note>Vulcan</note>; Neptune a pirate; and Bacchus and Ceres, who were merely farmers, ascended into heaven through the tongues and favors of their countrymen. As if this were not enough, even catamites and whores were granted Roman sacred honors. Truly, lest they should perish immediately from the memory of men and fall from their own heaven, they were not only worshipped with fixed and certain rites and sacrifices, but they also left behind for posterity certain animals as sacred to themselves—species that would always exist among men. 

Apollo, the flute-player, physician, and traveling medicine-seller, left the serpent; Jupiter left the eagle; Venus the doves; Juno the peacock; and each left something else. There are also trees and herbs consecrated to them through the invention of priests and the natural properties of the planets. Egypt was the inventress of this cleverness. Isis, the Queen of Egypt, is said to have devised this in the name of her husband Osiris after he had been deprived of his life by his brother and torn into twenty-five pieces <note>While most traditions say 14 or 42 pieces, Postel specifies 25</note> on account of the reputation of tyranny. She did this so that her subjects would not abandon or cast off the opinion of divinity which they had conceived regarding Osiris—both because of the greatness of his deeds and the belief in his divine origin. 

Once her brother was defeated, she recovered those twenty-five parts of her husband's body (which the brother had intended to send to as many governors of provinces as a sign of his deed). She took care to enclose each single part within individual statues larger than the human form, and to have them consecrated in as many dedicated temples in different provinces, as if the entire body of her husband lay hidden in each one. She established money for annual revenues for the priests who would promote this; for without the use of money, neither religion, nor laws, nor even the most useful arts can persist in the slightest in the adult world. 

Furthermore, although she wanted him to be believed to be anywhere in the provinces (as one who was said to be alone in heaven), she also wanted as many different animals to be held sacred as there were parts of the body. She did this to generate competition and a longer-lasting memory among the common people, who strive to outdo one another in the display of processions and ceremonies. Once an animal was consecrated anywhere, it was to be sacrosanct, not to be harmed even by accident, but to be worshipped with excellence and shown religiously—and this not frequently, nor without ceremonies or the vow of the common people. For even sacrosanct mysteries become cheap through constant use, but are commended by rarity. 

Thus, as if Osiris were reborn in each of those living creatures, he offered himself daily to the memory of the Egyptians. Nature has produced men with such a great sense of and desire for glory that they are spurred to noble deeds by its sting; however, wickedness translates this desire for glory only into fame and celebrity, rather than into virtue. This has left behind far more men like Paris, Cambyses, Herostratus, Dionysius, Claudius, Nero, and Heliogabalus <note>a list of infamously decadent or destructive ancient figures</note> than it has left men like Saturn, Janus, or Augustus. The more shameless these men were, the more ardently they attempted to seize heaven to wash away the stain of their wicked lives. This was the fountain of <term>idolatry</term> <note>original: "εἰδωλολατρείας"; the Greek term for image-worship</note> and the nursery of false persuasion. From this came the bow, the arrow, the sacred shield <note>original: "ancyle"; a reference to the legendary shield that fell from heaven in the time of Numa Pompilius</note>; from this, anything at all was forced into religion. Thence, divinity was believed to be absent from nothing. From this came the ruin and contention of the world, and the variety of burial, which seemed to be the door to divinity...
