<header>ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD</header>

The King of the African Indians <note>Postel likely refers here to the legendary "Prester John" or the Ethiopians, whom Renaissance thinkers often associated with a pure, ancient form of priest-kingship</note> is accustomed to responding on matters of religion and selecting the high priests to whom he gives instructions. King David was more beneficial in the name of prophecy than through his royal power. Each of these powers—the secular and the sacred—ought to be tempered by the other. He who possesses the things without which neither power can stand must moderate the judgment of all things regarding external matters. For no one is unaware that one holds the place of the soul, and the other acts as the body of the **Commonwealth** <term>Republic (Respublica): the "public thing" or organized state</term>; if these are disjointed and scattered, the state must necessarily collapse. For if one is placed apart, it withers in idleness unless it is stirred by proper observation, or unless the bridle of the other sets a limit on greed.

The strongest evidence for this is that all religions first perished in the very places where they were first established. And unless the diligence of princes had restrained luxury, they would have been destroyed by those very people who were for a long time the self-appointed guardians of those religions. In matters of the soul, however, sacred power ought to be absolute. But while the <term>mystæ</term> <note>original: "mystae"; refers to priests or initiates of sacred mysteries</note> favor themselves more than is right or consult only their own interests, they do not sufficiently weigh the utility of everyone; instead, they naturally tend to care for their own livelihood (since that is how they are maintained). Although their income is intended for the longevity and preservation of their order, no one should consider it a miracle if it is consumed by someone else. For they do not set a limit for themselves; rather, a fairer judge and the best arbiter of the Commonwealth ought to do so. It will be discussed later by what primary means all persuasions have perished or are destined to perish. Now, we must explain in a few words how various forms of worship crept into the world.

### The origin of ABSURD RELIGION and
### IDOLATRY <note>original Greek: εἰδωλολατρεία (eidōlolatreia)</note>. CHAPTER VI.

Since this temple of nature and the immensity of its blessings draws men into stupor and admiration, they desire to direct their gratitude toward some unknown cause. But the ignorant man, not knowing to whom he should give thanks (for blind mortality cannot conceive of the appearance of divinity), offers both fear and gratitude to whatever thing is introduced and presented by priests and "wise men." The priests, appointed to preserve this received opinion, increase and confirm it through divinations, riddles, thorny difficulties, and cunning. 

It was therefore sufficient for tyrants and those who once held the reins of power to restrain the minds of the people with even the most false religious opinions. Regarding the decrees, responses, or oracles of the gods—or the priests who taught their worship—no one was permitted or accustomed to demand a reason. The "wise," who knew the true nature of things but pretended to approve of these rites, served as an example to the ignorant common folk; as authors of the status quo, they ensured the received opinion of the gods was maintained, while the prince compelled both groups through fear for the sake of public peace. 

In ancient times, when the world was not yet "sharp-nosed" <note>original: "nasutus"; a Latin idiom for being discerning, critical, or skeptical</note>, those crafty princes and scoundrels were led by the credulity of the commoners and the multitude. Seeking to make the memory of themselves last as long as possible through rare or famous deeds—whether by glory, reputation, benefit, or trickery—they wanted the unskillful crowd to be persuaded that after death they would become immortal gods and depart into **heaven**, where they would take care of mortal affairs. This was contingent, however, on all mortals (but especially those they had benefited or ruled) being busy in performing sacred rites for them with frequent sacrifices—that is, so that their memory might be preserved longer, they supported their priests. For without an annual human memory and a small offering <note>original: "stipe"; a small coin or donation given to temples</note> established for that memory, nothing lasts very long. Time obliterates all things, but it erases these things more slowly. From this came **apotheosis** <term>apotheosis: the process of a human being transformed into a god</term>, and the eagles [released] from the funeral pyre... <note>Postel refers to the Roman imperial custom where an eagle was released from a deceased Emperor's pyre to represent his soul flying to heaven.</note>

From this came the blight and the origin of evil; from this came all kinds of sacrifices and games; from this came the various types of funerals for those seeking the heavens. Thence arose sacred rites, increased and confirmed by lies. From this, a being began to be regarded as a God who did not even deserve the name of a man, but rather that of a most savage beast. From this, the predator and destroyer of cities, **Mars**, arose; from this, the sodomite and potter <note>original: "figulus"; Postel uses this term mockingly for Jupiter's role in "forming" or manipulating mortals</note> **Jupiter**; the impostor and smooth-talking **Mercury**; **Venus** the prostitute; the **Lemnian smith** <note>Vulcan, who was cast down to the island of Lemnos</note>; **Neptune** the pirate; and the farmers **Bacchus** and **Ceres**—all ascended into heaven by the tongues and favors of their countrymen. And as if that were not enough, even catamites <term>Cynaedi: young men kept for sexual purposes</term> and prostitutes were gifted with Roman sacred status.

Indeed, lest they should immediately perish from human memory and fall from their heaven, they were not only worshipped with fixed and certain rites and sacrifices, but they also left certain animals to posterity as sacred to themselves—species that would always be present among men. **Apollo**, the flute-player, physician, and traveling pharmacist, left the serpent; **Jupiter** the eagle, **Venus** the doves, **Juno** the peacock, and others left other things. There are also trees and herbs consecrated to them, through the ingenuity of priests and the natural properties of the planets.

Egypt was the inventor of this ingenuity. **Isis**, Queen of Egypt, is said to have devised this in the name of her husband **Osiris**. When Osiris had been deprived of his life by his brother and torn into twenty-five pieces on the pretext of tyranny, Isis recovered the pieces after defeating the brother. She did this so that her people would not abandon or cast off their belief in his divinity—a belief they had conceived both because of the greatness of his deeds and the opinion of his divine origin. The brother had intended to send those twenty-five parts of her husband’s body to the governors of as many provinces as a sign of his deed. Isis ensured that each individual part was enclosed in statues larger than the human form, and that these were consecrated in as many dedicated temples in different provinces (as if the entire body of her husband lay hidden in each one). She established money for the annual income of the priests who would persuade the people of this; for without the use of money, neither religion, nor laws, nor even the most useful arts can persist in the slightest in a mature world.

Furthermore, although she wanted it to be believed he was anywhere in the provinces (as one who was said to be alone in heaven), she also wanted as many different animals as there were body parts to be held sacred. She did this to generate competition and a longer memory among the common people (who strive to surpass one another in the display of processions and ceremonies). She decreed that once an animal was consecrated anywhere, it was **sacrosanct** <term>Sacrosanctum: something protected by religious sanction from any injury or violation</term>, not to be harmed even by chance, but to be worshipped exceedingly and shown religiously—and this not frequently, nor without ceremonies or the vows of the people. For even sacrosanct mysteries become cheap through constant exposure, but are held in high regard through rarity. Thus, as if Osiris were reborn in each of those living creatures, he offered himself voluntarily to the daily remembrance of the Egyptians.

Nature has produced men with such a great sense of glory and desire that they are spurred by a sting toward noble deeds; however, wickedness translates this desire for glory only into fame and notoriety, not into virtue. Thus, it has left behind far more men like **Paris, Cambyses, Herostratus, Dionysius, Claudius, Nero,** and **Heliogabalus** than those like **Saturn, Janus,** and **Augustus**. The more impudent these villains were, the more ardently they attempted to seize heaven to wash away the stain of their wicked lives. This was the fountain of **idolatry** <note>original Greek: "εἰδωλολατρείας" (eidololatreias)</note> and the nursery of false persuasion. From this came the bow, the arrow, the sacred shield <note>original: "ancyle"; the shield that fell from heaven in the time of Numa Pompilius</note>; from this, anything at all was forced into religion. Thence, divinity was believed to be absent from nothing. From this came the ruin of the world and contention, and the variety of burials, which seemed to be the door to divinity...

Man himself was devoted as the most pleasing sacrificial victim to the gods—whether guilty or innocent, slave or free, guest or native, stranger or parent. Nor was it enough that some held certain animals sacred for the sake of long-standing memory; certain others were cursed and customarily sacrificed to each of those scoundrels (I meant to say gods): a sow to **Minerva**, a goat to **Bacchus**, a donkey to **Priapus**, and so on; thus an Egyptian fiction prepared a foul destruction for almost the entire animal kingdom.

Sacred rites began to be performed for the underworld. Earthly gods were worshipped according to the decrees of **Pythagoras** <note>The famous Greek philosopher who taught about the harmony of the spheres and the soul</note> so they would not cause harm, while celestial gods were worshipped so they might be beneficial. A crowd of gods from the entire conquered world was brought into the city by the Romans—those subverters of human peace—so that wherever men flowed from, they might find and worship their ancestral gods at Rome. 

**Vacuna** <note>original: "Vacinna"; the goddess of leisure or rest</note>, **Pales** <note>deity of shepherds and flocks</note>, **Rubigo** <note>deity of grain mildew or blight</note>, **Pomona** <note>goddess of fruit trees</note>, **Pilumnus** <note>original: "Pylumnus"; a deity protecting infants</note>, **Vertumnus** <note>original: "Vertunus"; god of the seasons and change</note>, **Cupid**, **Pleasure**, **Lubentina** <note>goddess of sensual desire</note>, **Venus**, **Fever**, **Fortune**, and **Roman Fortune** were gods dedicated with temples. Temples and statues were even erected for **Faith**, **Mind**, **Virtue**, **Wealth**, **Liberty**, and **Victory**. 

The names of the heavens, planets, elements, virtues, vices, men, and demons were changed by clever and crafty men and drawn into religion. The First Cause, or Providence, began to be held in the utmost ignorance by all men until it became known again under the leadership of **Christ**. Furthermore, lest the authority of a religion once approved be diminished, or the mark of impiety be burned onto the tyrants themselves, the victors always spared the temples—as long as they could hide and disguise their thefts. For one can hardly find in the records of literature, among such a great number of kings, tyrants, or emperors (except for a few Persians or Romans), those who dared to despoil religious places and shrines. This is despite the fact that they knew almost all types of religion were false and devised by human cleverness. They did this primarily because they knew men are believed to be the authors and preservers of religion even more than the gods themselves. 

Moreover, if you remove the ancestral gods or overturn and despoil their temples, how will those you wish to obey your commands be able to come together for sacred rites? Certainly, he who diminishes the authority of the gods dissolves the union of the people, unless—with all things already settled and the empire strengthened, and the falsehood of the former religion demonstrated—he strives to provide something better. A new prince certainly ought not to attempt this unless he is far superior. Therefore, all princes, or those in power, were busy adorning and building temples with the greatest effort—either to leave an impression of their own piety upon the common people, or to strengthen religions, or for both reasons. They sought to decorate those temples with spoils snatched from human blood or even from other temples, which resulted in the common people being kept in their loyalty far more easily. These are the causes and origins of false religion. Now we must speak of its progress, growth, and orders.

...and you should make bases. All things are owed to the skilled hand. For all things, as if heaped together in a kind of **chaos**, have been gradually polished and moved into their proper orders by human prudence—driven by necessity, utility, hope, and glory, and by the greatest labor of mind and body—after the fashion of the divine providence that adorned this worldly mass. Indeed, the raw principles of all things have been cultivated through learning and a kind of natural refining; just as divine providence, using natural power and arrangement, organized the celestial and elemental order from a primary and confused mass (which could not rightly be called either **matter** or **form** <note>Postel refers here to the Aristotelian concepts of *materia* and *forma*, where "matter" is the raw potential and "form" is the identity or essence of a thing</note>, nor could it be grasped by the human mind, which did not yet exist). It balanced heavy things with light, the highest with the lowest, the incorruptible with the fleeting, and motion with rest. This order is preserved eternally by the **celestial element**, which some call the "fifth" <note>original: "quintum"; the *quintessence* or Aether, thought by ancient philosophers to be the unchanging substance of the heavens</note>, because it depends solely on the command of providence and does not contain within itself diverse or conflicting parts that could be infected by contagion.

Therefore, at the beginning of human society, before vice and greed demanded laws for their restraint, the prince, the people, and the priest were one and the same, and were equals. From there, the authority of the father over his children, the head of the household over the servants, the master or lord over the slaves, the judge over the province, the prince over the realm, and the priest over souls began to take hold, proceeding gradually by example and by the common consent of men. Once established, both the prince (or judge) and the priest performed the functions of all such magistrates before affairs grew large and empires expanded. For there is no need for a different order where one person is sufficient.

Once an opinion is born and has flourished for some time, as things become known and required, something is added daily to the small foundations of affairs and the beginnings of sacred laws, arising from the doubts or vices that crop up every day. Furthermore, there is the worship of the common people, though (as far as affairs are concerned) it is rarely done without a **contribution** <note>original: "stipe"; a small coin or donation given to a temple or cause</note>. For when a certain opinion regarding holiness, a miracle, or some unusual and useful thing or divinity has increased everywhere among nations—religion naturally propagating itself—wealth, which was either meager or nonexistent at the very beginning, grows gradually. It flows in from all sides through vows, so that things which are small at the start grow up and expand immensely, creeping along through both opinions and riches. For there are many who offer gifts and believe the stories being told. There are few who "open" the miracles and sacred rites (lest they become cheapened by frequent exposure), and few who receive such great gifts which the common people believe (as the priests assert) are most pleasing to the gods. 

This is the condition of religion and the growth of persuasion. This "art" has constructed massive temples out of mere shrines and groves, and has compelled the splendor of wealth to assist the words of persuasion. From here arose secondary laws, born of vices and doubts, which explain and confirm the primary ones. Then, in the name of buildings, ceremonies, processions, games, ornaments, rituals, and revenues, there is even the demanding of gifts. The people, enticed by the splendor of all sacred things, are even accustomed to offer them voluntarily, partly out of religion, and partly to share in the glory and the memory of their name. Princes, and those who possess great means, in order to leave a glorious record of their name behind them and to have the gods look favorably upon them—and to surpass and incite the zeal of the commoners—usually build shrines at their own expense and appoint numerous guardians of persuasion to amplify religion itself. Added to this is the industry and **economy** <note>original: "oeconomia"; in this context, the careful management or "stewardship" of resources</note> of the priests in increasing those riches, which brings in a vast offspring of wealth. Thus it happens (as mortal affairs can never stand still, and are the cause of both ruin and change if anyone abuses them) that sacred wealth grows immensely, according to the desires and means of the people; and if there is any luxury anywhere, since they are restrained by no one,

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
## BOOK III

...are fed, it is seen most especially in priests or high priests. Those reasons, based on persuasions that arose from the earliest beginnings and were preserved for a long time, have grown immensely. In the splendor of their wealth, there is almost no institution of any duration that has not easily surpassed the **Epicureans** <note>followers of Epicurus, often stereotyped in this era as seekers of luxury and pleasure</note> in luxury, or the public treasury in resources. Finally, it even pierces itself with its own sword, and through the allurements of pleasures and depraved morals, it destroys itself. Nor does this occur only in our own religion. Although we Christians profess a contempt for all things, this can neither truly happen nor be observed once a religion has reached maturity. A few people, holy in reputation and not corrupted by vile opinions, needed little at the time when the nascent persuasion of the Church was growing; now many people need many things, and the highest leaders need the most. It was certainly fitting that religion be poor and stripped of all things—indeed, that it should advocate for the contempt of wealth—when its practitioners were very few and most abstemious, not yet burdened by vices, opinions, doubts, and a large assembly that required governance. But as the orders increased and became distinct, it became necessary to have resources sufficient for the needs of the community. 

From this, in my judgment, those who wish to forbid Christian **priests** <term>original: "sacrificulis," literally 'little sacrificers,' a term Postel uses for the lower clergy who perform the rites</term> from having their own resources are entirely mistaken, especially since if they have anything themselves, they shamefully squander it on luxury. Certainly, it is the perverse use, not the wealth itself, that ought to be blamed. For who but a fool would refuse gifts, the most excellent kind of acquisition? Who would forbid great buildings from being constructed in the divine name? Who would condemn industry, especially when those things are done for the sake of the deity? Let it be permitted for those to whose judgment they are committed to use them both well and poorly. Thus temples and priests grow rich; thus the **dead gods** are wealthier than the living. 

Furthermore, as the ownership of things increased, in the progress of time one person could not be sufficient for handling, amending, and preserving all sacred matters; several people equal in dignity could not exist without arbiters, lawsuits, and crimes. It was necessary for a primary order to be established once, and it was necessary for a first arbiter of religion to give laws to those who were absent, and to prescribe rules for those more remote whose care was committed to him. Whether he is chosen by the one who is the author or preserver of religion, or by a prince, or by popular consent, or by a great council, it matters not. It is necessary for one to be over many, to whom the summit of affairs is deferred. For just as no one can be a judge for himself (except in the secrets of his own conscience), so without a certain supreme authority among those equal in dignity, one cannot pronounce the law, punish crimes, or respond to doubts. In the religions of all nations that have spread widely, there have been high priests, and there will be in the future, who prescribe for the others, either by the authority of the Prince, or the consent of the Republic, or a supreme council. Otherwise, there would be no order of things in human affairs, but a kind of **Chaos**, since the affairs of this mortality are always connected to corruption, doubts, lawsuits, and vices. For truth, friendship, and virtue are held here by name rather than in reality, except by those whom God has entirely changed through Christ. 

Finally, when regions subject to the same persuasion spread wider than can be conveniently reached by all to the high priest, a third order must arise. Men of middle authority must be established according to the nature of the places, to whom the high priest may both prescribe rules and impart his authority in certain matters. Antiquity called these men **pontiffs** <note>original: "pontifices"</note> because they **make a bridge** <note>original: "pontem faciant"; Postel employs the traditional etymology of "pontifex" as a bridge-builder between the divine and the human</note> for the religion that flourishes through them, and as if by handing it down, they carry it across to others and preserve it, lest it be endangered by being immersed in political cares. There are therefore three orders of preservers and explainers of persuasion: the highest, the middle, and the lowest—high priests, pontiffs, and priests. There is no civilized nation reigning for a long time under the same persuasion that has not had these titles and duties, even if they called them by a name different from ours. For the diversity of words, which differs in almost every people, does not forbid the things themselves from being the same. That there are sometimes middle [ranks] of various...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s analysis of religious growth. Having argued on the previous page that wealth and resources became necessary as the Church expanded, he now explains how that expansion required the development of a formal hierarchy—moving from simple, local gatherings to a complex structure of bishops, archbishops, and a supreme leader.</meta>

GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK II.

There is nothing to prevent the existence of equal orders. For although archbishops rank above bishops in dignity and certain legal rights, and one assembly may rank above another, all these middle ranks are equal in the sense that they obey the supreme **pontiff** <term>original: "pontifici summo," the high priest or Pope</term> or the highest authority. The Greeks had patriarchs; when they had disagreements—just as the Apostles themselves did—it was not one supreme man who presided over them, but holy councils. Would that this practice had been preserved in all Churches! For from the power of a single man, there often emerge many laws that follow personal emotion or private gain rather than reason. While such laws might be useful at certain times, they do not always seem suited to the needs and nature of everyone as times change. 

However, for a world that has reached maturity, it is far more useful and efficient in private matters for one supreme leader to be in charge and to set the rules. It is hardly possible to frequently assemble such a crowd of prelates and learned men, who should only come together when the most vital matters of state are at stake. Indeed, neither for princes nor for **pontiffs** <note>the chief religious leaders</note> (who are most concerned) would that expense be tolerable. Therefore, the use and establishment of middle ranks is usually decided by the necessity of things and times, or even by public opinion. 

If the practice of a particular belief existed in only one city or municipality, the same person could be the highest, middle, and lowest authority. Such were the ancient and nascent religions, when every city, village, or town used its own sacred rites, distinct from others. For as has been shown before, after the knowledge of the "First Cause" <note>Postel’s term for God as the original creator</note> was lost—which had naturally offered itself to the first humans—an unrefined antiquity gave names to any deity that presented itself. Just as a province did not swear its word to a single prince, so too it did not know only one God. 

But when the expansion of religions followed, not even the most powerful emperor could encompass all types of duties in a single man. Assemblies of equals in the first and second orders had to be granted a head. Those further removed from the original source and location required a present authority, so that doubts or vices would not spread too widely and turn into law through long usage before remedies could be sought from afar. This is why Paul, the highest overseer of our **persuasion** <note>Postel uses "persuasio" (persuasion) to refer to a religious faith or system of belief</note> after Christ, rightly said that "Orders are from God." He was speaking not only of the authority of princes who moderate these fleeting earthly things, but of the orders of religions. Thus, both wealth and authority were organized together in sacred matters. We must now see by what law they are maintained.

### ON STABILITY. CHAPTER VIII.

No one, except by common consent or a holy assembly, may place a Prince over the supreme pontiff; nor may they divert things once dedicated to sacred use, as if they were assigned to the heritage of an eternal religion. The supreme pontiff gives the primary rights to the middle ranks (however many there are), and likewise to the lowest. The middle ranks obey him and prescribe the law entrusted to them to the lowest ranks. The lowest are accustomed only to obey, and not to prescribe to men of their own order by their own authority. 

If an inferior person is negligent in his duty, the right to correct him belongs to the middle rank; if that person fails, it belongs to the supreme leader. By these leaders, the people are chiefly guided by the hand toward religion, sacred things are explained, and the mysteries are tasted. In short, almost whatever care is committed to the other orders is usually cast upon them (unless religion is accompanied by greed). They are like the forces and parts of the elements, directed by the heavens and the First Cause; they are like the hands and limbs of the other orders, though certainly very different from any natural comparison. This order follows the example of nature most closely so long as it performs its duty without laziness and strives to imitate the perpetual action of nature. For the heavens obey sacred Providence, as do its powers and all the lowest things consisting of elements, and the middle World itself...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument for the practical necessity of religious hierarchies. While the previous page touched on the equality of some middle ranks, here he justifies the transition from the poverty of the early Church to the organized wealth and structure of a mature institution, arguing that a single supreme leader and various sub-ranks are essential for maintaining order and resolving disputes in any widespread belief system.</meta>

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...are restrained, this is seen most especially in priests or pontiffs. By this reasoning, beliefs that arose from early beginnings and were preserved for a long time have grown immensely. In the splendor of their wealth, almost no religion that has lasted for any length of time has not easily surpassed the **Epicureans** <note>A school of philosophy often associated in the Renaissance with the pursuit of luxury and pleasure.</note> in luxury and the public treasury in resources. Finally, it even stabs itself with its own sword, and through the allurements of pleasure and depraved morals, it destroys itself. 

Nor does this happen only in our religion. Although we Christians profess a contempt for all worldly things—which certainly cannot be done or observed in a religion that has reached maturity—the situation has changed. A few people, holy in reputation and not corrupted by wicked opinions, needed very little back when the nascent belief of the Church was growing; now, many people need many things, and those at the top need the most. It was certainly right for religion to be meager and stripped of all things—and indeed, to urge a contempt for wealth—when its followers were very few and most abstemious. At that time, vices, conflicting opinions, and doubts had not yet been born, nor was there a large assembly for which rules had to be prescribed. But as the ranks grew and became distinct, resources became necessary to meet the needs of the situation. 

Therefore, in my judgment, those who wish to forbid Christian **priests** <term>original: "sacrificulis," literally those who perform sacrifices</term> from having their own resources are **completely mistaken** <note>original: "toto caelo errant," literally "err by the whole sky."</note>, especially since if those critics have anything themselves, they shamefully squander it on luxury. It is certainly the perverted use of wealth, not the wealth itself, that should be blamed. For who but a fool would refuse gifts—the most excellent way of acquiring things—or forbid great buildings to be constructed in the divine name, or condemn industry, especially when these things are done for the sake of the Deity, and when the person to whose judgment they are committed is permitted to use them for good or for ill? 

In this way, temples and priests grow rich; thus the dead gods are wealthier than the living. Furthermore, as dominion over worldly things increased, one person could not be sufficient over time to handle, reform, and preserve all sacred matters. Nor could many people of equal rank coexist without doubts, lawsuits, and crimes. It was necessary at one time for a primary order to be established, and it was necessary for a chief judge to give laws of religion to those who were absent, and to prescribe rules for those farther away whose care was committed to him. 

Whether he is chosen by the author or preserver of the religion, or by a prince, or by popular consent, or by a great council, it matters not. It is necessary for one to preside over the many, to whom the highest authority in all matters is deferred. For just as no one can be his own judge (except in matters of conscience and hidden things), so without some supreme authority, it is impossible to administer justice among those equal in rank, to punish crimes, or to provide answers regarding doubtful matters. 

In the religions of all nations that have spread widely, there have been **supreme pontiffs**, and there will be in the future, to prescribe rules for the others, whether by the authority of a Prince, by the consensus of the Republic, or by the authority of a supreme council. Otherwise, there would be no order in human affairs, but a kind of Chaos, since the matters of this mortal life are always tied to corruption, doubts, lawsuits, and vices. For truth, friendship, and virtue are held here more in name than in reality, except by those whom God has entirely transformed through Christ. 

Finally, when the regions subject to the same belief spread so widely that the supreme pontiff cannot be conveniently reached by everyone, a third order must arise. Men of middle authority must be appointed according to the nature of the locations, to whom the supreme pontiff may both prescribe rules and impart his authority in certain matters. Antiquity called these men **pontiffs** <note>The word *pontifex* is traditionally derived from *pons* (bridge) and *facere* (to make).</note> because they make a "bridge" for the religion that flourishes through them, and as it were, they carry it across by handing it down to others and preserve it, lest it be endangered by being immersed in political cares. 

There are, therefore, three orders of those who preserve and explain a belief: the highest, the middle, and the lowest—the supreme pontiffs, the pontiffs (bishops), and the priests. No civilized nation reigning for a long time under the same belief has lacked these titles and duties, even if it called them by different names than we do. For the diversity of words, which differs among almost every people, does not prevent the things themselves from being the same. That there are sometimes middle...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s discussion on the practical organization of religious institutions. Having previously argued that growth necessitates wealth and hierarchy, he now examines the specific tiers of leadership—archbishops, bishops, and the supreme leader—balancing the efficiency of a single head against the ideal of collective governance by councils.</meta>

->GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK II.<-

...of various orders, nothing prevents it. For although archbishops are superior in dignity and by certain rights to bishops, and one assembly to another, all of them are nevertheless "middle" ranks in that they obey a supreme pontiff <note>original: "pontifici summo"; here referring to the Pope or a highest religious leader.</note>, or the supreme power. Among the Greeks, there were Patriarchs; when they had disagreements—as was the case with the Apostles themselves—no single supreme man was in charge, but rather holy councils presided over them. I only wish this practice had been preserved in all Churches. For from the power of a single man, there often emerge many laws—driven by personal whim or self-interest rather than reason—which, even if they were useful at some point, do not seem well-suited to the needs and nature of everyone in the current age.

Yet, in a mature world, it is far more useful and efficient in private matters for one supreme leader to be appointed to preside and prescribe rules, since that great crowd of bishops and learned men can hardly be gathered as frequently as would be necessary. Such a gathering should only happen when the most important matters of state are at stake. Indeed, that expense would be intolerable for either princes or pontiffs (who have the greatest stake in it). Therefore, the use and establishment of "middle" ranks is usually determined by necessity, the requirements of the time, or even by common opinion. 

If the practice of a particular belief were confined to only one city or municipality, the same person could be the highest, middle, and lowest rank all at once. Such were the ancient and developing religions, when any city, village, or municipality used its own sacred rites, distinct from others. For as has been shown before, after the knowledge of the First Cause <note>The "First Cause" refers to the original, pure understanding of God that Postel believed was granted to the first humans before it was corrupted by history.</note> was lost—which had been offered freely to the first humans—unrefined antiquity gave names to any deity that happened to be presented. Just as a province had not yet sworn loyalty to the words of a single prince, it did not know only one God. 

But when the propagation of religions followed, not even the most powerful emperor could encompass all types of duties in a single man. Assemblies of equals had to be granted leadership in the first and second orders. Those further removed from the original source and location required an established authority; this was to prevent doubts or vices from spreading too widely and hardening into law through long usage before remedies could be sought from afar. Hence, Paul—the supreme leader of our persuasion after Christ—noted with good reason that "Orders are from God." He spoke not only of the authority of princes who manage these fleeting earthly matters, but of the orders of religions. Thus, both wealth and authority were arranged together in sacred matters. We must now see by what law they are maintained.

## ON CONSISTENCY. CHAPTER VIII.

No one, except by common consent, a holy assembly, or a Prince, is permitted to preside over the supreme pontiff; nor may anyone divert things once dedicated to sacred use, as if they were assigned to an eternal inheritance of religion. The supreme pontiff gives the primary laws to the middle ranks (however many there are), and likewise to the lowest. The middle ranks obey him and prescribe rules to the lowest within the jurisdiction entrusted to them. Those in the final rank are only meant to obey; they do not usually prescribe rules to men of their own order by their own authority. 

If a lower official carries out his duty too negligently, the right of correction belongs to the middle rank; if he fails, it belongs to the supreme leader. It is by these lower ranks especially that the people are led by the hand toward religion: the sacred rites are explained, and the mysteries are tasted. In short, almost whatever care is committed to the other orders is usually cast upon them (unless religion is accompanied by the pursuit of profit). They are like the forces and parts of the elements, directed by the heavens and the First Cause, serving as the hands and limbs of the other orders—though clearly, this comparison is quite different from natural ones. This order follows the example of nature most closely so long as it performs its duty without sloth and strives to imitate the perpetual action of nature. For the heavens obey a sacred providence, as do its powers and all the lower things composed of elements; the World itself...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s discussion of the ecclesiastical hierarchy. He previously explained that while archbishops and bishops are superior in dignity to local priests, they all function as "middle" ranks subject to a supreme leader or council. He now transitions into how these middle ranks reflect the cosmic order and the administration of religious law.</meta>

the middle rank, representing our High Priests <note>original: "Antistitum"; refers to those standing at the head, such as bishops or overseers.</note>, acts only upon lower things, and exercises and impresses the powers entrusted to it by the First Cause <note>In Postel's Neoplatonic view, the "First Cause" is God, whose power flows down through hierarchies.</note>. The lower part of the world partly obeys nature, partly art <note>Here "art" refers to human skill or technology.</note>, and partly both. This is the image of the sacrosanct trinity, which *is diffused through all the limbs, as a mind moves the mass, and mingles itself with the great body*: <note>original: "Totam diffusa per artus, uti mens agitat molem, & magno se corpore miscet"; a famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid (VI.726-727) describing the world-soul.</note> when it departs, all things are in danger. Heaven belongs to God; the elements are open to both God and heaven, administered and produced by a hidden and open cause in a holy mystery. This system of orders, as far as it concerns the middle ranks, can be diverse. For some can rightly recognize the supreme arbiter of the law immediately without a middle rank, such as those who turn themselves to the First Cause without contemplating the intermediary nature: such are many holy assemblies and monasteries, which a flourishing persuasion <note>Postel uses "persuasio" to mean a system of religious belief or a specific faith.</note> now lacks. Furthermore, since no rationale of religion is usually rendered except in a chosen assembly, daily opinions are usually joined to other opinions, whence many private individuals (so long as there is a cause of belief) even create religious gatherings. But this has nothing to do with the established orders, nor is that crowd necessary if the Republic can do without them; and a province that obeys a belief stands much more happily before so many various cults and assemblies of orders disturb and increase the total number, unless they are introduced by necessity. The law of sacred things is usually handed down first by the supreme pontiffs, and then by the middle ranks; it is proclaimed either by them or by those to whom they have given the power of proclaiming the law. Indeed, it is necessary for them to have vicars <note>Deputies or representatives.</note>, who are accustomed to proclaim the law concerning sacred things to the multitude. For even if they themselves were Briarei <note>Briareus was a mythological giant with one hundred hands; Postel means that even with superhuman capacity, leaders cannot do everything alone.</note>, they would not be sufficient for themselves. They have, therefore, their own judges, who decide matters concerning sacred things or things pertaining to the sacred based on the authority handed down to them, not without the various attachments of the courts. This will be revealed next at the end of the book, where the judges of Princes or of profane <note>Secular or non-religious law.</note> law will be treated.

### ON THE HANDLING, USE, AND CORRU-
### ption of persuasions. CHAPTER IX.

This especially must be noted diligently: all the decrees of religion have the force of law, and all those subject to the jurisdiction of any bishop are held by them. For it is much less beneficial to the tranquility of the Republic to infringe upon divine matters than human ones, unless it happens through rare and not lazy negligence. Truly, it is not the place of a private man to resist in words, unless it is commanded divinely, or by a supreme and more powerful prince. The authority of the supreme pontiff, or whatever stands in his place, binds everyone with laws. The right of bishops is like civil law, and does not reach everyone. For there are many things approved by usage or by the decrees of pontiffs everywhere among nations (concerning rites and ceremonies) which are neither guarded by the highest pontifical law, nor usually observed by others, yet they obtain the force of law, provided they do not oppose human law. For since not only every province, but even every sacred place has its own as it were tutelary gods <note>Patron saints or protective spirits associated with a specific location.</note>, it is right for them to be worshiped by their own and accepted rite. Laws of this kind affect those subject to those places, but do not affect others in the same way. Divine law—after customs have been handed down and piety and worship toward the gods have been established (which is the first source of belief)—deals, much like civil law, only with sacred things and dedicated persons, or things held in the opinion of being sacred. The first concern is about divine worship, so that it occurs on certain fixed days with prayers and ceremonies: it encourages probity and duty, suggests the law of reason, and preaches virtue (unless it suffers from foolishness, as many ancient ones did of old) by the example, love, or fear of the gods. It prescribes to the sacred orders the manner in which everything held to be sacred should be observed. In the second place, the dignity and duty of persons must be addressed...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s analysis of the institutional structure of religion. # GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK III.

...by which duty each person, evidently, may perform their office, be initiated, be supported by what gain, and with what character, worship, and sacred vestments they should be endowed. For because the unrefined multitude of things easily admires and looks up to what is rare and theatrical <note>original: "personata"; literally "masked" or "played like a character in a drama."</note>, it is for this reason—so that through their finery the overseers of religions might be recognized immediately without questioning, and be set apart from the profane crowd by their very ornaments—that a good part of religions is placed in varied dress. This dress is even proven by its own interpretations to be necessary and essential, as if the divinity had commanded that its rites ought to be performed with such ritual, otherwise it would not hear mortal prayers. That appearance of the persona in a man dedicated to sacred things has always been the greatest part of persuasion <note>Postel uses "persuasio" to refer to a religious system or a specific set of beliefs.</note>. If, however, there are those to be initiated into the mysteries, or those about to give their names to a religion, it ought to be handed down in this place; for certain mysteries pertain to all, some to a few, and some to none except the high priests. But because it is a matter of opinion how many or to whom these are owed, it shall be enough to know that this law and the knowledge of it must be sought from the pontifical sanctions <term>Pontifical sanctions: the decrees or laws issued by the high priests or church authorities.</term>, and the reason for what is committed, or the decision of a doubt, must be had from that place whence the authority flowed.

The next place after the mysteries in mature persuasions <note>systems of belief that have reached a stable, institutionalized state.</note> ought to be for providing for the priests <note>original: "sacrificulis"; literally "little sacrificers," a term Postel often uses for those who perform the physical rites of sacrifice.</note> from those resources which are added, or are already dedicated to sacred things—which laws themselves, being absolute, cannot be published for those just being born before the resources have been acquired. For there must be property, and there must be dispute concerning it, before a law can be established about it. Therefore, nascent religious laws, just as they are simpler, are also closer to equity, because they either follow the offered goal of divinity, or at first they pretend to aim at it, and do not immediately mix the factions of wealth with piety. For this reason, princes comply with a nascent religion and support it for a very long time while it is content with moderate things, until they begin to use the law granted to them perversely.

But when either their faction, or their morals, or their resources begin to be greater than is right, and become an object of hatred or envy to princes—not rarely becoming formidable and a hindrance to the state—then the rights of choosing dignities begin to be taken from them, and their wealth diminished. For you might rather break than correct those things which have hardened into depravity. No one indeed, unless compelled, or moved by a rare religious conviction, can easily relinquish pleasures and utilities, the abundance of which he holds through his resources, and which nature has taught him to seek. Habits, therefore, creep into the place of piety, and occupy the place of the practice of virtue, and pass into custom. Thus, gradually, the law is usually either removed or diminished by the prince’s authority; wealth likewise. Otherwise, in the progress of time, a good part of the treasury <note>original: "fisci"; the public or royal purse.</note> would creep into the sacred realm; a luxury more than Sybaritic <note>Sybaris was an ancient Greek city famous for its extreme decadence and love of luxury.</note> would infect the sacred order. And since there are no priests anywhere among the nations who are not for the most part immune from war and the physical protection of the state (for they are born and instituted for retaining, driving, and composing souls), and since they are the wealthiest there, they would undoubtedly exhaust the treasury, never helping except with sacred rites, and always receiving; hence the envy of the treasury comes forth against them.

A thin persuasion is gradually increased by both laws and wealth; having increased, it stands at its manhood; from there, as if gasping for wealth and suffocated by it, it perishes in old age, its law first being diminished and its resources gradually reduced back to the treasury. But if princes could, in their own name, "wipe the nose" <note>original: "emungere"; a colloquialism for cheating someone out of money or "cleaning them out."</note> of the place of the gods, the sacred possession would not be so ample or so long-lasting. But since they would see the state of affairs endangered when the authority of a persuasion is derogated (for the common people listen to complaints), certain princes and magistrates of a corrupted world have devised a certain mixed law from the sacred and the profane, and a joined power for sacrificial kings. For it is the highest thing for striking terror among mortals that gods should accompany kings. If, however, the sacred order is allowed to grow in wealth without reins and at its own will, it undoubtedly brings destruction upon itself, the state, and religion. And since resources can never exist without the pleasures and the crime of which they are the suppliers, and they overflow the more because they lack censors:

<meta>This page continues Postel’s discussion on the institutional stability of religions. He transitions from the external appearance and dress of the clergy (discussed on the previous page) to the internal rot caused by excessive wealth, eventually proposing a set of universal "canons" or rules that he believes should govern any stable religious system.</meta>

->ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-

It is then, finally, when the priests are most wealthy—those who ought to approach the gods purely and live more holily than others—that they betray themselves to the common people. Even if the ruler is silent, they bear witness against the gods (as that famous saying goes). From this arise the obvious deceptions felt by the common folk, who believe they have been cheated; they develop a mind not only against giving more, but of taking back what has already been given, if it were possible. Thus the right and authority of the priests perish. In this way, all types of religious systems <note>original: "persuasionum"; Postel uses this term to describe organized religions or belief systems.</note> have perished. This is the outcome and the end of all things when the institutions themselves struggle under their own mass, and when no one wishes to look within themselves and return to a moderate path: *Great things collapse upon themselves, and fall heavily under too much weight.* <note>Postel is likely quoting the Roman poet Lucan here, referring to the collapse of the Roman Republic.</note> I do not wish to add here the violent ends of religions that happen due to external powers. For necessity sometimes imposes an end, not only upon sacred laws but also upon secular ones, though rarely without some great wickedness from those who are falling. This happens when Providence—or some cause unknown to us, usually attributed to Providence—seeks punishment for a shattered order and a shameful life.

There were once many, and there are even now other magistrates among certain foreign peoples <note>original: "barbaros"; in the classical sense, meaning non-Greeks/non-Romans, or simply "foreigners."</note>, whose responses and decrees were customarily observed with superstition in the early stages of their affairs: such as Augurs, Soothsayers, Prophets, Sibylls, and any other kind of office that once restrained and held back the minds of unlearned men. Truly, these things were ridiculous to other nations and relied only on opinion. For beyond the social orders and the law itself, by which the common people are usually kept in their duty, absolutely nothing is usually approved by the decrees and natural consensus of all religions. Now, however, in a few "aphorisms," as it were, religion itself must be summarized in brief definitions <note>original: "ἀφορισμοῖς" (aphorismois); Greek for definitions or short, pithy statements.</note>, insofar as it is agreeable to all, or ever will be agreeable. For I refrain from passing down those things which belong to only one group, because all religions—even the most excellent ones—are mutually ridiculous to one another (except where they agree in general terms): *For what you marvel at is a joke to others.* <note>original: "σὺ γὰρ ὃ θαυμάζεις, τοῦθ’ ἑτέροισι γέλως"; a Greek proverb emphasizing religious and cultural relativity.</note>

# COMMON CANONS OF ALL PERSUASIONS
## Chapter X.

Let it be a conviction for all that there is a God, the author of all things, from whom we should fear dire things and hope for the opposite.
All things are believed to have been made by God for a hidden cause.
It shall be a provision of the sacred laws that the ancestral deities must be both accepted and worshiped by all those enrolled in the State, or by the inhabitants of that place where the persuasion is approved; or at least, if one worships his own gods, he shall not contradict the accepted religion in words.
Let him who has been initiated not retreat.
Let everyone acquiesce to the accepted rites.
For the sake of public peace, let everyone observe the things established by sacred laws.
Let no private person have his own private gods.
Household shrines <term>Lararia: small shrines in ancient Roman homes dedicated to the Lares, the protective spirits of the household.</term> shall be permitted.
Public temples shall be maintained in suitable locations.
The deities shall be represented by statues.
It shall be provided that priests preside over all the rites of the divine beings.
The High Priests <term>Pontifices: the highest-ranking priests in the Roman religious hierarchy; Postel applies the term generally to religious leaders.</term> shall take care of this.
No private or profane person shall preside as a leader of mysteries <note>original: "mystes"; an initiate or priest of mystery religions.</note> without the highest consent of the State.
They shall reveal the secret mysteries of the persuasion to only a few.
Let no curious inquirer publish or despise them.
A certain portion of the annual yield shall be given to the ministers of the sacred rites.
They shall use and distribute the offerings, expiations, and vows.
There shall be a right to receive offerings from anyone.

He intends these to serve as a universal legal framework for a purified religious and social order, drawing inspiration from ancient Roman legal styles (like the Twelve Tables) to define the duties of priests, the protection of sacred property, and the administration of justice.</meta>

### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK III.

Let religious patrimonies <note>original: "patrimonia"; referring to the inherited property or endowments of a religious institution.</note> be held as sacrosanct.
Let them not consecrate an inheritance if there is a legitimate heir; but let it be lawful to do so in part.
Unless vows are protected by law, let them be voluntary.
Let him who has sinned make atonement through the prescribed legal rites.
Let the power of the Divine be believed to be eternal.
Let the primary concern in sacred matters be the keeping of faith.
Whoever violates faith, let him be an enemy to the gods and hateful to men.
Let him suffer the penalties of violated faith; let him be punished by *talion* <note>original: "talione"; the principle of "an eye for an eye," where the punishment matches the injury.</note>.
Let sacred persons, or those devoted to sacred things, be sacrosanct.
Let them be violated by no one.
Let there be a right of asylum in public sacred places, until the facts of the case are clear.
Let it be the right of anyone to flee there.
Whoever abuses this right, let him lose the privilege and be removed.
Let the priests <note>The original text "facer" is likely a printer's error for "sacer" or "sacerdotes."</note> perform the initial tasting of the sacred rites.
Those who are substituted for them shall be initiated by receiving sacred rites.
Whoever brings harm to a sacred person, let there be a penalty.
Let the arbiter of the law be the avenger of any injury brought upon sacred things.
Let the priest not carry a sword; let the sacred mysteries serve as his defense.
Let the impious man not attempt to appease the gods without consulting a priest.
Let those who have committed offenses against the gods be excluded from the sacred rites.
Let violence be far from sacred things.
Let the magistrate repel injury and settle seditions.
Let the beginnings of all things be hallowed by sacred rites.
Let there be fixed and specially appointed rites according to the needs of the occasion.
No one shall detract from the decrees and responses. If anyone does otherwise, God and the Prince-magistrate shall be the avenger.
If anyone sins in secret, let him atone for his crimes through sacred rites, open his mind <note>Likely referring to the act of confession.</note>, and believe the gods are favorable to those who repent.
What has been established in words, let them ensure it is carried out in counsel, in work, and in deed.
Let them restrain vices with exhortations and praise virtue.
Let the priests <note>original: "sacrifices"; those who perform the sacrifices.</note> impose punishments and rewards according to merit.
What they teach, let them also perform in deeds.
If they sin more gravely against God or nature, let there be a double penalty.
Let them be removed from their rank.
Let the priest be accursed before he pays the penalties.
Law concerning all sacred matters shall be prescribed by the supreme pontiff <term>Pontiff: A high priest or chief religious authority.</term>, the supreme power, or their mediators; those who have been granted authority by them shall speak the law, even if they are unwilling.
Nothing shall be permitted in sacred matters without authority, unless it is a gift or a vow.
Let them reveal proven crimes to the judge, and let him be the avenger.
Regarding matters not yet established, let those performing the sacred rites grant the laws.
Let them ensure that responses are kept according to the jurisdiction of the power.
Let them give forewarning of the wrath of the Divine because of crimes.
Let them report the disasters received due to neglected virtue and piety.
Let them pray for useful things and turn away from contrary things with rites.
Let them follow the customs of the fathers.

Then at last, when the priests <note>original: "sacrifices"; literally "those who perform sacrifices," referring here to the high clergy.</note> are at their most wealthy—men who ought to approach the gods purely and live more holily than all others—they betray themselves to the common people. Even if the prince is inactive (as that man used to say), they bear witness against the gods. From this come the open frauds against the common people, who believe themselves to have been imposed upon; they develop a mindset not only of refusing to pay out, but if it were possible, of demanding back what they have already paid. Thus perishes the right and the authority of the priest. Thus all types of persuasions <note>Postel uses "persuasio" to refer to a system of religious belief or a specific faith.</note> have perished. This is the outcome and the end of all things, while the institutions themselves labor under their own mass, and while no one wishes to look into themselves and return to a middle ground: *Great things rush headlong into themselves, and heavy things fall under their own excessive weight.* <note>Postel is quoting the Roman poet Lucan from his work *Pharsalia*, describing the internal collapse of great empires.</note> I do not wish to add here the violent ends of religions which occur due to external power. For necessity sometimes imposes an end without fault, not only upon sacred laws but also upon profane ones; yet this rarely happens anywhere without the great wickedness of those who fall, when providence (or some chance unknown to us, though usually ascribed to providence) seeks punishment for an undermined order and a shameful life.

There were once many, and are still others, magistrates among certain barbarians whose responses and decrees were superstitiously observed in the early stages of matters: such as Augurs, Soothsayers <note>term: "Aruspices"; ancient Roman priests who interpreted the divine will by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals.</note>, Prophets, Sibyls, and any other kind that once restrained and held back the minds of unskilled men. But these were ridiculous to other nations and relied only on opinion. For besides the established orders and the law itself, by which commoners are usually kept in their duty, nothing at all from the decrees of all religions or from natural consensus is usually approved. But now, in a few pithy sayings as it were, religion itself must be enclosed in aphorisms <note>original: "ἀφορισμοῖς"; Postel uses the Greek term for concise, defining statements.</note>, insofar as it is suitable for everyone, or ever will be. For I refrain from passing down those things which belong to only one religion, for the reason that all of them—even the most excellent—are mutually ridiculous (except where they agree in general kind): *For what you marvel at, is a joke to others.* <note>original: "σὺ γὰρ θαυμάζεις, τοῦθ' ἑτέροισι γέλως"; a Greek poetic sentiment on the relativity of religious customs.</note>

## THE COMMON CANONS OF ALL PERSUASIONS
### Chapter X.

Let everyone be persuaded that there is a God, the author of all things, from whom we should fear dire things and hope for the opposite.
Let it be believed that all things were made by God for a hidden cause.
By all those enrolled in the Republic, or the inhabitants of that place in which the persuasion is approved, let it be established by sacred laws that the ancestral deities must be both accepted and worshipped: or, if one worships his own gods, let no one contradict the received religion in words.
He who has been initiated, let him not draw back.
Let everyone acquiesce to the received sacred rites.
For the sake of public peace, let everyone observe all things established by sacred laws.
Let no private person have his own gods. <note>This canon mirrors the ancient Roman laws of the Twelve Tables, which sought to prevent private, unapproved cults from destabilizing the state.</note>
Let household shrines <note>term: "Lararia"; in ancient Rome, these were small shrines dedicated to the Lares, the guardian spirits of the household.</note> be lawful.
Let public temples be maintained in a suitable place.
Let the deities be fashioned in statues.
Let it be provided that priests preside over all the rites of the divine ones.
Let the Pontiffs <note>term: "Pontifices"; the high-ranking priests in the Roman religious hierarchy who oversaw the state's religious laws.</note> take care of this.
Let no private or profane person preside as a minister of the mysteries <note>term: "mystes"; a person initiated into secret religious rites.</note> without the supreme consent of the Republic.
Let the secret mysteries of the persuasion be opened to only a few.
Let no inquisitive person publish or despise them.
Let a certain portion of the year's produce be given to the ministers of the sacred things.
Let them use and distribute gifts, expiations, and vows.
Let there be a right of receiving offerings from anyone.

### ON THE LAW OF NATIONS AND
#### Civil Law. CHAPTER XI.

Secular law consists of either nature, the law of all nations, or the law of specific ones. Natural law encompasses everything that nature has taught animals to seek or avoid <note>Postel follows a traditional Roman legal definition (associated with the jurist Ulpian) where "natural law" is shared by all living creatures, such as the urge to procreate or protect offspring.</note>. But since "law" is spoken of in respect to what is just and unjust (matters which nature, being devoid of reason, cannot err in, nor reach by its power), there is no doubt about it now: rather, whatever is within that natural law, we shall translate for the use of men—namely, into the Law of Nations. Therefore, the law of men, or of nations (which is the same thing), is that which is approved by almost all mortals either by nature, reason, or necessity, and is established for the purpose of public peace. Nature indeed suggests that in this law, good should be sought and evil avoided: "good" being that of the body, the soul, or of fortune—which usually shifts back and forth like a game, and which they call "external good." But "evil" is that which can undermine any of these.

Reason indeed is accustomed to suggest many things which prudent men naturally judge should be observed or changed—even if it is not immediately apparent in the first instance of nature—due to the circumstances of time, place, persons, or status. Examples include those things known to contribute to the preservation of commonwealths, the status of cities, or their dignity. For although cities and gatherings of men are not created by nature itself, but rather established by human art and prudence, they nevertheless seek their own preservation just like natural things do: since all change is contrary to nature and stability. And therefore, they often do many things against nature [in the animal sense] by the authority of natural law [in the human sense]. It often happens that something is done with nature acting as a guide alongside human opinion, even though it may seem to contradict the way nature itself acts.

If two cities, or any gathering of men, desired something that seemed necessary for the preservation of both, without doubt each must strive for its own protection to obtain it. In that desire for its own safety, one city can and should fail the other, unless the thing sought can satisfy both; in that case, equity must be used. For it is better for one to be deprived of their desire than for one to be made a servant to the other and, contrary to nature, be deprived of their natural liberty. Therefore, that law is usually joined to violence if the rights of both parties are equal, and it takes its origin from force itself. Necessity naturally has a place in the Commonwealth when we arm ourselves against the nature of others to keep ourselves and our people safe; we hold those others as captives and slaves, so they may not harm us and may instead be useful. This we do against nature, and it is by far the most violent part of the law.

...the most just <note>original: "tissima," completing "iustissima" from the previous page</note> aspect of natural law, though I do not know if everyone will approve of it unless it takes its origin from the law of nature itself, which is stronger than any other. For since man is born destitute of all the protections by nature—which a more kind parent granted to the other living creatures—he has his entire life bound up with both a natural anxiety and a necessity to protect himself and his belongings. From this "necessity of evil" (as it is commonly called), so that we would not grow sluggish in idleness, there arose whatever there is of the arts, of higher learning, and of the human condition. From this came the variety of foods, in place of the acorn. From this, in place of clothing made from bark and the inner layers of trees, came linen, wool, and silk. In place of huts and hovels came spacious houses, palaces, camps, and cities. In place of things growing wild, things were produced by industry and art; which, though acquired by necessity, received further growth through luxury. It can therefore be said that what we most greatly dread is and has been most useful to nature: namely, necessity itself, which daily drives us toward noble deeds.

Opinion is the daughter of Necessity; she is the one who usually incites us to all the greatest things through a desire for glory. She compels us to know the arts that produce wealth and that are, or can be, for profit and glory. She makes us commend ourselves to posterity through noble deeds and, in short, causes us mortals to undertake and complete the greatest things, closest to the gods. From necessity, laws were established, cities were girded with walls, roads were paved and cleared, bridges were built, aqueducts were brought together, and temples were erected for the observance of religions and the admiration of the common people—along with many more things of this kind, without which the life of mortals could hardly endure.

But something must be said about that law which applies to a few people, which they therefore call **Civil Law**. <term>Civil Law: From the Latin "ius civile," referring to the specific laws governing the citizens of a particular city-state or nation, as opposed to universal Natural Law.</term> To me, reflecting on where this law took its origin, it does not seem clear whether it should be referred back to nature, or to her sister, **Custom**, or to both, or to chance and the character of a place. For it is admitted by all that individual peoples use certain specific laws of their own, and these are joined to nature. Indeed, it is that very point on which we taught a little earlier that all nations agree in their principles and in the lessons of nature or wisdom. 

But besides that, according to the character of the place, the nations, the accepted morals, and the practice of custom, almost all peoples have something in the place of law, either written down or accepted into their morals by silent consensus, which others might not only fail to observe, but even despise and mock. Such laws are commonly called **Usage and Customs**, or **Local Law**. <term>Local Law: "ius locale," the legal traditions unique to a specific region.</term> This example is evident not only in various peoples, regions, and places regarding secular matters, but most especially in religions accepted through long usage. For the Hebrew mocks the Christian and disapproves of his morals as approved by law (as has always been the practice in matters of persuasion); the Christian mocks the **Muslims** <note>original: "Muhamedicos"</note>, and the Muslims mock both; and they are affected by implacable disagreement. Finally, every religion, even when distracted into various sects, is known to have far more factions than civil ones; this indeed takes away the ability to converse, travel, and visit many regions. Yet, for individual peoples, this arises from contention with their neighbor and from their differences, and it brings no small stubbornness in retaining their religion—a thing than which nothing in a Republic can be greater or more useful. Therefore, custom, confirmed either by the silent judgment of men or even in writing, is both usually and rightly observed according to the character of the place. But where it has endured for several years (which ought to be more or fewer years depending on the usage of the matters and the fatherland), then at last it takes on the force of law. Therefore, it is right that what differs from common law should be established by the character of the place. Otherwise, by chance it often

It happens that many peoples, before they were bound by any written prescription of laws, created **civil law** for themselves by assenting to certain things through a kind of tacit agreement. Therefore, **natural law** ought to follow nature in all things; however, the **law of nations** follows nature first, but a nature joined to necessity and arranged by human reason—which itself, for the sake of the utility and preservation of the **Republic**, not infrequently differs diametrically from natural law. For a good man and a good citizen are often very different, just as are the prudent man and the wise man. **Civil law** follows customs received for any reason and approved only by those for whom they are in use; yet it does this most especially when it has received the force of law through time or formal decree. For without custom, approval, or power, no law is ever accepted.

## ON THE CAUSES OF ANY LAW WHATSOEVER. CHAPTER XII.

When we take up something to be treated and taught through demonstration, we are accustomed—after the manner of the Philosophers—to ask whether it exists, what it is, for what ends it is prepared, or from what causes it arises. That there is some form of law among those men who live a more ordered life is well-established; and we have seen what it is. It remains to weigh those final and primary causes. The end toward which the constitution of law tends is the peace of the entire Republic and its parts, so that everyone is kept in their duty, and whatever duty proceeds from him is contributed to the use and preservation of the Republic; or (as **Cicero**) <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman orator and statesman who wrote extensively on the philosophy of law.</note> says, the preservation of a lawful and customary equality in matters and cases. 

The primary cause is reason itself, partly implanted in the minds of men by providence, partly refined by the experience of things and the order of nature itself. To invite men to the preservation of order and to a likeness (as much as possible) of God—the highest being proven in religion—this reason prescribed law, either in writing or by unwritten custom, for posterity to use. And because no mortal could provide by law for all the errors of all people, laws gradually took their occasion from vices, ambiguities, or lawsuits; and one might not undeservedly call them the daughters and indicators of sin or error. Error was indeed the cause for the most part, but only an accidental one; prudent and just men are the primary cause. For unless those men had provided remedies suited to vices and certainties for doubts through their distinguished and just judgment, their decrees would undoubtedly never have obtained the place of law. 

Indeed, it is necessary for laws to consult the utility of all, or the majority of people, before they can be received. Laws are established, which all are held to obey, by the consent and authority of all, or of a few, or of one person, to whose words everyone must swear. Laws are enacted by the consent of all when a law is usually proposed on the <term>trinundinum</term> <note>original: "trinundino die"; a period of three market days in Roman law used for the public announcement of a proposed law before it could be voted upon.</note>, or on any fixed days, with the people called together in any known and public place—such as before the Rostra in **Rome**, or before certain other statues (as it was the custom in **Athens** to post them at the <term>eponyms</term> <note>original: "eponymis"; refers to the bronze statues of the Eponymous Heroes in the Athenian marketplace where new laws were displayed for public scrutiny.</note>). There, all the common people discern whether something is useful or useless; nor is it ratified, nor should it be, until all or the greater part have consented to it. 

Thus laws were introduced in a popular state (which the Greeks usually call a <term>democracy</term> <note>original: "democratiam"</note> or <term>polity</term> <note>original: "politiam"</note>); thus they were enacted wherever there was any degree of liberty under any administration. But the first method of enacting, gathered from the usage of all, first came forth either from all, or from a few, or from one. Whether all or a few had a law to be proposed and examined, it was still necessary for it to be done by a magistrate "asking" in the name of all, who would both post the notice and collect the votes cast regarding the law. Sometimes eloquent private individuals were able to involve themselves, such as the rhetoricians in **Athens**; on the contrary...
