### WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK III.

For those <note>The orators or legislators mentioned on the previous page.</note>, very heavy penalties were established so that they would not deceive the common people with false persuasions or pass a law without a popular vote. For what could **eloquence** not subvert if the reins of government were handed to it? Suppose it is joined to a most excellent man: certainly the opportunity for increasing one’s wealth, or capturing glory, or factiously favoring certain people can, in truth, turn the best man into the most wicked, the simple man into one who is deceitful—to put it briefly—and create a tyrant out of a private citizen. These things have been seen quite often in those cities or provinces that have been led around by a more long-winded eloquence.

For just as we owe the benefit of every more civilized constitution to a skill in speaking that is joined to **prudence**—as well as the better parts of our deliberations and the drawing of neighboring peoples into our own opinion and utility—so too, when eloquence continues to be abundant once affairs are already established, and is destitute of justice and equity, it undoubtedly tends to bring not safety, but the ruin of the **Republic**. 

Therefore, when many approve of a law, a proclamation—which they call a *signification* <note>original: "significationem"</note>—is made by the magistrates themselves or by men admitted for that purpose. For nowhere are all people admitted to that process of approval. Indeed, it would be superfluous and turbulent to admit the commoners and the more unrefined, the rustics, and the craftsmen <note>original: "sellularios," referring to those who work sedentary jobs or at a workbench.</note> who are generally devoid of common judgment. It is enough for there to be present from individual wards, villages, and townships either some of the more sharp-witted men or a few who will speak their opinion in the name of everyone and bring forth arguments back and forth; and this is only in **secular matters**. For it is never permitted to hesitate or dispute concerning **religious matters**, except among the Pontiffs, the priests, and those whose duty it is to preserve them. 

Laws are established by a few, which the whole body recognizes, either when the whole people is subject to an **aristocracy** or **democracy** and approves the judgments of some holier senate or order; or, on the other hand, when the common people possess such great authority that even men of great power and the leading citizens obey their decrees. Such were the **Roman plebiscites** <note>original: "plebiscita Romana," laws passed by the assembly of the common people.</note>, enacted during the reign of the tribunes of the plebs, passed either for the favor or the necessity of the commoners so that they would not be oppressed by the [wealthy] citizens and the nobility. 

Because the administration of the "Best Men" <note>The *Optimates*, or the aristocratic faction.</note> is full of equity, its edicts are easily approved by everyone as being most fair, without the common people being called away [from their work]. But when those leaders begin to turn the Republic toward their own private gain, the people are indeed conveniently bound by the ancient bond of laws, but then they are miserably plundered by the laws being passed; the Republic, which ought to have been preserved, is undermined, and it hastens its own ruin. **Decrees of the senate** <note>original: "senatusconsulta"</note>, the sanctions of the courts, and **judicial rulings** <note>original: "aresta," likely referring to the French "arrêts" or court decrees.</note> also establish law for those who approve of their judgments, on account of a remarkable observance of the fair and the good (which is usually found either nowhere or among them). 

One person has the right of making laws, either by his own authority, or by granted authority, or by a mixture. For he is either appointed, or he appoints himself, or both. Any **Prince**, being powerful enough to use his own and pure power over his subjects—since they, for the sake of public peace and by right or rather by injury, must obey more quickly than they can reject the yoke of command—is accustomed to prescribe to them what condition of affairs he wishes to be held in the name of everyone and for the public utility. Thus, he would rather remove from the midst or compel certain people who refuse to do what is commanded, than suffer his authority to be easily diminished—unless he is granting **privileges** (which do not serve as a general precedent) or is venting his rage against everyone. 

From this, the edicts of Princes are usually called **pleas** <note>original: "placita," from "placuit," meaning "it has pleased [the ruler]."</note>, because they are for the most part proposed by absolute will. No private individual is permitted to oppose or resist these, just as laws derived their name from the "counsel and prudence" of the **senate**, or from the "resolutions" <note>original: "scitis," related to *plebiscita*.</note>—that is, things known and recognized—of the **common people**. Therefore, the most excellent of the governances of republics, when it is kept well and holily, is **royal** or **imperial power**. For if you remove the names from the midst: the leaders, kings, emperors, and men of any other dignity, who...

Having previously addressed how laws are proposed through eloquence and approved by magistrates, he now moves to the authority of the Sovereign (Princeps) and the various historical forms of legal interpretation across different cultures, including Roman, Islamic, and Jewish traditions.</meta>

->ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD<-

Those who are able to exercise absolute power over certain people possess the same right; this right arises not from nature, but from the customs of peoples or the ambition of Princes. Therefore, that one individual who holds power, acting as a **living law** <note>original: "lex viva"</note>, ensures that established rules are preserved, and he either corrects those that are failing or proposes new ones from his own authority. No private citizen can or should demand a reason for these actions, except in cases where the Prince receives moderation from a senate. Indeed, it is likely—unless the Prince is, to use the Greek term, **most tyrannical** <note>original: "τυραννικώτατος" (tyrannikōtatos)</note>—that those things he wishes to be ratified have been examined in a council of wise men and those who preside over the administration of affairs for the safety of all. If this has been done, it is not within the capacity of any person of private station to dismantle or scrutinize it. For the **Principate** <note>The office or period of rule of a chief or monarch.</note> is a sacred thing, nearly a matter of religion: to seek a reason for its judgment, as with religion itself, is not without danger. Since human affairs have a need for stability, and their very life consists of duration and constancy, undoubtedly whatever contributes to the preservation of peace and integrity must be most strictly maintained, even if some parts are unjust. For it is certain that if the head of the **Republic** is overturned (which must happen if the command of the Prince is rejected), the members will collapse, be separated from one another, and be mutually abandoned. Nor is it only the laws which he himself brings or could bring that perish when a Prince is destroyed (unless another more just ruler were already taking over), but all those laws received from the ancients under his command will be afflicted and so diminished as to almost vanish—especially if another ruler is introduced by some violent movement or sedition; otherwise, they are changed daily.

Furthermore, the origin of Princes who use absolute power once arose from **virtue**; and therefore the reins of all affairs were permitted to them by their subjects because of their merit, so that what was once granted by authority now stands by its own right. Thus, new principalities are for the most part granted by authority, which in the course of time they pull toward absolute power, and they eventually use their own will as an ancestral right, being confirmed by the long passage of time. There are also mixed systems, which partly establish and partly receive laws: such as Princes moderated by **aristocracies** <note>A form of government where power is held by the nobility or a privileged class.</note>, who are created by election rather than by hereditary succession; one must stand by the decisions of all such rulers. Quite different is the power received by **praetors** <note>Roman judicial officers.</note>, whose edicts—supported by the authority of the Princes or powers to whom they are subject—pass into law; this is the type of law the Romans call **honorary law** <note>original: "ius honorarium"</note>. 

But because the one who establishes laws must be, as we have said, most prudent, Princes have therefore granted the power of responding on matters of law to the wise and prudent, imparting their own authority to them. This part of the law is by far the most excellent, as it is entirely free from personal passions. For that reason, a good portion of the written law among all nations consists of the **responses of the wise**. Not only did the Roman state grow by these and by the decrees of the **Pontiffs**, but so did all those states that endured for a long time. For this reason, even now, all who use the Latin language use that law. For the **Pandects** <note>A massive compendium of Roman civil law, also known as the Digest.</note> are nothing other than the responses of the wise who clarified the edicts of the praetors or contributed their own. The **Muftis** <note>original: "Muphtij"</note> among the Arabs have that legal standing. Once, among the Hebrews, the seventy elders chosen by Moses and Jethro held it; their responses were never made public until **CHRIST**, the restorer of that religion and the founder of the new one, revealed and made public the hidden **impasses** <note>original: "ἀνεξοδίαν" (anexodian) - referring to legal dead-ends or complexities used to trap people.</note> and **cunning** <note>original: "vafriciem"</note> within them, and disapproved of them. For all things, even the best, if they do not become worse through long use, are certainly prone to being circumvented by sharp-witted men. Yet not infrequently these responses, when they are joined to opinions, religions, and personal affections, also possess their own share of injustice.

<summary>Postel argues for the divine and practical necessity of a central sovereign as a "living law" to maintain social stability. He traces the evolution of legal authority from virtue-based leadership to formal systems like Roman civil law, Islamic Muftis, and the Hebrew Sanhedrin, while noting how human cunning can corrupt even the best legal traditions.</summary>
<keywords>sovereignty, living law, absolute power, Republic, praetors, honorary law, Pandects, Muftis, Sanhedrin, legal cunning, Christ as reformer</keywords>

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK III.

...reason. Therefore, those laws that are joined to religion or to the preservation of a greater power tend to weigh equity and reason less than those given without any personal bias by private individuals. For those who hold the reins of affairs, or who desire to gratify someone by their own authority, accommodate many things to favor. Those who propose nothing for themselves except the **fair and the good** <note>original: "æquum & bonum"; a traditional legal principle in Roman law emphasizing justice over strict literalism</note> are certainly far more equitable in providing for the interests of **posterity** <note>Future generations.</note> than a Prince or a Magistrate; for the latter, while often seeking their own advantage more than is fair, or looking out for the customs of their own age or State, tend to establish many things that are unfavorable and useless to posterity. 

There is also another origin and cause of law which does not pertain to everyone who is subject to a single Prince, but whose utility is nevertheless referred to the good of the State (for otherwise it would not be considered law); this law must be prescribed and approved according to the various conditions of men. For each individual assembly of mortals—whether in secular or religious matters—possesses, besides laws received through long usage or recently passed and based on religious, natural, civil, or international law, certain rules proper to their own conditions or crafts which do not extend beyond that specific status. 

Concerning these matters, neither judges can pass judgment, nor can the craftsmen of other arts speak, due to their ignorance of them. Hence the sailor has nautical laws; the stonecutter and the smith have theirs; and the goldsmith has his own regarding gold items according to the usage received in his craft. He explains the matters of the craft to the judge; and this is done not only by the reason of the art itself or the materials usually handled within it, but also by the usage of specific places and men. That part is truly by far the most difficult to understand, and it cannot be handled by **common law** <note>original: "iure communi"; here referring to general laws applicable to everyone, rather than the English legal system</note>, because it is most closely joined to the varied opinions of men. However, once the utility to the fatherland is proven by a judge, he gives strength to those laws that have been approved by **silent consent** <note>original: "tacito consensu"; the idea that a law or custom is valid because the people and the ruler accept it without formal protest</note>, whereby even the Prince is seen to mediately approve them through that same silent consent. 

Laws are never formally published regarding those arts because that "sacrosanct struggle"—that contention by which one man strives to surpass another in his craft—tends to preserve those laws diligently enough, not indeed through evil means, but through better skills. For everyone strives to be the best in his own art. A measurer <note>A surveyor or one who calculates dimensions and weights.</note> measures as best as he can; but if he should state a false measure, it is necessary that the error be detected by a more skilled measurer and revealed to the judge as proven. Finally, the judge determines whether the error is to be punished. For although there is no **consent from one who errs** <note>A legal principle: an agreement based on a mistake is not a true agreement.</note>, nevertheless, when someone professes an art of which they are ignorant, they must be held responsible for the loss caused by the error they committed. 

But this topic is broader than can be conveyed in a few words. Therefore, the judgments and understandings of all arts must be referred back to the experts of the art, who—according to the laws received among the most excellent practitioners—may decide on the nature of the fault, error, vice, or virtue committed, and then report it to the judge. We can call this part of the law "unwritten," just as many things are in the civil law of individual places. On the other hand, we see written law everywhere among nations which proceeds from religion and the command of the Prince, the ignorance of which should excuse no one. For if ignorance of the law were admitted even once, it would be the same as if it were not written at all. For any litigant would pretend not to know that part of the law which seemed to work against him. But the law and custom of particular assemblies

### in Civil Law, Chapter XIII.

--- Page 319 ---
<meta>This page continues Postel’s legal and philosophical framework. Having established that laws are often adapted to the specific conditions of people or crafts, he now begins a formal classification of the types of law (sacred, civil, mixed) and the types of "things" (corporeal, incorporeal) they govern. He concludes by focusing on "Man" as the central subject of law, beginning a discussion on the social status of individuals—specifically the distinction between freedom and slavery.</meta>

->ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD<-

All law treats either of persons, or of things—which may be sacred, profane, or mixed. Pontifical laws <note>Original: "iura pontificia"; the body of laws governing the Church or priesthood, often called Canon Law.</note> and the primary prescriptions of all religions deal with sacred matters. Civil laws <note>The laws of the state or "ius civile."</note> do indeed prescribe concerning sacred things, but only insofar as it is necessary for their preservation; they do not likewise deal with their institution, restoration, management, or use. Civil law treats profane <note>In this context, "profane" simply means secular or non-religious.</note> things. These are either public or private: that is, involving the affairs of the entire body of the Republic, or of individuals. Mixed are the affairs of religion, such as whatever land or movable goods are attributed and granted for the use and preservation of religion. For the law itself as it pertains to the thing is sacred, yet the things themselves are profane. But since they can never be separated (for if the thing did not exist, the law would not; and vice versa), one might deservedly say they belong to "mixed law."

The volume of our law which they call the *Decretals* <note>The "Decretales" were collections of papal decrees that formed a core part of medieval Canon Law.</note> deals mostly with this genre. For that book was published when religion had already increased in wealth but piety was afflicted; whereas in earlier times, the decrees of the holy fathers had treated abundantly of piety itself, ceremonies, and spiritual matters. Thus the character of the times changes the laws. 

Furthermore, some things are corporeal <term>corporeæ: tangible objects that can be perceived by the senses</term>, others are incorporeal <term>incorporeæ: intangible rights, such as the right to inherit or a legal action</term>. Corporeal things are men or their goods subject to the senses. Incorporeal are the laws themselves regarding things: such as a legal action, a sale, hiring, leasing, or an inheritance. And likewise, some things are public, others private. The latter are among the goods of individuals; the former belong to no one in particular, but belong to everyone. But since all laws were established for the sake of man: we shall treat first of him, as if he were the prince of all things—first of his condition, then of his possession, and finally the mutual relationship of all men must be addressed.

### DIVISION OF THE CONDITION OF
### men. Chapter 14.

All men are either free (and free-born), or slaves, or mixed. We understand the free to be those who use their own judgment plainly in conducting their affairs—provided they commit nothing against equity and the good, or against received laws. For nature intended all men to be produced as such for the most part. Necessity introduced the condition of slaves against nature, when men who had been adversaries began to be "kept" <note>Postel is using a traditional (though folk) etymology for the Latin word for slave, "servus," deriving it from "servare," meaning "to save" or "preserve" a captive instead of killing them.</note> by other men. For in olden times, it was customary to kill all enemies in war. Eventually, partly through utility and partly through piety, they began to keep them for the use of their labor, and to deprive them of natural liberty so they might not do harm and that their works might be profitable. 

Thus, they entirely lost the right of nature by the consent of masters, and began to be as nothing within the Republic. They are permitted to do nothing unless it yields to the interest of their masters. No legal actions or contracts are permitted to them: because they hold no legal right, not even to sacred matters, which nevertheless tend to belong to everyone. They procreate for the master, they acquire for him, they live for him—not for themselves. Yet by natural law they are all held <note>bound by moral or natural duties</note> as long as they are human beings. 

When this servitude exists in a man of very great talent and great resources, it is certainly most contrary to nature, because the most worthy is sometimes subjected to the most unworthy. But if one is a little more stupid, and more inept at conducting affairs, and serves a wiser master by whom he is, as it were, led by the hand—the prince of philosophers, Aristotle, asserted and demonstrated this in his *Politics* <note>Aristotle’s "Politics" argues that "natural slaves" lack the faculty of deliberation and benefit from being ruled by those with reason.</note>. For it goes happily with such a person when that which nature had given as maimed and inept is corrected by a master and made fit for conducting affairs for the use of the Republic. Those who are "mixed" are they who, although they can now use the prescriptions of the laws according to the custom of the Republic, nevertheless...

### WILLIAM POSTEL BOOK III.

...they also acknowledge both patrons and those to whom they are indebted, either in all things, or in certain matters in which they are physically obligated. Personal duties of this kind are those that subject men to other men. The freedmen <note>Original: "Libertini"; former slaves who have been legally freed.</note> of the Romans were under this mixed law. For that reason, it was entirely forbidden—out of reverence—to bring a legal action under a defamatory name against a patron and his closest relatives (just as it is forbidden for a slave to do so against a master). The law differs between these two in this respect: masters have the power of life and death over slaves (though the prince <note>In a legal context, "prince" refers to the sovereign or the head of state.</note> takes care that this is not exercised too severely by private individuals); patrons no longer have that right over freedmen. 

Freedom is restored in any way by the will and consent of the master, unless it is done either to defraud creditors or by a master of "imperfect judgment" whom a slave could easily manipulate—such as minors, the insane, or the mentally impaired. For if sound judgment is present, every manumission <note>Original: "manumissio"; the formal process of releasing a slave from bondage.</note> usually proceeds in favor of liberty. It makes no difference whether one was born a slave or made one, since all are under the same law if that opinion has prevailed. 

Again, free men live either by their own right alone, or partly by their own and partly by another's. A father, master, tutor, or curator acts by his own right, provided they improve the condition of a ward or an insane person. A son, a minor, or an insane person acts partly by his own right and partly by another's. Because they are incautious and inexperienced in affairs, they are restrained by parents or tutors so they do not worsen their domestic estate or abuse it through the heat of youth or imprudence. Therefore, they are allowed to improve their condition without the authority of tutors or fathers, but not to make it worse. 

The insane can, while they have "lucid and clear intervals," enter into contracts both for and against their interests; otherwise, neither is permitted without a curator <note>A court-appointed guardian for someone who is mentally unfit.</note>. There is also a certain "imitation of nature" introduced among many men, such as when someone seeks children for himself from elsewhere through adoption, in which matter it seemed appropriate to imitate nature: for a younger person cannot adopt an older one. Furthermore, the first degrees of affinity are usually preserved among brothers, sisters, twins, and adopted children; nor can they contract marriage unless emancipation <note>Original: "emancipatio"; the legal act of releasing a child from the power of the head of the household.</note> precedes it, and this according to Roman law. 

For these matters are based on opinion, and are therefore part of arbitrary law. But it has seemed most important to follow nature in transmitting law. 

**Another division of men.** All men are either for the purpose of pronouncing the law, explaining it, or merely hearing it. In this all agree: when their own affairs are being treated, individuals (even if they are the greatest magistrates or princes) must hear the law. It is accepted everywhere among nations that two types of men pronounce the law. For judges are appointed either by princes or by the litigants themselves. 

Since the duty of princes, newly established among men, was to pronounce the law, and there arose daily a greater abundance of lawsuits than one man was sufficient to terminate, princes granted their authority to judges. This was done so they might settle matters between litigants with equity, and their sentences were to be upheld no differently than the decrees of princes—though more cautious times invented the benefit of appeal—which, for the sake of the peace of the Republic, may not be resisted. 

Simple or compromise-based arbitrators are also judges in any Republic, to whose sentence the plaintiff and defendant usually agree and swear, either by a pact not to withdraw or otherwise. This was indeed invented as an aid to judges and for the convenience of litigants. There are truly many types of such judges. For any Prince reserves the legal investigation of certain matters for himself, and the highest magistrates take cognizance of all business, or only some. But more on that a little later. 

Those who explain the law, or present cases to judges according to the law, are either advocates or proxies <note>Original: "procuratores"; legal representatives or attorneys who act on behalf of another.</note>, since the litigants themselves are frequently ignorant of the law. Men of private condition only hear the law, unless perhaps they are occasionally appointed as arbitrators to pronounce it. Others, besides private individuals, in addition to pronouncing the law, also by hearing and obeying...

[subject to another's] right. The final division of men is this: All men are either noble, commoners, or are dedicated to religion. Among all nations, virtue—especially military virtue or that which preserves the state—has brought a reward to its possessor by the consensus of those who experienced or recognized it; that reward is a certain fame and the memory of a benefit once conferred upon the republic, from which the families of illustrious men in every nation arise. Not infrequently, a great force of wealth achieved this, and from it came authority, force, and power, so that a man was believed to be greater than ordinary people, and thus acquired confirmation and authority—and even tyranny—from public opinion. Therefore, some nations have allowed that greatness to pass to posterity; others allow it only to those who acquired virtue by their own industry, so that the descendants might not take pride in a false title without their father’s virtue and glory. This latter opinion usually incites more people daily to virtue. Those who support the Republic either with wisdom or wealth are deservedly held in the same rank. These are the origins of nobility. Commoners <note>Original: "ignobiles"; those not belonging to the noble class.</note> are those who have performed no outstanding deed in the state: or if they did, they were deprived of their reward (as happens very often) by an ungrateful multitude, or by a prince (who tends to fear or envy those who are a bit too illustrious), or they perished, robbed of the memory of their ancestors. For nature produced all men with a similar origin, body, and mind; it is virtue and opinion that elevate them. Dedicated to religion are those upon whom the care of increasing and preserving religion rests. And these types of men preserve the condition of either souls, bodies, or external things. Religion and philosophy care for souls; the soldier, the judge, and the doctor care for bodies; the judge and the soldier care for the goods of fortune—unless the proper use of things is inverted. For who will guard the guards themselves? <note>Original: "Quis custodiet ipsos custodes?" A famous quote from the Roman poet Juvenal.</note> But these men, however wicked they may be, are to be tolerated rather than removed.

### WHAT RIGHTS MEN MAY POSSESS
### by benefit, and how they lose rights and
### change conditions. Chapter XV.

In the affairs of individual men, there tend to be natural rights—that is, liberty; the rights of the place where one was born or received, which the Romans call citizenship; and rights of blood, which we call family. For every man is born free, and is usually born somewhere and from someone. Therefore, he has from nature the right of using his own judgment: of preserving himself, and of possessing things for his own protection. He usually obtains these by the benefit of the law used by the people where he is born, and he is necessarily assigned to some family from which he was born, as if by descent. Natural rights are lost either by one's own fault or by the actions of another. When someone allows himself to be sold into service for a price, or when by his own act his body is bound to service—as when he owes a debt of money or labor that he must provide—then he himself divests himself of his natural right. He also incurs infamy along with his loss, while he perishes by his own will. By the action of another, a man loses his rights when he is captured by any enemy and led into slavery; from which, when he has extricated himself, he returns to his own status by the "right of return." <note>Original: "iure postliminium"; a Roman legal concept where a person who returns from captivity recovers all their former rights and status as if they had never been away.</note> For misfortune brought about by necessity does not usually, nor should it, hinder one's birthright or natural right. In the law of citizenship, we possess either only public things, or both public and private things—that is, our own property. Although public things are in no one's private ownership, they are nevertheless for the use of everyone; a person stripped of all resources can no less enter sacred places anywhere in the world, or walk on a public road, or spend time in the forum and places dedicated to public utility, and use the air, water, and fire, just as a wealthy man does. Moreover, laws are established for his preservation, just as for the rich man. For the laws follow nature, not fortune, and whatever they deal with regarding property, they do so to serve the preservation of nature. Furthermore, since by the benefit of laws it is permitted to possess one's own things anywhere on earth, we also [owe] the preservation of our things to them.

we owe. For either our things and our works are made our own, or we make the things of others our own through purchase, exchange, or occupation. The works of others also come to us through gifts and inheritances, which we make ours by accepting or entering into them, which we owe to the laws themselves. For unless the laws and the will of the magistrate made contracts valid, kept us in our possessions, and established the heir as the living possessor immediately upon the death of the former owner—whom we therefore call the heir (whether he be a <term>legitimus</term> <note>A "legitimate" heir under the law of the Twelve Tables.</note>, a <term>suus</term> <note>A "self-successor," typically a child under the father's direct power.</note>, or a <term>necessarius</term> <note>A "necessary" heir, often a slave freed by will to take the estate.</note> heir)—and unless the laws willed that a thing belonged to the one to whom it was gifted, we would undoubtedly possess nothing certain. We would be tossed about; everything would be acquired by the stronger party; and all things would occur which usually happen in the total overthrow of affairs.

Therefore, the jurist Paul <note>Julius Paulus, one of the most influential Roman legal scholars of the 3rd century AD.</note> rightly ascribed to the "City" <note>Original: "Civitati"; referring here to the organized State or Commonwealth.</note> everything that is within our property, so that we may understand the City to be the force and majesty of the laws approved in any given place. For men come together through laws; those who come together are either citizens, or like citizens. Citizens are those who may hold office under the laws; "like citizens" are those who find it necessary only to obey. These matters exist within the City.

We either have a family, or we are held by a family, or both, or neither. It was the custom of the Romans that all who were born from male children—whether they were sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, or great-great-grandsons—were in the family of the patriarch as long as that father and author of the family survived. That family was required to follow and obey whatever the parent prescribed as fair in the first place, both those of the male and female sex. That entire family always fell back under the power of the elder, except when the young women were led away in marriage. For then, they passed from their father's power as if <term>manumitted</term> <note>Released from legal control, like a slave being freed.</note> and moved into another family where they would give birth to children—belonging not to the power of the father from whom they came, but to the husband or the husband's father. This was called "losing status" <note>Original: "capite minui"; a legal term meaning a change or reduction in a person's civil rights or status.</note> and "losing one's family." 

Unless manumission, or a transition into another power (such as adoption), exempted the males, or unless they were deprived of their father's goods due to ingratitude, they never left the family. Lastly, those who have not yet fathered children are only "held" in a family. Only he who has lost his elder parents, or who has entirely moved away from their location, region, and laws and fathered children in another Republic, "has" a family. He who is of his own right <note>Original: "suo iure"; legally independent.</note> is both among parents and is held. He who is in the middle between these extremes neither "has" nor "is held." He who is a stranger anywhere among the nations where he has not fathered children is in a place where, out of reverence and the honor of marriage, children are considered illegitimate and "conceived by the multitude" <note>Original: "vulgo concepti"; children born outside of a legal marriage.</note> before they have fathered their own, unless the law or a Prince aids them by inscribing them into the family of a certain father. There are those in a state of servitude who, if they father children, they father them for their masters; because they were born into this status, they have suffered the "greatest loss of status" <note>Original: "capitis maxima diminutione"; the total loss of liberty and citizenship in Roman law.</note>. For they are effectively non-entities as far as Roman rights are concerned, except in matters regarding the master.

The common usage of mortals only attributes the family to the father until the children have taken wives or have reached an age fit for administering an inheritance; then they are clearly made of their own right, just as those who are emancipated are accustomed to be. But these are matters of opinion. It is sufficient that a natural father presides over his own with authority as long as they are sound in body and judgment, and that he rules the family himself and looks after his affairs well. For this is proven by the example of all nations and all living creatures, so that there may be greater liberty. Roman law looked after the role of the parent until the twenty-fifth year, because it seems that human judgment is weak and insufficiently refined, and that no one before that age ought to be destitute of a father. Otherwise, a various opinion regarding the "just age" for administering affairs must be followed. For it is necessary that reason and judgment be perfected by the experience of things, not prepared by nature alone. Therefore, where a father has left surviving children before that age, it ought to be established by law that <term>tutores</term> and <term>curatores</term> <note>Guardians for minors (tutors) and those who manage the property of young adults or the disabled (curators).</note> should perform the role of the father. For unless a dying father has appointed a guardian for the children, the nearest relatives ought to care for them; otherwise, by the authority of the pre-

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

a guardian or curator is assigned to them, as well as to those who suffer in their mind, because it is in the interest of the Commonwealth that no one should use their own affairs poorly. For this reason, those in such human conditions are especially helped if they have committed anything to the detriment of their own affairs, even if it was done through a contract. One who is excluded from a family, or departs from it willingly, provided he is still able to act, is considered to have undergone a <term>minimal reduction of status</term> <note>Original: "minima capitis minutione." In Roman law, this refers to a change in a person's family standing, such as being adopted or emancipated, without losing citizenship or freedom.</note>. If we lose the right of citizenship without having committed a crime, it is also necessary to lose the family; such is the case for those deported, those <term>relegated</term> <note>A milder form of exile where the person was sent away but kept their property and citizenship rights.</note>, and foreigners. There is also a <term>medium reduction of status</term> <note>The loss of citizenship and family, but not freedom.</note>, and when we are slaves, we are afflicted by the <term>maximal reduction of status</term>, stripped of every right. For in that state, even what nature had given is lost.

Indeed, antiquity knew two kinds of slaves. One was the common kind, born without a crime, who were usually captured because they wished to preserve their fatherland or their faction; these were permitted to recover all things by the <term>right of postliminy</term> <note>The legal right of a person captured in war to have their previous status and property restored upon returning to their home territory.</note>. The other kind arose from crime, whom the Romans were accustomed to call "slaves of punishment" <note>Original: "servos poenae." These were criminals whose sentence involved the loss of all civil rights and liberty, often involving forced labor.</note>. For however atrocious the crimes were, antiquity spared human life as much as it could. 

He who took up arms against the Commonwealth in which he was born, raised, and preserved, or who conspired in secret; he who attempted to overturn religion; or he who laid snares for the life of a man (to whose mutual protection nature created us to be dutiful); he who killed a man willingly and with premeditation (unless while defending himself); he who plundered the property of others; or he who, against the laws and the will of the master, rose up to the destruction of nature and public peace—such a person is deservedly deprived of the help of human society and ought to be cut off like a rotting limb. 

Yet the wisdom of the ancients knew that men are able to return to a fruitful state just as they are able to sin. For that reason, in place of the death which the delinquents deserved, they devised various kinds of punishments. A judge had the power to determine these according to the prescription of the laws, moderated by equity and the "living law" <note>Referring to the judge's role as the voice of the law in action.</note>. Those who were afflicted with the heaviest punishment were usually relegated to the mines to dig for the use of the Commonwealth, where a man—even with the healthiest body—hardly lasts for five years. Others were punished with perpetual exile, or were relegated to islands or certain foreign provinces for a time. They tried everything so that they might keep the man alive, even though he deservedly ought to be deprived of laws, family, and nature. For life is the highest thing; death is the lowest and most useful, even to be hoped for by the wretched. A long-lasting punishment is heavier than death among any nation. He who contravenes the laws is usually deprived of them, either by death, or the penalty of exile, proscription, or any other punishment. But let these things be said concerning the possession of men and the change of their condition.

### WHAT MEN CAN MUTUALLY PROVIDE TO ONE ANOTHER,
### and how they can hinder each other. Chapter XVI.

It is established that whatever right exists is placed in <term>duty</term> <note>Original: "officio." This refers to moral and social obligations or "appropriate actions" that sustain human society.</note> (if men would observe this mutually with nature as their guide). Truly, that part of duty which brings a benefit to us or our affairs, we all easily receive, seek after, and strive for; but we frequently neglect to pay it back, unless compelled by shame or the force of the laws. For since nature brought us forth naked, it also left us with a certain desire, not only for accumulating things for the present, but as if we were going to live for eternity, without any limit to greed. To this necessity was added the ruin of the world—the "opinion"—so that we desire things for the future not only for use, but for glory. Care for posterity, lest they fall into miseries we have seen, has increased the vow of having, and has forced equity and gratitude to go into exile from among men. Once those were driven out, men began to act through repayments, trusting in wealth rather than in man or his faith (which nevertheless was always the greatest bond among good men), but rather in the things themselves, which mutually consist of three parts, for whatever...

### BOOK III OF GUILLAUME POSTEL

For what one human can provide to another consists either in the presentation of a thing, in its use, or in a human action. We give a thing that is movable, self-moving, or immovable, or the rights to obtain them. A **movable** thing is whatever lacks life and exists outside the soil; **self-moving** refers to all living beings <note>This category typically includes livestock and animals.</note>. **Immovable** things are the soil, water, and buildings. These are usually handed over either simply for the sake of future favor, for the preservation of nature, or by a specific vow of the giver: such as donations, inheritances, legacies, and other types of gift. For he who gives receives nothing except the goodwill he hopes for rather than possesses; conversely, if something is done contrary to the agreements made in the donation, the recipient is rightly noted for ingratitude. He can be deprived of the donated thing as an ingrate, unless the gift was made unconditionally. For if a terrible crime is committed against the giver, the laws rightly moderate such attempts with their severity. For laws live in the place of the deceased and the absent: and for that reason, they make valid those things established by them.

Things can be exchanged for other things (now I subtract money for a moment) when solid objects are given for objects without any external valuation, a kind of trade with which unrefined antiquity used to conduct its commerce. Since there was much labor in this—driving and carrying things back and forth—mortals devised something for the greatest good of all. First (which however eventually turned to their ruin), they created something that could easily be exchanged in the place and name of all things, and which was of minimal mass: namely, **money** <term>pecunia: derived from "pecus" meaning cattle, the original form of wealth</term>. Whether it be made of iron, lead, leather, wood, gold, or silver, or from any other material (as it certainly was once), it mattered not, provided that by the consensus of laws and peoples, or by the command of princes, it was valued as much as the things themselves. 

But when, after the "youth of the world," other materials were recognized as subject to the falsification of marks <note>Counterfeiting or debasing of coinage.</note>, greater bulk, and corruption, by the consensus of almost all peoples in the world, gold and silver began to be approved; it is clear this was also done by necessity. For since many provinces were not self-sufficient and were forced to seek necessary supports from neighboring regions, yet the force of those local laws which gave a price to money elsewhere was unknown, almost all mortals were forced to embrace **gold**. It was chosen for its minimal bulk, because it is minimally or hardly subject to corruption, and because its weight is equal everywhere; its power, like that of a God, would be equal everywhere. 

Before its frequent use, gold was neglected in many regions and used no differently than iron for making chains for criminals; a good part of the recently discovered world <note>A reference to the Americas, which Postel views through the lens of European contact.</note> was even ignorant of its use before that plague of the corrupt world, greed, arrived there. Now, therefore, in the whole world, gold is sought after, under whose dominion is placed whatever the earth produces or hides: in whose name one may obtain the thing, the use, and the deed from any person. For this reason, the ancient fictions of the poets rightly called the king of the underworld **Dis** or **Pluto** <note>In mythology, Dis Pater and Pluto were gods of the underworld and, by extension, the mineral wealth found underground.</note>: because whatever was dug up from the innermost bowels of the sea and earth was under his jurisdiction.

Sometimes one or more things are given for the use of another. Furthermore, what **use** <term>usus</term> is, is clear enough: it is the right to use another's property for a certain time—whether continuous or interrupted by intervals—while preserving the substance of the things themselves. When this extends more widely, namely to all the "produce" of things, then it is called not "use," but **usufruct** <term>ususfructus: the right to enjoy the use and advantages of another's property without destroying it</term>. For in "use," the necessity of the user is considered; in "usufruct," both the convenience and whatever consists in the profit of the thing are considered. Although both use and usufruct are "things" in the sense of being rights, yet in law we more properly call "things" those objects for the sake of which, or from which, utility can be drawn. He who contravenes the laws is usually deprived of them, either by death, or by the punishment of exile, proscription, or any other penalty. For what one human can provide to another exists either in the delivery of a thing, in the use of that thing, or in a human action. We give a thing that is either "movable," "self-moving," or "immovable," or the rights to obtain them. A **movable** thing is whatever is apart from the soil and lacks life; **self-moving** things include all living creatures. **Immovable** things are the soil, water, and buildings. These are usually handed over either simply in the hope of receiving favor, for the preservation of nature, or by a specific vow of the giver: such as donations, inheritances, legacies, and other types of gifts. For he who gives receives nothing except that goodwill which he hopes for rather than possesses. Conversely, if a contract is made regarding a donation and something is done against it, it is rightly noted as ingratitude, and the ungrateful person can be deprived of the gifted thing, unless the gift was made unconditionally. For if a dreadful crime is committed against the one who gave, the laws rightly moderate such attempts with their severity. For laws live in the place of both the deceased and the absent; and for that reason, they ratify the things established by them.

Things can be exchanged for other things (now I withdraw money from the discussion for a little while) when solid objects are given for other objects without any external valuation, which is the type of trade by which unrefined antiquity used to carry out its commerce. Since there was much labor in this matter, in driving and carrying things back and forth, mortals devised something for the greatest good of all. First—though it eventually turned to their own destruction—they found something that could easily be exchanged in the place and name of all things, and which was of the smallest bulk: namely **money** <note>original: "pecuniam"</note>, which takes its name from the primary possession of the ancients, which was in **cattle** <note>original: "pecudibus"; Postel is noting the etymological link between "pecunia" (money) and "pecus" (livestock)</note>.

Indeed, it did not matter whether it was made of iron, lead, leather, wood, gold, or silver, or from any other material—as it certainly was in the past—so long as it was valued as much as the goods were, by the consensus of laws and the people, or by the command of princes. But when, after the "youth of the world," other materials were recognized as liable to adulteration (as with wood), or to greater bulk, or to corruption, the consensus of almost all peoples of the entire world began to approve **gold** and **silver**. It is established that this was also done out of necessity. For since many provinces were not self-sufficient and were forced to seek necessary supports from neighboring regions, and since that force of law which had given value to money elsewhere was unknown there, almost all mortals were forced to embrace gold—both for its minimal bulk and because it is least, or only with difficulty, subject to corruption, and is of equal weight everywhere. Gold became as a God, having equal power everywhere.

Whereas before its use became so frequent, gold was neglected in many regions, and was used no differently than iron for making chains for criminals. A good part of the recently discovered world <note>A reference to the Americas and the "Age of Discovery"</note> also ignored its use until the plague of the corrupted world—**greed**—arrived there. So now gold is sought after in the whole world, and under its dominion is placed whatever the earth brings forth or hides; in its name, one may obtain the thing, the use, and the action from any man. For this reason, the ancient fictions of the poets rightly called the king of the underworld **Dis** and **Pluto** <note>Postel links the names of the Roman/Greek gods of the underworld to "wealth" (Greek *Ploutos*), as riches come from the depths of the earth</note>: because whatever was dug out from the innermost bowels of the sea and the earth was under his jurisdiction.

What "use" <note>original: "usus"</note> is, then, is clear enough: it is the right to use the property of another for a certain time—whether continuous or separated by intervals—while the substance of the things themselves remains intact. When this extends further, namely to the entire produce of the things, then it is called not "use" but **usufruct** <term>ususfructus: a legal right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another</term>. For in "use," the necessity of the user is considered; in "usufruct," both the convenience and whatever is situated in the profit of the thing are considered. Although "use" and "usufruct" are themselves "things" (inasmuch as they are rights), we nevertheless more properly call those things "property" in law for the sake of which, or from which, utility can be drawn. <meta>This page continues Postel’s legal and philosophical exploration of human society. Following the previous discussion on the transfer of physical goods, he now examines the legal concepts of "actions" (performances), the role of the State (the Republic) in upholding justice, and the psychological origins of wrongdoing.</meta>

...receive use, or the "usufruct" <note>original: *usumfructum*; the legal right to use and enjoy the fruits or profits of another's property without owning it</note>, or the reverse. The reasoning for an **action** <note>original: *facti*; in Roman law, a *factum* refers to a specific deed or performance required by a contract</note> is very widely evident. For it can exist in duty, in obligation, in negligence, or in something left undone. Indeed, a thing is very frequently accustomed to be paid in place of an action: as if I give you that field, or that object, so that you may do this for me: you owe me the action, just as I provided the object. From this arise countless types of contracts, which, although they are only about a thing, a use, or an action exchanged individually or together, nevertheless are usually measured by money—whenever the question of "how much it matters" is required—by **arithmetical equality**; or by how much that thing was, or is, worth. By a manifold bond of obligations, men owe these three things to one another and are accustomed (if they follow the laws) to provide them. But if they persist in being unjust and unfair toward those to whom they are bound—doing so because they act against the law itself, which preserves the actions of mortals in place of an exiled "faith" <note>original: *fides*; here meaning trust or reliability in social dealings</note>—they not only neglect the faith bound to them (either by themselves or by those whose rights they use, or born from the condition of things), but they even contravene the contracts, pacts, and agreements themselves, which it is right for all mortals to observe. From this were born **legal actions** to pursue what is right. For the **Republic**, like a most pious mother, when she has taken us up to be cherished in her bosom, also takes care that we may obtain from her power whatever is our right; lest we should ever happen to be destitute of the duties useful and necessary for living, or lest contempt for one's self—namely, injustice—should reign among men. From this comes the ruin of both nature and human affairs. Therefore, even if we are unable to pursue our thing, use, action, or right, or if we neglect them—whether an injury is done to us regarding our property or our person—the State itself takes it upon itself to avenge or help her citizens, wherever in the land they may be, using a specific name. She **puts the womb into possession** <note>original: *ventrem in possessionem mittit*; a Roman legal procedure where a pregnant woman was granted possession of an estate to protect the inheritance rights of the unborn child</note>, gives guardians to orphans, curators to adults and the insane, avenges the injured, and punishes the guilty, even with no one demanding it. We are compelled to confess that we owe this much to nature, prudence, reason, and well-placed laws, and thereby to the author of all things, **God, the Best and Greatest**. Thus, men are harmed when they are forced by the power of laws to seek from one another what right and reason ought to have persuaded them to do, give, or refrain from doing.

## ON THE ORIGIN OF INJURY,
### CHAPTER XVII.

It can be clearly evident to one looking closely that **necessity**, **ambition**, and **greed** are the causes of injury <note>original: *iniuriae*; in this context, it refers broadly to injustice, legal wrongs, and personal insults</note>. For he who inflicts an injury upon the body is led by a desire for vengeance or glory, because he is, or seems to be, superior to the other; he who sins against property is surely tormented by greed, necessity, or ambition. Furthermore, there are three types of injury: **impiety**, **greed**, and **injury or insult**. **Impiety** despises the gods, religion, and things assigned to religion and the gods—such as sacred objects or persons, and the deceased—and it affects them with reproaches, as well as one’s parents and fatherland. For these ought to be sacrosanct not only by profane laws, but also by sacred ones. Therefore, he who sins against these sins most gravely, at the very least twice over. For he commits an offense against both men and the prescriptions of both types of law <note>meaning both civil/human law and divine/canon law</note>. **Greed** properly, along with **necessity**, makes people into craving plunderers of what belongs to another. For this occurs regarding things acquired for the duties of life. We inflict **injury** on another either by words, by slander, or by blows. One sins against reputation with words and insult, and against bodies with blows. Truly, the cause of inflicting injury arises in a human either from necessity, or opinion, or will, or persistence and fraud. **Opinion** persuades things to be otherwise than they are, toward the following of which men are for the most part more inclined than toward the [truth]...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s critique of the corruption of justice. Having previously discussed the exchange of goods and the nature of obligations, he now turns to how the concepts of private property—"mine and thine"—and the manipulation of legal interpretation lead to social decay and the subversion of the Commonwealth.</meta>

[... truth]. <note>original: *ritatem*; the end of the word *veritatem* from the previous page</note> From this comes the destruction of the world: "mine" and "thine." When these are confused, they generate lawsuits for us. For while I believe your things to be mine, and you conversely believe mine to be yours, we feed the crows excellently—I meant to say **lawyers** <note>original: *patronos*; in the Roman legal sense, these were protectors or advocates. Postel makes a pun here, calling them "crows" (*corvos*) who feast on the carcasses of legal disputes</note>—and we prefer to contend by the **utmost letter of the law** <note>original: *summo iure*; a reference to the legal maxim *summum ius summa iniuria*, meaning "the extreme law is the extreme injustice"</note> based on a mere opinion, rather than living peacefully after submitting our false opinions to arbitrators so they might elicit the truth to which we should agree.

Pure will—the mere desire for possessing things by right or by wrong—even openly breaks through the law; by its own lust, it seizes, weakens, and overturns what belongs to another, and in most cases, this lust stands in place of reason.

The third type of corruption is the most ruinous: when a large portion of mortals use the law itself not for the safety of the **Commonwealth** <term>original: *Reipublicæ*; the "public thing" or the State</term>, as it was designed, but for the subversion of justice. This is eventually the end of even the most excellent things: those things which were once healthily established anywhere among nations for the safety of the Commonwealth tend to be twisted into a perverse meaning through the constant handling of men—especially the wicked—unless you completely renew them in every single century. Indeed, nothing can be more unfortunate than this. 

For when the law is made clear to one who was held by a false opinion, he yields, and is not usually so unwilling to acquiesce to the judge. When force is openly applied, it can hardly happen except by a tyrant, or in a place where there is nothing sacred or legal. But who can bear those who, using the sacrosanct prescription of the laws to ensure their cleverness is not exposed at first glance, immediately cover their frauds and strive to commit the greatest injustice through the law? 

Truly, such is the condition and misfortune of laws—both divine and human—that it is like that of pavements. For if they are new, level, and on a well-placed path, no one could easily say how much benefit those who walk upon them receive. But if once they are overturned and mixed with heaps and pits, no one makes the journey safely; everyone receives the greatest harm, and everyone would prefer to walk on a muddy road rather than on such a pavement. 

And so, when laws begin to be born and established among men, they keep at least as many as possible (if not all) in their duty. But when their meaning begins to be circumvented by crafty men, then instead of good faith, there is deceit; instead of truth, falsehood; instead of justice, iniquity is prepared against the heads of innocent men under the cover of the law. 

Religions, through the trickery of crafty men, turn piety into a hunt for wealth, and turn innocence into a thousand arts for doing harm safely. This is not so permitted in secular laws, except for the more powerful and those who can supply lawyers. These things happen partly through the wickedness of men, and partly through the excessive mass of opinions stitched onto the law. From this it happens that no one has such an unjust case that he cannot pluck something from that heap of opinions; even if he does not win by it, he may at least torment his adversary excellently.

### IN HOW MANY WAYS, BY WHOM, AND AGAINST WHOM
### Sin is Committed. Chapter XVIII.

The term **sin** <term>original: *peccatum*; a moral failing or "missing the mark"</term> extends wider than **injury** <term>original: *iniuria*; a specific legal wrong against another</term> itself. For many sins are not injuries, but all injuries are sins. For since an injury is not done to one who is willing, when a man sins against himself or his own property, because he does it and suffers it willingly, he indeed sins, but he does not commit a legal "injury." 

Truly, all sins are committed either against religion, against nature, or against men. He acts against religion who neglects to observe it through external signs and accepted customs; and he does so all the more, the greater his status, if he—as a private individual—strives to tear it down with words, or acts contrary to it, or differently than usage requires or has received. For all these things lead to its subversion. Likewise, one who violates things assigned to religion—such as one who violates tombs, who defiles sacred virgins, or who affects persons dedicated to sacred things with any injury, or who [steals] things...

He also begins a classification of "sin" (peccatum) as a concept broader than "legal injury" (iniuria), categorizing offenses against religion, nature, and humanity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal foundations of society. The previous page ended with a critique of how "mine" and "thine" cause social discord and how legal advocates ("crows") profit from disputes rather than seeking truth.</meta>

[... truth] <note>original: *ritatem*; the end of the word *veritatem* from the previous page</note> may receive use, or the fruit of use <note>original: *usum fructum*; the legal right to use and enjoy the profits from property belonging to another</note>, or conversely. The reasoning for a **deed** <term>original: *Facti*; an action or performance required by a contract</term> is broad indeed. For it can exist in a duty, in an obligation, in negligence, or in a thing left undone. A "thing" is also very frequently given as repayment in place of a deed: as if I give you that field, or that object, so that you may do this for me; you then owe me the deed, just as I provided the thing. From this arise countless types of **contracts** which, although they are specifically or collectively about an exchange of things, use, or deeds, are nonetheless usually measured in money—according to an arithmetic equality of how much it matters or how much that thing was or is worth.

In the manifold bond of obligations, humans owe these three things to one another and are accustomed to provide them, provided they follow the law. But if they persist in being unjust and unfair toward those to whom they are indebted—acting against the law itself which preserves human actions in place of a now-exiled **faith** <note>original: *fidei*; here meaning "good faith" or "trust," which Postel laments is disappearing from society</note>—they not only neglect the faith bound by themselves, by those whose rights they use, or by the nature of things, but they even contravene the very contracts, pacts, and agreements which all mortals ought to observe. 

Hence were born "actions" <note>legal lawsuits or claims</note> to pursue one’s rights. For the **Commonwealth** <term>original: *Respublica*; the "public thing" or the State</term>, like a most devoted mother, when she has taken us into her bosom to be nurtured, also ensures that we may obtain through her power whatever belongs to our rights. She does this lest we be deprived of the things necessary for living, and lest a contempt for one's fellow man—that is, injustice—reign among us. From such contempt comes the ruin of both nature and human affairs. 

Therefore, if we either cannot or neglect to pursue our property, its use, a deed owed to us, or our right—whether the injury is done to our things or our person—the State takes it upon itself to protect or help us under a specific legal name, wherever its citizens may be. She grants possession of an estate to protect an unborn heir <note>original: *Ventrem in possessionem mittit*; a Roman legal procedure protecting the property rights of a pregnant woman for her future child</note>, gives guardians to orphans, provides curators for adults and the mentally ill, avenges the wronged, and punishes the guilty even when no one asks for it. In this, we are forced to confess how much we owe to nature, prudence, reason, well-placed laws, and thereby to the author of all, God the Best and Greatest. Thus, people are harmed when they are forced by the power of laws to seek from one another what reason and right should have persuaded them to do or give (or not to do) of their own accord.

## ON THE ORIGIN OF INJUSTICE,
### CHAPTER XVII.

It is clear to any keen observer that necessity, ambition, and greed are the causes of injustice. For he who inflicts injury upon the body is led by a desire for vengeance or glory (wishing to be or seem superior to another); while he who sins against property is surely tormented by greed, necessity, or ambition. Furthermore, there are three types of injustice: impiety, greed, and insult. 

**Impiety** despises the gods, religion, and the things assigned to them—such as sacred objects, holy persons, or the deceased—and treats parents and the fatherland with disgrace. These things ought to be sacrosanct not only by secular laws, but also by sacred ones. Therefore, he who sins against these commits at least a double sin: he offends both humanity and the prescriptions of both types of law <note>meaning both "human" civil law and "divine" canon law</note>. 

**Greed**, along with necessity, makes people hungry for and thieves of what belongs to another. This occurs regarding the physical things acquired for the duties of life. 

We inflict **injury** on another either by words, by slander, or by blows. One sins against reputation with words and insults, and against the body with blows. The cause for inflicting such injury arises in a person either from necessity, from opinion, from will, or through stubbornness and fraud. **Opinion** <note>here meaning a false belief or subjective impression</note> persuades us that things are different than they truly are, and people are generally more inclined to follow this than the truth...

...truth. <note>original: *ritatem*; the conclusion of the word *veritatem* from the preceding page</note> From this comes the destruction of the world: "mine and thine," when they are exchanged, generate lawsuits for us. For while I believe your things are mine, and you likewise, we nourish those "crows" magnificently—I meant to say legal advocates <note>original: *patronos*</note>—and we prefer to contend by the strictest law <term>original: *summo iure*; a legal principle where the rigid application of the law without equity can lead to injustice</term> based on opinion, rather than living peacefully once our false opinions are yielded to arbitrators so they might elicit the truth we should agree upon. A mere desire to possess things, whether by right or by wrong, even openly shatters the law; it seizes, undermines, and overturns the property of others by its own whim, and for most, this whim stands in place of reason. The third and most wretched kind of corruption is that a great part of mortals uses the law itself—not for the safety of the Commonwealth <note>original: *Reipublicæ*</note>, as it was intended, but for the subversion of the law. This is ultimately the end of the most excellent things: those which were once wholesomely established anywhere in the world for the preservation of the Commonwealth are usually twisted into a perverse sense through the constant meddling of men, especially the wicked—unless you completely renew them every century. Indeed, nothing can be more unfortunate than this. For when the law becomes clear to one who was held by a false opinion, he yields and is usually not so unwilling to acquiesce to the judge. When violence is openly used, it can hardly happen except by a tyrant, or in a place where there is nothing of law or sanctity. But who can bear those who, under the sacrosanct pretext of the laws, immediately cover their frauds at first sight so that their cunning is not exposed, and strive to commit the greatest injustice through the law? Truly, such is the condition and misfortune of laws—both divine and human—as is common with pavements. For if they are new, level, and on a well-laid path, no one could easily say how much benefit those who walk upon them receive. But if they are once overturned and mixed with heaps and pits, no one travels that way safely; everyone receives the greatest harm, and everyone would prefer to walk on a muddy road than on such a pavement. Therefore, when laws begin to be born and placed among men, they keep—if not all—certainly as many as possible in their duty. But when their meaning begins to be circumvented by cunning men, then in place of good faith comes deceit; in place of truth, falsehood; and in place of justice, iniquity is prepared against the heads of innocent men under the cover of the law. Religions, through the trickery of crafty men, turn piety into a hunt for wealth, and turn innocence into a thousand arts for doing harm with impunity. In secular <note>original: *prophanis*</note> laws, this is not permitted to such an extent, except for the more powerful and those who can supply legal advocates. These things happen partly through human wickedness, and partly through the excessive mass of legal opinions added to the law. From this it happens that no one's legal case is so unjust that he cannot pluck something from that heap of opinions: which, if it does not win the case, at least twists the adversary magnificently.

### IN HOW MANY WAYS, AND BY WHOM, AND AGAINST WHOM
### sin is committed. Chapter XVIII.

The term "sin" <term>original: *Peccati*; here used in a broad sense of transgression or moral failure</term> is broader than "injustice" <note>original: *iniuria*</note> itself. For many sins are not injustices, but all injustices are sins. For since an injustice is not done to one who is willing <note>referring to the legal maxim *volenti non fit injuria*</note>, when a man sins against himself or his own property—because he does and suffers it willingly—he indeed sins, but he does not commit an injustice. Truly, all sins are committed either against religion, against nature, or against men. He acts against religion who neglects to observe it with external signs and received customs; and he does so all the more as he is greater, who as a private individual strives to tear it apart with words, or who acts against it in a way other than what custom demands or has received. For all these things lead to its subversion. Likewise, he who violates things ascribed to religion, such as one who violates tombs, who defiles sacred virgins, who affects persons dedicated to sacred things with any injury, who [violates] things...

...plunders sacrosanct things by theft. Nor indeed are only religious things sacred, but also those things which contribute to the safety of all—such as whatever serves convenience: roads, the forum, or walls. Because these are assigned to the public, they all ought to be treated as if they were sacred things. If anyone should willfully and knowingly overturn, scatter, steal, or violate these, it is established that he has sinned greatly. In these and similar cases, beyond the crime committed—which would be punished even if it were done to a private individual—satisfaction must also be made for the damage suffered by the whole body of the Commonwealth <term>original: *Reipublicæ*; the state or organized political community</term>. There is not, nor ever was, any nation that did not place these among the most serious crimes.

Opinions regarding tombs have certainly varied. Some preserved them with spices and glass; others with spices alone; some with the bodies of parents, as the Scythians <note>An ancient nomadic people of Central Asia; Postel refers here to their specific ancestral burial rites</note> did for their fathers; some by dogs, others by fire, many by earth. But it was common to all nations to make the place where either the whole body or the ashes were laid religious <term>original: *religiosum*; in Roman law, a 'religious' place was one specifically dedicated to the gods of the underworld, making it legally protected and inalienable</term>; so much so that in some regions it is the custom to create a road even where the dead man was carried in, even if it did not exist before and was private property. Nor is it a wonder that, by the consensus of all nations, the law also wished those to be sacrosanct to us, from whom we received both our existence and the laws themselves. 

Christians alone make a place religious before they bring in the dead; in other religions, the body itself brings the religious quality to the place. Although the customs received by any religion may seem ridiculous to neighbors, whatever they are, care must be taken to do nothing against them in the places where they are approved. For that is to disturb and overturn the head of the Commonwealth and to diminish the respect for religion—unless this is done with such great modesty that you can introduce a better one before the accepted one is overturned, and you are capable of doing so, prevailing primarily through authority. For it is by those religions that people most strongly coalesce, and they are held under laws and Princes <note>sovereign rulers</note> by terrors; this is the primary utility of the Commonwealth. 

Whoever attempts anything that brings destruction to one or more humans sins against nature—which is a crime full of the highest inhumanity in a private person. For for the sake of retaining or obtaining peace, any Commonwealth can (after coming to the miseries of desires and opinions) either slaughter neighboring cities or regions to the point of extinction if they are harmful, unless they surrender. For it is better, when all things are done for the sake of peace, that a few live in quiet than many in constant miseries and conflict.

Furthermore, by a certain process of nature—hidden indeed from men and therefore mysterious <note>original: *religioso*; here meaning something veiled or divinely ordained</note>—when human affairs have reached their peak and overflowed into pleasures, and there are more people everywhere on earth than can be sustained in one place, it is necessary that destruction be prepared either by themselves for themselves or others, or from the opposite side. In this matter, since fate and the whim of Princes can do much, I do not know if anyone sins greatly. Truly, no private person is permitted to harm another. Therefore, he who kills or attempts to kill a human—for whose birth and preservation Nature is most diligent, and for whose use all laws and other things are prepared—is said to have sinned against nature, because he has removed from the midst the summit and peak of nature's things: namely, an innocent human and a brother. 

For this reason, in all Commonwealths, there are magistrates <note>public officials or judges</note> as avengers of this injury. But he who plots some ruin for many, such as one who takes care to infect the water or air which many use, who sets traps, or creates danger by any means that tends toward the destruction of the lives of many, is by far the most wicked and must be removed from the midst. Therefore, he who creates a present danger to the life of a human...
