<meta>This page continues Postel’s legal and ethical philosophy within the framework of the Commonwealth. Following the discussion on the sanctity of public infrastructure and burial grounds, he now examines the hierarchy of "sins" or offenses—distinguishing between those against nature, against other individuals, and against oneself—and argues for the state's right to intervene in the management of private property for the public good.</meta>

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK III.

But indeed, such a person offends against nature and against man. For he sins against nature because he strips her away, despoiling himself of the very humanity <term>original: *humanitate*; here referring to both the quality of being human and the kindness owed to others</term> she had bestowed. He sins against man because he was preserved by the laws for the sake of mutual protection and duties, yet he not only cheats him of duty but deprives him of life. 

However, one who commits an offense against a man’s reputation, or against men in general, or against their property, is said to sin against man but not necessarily against nature. Nevertheless, if the victim is likely to perish immediately as a result of the crime committed, the crime is then seen as being committed against nature as well. 

A man may sin against one person, against many, or against all. Against one person: either himself or another. Anyone can offend against themselves through negligence or through action, whether in matters of the soul, the body, or fortune—which are called "external goods." We are negligent when we do not frequently care for our souls, fail to adorn them with virtues, or neglect to exercise them with great contemplations; from this neglect, every kind of error creeps in. We busily infect ourselves with vices and never cease to undermine our thoughts with unjust actions. Because the danger of these internal matters pertains only to ourselves, and because human thought cannot be seized by other men, there is no legal penalty to avenge them. Instead, the expiation of the fault is referred to religion and the fear of God, who will be the punisher of those who neglected to cultivate and preserve the reason divinely composed for them within this harmony of the body.

If anyone should negligently care for the health of their body, or approach danger, and bring evil upon themselves by chance or by will, they must undoubtedly credit it to themselves; no law exists to punish that sin. For nature has given such a great concern for preserving life—not only to humans but to all living creatures—that there is no need for law in that regard. Hence, death is the greatest fear, and life (and those things which support it) is the highest joy; nature has persuaded us that all things are secondary to it. There are indeed remedies for the vices of the body, but no one should be forced to take them against their will. Nature has sufficiently taught what should be sought or avoided without anyone needing to prescribe it. If a person suffering in body does not wish to be cured—since "no injury is done to one who is willing" <note>original: *nolenti non fit iniuria*; a fundamental legal maxim suggesting that if someone consents to an act, they cannot later claim to have been legally wronged by it</note>—they must enjoy their own misfortune, unless they suffer from a defect of judgment, age, disease, or nature. For such people, if parents are lacking, the laws ought to stand in the place of a father, as is customary in well-constituted Commonwealths. 

When someone recklessly squanders and consumes their external goods and the supports of life on uses that are useless to themselves or the Commonwealth, they certainly sin against themselves. Yet, because it is in the interest of the Commonwealth that no one makes bad use of their own property, such a person should be restrained by the laws. For the Commonwealth receives a detriment when those who have squandered their means on delicacies <note>original: *abliguriere*; specifically to waste money on fine food or luxury</note> or have otherwise ruined their estate are forced to beg, to abandon their families, and thus to die while still living. 

A private individual’s discretion over their own property ought not to extend so widely that they may abuse it. For one ought to live for the Commonwealth, not just for oneself. The majesty of the laws, almost everywhere among nations, has seen to it that this should not happen; it has given curators, tutors, or administrators to certain people. These guardians are permitted to improve the condition of the things committed to them, but they are not allowed to make them worse. This is most clearly evident in the "sinews" <term>original: *neruis*; the structural strengths or essential components</term> of the Commonwealth. I call the powers of both laws—secular as well as sacred—the "sinews." Since men must necessarily preside over the administration of these laws, and since places and resources must be provided for them, anyone who wishes is permitted to increase and improve these resources, but never to diminish them. For established resources exist so that they may grow, persist, and endure, as far as the efforts of the Commonwealth can achieve. Therefore, no one should be allowed so much license over their own property, especially inherited estates...

# OF WORLD HARMONY

...renders men, who are insufficiently prudent (as the far greater part are), effeminate and prone to luxury and sedition. These men are usually kept in their duty more by laws than by their own reason, and it is more useful to restrain them like wild beasts than to try to correct them. For he who would remove all wicked men will command either few or perhaps none at all. Hence, while we are incited by the vices of either the people or ourselves, we rush headlong into wars and deaths, and we either attack others, repel injuries, long for things belonging to others, protect our own, or not infrequently even undermine our own while seeking shortcuts through greater expenses. 

Heavenly virtue also, and a hidden cause, contributes not a little to this matter. Necessity, and the likeness of natural things, incites it. For he will not desire to eat whom hunger has not tormented; nor to drink, he who has not thirsted; nor to rest, he who has not labored. For Nature placed all things in a cycle of change, joined to necessity: so that while we maintain the middle path between extremes, we are gifted with virtue. 

But it shall be enough to know this: that everyone—or the <term>Prince: *Princeps*; the sovereign ruler or head of state</term> in the name of everyone—when he procures through wars, slaughters, and plunders those things which lead to the preservation and increase of the state, even with injury to one, many, or all the people of another <term>Commonwealth: *Republica*; the organized political community</term>, does not sin, except regarding religion; to which the Prince, as much as the commoner, must give satisfaction. For (as the <note>original: *Lyricus*; referring to the Roman poet Horace, Odes 3.6.5: "Dis te minorem quod geris, imperas."</note> Lyric Poet says) *Because you bear yourself as less than the Gods, you rule.* It has never been otherwise according to the laws and sovereignty received among men, nor will it ever be so in this mortality as long as our life is joined to the necessity of change, unless nature grants another order of life. 

I would discuss in how many and in what ways those injuries and sins are redressed, if the authority of all men, and especially the dignity described by the orators, were sufficiently established. But it is necessary first to deal diligently with persons, before we come to the things and actions by which injuries are redressed. For before we can act to pursue or preserve our things, or by an action for injuries—and to include everything, whether the action be against a thing or a person—there is need for a judge destined for that matter about which we are to act to exist in the Commonwealth: a person who either assesses the matter for me, or asserts it, or takes it away. Therefore, we must speak of magistrates and their jurisdiction.

## ON JUDGES AND MAGISTRATES. CHAPTER 19.

Since every kind of Commonwealth tends toward the same ends—namely, toward peace, duration, and stability—and is nourished, preserved, increased, and thrives by the same things, and is endangered by similar things, it is nonetheless a wonder that the very mode of administration in the constitution of magistrates differs so much that, except for number and order, almost none agree with another. 

However, since it would seem both an infinite task and little necessary (unless there are illustrious examples, as we showed in our <note>Postel likely refers here to his own academic work on the Athenian system.</note> *Athenian Magistrates*) to report the institutions of all those that exist or are recorded in literature, we shall hand down, based on the necessity and use of things, those kinds of magistrates that exist in any Commonwealth, if not in a specific office, certainly joined with another. It is clear that magistrates were primarily established from the imitation of nature and arose gradually from the necessity of things. For nature taught all living creatures to have care for their offspring until the offspring themselves can look out for themselves and seek by themselves whatever leads to sustenance. Then, in brute animals, she took away that affection, so that they might hurry to the procreation of other offspring. She willed that a perpetual care and knowledge of his own be left to man, so that what the father acquired through longer experience for the support of life, he might always instill in his children and gradually instruct them, and...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s exploration of the social contract and the origins of human law. ### WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK III.

And [Nature] was to lead him toward that perfection which would also be an aid to his future family and posterity. Thus, the **Father** first began to rule over his children in those matters which were necessary; he prescribed—either through signs (before languages were devised) or through words—what should be sought and what should be avoided. When the children obeyed his command, they began to live far more happily than those who were destitute of such guidance. And that was the first mode of governing.

But as men grew to adulthood and increased into a greater multitude, they were oppressed by injury. Families rose up against families, either for the sake of lust or necessity, and they inflicted mutual injuries upon one another. It then seemed right to **imitate nature**: by the consensus of certain people, they chose one man from the whole assembly who was distinguished by virtue or reputation. To him was given the power, in the name of all, to punish crimes and to ordain that whoever committed such acts in the future should be afflicted with such punishments or penalties. From this, it is established that not only the defense of individuals but the protection and care of everyone was both entrusted and received.

Thus municipalities, villages, cities, peoples, and provinces were created, while mortals, in imitation of nature, chose for themselves **one head**, and as it were a parent, who would seek out what was to be sought and—endowed with the authority of all—would provide for those things to be avoided. I do not dwell on the fact that princes immediately degenerated into tyrants; once these were removed, power was permitted to many good men, which is called an <term>Aristocracy: *aristocratia*; rule by the "best" or the elite</term>. Passing into a tyrannical <term>Oligarchy: *oligarchia*; rule by a few</term>, it gave birth to <term>Democracy: *democratia*; rule by the people</term>, and from there to an unjust <term>Ochlocracy: *ochlocratia*; mob rule</term>, or a confused empire.

For although there are three flawed types of administration and three desirable ones, it is better to be ruled even by evil and unjust men than by none at all, and to rage in mutual slaughters. If a Prince, or whoever holds the authority of the laws, is absent, we feel the presence of any tyrant we happen to meet. By the desire for vengeance, ambition, and glory—placed in our minds by nature—and even by necessity itself, we become tyrants to others and rage and act cruelly toward one another.

This is evident in the peoples recently opened to the whole world <note>Postel refers here to the indigenous peoples of the Americas and other lands reached during the 16th-century Age of Discovery.</note>, who, although they are far more numerous than those inhabiting all Europe and know nothing of a more refined nature, nor have written laws or letters, nevertheless have **Princes** as punishers of injury or leaders for seeking vengeance. Nor is there any nation so barbaric that it lacks some leader. This is evident even in the smallest of almost all living creatures, namely in **bees**.

Therefore, that power—as if it were sacrosanct—must be religiously observed, as without it, no human conversation would be safe. This is most clear when you see men prowling in mutual slaughters and even devouring themselves. Nor should it be immediately thought that this "humanity" belongs entirely to nature; rather, it is gradually instilled in us by the authority of parents, laws, and Princes. (For it is enough that nature produced us as **capable of being taught**, not already taught). Indeed, all people, wherever they are on earth, would be held by the same skill and humanity if they were produced as such by nature alone. 

For there are many who neither speak, nor have laws, nor are led by a shame for anything (which we believe most especially comes from nature), nor do they know laws or religions; they neither sow nor reap. From this it is clear that these things were discovered by **prudence**, infused into a nature capable of being taught, and offered to that tender age which is capable of all opinions. This can become known to us as well, when we look more diligently into our own beginnings and consider the things handed down in records. For there was almost never a nation that did not hold human flesh as a delicacy—to the point that they gave what they held most dear as a most pleasing <term>Victim: *uictima*; a sacrificial offering</term> to the gods. Who among the grown republics of today would not shudder at this? Every <term>Scythian: *Scythica*; historically, nomadic people from Central Asia, used here as a symbol of the "barbarian"</term> nation held the bodies of enemies among their most pleasing foods, which is still evident today in many places; they even held in delight the bodies of their aged parents, among whom, at a mature age, they would...

...the fear of death had not been instilled, so that they might gladly offer themselves up to be slaughtered and devoured in feasts by their parents. <note>Postel is likely referring to classical accounts of "barbaric" tribes or perhaps early mythological accounts of cannibalism to contrast with "civilized" life.</note> Therefore, we owe so much not to nature—which created us destitute of all things and the most miserable of all living creatures (unless hope, the knowledge of God's religion, and the desire for life and glory raised us up)—but to God, to religion, to wisdom, to the laws, and to the princes who keep us within the bounds of humanity. They daily lead us toward the refinement of our character and make nature itself, which is incomplete <note>original: *mancam*</note> on its own, corrected within us. Indeed, as needs demanded, not only did individuals rage against one another, but many against many, moved either by vengeance, necessity, or glory, while they were either seized by the pursuit of some goal or strove to possess what their neighbors held. Therefore, for the purpose of repelling that multitude which rises against another, the **Prince** prepares for war. He spends the resources prepared and collected from everyone for the sake of protecting liberty at his own discretion—as if, as I was saying, he were the condensed body of the Commonwealth <note>original: *compendiarium Reipublicæ corpus*</note>—and he overthrows the enemy. For I wish to take my example from the victorious people and the Prince, since the conquered usually receive the laws of the victor. And once war has arisen, both while it lasts and after it is finished, it is necessary for at least three types of <term>magistrates</term> <note>In this context, a "magistrate" refers to any high-ranking civil officer or administrator, not just a judge.</note> to emerge: those who repel injury at home, those who do so abroad, and those who collect the strength from each individual of the Commonwealth for both purposes. For before a war, one person acting in the name of all could have been enough to lead. These were the kings or **Princes** (for the difference is in the title, not the reality), and they were both judges and priests of the divinity under whose protection the cities or assemblies are administered—provided that a religion had already been devised and established. Therefore, since he has two locations to manage, unless he compels both peoples to live in one place, and since he can only conveniently perform the duty of the prince in one, he must necessarily be absent from the other. For I am speaking of such places that show the world has already reached adulthood. Suppose one magistrate acts in one place and another in the other to declare the law among contenders and to restrain those who act against the laws; then another must be appointed to collect power for the Prince from the individual members—namely, a **Quaestor**, <note>A term borrowed from Roman administration, here referring to a financial officer in charge of the treasury and taxes.</note> for the purpose of collecting taxes <note>original: *vectigalia*</note> and who perhaps also manages the levy of soldiers.

---

# THE DIVISION OF CIVIL ADMINISTRATIONS,
## and their explanation. Chapter 20.

Every magistrate, therefore, either drives off domestic injury or external injury; or collects the power by which both can be done; or is an appendix to those who care for such things. There are, therefore, three primary elements: the **Judge**, the **Quaestor**, and the **Prince**. The first rules internal affairs; the second gathers power; the third opposes both internal and external violence. For the Prince also provides the Judge with salaries so that he may more conveniently perform his services for the Commonwealth; he provides the soldier with expenses and creates for himself and the state the "sinews" of wealth and resources. For although he has been gifted with authority by the consensus of all, unless he were wealthier than a private citizen—so that he might make himself favored by his friends and formidable to his enemies and wrongdoers—his authority would undoubtedly be in vain. For the Commonwealth, however well-disposed it might be toward him, cannot supply on the spot, as if by begging, those things which are immediately required to correct crimes or avoid dangers. Moreover, the Prince imparts his own authority to the Judge himself, so that the Judge may use it, not indeed according to his own whim, but according to the laws of what is fair and good <note>original: *aequum et bonum*, a standard legal phrase for equity.</note> and according to the Prince's prescription. For the Prince alone ought to possess pure command <note>original: *mero imperio*, referring to the highest form of legal power, including the power of life and death.</note> so that no private person gifted with it might think he is permitted more than is right. Truly, our empire must be increased, and through victories, our Prince must be led to the greatest heights, and finally, our simple magistrates must be multiplied. Let us grant, if it could be done, **one Prince for the whole world**. For that is most especially in the likeness of the one Divinity, upon whom the order of nature depends.

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK III.

...hangs, and lasts eternally, so that Homer’s opinion may be preserved: **It is not good for many to rule; let there be one ruler.** <note>original Greek: *οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη, εἷς κοίρανος ἔστω* (Iliad 2.204). This was a common Renaissance argument for monarchy.</note> Or if it cannot belong to the entire world—since surely not even a tenth of it can or ever could be held by one king—let it be as large as it can be for the preservation of its own people. For it is no less a virtue to protect what has been acquired than to seek it out; yet he who possesses more can scarcely do this, as he can hardly restrain those who revolt in his presence, especially if he should reign for a longer time. For that reason, no empires that attempted to grow larger than their own strength could endure; smaller ones lasted the longest. Because the first and primary cause for the institution of princes was to settle and avenge domestic injuries and complaints, and the second was to repel external danger.

I shall first speak of the judges: how many types there ought to be, or are, in a well-constituted state <note>original: *politia*</note>. All judges, as I said regarding religion, are either supreme, middle, or lowest. The supreme judge is, in certain cases, the Prince himself, who rightly reserves such matters for his own knowledge. In the second place after him are the supreme magistrates, who usually give judgment particularly among the "middle" judges in those matters which the Prince does not wish to be finished by inferiors, or which were wrongly decided, or which come into dispute—to put it in a word, they preside over everyone.

In our France, so that matters may be more precise, there are two magistrates of this kind. First is the **Sacrosanct Council** <note>The *Conseil Privé* or Privy Council</note>, in which the prince himself is frequently present; however, as many great men as are distinguished by their wisdom and experience in affairs, and to whom the prince has granted this on account of their merits, are usually admitted into such a holy assembly. Otherwise, only a few and the most eminent enter, especially if the matter is secret or more private. For this reason, they call it the **Private Council**, because matters are settled or established by the Prince as if privately, partly by reason and partly by his own judgment. To fail to obey this decree is a crime and a sacrilege. But because any injured person could not easily gain access there, princes have always had certain men of remarkable experience and knowledge—the **Masters of Requests** <note>original: *libellorum supplicum magistros*</note>—to offer petitions to the prince in that assembly and to make themselves available everywhere to all those seeking remedies.

The other assembly of judges is called the **Great Council**, where they primarily deal either with those things which the prince wishes to be known by them through special privilege, or they debate the law, jurisdiction, refusal, and contention of inferiors. And since both those things done in the Supreme Council and the Great Council require singular examination and endurance, it must be seen everywhere whether the petitions are based on truth and the utility of the Commonwealth. And if the petitions rest upon truth, a man is appointed by the prince—one of the greatest wisdom, knowledge, and long experience in affairs, with a mind sharpened in all things—to look into whether what has been decreed should be ratified (for false and useless things are not rarely urged upon princes). Only then does he fortify the act with the confirmatory seal of royal authority (without which nothing receives the force of public law) and join the acts to the power of the laws, provided that nothing is found therein except what is fair and good. Otherwise, he is accustomed to **cross out** <note>original: *cancellare*</note> and break the legal instruments; therefore, in French, he is called the **Chancellor**. His decision is also held as ratified for those doubting the jurisdiction or for those complaining. 

Although it is my purpose to hand down not the civil law of the Romans or of another people, but that which is either approved, to be approved, or probable by the consensus of all nations, I nevertheless wanted to take this example from our own Commonwealth as something that no man could easily find fault with. For things instituted by the wise, proven by long use, confirmed by the consensus of all, and constant in both war and peace, are surely to be sought by any mortal. There are also other supreme magistrates, usually appointed daily by any prince, but not for the care of the whole Commonwealth; rather, they are appointed for the investigation of a particular business or case, who, once their sentence is delivered, can decide and decree in that matter no differently than the prince. But I come now to the middle judges, whom the Greeks call *hypallelous* <note>original: *ὑπαλλήλους*</note> and the French call **subalterns**; these will certainly be much clearer once the lowest ones have been declared. They are...

### BOOK III

Therefore, the lowest are all the "pedanean" <term>pedanei: literally "judges of the feet," referring to minor officials who sat on low benches rather than elevated tribunals</term> and municipal judges. These are stationed by the Prince in specific locations, conveniently arranged so they can be easily accessed by all, to deliver the law to citizens or the common people. Below these, no one has the power to grant a legal ruling. These judges are like the "dregs" of the judiciary, and are not particularly skilled in legal matters. For this reason, they are only permitted to hear cases involving a certain fixed sum of money; they are not allowed to decide capital cases on their own unless they convene a consensus of several judges, or unless the merits of the case are formally exhibited and explained to a higher authority. If any error is made in their sentencing, the injured parties are usually helped through the benefit of appeal <term>appellationis: the legal process of referring a case to a higher court for review</term>.

The "middle" judges are those who recognize a superior above them and have inferiors below them from whom cases can be appealed to their court. These are of three kinds. Some depend directly on the Prince without any intervening right of another. Some are assigned to religious assemblies <note>Postel refers here to ecclesiastical courts or judges within religious orders</note>. Others are granted to men who have been gifted with nobility for the sake of their merit, virtue, and good faith; these noble judges may serve as middle or even lowest-tier judges.

The Prince desires that these men—whether they be religious communities or men who have served the Commonwealth <term>Respublica: used here to mean the state or the well-ordered public body</term> well—be granted not just the property itself, but the authority to defend it and to assist the State within their jurisdiction. He does this to preserve and increase religion and to promote and stir up virtue in men. For when these men recognize the benefit they have received from the Prince and strive to be like him, they act as the hands and supports by which the Prince manages other men and can more easily exercise his power.

Such is the nature of the nobility, of which I have already spoken. It is difficult to judge whether it is better for nobility to be hereditary <note>original: "diuturnam, & in liberis locum habere" (long-lasting and having a place in children)</note> or to be granted only to those who have personally earned it. However, it is more certain than certainty itself that we undertake far more for the sake of our posterity than for ourselves; we are gripped by a much greater zeal for increasing and preserving a legacy that will benefit our descendants than if we were merely protecting our own interests. For this reason, we cultivate and defend the State with greater devotion than if we were merely temporary residents here, keeping the glory of virtue for ourselves alone rather than leaving it to our children. Therefore, a Prince reigns far more securely when he has an ancestral nobility—even if they rely on "paternal glory" by a false name—than one who relies on a "true" nobility sought from the lowest origins. For that "true" but new nobility has hardly taken root before it is pulled out. The ancestral kind, however, has grown and remains standing through the immense benefit of industry and private wealth, which is the very "sinew" of the State.

This nobility, therefore, has the license to appoint judges, categorized into three types:
1. Some can only restrain the guilty so that they may be handed over to other judges; they cannot punish them with lashes or fines.
2. Others can both restrain and impose many fines (either fixed or arbitrary) or corporal punishment.
3. Others can restrain, punish with death, or proscribe individuals from their jurisdiction, sentencing them to either perpetual or temporary exile.

In these judgments, there must always be the remedy of appeal. Truly, great care must be taken that a judge does not abuse the authority granted by the Prince according to his own whim, believing that power to be his own when it is not, but depends entirely on the Prince’s power. For all men, and especially those gifted with authority, tend to grow habituated to power <note>original: "inolescunt," suggesting the way habits or vices become "grafted" onto the character</note> and permit themselves many things, unless continuous virtue and a love of justice restrain them, or the fear of the law and immediate punishment keeps them in check.

Among our middle judges, there must be some who are "supreme," established in the highest dignity, authority, and fellowship. Someone most worthy of supreme authority should preside over them. These judges decide particularly on appeals and the errors of inferior judges. From their sentence, it is not permitted to appeal further, lest lawsuits become eternal—unless the Prince, by his own pleasure (which should be done only with difficulty and for the sake of some public utility), decides something to the contrary. For a Prince subverts his own State when he diminishes the dignity and authority of the courts and creates eternal lawsuits while... <note>The text cuts off here as the catchword "tes" suggests the next word is "testatur" or similar on the following page.</note>

One thing must be noted: that in matters of religion, there is also a right of appeal to the highest prelates of religion, except in cases involving sects that cast doubt on the accepted religion. Because such a thing tends toward the disturbance of the Commonwealth, once it is proven—even by slight evidence or by witnesses who are otherwise considered dishonorable—the judge of civil causes delivers the law regarding it.

### ANOTHER DIVISION OF JUDGES. CHAPTER XXI.

All judges are appointed or established either for punishing capital injuries <term>capital: crimes involving the loss of life or status</term>, for ending civil controversies, or for both; and they have jurisdiction either in a single place and matter, or in all of them. They are either "ordinary" <note>regular judges with standing jurisdiction</note> or sent as "subsidiary" <note>extraordinary judges sent to assist</note>, and they take cognizance of either private matters or public matters of the treasury. The first priority is the prosecution of crime or the punishing of public injury, for it was for this reason that princes were first chosen and supported by the public: so that justice might be rendered if any injury were done to one person by another. Indeed, a sin involving property is far lighter than one involving bodies. It was not considered a crime requiring atonement to offend against property, except in cases of theft or intentional harm—which some were once accustomed to punish by death, others by a fourfold penalty, and others by various other fines. Among the Spartans <note>original: "Lacedæmonijs"</note>, it was once considered a matter of glory if one was not caught, making them both more cautious in plundering the property of enemies and more attentive in preserving their own. A capital crime, however, is certainly committed not only against the person to whom it is done, but also against all their kin. Many injuries are indeed based on the opinions of various nations, some of which consider certain acts as nothing, while others even hold them in honor. But to have killed any human being (except for enemies, or those whom it is permitted to kill with impunity by an accepted law) whether by poison, or by a weapon, or by a plot, or to have slain or sought to slay them by any fraud whatsoever—this is permitted nowhere among any people. Furthermore, in demanding penalties, the judge ought to follow the prescription of the laws and the opinion accepted for the sake of public peace, and this must be done severely toward those accustomed to sinning, especially while the benefit of appeal remains. Otherwise, for a supreme judge, equity <note>original Greek: τῇ ἐπιεικείᾳ (tē epieikeia) — the principle of fairness or mercy that tempers the strict letter of the law</note> must be preferred to the strict letter of the law, and the case must be moderated by this fairness. In the second place are those who resolve controversies concerning property. A judge can also be established for both types of inquiry at fixed hours, when there is either a scarcity of cases or a shortage of judges. Lest judges permit themselves too much, contaminating their duty through either license or negligence, guardians are given to them by the prince, or ought to be given, with the highest authority. These are like judges or advocates or procurators of those matters which pertain to the conservation of the Commonwealth, holding care even as "guardians of the guardians," without whose authority nothing can be decided that tends toward the loss of the treasury or of nature. When these guardians make requests or offer resistance in such matters, they must be obeyed as if they were the prince; otherwise, they may report the matter to the prince themselves. For this duty, many Republics have had "censors," and some permitted anyone who wished to accuse those who had finished their term of office. All these things were invented to keep judges in their duty, serving as the eyes of the supreme authority. However, where there are not many lawsuits or where injuries are rarer, a judge can indeed deliver the law in many places. # ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
## THE HIERARCHY OF JUDGES

...therefore, all the lowest judges, the petty and municipal judges <term>petty judges: originally called *iudices pedanei* or 'foot-judges' because they often heard minor cases in public spaces or while standing</term>, who serve in places established by the sovereign <note>original: *principe*</note> that are conveniently located so they can be reached by everyone, administer the law to the citizens or the common people. Below them, no one can grant judgment. These are, as it were, the lowest tier of judges, and are not particularly skilled in legal matters. For this reason, they are only permitted to hear cases involving a certain sum of money, and they are not allowed to decide on capital cases <term>capital cases: legal matters involving the death penalty or the loss of a person's civil rights and status</term> by themselves. They may only do so if a consensus of several judges is gathered or consulted, or if the merits of the case have been fully presented and explained. If any error is made in their sentences, it is customary for the injured party to be helped through the benefit of an appeal.

The middle judges are those who acknowledge a superior above them and have subordinates beneath them from whom appeals can be made. These judges are truly of three types. Some depend directly on the sovereign without any intermediary right; some are assigned to religious assemblies; and some are permitted to men who have been granted nobility because of their merit, virtue, and good faith. These noblemen serve not only as middle judges but as the lowest tier as well. The Sovereign <note>The "Prince" or head of state</note> intends for all these groups—whether religious communities or men who have served the Commonwealth <note>original: *Reipublicae*</note> well—to be gifted not only with property but with the authority to defend that property and assist the state within their jurisdiction. This is done for the sake of preserving and increasing religion and promoting virtue among men. For when these men recognize the benefit they have received from the Sovereign and strive to be like their own kind, they act as the hands and supports through which he governs other men and more easily exercises his power.

Such is the nature of the nobility of which I have already spoken. Whether it is better for nobility to be hereditary and held by one’s children, or granted only to those who have personally earned it, is a difficult matter to judge. However, it is more certain than certainty itself that we undertake far more for the sake of our descendants than for ourselves. We are held by a greater desire to increase and preserve a legacy that will benefit our posterity than if we were protecting only our own immediate interests. For that reason, we cultivate and defend the Commonwealth with greater zeal than if we were merely temporary officials who held the glory of virtue for ourselves alone without leaving it to our children. 

Therefore, a sovereign reigns far more securely when he has a nobility that is ancestral—even if it relies on a father’s glory under an inherited name—than one who possesses a "true" nobility sought from the lowest place. For that "true" nobility has scarcely struck roots before it is pulled up, whereas the ancestral kind has grown and stands firm through the benefit of vast industry and family wealth, which is the sinew of the Commonwealth.

This nobility, therefore, also has the license to appoint judges, divided into three categories of power:
1. Some can only compel suspects to be handed over to other judges, but cannot punish them with beatings or fines.
2. Others can both compel and impose many predefined or discretionary fines, or even physical beatings.
3. Still others can both compel and punish with death, or banish someone from their jurisdiction, punishing them with either permanent or temporary exile.

In all these judgments, help should always be available through appeals. Yet great care must be taken that no one abuses the authority given by the sovereign according to their own whim, believing that this power is their own when it actually depends on the sovereign’s power. For all men, and especially those gifted with authority, easily become insolent and grant themselves many liberties unless continuous virtue and the love of justice restrain them, or the fear of the law and immediate punishment keeps them in check.

Among our middle judges, some ought to be supreme, established in the highest dignity, authority, and fellowship, presided over by someone most worthy of the highest authority. These should primarily judge and decide on appeals and the errors of inferior judges. From their sentence, it should not be permitted to appeal—lest lawsuits be eternal—unless the sovereign’s pleasure decides something to the contrary (which should happen rarely and only for the sake of some public utility). ### ANOTHER CLASSIFICATION OF JUDGES. CHAPTER 21.

All judges are appointed or established either for punishing capital crimes, for settling civil disputes, or for both; they have jurisdiction either in one specific place and matter, or in all. They are either ordinary judges or sent as assistants, and they preside over private matters, public matters, or the treasury <term>treasury: the *fiscus*, referring to the state's public funds and financial interests</term>. The primary reason for judges is the prosecution of crime or the punishment of public injury; for it was for this purpose that rulers <note>original: *principes*</note> were first chosen and supported by the public: so that justice might be rendered if any harm were done by one man to another. Among the Spartans <note>original: *Lacedæmonijs*</note>, theft was once a point of glory, provided one was not caught, making them more cautious both in plundering the property of enemies and in guarding their own. # ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

...lest it should hinder or disturb authority, it is best that the seats of all judges be fixed and established. It is necessary for each to speak the law <note>original: "ius dicere," the formal act of rendering a legal judgment</note> and provide justice in specific, predetermined places and times; otherwise, affairs would be in a state of total confusion. Therefore, they have their seats throughout all lands, which they must neither step outside of—unless permission is obtained from a neighbor—nor abandon. In these places, no one can perform the office of a judge unless they have been granted the authority to speak the law there by the supreme magistrate or the prince. 

But since a judge himself may be hindered by illness or by other necessary business—as happens when he frequently attends higher courts to fulfill his duties—provision must be made so that the seat does not remain empty. Therefore, someone must be appointed by the prince, or chosen for his integrity, to speak the law in the judge's absence. 

In truth, a grave error has now been committed in this matter by the French State <note>original: "Gallica Republica." Postel is critiquing the 16th-century French practice of "venality of office," where positions were bought and sold</note>. For those who were once granted very large salaries for the purpose of exercising their duty—the praetors in individual provinces—now receive those payments while being completely unskilled in judging. They shift the entire burden of the office onto sub-prefects <note>These were the "lieutenants" who did the actual legal work</note>, who are indeed learned and good men, but poorer and with a salary lower than what is sufficient to maintain a judge's integrity and avoid "filth" <term>filth: *sordes*, a term for bribes or sordid financial gain</term>. This is something that should be avoided at all costs. For from this source, the first stain of evil and the cause of crimes arises among the very arbiters of justice. 

Furthermore, because in individual provinces there are usually some scoundrels, robbers, and bandits who infest entire regions and fly here and there like nomads—wandering without fixed homes to the great injury of the local people—they cannot easily be restrained or caught by stationary judges. There was a need, therefore, for another kind of "wandering" <note>itinerant or circuit</note> judges, who could pursue and apprehend these vagabonds anywhere in the land. Once caught, and with the local provincial judge or several wise men of that area brought in, these judges could determine and carry out capital punishment, or whatever penalty the crimes deserved, without the possibility of an appeal. These judges do not touch private matters, unless perhaps to prevent them from stagnating; they occasionally prepare lawsuits for the stationary judges, or, at the request of the parties, elicit the truth of a particular fact to be presented to a judge. 

Furthermore, as new diseases arise, new remedies must be sought. For it often happens through the craftiness of men, or even the negligence of judges—or both causes (for the more you restrain men, the more they strive to slip away like eels)—that an immense number of punishments and lawsuits, both criminal and private or civil, arises. To this, wicked men, the more they are investigated to give an account of their lives, the more stubborn they tend to be, and less obedient to judgments because of their guilty consciences. To cure this vice, the Prince or the supreme power of law-giving ought to select the best men from the Great Assembly <note>likely referring to the Estates-General or a high council</note>. Or, if this is not possible due to the number of courts, he should grant authority to certain men to go through those regions to purge them of evil men and put an end to the multitude of lawsuits as quickly as possible. They should do this according to the needs of the situation, every second, third, or fourth year in each province. For in this way, they will heal the world through terror, punishment, and remedies. 

Moreover, factionalism and a certain partiality are not rare among the judges themselves, due to the variety of provinces, places, and offices; the more they excel in authority and wealth, the more influential they tend to be. Therefore, no wise State <note>original: "Respublica"</note> is accustomed to allow them to speak the law in their own interest or that of their kin, nor to permit any right from which it might happen that, by the favor of a prince, many are exempted from the jurisdiction they are under or in which they are litigating because of the hostility of the judges. Instead, they have "delegated judges," as they say, who can speak the law there only for that specific case. Regarding all crimes or disturbances of the State and lawsuits which in man...

Having previously addressed the roles of primary judges and the flaws in the French system of delegating authority to sub-prefects, he now transitions to the supporting officials—the "appendages"—necessary for a functioning legal system as a society grows in complexity.</meta>

...whether arising from private individuals or those endowed with authority, or even from the affairs of the assemblies themselves, judges are appointed or can be so appointed. There remain for us those who handle and protect the affairs of the treasury <note>original: "fisci," referring to the public purse or the state's financial interests</note>; we shall speak of them only after we have described the appendages of the courts.

---

## ON THE APPENDAGES OF THE COURTS.
### CHAPTER XXII.

By "appendages," I mean those magistrates, titles, or duties without which an enlarged and long-enduring Republic <note>Postel uses "Respublica" in the broad sense of any organized state or commonwealth</note> can hardly stand. For new Republics, not yet shaped or expanded by long experience—or even older ones that were once ignorant of crimes—were able to do without them, either because vices had not yet been recognized or had not yet arisen, or because the remedies were unknown. 

For a greater knowledge of things, greater prudence, and a more flowing abundance of resources—be they goods of the mind, the body, or fortune—are considered the "highest good" in this life according to the common opinion of virtue, and are therefore sought after by everyone. However, if the use of these external things lacks justice and moderation, they undoubtedly become the fuel for all vices. Thus, in the past, young Republics committed few errors due to their ignorance and meager resources. Their concern reached only as far as necessity, not toward glory or reputation; lacking examples of such things, they proceeded simply. Man is an "ape of man" <note>A proverb suggesting that humans naturally imitate the behavior—and the vices—of their neighbors</note>, yet this moderate ambition is of the greatest use if there is a "measure in things" <note>original: "modus in rebus," a famous phrase from the Roman poet Horace meaning moderation</note>—which ought to be placed in the soul, not in the abundance of possessions.

Indeed, judges require three types of men. Some are appointed for the beginnings of cases, others for the middle, and others for the final execution of matters in which a judge can hardly spend his own effort. For there are, or should be, those who can apprehend criminals—whether caught in the act, or noted as guilty through investigation, witnesses, judgments, or conjecture—without a specific command from the judge, and bring them before the tribunal. The Latins called them <term>apparitores</term> <note>Apparitors: court officials or bailiffs; named because they make the accused "appear" (apparere) before the judge</note>; at other times they are called <term>viatores</term> <note>Viatores: literally "travelers," serving as messengers or summoners for the court</note>; in French, they are called "servants of the court" <note>original: "curiæ seruientes," referring to the *sergents* of the French legal system</note>, because they are the ministers of justice. 

The watchmen <note>original: "uigiles," the night watch or city guards</note> among any people have the same legal standing. Because the greatest power for doing harm exists at night, the law allows them to restrain with chains and present to a judge anyone wandering at unusual or prohibited hours, or those who have committed a crime, or those approaching the guard posts without a password, or anyone committing a deed considered a vice in that Republic. 

There are also <term>quaestores</term> <note>Quaestors: here meaning investigating magistrates or "seekers" of evidence</note>, not only for "parricide" <note>In Roman law, *parricidium* often referred to any especially heinous murder or high treason</note> but for any more serious crime committed. They visit the locations and conduct the investigation, either at the request of the victim, by order of the judge, or even by their own office, preparing the lawsuits and questions for the judge. The judge, having learned the merits of the case, then decides whether the accused should be summoned or arrested (though citation is permitted unless the crime is grave or there is a risk of flight). If the accused does not obey by the appointed day or prescribed time—or a time extended by reason of law or the case—they are ordered to be thrown into chains, or a sentence is pronounced in their absence. For such a person is guilty of <term>contumacy</term> <note>Contumacy: the legal term for a stubborn refusal to appear in court or obey a judicial order; contempt of court</note>.

In the past, it was permitted in all Republics for anyone to seize criminals caught in the very act and bring them to the tribunal. Now, under French law <note>original: "iure gallico"</note>, this power is granted only to certain people, so that there is no room for mutual slander or injury. Truly, in the case of a public injury, this power ought to be open more widely, so that everyone might be a protector of the law. Nor did the Romans permit this only in crimes; in civil matters, too, the power was given to anyone to call their defendant into court in the presence of one witness, whom the defendant was not allowed to dismiss. This was separate from the work of the *apparitores*, who provided the service to the Republic of forcing those to come who, having been called to court, refused to appear...

<summary>Postel describes the necessary "appendages" of a legal system—bailiffs, watchmen, and investigators—arguing that as societies grow wealthy and complex, they require specialized officials to suppress the vices that naturally arise from abundance.</summary>

->ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-

...and they would be presented to those [judges]. However, nearly every place has its own custom. For **Summoners** <note>original: "Viatores," literally "travelers," these were officials who served as messengers or bailiffs for the court</note> may be appointed both permanently and temporarily, either for a specific matter or multiple pre-defined matters. At the request of the litigants, they call people to court and restrain the lawless, whether the subjects obey voluntarily or by the judge’s command. This power ought to be common to all for the sake of public peace, provided that their right does not extend further—whether in summoning to court, taking pledges, or seeking out criminals—than the province of the judges under whom they serve. For they cannot perform these duties in another’s jurisdiction without obtaining permission, unless they possess such authority either previously granted by the prince or specifically permitted for that business, so that they may perform their duty anywhere. Therefore, by means of a legal petition <note>original: "Libello"</note>, either at the plaintiff's request or the judge's order, once the defendant is presented and ordered to come to court, the judge learns the main points of the case there through the report of the **Summoner**; from there, he asks the litigants to provide him with supporting evidence.

From this, due to "human ignorance" (as they say), **Patrons** and **Procurators** <note>These roles correspond roughly to modern advocates/barristers and proxies/attorneys</note> have come into use. They explain the facts and merits of the case to the judge. They are used in the midst of litigation, and specifically in Republics that have already become depraved. Since the judge himself ought to necessarily grasp whatever law is relevant—either by himself, from the legal instruments and acts, or from the words of the litigants—regarding the knowledge of the case, he could certainly do without those aids and hear anyone speaking for themselves. For this reason, many nations lack such men and leave those matters to be weighed by the judge, since the **Patrons** themselves can add nothing to the case except a certain order and a polished style of words.

But in truth, in such a trial, help must be given through these men to those who are absent, as well as to those hindered by language, women, wards, the unfit, the mentally impaired, and those who suffer from such a defect that they cannot explain their own right or the feelings of their mind, or what legal standing they have. I believe **Advocates** were first established for their sake, just as there are still many Republics where they speak the law even for those accused of the greatest crimes. Thus, the **Procurator** opens up to the **Advocate** those things which must be done according to the practice of civil law <note>original: "ius civile"</note>; the Advocate then explains these to the judge in writing or by voice, adding the arguments which are usually sought from the Law of Nations <note>original: "ius gentium," refers to laws or customs common to all humanity</note>. Not infrequently, judges also prepare lawsuits for other judges. 

Under Roman law, all may be admitted to the office of **Procurator** except minors, women, the insane, those marked by infamy, and those enrolled in religious orders (who may only be procurators or syndics in sacred matters). If any are usually exempted anywhere by the opinions of civil laws, they may be appointed for either a single business matter or for all matters, for any length of time. If, however, someone manages another’s affairs without a mandate <note>original: "mandatum," a formal commission or contract</note>, he is usually called a **Manager of Affairs** <note>original: "gestor negotiorum"</note>, not a procurator. If he is appointed by a mandate—whether by word, letter, or formal notice—he is not usually approached by the judge as a procurator, which seems to have been established quite unfairly. For it is right that everyone be heard either in person or through a friend or one appointed by mandate. Yet, many "crows" <note>A metaphor for greedy or predatory people</note> gasping for the wealth of others would be put at risk. For that reason, it is better to nourish them at the expense of the Republic than to abolish them.

There remain for us those who assist the judges after the case is decided, as if by dictation. The **Scribe** <note>clerk of the court</note> is in charge of this matter: first while the parties are being interrogated, or when the merits of the case are reported in criminal matters; in civil matters, however, while the judge delivers the sentence, the scribe transcribes it and creates, as it were, codicils. Later, showing these to the judge and conferring with him, he polishes them, and from there produces the petition or the instrument of the judgment. He gives this to the one in whose favor the judgment was made. In order for that instrument to have the strength of laws, it must be protected by the seal of the prince or of the one under whom that jurisdiction is administered; finally, its effects must follow. For the law would be spoken in vain unless its effects were afterwards realized in actual affairs. Therefore, nothing should be determined or judged by any judge without it being immediately taken down by the **Scribe** and placed at least in a diary, or into an instrument or petition if the matter requires it. When someone, having been warned, does not obey the judge...

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK III

...cannot be free from deceit. Therefore, either the one who orders a party to appear in court, or another official who is called by our people a **doorkeeper** <note>original: "hostiarius," a gatekeeper or usher</note> or a **commissioner** <note>original: "commissarius"</note>, compels the defendant to obey. This is done either by force or by seizing **pledges** <note>assets taken as security to ensure legal compliance</note> equal to the value of the matter at hand. For wherever in the world people contend in court over their affairs, matters are usually settled so that it is practical for the judgment to be paid or carried out; otherwise, both princes and judges would be established in vain. But these remarks concern judges and their ministers. The rest of these matters are based on human opinion.

->ON THE MILITARY ORDER AND<-
->AUTHORITY. CHAPTER XXIII.<-

Now we must briefly treat those who were established to repel external injuries, since they do not contribute to the knowledge of the law itself, but not infrequently lead to its subversion. As long as human affairs were very small, not yet increased by personal ambitions, and while the dominion of republics or princes did not extend far, the prince undoubtedly presided over sacred rites, the administration of justice, and the repelling of external injury. For in those times, lawsuits and injuries were rare, religious ceremonies were few, and enemy attacks were neither frequent nor formidable. 

But when that power had to be divided, the pinnacle of religion <note>Postel refers here to the "apex" or supreme spiritual authority</note> could be retained by the prince in terms of supreme power; however, the administration of justice had to be permitted to others due to more frequent lawsuits, as we have taught. The force and power of arms were concentrated in a single prince. That power ought to be divided three ways: into internal, external, or mixed. For civil seditions and uprisings of the common people must be restrained with a force greater than that of the law, lest they rise up against the judges or the prince himself. Strength must also be prepared against foreign enemies. Finally, forces must be established for both purposes when the prince cannot be everywhere at once. 

This is seen, for example, on the borders of regions, where the common people tend to have inconsistent minds and loyalty due to the various rumors spread by neighboring princes. Therefore, this **guardian** <note>original: "custodem"; Postel is referencing the "Phylakes" or Guardians described in Plato's Republic</note> (for so Plato calls the soldiers established for guarding the state) must be most faithful to the prince, most loving of the republic, and most prudent. He must be a man who can move minds through eloquence just as he moves bodies with arms, drawing them to his own opinion and keeping them in loyalty to his prince. He must be ready to take up powerful arms for the prince even against a neighbor or friend. 

To ensure he does this more from the heart—and is not tempted by the allurements of fortune (to which both nature, necessity, and public opinion have made men inclined) by an adversary—the prince ought to gift him with wealth located in the heart of the kingdom. Or, the prince should establish him as a wealthy inland resident, so that he does not easily follow the loyalty of enemies. For wealth and established property keep a man in his loyalty more than anything else; nor has any loyalty anywhere been long-lasting without a stake in the land. Therefore, no one would easily break faith by merely chasing another's hope and seeking uncertainties while abandoning certain things. 

He who is poor, unless he is held strongly by love for his own people and for justice, is certainly for sale. It is common to all those devoted to military service that, once the **oath** <note>original: "sacramentum," the Roman military oath of allegiance</note> is offered for the benefit of the country and religion, they swear to the loyalty and safety of the prince and the republic. If they commit any offense against this oath, they are to be discharged and stripped of their rank as befits wicked and shameful men. This serves both as a punishment for them—as those who have most gravely offended against the republic—and as an example of the dishonor that strikes fear into us by its very nature. Therefore, in the highest matters, a soldier must offer that oath of loyalty; for it is like a sacred marriage of both types of law <note>likely referring to the union of civil and military law, or human and divine obligation</note>. For while the soldier is asked by the oath...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
## BOOK III

...some name, or power, or a matter based on opinion (whose authority is **most holy** <note>original: "sacrosancta"</note> and which ought to, and usually does, strike fear into anyone who neglects the **sacred oaths** <note>original: "sacramenta"</note> taken in its name) ought to be asserted and interposed. We affirm that our faith will endure in this way, just as we believe and desire that that by which we swear is true and everlasting. If it should happen that someone neglects this, an injury is done not only to human witnesses but to the gods, and moreover, a crime has been committed. Therefore, those who commit **perjury** <note>swearing a false oath</note> are deservedly either punished as **treaty-breakers** <note>original: "foedifragi"</note> or marked with infamy. For there is no nation that has received a form of worship and approves and accepts laws that does not keep the faith which it believes and desires to be kept toward itself. He who breaks his word, therefore, ought to feel both God and men as his avengers.

But I return to the prince, who, since he is but one person, cannot be present in all places at once (except through his authority). It is necessary, therefore, for him to appoint **magistrates**, **leaders**, and **military tribunes** to head those armies, who may command them to carry out their orders, see that they are done, and administer justice among them. For it is necessary that that race of men—furious and **consecrated to Mars** <note>The Roman god of war; Postel implies soldiers are naturally aggressive</note>, born to inflict injury unless you constantly watch over them—be restrained not by the gentleness of laws, judges, and provincial officials, but be immediately warned, terrified, punished, or **discharged** <note>original: "exauthorari," meaning removed from military service</note> by their own leaders. Otherwise, they would turn everything into license, undermine everything, and hold nothing as holy or sacred. 

Besides the leaders, who frequently neglect what is right, **judges** must also be appointed to punish the **guilty** <note>original: "fontes," literally the 'sources' of the crime</note>, not only in the army but also in the courts. For those who are physically strong could not be restrained in any other way except by those equal in dignity, but supported by a greater authority or greater force.

In this matter, the **Turks** <note>original: "Turchæ," referring to the Ottoman Empire</note>, who are now the most extensive masters of the world, are wonderfully wise and severe because of their one well-established military system. For if a **decurion** <note>a leader of ten men</note> neglects to punish a crime in war, or neglects to maintain order or the duties of his office, and it becomes known to the **centurion** <note>a leader of a hundred men</note> that he either neglected it or was unwilling to punish it, the decurion is immediately punished in place of the criminal. Likewise, if the centurion fails, he is answerable to the **chiliarch** <note>original: "Chiliarchæ"; a commander of a thousand men</note> (for each has their own jurisdictions); and if the chiliarch fails his own general, they are all accustomed to pay the penalty for the sake of military utility according to the law, in place of the guilty parties. Nor is the criminal soldier punished any less if he is caught later. Indeed, in war, the punishment is **ten times more severe** because where the opportunity for wrongdoing is greatest, the punishment there ought to be larger and heavier. 

In the interior regions, where soldiers are stationed permanently, there is a need for judges rather than generals, or rather for both in two different orders. Truly, since all soldiers are either **cavalry** or **infantry**, they are usually assigned to duties at the prince's discretion. But this is by far the most certain arrangement: ten men to a decurion, ten decurions to a centurion, ten centurions to a chiliarch, and ten chiliarchs to a general. Finally, all generals are subject to the one who has care of the entire army. It matters little if they are organized by another number, provided they can be easily managed by one person. Thus it happens that if something must be done or decided, the commands immediately reach from the highest to the lowest; they immediately come to assemblies and carry out what is commanded.

These men, therefore, because of their untamable nature, and because the duties of military service are little known to civilian judges, and because one class usually hates the other, ought to have **their own courts** <note>military tribunals</note>. Otherwise, vengeance rather than equity would be observed. For this reason, princes are also accustomed to assign those of their own household to certain tribunals, lest they be hindered (as they say) from the prince's service elsewhere. Truly, these are matters of opinion. For a single order of judges ought to investigate every crime without selection or regard for persons, having the strength to restrain even the greatest crowds and...

In courts and armies, however, which are like unbridled and wandering cities, there is a need for those whom we said should be of the same kind <note>Postel refers to the specific military magistrates mentioned at the end of the previous page.</note>.

### ON THE EXPEDITION. CHAPTER 24.

Furthermore, provision must be made for the soldiers themselves, so that they have both what is necessary for life and the use of arms, as well as what is required for the journey and the expedition. First, therefore, there is a need for a **magistrate** <note>original: "magistratu"</note> appointed for that specific time, for as long as the expedition lasts, upon whom the care of all—or at least the more important—duties shall fall. He must possess such authority that no one would dare resist his command with impunity. This official should have the primary care of preparing necessities for the sustenance of both men and horses. Grain, wine, and fodder must be brought in from the neighboring fields, and care must be taken so that they can be sold at a lower price. For when a soldier is forced to purchase his **provisions** <term>annona: the state-regulated grain supply or its market price</term> at a massive cost, he immediately refuses his duties while he is occupied with seeking out necessities, or he is forced to spend more than he receives in his **wages** <note>original: "stipendijs"</note>. For it must be especially noted that this class of men, for the sake of profit and a more splendid fortune, seeks to make a living at the risk of their lives; unless they believe they can obtain profit, they never perform their duties with a liberal spirit. Therefore, care must be taken to ensure the grain supply is as cheap as possible. For there is no prince who can include in a soldier's wages those expenses commonly incurred outside the military art; and even if he did, no soldier would be willing to expend all the sweat of his life for it. Provisions are gathered either into one place or along one route. If along a route, it is done for transit. If in one place, it requires great diligence. If we are to attack, and fresh crops are available, only the quantity is required; but if we are besieged, we need those things that can be preserved for a very long time, such as rice, millet, wheat flour, rye, and barley. For when these are ground down, they do not rot easily because they do not trap air within their body. In the second place are all salted things: cheese, meat, and fish. In the third place are wheat, barley, and oats, kept in a place where they are frequently moved so they do not spoil from trapped air. Live animals are not to be kept alive for long during a **siege** <note>original: "obsidione"</note>, lest they consume the very things that allow horses and men to sustain life longer. Furthermore, they can be best preserved and hardened with salt. For unless fodder is supplied in abundance, the animals are slaughtered at home, as they usually cost no small amount to feed. So much for the siege. Regarding tools for the road and **engines** <note>original: "machinis"; refers to siege engines like catapults or rams</note> for attacking or defending, care must be taken that nothing is lacking when the time comes. For while a soldier is stuck in the narrows of a road, or cannot move his engines, or waits for a bridge, or is delayed for any other reason, he incurs expense; and eventually, that which should have been foreseen and done long ago must be done in the greatest chaos. Thus, the greatest loss occurs in such matters. To ensure the roads are level for moving engines and transporting soldiers, the first care is to have a plenty of **levelers** <note>pioneers or combat engineers who prepared the way for the main army</note>. Military roads suitable for moving troops should be built in the Roman fashion by the local people and select men. If bridges are lacking, timber must be brought from elsewhere long in advance and prepared in suitable places. For this, it is necessary to have a scout who is an expert in the regions; otherwise, if wood is lacking, **skins** <note>original: "corijs utres"; leather bladders or wineskins</note> must be prepared and inflated so the soldier may swim across. If there are not enough of these, they can be sent back to comrades by a rope. Beams, barrels, planks, and so on can serve as a bridge in summer, but **recruits** <term>tyronibus: young or inexperienced soldiers in training</term> ought to be practiced in this art. However, when we are near the enemy...

ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...some name, power, or matter established in opinion (whose authority is most sacred, and which ought to, and usually does, strike fear into anyone neglecting the sacraments taken in its name) must be asserted and interposed; and we affirm that our faith shall endure in the same way as we believe and desire that that which we swear by is true and lasting. But if it should ever happen that this is neglected, because an injury is done not only to men but to the gods, and moreover a crime has been committed, those who commit perjury are deservedly either punished as **treaty-breakers** <note>original: "foedifragi"</note> or marked with infamy. For no nation that has received a cult and approves and accepts laws fails to keep the faith which it believes and desires to be kept toward itself. He who breaks faith, therefore, ought to feel both God and men as avengers. 

But I return to the prince, who, since he is but one person, cannot suffice to be present in all places (except by authority). He must therefore appoint magistrates, leaders, and tribunes of the soldiers over those armies, who may command them to do what is ordered, see to it, and administer justice among them. For that race of men, furious and **dedicated to Mars** <note>original: "Marti sacrum"; a reference to the Roman god of war, used here to describe the naturally violent or volatile temperament of soldiers</note>, and born to inflict injury unless you watch them closely, ought not to be restrained by the mildness of laws, judges, and provincials, but should be immediately warned, terrified, punished, or discharged by their own officers. Otherwise, everything would turn into license, they would undermine everything, and hold nothing holy or sacred. 

Besides leaders, who frequently neglect what is right, there must also be appointed judges to punish the guilty, not only in the army but also in the courts of the palace. For those who are powerful in strength could not be restrained otherwise than by those equal in dignity, but supported by greater authority or greater forces. In this matter, the **Turks** <note>original: "Turchæ"; Postel, like many Renaissance thinkers, felt a mix of fear and admiration for the Ottoman Empire's rigid military discipline</note>, now the masters of vast affairs, are wonderfully prudent and severe because of a single well-constituted military system. For if a **decurion** <term>decurio: a commander in charge of ten men</term> neglects to punish a crime in war, or to keep order or the duties of his office, and it becomes known to the **centurion** <term>centurio: a commander of one hundred men</term> that he either neglected it or was unwilling to punish it, the decurion is immediately punished in place of the criminal. Likewise if a centurion fails, he is punished by the **chiliarch** <term>chiliarcha: a commander of one thousand men</term> (for each has their own rights); similarly, if a chiliarch fails his general, they are all accustomed by the established law of military practice to pay the penalties in place of the guilty, nor is the criminal soldier punished any less if he is caught later. 

Indeed, in war, the punishment is tenfold more atrocious, because where the opportunity for wrongdoing is greatest, the punishment there ought to be greater and more severe. In inland regions, where there are stationary soldiers, there is a need for judges rather than leaders, and for both in the other two orders. Since all are either cavalry or infantry, they are usually assigned to duty at the prince's will. 

But this is by far the most certain method: ten men to a decurion, ten decurions to a centurion, ten centurions to a chiliarch, and ten chiliarchs to a general; finally, all leaders to the one who has care of the whole army. It matters little if they are organized by another number, provided they can be easily managed by one person. Thus it happens that if anything is to be done or decided, the commands immediately reach from the top to the bottom; they immediately come to assemblies and do what is commanded. These men, therefore—both because of their intractable nature and because military duties are little known to civilian judges, and because one class usually hates the other—ought to have their **own courts** <note>original: "iudicia propria"</note>; otherwise, vengeance rather than equity would be observed. For this reason, princes also tend to assign their own household members to certain tribunals, lest, being hindered elsewhere (as they say), they be absent from the prince's service. But these are matters of opinion. For a single order of judges ought to investigate whatever crime exists without distinction or regard for persons, and have the power to restrain even the greatest crowd and...

...supported by authority, to be ready in any part of the world. In courts and in armies, however, which are like cities without restraints and wandering about, there is a need for those whom we have said should be [magistrates], namely, of the same kind <note>The author refers to the earlier point that soldiers must be governed by those who share their nature but possess higher authority</note>.
