### ON THE EXPEDITION. CHAPTER XXIV.

Furthermore, provision must be made for the soldiers themselves, so that they have what is necessary for life and the use of arms, as well as what is required for the journey and the expedition. In the first place, therefore, there is a need for a magistrate appointed for that time during which the expedition specifically lasts, upon whom the care of all, or at least the more important duties, shall fall. This person must possess such authority that no one would dare to resist his command with impunity. He should have the primary care of preparing necessities, both for the sustenance of men and of horses. Grains, wines, and fodder must be brought in from the neighboring fields, and care must be taken so that they can be sold at a cheaper price. For when a soldier is forced to purchase the **grain supply** <note>original: "annona"; refers to the yearly produce or the state-regulated food supply</note> at a massive price, he immediately refuses his labor while he is occupied in seeking out necessities, or he is forced to spend more than he receives in wages. 

For this must be especially noted: that this class of men, for the sake of profit and a more splendid fortune, seeking to make a gain at the risk of their lives, never carries out its duties with a liberal spirit unless they believe they can obtain a profit. Care must therefore be taken that the grain supply be as cheap as possible. For there is no prince who puts into the soldier’s wages those things which can commonly be spent outside the military art; and if he did, no soldier would want to expend the total **toil of his life** <note>original: "uitae sudores"; literally "the sweats of life"</note>.

Resources are gathered either in one place or along one route. If along a route, it is done for transit. If in one place, it requires great diligence. If we are to attack, we need the current crops and only quantity is required; but if we are besieged, we need those things which can be preserved for the longest time, such as rice, millet, wheat flour, rye, and barley. For when these are ground down, they do not rot easily because they do not trap air within their body. In the second place are all salted things: cheeses, meats, and fish. In the third place are wheat, barley, and oats, kept in a place where they may be frequently moved so they do not perish by trapping air. Live animals are not to be kept alive for long during a **siege** <note>original: "obsidione"</note>, lest they consume those things by which horses and men might sustain life longer. Moreover, they can be best preserved and hardened with salt. For unless fodder is supplied in abundance, they are killed at home, and usually cost no small amount to feed. 

These things concern a siege. As for the instruments for the road and the machines for attacking or defending, care must be taken that nothing is lacking at the proper time. For while a soldier is stuck in the narrow parts of a road, or is unable to move the machines, or waits for a bridge, or is delayed for any other reason and incurs expense, that which ought to have been foreseen and done long ago must finally be done in the greatest confusion. Thus, there is the greatest loss in such a matter. To ensure that the roads are level for moving the machines and transporting the soldier, the first care is that there be a plenty of **road-levelers** <note>original: "complanatorum"; workers or "pioneers" who cleared and leveled paths for the army</note>. Military roads, suitable for moving troops, ought to be built in the Roman fashion by the local people and selected men. If bridges are lacking, material must be brought from elsewhere long in advance and prepared in suitable places; for which reason it is necessary to have a scout who is an expert in the regions. Otherwise, if wood is lacking, **leather skins** <note>original: "utres"; inflated animal skins used as floats</note> must be prepared and inflated, by which the soldier may swim across. If these are not enough, they can be sent back to companions by a rope. Beams, barrels, planks, and so on, can serve as a bridge in summer, but this art ought to be practiced among the **recruits** <note>original: "tyronibus"; young or inexperienced soldiers</note>. However, when we are near the enemies...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on military logistics, shifting from the preparation of supplies to the qualities of a commander and the financial structures needed to support both the military and the judiciary.</meta>

[The commander] must possess such diligence that he anticipates all the enemy's plans and employs the most faithful scouts, so that he may provide remedies for the situations he foresees. For we easily **drive out one nail with another** <note>original: "clauum clauo"; a proverb meaning to counteract one force or problem with an equal and opposite one</note> if there is foresight. Even a straw terrifies the unprepared. Because every region has its own methods of defense and attack, there is no need to discuss them individually. The first requirement in any leader is that mature plans be put into effect with extreme speed; if he senses that an adversary is guarding against his usual tactics, he should know that he must immediately resort to another. Indeed, he must be a **Proteus** <note>In Greek mythology, Proteus was a sea-god capable of changing his shape; Postel uses this to mean a leader must be adaptable and unpredictable</note>. 

However, we must return to the overseer, who, like other magistrates, must necessarily have three ranks of men under him. He ought to place certain officials in charge of a larger province, to whom several subordinates are obedient. First, let him ensure that the **sinews of war** <note>original: "neruum belli"; a classic metaphor referring to the money and resources necessary to sustain a conflict</note> are reported to the leader. He must keep the roads cleared of criminals; secondly, he must oversee things necessary for the sustenance of men; thirdly, for horses; and fourthly, for the baggage, including the arms required for both men and horses as well as the entire army. Nothing prevents different magistrates from being assigned to these various duties. But no one would deny they should follow the order I have described, for in human affairs there is a certain design that depends on a single head and is distributed into many parts in an orderly way. He will choose individuals faithful to himself, and he will pledge their loyalty to the prince. If any fault is committed by them, he must compensate for it; therefore, he must have the highest authority over them to restrain them. Once he has restrained them, if they are at fault, they are to be fined; if he chose bad men himself, he can be punished or pay the penalty. For when many people hold the same office, a certain envy arises in human affairs, causing them to betray one another, inflict injuries, and accuse each other; instead of attending to public business, they look after themselves and pursue their own factions. Truly, wealth must now be gathered for both duties: namely, for the salary of judges and for military requirements.

## ON THE FIRST ELEMENTS OF WEALTH,
### *and on the distinction of things.* CHAPTER XXV.

There has been a great and immense variety among men in collecting that power [of wealth] which the consensus of people wishes to be granted to the head of the republic. For after wealth was first granted to princes so they could provide for themselves while caring for the state, the ancients used to give such funds only to a magistrate created for that purpose, who would demand from everyone what was fair. At that time, the **municipalities** <note>original: "municipia"; self-governing towns or cities</note> themselves used to choose either one or several men suitable for military service and pay their expenses by public consensus. Others collected two types of money—their own and the military fund—while the judges were paid from local sources. Some collected for the judges, themselves, and the military: once this practice became common, **taxes** <note>original: "uectigalia"; refers to various forms of state revenue or tolls</note> began to be extended through a single process, and the power of demanding them rested with the prince. 

Thus, some used to collect tax assessments from persons, some from things, and some from both. Gradually, whatever exists from which some utility can be gained began to be monitored and made subject to the **treasury** <note>original: "fisco"; the state's central chest or financial department</note>. Whatever the custom may have been, those three types mentioned just before encompass everything. For if you demand from persons, persons possess everything; if from things, all are subject to the eyes and senses; if from both, the law will be the same. The first republics used to assess "heads" [poll taxes], and payment was made to the treasury according to the ratio of the **census** <note>original: "census"; the official list of citizens and their property value used for taxation</note>. Many republics in **Germany** even now do this by a simple oath without any detailed description of the census. For you would hardly know what individual goods a person has unless there were some man so honest that he immediately revealed how much he possessed—which is certainly a **rare bird** <note>original: "rara auis"; a Latin idiom for something extremely uncommon or unique</note>. -># G U I L L A U M E  P O S T E L  B O O K  I I I.<-

...for no one would willingly say something that contradicts himself. As for what is held in the way of resources, it is multifaceted. For wealth is situated either in the land or in the water. In the waters, resources are movable, immovable, or partially both. On the land, they are movable, immovable, or self-moving <note>i.e., livestock and animals</note>. The Roman <term>republic</term> <note>original: "respub."; the Roman state and its legal traditions</note> and many others desired that no <term>tax</term> <note>original: "uectigalis"; a toll or duty paid to the state</note> be taken from the utility of water, on the grounds that one cannot live without its use. For they wished the use of seawater, fisheries, the seashores, and wild animals to be common to all, and for everything to become the property of the occupant for as long as they possessed it. The banks of rivers, however, have always been private property.

From the sea come <term>merchandise</term> <note>original: "mercimonia"</note>, fisheries, and salt. Merchandise is a movable thing. The right of fishing—if it is available everywhere equally, or if it is restricted somewhere, such as on a specific occupied and private shore—those things from which the utility is sought are considered immovable. If a thing cannot be produced without the use of a specific shore—as is the case with salt, which is produced partly by art and partly by nature—it occupies a middle condition. For insofar as the thing remains in the soil, it is immovable; insofar as it is extracted and carried elsewhere, it is movable. 

The right of rivers is like a road, and governed by the same law, except regarding fisheries; in the more civilized and cunning parts of the world today, these are almost entirely private, though otherwise they are held by common right. Waters enclosed within certain limits of soil, such as lakes and ponds, are public or private depending on the custom of the region. If someone has them enclosed on their own land, it is certain they belong to him. The status of shores or riverbanks, unless otherwise established by law, grants rights to the neighbors. 

Running water can also be subject to a perpetual tax—for instance, if a channel is diverted from its natural course and led into a region that it makes far more productive through irrigation. In that case, the person by whose labor this was achieved can, for as long as the water flows usefully there, demand a tax from individual landowners. The water is granted by <term>inch-measures</term> <note>original: "unciales mensuras"; a system of measuring water flow by the diameter of the pipe or opening</note> for established hours and days. This source of revenue exists in many places, but it is by far the most abundant in <term>Cisalpine Gaul</term> <note>Northern Italy</note>, which they call <term>Lombardy</term>. For more diligent republics or princes have drawn <term>Niles and Euripuses</term> <note>Postel uses the names of the Nile river and the Strait of Euripus as metaphors for large-scale irrigation canals and artificial channels</note>—either collecting water from the mountains into lower regions, or diverting channels from the Po, the Adige, and other rivers into the flat and level plains.

Regarding things usually obtained through the convenience of waters: because a prince defends and protects merchandise no less than the things born of the soil (even if they are brought from elsewhere or are to be exported), he can nonetheless take a tax from them, and especially from salt. Indeed, these matters are placed at the discretion of princes. 

On the land, there are sown crops, trees, meadows, pastures, and forests. By "sown crops," we mean legumes and grains, and things usually sown and gathered annually. Of trees, some are fruitful, others sterile, some are in wild forests, and others in <term>coppices</term> <note>original: "cæduis syluis"; forests managed for periodic cutting</note>. Although meadows and pastures can be aided by human industry, they are primarily situated in the benefit of nature. The uses of forests are many: they are preserved for domestic use for fire, for tools, for building, for grazing, and for hunting. From these come the trade goods born from the surface of the earth: wood, legumes, hay, fruits, and herds. 

There are also <term>metals</term>, which cannot be rendered pure without the benefit of forests; for this reason, we place their origin in the bowels of the earth, but their perfection in the use of wood for smelting. These are gold, silver, tin, copper <note>original: "Cyprium æs"; literally 'Cypriot bronze'</note>, <term>brass</term> <note>original: "aurichalcum"; orichalcum</note>, lead, iron, quicksilver, and other minerals, as well as stones, pebbles, gems, and whatever else nature produces for those who look more curiously. There remains the class of self-moving animals, which, when accounted for by head or by herd and led elsewhere as merchandise rather than staying on their native soil, also constitute great wealth. 

We can therefore very easily provide another division for both what is held by land and by sea. For everything is either under the surface, or on the surface, or partly inside and partly outside. On the surface of the earth are all living things of the land and air; and, partly above and partly below, whatever vegetable the earth produces. Below the surface are all metals, or medic- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; likely "medicamenta" (medicines/minerals)</note>

-># ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-

...ornaments, gems, and whatever is of high price. In the sea, there are fisheries, navigation, and salt. There remains for us the most extensive part of wealth—which is as rich as it is difficult to understand. For, arising from necessity, it is drawn entirely into the realm of public opinion; industrious men, anticipating what things a particular region might most delight in, without regard for utility or necessity, provided they make a profit, bring foreign goods there and—if one may say so—often undermine the stability of the world. For man, by nature, besides the unique gift of speech which distinguishes him from other animals, also has this trait: he admires all things foreign, is amazed by the unusual, and is more captivated by useless imports than by proven domestic goods. 

Wealth is also gathered by other skills, yet still from those elements we have mentioned. A good part of the first men lived by hunting; others by theft committed on land or sea; some by pastures or animals; others by agriculture; others by "opinion," such as those who increased their wealth through religious offerings; some by the labor of the body; others by the benefit of their intellect—who alone among mortals are usually the most beloved in the state and least liable to the <term>treasury</term> <note>original: "fisco"; the state's financial department</note>. For the gifts of the mind usually earn true nobility almost anywhere in the world, provided they are turned toward the use of the state. 

From all these, or most of these elements of wealth, the treasury can take a portion for the preservation and protection of the state. Also, things which cease to have an owner, or which return to the treasury as if by <term>right of recovery</term> <note>original: "postliminio"; a legal concept where property rights are restored to the original state</note>, should belong to the prince: such as the goods of the proscribed, or those marked by a capital crime. Some place in this same legal category the goods of those who, born elsewhere, die while possessing or acquiring property on foreign soil, not having obtained the favor of the prince to become citizens or <term>subjects of the land</term> <note>original: "populi fundi"; those who have the legal status of residents</note>—a right used by the King of the French <note>A reference to the *Droit d'Aubaine*, where the French crown claimed the estate of an alien who died in France</note>. For he joins the goods of those born elsewhere and dying in his jurisdiction to the treasury, lest more unknown foreigners gradually creep into the region. Indeed, these are the main sources of wealth.

## ON THE TREASURERS OF THE PUBLIC COFFERS,
### CHAPTER XXVI.

When taxes began to be extended, and there were only princes of one or two cities or municipalities, there was no need for a great or numerous magistracy to collect them, since the wealth of any private person could easily be known to a prince acting as an arbiter of equity. But as wealth and dominions increased—whether things had to be looked at individually, by estimation of the soil, or by the power of men—there was first a need for an arbiter of the <term>census</term> <note>original: "census"; the official registration and valuation of property for taxation</note>, of resources, and of things. This official divides the sum proclaimed by the prince and ordered upon any province; after diligently considering the resources of all places, he distributes the portions of the greater requested sum according to cities, villages, gatherings of men, and districts, by assessing them for what they can pay. 

Once this is proclaimed, there is a need for a municipal magistrate who, having summoned those more skilled in private matters, imposes a fair share of the payments according to the strengths they have disclosed. In this matter, it is amazing how much those whom the French call the <term>Elect</term> <note>original: "electos"; the *élus*, royal officials in France responsible for tax assessment</note> allow themselves. With supreme injustice, they exempt some who have corrupted them with gifts, and heavily oppress others, unless they receive from both. The municipal <term>treasurers</term> <note>original: "quaestores"</note> present the sum collected from private individuals to the provincial treasurer, who accepts it with signed documents and witnesses. He, in turn, presents it to the high treasurer, who returns it to the <term>exchequer</term> <note>original: "aerarium"; the public treasury of a state</note> or spends it on those uses which the prince has established. In these matters, it can hardly be seen whether fraud lies beneath. Nevertheless, a <term>comptroller</term> <note>original: "antigrapharius"; an official who keeps a duplicate record to check against the main accounts</note> ought to be everywhere and enter into a journal whatever is received by the treasurers themselves. And lest the treasurers and the comptrollers commit some wrong together, there is a need for <term>masters of accounts</term> <note>original: "magistris rationum"; senior auditors</note> (whom it is fitting to have everywhere) who [receive]...

-># WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK III.<-

...and examine the accounts of expenses and record them in the public ledgers. But when the King or Prince gives as a gift something that had been acquired by the <term>treasury</term> <note>original: "fisco"; the state's central fund</note>—such as confiscations or anything else—it is necessary that this also be recorded in the accounts by those in charge of the treasury, a department which many commonwealths lack. For it is enough for the sake of accounting that all who owe the treasury, or who receive from it, be held accountable. Yet this matter is so slippery that it can scarcely be restrained by those bonds. Therefore, whether the assessments—commonly called <term>tallages</term> <note>original: "taleas"; a form of arbitrary tax levied by a lord or king</note>—are personal (meaning they track the estimation of even hidden wealth) or real (meaning they apply only to land and visible property), that order must be maintained, just as it is in military affairs. Because the "food" of the commonwealth is for public opinion to be strong, and because no private citizen is permitted to question the decision of the prince, these matters do not suffer delay, much like the demands of the stomach. For once pledges have been seized, everyone is immediately compelled to pay; and if a fine is involved, they are usually confined in body so that they either perish or are released from payment by their friends. These men, therefore, are the <term>treasurers</term> <note>original: "quaestores"</note> of fixed assets.

The same order applies if anything is demanded from other classes, which has always been done with religious institutions when they have become immensely wealthy. For wealth, in whatever way it is held, is still wealth; it is useful to the state and liable to the treasury if the state is in need. Otherwise, it would be possible to assign all property to sacred uses and leave the commonwealth destitute. For those things which come to the treasury by chance, there must also be a specific treasurer—such as when fines must be collected, for which there is a designated official. Those profitable offices which are not connected to the courts return to the state's fund upon the death of the holder and are usually sold again. 

There are also <term>customs duties</term> <note>original: "uectigalia"</note> whenever any merchandise is driven or carried through fixed locations. For from these, the commonwealth that protects them can take a toll, excluding those things without which one cannot live comfortably. For everyone pays what the treasury takes; the merchant does not truly pay the profit out of his own pocket, as he immediately recovers it from the buyer, which is why that part of the tax is a burden on the commonwealth. Do not drive away the merchant, provided the goods he brings are useful to the state. Let him be free to sell what he has finished. If he sells useless things, punish him with a tax. When he takes from you something he necessarily needs, then tax him, but not so much that he is deprived of his profit; for then he would not come, but rather so that you might become a sharer in his gain. 

Furthermore, "the smell of profit from any source is good" <note>original: "ex re qualibet lucri bonus odor"; an allusion to Emperor Vespasian’s famous defense of a tax on public urinals</note>, and according to the whim and tyranny of princes, various types of exactions are devised daily. For some, like the Turk <note>referring to the Ottoman Sultan</note>, have willed that even the bodies of the poorest men, committed to the faith of Christ or Moses, be subject to tax; because they cannot pay this, either their bodies are detained or they are released from communal taxes if there is a fixed annual sum. Millions upon millions of coins must be collected under the pretext of maintaining roads and supporting the military. 

But because this wretched condition of life daily removes some from our midst and brings others forth, it is necessary that magistrates be so established that some are supreme, some middle, and some lowest. The greatest depend on the prince, the middle on the greatest, and the lowest on the middle, in matters of judgment and in preparing and commanding the military. Among the treasurers, they function by distributing what is commanded, collecting what is distributed, and reporting it. For unless you report it, you have accomplished nothing. These are the accounts of persons, the ranks, and the duties which are necessary in well-constituted commonwealths, upon whose authority depends—or by which is handled—whatever causes can arise in law. The law of obtaining one’s own and keeping one's property for oneself is a single law among all nations. But because every region tends to use its own formulas for legal actions, those things pertaining to practice cannot be handed down with as certain a method as those looking toward theory. Therefore, that discussion must be left to common usage. For it was enough to have explained these elements—

...ornaments, gems, and whatever else is held in high price. In the sea there are fisheries, and from navigation comes salt. There remains for us the most extensive part of wealth, which is by far the most opulent yet also the most difficult to understand. For although it arises from necessity, it has been entirely diverted into the realm of "opinion." This is because industrious men, sensing what things a particular region might most delight in, bring in foreign merchandise without any regard for utility or necessity, provided they make a profit; in doing so, if I may say so, they often undermine the stability of the world. For man, by nature—beyond the unique gift of speech which distinguishes him from other living creatures—also possesses this trait: he admires everything foreign, stands amazed at the unusual, and is more captivated by useless external things than by those that are domestic and proven. Wealth is also amassed by other arts, yet it always stems from those things we have mentioned. A good portion of the first men lived by hunting; others by theft committed on land or sea; some by pastures or livestock; others by agriculture; others by "opinion," such as those who have increased their wealth through religions; some by the labor of the body, and others by the benefit of their talent <note>original: "ingenii"; referring to intellectual or creative work</note>. These last are the only mortals who are usually the most beloved in a <term>commonwealth</term> <note>original: "rep." or "respublica"; the state or public body</note> and are the least beholden to the treasury. For the gifts of the mind, provided they are turned to the use of the commonwealth, usually procure a true nobility almost anywhere in the world. From all or many of these elemental sources of wealth, the <term>treasury</term> <note>original: "fiscus"</note> can pluck something for the preservation and protection of the state. Furthermore, things that cease to have an owner, or which return to the treasury as if by a "right of recovery," belong to the prince: such as the goods of the proscribed, or those marked by the shame of a capital crime. Some place in this same legal category the goods of those who, having been born elsewhere, die while possessing or acquiring property on foreign soil without having obtained the prince's favor to become citizens or subjects <note>original: "populi fundi"; a legal term for those who accept the laws of a territory</note>. This is the law used by the King of the French <note>Postel is referring to the "Droit d'aubaine," a law where the crown inherited the property of unnaturalized foreigners who died in France</note>. For he joins the goods of those born elsewhere and dying in his jurisdiction to the treasury, lest too many unknown foreigners gradually creep into the region. Truly, these are the primary sources of wealth.

### ON THE TREASURERS OF THE TREASURY,
### CHAPTER XXVI.

When <term>taxes</term> <note>original: "vectigalia"; revenues or tolls</note> began to be extended, and there were princes of only one or two cities or municipalities, there was no need for a great or numerous magistracy to collect them, since the wealth of any private citizen could easily become known to the prince as an arbiter of equity. But as wealth and dominions increased—whether things are viewed individually, or by an estimation of the land, or by the power of men—there was first a need for an arbiter of the census, of resources, and of property. This official divides the total sum proclaimed and commanded by the prince among the various provinces; after carefully considering the resources of all places, he distributes the portions of the required sum among the cities, villages, assemblies of men, and districts, taxing them according to what they are able to provide. Once this is decreed, there is a need for a municipal magistrate who, having called upon those more skilled in local matters, imposes a fair share of payment upon the people according to the strengths they have disclosed. In this matter, it is a wonder how much those whom the French call the <term>Elects</term> <note>original: "electos"; the "Élus" were royal tax officials in France who oversaw the assessment of the "taille" tax</note> permit themselves to do. With the greatest inequity, they exempt some who have corrupted them with gifts, and they heavily oppress others, unless they have received bribes from both sides. When the municipal treasurers have collected the sum from private individuals, they present it to the provincial treasurer—who records it with signatures and witnesses—and he in turn presents it to the high treasurer, who returns it to the <term>public treasury</term> <note>original: "aerarium"</note> or spends it on those uses which the prince has established. In these matters, it can hardly be seen whether fraud lies beneath the surface. Nevertheless, there ought to be a <term>counter-registrar</term> <note>original: "antigrapharius"; a clerk who keeps a duplicate record to prevent embezzlement</note> everywhere to record in a diary whatever is received by the treasurers themselves. And lest the treasurers and counter-registrars commit some offense together, there is a need for <term>masters of accounts</term> <note>original: "magistri rationum"; senior auditors</note> (who should be present everywhere) who [examine] the receipts...

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK III.

...and they should examine the accounts of expenses and record them in the public ledgers. But when a King or Prince gives as a gift something that had been acquired by the <term>treasury</term> <note>original: "fisco"; the state's central fund</note>, such as confiscations or anything else, it must also be recorded in the accounts by those in charge of the treasury, a department which many commonwealths lack. For it is sufficient for the accounting that all who owe the treasury, or who receive from it, are held accountable. But this matter is so slippery that it can hardly be restrained by any bonds. Therefore, whether the assessments—commonly called <term>tallies</term> <note>original: "taleas"; a traditional method of recording debts using notched sticks</note>—are personal (that is, they follow the estimation of even hidden wealth) or "real" (that is, based only on land and visible assets), the same order must be observed as is found in military matters.

Since being strong in resources is the "food" of the <term>commonwealth</term> <note>original: "reipub."; the public state</note>, and because no private person is allowed to question the prince's judgment, these financial matters—much like the stomach—do not tolerate delay. For when pledges are seized, everyone is immediately compelled to pay; and if a fine is involved, one is usually confined in body so that they either perish or are freed by friends through payment. These <term>treasurers</term> <note>original: "quaestores"; officials responsible for managing public funds</note> are therefore the managers of fixed assets. 

The same order applies if anything is required from other classes of society, which has always been done to religious institutions when they have become immensely wealthy. For wealth, however it is held, is wealth; it is useful to the commonwealth and subject to the treasury if the state is in need. Otherwise, it would be possible to assign everything to sacred purposes and leave the commonwealth destitute. 

There must also be a treasurer for those things that fall to the treasury by chance, such as when fines—which have their own treasurer—are to be collected. Those profitable offices that are not involved in judicial matters return to the public fund upon the death of the holder and are usually sold again. There are also <term>customs duties</term> <note>original: "uectigalia"</note> whenever any goods are driven or carried through fixed locations. From this, the commonwealth that protects those trade routes can take a duty, excluding those things without which one cannot live comfortably. For each person pays what the treasury has taken; yet the profit-seeking merchant does not truly pay it himself, since he immediately recovers the cost from the buyer. For this reason, that part of the duty is actually a disadvantage to the commonwealth's own citizens. 

Do not drive the merchant away, provided the goods bring utility to the commonwealth. Let him sell freely. If he sells useless things, penalize him with a duty. When he necessarily brings from abroad what you lack, then tax him—but not so much that he is deprived of his profit (for then he would not come), but rather so that you might become a participant in his profit. 

Furthermore, "the smell of profit is good from any source" <note>An allusion to the Roman Emperor Vespasian's famous phrase *pecunia non olet*, "money does not smell," used to justify a tax on public urinals</note>, and according to the whims and tyranny of princes, various types of exactions are devised daily. For some, like the <term>Turk</term> <note>referring to the Ottoman Sultan</note>, have even willed that the bodies of the poorest men—those devoted to the faith of Christ and Moses—be subject to a tax. Because they cannot pay this, either their bodies are detained, or they are freed by the local citizens if there is a fixed annual sum. Thousands upon thousands of coins are collected into his treasury under the pretext of supporting the judge and the soldier. 

But because this miserable condition of life carries some away daily and produces others, <term>magistrates</term> <note>government officials</note> must be so constituted that some are supreme, some middle, and some lowest. The highest depend on the prince, the middle on the highest, and the lowest on the middle—both in matters of justice and in preparing and commanding the military. Among treasurers, this hierarchy exists for distributing what is commanded, collecting what is distributed, and reporting it. For unless you report the accounts, you achieve nothing. These are the categories of persons, the orders, and the duties which are necessary in well-constituted commonwealths; upon their authority depends whatever legal cases may arise. 

There is one law everywhere among nations for pursuing one's right and preserving one's property. But because every region tends to use its own formulas for legal actions, those things pertaining to practice cannot be handed down with as certain a method as those looking toward theory. Therefore, that discussion of practical law must be left to common usage. For it was enough to have explained by these basic principles...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
## BOOK IV. ON THE CONVERSION FROM FALSE PERSUASIONS 
## TO THE TRUE ONE.
### ON THE SKILLS NEEDED BY A PRINCE
->who intends to change religion and substitute the true faith for a false one.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'E' featuring a profile portrait of a classical figure, possibly Agrippina, with the inscriptions 'AGRIP' and 'ANO' visible within the frame.</image-desc>Of all the ideas that move our minds, none is usually accepted with more reluctance or abandoned with greater difficulty than the opinion held concerning religion. It hardly ever happens—unless by extreme force or by a long-term effort of instilling different ideas—that it can be altered at all without bloodshed or a total revolution in affairs. Therefore, <term>Plato</term> <note>A reference to Plato's *Laws*, where he argues for the stability of religious traditions to maintain social order.</note> advises in his *Laws* that the belief about God accepted in any <term>commonwealth</term> <note>original: "repub."; the state or public community</note> should not be disturbed rashly. For it happens that if a prince, or anyone else, unwisely dissolves old beliefs in people's minds before binding them with a new religion, popular harmony and the common bond are undermined; once the people are released from their old faith, they will hardly admit another, even the most excellent one. Indeed, this happens for many reasons, which we must carefully attend to before we proceed further to discuss the banishing of <term>adulterated beliefs</term> <note>original: "adulterinis"; meaning corrupted or fake religions</note> and the substitution of the true one. 

In the previous book, it was demonstrated that it is common to all men that, even if they are ignorant of what kind of God they ought to have, they all nevertheless agree that one must be held. This itself proceeds from an opportunity given to everyone by nature to show gratitude. For it is impossible that this wise animal, full of reason <note>Postel is referring to Man.</note>—though by nature lacking in all things and, as it were, exposed to every kind of misery—does not desire to recognize the giver of such a great gift when he realizes that this whole "machine of the world" was prepared for him to compensate for and banish those miseries. Thus, he worships whatever he has heard from his parents is held in the place of God. 

Added to this gratitude and compensation is that most tenacious age <note>Childhood.</note> which, as the poet says, "long preserves the scent of what it was once soaked in" <note>original: "quo semel... imbuta est, odorem diutissime seruans"; a reference to Horace’s *Epistles*, likening a child's mind to a new jar that keeps the smell of its first contents.</note>. This age, surrendering itself to habit as if to a second nature, retains and defends the false just as bite-mindingly <note>original: "mordacissime"; tenaciously or "with teeth."</note> as the true once it has received it; it believes nothing is truer than what it received from its parents. 

Furthermore, the more false an opinion about the gods is anywhere in the world, the more ardently the <term>little priests</term> <note>original: "sacrificuli"; a diminutive, somewhat derogatory term for priests of false religions.</note> contend—at the persuasion of Satan, the author of false persuasion and evil opinions—that it must be retained and approved by everyone. This is evident from these arguments: A good man, conscious of his own virtue and content with his own conscience, does not usually peddle his own wares or care much for the judgment of others. He knows that nothing in the nature of things is changed by the words of men, and he knows that true praise is to be expected only from the good. 

Conversely, a criminal man, conscious of his own evil, thinks everything is being said about him; he puffs himself up, preaches, and forces himself on others so that he may cover the "fox he carries in his chest" <note>A classical idiom (from the poet Persius) referring to someone who hides a cruel or crafty nature behind a mask of virtue.</note> with the reputation of a goodness improved by the votes of others. Hence, you see the most vain men daily peddling their own merits and belittling others. In false religions, it is exactly the same. For this reason, they used to elude people with ambiguous answers and seemed to satisfy everyone. This is what antiquity meant when it called Apollo <term>the Ambiguous</term> <note>original: "λοξιαν" (Loxian); a Greek epithet for Apollo referring to his cryptic or "slanting" oracles.</note> and the father of the gods, Saturn, <term>the Wily</term> <note>original: "ἀγκυλομήτην" (ankylomētēn); a Greek Homeric epithet meaning "crooked-counseled" or "devious."</note>.

He warns princes that old beliefs must be replaced carefully to avoid social collapse and compares the defensiveness of false religions to the vanity of a guilty man.</summary>

...wished. There were added <term>most sacred dances</term> <note>original: "tripudia solistima"; a technical term from ancient Roman divination referring to the favorable rhythmic "dance" of the sacred chickens while eating, used to determine the will of the gods.</note>, auguries, the inspection of entrails, divinations, and those obscurities by which both the wise and the common people were deceived. If anyone, however, had dared to speak against these things, they were punished with death. For this is the nature of false persuasions: however badly they were urged, they want to thrust themselves upon everyone, they must be proven by the presence of a sword, and no one dares to dispute them under penalty of capital punishment; thus, he who dares not even open his mouth against them for fear of death may seem to approve them, at least through fear and silence. 

Therefore, those who are unskilled in discerning the false from the true are bound to false religions all the more vehemently the more they are pressed by the <term>sacrificers</term> <note>original: "sacrificulis"; a term often used pejoratively by Postel to describe minor priests of superstitious or "false" rites.</note> and their priests, and they are cured of them with greater difficulty. For they share the principles of belief with good things: age is added, custom compels, and falsehood presses. Because of this—since no one cares for or considers such things—it happens that the truth is not widely known; falsehood thrusts itself everywhere, flourishes, and is approved. For any prince considers it enough to keep the people in peace and to spend those things belonging to the treasury for his own legal and military affairs. 

The soldier is hardly restrained by any laws, whether secular or sacred. The judge punishes injuries, and resolves doubts, lawsuits, and quarrels. The common people do not grasp the mysteries. Only the holy magistrate <note>The religious authority or high priest of the state.</note> has the care of religion; and because he takes a profit from it, he never allows it to be changed, even if it is utterly corrupt. He incites the common people, threatens them with coming plagues, and foretells disasters, by which things he strikes the minds of almost everyone. In such consternation of mind, hardly any free judgment of things remains for anyone. And if someone, judging things freely and incorruptly, should wish to be heard, he must inevitably rush into danger and willingly undergo immediate death. Yet since nature has taught that death is to be feared, no one wants to undergo it unless they are driven by a divine spirit and completely transformed—just as the witnesses of Jesus Christ were.

Having carefully weighed these things, the moderator of the <term>commonwealth</term> <note>original: "reipub."; the state or public community.</note> should, gradually and without a great assembly of men, communicate what he wants changed in the commonwealth to the leading nobles. He should persuade them through reasoning and gentle enticement regarding what he thinks should be changed in religious matters. Once they have approved (for if it displeases everyone, one must either wait and persuade, or compel—though the latter is hardly safe for a ruler who governs by the judgment of others), then the highest judges in various provinces must also be compelled: so that, when preachers advocate such things as the prince wishes, the judges permit those who wish to gradually persuade the people. 

In the third place, once the power of both the nobles and the judges has been won over—so that they do not resist those making the effort by forming factions—the <term>high priests</term> <note>original: "pontifices"</note> must be called. The high priest must be compelled, whether he likes it or not, to advocate (or permit to be advocated) those things which the prince has approved as best and has examined with the consensus of the most learned men. He should not dare to oppose even with a word those who have been sent by the prince for the sake of teaching. 

The prince ought to choose men suitable for persuading the true faith, trained in all arts as much as possible, but especially most practiced in the doctrines of the true religion. To solve the objections of the false religion, they should be well-instructed in philosophy. Since few such men can be found, they should travel through entire regions as most sacred and inviolate persons (guarded by watchful custody if necessary). They should initiate those who are willing to approve the doctrines of the true religion, but leave the <term>freedom of belief</term> <note>original: "libertatem credendi"</note> to everyone else. For what is done by force hardly ever bears fruit. Therefore, the true religion forbids force to be used against anyone of right and constant judgment; and it disapproves if someone is imprudently driven to the truth by force. 

For God wants free minds. It is true that if there are a few infidels among many, and a stain spreads from them to the multitude, a day may be set for them to either cross over into persuasion [convert] by their own will, or be compelled to leave the region against their will—lest the rot spread from a few decayed members to the whole body and bring ruin. These are the princi- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page; the catchword "princi-" suggests the word "principia" (principles) or "principes" (princes/rulers).</note>

# THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD, BOOK IV.
<meta>catchword: held</meta>

...the prince's arts, by which, with absolutely no loss but with the greatest gain and ease, he can persuade his subjects of the truth without uproar or bloodshed. The visions and dreams of princes, when they align with the truth, are to be held by the subjects as revelations; the false is to be hissed out, and the true confirmed. For even if the truth was already true and the false was false, yet when it is repeated through the benefit of a person in a position of authority, it is believed by the common people—who depend on authority—as if it were something new. Indeed, a falsehood is far more easily approved by authority than the truth demonstrated by reason from a humble man. Therefore, why should we not think a prince can persuade people of the truth, since he can persuade them of falsehood by authority alone? 

Before all else, the prince—having gathered a group of most excellent men of the true religion—ought to have conclusions reduced to brief <term>axioms</term> <note>original: "axiomata"; concise, self-evident principles or foundational statements of doctrine used for teaching.</note>. If possible, he should even know and commit them to memory, so that from his own mouth—with great authority, whether sacred or secular—men may hear those things which the learned men and professors are tasked to urge, persuade, and confirm. In the first book, I have most fully provided, urged, and confirmed those conclusions which are necessary for one intending to persuade others of the true religion. They can be sought from there.

->BY WHAT WAYS TRUE FAITH MAY BE PREACHED WITHOUT GIVING OFFENSE TO ANYONE: and concerning the duty of him who takes up the care of correcting or entirely overturning a false persuasion.<-

It is necessary that he who has received from the prince the task of persuading others of the truth be no less skilled in those things which the adversaries of truth approve than in the truth itself. For the truth must not only be taught and confirmed, but false objections must be solved and arguments dissolved. This cannot happen except by a <term>comparison of points</term> <note>original: "collisione locorum"; literally a "clashing of places," referring to the dialectical method of comparing contradictory theological or logical "topics" or commonplaces to find the truth.</note> with the false. 

Furthermore, one must see to it that they become "all things to all men" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 9:22, a core principle of Jesuit and early modern missionary strategy.</note>; that is, they should so accommodate themselves to those they wish to be taught that they seem to begin with the approval of their laws. Eventually, once their attention is secured and conclusions elicited, we may either confirm our own positions or show those of others to be insufficiently firm. This must be observed above all: that which the people hold as hated or disapproved should not be named before its description has been carefully handed down. For that would make us suspect from the start and would turn the minds of the listeners away from goodwill and attention—without which (unless by a miracle of the Holy Spirit) you can persuade no one. 

Therefore, so that the minds of the people (for whose salvation these things are done) may be won over, one must consult their weakness at the beginning. Even those who are "half-wicked" or "half-impious" should be praised and approved as if they were good. Thus, while they partly acquiesce and begin to frequent the company of those who teach the truth and prove it by their deeds, they may be gradually corrected and changed through constant association. For conversation and constant refinement over a long period of time will bring about what you would never obtain at first glance. Moses received the children of Israel in such a way. Paul became "all things to all men" in this way, regarding his social interaction. For this reason, Jesus Christ, though about to fulfill the Law, wished also to be subject to the ceremonies of the Law.

He who teaches must always have his mind intent on three things. He must always set this before his eyes: the first power of teaching comes from the character of the speaker; the power of urging comes from the listener's soul; and the power of persuading comes from the matter itself. Therefore, let the herald of truth be of the highest innocence of life and, as far as is possible among men, beyond reproach. He should know the listener's soul—what pleases or displaces him vehemently. Thirdly, he should be of such erudition that regarding whatever matter he must speak, he deserves silence and a hearing for his own sake. If, however, the mind of the people is not clear to him, nor how easily they might acquiesce to the truth, let him bring forward common principles known to everyone, and having captured the audience by these, when they are already attentive...

### A FORMULA FOR PERSUADING THE
#### *Muslims, from God.*

In the second book, it was seen what we have in common with the Muslims and what is different. For they confess whatever we hold concerning divine matters, though in their own way; except for those things regarding the divinity of Jesus Christ and his death, which are most proven to us. Because they are vehemently offended if they hear Christ called God—since that lying impostor Muhammad <note>original: "Muhamedes"; Postel’s language reflects the harsh polemical style of the Renaissance era toward the Prophet of Islam.</note> wished to persuade them of the contrary throughout the entire <term>Quran</term> <note>original: "Alcorano"</note>—therefore, nothing should be dealt with regarding that subject from the beginning of the persuasion. This is so even though the goal of the whole true religion resides in Him, just as in His death and resurrection. If anything is said concerning Christ, it should not exceed those things which are handed down about him in the Quran, lest the <term>Alphaquis</term> <note>original: "Alphachijs"; from the Arabic 'al-faqih,' meaning a jurist or scholar of Islamic law.</note>, becoming aware, call the people away from listening in secret where it is not permitted openly. 

One must, therefore, declaim concerning divine benefits in as ornate a manner as can be done. For although the Arabic and Turkish languages are capable of their own eloquence, nothing is more inept than those persuasions made by their own scholars. One should subjoin the variety of the world, of fruits, animals, and kingdoms in a certain order; so that, captured by the light of order and enticed by a new kind of teaching, they may become most attentive and frequent in attendance. Once a larger audience has been gathered, one must deal with the power and benefits of the Creator, but with a deeper method than before. For the mystery of the most holy Trinity must be touched upon with easier demonstrations. For the Muslims who excel in any kind of learning are most greedy to hear of it. 

The first example is most familiar, drawn from the intellect, introduced thus: Whatever things are perfect, good, just, and absolute in any perfection, they have that from God. That which comes from a certain principle most abundantly into certain effects and particulars must necessarily be far more perfect, more abundant, and greater in the cause than in the effect. For example, if many very beautiful houses are made from the conception of a most excellent craftsman, no one will deny that there is an infinite power in his mind for designing infinite similar or more beautiful houses. Thus, it is certain that what is most excellent in us, and established in all things, also has its image in God. But nothing in things or in their action, however simple, lacks a trinity. For nothing can be done without a <term>ternary power</term> <note>A philosophical argument common in the Renaissance that because humans have power, knowledge, and will, God—as the ultimate cause—must possess these three attributes in perfect unity, mirroring the Trinity.</note>. For even if you have as much power as you like for doing anything, unless there is present the knowledge of how to do it, and of those parts which...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
<meta>catchword: uege</meta>

For a work to be accomplished, knowledge is required, as well as a supreme and equal power of wisdom; and to those two properties, there must be added the will to achieve it and the love of preserving it. Certainly, no thing at all can exist in reality or be made without these. But if this exists in the most excellent part of ourselves—namely, in the soul—certainly God possesses that Trinity in the most excellent way. For even though He is powerful, unless He had possessed wisdom and the will and love for creating from eternity, He could not have brought anything into being when it seemed right to Him.

Therefore, God is three and one. For the same divinity exists in power, the same in wisdom, and the same in love; and yet there are not three divinities, but one divinity. It is just as when I think, I express, and I act: these are different actions, and yet they are not three things, but only one. I think of the form of a building, I explain the same in words, or in writing, or in a floor plan <note>original: "ichnographia"; a technical term for a ground-level architectural drawing</note>, and finally, I see to its construction. There are, therefore, three considerations of the building: first, as it is in the mind; second, as it is in the explanation; and third, as it is in the finished work. And yet, they are not three buildings, but one.

Thus, God the Father is as Power, the Son is as Wisdom, and the Holy Spirit is as Love and Effect. These things must be confirmed and driven home <note>original: "inculcanda"; literally "trampled in" or impressed upon the mind</note> with many examples. One must also speak out against those bad Christians who used to say, before the Prophet <note>Postel likely refers to Muhammad here, addressing the Islamic critique that Christians worship three gods.</note>, that there are three gods; since there are not three gods, but one God. While these things are frequently repeated, they seem to work in their favor.

This point, which has been seen as necessary, must be confirmed by the likeness of all things, and especially the most excellent ones. The Sun can do nothing at all without the number three <note>original: "ternario numero"</note>. For it consists of a body, light or rays, and power. For the luminous body is not the ray, nor vice versa; but the ray proceeding from the body differs from its source, and the effect of the heat is distinguished from both. And yet, there are not three actions, or powers, or heats. So it is in all things. In the arts, there is a most familiar example: for a potter could never form a single jar, or any other earthenware, unless the knowledge of the power and the will proceeding from both were present. For anyone established in their craft can only do a thing when they have the knowledge and the will to form it. Since this is most excellent in man, it must necessarily be far more excellent in the Archetype <term>Archetype: The original model or "Ideal" in the mind of God from which all created things are copied.</term>, just as much as God is greater than man. For just as the whole art is in the power of the craftsman, so also the whole art is in his knowledge, and the whole art is in his will and effect; yet there are not three things or three arts, but one art. Likewise: nothing can be done by art or nature unless there is in the action an abundance, a process, and a will—or, as I have said, a fertility, a birth, and love. For if from that power of art which one possesses, there could be no progression or generation proceeding forth, he would do nothing at all. And unless he took delight in the action and made a choice of the material in which to act, undoubtedly nothing could be made by the craftsman.

In natural things, the example is even easier. Unless pepper or ginger had a constant and inexhaustible abundance of burning and stinging from which a biting sensation and burning always proceeded, and unless nature delighted in it and wished to always act in that way in its own manner, undoubtedly it could not exist.

The fact that even inanimate things seem to have a kind of "choice" is proven by the fact that all actions are directed first toward the most disposed subject. Pepper indeed burns, but not everywhere. When the pores of the body are opened by sweat or exercise, it acts a little; on flayed flesh, it acts most vehemently; but in the most excellent way, it acts on the tongue, because that member is suited for tasting and sensing things. If fire is placed next to sulfur, flax, straw, dry twigs, solid logs, and finally thick wood in the middle of a forest, it will never err in choosing its object or in acting.

So too a stone—whose nature, besides its hidden properties, is to tend downward—settles very little upon a literal earthy body; it sinks more in mud, greatly in water, and in the air until it reaches the earth. Thus all things make their choice.

Furthermore, we must come to actions: none of which can be performed without a **triad** <note>original: "ternario"; a group of three</note>.

We must discuss matter and form even with the learned and those skilled in natural things. Since their concern revolves around things so that they might know God as He is, we must insist most strongly on this point. For once this is demonstrated and persuaded, many most excellent things will follow. Specifically, that God has a Son, and generates Him from Himself from eternity, without whom nothing can be made; and from both proceeds the will, love, and effect, which we call the **Holy Spirit**. It will also follow that there is falsehood and lies written even two hundred times in the **Quran** <note>original: "Alcorano"</note>, since it is repeated there so often that "God neither begets, nor is he begotten, he has no son, he is not a trinity," etc. If some **Imams** <note>original: "Imamin"; Islamic prayer leaders or scholars</note> object to these sentences from the Quran, and they must be satisfied (while the work is not yet refuted) so they do not stir up trouble or seem to pressure the **Evangelist** <note>Postel uses this term for the Christian missionary or teacher of the Gospel</note> as if he could not respond, he ought to satisfy them in this way: He should say that these sentences are indeed written in their prophet's book, but that they must also test them against other sentences of the law. He [Muhammad] wrote in two places that no one ought to or can provide the interpretation of the sentences of the Quran except the prophet himself. Furthermore, it is written in the traditions received from his mouth that out of twelve thousand <term>Aiet</term> <note>original: "Aiet"; referring to *Ayat* or verses, which Postel equates here with "words or miracles"</note>, only three thousand are true, while the rest are false. However, so that they might freely call all things either true or false, he did not distinguish between them. Therefore, the Evangelist must say that those words which are contrary to natural reason are false and should not be followed, while the others are true.

### Another argument from man.

When they have begun to think correctly about God and that opinion is confirmed, then man and his gifts—of both mind and body—must be extolled. To these things, virtue itself, of which man alone is capable, must be praised with every kind of honor; among these, **chastity**, **humanity**, and the **preservation of human life** must be placed before their eyes most urgently and frequently. For this reason, angels and God are most excellent because they are never polluted by the **stain of Venus** <note>original: "Veneris labe"; a classical reference to sexual lust</note> and always attend to the preservation of men; whoever does the opposite is unjust and is armed against nature. For nature willed man to be created so that he might be as similar to God as possible. And because they listen most gladly to the lives of the saints of the early Church, the Evangelist must have a supreme knowledge of them, so that the power of the Gospel and the ornament of all virtues may be seen in them. For we are incited to noble deeds more easily by examples than by words. We must begin with the miracles of the Old Testament, and God must be praised in his saints. However, it must always be noted that all miracles performed before Christ were done by invoking the name of God, by pouring out prayers, or by a command received from God. But **Christ**, in his own name, as the true God, performed every kind of miracle. The Gospel must be used as testimony in these matters. For the **followers of Muhammad** <note>original: "Muhamedici"</note> are more studious of it the more learned they are and the more they are freed from the captivity of trifles. Observing this, the **Caliphs** <note>original: "Chaliphæ"; the civil and religious leaders of the Islamic community</note> keep them as far as possible from the reading of philosophy and the Gospel. For as many as are learned either become Christian in opinion or die entirely without any religion. For they cannot conceive in their minds the kind of God that Muhammad described. For besides the fact that he appears to be the author of evil, he also seems to be the author of murder, idolatry, crime, robbery, lust, pleasure, and **pederasty**...

### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
### BOOK 4

...pederasty <note>original: "pederastiæ"</note>, and the principle and precept of brutal intercourse is attributed to him—things which you would shudder even to believe of a man contaminated by every kind of crime. Above all, the preacher must take care to have with him countless copies of the **Gospel** printed in **Arabic**, so that he may communicate, give, and distribute them to anyone who wishes. Once the Gospel has been introduced and the life of Jesus Christ seen, those things concerning Christ found in the **Quran** <note>original: "Alcorano"</note>, its interpreters, and the **Sunnah** <note>original: "Suneh"; the body of traditional social and legal custom and practice of the Islamic community</note> must be gathered into one and placed before their eyes; He [Christ] must be exalted as much as possible. Indeed, it must be added to His praises that the Sunnah affirms **Jesus Christ** will be the future **judge of the living and the dead**. From this, it must be confessed that He is God. For judgment belongs to God alone, who knows all things. Therefore, God the Father would never permit the judgment—in which all things whatsoever from eternity and from the creation of the world must be known and weighed—to Jesus Christ, unless He Himself were the **all-knowing God**. To this, since He was truthful and called Himself God (as He was), He must be believed. For prophets illuminated by God could never lie. Otherwise, they would not be prophets, nor would our Evangelists be gifted with the grace of the Holy Spirit. **Augustine** used to say that if a single lie were found in the entire Gospel, it should be believed in no way at all.

However, since **Muhammad** wrote nine thousand lies, he could not be a prophet. For the all-knowing God cannot deceive. Therefore, if this law had been from God and His angel, in whom neither forgetfulness nor ignorance falls, it could have contained nothing contrary, superfluous, or false. But one must not yet act against the prophet or the law before God is made known and Christ is accepted through ancient testimonies, their own words and works, and even the confirmation of adversaries and the deeds of his own followers. When we have obtained this, it will immediately be clear to all, without any specific pointing out or hateful dragging through the mud of his name, what kind of man Muhammad was. For the **Light** will both put to flight and expose the **darkness**.

One must proceed, therefore, with inductions of this kind. No one will doubt that whatever things are more excellent ought to be chosen. Which is more excellent: he who lives chastely, or he who is entirely overflowing with lusts? He who gives, or he who snatches away? He who heals, or he who hurts, crushes, and kills? He who brings nature’s peace, or he who brings war? The choice is easy. And yet, though many have been perfect as far as a human is allowed, no prophet was ever greater, holier, or more divine than **Isa** <note>original: "Hiſſa"; the Arabic name for Jesus</note> himself, that is, **Jesus**. Therefore, nothing is holier than His law, His precepts, and His imitation. The law of Christ is thus more excellent than all laws. 

And likewise: if a certain man is given who was conceived of the Holy Spirit and a Virgin, famous for miracles from his very birth, gifted with divine wisdom, most innocent in life, most humane, who restored life and health to many, who never wished to possess any earthly things, and who taught and wished his followers to live so; and on the opposite side a man is given who was conceived in the manner of others, educated in idolatry, practiced in trade, famous for no miracles, suffering from disease of mind and body, who plundered the goods of others, killed, hurt, and oppressed countless men, who referred all things to profit, and taught his followers to draw the sword against other mortals—which of these shall be judged more excellent? Who is more useful to nature? To whose laws would you think one should rather obey? Do not laws smell of the character of their authors? The former dictates things friendly to nature, the latter things hostile. The former nourishes nature, the latter is armed against it. That one brings salvation, this one brings destruction. I say nothing of the gifts of either. For if I grant divinity to Christ, and a resurrection performed without the prayer of any saint; and to Muhammad those titles which I blush to think of—who will not see whose examples we should follow? Thus, with many such comparisons <note>original: "exaggerationibus"; used here in the sense of rhetorical heightening or accumulation of points</note> taken from the life of each, Christ must be named, and Muhammad suppressed, until the divinity...

## WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK 3.

Let [faith] in Christ be persuasive, and let Him be displayed to all, depicted in His true colors. For the sake of satisfying [dissenters], we will not simply dismiss falsehoods, but we shall tell the Prophet <note>Postel refers to Muhammad here</note> that the Jews, out of hatred for Christ, persuaded men of many things contrary to the Gospel—as they indeed did. Among other things, it is clear they wished to strip away His divinity (which is evident from the Universal Judgment and the lives of Christ's disciples). And [Muhammad] believed them, since they were his first instructors and followers. Furthermore, those words in the **Quran** <note>original: "Alcorano"</note> concerning the Trinity, Christ’s divinity, and His death, are not <term>muhchemat</term> <note>From the Arabic *muhkamat*, referring to "decisive" or "clear" verses of the Quran that are not subject to interpretation</note>, that is, they are not judicial or true. Certainly, the true reason Christ’s divinity was removed in the Quran was so that glory would not be shared between Muhammad and Christ, or Moses. For had he subscribed to either, the glory would have fallen back upon them, and his own acquired wealth would have perished. Now, therefore, having spoken of virtue and of all men, and having made frequent inductions against those vices with which the false prophet teemed, as I have said, Muhammad will betray himself by his signs, and by the same work Christ and the apostles shall be exalted. Therefore, so that there may be an abundance of evidence by which we may persuade men, I have decided to subjoin for the sake of example a brief compendium of the lives of certain apostles and some other saints, who as followers of Christ provided testimony of His divinity through both words and deeds.

By this gift, they attained the knowledge of **all languages**, than which nothing in all of nature is more miraculous. Indeed, they performed such innumerable miracles wherever on earth they traveled that they could not be contained in writing. Indeed, the multitude was so great that ten thousand believers came to the true faith on that day. Once the **Gospel** has been introduced and the life of **Jesus Christ** has been seen, those things which are held concerning Christ in the **Quran** <note>original: "Alcorano"</note>, its interpreters, and the **Sunnah** <note>original: "Suneh", referring to the body of traditional social and legal custom and practice of the Islamic community</note> must be gathered into one place and set before their eyes. He <note>Christ</note> is to be extolled as much as possible.

Indeed, it must be added to His praises that the **Sunnah** affirms that **Jesus Christ** will be the future judge of the living and the dead; from this, it must be confessed that He is God. For judgment belongs to God alone, who knows all things. Therefore, God the Father would never permit the judgment—in which all things whatsoever that have existed from eternity and from the creation of the world must be known and weighed—to **Jesus Christ**, unless He Himself were God, knowing all things. To this, since He was truthful and said that He was God (as He was), He must be believed. For prophets illuminated by God could never lie. Otherwise, they would not be prophets, just as our **Evangelists**, gifted with the grace of the Holy Spirit, would not be. **Augustine** used to say that if a single lie were found in the entire **Gospel**, it should be believed in no way at all.

However, since **Muhammad** wrote nine thousand lies, he could not be a prophet. For the omniscient God cannot deceive. Therefore, if this law had been from God and His angel, in whom neither oblivion nor ignorance falls, it could not have contained anything contradictory, superfluous, or false. But one must not yet act against the prophet or the law before God is made known and Christ is accepted through ancient testimonies, his own words and works, and even the confirmation of his adversaries and the deeds of his followers. Once we have obtained this, it will immediately be clear to all—without any specific designation or hateful naming—what sort of man **Muhammad** is. For the light will both put the darkness to flight and expose it. 

Therefore, one must proceed with inductions of this kind. No one will doubt that whatever things are more excellent ought to be chosen. Which is more excellent: he who lives chastely, or he who flows entirely with lustful desires? He who gives, or he who snatches away? He who heals, or he who hurts, crushes, and kills? He who brings the peace of nature, or he who brings war? The choice is easy. And yet, though many have been perfect as far as a man is allowed to be, no prophet was ever greater, holier, or more divine than **Isa** <note>original: "Hissā", the Arabic name for Jesus</note> himself, that is, **Jesus**. Therefore, nothing is holier than His law, His prescriptions, and His imitation. Thus, the Law of Christ is more excellent than all laws. 

And likewise: If a man is presented who was conceived of the Holy Spirit and a virgin, famous for miracles from his very birth, gifted with divine wisdom, most innocent in life, most humane, who restored life and health to many, who never wished to possess any earthly things, and who wished and taught his followers to live thus; and on the opposite side a man is presented conceived in the manner of others, raised in idolatry, practiced in trade, famous for no miracles, suffering from disease of mind and body, who plundered the property of others, killed, injured, and oppressed countless men, who directed all things toward profit, and taught his followers to draw the sword against all other mortals—which of these shall be judged more excellent? Which is more useful to nature? Whose laws do you think should rather be obeyed? Do not laws smell of the character of their authors? The former dictates things friendly to nature; the latter, things hostile. The former cherishes nature; the latter is armed against it. The former brings salvation; the latter brings ruin. I am silent regarding the gifts of each. For if one considers the divinity of Christ and his resurrection, accomplished without the prayer of any holy man; and to **Muhammad** those titles which I blush even to think of: who will not see whose examples we should follow? Thus, with many comparisons <note>original: "exaggerationibus"</note> taken from the life of each, Christ must be named, and Muhammad suppressed, until the divinity...
