For Christ had said: *Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate.* <note>Matthew 23:38</note> And likewise: *Amen, I say to you, there shall not be left in the Temple one stone upon another that shall not be thrown down.* <note>Matthew 24:2</note> Furthermore, that wicked Emperor paid the penalty for his treachery. For while he held camp near the city of Ctesiphon, located on the borders of Assyria and Media, a spear was vibrated into the man’s chest by divine power. He ended his life, crying out these words against Christ: <term>“You have conquered, O Galilean”</term> <note>original: "Vicisti Galilæe." Tradition holds these were the dying words of Julian the Apostate, acknowledging Christ's victory over his attempt to restore paganism.</note>. Thus he surrendered his soul, which had been besieged by a demon. The fact is well-established; the authors are pagan <note>original: "prophani"; referring to non-Christian historians like Ammianus Marcellinus who recorded these events.</note>. Indeed, to his quaestor Libanius—who was then a stranger to the religion and who had educated Julian in literature—the Christian soldier Saint Mercurius appeared in a vision on the night closest to the Emperor's death, twisting a spear into Julian and finishing the Emperor off. When Libanius learned the truth of this the following day, he put faith in the dream, left his office, hurried to Saint Basil, and professed Christ through baptism. He did this all the more ardently because, while the Apostate was being finished, the same thing had occurred in a dream to both Basil and Libanius. 

Nor was it only Julian who paid the penalty for violating Christ and for neglecting and making light of his religion; Arius <note>The priest whose teachings led to the Arian heresy, which denied the full divinity of Christ.</note> paid the penalty for his impiety when his bowels spilled out in a latrine. One Herod was consumed by a disease of lice <note>original: "morbo pediculari"; often interpreted as a horrific infestation of worms or lice, seen as a divine punishment for tyrants.</note> because of his pursuit of Christ’s infancy and his most cruel slaughter of the Innocents; another <note>Herod Agrippa I.</note> for lusting after honors due to Christ. The same plague consumed Lucius Hieronymianum in Cappadocia, a most savage attacker and persecutor of Christians. By a not dissimilar end, Galerius and Maximinus, who had finished off the martyrs of Christ with every kind of cruelty, closed their unhappy lives. The same happened to the King of the Vandals <note>Likely referring to Huneric, known for his persecution of Catholics.</note> who rose up against the established religion. Emperor Arnulf paid an equal penalty for despoiling the temples of Christ and afflicting the sacred orders. Constantine, nicknamed <term>Copronymus</term> <note>original: "κοπρώνυμος"; meaning "named from dung."</note> and <term>Ainomases</term> <note>original: "αἰνομάσης"; meaning "of a hateful name."</note> because of his treachery, gave up the remains of a body filled with worms to leprosy. Aegeas, the proconsul of the Peloponnese, after he had afflicted the Apostle Andrew with tortures, suddenly expired, driven into a madness by a demon. For the Eastern Emperor Valens, who also afflicted the sacred orders and forced men dedicated to the sacred mysteries into military service, a miserable end to his life was predicted by Paphnutius; he was cooked rather than burned by a fire of straw set by his enemies, the Goths and Vandals. Nero partly laid hands on himself and was partly stabbed by his own people. A domestic servant cut the throat of Domitian. Commodus—who was an "inconvenience" to everyone <note>A pun on the name "Commodus" (convenient) and "incommodus" (inconvenient).</note> and was also savage toward our people—was strangled. Macrinus had the sort of exit he deserved. Elagabalus closed his days with a worthy end, because it had not been enough for him to have suffered most uncontrollably from every vice and to have dragged others into crime, unless he had also robbed the Pope Callixtus of his life along with many martyrs. Maximinus, stabbed by his soldiers, perished by divine vengeance because of the innumerable deaths and slaughters of Christians; otherwise, he was most burdensome to the soldiers, by whom the Emperor was called an ignoble man. Decius died not much more happily. Valerian was killed in Milan. A servant took the life of Aurelian. To run through them all, no Emperor of the Romans, or of others...

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK IV

### THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...of all the princes who persecuted the Christians, not one escaped being consumed by a violent death, except for **Diocletian**. <note>Diocletian (r. 284–305) led the last and most severe persecution of Christians but was unique among his peers for retiring voluntarily.</note> To ensure that the same fate which had befallen nearly everyone before him did not happen to him, he laid down the insignia of the empire and grew old in private life until he passed away. Now, although the condition of a soul should not be judged entirely by the death of the body—since God reserves eternal punishments for the impious—nevertheless, since God gave the use of life not so that it should be ended violently, but so that death might be undergone with quiet senses and a prepared mind, it is a certain argument for future perdition when God allows a man to perish in such a way. Infected with a <term>Lerna of crimes</term> <note>Lerna was the swamp home of the multi-headed Hydra; here it signifies a bottomless pit of wickedness.</note>, such a man cannot even think of the **First Cause** <note>God, the origin of all things.</note> except for his own condemnation. God wishes to terrify the impious with these examples, so that even if they judge that souls are nothing after the funeral, they may still be deterred by the example of a most shameful and unhappy death. Such men direct all their efforts toward leaving behind the longest and most honorable memory of themselves.

Let the histories of all nations be revolved most diligently, and let the deeds since the birth of Christ be weighed; where Christ was not received, barely one prince in ten approached the <term>son-in-law of Ceres</term> <note>A poetic reference to Pluto, king of the Underworld; Postel means they died a violent rather than a "dry" or natural death.</note> by a peaceful death. Among Christians, however, barely one in ten has perished by an ill-fated death. I except certain petty kings and princes of a "Roman heart," as they say, who always have Christ in their mouths by way of blasphemy, but think the word "God" is just a name. For although they act under the empire of Christ, they think nothing is more noble than to kill a man. If <term>talio</term> <note>The law of retaliation; "an eye for an eye."</note> is frequently visited upon them, it is no wonder.

But **Machiavelli**, that parent of the impious, will say that Christian men, born for slavery, know nothing of liberty and therefore cannot overthrow their princes. He argues they accept any empire, no matter how unjust, with a level head, and thus it is no wonder that no princes are finished off among them. If he had weighed the powers of nature, and what has been done by Christians now and for a thousand years, he would undoubtedly never have asserted that a mind conscious of its own goodness diminishes the strength of the body. On the contrary, a man with a guilty conscience has everything filled with trembling. 

Nor is there any reason for him to oppose us with the example of the ancient Romans. For if the Romans were to come back to life today, victory over all peoples would not be as easy for them as it was once over worn-out or unarmed regions. It is not a loss of liberty or oppression by Christ that causes unjust princes to be endured, but **prudence and public peace**. For it is better, when things are well-arranged under a tyrant, to endure his commands (however unjust) at some cost, than to experience as many tyrants as there are neighbors and magnates while he is being removed through sedition. 

An unjust prince invades fortunes but spares bodies. In a change of government, however, it is necessary for everyone to be plundered by altercations and factions; many are even killed if they oppose the change. Everything must be permitted to the soldier who chooses the prince and removes him when he wishes; for he who commands the commander never pays the penalty. How great was the unhappiness of the Roman people from **Julius Caesar** to the Emperor **Constantine** for nearly four hundred years? Certainly, whoever among those emperors was most outstanding in luck is not to be compared with even mediocre Christians. Therefore, there is no better condition of affairs (although among Christians there is no lack of scoffers, plagues, and extreme craftiness) than where Christ is heard. Everywhere in the world there are lost men; but they are more noticed among Christians because a person is more wicked who is evil under the best law, and because wickedness betrays itself more among many good people, as opposites reveal one another. By these persuasions, the heathens are to be gradually drawn to the knowledge of the truth: so that while they repent out of terror of the punishments inflicted on the wicked (lest the same happen to them), they may also be invited to good things by the hope of a better fortune and condition of the state. For they will finally become true followers by the example of the good, even for the sake of the **Highest Good** itself. In this way...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument for the universal truth of Christianity by appealing to non-Christian sources. # THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

Moses used the art of enticing a stubborn people toward a happier fortune, even though the ultimate end of his religion was eternal life, just as it is in the Christian religion. While he promises a land flowing with milk and honey, while he promises longevity and "earthly goods," as he calls them, he keeps the people constrained under the law until the truth of happiness itself should arrive. David calls these the "good things of the Lord," not earthly things, but in the "land of the living," <note>original: *terra viventium*</note> when he says: *I believe that I shall see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living.* And elsewhere, he says: *I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.* To these must be added the prophecies of the Sibyls, the responses of the oracles, and whatever else bears witness to Christ. 

The Sibyls—a race of women divinely inspired—left writings many years before Christ concerning him, his divinity, and his wonderful works, which we both prove and affirm through Gospel truth. What could be more divine than those poems produced by the **Erythraean Sibyl** thirteen hundred years before Christ was born? In the headings of these poems (lest it be believed they could be understood as referring to anyone else), the name of Jesus Christ was noted with these letters: **Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior**. <note>original Greek: *ἰησοῦς χριστὸς θεοῦ ὑιὸς σωτήρ*</note> There are as many verses as there are letters in that title. <note>This refers to a famous acrostic where the first letter of each verse spells out the title of Christ.</note> Lest these be thought of as inventions of the Christians, they were brought to the Romans from their own archives and Sibylline books, and they were circulated in the hands of everyone. How would a class of men destitute of authority, as the Christians were for three hundred years, have dared such impudence as to propose these to the Senate and the Emperors and claim they were from the Sibylline books, unless the text itself revealed it immediately when the book was produced? These Greek verses exist in the *Imperial Oration* <note>original: *en tō logō basilikō*</note> found in **Eusebius**. They are also cited by **Ludovico Vives** in his commentaries on **Augustine’s** *The City of God*, Book 18, Chapter 23, where Augustine translates those verses into Latin. They deal with the future judgment, the second coming of Christ, and the transformation of all things. 

Furthermore, even a demon in the temple of **Apollo** was forced to confess Christ when it was consulted as to what kind of man he was. The oracle said: "He was mortal according to the flesh, but wise and famous for wonderful works; but seized by Chaldean judges, beaten with whips, he died a cruel death." Let **Lactantius**, **Justin Martyr**, Augustine’s *City of God*, and the history of **Orosius** be read diligently. Innumerable testimonies concerning Christ are found in them, drawn from pagans against pagans, which both overturn the worship of idols and confirm the true religion. But we must now look at the practice—how modern forms of worship are to be approached.

## ON THE VARIOUS MODERN 
## religions, and how they may be refuted.

Besides the Muhammadan <note>Islamic</note> and Mosaic <note>Jewish</note> religions, there is the vast religion of the demon. For wherever people worship spirits <note>original: *lemures*</note>, the foul image of the demon frequently represents itself there and deludes the minds of men. This is worshipped openly and professedly in almost all of **India**, and in the **New World**, along with the islands. The Sun is worshipped by many of the **Tartars**. The regions lying under either pole are not yet known to us; therefore, we cannot say what religion they follow. **Olaus Magnus** the Goth <note>A Swedish historian and geographer (1490–1557) known for his descriptions of Northern peoples.</note> reported that certain people very close to the Lapps worship a square fragment of red cloth. Certainly, we will be able to overcome falsehood in all of them by refuting them from their own sayings, as I noted above. For in all things, but most especially in divine matters removed from the senses, it is easier and better to argue against the false than it is to grasp the truth. Imagine, then, that a most foul demon, the author of false worship, is presented to you (for under him all species of idolatry are fostered) and is held to be a god, as among the **Indians on this side of the Ganges**; if they confess one supreme God (which almost all do), since it is far more excellent to give...

### WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK III

To enlist in the army of a prince rather than a commander of soldiers, and to join him rather than a **chiliarch** <term>a commander of a thousand men; from the Greek *chilias*</term>, and the chiliarch rather than the centurion—and so on for the rest—how does it happen that men are so dismayed in spirit that, while they acknowledge God as the creator of heaven and earth, under whom even Satan trembles, they choose to act like slaves? Why would they neglect the person of the Prince to live instead under the protection of a mere inferior and a lost soul? What soldier is so insane (even assuming Satan were good) that he would not strive to prove himself to the Prince rather than to a leader of the lower ranks? Does not everything tend toward this: that we receive the grace of a good deed from the supreme leader, and that we acknowledge Him who is supreme? If an injury is done to us, from where do we seek a power to avenge us, unless it proceeds from the highest power? From whom do we either fear the punishment for a misdeed or hope for the reward of a benefit? Certainly, all things tend toward the highest; they proceed from there, and they return there. Many examples must be proposed from the arts, from ranks of dignity, and other such things which are familiar and known to those peoples among whom one is working, so that they may become more attentive when persuaded by a familiar introduction. 

In the second place, one must insist upon honor and **violated majesty** <note>original: *violata maiestate*; refers to the legal concept of *crimen laesae maiestatis* or high treason</note> by dealing with examples and instances such as these: If anyone were to serve as a soldier under any leader who depended on a supreme power, and he knew that primary power and encountered it, yet thought he should neglect it and only honor and observe the one in whose battalion he was enrolled—would not that supreme authority (whether it belongs to one, a few, or all, but united in one head) rightly be angered? Would it not not only discharge that soldier but also condemn him as one guilty of treason and the author of sedition? For what order could ever be held or preserved in a Republic unless everyone bowed their necks to the primary power? To not acknowledge a leader as the leader is the same as if you wished to be held as the leader yourself. Therefore, he is immediately held guilty of treason who does not defer all things to the primary power. 

You therefore, O **Indians** <note>Postel uses "Indians" as a general term for non-European peoples or those in the "New World" and East</note>, and all **devil-worshippers** <term>original: *διαβολόσεβοι* (diaboloseboi)</term>, live as those guilty of treason against God, buried in error and perdition. As for your claim that you worship this foul power so that he may not harm you, and that you wish to provide rest to the supreme God so that He is not intent upon or occupied with the labor of condemning and directing you—what is this but contradicting yourselves and denying Him to be the one you confess as God? If He is God, as He truly is and as you yourselves affirm, He must be omnipotent. If He is omnipotent, He is always omnipotent; He is not burdened by any labors in governing the world as you think, but He surveys and penetrates all things. 

Therefore, consider your demon, whom you worship as the executor of God's justice so that he might not be cruel when you must pay the penalties for iniquity: if he were able to do anything against God's prescription and permission, would he not first look out for himself? Would he not cancel the sentence of the supreme judge and accept less punishment upon himself than has been inflicted on him by God? How could it be that he would punish you more lightly than God wishes—he who was damned immediately at the creation of the world and is exiled from heaven and the blessed company? You believe these things falsely, O Indians. He who fails himself through impotence will not be able to help others. 

Furthermore, since every law and religion ought to, and usually does, lead men toward a better hope and toward happiness, how does it happen that through a multitude of sacrifices, the blood of men, the countless injuries of unviolated serpents, and the supreme expense of life, you wish to undergo hell and the punishments of the devil? For there is no need of religion to go to hell! The more wicked someone is, the closer he is to your "happiness" and your end; and yet you want these things prepared for you through so many labors and dangers. You deny God, O Indians, you deny God when you think the choice of moderating His sentence is permitted to the devil. The devil has no right in inflicting or moderating punishments. The state of your affairs is just as if—

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK III

[It is better] to give one's name in the army to the prince rather than to the master of soldiers, and to him rather than to the chiliarch <term>original: *chiliarchæ*; a commander of one thousand men</term>, and to the chiliarch rather than the centurion, and so on with the rest. # ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD
### BOOK III

If the citizens of a single Republic—knowing that they could at any time deserve punishment by sinning (as no one is without sin) and thus face a death sentence—were to honor, serve, and seek to win over through obedience no one in the entire Republic except for the **executioner**, while meanwhile neglecting the judges and those who have the power to decree and condemn: what prince would tolerate such foolish citizens in his empire? Indeed, what private citizen would tolerate a son, a house-born slave, or a servant, if that person chose to recognize authority from any source other than the father or the master? What household can remain intact for long unless all things are referred back to the judgment, praise, and glory of a single head? You must acknowledge the **Supreme Commander** of the whole world, who commands even the wretched demon; otherwise, you will burn in eternal punishment, and there will be no moderation of the divine sentence for you. Until this day, you have all perished. Repent, you miserable people, and if the calamities of eternal life do not warn you, let the condition of your present life incite you.

Consider how much misery this unspeakable persuasion has brought upon you and urged you toward until now. What animal has nature produced that is more terrifying, harmful, and hostile to human nature than serpents? Yet they are so sacred to you that you do not dare to harm them or even speak ill of them. What has God given to man among external things that is dearer than his own children? Yet their death is considered most happy if they are devoured or killed by serpents. What greater care has nature given to man than that of preserving his own life? Yet the devil has persuaded you to end it voluntarily by the most cruel death in the flames. <note>Postel likely refers here to reports of *suttee* (widow burning) or ritual sacrifices in the East and West Indies.</note> What greater plague can strike terror into even a strong man of sound mind than the hideous image of a demon? Yet when your people draw their final breath, if the form of the foul specter is missing, he has taught physicians, priests, and sacred officials <term>original: *hierophantas*; a priest who interprets sacred mysteries</term> to visit those breathing their last, wearing masks fashioned to look as hideous as possible. Certainly, in America, the foul image of the demon is present to anyone either dying or suffering from a very grave illness—even without the help of others—and is accompanied by a large retinue of the same kind. These are the fruits of your religion, Indians. To you, a serpent is holier than a man, more precious than your own children; a hellish life is more valuable than your own, and the devil—the destruction of human life—is placed before God, the supreme author of all things.

Through these and similar arguments drawn from false religions, the false religion must be discouraged and the true one offered. For there is almost no one who—even if they do not immediately confess one supreme God (as those on either side of the Ganges <term>original: *Cisgangetani & Transgangetani*; peoples of the Indian subcontinent</term> do)—will not at least acknowledge that there are various kinds of demons. Everyone will concede that among various and diverse things, there must necessarily be one highest, than which nothing greater can be given. For even the inhabitants of the Western Isles of **Cuba**, **Paria**, <note>A region in modern-day Venezuela, then considered part of the "mainland" of the Indies.</note> and the whole continent, all confess that certain demons are superior to others. It is indeed the work of the Evangelist to be armed against these pests with the highest faith and, as Jesus Christ says, with prayer and fasting. Victory in the cross will be certain. We ought to hope for this future as a thing more certain than certainty itself. For the supreme power of **Jesus Christ** has not vanished, as our impious people think. Christ, or the **Holy Virgin**, and his saints, hear their own no less today than in the past; provided that work is done especially among those who have never heard of him.

This is clear from these examples. **Jerome of Prague**, after spending a life in solitude for twenty years during the time of the Hussite faction, was sent from Poland to **Lithuania**, a region devoted to various and false cults. King Władysław of Poland <note>Władysław II Jagiełło (r. 1386–1434).</note> had sent him with letters of recommendation to Prince Vytautas of Lithuania <note>Vytautas the Great (r. 1392–1430).</note>, so that, having expelled false superstition, he might substitute the true religion. Some worshiped household serpents, others a sacred and perpetual fire, others a hammer along with the sun, and the vast majority worshiped forests. He immediately exploded <note>original: *explosit*; meaning to drive out with scorn or refute utterly</note> the first three superstitions. In...

Among these events, a first miracle occurred: though they were accustomed to nursing serpents at home on the most delicate foods and soft bedding, and had brought them out to the middle of the marketplace to be burned, one serpent of unusual size was so protected by its prince, the demon, that it remained unharmed in the great fire while the others were consumed. It could not be destroyed until the sign of the cross was made and the name of Christ invoked, at which point the multitude crushed it. 

Furthermore, there were forests that had been untouched and held as sacred by the people for countless ages, in which (if anyone had previously violated them) they immediately suffered harm from a demon. When **Jerome** <note>original: "Hieronymus"; likely referring to Jerome of Prague (c. 1379–1416), a missionary known for his work in Lithuania where he destroyed sacred groves</note> himself took an axe and began to cut them down, the crowd followed his lead and began to fell innumerable trees. Finally, they came to an ancient oak of extraordinary thickness, famous for its religious significance. While everyone else feared to touch it, one man, bolder than the rest, swung his axe to strike; however, he struck his own leg and fell with a great cry. The common people began to accuse Jerome, lamenting the violation of the most holy grove—the home of the gods—and, being terrified, they began to incite a riot. Having secured silence, Jerome showed them that these were the illusions of a wicked demon and that the man had suffered no real evil; taking him by the hand, he raised him up fully healed. At this, all were astonished and turned against the sacred oak, cutting down the entire grove. So present is Christ whenever his glory is at stake. These are the true powers of faith. This history is treated more at length by **Aeneas Sylvius** <note>Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini, who later became Pope Pius II (1405–1464)</note> in his work *Europe*.

But a far more famous and recent miracle must be placed before your eyes, so that we may show that the presence of the **divine Virgin mother of Jesus Christ** is also with her worshippers. **Peter Martyr** <note>Peter Martyr d'Anghiera (1457–1526), an early chronicler of the "New World" explorations</note> writes of this, a man not at all superstitious, but of singular faith in delivering his description of the New World. I know that some will laugh and mock this narration of mine, thinking me possessed of such simplicity as to believe these things; yet I am persuaded of these and far greater things concerning the divine Virgin. But let them listen and weigh whether all miracles are performed by the author of demons. 

When a certain sailor, seized by ill health, was left behind by his companions on the shores of **Cuba**, seeking someone he might meet in whose house he could recover, he came upon a certain chieftain who took pity on him and cared for him at his home until his health was restored. Mindful of this kindness, the sailor began to diligently manage the affairs of that prince, eventually being placed in charge of his army. Indeed, he fought very often and most successfully in the prince's name, for he always brought back victory. 

Once he had gained skill in the language of that region, the chieftain asked by what divinity or power he was always so successful. The sailor (as common people are often more simple regarding sacred matters) replied that the **divine Virgin Mary**, whom he worshipped daily and whose image he wore hanging from his neck, granted him those victories. He explained that the <term>Zemes</term> <note>original: "Zemes"; the Taíno spirits or deities of the Caribbean</note>—that is, those whom they falsely believed to be gods—were most pernicious demons who distracted men from the knowledge of the true God and would eventually plunge and lose them in destruction and the abyss. He told the prince that if he would accept the Virgin and her son, and be baptized in the name of Jesus, it would come to pass that no enemy would ever harm him. 

Immediately the <term>Cacicus</term> <note>original: "Cacicus"; a Taíno word for a chieftain or tribal leader</note>—that is, the ruler—believed. He built an altar to the Virgin using the image given by the sailor. The sailor recited the *Hail Mary*, and the subjects followed. The ceremonies they had previously established for the **Zemes**, they now applied to the image of the Virgin set up on high. Around the image are various pots filled with meat, with vessels full of water and various necklaces, which they were persuaded their **Zemes** (that is, spirits) would take and use. Thus, the places sacred to the **Zemes** were cast down, and the ruler asked that he might receive baptism. ...the inhabitants of Hispaniola were called. Once they had been shaped and instructed in religion, the sailor departed with his crew for Hispaniola, leaving them no other instruction than that they should recite the "Hail Mary" <note>original: "Aue Maria"</note> and, in times of danger, cry out in the Spanish tongue, "Holy Mary, help us" <note>original: "Santa Maria aiuda nos"</note>. The chieftain Anciso <note>Martin Fernández de Enciso (c. 1470–1528), a Spanish conquistador and geographer</note> recounted these and the following miracles to the governor assigned to the shores of Cuba, and confirmed them with countless witnesses; Anciso then reported this to Peter Martyr <note>Peter Martyr d'Anghiera (1457–1526), the first historian of the Spanish explorations in the Americas</note>. Since the commander was so fortunate in his victories, he began to be feared by his neighbors. Therefore, those worn down by wars made an agreement to test, without bloodshed, which **Zemes** <term>Zemi: ancestral spirits or deities represented by idols, worshipped by the Taíno people of the Caribbean</term> was more powerful: the one whom the commander had recently received (for so they called the Virgin), or their ancestral ones. They agreed that from the opposing forces, individual youths would be bound with very tight chains, and the adversary would perform the sacred rites of whichever **Zemi** freed its youth first. 

Once the youths were bound and prayers were poured out on both sides, the youth who immediately called out, "Holy Mary, help me" <note>original: "Sancta Maria adiuua me"</note>, saw the Virgin appearing before the eyes of all. She carried a rod in her hand, with which she put to flight a foul demon—who was present even as a ghost (a sight familiar to them)—and touched the chains of the baptized youth. Immediately, before the eyes of everyone, those chains bound the other youth. Thus it happened that not only was the first youth freed, but his opponent was bound with a double knot. According to the pact, the losers wanted to hand over the "herb" <note>likely a symbolic gesture of surrender or peace</note>; however, certain elders, claiming this was done not by the excellence of the opposing deity but by human trickery, refused to stand by the agreement unless it happened again in their presence. 

Therefore, eight of the most prudent men (as is their custom) were chosen, and the same pacts and deeds were repeated as before. While they were calling out, the Virgin appeared to some, while to others, a most foul demon—in the form he is commonly painted—was observed by the eyes of all. With her rod, the Virgin drove away the demon so that he could not free his own follower; and, touching the chains of the commander’s youth as before, she transferred them to the opponent. Seeing this, everyone—both elders and youths—hastened to profess the holy religion. Therefore, when Anciso reached that region, they asked him for priests to initiate them. Indeed, one hundred and thirty of the commander's former enemies were baptized in a single day. These men reported not only that they had seen those two miracles, but that whenever they had fought against the commander (since he was a Christian), they had seen the same Virgin standing before the battle line holding a scepter and terrifying them with a threatening countenance. Compelled by this, they had converted to the true religion, moved more by these sights than by the later miracles. 

In this way, God willed the angel to go before the children of Israel in a visible form; thus the angel of Joshua was present before Jericho; thus Sennacherib was struck down and put to flight. The hand of the Lord is not shortened, so that he cannot save. When the French, led by **Godfrey** <note>Godfrey of Bouillon (c. 1060–1100), a leader of the First Crusade</note>, set out to liberate the Holy Land from the Muslims <note>original: "Muhamedicis"</note>, and while in Asia Minor—their forces not yet assembled and exhausted by the long journey, with even the Emperor of Constantinople plotting treachery against our men—they were met by **Soliman** <note>Kilij Arslan I (d. 1107), the Seljuk Sultan of Rûm</note>, the leader of the Turks, with three hundred thousand men. Against these, thirty thousand Christians in their own regions routed, killed, and put them to flight. 

A most wonderful thing happened there: although our men had followed the retreating enemy for barely a single day's journey, a massive slaughter was nevertheless carried out for the space of three days. By whom this was done was never known, except that certain captured Turks reported the slaughter was carried out by three knights in white armor and on white horses. Certain men of the Greek religion <note>Eastern Orthodox Christians</note>, held in high opinion for their holiness, said these were **Saint George**, **Theodore**, and **Demetrius**. Whoever they were, it is certain they were not men. ...though it is expressed neither in Latin, nor French, nor even with proper grammar, I hold it with such faith that I would not give greater credit even to Thucydides <note>The ancient Greek historian known for his strict standards of evidence-gathering</note>. For truth is found in simplicity, whereas in eloquence there is a freedom to amplify that often mixes many falsehoods with the truth. Inspired by these examples and the deeds of the apostles and martyrs, an Evangelist <note>Here referring to a missionary or spreader of the Gospel</note>—raised up in hope, armed with faith, relying on innocence, burning with charity, glowing with divine love, intent on fasts and prayers, and trembling with humility—ought to expect anything from God. God will always be present for him and will confirm his efforts. 

For if God was present not only for the greatest apostles and martyrs, but also sent an angel to a soldier who was hardly righteous; if even the wicked and those estranged from Him have performed miracles in Christ’s name; if the Virgin Mary was present to sailors and semi-pagans who invoked her, for the sake of confirming their faith in her Son; and if He shines forth daily with miracles in countless places at the prayers of a good man who calls upon Him from the heart and with faith, then surely He will not fail such a man. I know that no one is so righteous that, by his own merits—which are like a "menstrual rag" <note>original: "pannus menstruatae"; a reference to Isaiah 64:6, used here to mean "filthy rags" or "polluted garments," suggesting human righteousness is nothing compared to God’s holiness</note> if compared to divine goodness—he could deserve divine favor. This is a gift of God; no one can "demand" miracles. Yet, because no one can be considered righteous when compared to God, one should not live like certain people who wickedly abuse the liberty of the Gospel—I might almost say in the manner of the Epicureans <note>A school of philosophy often stereotyped in the Renaissance as being solely devoted to physical pleasure and denying divine providence</note>. One must fast and pray at appointed days and hours. It is something to advance "thus far," even if it is not granted to go further <note>original: "Est aliquid prodire tenus, si non datur ultra"; a quote from Horace's Epistles</note>. 

But what need is there to speak of these things in general? The best of those people <note>Referring to the indigenous peoples being described</note> never drink unless they are thirsty; they do not eat unless prompted by hunger; they do not grow angry unless you do them an injury; they do not engage in sexual acts unless they are aroused. Is this not living according to the Gospel? Certainly, although this practice of the Gospel does not differ from the ways of the ungodly, it would still be tolerable if the law of Christ had not been made so wide through the interpretations of a people most inclined toward their bellies, so that among those "Evangelists," nothing is certain. Indeed, an Evangelist must certainly not live in the Epicurean manner, even if he holds a most free faith.

But I return to the plan. As we said above, the Indians <note>A general term for the indigenous peoples of the Americas</note> who confess and acknowledge a Supreme God shall be refuted by the arguments I have given. Because these people very frequently suffer from the presence of demons, they must also be warned of the unhappiness they experience from that pestilence. Finally, if those pests oppose them, they are to be put to flight by the sign of the cross and by invoking Christ and His saints. These people cross over to the rule of truth far more easily than a Jew or a follower of Muhammad. Already, almost all of New Spain <note>Colonial Mexico and Central America</note> has crossed over to the truth. For a countless multitude approaches Christ every day. In the kingdom of Narsinga <note>The Vijayanagara Empire in Southern India</note>, not a few also listen most willingly to teachings about Christ. I say nothing of other superstitions, as they will destroy themselves. 

When these men have crossed over into the true knowledge of God, they should be burdened with rituals only moderately. They should be invited to the truth of worship and holy institutions through persuasion, not compelled. If they wish to keep the ancient ceremonies of their false worship, that vanity is to be gradually driven out, unless it contains inherent sin. It should be permitted that the worship which was once offered to an idol—if it can be done without a loss of natural dignity—be ascribed to Christ. By this, as if nourished by the "milk of infancy" and confirmed in the true religion, they may eventually become capable of "solid food" <note>An allusion to 1 Corinthians 3:2 and Hebrews 5:12, suggesting converts should be taught gradually</note>, seek God from heaven, and become like the best of men. Thus, in a few days, religion shall grow to maturity. Against their nefarious sacrifices, such as those who sacrifice their own children to the **Zemis** <term>Zemi: ancestral spirits or deities represented by idols, worshipped by the Taíno people of the Caribbean</term> or to whatever idols, one must begin from the dignity of nature and the enormity of the crime. One must first persuade them not to commit such acts against their own children, parents, friends, and servants; and finally, that all men must be exempt from these nefarious sacrifices. ## THE METHOD OF BRINGING THE JEWS TO THE KNOWLEDGE
## *and faith of Jesus Christ.*

**S**o many brilliant minds, so many learned men, so many people instructed in every kind of art and discipline have occupied themselves in vain with this stiff-necked nation <note>original: "cervicosa isthaec gens"; a common biblical idiom for the Israelites' perceived stubbornness</note>. So much has been written against their treachery that even I—most unskilled in eloquence and stammering, ignorant in knowledge, confused in method, and to sum it up in one word, barely commendable in any way—might think I would be wasting my effort. I might wonder if I could achieve anything where the wisest men have profited nothing. 

Indeed, I do not think—I truly do not think—it will ever happen that the Jews can be persuaded and led to the truth by any art, however perfect in every part, because it was predicted by the Holy Spirit through the prophets, and by Jesus Christ—blessed man and God—that the race of Israel will not perceive a universal liberation from the captivity in which they now remain, until Jesus himself comes a second time, terrible, to judge the whole world. 

However, although most excellent men have achieved almost nothing by their writings against the stubbornness of this hardened nation, I do not think I should therefore abandon this task. For it very often happens that a city which could not be captured by the skill and industry of the most excellent commanders, despite frequent attacks, is finally conquered by the efforts of a common soldier. Not rarely has a recruit <note>original: "tyro"; a beginner or novice soldier</note> shown an example of himself that a veteran could admire rather than imitate. 

Before Christ’s terrifying advent, the whole nation will not be gathered. Furthermore, the things said about their dispersion do not imply a loss of truth, nor do they take away the choice of salvation, but they do remove their status and governance, which they have now experienced for one thousand four hundred and sixty years <note>Postel is dating the Jewish Diaspora from the destruction of the Temple in 70 AD; adding 1,460 years brings him to roughly 1530, the period of his writing</note>. For although that nation is most spirited in defending its salvation and liberty, and most ready to obey anyone in the name of a prophecy or an Israelite leader, yet from the moment they put Christ their Savior on the cross, they have always been miserably oppressed in all their endeavors. And what is more marvelous—and a greater confirmation of the faith of Jesus Christ—the Jew is in a worse condition among the pagans and those entirely foreign to our religion than where the followers of Christ dwell. 

Yet they are never free from afflictions, fasts, prayers, Sabbath-keeping <note>original: "sabbathismis"</note>, and other rituals. From this it becomes clear that they have committed a sin more serious than the idolaters themselves and have sinned incredibly against God, the parent of all nature. For they know for certain that they perform sacred rites to Almighty God, and they venerate Him with the very same worship as when God was present to all their prayers; and yet He does not permit them to protect themselves with any liberty or governance—despite those sacrifices once so pleasing to Him, fasts once so accepted, prayers once so welcome, and a people once so pious—while the impious and the idolaters themselves [enjoy] festive peace...

### The First Approach

I will not deal with you through the Scriptures at the beginning, O Jews, since you elude everything brought forward for your benefit and for the confirmation of the truth by using interpretations that are alien to the true meaning of the authors, yet approved by the authority of your Rabbis. Instead, a Reason <note>original: "Ratio"; Postel appeals to the Renaissance concept of universal logic shared by all humanity</note> common to us, to you, and to all other men will be brought into the open. If you dare to deny what is consistent with that Reason, let the consensus of the whole world at least stand as witness to your faithlessness. For I do not think it will happen that you will agree with it; faithlessness and obstinacy contend for greatness within you to such an extent that even when truths are admitted, you resist them—if not in words, then at least in your actions or inactions. 

We shall begin, therefore, first from the principles and ends of the parts of this world, so that from demonstrations drawn from there, we may finally construct those syllogisms <note>logical arguments where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</note> which are not far from the truth. You admit, along with the philosophers, that God established this entire temple of nature for the sake of man, and man for the sake of God—to be worshiped, honored, and loved above all things for these benefits. I do not think you wander in your understanding of God. For whatever is supreme, eternal, infinite, incomprehensible, and above all matter and form, I believe is called "God" by you, as it is by the consensus of all wise men. It is established, therefore, that all things were made mediately for the sake of God, and immediately for the sake of man. 

Furthermore, just as God is "Pure Act" <note>original: "actus purus"; a philosophical term from Aristotle and Thomas Aquinas meaning a being with no unrealized potential, who is eternally active and complete</note>, always attentive to the three parts of the world—the highest, the middle, and the lowest—so too must man, for whose sake those parts exist, have a certain goal. For man, made for the sake of the knowledge and praise of God, ought not to be idle. Therefore, man, created in the image of God—that is, excelling in the reason which is akin to divinity and endowed with free will—must also be always attentive toward three things: namely, that he directs whatever he does to the glory of God, the innocence of himself, and the utility of his neighbor. Whatever he wishes to do, he should weigh most diligently, so that if he should sin against any of these three, he may flee from it entirely; but if he understands a deed to tend toward any of these, he should not doubt that it is beneficial to all three. 

Yet his chief care ought to be to prove himself to God primarily by helping his brother, another human being. For both sacred and profane matters must be set aside when it comes to preserving a human life. Therefore, the name of religion is falsely used as a pretext when a brother’s need, which could be helped, is neglected. This principle of a human helping a human is by far the most approved by the philosophers, whereas Moses—because of you and your obstinacy—wrote by God's command that you should hold not all men, but only your friends in the place of brothers. He knew you to be so stiff-necked and rebellious that he gave you scarcely half-just precepts, as is clear in many places of Holy Scripture. For those precepts were later explained more broadly and humanely, and frequent mention of your obstinacy was made. 

Is it not clear enough that even while Moses was still alive, you practiced that obstinacy and abused circumcision? For in Deuteronomy 10 it is written: *Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no longer stiff-necked. For the Lord your God, etc.* But since there are so many testimonies of your hard necks, it is clear enough from your deeds. When Moses wanted to be your champion, you drove him away; after seeing miracles in Egypt, you murmured at the Red Sea; and when the sea was divinely parted, you judged God incapable of feeding you in the desert. If I wished to [record] all...

...to run through sacred history, almost nothing will present itself more frequently than your faithlessness <note>original: "perfidia"; in this context, Postel uses the term to describe a perceived failure to recognize Christ as the fulfillment of the Law</note> toward God. That those precepts which God gave to you at first glance were accommodated to your weakness and wickedness, and were not absolute, is most clearly evident from those things which were handed down to you in many places concerning the love of neighbor. For in the first place, Moses says:

> You shall love your friend as yourself. <note>original: "Diliges amicum tuum sicut teipsum." A variation of Leviticus 19:18, where Postel uses "friend" (amicum) rather than the more common "neighbor" (proximum) to emphasize a limited scope.</note>

Thus God was accommodating Himself to you, so that He might not give you a greater commandment than that which even the gentiles and those lacking the Law were using. For there is no man so impious that he does not have some friend whom he loves vehemently. Indeed, many living creatures destitute of reason have a sense and a fellowship of friendship. Why then is such a meager commandment given? This is the reason, O Jews: because you were the worst of mortals (even though you preserved some memory and the ceremonies of the law of Abraham), you were hostile even to your friends. You loved in word and tongue, in the manner of the court; but toward friends who followed your own faith, you so abused them with deceptions and faithlessness that there was clearly no faith among you. By pleasing yourselves with certain ceremonies, you were even far worse than many beasts, and more wicked than all other hypocrites. For otherwise, if there were no sin in that regard, it would not have been necessary to give you that law—which one cannot find in civil laws because it would be superfluous. For no one fails to love a friend of their own accord.

One may even derive the contrary law from this. For so that God might encourage you to kill those peoples who had lived in the holy land before you—who were, as it were, declared enemies—and so that their stain would not creep into you (which later happened extensively), and so that they might be entirely exterminated, He wished to arm you with hatred against them, as if He had said:

> You shall love your friend, and you shall hate your enemy. <note>original: "Diliges amicum tuum, & odio habebis inimicum tuum." This is the traditional interpretation of the Law that Jesus critiques in Matthew 5:43.</note>

For you know better than anyone that almost all precepts introduce their contrary. For the same reason, Moses wished to accommodate himself to your weakness in the same verse when he said:

> You shall not take revenge, nor shall you take vengeance upon your fellow citizens. <note>original: "Non ulciscêris, nec sumes de ciuibus tuis uindictam." From Leviticus 19:18.</note>

For this same law held place in all the cities of the heathens. By that law, the "living laws" <note>a term for judges or magistrates</note> were everywhere the judges themselves, who took punishment on behalf of everyone against wicked men. By the opposite sense, He wished you to be incited against the enemies of true religion, yet not to rage with eternal hatred against nature itself. For in his song, which is as it were the climax <note>original: "catastrophe," used here in the classical sense of a final resolution or turning point</note> of the entire law, he says that vengeance belongs to God, so that He might eventually destroy you fundamentally on account of the iniquities usually committed by you under the holy law. 

He wished you, therefore, to use vengeance only insofar as you had established a commonwealth after the unworthy inhabitants were driven out, but not for men to be armed in the future under any pretext of religion. For vengeance properly belongs to Him who knows the gravity of the crime and has weighed the spirit with which things are done: which cannot happen for a private man, who is either moved by emotion or weighed down by ignorance. ...[that He] might require less of you. Specifically, **to practice judgment, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with God.** <note>original: "facere iudicium, diligere misericordiam, & humiliter cum Deo incedere" — a reference to Micah 6:8.</note> This is the goal of man regarding man: to live justly with him—that is, to do for him whatever you wish him to do for you—to have mercy on the sinner, and to satisfy the hungry. Although Moses did not say this explicitly regarding all men, he nevertheless showed well enough where the perfection of the Law was intended to be when he left written: *If you encounter your enemy’s ox, or a wandering donkey, lead it back to him. If you see the donkey of one who hates you lying under its burden, you shall not pass by without helping him to lift it up.* <note>Exodus 23:4-5. Postel uses these specific laws about livestock to argue for a broader moral principle of loving one's enemies.</note> These duties show that even enemies are to be loved, or at least that they should be won over by duty as if they were friends. For it cannot happen, if there is a place for fostering quarrels and hatreds, that a <term>republic</term> <note>original: "respub." (respublica). In this period, it refers generally to any organized political community or the "commonwealth," not necessarily a representative democracy.</note> can ever be happy. 

Lest the reasoning of such duty be thought applicable only among one's own people, Moses added: *You shall not trouble the foreigner.* For you know the condition of strangers, since you were strangers in the land of Egypt. He also wishes that no injury be inflicted on anyone by reason of **false religion**, nor should anyone be held as an enemy on that account (unless they apply force). From this it is clear that, although Moses accommodated himself to the nature of the people he led, he nevertheless felt and judged that no one should be considered an enemy, since everyone should be won over by kindness. 

I wish these things were well-urged and persuaded to the Jews, because they strive to overturn the true aim of man with the prescriptions of their own Law. Truly, man is born for the sake of another man, and toward all (with those close to us and those of true persuasion placed in the first rank) he ought to be equally disposed. Just as all people share one God, one nature, and one common condition of being born, living, and dying, so they should help each other as brothers through mutual duties. Man is certainly more perfect the more he is like God. And yet God is equally beneficial toward all; the more He communicates a benefit, the more He does things worthy of God. Indeed, He nourishes enemies just as He does friends—and not rarely more mercifully—so that, burdened by benefits, they might recognize the Giver; or, being deservedly infamous for ingratitude, they might pay the penalty in perpetual punishments for not acknowledging such great benefits.

If, therefore, you grant me, O Jews, that the man who is most like God is by far the most excellent—one who strives to prove himself to God the Father by bestowing benefits upon all, who preserves himself in the highest innocence as a son of God, and who places the **Supreme Good** in the contemplation of God the Father (that is, of Truth) and in the admiration of His creation—then we are now in agreement. But if you dare to deny this, I shall refer the matter to the most holy reason of the Divine Majesty with the consensus of the whole world present. Since you have reached such a point of impudence that you would rather strip away reason than subscribe to the truth, [this reason] shall rightly bind your **faithlessness** <note>original: "perfidiam." Postel uses this term in the medieval sense of "misbelief" or refusal to accept what he considers the rational truth of Christianity.</note>—which allows itself neither to be directed by law nor conquered by reason—with the laws of stubbornness and damnation, and shall adjudge you, willing and seeing, to eternal punishments.

But I think you will acquiesce to such clear principles, known to all. For if you were to resist, you would be defeated by this one argument known to you. Postel is referring to the philosophical idea that man is a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</note>; and that the world itself, both small and great, visible and invisible, exists for the sake of God. If, therefore, all lower things are for the sake of man, since man is in the lower world, it is necessary that he also exists for the sake of man. If for the sake of man, then for himself and for another; therefore, he who was made for the final cause of God’s grace, exists both for himself and for other men. From this, the truth of the assumption is clear. It is not without cause that I insist you subscribe to this opinion, for it contributes greatly to the discussion of what follows. Let us proceed. ...if you run through [your history], almost nothing will offer itself more frequently than your betrayal of God. In this way, God accommodated Himself to you, so that He gave you no greater commandment than that which the <term>gentiles</term> <note>Non-Jewish nations or peoples.</note> and those lacking the Law already practiced. For no man is so impious that he does not have some friend whom he loves vehemently. Indeed, many creatures devoid of reason possess a sense and fellowship of friendship. Why then is such a meager commandment given? The cause is this, O Jews: because you were the most wicked of mortals (although you kept some memory and ceremonies of the law of Abraham), you were hostile even toward your friends. You loved with word and tongue, in the courtly manner; but as for friends who followed your same faith, you so abused them with impostures and betrayal that there was clearly no faith among you. You were—while pleasing yourselves with certain ceremonies—far more wicked than many brutes, and indeed more deceitful than all other dissemblers. Otherwise, if you were not sinning in that regard, it would not have been necessary to give you that law, which one cannot find in civil laws because it would be superfluous. For no one fails to love a friend by their own choice. 

A contrary law can be derived from this. For so that God might encourage you to kill those peoples who had lived in the holy land before you as declared enemies—and so that their stain would not creep into you (which later happened extensively)—He wished to arm you with hatred against them, as if He had said: 

> You shall love your friend, and you shall hate your enemy. <note>This "antithesis" is famously quoted by Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:43) to show how the New Law expands upon the Old.</note>

> You shall not take revenge, nor take vengeance upon your fellow citizens. <note>Leviticus 19:18.</note>

For even in all the cities of the pagans, the same law held place. Under that law, the "living laws" were the judges themselves, who took punishment from wicked men in the name of everyone. By a contrary sense, He wished you to be moved against the enemies of the true religion, rather than to rage with eternal hatreds against nature itself. For in his song, which is like the <term>catastrophe</term> <note>Postel uses this term in the classical sense of a "turning point" or "final conclusion" of a drama—here referring to the Song of Moses in Deuteronomy 32.</note> of the whole Law, he says that vengeance belongs to God, so that He might eventually destroy you completely because of the iniquities you were accustomed to admit under the holy law.

Therefore, true vengeance belongs to God alone; otherwise, it must be referred to a judge, lest we immediately slay those neighbors we hold as enemies under the pretext of injury. For unless our <term>libido</term> <note>In this context, "unchecked desire" or "unbridled passion."</note> were bridled by laws, there is no one who would not, in the heat of passion, wish to take a brother's life for the smallest injury. # ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...lest he should fail to represent to him that glory of the whole universe which He deserves for the sake of created things, and so that he could not plead any ignorance in matters pertaining to that goal, He willed to create man in His own **image and likeness**—that is, adorned with the guidance of reason. He did this so that as often as man recalled the form of his Original Model, he might strive to become as like Him as possible (as far as our frailty allows). From this, the axiom already assumed is clear: namely, that **men are more excellent the more they are like God.** 

However, so that we may see and more diligently observe what is placed within the duty of a good man, we must look at what kind of being God is, and how and what He does. Because I am dealing with a **stiff-necked people**, <note>original: "ceruicosa gente." This is a traditional biblical idiom (Exodus 32:9) used here by Postel to address his Jewish readers who might resist the Christian doctrine of the Trinity.</note> I wish to bring here a brief summary of those points in the first book which demonstrated that God is **three and one**. 

The Jews confess with us that God is most simple, infinite, most just, most powerful, most wise, most benevolent, and most adorned by far with all other titles of goodness and virtue—or (if I can express anything worthily of Him) most endowed and most absolute. However, when we ascribe to Him those qualities from their effects (even though He is free from them as mere "qualities" in a human sense), we must attend most diligently to those properties He possesses as Creator, without which a Creator cannot be understood. 

Although He is most powerful, unless He had possessed within Himself both the wisdom to create all things and the absolute knowledge of even the particular parts, and had been moved by benevolence and love to create what He was able and knew how to create, He could never have created anything. For any power, unless it knows what it is to do, acts not; and if it knows, but does not will it, the result is the same. Therefore, **God is three and one.** 

For as the Powerful One, He is the Father and Author, from which Power is generated for eternity the Wisdom which is the Son; and from both proceeds the Love of acting, which is the Holy Spirit. Power is almighty, Wisdom is almighty, Love is almighty, yet there are not three almighties, but one Almighty. Nor, however, is the Holy Spirit the Father or the Son, nor is the Son the Father or the Holy Spirit; rather, the persons are co-equal to one another, distinct by their properties, while they are only one divinity. 

This ought to be conceived, as far as is permitted, by an example familiar and daily to us. When I think of anything to be done—for example, a **castle** <term>castrum</term> <note>Postel uses the building of a fortified castle as a metaphor for the Divine "architectural" process of the Trinity.</note> to be built—it is necessary that I have it entirely in my mind and knowledge before any firm notion of it exists. Yet I do nothing unless I reveal the form by voice, or by a drawing which I have conceived in my mind. Nor do I achieve anything unless the conception, the diagram, the explanation, or the description comes to the work. Therefore, the whole castle was in the mind, the whole in the diagram, and the whole in the work. Yet there are not three castles, but there is one castle. Thus the castle in the work is not the castle in the diagram, the voice, or the writing; nor is the castle in the voice the castle in the mind or in the work. Rather, they differ from one another by certain properties, even though the thing is one, and it is as simple as possible within its own kind. 

It could not happen that in things existing in nature there would be anything in which all things agree, unless it proceeded from a common principle in which that thing was most perfect. There is no thing that does not require the **number three** for the completion of its essence, however simple it may be. For example, take any grain of seed: unless it has fertility (or the power of acting) from the time it received its completion until it ceases to be, along with the progress and the love or will of acting, nothing can be produced from it. Let us take an **acorn**; when it has been buried in the earth, unless it possesses the fertility and power of producing a tree from itself, it will not produce it. If the progress from that power is lacking, it will do nothing. If it does not "love" to nourish its own tree in such a soil and form, the tree will never be produced or sustained. Yet the whole tree, and the seed...

### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK 4

...is power, and likewise process, and love or natural delight; and yet they are not three trees, but one tree. So it is in all of nature. Therefore God, who is the cause of all things, is most greatly three and one. Since God is most greatly one, there is nevertheless in all of nature a unity before number, an eternal equality before the difference and inequality of things, and a connection before separation. Unity is the Father, equality the Son, and connection the Holy Spirit; and yet there are not three gods, but one God. 

In the soul, which is one and the image of God, powerful reasoning—by apprehending and handing over all things to comprehension or perfect knowledge and discernment—commands the memory so that it can be repeated through recollection. The whole intellect comprehends, the whole knows, the whole remembers; yet there are not three intellects, but one. The souls of brute animals <note>Postel refers to "brutes" in the classical sense of non-rational animals, such as livestock or wild beasts.</note> possess fantasy, thought, and memory. Sensation consists of essence, life, and sense. All things—matter, form, and the composite—arise from both proceeding. In the arts, we see thought, explanation, and the art itself; or the artisan, the instrument, and the material, etc., as was taught in the first book. 

Not only is God simple, three, and one, but His action always looks toward a threefold world: the highest, the middle, and the lowest. Whatever He does, He does for the sake of use and purpose; hence He wills to be the author of good to all equally, and the author of evil to no one. For to believe He is the author of evil is wicked. If He sets out His goods in common for everyone, He also wills them to be distributed with the highest justice. Therefore, whatever can be thought of to protect this thin mortality—and far more than anyone can ever grasp in their mind—He willed to do for the sake of man, so that He who is held to be the father and author of all might also set out things most worthy of such a father for the common good. 

Hence the philosopher's saying: *The more common a good is, the more divine it is.* <note>original: "Bonum quo communius, eo diuinius." This was a popular medieval philosophical axiom suggesting that true goodness seeks to share itself with as many people as possible.</note> God willed that the Jewish people, who were most addicted to greed, should learn this not only from the natural use of things but He confirmed it in the desert for forty years, so that the nation ought to have been persuaded of nothing more than this. For when manna rained down upon them in far greater abundance than was enough to feed such an army, anyone who out of disobedience to the divine <gloss>divine</gloss> commands, or for the sake of more than one person, had collected more (except on the eve of the Sabbath), found that not only did they have nothing more than the others, but while it remained uncorrupted on the surface of the earth, it bred worms and rot at home. 

In this matter, God wished to prove that the efforts of mortals to pile up wealth beyond necessary use are in vain. For one cannot see what else someone who burns with the desire for possessing feels or acquires, other than their own miseries, in amassing things from everywhere for the sake of children, necessities, relatives, or even luxury. Certainly many are accustomed to leave behind to those they wish to be enriched by their wealth the instruments of sloth, idleness, pride, luxury, and all pleasures; no one has ever prepared virtue with wealth. As for that part of virtue usually exercised with the help of riches, no one is at fault who, lacking them, does not exercise it. But he who has the assistance of wealth can be in the gravest guilt, and a double one at that. For if he does not give as much as he ought, he is already liable to give an account; if he seeks and ascribes to himself the glory of those things he bestows, it would have been better to have given nothing. 

The Creator, therefore, since He placed all things in common, willed that those who have obtained more should distribute them so that they keep nothing for themselves beyond necessities; for the <term>management of wealth<note>original: "dispensatio." In Postel's theology, the rich do not "own" their money but are merely stewards or administrators of God's property.</note></term> has been entrusted to the rich. We must now come to our human being. He is most like God who is always most attentive to a three-part goal: who refers all things to the honor of God, the innocence and cultivation of himself (that is, of his soul), and to the charity and use of his neighbor; who would never do injury to anyone; who would rather die than act against the right judgment of his soul; who desires that whatever is placed within him be ready for his brothers, that is, for all other men, and has...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...is bound, who seeks no glory from his own deeds. For glory and honor are the unique gifts of God; therefore, a person is better and more useful to nature the more they approach this condition. And the precepts are holier the more they command, encourage, and teach these things. Therefore, Christ is better than Moses—more just, more holy, more useful to nature, and more like God in the flesh. The Gospel is more excellent than the Old Law, and Christians are far more excellent than the Jews. From this, it is certain that salvation and the true way of salvation reside in our religion. Either you must deny the first principles, or you must concede the final conclusions; for there is no room for escape in this argument. The Evangelical precept <note>Referring to the teachings of the Gospel</note> is entirely consistent with God and nature: *Whatever you would wish that men do to you, do the same to them.* This is far more widely applicable than where it is written:

> Do not do to others what you do not want done to you.

For this latter phrase is as if you were to say, "cease from evil"; the first is as if you were to add, "and do good." For just as no one wants to suffer injury, so one ought not to inflict it on anyone; but to be most like God, you ought to do for others whatever you would wish they did for you. 

But a certain Rabbi will object to me that the law of Christ does not seem good because it has removed the greatest part of the ceremonies of the Old Testament, even though not one apex <note>original: "apex"; referring to the smallest stroke or "tittle" of a Hebrew letter, implying the smallest detail of the Law</note> of the law should be omitted. I shall provide satisfaction. The Jews approve of the Prophets and the Hagiographa <note>The "Writings" or *Ketuvim*, the third section of the Hebrew Bible</note>; although, because there are weightier and more urgent testimonies in David and Daniel, the modern Talmudists have rejected them among the Hagiographa so that they might appear to have less authority <note>Postel refers to the Jewish categorization of the Tanakh, arguing that moving Daniel and David's Psalms out of the "Prophets" section was a tactic to lessen their messianic weight.</note>. > Hear, he says, the word of the Lord, princes of Sodom; give ear to the law of our God, people of Gomorrah. To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices to me, says the Lord? My soul hates your Calends <note>The first of the month</note> and your solemnities; I endure these things with difficulty. Wash yourselves, be clean, take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes. Cease to act perversely, learn to do good. Seek judgment, succor the oppressed, judge for the orphan, defend the widow, and come and let us reason together, etc.

If the worship of the Law and that number of sacrifices and ceremonies had made people holy, and if they were to last forever, how is it that the most holy prophet, having rejected them entirely, relates the whole of religion to the piety of the heart and interior goodness? Would it not have been enough for him to have either rebuked those vices committed under the pretext of sacred rites, or to have commended virtue without attacking the rites themselves? Since they were instituted by Moses, they could not be the cause of vice. Certainly, the prophets knew entirely that they were to be abolished, because not only Isaiah, but Jeremiah also dared to diminish them. > Do not trust in the words of the Lord, saying, "The Temple of the Lord, the Temple of the Lord is this." For if you truly direct your ways and your efforts, if you execute judgment, etc.

And therefore the prophet forbids praying for the people, because the Lord will not hear; this certainly cannot be understood as referring to the Babylonian captivity, since you were led back from it and were heard. ### GUILLAUME POSTEL BOOK IV.

...to those who long for the day of the Lord, why do you desire it? That day of the Lord will be darkness, and not light. Is not the day of the Lord darkness and not light, gloom and no brightness in it? I hate and reject your festivals, and I will not take delight in the scent of your assemblies. Even if you offer me burnt offerings and your gifts, I will not look upon them; I will not accept the peace offerings of your fatted beasts; take away from me the noise of your songs, etc. <note>A quotation from the prophet Amos 5:18–23</note> These things not only predict the abolition of sacred rituals at the coming of Christ, but they assert that the coming of the day of the Lord will be ruin, darkness, and gloom for you. All things were meant to be removed by the coming light of the Gospel. But it is also pleasing to hear David's opinion on this abolition. In *Psalm 50*, <note>original: "Cantico 50"</note> he writes thus:

> Hear, O my people, and I will speak, *Israel*, and I will testify to you that I am your *God*. I will not rebuke you for your sacrifices, nor for your burnt offerings, which are always in my sight. I will not accept calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks, etc. Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise.

Do these words not overturn the sacrifices and convert them into a pious worship? If they were not meant to cease eventually, why would the holy prophets have debated them? All external things, even circumcision itself, were meant to cease with the coming of Jesus Christ. Moses himself in *Deuteronomy 30* says:

> If you are scattered to the corners of the sky, *Israel*, from there the Lord your God will draw you, and take you up, and lead you back into the land which your fathers possessed, and you shall obtain it; and blessing you, he will make you more numerous than your fathers were. The Lord your God will circumcise your heart, so that you may love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live, etc.

Likewise, we cited this ten chapters earlier. *Jeremiah* has the same in chapter 4:

> Be circumcised to the Lord, and take away the foreskins of your hearts, O men of *Judah* and *Jerusalem*.

From these things it is clear that not only were the ceremonies to be removed at Christ's coming, but also the circumcision of the foreskin was meant to be changed into the circumcision of the heart. But meanwhile, Moses' opinion must not be passed over with a "dry foot" <note>original: "sicco pede"; a Latin idiom meaning to pass over a subject quickly or without getting involved in the details</note> (as they say); it must be examined diligently, because the Jews find protection for themselves in it, thinking it will come to pass that God, with the *Messiah* as leader, will bring them back and place them again in the holy land. It is clear enough that this return is not to be understood as being from *Babylon*, because circumcision continued for nearly five hundred years afterward. It must therefore be understood as the restoration in the time of the *Messiah*, by whom circumcision was to be abolished. When he speaks of the land in which they will be restored, it cannot be understood as *Palestine* or *Judea*. For it is entirely impossible that there could be greater wealth or people there than when things flourished under *Solomon*. For that region could not support such a multitude of people. 

He calls it the "land of the fathers," after the manner of *David*, who, although he was the wealthiest and most fortunate, and in every respect a blessed prince, nevertheless said he would see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. For in this life, however fortunate we may be, we are entirely in the land of the dying. Thus, while he seems to promise you one thing, he means another; just as when he promised you *Palestine*—a region almost entirely barren except for a few fertile valleys—he said he would give you a land "flowing with milk and honey," so that he might draw you toward hope and the evidence of heavenly things. For springs of honey or milk were never seen there. 

But if Christ has come, they say, how was he not the King of *Israel*? How did he not lead the *Jews* back, gathered from the whole world, into some region which they might inhabit far more happily than before? How could it be that he whom you call *Christ* had no attendants, no power, and lived in the greatest poverty and contempt? Many points are proposed here, and each must be addressed individually. Certainly, around the time of Christ's coming, the Jews from the whole world—

Just as no one wants injury brought upon themselves, so he should bring it upon no one. But so that you may be most like God, whatever you would wish to be done for you by others, you ought to do the same for them.
