to be handed down: the **natural law**, the **law of restoration**, and the **law of grace**. The **natural law** was given to all people, but in Adam and his descendants it became so corrupted that, although everyone may judge themselves to be acting wrongly, they cannot amend their ways for the sake of salvation without a special privilege from God. The second, the **law of restoration**, was given to Moses so that he might explain it to the Israelites. The third, the **law of grace**, was to be given by Christ, its divine author, in such a way that remedies for our corrupted nature would be offered to all people within it. These eras are connected to one another like the past, the present, and the future. Since the first and the last laws belong to everyone, they were not restricted to any specific locations. The Jewish law, however, held only a specific place; once it lost that place entirely, it also ceased to have any power. For as long as God wished to sustain that law, He diligently sent it prophets, gave it teachers, and ruled it through judges, kings, and leaders; nor did He send it any calamity without first announcing it along with its conclusion, as was evident in the Babylonian captivity. It follows, therefore, that since the prince, the priest, the prophet, the kingdom, the location, the miracles, and the Temple have been lost to that nation—without any hope of liberation or any prophecy of return—that law has also reached the end of its power. For it is impossible for that law to retain its force when all its supports have utterly collapsed, and when the world has now been without that law for fifteen hundred years.

Since there is no gap between these laws, it follows that the **law of the Messiah** was instituted in place of the **Mosaic law** when the latter perished. The law of God and of the true Israel remained continuous in Judea along with the Mosaic law, which Jeremiah hinted at when he said in his thirty-third chapter: <note>Jeremiah 33:17–18</note> *David shall never lack a man to sit upon the throne of the house of Israel, nor shall the Levitical priests lack a man before me to offer burnt offerings, and to kindle grain offerings, and to sacrifice every day.* It is clear from this passage either that the prophet lied (which is a sin even to imagine) or that we Christians are the **True Israel**. For sacrifices have been offered by us now for fifteen hundred years. In that place, Christ succeeded to power after **Simeon** <note>original: "Simhoni." Likely referring to Simeon the Just, a High Priest whom Postel identifies as the last of the legitimate Jewish authorities.</note>, who was the last of the good leaders, though Christ came without outward ceremonies, for he had come to do away with them. He was succeeded by **James the Just** <note>The brother of Jesus and leader of the early Christian community in Jerusalem.</note>, and the others in order. Although our circumstances there are now afflicted, they nonetheless possess power. For in this our Israel differs from yours: we are not bound to specific places or earthly things. The rewards of your law, however, were an abundance of all corruptible things, depending entirely upon the land of Israel.

From this consideration, it is clear that the Christians have preserved that power which you have lost. Moreover, the **Throne of David** is the Church of God and the fellowship of the faithful. The prophet Nathan revealed this to David after he had rested from his enemies, in the second book of Kings, chapter seven: <note>2 Samuel 7:16. In the Vulgate, 2 Samuel is often titled 2 Kings.</note> *And your house shall be faithful, and your kingdom shall stand forever before your face, and your throne shall be firm continually.* This cannot be understood literally as a kingdom supported by corruptible things; therefore, it must be understood as being said of the power of the faithful who follow the faith of David. Hence David says in the Psalms: *Your throne, O God, is forever and ever,* etc.

There is also another condition for the people living under the law. For they were to be weighed down by three kinds of captivities: the first, like small children under the Judges; the second, for seventy years in Babylon; and the third, an eternal one—namely, when the grace of the Law was to be exchanged for the grace of the Gospel. Therefore, all those things for which God said through the prophets that He would not grant forgiveness must be referred to this final captivity, from which they will not be liberated unless they become Christians. There are also three ways of understanding **Israel**: under the law of Moses, under the Gospel (as we have seen from Isaiah), and under the rejection and wrath of God. There are also...

That only a very few were to be gathered in the second congregation is evident from the book of the *Sanhedrin* <term>Sanhedrin: A tractate of the Talmud dealing with the Jewish high court and messianic expectations.</term> in the chapter *Helec*. To whom will the Law be credited, to Moses or the Messiah? But one further condition of things must be noted before we address objections. The multitude of people was divided into three parts when the Messiah came. It is because of their impiety and craftiness that you suffer all these extremes. For they laugh at you, and you seriously believe them, even though you have been in such a long captivity and have lost your prophets, priests, judges, kings, and miracles. The power of the Law has perished for you. Nor can the Jews be anything other than impious and treacherous for these past fifteen hundred years.

One third you shall burn in the fire in the midst of the city when the days of the siege are finished; and you shall take a third and strike it with the sword all around the city; and another third you shall scatter to the wind, and I will unsheathe a sword after them. Before I deal with the *Nizahon* <note>original: "Nizahon." This refers to the *Sefer Nizzahon* ("Book of Victory"), a prominent medieval Jewish polemical work that challenged Christian interpretations of the Bible.</note>, I wish to note certain things in this passage of the prophet, so that you may pay closer attention. I pass over that in the beginning he compares you to hair—that is, the most useless waste of the body, and that which alone nourishes no living creature except the bat, but when shaved off it immediately perishes. So among men who depend on God, you were the greatest "shadow-dwellers" <note>original: "tenebriones." A play on words suggesting both those who live in darkness and swindlers or cheats.</note>, carrying around nothing else but darkness under the pretext of God's law. 

One part was burned under Titus <note>Titus, the Roman general (and later Emperor) who destroyed the Second Temple in 70 AD.</note>. For Jerusalem was set on fire, in which eleven hundred thousand men perished by war, famine, plague, and fire; nearly one hundred thousand were reserved for slavery and spectacles. Moreover, in the whole war, six hundred thousand men were lost. If you look at that multitude which was led out of Egypt, three times as many and more were slain. And yet that is only one-third part. For forty hundred thousand <note>i.e., four million.</note> (namely, the other two-thirds) were destroyed in Bitter <note>original: "Bitter." This refers to Bether, the final fortress of the Bar Kokhba revolt in 135 AD. Postel is citing the massive casualty figures found in Jewish tradition (Midrash/Talmud) to emphasize the scale of the disaster.</note>, at the very least. I do not wish here to bring forward what Josephus—a Jewish man of great authority among your people—has related. That author remains. You will believe him where he does not speak of Christ. 

A third part was destroyed by the sword; another third is a laughingstock to the whole world as fugitives to this present day. From that whole multitude a few were saved and bound in the covenant <note>original: "patio," likely a misprint or variant for "pacto" (covenant).</note>, that is, made Christians, and yet not all were good. For Simon the Samaritan <note>Simon Magus, a sorcerer mentioned in Acts 8 who attempted to buy the power of the Holy Spirit.</note> was baptized, and wished to abuse the Holy Spirit for magic; finally, having become impious and treacherous, he led many into error. And finally at Rome, while he falsely believed he could fly to heaven by the help of demons, he fell by the prayers of Peter and Paul, and was carried down to hell in the 11th year of Nero. Immediately after his death, the destruction was decreed, and the war was committed to Titus. Whence fire came upon the whole house of Israel. 

What truly is the cause? Because Jerusalem was more impious than the nations. For the nations, as soon as they heard of Christ and his doctrine, were converted; in Samaria, in Damascus, in Antioch, and in neighboring cities, we were already called Christians, while Jerusalem was still afflicting our people with all punishments. To you, before the Messiah came, nothing was in common with the nations. Nor was there anything in which you ought to have taken an example from them under Moses; indeed, it would have been damnable. For they were idolaters, and just as bad in morals as you. Therefore, you had to flee the example of the nations in all things. For you were led into captivity because of the imitation of the nations. 

Now, however, God says he wishes to establish all extreme examples against you because you do *not* follow the nations. It was necessary, therefore, for the nations to have had something from God in common with you and the rest of the nations, and which the nations would have received before you. But there is no such thing except the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the seed of Abraham, in which all nations were to be saved. For it was a small thing, as Isaiah says, that the Messiah should be the God-man for the salvation of Israel...

Therefore, God had placed him <note>Referring to Jesus Christ</note> for the salvation of the nations. But it was necessary for the scriptures to be fulfilled: so that God might call a "people" those who were "not a people," and "beloved" she who was "not beloved." <note>A reference to Hosea 2:23 and Romans 9:25, interpreting the conversion of the Gentiles as a replacement for the rejected Israel.</note> Therefore the fishers of men <note>The Apostles</note> used to say: *It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you first, but because you have made yourselves unworthy, behold, we turn to the nations.* <note>original: "Oportebat primum uobis loqui uerbum Dei, sed quia uos indignos fecistis, ecce conuertimur ad gentes." See Acts 13:46.</note> If you had acted according to the judgments of the nations, at that time Israel would undoubtedly have been saved. But because you rejected the Gospel, and dared to blaspheme it, and to kill Christ Jesus the Messiah—whom Pilate believed to be most innocent (though led by greed and the stubbornness of the Jews, he gave him up to be crucified) and whom he judged should be released several times before he yielded to your shouts—therefore God established so cruel an example of you in the sight of the nations, that nothing like it existed before, nor shall there be in the future.

He so favored the ethnic leader <note>The Roman general and future Emperor Titus</note> who was raging against you, that in the midst of your army, Titus, while besieging the city, could never be harmed by anyone. In a place where there was not a great supply of materials, in three days he encircled your city with a very wide and high wall, thirty-nine stadia <note>A "stadium" was an ancient unit of distance; 39 stadia is roughly 4.5 miles.</note> long. There, eleven hundred thousand <note>1,100,000</note> people were trapped; no one dared to come forth in legitimate combat. There, mothers cooked and ate their own children; there, dung and filth were the most pleasant food and highly priced; there, houses were filled with corpses and those dying of hunger. There, the crowd of the dying was so great that the earth of the city lacked space for burial. There, because of the stench, bodies were thrown headlong from the walls, filling the trenches in such a multitude that when Titus saw them and turned his eyes to heaven, he said: *I call God to witness that I am not the cause of this misery.* <note>original: "testor Deū, quia in causa huius miseriae non sum." Postel is drawing these gruesome details from the historian Flavius Josephus's account of the Siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD.</note> Finally, there, no father could embrace or love his son, or weep for him when dead. There also (though Titus otherwise had the most obedient soldiers), he could not, even by forbidding it, prevent them from destroying the Temple by fire and turning Jerusalem into a heap of stones.

And yet the survivors did not recognize Christ, but again they were gathered from the whole world at Bitter <note>Referring to Betar, the final fortress in the Bar Kokhba revolt against Rome in 135 AD.</note> against the Holy and Just One. How much misery was there, one may judge from this: they were in a city surrounded by a wall far greater in circuit than Jerusalem, nearly four times the number, and they endured a three-month siege. What the Jews suffered there, I leave to be imagined from the history of Jerusalem, for no historian has described the calamities of this slaughter in full detail. Let the histories of all nations from the creation of the world be read, and no slaughter similar to this will ever be found; whence it must be confessed that the Jews committed a sin so immense that no greater has ever been, or will be, since the world was made.

From this deed alone, one can certainly estimate the divinity of Jesus Christ. For God would never have exacted such bitter and unheard-of punishments for the killing of a merely holy prophet of the world—since a man holier than Isaiah, or Zechariah the son of Jehoiada, could not be given—and yet God forgave both those deaths and the people's idolatry after seventy years <note>The Babylonian Captivity</note>, and cherished his people still for nearly five hundred years. Yet now, alienated from Him, they have been in exile for fifteen hundred years. Therefore He does not spare you, nor will He ever spare you, unless you believe in His Son, the Messiah Jesus, who was violated and killed by your ancestors. For He is pious, and waits for you with mercy; though you weaken yourselves with fasts, pour out prayers, support one another, and perform ceremonies, you must not hope that He will ever hear you—He who has not heard you crying out for fifteen hundred years, while you are dispersed, hated by the whole world, and born to be the reproach and laughingstock of the nations.

Now let the armored *Nizahon* <note>The *Sefer Nizzahon*, a Jewish polemical text. Postel personifies it here as a heavily armed knight or "cataphract."</note> come forth; let us join battle. Although I am equipped with light armor, scarcely a spear and a small shield, yet with the faith of Jesus Christ as my guide, I hope it will easily come to pass that the more naked I am, and the less prepared with sacred equipment, the more He will supply me with greater strength. Thus, by movement, agility, and spirit, I may be able to finish off this Goliath, who is supported by such a crowd of opinions. First, he will object that we are not the people of God, because the seal of the Law, circumcision...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD #

<page-num>186</page-num>

...that we should not observe [the law], even though Christ himself observed it. I have already shown that we are the people of God because we succeeded immediately after the Law of Moses was cut off—with its privileges, ceremonies, signs, magistracy, priesthood, prophecy, and power all ceasing. The fact that we are not circumcised teaches perfection. For Moses in Deuteronomy and the prophets, as I have already shown, preferred the circumcision of the heart to the circumcision of the flesh; I have already cited those passages. Why, then, was Christ circumcised? He did it to make both [Jews and Gentiles] one, to join the Jews to the nations, and so that as a mediator he might receive both extremes into himself: baptism and circumcision. He did it to approve the Law as good, since it was given by him, and to accommodate himself to your weakness, so that as God and man he might show us through total humility that we must obey received laws that do not fight against God. But now that he has departed, if we were to be circumcised, Christ would be of no benefit to us. The primary reason for his circumcision was the approval of the Law up until his day, and to connect the extremes, so that just as he consisted of two natures—divine and human—he might also join the law of physical reward with the spiritual, making both into one.

The Jews object to <term>idolatry</term> <note>Postel is addressing the common Jewish and Muslim critique that the Christian use of icons violates the Commandment against graven images.</note>, claiming that we worship images of the saints and of Christ. We do not adore them, nor do we believe there is anything of divinity within them; rather, we keep them in memory of Jesus Christ and the saints, especially since—due to our own negligence—few people know the Holy Scriptures. This was not a practice foreign even to the ancient Law. For some thought divinity dwelt in the <term>bronze serpent</term> <note>A reference to Numbers 21, where Moses set up a bronze serpent to heal the Israelites; it was later destroyed by King Hezekiah because people began worshipping it (2 Kings 18:4).</note>. Moses had instituted it, but Hezekiah removed it because of popular abuse. There were also two Cherubim in the Temple, which can and should be depicted even though they have a figure far less physical than a holy man. Yet the people who saw those signs in the Temple did not worship them. In the same way, our people do not adore the images of holy men, but they look upon them in memory of those they represent. The prayers they pour out before them—asking that the saints might appeal to God on our behalf—begin with God and end through Christ our God. 

It is truly reasonable that the saints, who were heard by the Lord on behalf of the people while they were in mortal bodies, can easily obtain what they ask for now that they are joined to him, as they feel compassion for our miseries and seek remedies for them. This is evident in many other places and specifically from that passage in the prophet where he says: *Even if Moses and Samuel stood before me to pray for this people, I would not listen.* <note>original: "Si steterint ante me Moses & Samuel, ut orēt pro populo hoc, nō exaudiā." See Jeremiah 15:1.</note> From this passage, it is clear both that the saints are able to pray, and also that no one—not even the holiest—can obtain anything from God in your name until you believe in Jesus, whom you crucified. 

I wish that rather than being a cause of offense or error to anyone, the Church would remove those images for a time, until the <term>Muslims</term> <note>original: "Muhametani"</note> and the Jews embraced Jesus Christ from the heart. If it were only for that reason, you could become Christians; the Church would accommodate itself to you in this, or provide separate temples where you could worship Jesus Christ according to your own judgment. 

It is also said that we neglect the choice of foods and "transgress the Law" <insert>you say</insert>. If those observations had been necessary for salvation, the Holy Spirit would never have sought to dismiss them so freely through the mouths of David, Isaiah, and the other prophets. Therefore, the one Law permitted or prohibited all those things because of the hardness of your hearts and for a time (until Christ, the Sun of Justice, should shine upon you), so that you might remember God more frequently by seeing what was permitted or forbidden. Truly, there can be no evil in those things, because what God created is good; it cannot generate evil or sin in a human who is a worshiper of God and possesses total purity of heart. For sin does not occur except by the will. Whatever was a sin regarding those things while the Law of Moses lasted was so not because the thing itself was evil, but because it would have been evil to break the Law. He commanded those ceremonies with which you were [familiar] in Egypt. Therefore, we do not sin by using those things which are not evil in themselves and which were discussed by the prophets. For it would have been far more serious to omit the daily sacrifice of the Temple—namely, the two rams—than to have eaten pork. And yet the prophets, looking toward the times of the Messiah, said: *Who has required these things from your hands?* <note>original: "Quis hęc requisiuit de manibus uestris?" See Isaiah 1:12.</note> Therefore, the true Law was to practice mercy and judgment, to help the oppressed and the widow, and to be most like God by doing good to all.

If Christ was God, says the <term>Nizahon</term> <note>Refers to the *Sefer Nizzahon* (The Book of Victory), a famous medieval Jewish polemical text used to counter Christian missionary arguments.</note>, and all-knowing, why did he tell his disciples he did not know the day of the resurrection? Because it is not expedient for men to know it...

-># WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK IV.<-

<page-num>187</page-num>

God willed to cover [the end of the world] in silence and obscurity. For knowing the cycles of things belongs to God alone, who cannot err; but for man, upon whom death always looms and the judgment of God always presses, yet who still does not abstain from evil, it is not his place to know the end. For if a man commits so many crimes even while placed in the fear of death and God’s judgment, what would he not do if he knew that a certain truce <note>original: "inducias," referring to a granted delay or period of safety</note> had been given to him? Therefore, God willed to accommodate himself to his disciples and to an audience that was not yet firmly established. Among them were many very dear friends, especially among the disciples. There were also the relatives of his mother, who, if he had confessed to knowing something so difficult, would have importuned him to reveal it. If he had refused to do so, they would have taken it poorly and judged that he did not have enough faith in their integrity. For it was necessary for him to accommodate himself to their tender ages in the faith, since even after seeing so many miracles, few believed in his resurrection (which he had often predicted) once he was dead. 

But a Jew will say to me: "If he knew, and denied it against the sense of his mind, he lied, which is foreign to a prophet." Yet he both knew, and by saying he did not know, he did not lie. For as a human, no mortal knew, but as God, he knew all things. For since he was both God and man, having two extreme natures in himself—the highest of the high and the lowest of the low—he also had two knowledges and two wills. I believe, O more sensible Jews, that you will not deny this to me, since you consider that the Messiah will be a man more excellent than any who could ever exist in the world. But if he were only a man, another greater than him could be made by God who was both God and man at once. Therefore, it was necessary for him to be God, endowed with two natures, and also with two wills, two knowledges, and qualities of the soul which appear different in God than in a human mind. 

But you will say it is evident that he was ignorant of something even common. For when he came to the sterile fig tree <note>A reference to the Gospel story where Jesus curses a fig tree that has no fruit.</note>, he told the disciples to look and see if there were figs on it. Look here, my good Jew, do you not see that God also acts as if he is ignorant of you, when he confessed to similar instances of ignorance? Why did God say to Adam, "Where are you?" Was he ignorant, or could he not find him? If he could find him, why did he ask where he was? And likewise: "I will go down," says God, "and I will see whether they have completed the work." Was he ignorant of whether they were building the tower <note>The Tower of Babel.</note>? Does he have need of local movement? Is he ignorant of anything? The same must be judged concerning the visitation of the Sodomites. These are familiar phrases of speaking in the sacred writings; God accommodates himself to us, and acts only effectively <note>meaning God produces the effect of a human action for our benefit</note>, not through passions of the mind in our manner. He is seen to be led by repentance for having made man—did he therefore not know from eternity that man would sin? These things are accommodated to our senses, because otherwise we would not grasp them. Christ willed nothing else except that, while he had everyone attentive to the fig tree, he might both terrify them with the power of a divine miracle and incite them to good works.

As for the fact that he had knowledge of the future, he taught this sufficiently by predicting his resurrection at a certain and fixed time; he predicted the sending of the Holy Spirit, the deaths and miracles of his followers, he predicted the disaster of Jerusalem, he predicted the resurrection of all, the future judgment, and the refining of matter through fire. But why did he not add the precise times, so that they could have taken precautions? Here I shall interrupt, and unless you solve a similar question for me by returning like for like, I am not going to satisfy you.

Could all the prophets, using divine revelation and inspired by the Holy Spirit, pronounce things to come and predict the truth at a precise time, or not? You will not deny they could, because the 70 years of captivity were precisely announced, and the ruin of the Temple after 70 weeks <note>A reference to the "Seventy Weeks" prophecy in the Book of Daniel.</note> was also announced. Why then did they not hand down all future calamities precisely, so that the men in whose times they were to happen could protect themselves? You will say it would have been inconvenient. For then there would have been no merits of hope and faith; the impious would have acted wickedly freely right up to the end, and fear would have been removed until that very hour. There would have been no place for the choice of believing—which is the merit, the source, and the basis of religion. Your Messiah, and the Messiah of the whole world, would have been oppressed while still an infant. For if you had known the fixed and stated day he was to be born, you would have flocked there from the whole world, and you would have stirred up a power formidable to neighboring princes and republics, and undoubtedly excited factions to exalt him, and you would have oppressed both yourselves and him before there was a place for the Gospel. This is most evident because, although he willed to be born in the greatest obscurity,

[God] willed it, yet it could not be otherwise than that Herod—because of what he had heard from the Magi—destroyed all the youth from two years old and under in the borders of Bethlehem and in Ramah. Regarding this matter, if you do not accept our views, hear Macrobius (whom I cited above) writing thus about the jokes of Augustus:

> When Augustus had heard, he says, that among those boys under two years old whom Herod had ordered to be killed in the borders of Bethlehem, his own son had also been killed, Caesar said: "I would rather be Herod's pig than his son." <note>This is a famous pun attributed to Emperor Augustus. In Greek, the words for "pig" (hus) and "son" (huios) sound similar. Since Herod was Jewish and did not eat pork, a pig in his household was safer than his own children, whom he famously executed out of paranoia.</note>

That author [Macrobius] is a stranger to both you and us, and clearly a pagan <note>original: "impius," literally ungodly, used here to mean someone outside the Judeo-Christian faith</note>, so far is it from the truth that you could say he was coached by us. The crime is established. It was not enough for Herod to have taken from you the kingdom, the priesthood, the judgment, and the royal offspring, unless he also pursued Jesus among the innocents. What would have happened if he [the Messiah] had come with royal pageantry? For that reason, the prophets did not wish to touch upon the specific day or month, lest he who was in "Shalom"—that is, the Prince of Peace—should bring war immediately from his cradle. What a crowd and world confusion would have been present for the true Messiah, since after two million men were killed in Judea and the chief cities were overturned, yet forty million—or as others prefer, four thousand myriads—flocked to the false Barcozaba <note>A derogatory name for Simon bar Kokhba, leader of the Jewish revolt (132–136 AD). "Bar Coziba" means "Son of a Lie."</note>. 

Religion is not accustomed to decreeing precise times, so that the freedom to acquiesce to the truth, or not to acquiesce, might be left to us. In this matter, Jesus Christ wished to be like the prophets, so that he might encourage his own toward faith and lift them into the hope of things to come. Indeed, he foretold the sending of the Holy Spirit, yet not precisely: but he said, "Not after many of these days." On the fiftieth day from the resurrection, however, and the tenth from the ascension, he sent the Paraclete <note>The Holy Spirit, from the Greek "Parakletos" meaning Comforter or Advocate</note>, whose name the impostor Muhammad, six hundred years later, wished to seize with your favor and assistance. Therefore, you bring nothing regarding the ignorance of Christ; otherwise both God the Father and the prophets, by the guidance of the Holy Spirit, would have been ignorant—which is impious to believe of them, as it is of Christ. That we are called the "True Israel," the other having been expelled, was made clear enough above; and we have seen Christ in the flesh. 

Regarding what Nizahon <note>A reference to the "Sefer Nizzahon," a common title for medieval Jewish polemical works that argued against Christian interpretations of the Bible</note> objects to us—that we ought not be called "Israel" because of the interpretation "one who sees God"—then by that same reasoning the Hebrews were falsely named, for they never saw Him. We know that Divinity cannot be discerned by the eyes; and we assert that we now see God as if through a mirror in an enigma <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12: "For now we see through a glass, darkly."</note>, until, released from the bonds of the body, we may see with a free soul face to face. 

But a place presents itself in which Nizahon exults and seriously triumphs as a victor: "If the Messiah or Jesus is God, why did he enter into a woman, since a woman is an unclean vessel, from which God willed the Israelites to abstain for three days before they received the Law?" A difficult question indeed. Suppose even (O pestilential man) that the divine virgin was a woman—whom you think you can defile with your blasphemous mouth with an even fouler name. Can God for that reason conceive a stain in Himself, because He daily sees and tolerates the foulest sins of men, than which nothing is more foul? Can He, penetrating into His world—in which are found even down to the underworld those more infamous than all infamy, as David says—conceive a stain? Or because He sustains, sees, and endures such infamous harlots? If He could have been shaken by wickedness, He would long ago have ceased to be God. 

Could He not, therefore, enter without a spot (supposing God to be a body) into a female body? See how powerless you make Him, and inferior to the sun! For the sun's rays touch sewers, putrid lakes, serpents, and whatever there is of putrid and stinking poison, yet they always remain in their own integrity. But if incorruptible and supreme things could conceive a stain from inferior things by touching them, there would long ago have been no sun; its rays would be foul and would bring destruction rather than health. See to what a state of impotence you reduce God, or where you might fall, while you compare His power (which is incapable of vice) to a human, whose "all righteous acts are like a menstrual rag" if compared to God. Or you make Him inferior to His own creature, like a candle or a household fire. For place a candle in latrines (pardon the expression <note>original: "honos sit auribus," a traditional phrase used when a speaker is about to say something potentially offensive or "dirty"</note>) as long as you wish; place it even in any darkness; when you take it out, the light itself brings back clearly no defect. And do you, most lost of men, not hesitate to assert that the majesty of God is inferior and more powerless than that? His holy majesty could even enter the vilest harlot without stain and purge her, making her worthy of God—which He does daily through grace while He converts female sinners. For neither more of the body...

->## GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK IV.<-

<page-num>339</page-num>

<sig>KK 3</sig>

God possesses grace just as he exhibits power. Truly, the most holy mother of our Lord Jesus Christ was not a harlot—as you dare to assert, and which I shudder to repeat—nor was she a "woman" (that is, one who has known a man), but an eternal virgin. It was a most worthy work for Jesus Christ that, just as he possessed two natures within himself, he should likewise receive two modes of creation within his own sweet flesh. For just as God formed the first man from clay without seed or a vessel suited for generation, while he willed all others to be born from that man through the instruments of nature; so the Son of God, the Wisdom of the Father, Jesus Christ, willed to encompass both modes in his own birth. For just as the most powerful God created all things through Wisdom—the Word, or his Son—in the Holy Spirit proceeding from both, so he willed the human nature procreated by God the Creator to be united in one subject of divinity and humanity participating in both, and to obtain such a generation among humans that he might have within himself the two preceding modes and proceed from them. 

There are two things to be considered in generation: the seed, and the vessel <note>The "vessel" refers to the womb or the female biological role in reproduction, common in early modern anatomical language.</note> suited for receiving and nourishing it. The first man [Adam] lacked both; all other humans have both; the third man [Christ] had only one. For by the guidance of the Holy Spirit, without any seed, he began his growth in a virginal vessel. 

O wretched and faithless Jews, let you at least have pity on yourselves! Let it be enough that the faithlessness <note>original: "perfidia," a term Postel uses here to mean a rejection of the Christian "truth," common in the polemics of his time.</note> of your Rabbis has resulted in countless people from among you being condemned for 1500 years. See the magnitude of the glorious Messiah—how all things in him harmonize with one another; how no greater man could be given or imagined than he who is at once both man and God. Consider how he could not have been born more worthily than from a most holy virgin; how he willed to enter the world in no better way than humbly and obscurely at first; how he could not have been more like God than by doing good to all, and by bringing the truth while receiving and enduring countless insults upon himself—he who valued humanity so much that, since humanity was unable to pay the debt in its own name, he satisfied the Father. If you believe all the highest things about him, then everything we believe about him must be proven to you. 

Furthermore, the prophets did not pass over such a great mystery in silence. Isaiah says: *Hear then, house of David: Is it too little for you to be troublesome to men, unless you are also troublesome to my God? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, a virgin shall be with child and shall bear a son, and shall call his name Emmanuel. He shall eat butter and honey, that he may know how to refuse the evil and choose the good.* <note>Isaiah 7:13-15. This is a central text in the debate between Christians and Jews regarding the word "Almah," which Christians translated as "virgin" and Jewish scholars often translated as "young woman."</note> These things are most clear; they would require no interpretation were it not that the Rabbis dared to corrupt them in order to pour clouds over your eyes. 

Because that ruined man Ahaz—who was worthy of a faithless people, being estranged from God and distrustful—had refused to consult the Lord in the danger of war, the prophet spoke those things by the oracle of the Holy Spirit. It was as if he said: "O house of David, and King Ahaz of Israel, you who do not wish to test whether God preserves his people, nor wish to ask a sign from him (as if he had deserted us), do you not find it enough to despise holy men and prophets, that you must also provoke God? However much you may hold him in contempt, you will not prevent God from bringing forth a sign by far the greatest among his people. For a virgin being with child shall bear a son, and shall call his name not 'man,' but 'God who is with us' [Emmanuel]. And when the boy is raised in the ancestral manner on honey and cream, he shall know how to reject the evil and disobedient peoples, and choose the good and faithful." 

The following passages are clear regarding the rejection of Israel and the land that was to be abandoned. Moreover, you all confess that Simeon the Just <note>A figure in Jewish tradition (Simeon HaTzaddik) whom Postel identifies with the Simeon in the Gospel of Luke.</note> was the last of the fortunate priests, and that the "tongue of fire" <note>Postel refers to the Jewish tradition that a scarlet thread in the Temple would miraculously turn white on the Day of Atonement to show God's forgiveness, a sign said to have ceased 40 years before the Temple's destruction.</note> ceased to be carried in his right hand at his death, and that those who followed did not bless the people with the name *Arba Othioth* <term>Arba Othioth: The Hebrew "four letters" or Tetragrammaton (YHWH), the sacred name of God.</term>, and that other miracles gradually vanished. From this, your rejection was manifest even before the boy Jesus, Emmanuel, was weaned. For in the year that he held Christ in his arms during the purification of Mary, Simeon the Just died. All these things are in agreement. 

Indeed, who would not marvel at and shudder at the impiety and the zeal of your Rabbis for corrupting the scriptures? "Emmanuel" fits the name of the Messiah alone, for then God was to be with men—he whose generation no one could declare. They [the Rabbis] want that saying to refer to the daughter of the prophet, or some other woman as they dream up, and they claim a man was the father of Emmanuel. But what kind of great "sign" is it if a woman conceives and gives birth in the common way? Signs are rare and beyond nature, but...

...to conceive a child from a man—what is miraculous about that? When the daughter of Ahaz, or the prophetess, gave birth, did you not lose your land and did ruin not come? <note>Postel is arguing against the interpretation that the "young woman" mentioned in Isaiah 7:14 was simply a contemporary woman of the prophet's time, which would make the birth a mundane event rather than a divine "sign."</note> O reprobate men: are you not ashamed to follow such delusions, O wretched ones? To this, who could speak of a "virgin" and "pregnant" without a contradiction of falsehood, if one understands it by the common custom of conceiving? If she conceived by a man, she is not a virgin. Therefore, when he says "virgin" and "pregnant," he describes a supreme sign and a miracle. Indeed, so that there would be no ambiguity, he used the word *harah* <note>original Hebrew: הָרָה (harah), meaning "pregnant" or "to conceive."</note>, which (as I said) if understood as a deflowered woman, implies a contradiction. 

Therefore, he refers only to the Virgin Mary, who conceived without a man and remained a virgin. For from her, having assumed flesh, Jesus Christ proceeded; just as he went along, passing through the midst of those who wished to seize him, and as he vanished on the mountain from which they wished to throw him headlong. <note>References to the Gospel of Luke, where Jesus miraculously escapes crowds in Nazareth.</note> Mary, the mother of Christ, was a virgin during the birth and after the birth. God is therefore not defiled by descending into the holy virgin. 

The Temple of Peace in Rome collapsed when the Virgin gave birth. The Romans thought that new work was eternal, but when that mass fell, touched by heaven, it gave place to the true Prince of Peace. <note>A popular medieval legend claimed that the Roman Temple of Peace would stand until a virgin gave birth; it was said to have collapsed on the night of the Nativity.</note> An altar had previously been placed in the temple of Isis in Egypt for the "Virgin about to give birth"; likewise in Gaul, in the time of the Druids of the Carnutes <note>The Carnutes were a Celtic tribe centered around modern-day Chartres; Postel refers to the legend of an ancient druidic statue of a "Virgin who will give birth" (Virgo Paritura) discovered there.</note>, an altar was placed which was later dedicated to the woman in childbirth. Oil flowed from a fountain in Rome for an entire day following the birth of the Lord. A golden rainbow was seen that day, a star led the Magi, and three suns merged into one. All these things are noted in the annals of various nations and are consistent with prophetic writings. 

Jeremiah mentions the same miracle in other words in chapter 31: "How long will you turn here and there, O rebellious daughter Jerusalem? Surely the Lord has created a new thing upon the earth. A woman shall encompass a man." <note>Jeremiah 31:22</note> This is the "new thing" that the Lord does: a woman encompasses a man without any manly work. For what else would be "new" if she conceived in the manner of all others? Therefore, a little later he speaks of the old law being abolished and of the new law of that man—whom the woman encompasses—being received. He who was called a "man" in his mother's womb because of the divinity as his perpetual companion, both inside the womb and out. Because of this, Isaiah says, where he deals with his death in chapter 53: "Who shall declare his generation?" as if to say: no one, unless God reveals it. For from eternity, Wisdom, the Word, and the Son of God exists as begotten, and he is always with the Father, a Son without a mother, through whom the world was created in love and the Holy Spirit. Thus, in his second generation, he had a mother without a father, from whom he came to redeem by assuming flesh, and to lead back into the way of truth those whom he had created. 

But I return to Nizuah <note>original: "Nizuah." This likely refers to the *Sefer Nizzahon* (The Book of Victory), a famous medieval collection of Jewish polemics against Christianity, which Postel is here personifying as an opponent.</note>. He says: "In your Gospel of John, it is written that Christ said he had from the Father and God whatever he had; therefore, he was not God." This argument is the same as if you were to say: "I did this by the impulse of my mind, therefore I am inferior to my mind." Jesus is less than the Father according to his humanity, but equal according to his divinity. For as seen above, the explanation of all things in the Word is equal, just as it is in the mind and in the work. Thus the whole wisdom of the Father is in the Father, and the whole is in the Son; for as the man Christ, he takes the "form of a servant." Otherwise, he is equal in divinity, since there is one and equal deity in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in distinct persons. 

Another objection: "God did not choose the Christians as a people, since it is written: *He has not done so for every nation, and his judgments he has not manifested to them.*" <note>Psalm 147:20</note> That is understood regarding the Law. For elsewhere it says: "All nations, clap your hands; shout to God with the voice of exultation," since Zion is founded in the joy of the whole earth, etc. For all nations were to come and adore you, Lord. Truly, since the eternal Israel is in Jerusalem, it follows (as we hold) that Jerusalem was and is the Church of God, which you alone held under Moses. But for 1,500 years it has been open to the whole world, and it has become clear that the "True Israel" is the people of that Church. 

But a far greater and difficult question presents itself. "If Jesus was God," says Nizuah, "why was he hanged, and why did he endure all kinds of afflictions in himself? Why did he cry out that he was forsaken by God?" etc. I will satisfy this first with reason, and finally with authority. Let us return to the beginning. It has already been said often that a man is more perfect the more similar...

# BOOK IV OF GUILLAUME POSTEL

...one becomes more like God, and conversely <note>That is, one becomes less like God by doing the opposite.</note>. God gives to all and receives nothing; He bestows His goods upon enemies and blasphemers just as much as upon friends; He does all things for the sake of man; He exercises the greatest charity toward all; and He makes truth perpetual in the world through the continuation of species in matter. For this reason, He rejects things that are disordered, evil, and false. Since the Messiah was meant to be the most perfect man—and one greater than him cannot be granted—he ought to have become like God in all his actions. Therefore, he had to be utterly poor, possessing nothing, generously bestowing whatever was within him, but receiving from no one. He loved all men equally, as when he prayed for those crucifying him; he also did all things for the sake of man’s salvation. For man, without God, could not return to the innocence lost by Adam, a point proved most extensively in the first book. 

If having the greatest charity toward all is what makes one most like God, then no one can have a greater charity than when he lays down his life for the sake of the salvation of many and dies willingly. This is what Christ willed through his divinity, though in his body he surely shuddered, even to the point of sweating blood. <note>A reference to Jesus’ agony in the Garden of Gethsemane (Luke 22:44).</note> Furthermore, whoever wishes to show the greatest charity to a brother must necessarily have the primary care for the salvation of that brother's soul. He who takes up the care of souls takes up the assertion of the truth; and he who takes up the assertion of the truth must necessarily displease the powerful. For they foster vices in their commonwealths for the sake of their own utility and opinions; whatever the truth-teller stirs up, he seems to censure those vicious persons. Hence the proverb: *truth begets hatred.* <note>original Latin: "veritas odium parit," a famous line from the Roman playwright Terence.</note> Hatred immediately prepares evil for the one who asserts the truth. 

But if a man is to be most like God, he ought not to be swayed; he ought rather to die than to suffer the loss of truth. For what God does in the perpetuity of the species, so also the servant of truth ought to do concerning the assertion of truth; he must see as diligently that the vice of falsehood does not creep into the soul as God ensures that no blemish or disease creeps from nature into the body. Whoever is such a person must undergo death. Indeed, the prophets reveal these things more extensively, as will be evident in the prophetic Gospel. I will be content with one passage for now, as if pointing it out with my finger: Isaiah 53. *The Lord has laid on him the iniquities of us all, and by his bruises we are healed. He was wounded for our iniquities, bruised for our crimes.* <note>Isaiah 53:5-6, the "Suffering Servant" passage central to Christian claims that the Messiah was meant to suffer.</note> It is necessary to understand those words as referring to the Messiah, however much the Rabbis may distort them. 

Therefore, if your Messiah was to be most excellent, he had to excel by far in the goodness of his soul and always profess the truth, rather than having a "courtly"—that is, an outward—justice, which anyone who is eager for worldly splendor must possess. The soul is far more excellent than the body; therefore, its virtues are superior to the virtues of the body. Thus, the Messiah was to be of a better kind of excellence. For he who flourishes in abundance of things and worldly power cannot be good and most like God. Since there will always be poor and needy people in the whole world, if they are despised by him who possesses something, that possessor is not perfect, because he keeps things for splendor and vain reputation while the others do not have what is necessary; brothers die of hunger while one man devours everything. If he gives to all equally, he will immediately be like them: poor. If he gives but always remains in abundance, he must despoil some to clothe others, becoming an unjust predator who bestows the blood of another. 

But the Messiah was not to have sin in himself; hence it was necessary that he be poor, humble, abject, hated by the evil, and approved by only a few good men—such as Jesus Christ was. But I proceed to the summary of the life of Jesus Christ, so that the Jews may see that it is not just one or two distorted passages that fit him, but that his entire history is contained in the prophets no differently than it is in the Gospels. Unless all these things had been said of him, it would not be possible for them to agree in every detail. Thus, they shall recognize what he was to be. At the end, I will run through the other objections and solve them in a few words, which the Jews object against his coming. For they are so stupid and so addicted to their Rabbis that, because there are two comings of Christ, they expect two different Messiahs. <note>Postel refers to the Jewish tradition of *Mashiach ben Yosef* (a suffering Messiah) and *Mashiach ben David* (a triumphant Messiah), arguing they are actually the same person appearing twice.</note>

We believe that Jesus Christ, the Son, the Word, and the Wisdom of God the Father, was begotten from eternity, acting with the Father before the ages as a distinct person of the same divinity; that he brought about the distinction and creation of things together with the Father and the Holy Spirit in time; and finally, having been promised...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...that he had been revealed by the Holy Spirit to Moses and the prophets, just as He had previously revealed himself to Abraham and Jacob. Secondly, that he was born in Bethlehem of Judea of a virgin, so that he whom the Father had formed as man might, through him, lead that same humanity—which had become entirely depraved—back to the way of justice. Furthermore, as soon as he willed to be born into the world, he embraced poverty through his very deeds; at that time, he altered the affairs of the Israelites and transferred them to himself. On the 12th day <note>This refers to the Epiphany, traditionally twelve days after Christmas, when the Magi visited Jesus.</note> he was adored by the Magi kings, and finally fled into Egypt. John the Baptist preceded him like a new Elijah, inviting people in the desert to repentance in his name. Then, when he had grown up and become a perfect man, he called the apostles—mostly fishermen—so that he might make them "fishers of men." To them, he began to explain the law that would be useful and salvific for the whole world, so that they might preserve true piety in their souls. 

He willed that what he taught be confirmed by the greatest and unheard-of miracles. Because of these miracles, an incredible envy was conceived against him by the leaders of the Jews, who sought an opportunity to destroy him. Then he entered Jerusalem while the people shouted "Hosanna," even though he rode as a very poor man upon a donkey. Yet he acted as a king when he dared to drive the "sacred trade" <note>Referring to the buying and selling of sacrificial animals</note> from the holy place, overturning the tables of the money-changers <note>original: *trapezitarum*</note>. 

A little later, through the trickery of one of his own, he was sold for 30 pieces of silver; the hour and place were named where he would be handed over. Having found an opportunity at night, the traitor led cohorts to the Mount of Olives, where Jesus was captured and his followers were scattered. When he was brought there, the leaders and Pharisees convened concerning his death. Because of him, Herod and Pilate became friends. Judas, led by repentance, returned the price of the betrayal, which the leaders refused to put into the treasury <note>original: *corbanam*, the sacred treasury of the Temple</note> but used instead to buy the potter's field, destined for the burial of foreigners. Jesus was afflicted with every shame, insult, and beating by those who ought to have cherished him. Finally, with false witnesses asserting false things about him, he was judged to death between two thieves. His hands and feet were pierced, and he was fastened to the cross with nails. The whole frame of his body was undone by torments and mangling, and his face was so deformed by spit and the blood flowing from his head that he appeared like a despised leper, the most abject of men. And so that he might not miss any kind of cruelty, they offered him vinegar from a sponge when he thirsted on the cross. 

Meanwhile, when the soldiers wanted to divide his clothes among themselves, they finally cast lots for whose they should be. At the end, though they opened his side, they did not break his bones. Furthermore, an eclipse of the sun and moon occurred at that time, which was impossible during a fourteenth moon <note>A solar eclipse cannot occur during a full moon (the 14th day of the lunar month), marking this as a supernatural event to Postel.</note>; it lasted for three hours. He was buried, he rose again, he walked with his followers, and he ascended into heaven. He sent the Holy Spirit to the Apostles and disciples, through whom—speaking in the languages of all nations—the holy law of the New Testament was published. It is preserved by us until he returns in his second coming, terrible to all those who despise his law. Then, when he shall judge the living and the dead, he will hand over the kingdom to God the Father, after all corruption has been abolished. These are certain main points in which the sum of the matter lies. If the prophets support all these things, it is not possible for them to be understood as referring to anyone other than Jesus.

### THE NEW-ANCIENT OR PROPHETIC GOSPEL
<note>original: *Evangelium Caenopalaeum*. Postel likely coined this from the Greek *kainos* (new) and *palaios* (old) to suggest a Gospel that is both a new revelation and the ancient fulfillment of prophecy.</note>

Although I have primarily resolved to bring forward those things we hold by faith through the authorities of the Old Testament, I have nevertheless decided not to neglect reason whenever it can support authority. All philosophers and Jews in whom there is reason will admit to me that God is the one creator of heaven and earth, of things visible and invisible. They cannot deny that it is impossible for anything to be created by God except by supreme Power, through supreme Wisdom, for the sake of some end in the Will. For Power would be in vain if it did not know by what art or in what way things were to be done; and both would be present in vain unless the Will and Love of a certain end induced the action. 

Therefore, the entire creation of things is in God the Almighty [the Father]; likewise, it is all in the most wise Son or Word [Wisdom]; and all in the almighty Will, Love, or Holy Spirit proceeding from both. And yet there are not three Almighties, but one Almighty. We see that we can do nothing in the "image of God"—that is, the soul placed within us—unless we have the whole matter to be done in the mind, the whole in the explanation, and the whole in the work and thought. There can never be a Will unless Power and Knowledge precede it. Moses, the leader of the prophets, showed these three in the first two periods...

# GUILLAUME POSTEL BOOK IV. 393

...placed in the periods of Genesis. "In the beginning," he says, "God created the heavens and the earth, but the earth was empty and void, and the spirit of the Lord moved over the waters." <note>original: "In principio, inquit, deus creauit cœlū & terram, terra aūt erat inanis & uacua, & ſpūs dn̄i ferebat ſup aquas."</note> There you see God, the Principle, and the Spirit. "In the beginning," that is, in the Son, God created all things, which by the effect of the Holy Spirit (acting as the "finger of God") received material existence. David indeed says in Psalm 32: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their power by the breath of his mouth." <note>original: "Verbo dn̄i cœli firmati ſunt, & ſpiritu oris eius omnis uirtus eorū." Reference: Psalm 33:6 in modern numbering.</note> There he also brings forward God, the Word, and the Spirit. For nothing can be brought into being without those three <term>middot</term> <note>Hebrew: "measures" or "attributes." Postel uses this Kabbalistic term to refer to the persons of the Trinity.</note>, that is, properties. And again: "He will send his word and melt them; his spirit will blow and the waters will flow." God sends his Word and Holy Spirit into all natural things, as if to give them form, and without these nothing happens. Yet there is but one reality, one action, and one God, doing all things in all.

I have frequently taught above—especially in my *Refutation of Muhammad* <note>Postel refers to his work *Alcorani seu legis Mahometi... confutatio*, where he attempted to explain Christian doctrines like the Trinity to a Muslim audience using logic.</note>—why that eternal Mind calls the Son "the Word." God has no name that can be bestowed upon him, or that can entirely bring his nature before the object of our mind; for if our mind could comprehend an absolute notion of the First Cause, it would be equal or superior to it. In this, we recognize our mind is greater than the sensible world: because we can encompass the immense mass of the heavens within our thought. Therefore, God, pitying our weakness in contemplating him (who is our ultimate goal), revealed names familiar to holy men, so that through their meaning and similarity we might arrive at a conjecture of such great majesty. Truly, to explain the Second Person in the divine, nothing could be given more familiar to our senses than "the Word." For just as we have nothing prior to a thought except to open that concept of the mind with a word, so Divine Providence—thinking eternally about this world-mass to be created and seeing all things in it before matter was created—immediately distinguished that same mass through the Word and Wisdom, and brought it into being when it seemed right. Therefore he called the Son "the Word," a term which the Greek philosophers borrowed and called <term>Logos</term> <note>original: "λογου", Greek for "word," "reason," or "discourse."</note>. Our Evangelist John, weaving the story of Jesus Christ's life on earth from the eternal generation of the Word, said: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him," etc. We shall speak of this Word in many places as the occasion arises. Regarding the Wisdom of God, who is Jesus Christ, Solomon says: "The Lord by wisdom founded the earth, and established the heavens by understanding." And David: "In wisdom you have made all things." From these, the image of the blessed Trinity and the mystery of creation are sufficiently clear.

Now we must come to the <term>prophetic</term> revelations about what God wished to say regarding that happy Wisdom, so that we may more diligently discern what sort of person the Messiah was to be. God promised Abraham, the leader of restored piety, that a son would be born to him, in whose seed all nations were to be blessed—and this not just in one place, but in many. God further added that he would give that land to his seed forever. Moreover, God confirmed those promises by giving offspring to the elderly Abraham and Sarah, even though by the natural course of things it was impossible either for him to beget or for her to conceive. This happened because they believed that all things are possible for God. These matters must be carefully <term>weighed</term> <note>original: "ppēdēda", from the Latin "perpendenda."</note>, because they are the basis of sacred history. The Messiah is promised in the seed of Abraham; therefore, he was to be a man. And in that same seed, all nations were to be blessed (that is, saved and led to the truth). Yet it is impossible for this to be done by a man alone. Likewise, it is impossible for a man to rule the whole world, since God—while the free will of man lasts—cannot maintain earthly power through a mere human. Yet it was to happen, because the truthful God said so. Therefore, the promised Messiah was to be both Man and God: Man, because he was truly of the seed of Abraham; God, because he had to save all nations, for a man cannot do that. In truth, even in fleeting matters, God does not rule the whole world by force, as I taught above. Yet he shall rule and does rule; from which it follows that the empire of the Messiah and his law are spiritual, since otherwise it would not endure forever, as this world is not eternal but temporary. But the seed of David and Abraham must reign in the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end. Therefore, the promised Messiah had to be God and man, his empire purely spiritual, and the land of his faithful the fellowship of the holy Church. And you, in many places in your <term>gemaras</term> <note>original: "gemaris", referring to the Gemara, the rabbinical commentaries that form part of the Talmud.</note>, hold such a happy and great law of the Messiah, and the...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...was from Moses and the prophets, revealed by the Holy Spirit, which He had previously opened to Abraham and Jacob. But in the second birth, He was born in Bethlehem of Judea from a virgin, so that He—through whom the Father had formed man—might lead that same man, who was entirely depraved, back to the path of justice. Furthermore, as soon as He willed to be born into the world, He embraced poverty in His very actions, and thus altered the affairs of the Israelites and transferred them into Himself. Born on the 13th day <note>This refers to the Epiphany, traditionally celebrated 12-13 days after Christmas.</note>, He was adored by the Magi kings, and finally fled into Egypt. Then, when He had grown up and become a perfect man, He called the apostles—mostly fishermen—so that He might make them fishers of men. To them, He began to explain the law that would be useful and salvific for the whole world, so that they might preserve piety entirely in their souls. 

He willed that what He taught be confirmed by the greatest and unheard-of miracles. Because of these miracles, an incredible envy was conceived against Him by the leaders of the Jews, who sought an occasion to destroy Him. Then He entered Jerusalem, with the people crying "Hosanna," even though He rode as the poorest of men upon a donkey. He acted as a King when He dared to drive the "sacred market" from the holy place, overturning the tables of the money-changers. 

Shortly after, by the deceit of one of His own, He was sold for 30 silver coins; the hour and place were named where He would be delivered into their hands. Having found an opportunity at night, [Judas] led cohorts to the Mount of Olives, where [Jesus] was captured and His followers dispersed. Once He was brought there, the leaders and Pharisees met concerning His death. Herod and Pilate became friends because of Him. Judas, led by repentance, returned the price, which the leaders did not want to put into the *corban* <note>original: "corbanā". This refers to the Temple treasury or the chest for offerings.</note>, but used for the purchase of a potter's field destined for the burial of pilgrims. 

Afflicted with every shame, insult, and lashing by those who should have cherished Him, He was finally sentenced to death between two thieves by false witnesses asserting false things about Him. His hands and feet were pierced, and He was fixed to the cross with nails. The entire framework of His body was undone by torments and mangling, and His face was so deformed by spit and the blood flowing from His head that He seemed like a despised leper, the most abject of men. And so that He would feel every kind of cruelty, they offered vinegar from a sponge to Him as He thirsted on the cross. Meanwhile, when the soldiers wanted to divide His clothes among themselves, they finally settled by lot whose they should be. Finally, though they opened His side, they did not break [His legs]. 

An eclipse of the sun and moon occurred at that time—impossible during the fourteenth moon <note>This refers to the full moon of Passover; a solar eclipse is scientifically impossible during a full moon, which Postel cites as proof of a miracle.</note>—and lasted for three hours. He was buried, He rose, He walked with His followers, He ascended into heaven, and He sent the Holy Spirit to the Apostles and disciples. By them, speaking in the tongues of all nations, the holy law of the New Testament was published, and it is kept by us until He returns in His second coming, terrifying to all who despise His law. Then, when He judges the living and the dead, He will hand over the kingdom to God the Father, with all corruption abolished. These are certain chapters in which the sum of these matters lies. If the prophets support all these things, it is not possible that they refer to anyone other than Jesus.

### THE NEW-ANCIENT GOSPEL, OR THE PROPHETIC GOSPEL.
<note>original: "EVANGELIVM CAENOPALAEVM". Postel uses the term "Caenopalaeum" (New-Old) to argue that the Christian Gospel is actually the most ancient and original truth restored.</note>

Although I have primarily set out to bring forward the authority of the Old Testament for those things which we hold by faith, I have nevertheless decided not to neglect reason whenever it can support that authority. All philosophers and Jews alike in whom there is reason will admit to me that God is the one creator of heaven and earth, of things visible and invisible. They cannot deny that it is impossible for anything to be created by God unless it is done by supreme power, through supreme wisdom, and by the will for the sake of some end. 

For Power would be in vain if it did not know by what art or in what manner things were to be done; and both would be present in vain unless the will and love of a certain end induced it. Therefore, the entire creation of things is in God the Almighty; it is likewise entirely in the most wise and almighty Son or Word; and it is entirely in the almighty Will, Love, or Holy Spirit proceeding from both. And yet, there are not three Almighties, but one Almighty. We see that we can do nothing in the image of God—that is, the soul placed within us—unless we have the whole matter to be done in our mind, the whole in the explanation, and the whole in the work and thought. There can never be a Will unless Power and Knowledge precede it. Moses, the leader of the prophets, placed these three in the first two...

### WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK 4

...placed in the cycles of Genesis.
> "In the beginning," it says, "God created the heaven and the earth; but the earth was void and empty, and the spirit of the Lord moved over the waters."

In that passage, you see God, the Beginning, and the Spirit. "In the beginning"—that is, in the Son—God created all things <note>original: "In principio, id est in filio." A common medieval interpretation linking the 'beginning' of Genesis with the 'Word' in the Gospel of John</note>, which through the effect of the Holy Spirit, acting as the finger of God, received their material existence. Truly, David says in Psalm 32:
> "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the breath of his mouth all their power."

There also he brings forward God, the Word, and the Spirit. For nothing can be brought into existence without those three <term>middot<note>A Hebrew term meaning 'measures' or 'attributes,' referring here to the three persons of the Trinity as divine properties.</note></term>, that is, properties. And likewise:
> "He will send his word and melt them; his spirit will blow and the waters will flow."

In all natural things, God sends the Word and the Holy Spirit so that forms may be given to them; without these, nothing would exist. Yet there is but one thing, one action, one God, doing all things in all. Why that eternal Mind calls the Son "the Word," I have taught frequently above, most especially in the <term>refutation of Muhammad<note>Postel refers to his own polemical works against Islam, where he argued for the Trinity using philosophical logic.</note></term>. God has no name that can be bestowed upon Him, or that can entirely draw His nature into the focus of the mind; for then our mind would be equal or superior to the First Cause if it could comprehend an absolute notion of it. In this, indeed, we recognize our mind to be greater than the sensible world: that we can encompass the immense mass of the heavens within it. God, therefore, pitying our weakness in contemplating Him who is our goal, revealed to holy men names familiar to them, so that through their meaning and similarity we might arrive at a conjecture of such great majesty. Truly, to explain the second person in the divine nature, nothing could be given more familiar to our senses than the "Word." For just as we have no earlier way to reveal what we have thought than to open the concept of the mind with a word, so divine providence—thinking from eternity about the creation of this mass, and seeing all things in it before matter was created—immediately distinguished that same mass through the Word and Wisdom, and brought it into being when it seemed right. Therefore He called the Son the Word, a term which the Greek philosophers borrowed and called <note>original: "λογον"</note> **the Logos**. Our evangelist John, weaving the life of Jesus Christ on earth from the eternal generation of the Word, said:
> "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him," etc.

We shall speak of this Word in many places as the occasion arises. Concerning the Wisdom of God, which is Jesus Christ, Solomon says:
> "The Lord by wisdom founded the earth, he established the heavens by understanding."

and David:
> "In wisdom you have made all things."

From these, the image of the blessed Trinity and the mystery of creation are sufficiently clear. Now, after those things which God willed to say concerning that happy Wisdom, we must come to the prophetic revelations, so that from them we may more diligently discern what kind of person the Messiah was to be. God promised to Abraham, the leader of restored piety, that a son would be born to him, in whose seed all nations were to be blessed; and this not in only one place, but in many. God added, truly, that He would give that land to his seed forever. Moreover, God confirmed those promises by giving offspring to the elderly Abraham and Sarah, when it was impossible by the natural course of things either for him to beget or for her to conceive. This happened because they believed that all things are possible for God. Truly, these things must be weighed diligently, for they are the foundation of sacred matters. The Messiah is promised in the seed of Abraham; therefore He was to be a man, and in Him all nations were to be blessed—that is, saved and brought to the truth. But it is impossible for this to be done by a mere man. Likewise, it is impossible for a man to rule the whole world, since God (while man's free will remains) is not suited to holding earthly power <note>Postel argues that God does not rule the world through raw force but through spiritual influence</note>. Yet it was going to happen, because God, who is truthful, said so. Therefore the promised Messiah was to be both man and God: man, because He was truly of the seed of Abraham; God, because He had to save all nations. For a man cannot do that. Indeed, as I taught above, God cannot rule the whole world even in fleeting matters. Yet He will rule and does rule; from which it follows that the empire of the Messiah and His law is spiritual, since otherwise it would not endure forever, for this world is not eternal but temporary. But the seed of David and Abraham must reign in the house of Jacob forever, and of His kingdom there shall be no end. Therefore the promised Messiah had to be God and man, and His empire only spiritual, and the land of His faithful a fellowship of the holy church. And you, in many places in your <term>Gemaras<note>The Gemara is the component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis and commentary on the Mishnah.</note></term>, hold to such a happy and great law of the Messiah, and Him
