### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
<note>original: "DE ORBIS CONCORDIA"</note>

The Messiah was to come in such a way that the Law of Moses, and even Moses himself, would be almost nothing in comparison to him. Yet nothing greater than God-become-man can be given; this is Jesus, and his law is a spiritual law. In the use of natural things—from which religion seems to differ only slightly to those who consider it lightly—God teaches that the same process happens daily, by shaping individual men toward their children in the very same way. For the sake of virtue, and for the sake of the goals to be sought in the places where they are born, but especially to persuade them toward works of virtue and piety, parents incite their children—who are unskilled in all things due to their age—toward noble things. They give them those things by which they see them most easily held, and with promises of similar things to come daily, they soothe them if they continue in what they have begun, as if it would always be so for them. Meanwhile, they cover with silence what will eventually happen: that in another succeeding age, they will no longer seek **treats** <note>original: "crustula," literally little cakes or cookies used as rewards for children</note> or little gifts as a reward for virtue, but rather a good reputation. And finally, if they continue to be good, seeing that even fame is fleeting and an unworthy reward for such great labors, they will refer everything to the praise of the Creator alone, so that they seek no reward for themselves, committing all things to the judgment of Him who placed them here.

Since they consider this most just and believe it with certainty, they cannot fail to attain the most just things from Him (I am speaking here of a person instructed under true religion). Did those fathers who, with a single word, called all the rewards of virtue, little gifts, glory, reputation, and the hope of eternal life "**treats**," did they lie? Did they deliberately assert what was false? Not at all. For so that they might accommodate themselves to children—who could neither grasp nor desire other things—they offered and promised those things by which they knew they could then be captured. In a similar way, God promised the successors of Abraham, as a total reward, a fertile land and whatever accompanies it for happiness, if they would keep His precepts. 

The children of Abraham were soothed and occupied by those **treats** for about five hundred years, focused on pastoral matters, lacking a formal government, and with little ambition. Moses took them up as they were, so to speak, **leaving their youth** <term>ex ephebis<note>A Greek-derived term referring to young men reaching the age of maturity and entering social responsibility.</note></term>. Under him, they spent the following age in the greatest splendor of affairs: in a republic, in a kingdom, and in an aristocracy, right up until it was time to recognize those rewards as empty and to refer all things back to God. Two parts of this history went well, and with the highest favor of God; but when, at the **turning point** <term>catastrophe<note>Postel uses the theatrical term for the final resolution of a plot to describe the critical point in Israel's history when they were meant to transition to spiritual maturity.</note></term>, they committed an error and judged that the rewards of childhood and youth were also fit for old age, they went astray, wandering into a **depraved mind** <note>original: "reprobum sensum," an allusion to Romans 1:28</note>.

Just as in the ages of a man nothing is more certain than change, but nothing is more uncertain than the exact moment of alteration (for it is certain that a child becomes a boy, a boy a youth, a youth a man, and a man an elder; yet scarcely anyone knows when it happens until after it has already occurred), so it was in the Law. When they ought to have passed over to a greater fortune, they nevertheless forced Moses, their protector, to live in exile for forty years; and even then, they barely submitted to him in the name of God, despite daily miracles throughout those entire forty years. They flourished, indeed, under David and Solomon. But when he came who was to draw them from the fleeting and empty toward the perfect reward of virtue, after he had spent nearly forty years among them (a number falling within a decade, which pertains to that transition), they killed him most cruelly. Forty years later, they perished in a slaughter, until they were gathered there again, only to fall again a little after forty years. 

And yet—**if you can believe it** <note>original: "si dijs placet," a classical idiom expressing irony or indignation</note>—these people still expect to have youth and earthly rewards; they do not feel that they are nourishing a plague in their own bosom, even though they have now been without God for longer than their youth and the age of their strength lasted. But these are side-notes for the sake of interpreting this passage. In that seed of Abraham (as I had said), all nations were to be blessed; he was necessarily to be God and man together—most humble, with a spiritual law, possessing hearts and souls rather than things—the King of the whole world. When Jacob blessed his sons, being divinely inspired, he said:

-> "The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor a lawgiver from his thigh, until **Shiloh** comes, who shall be the expectation of the nations, tying his foal to the vineyard, and his donkey to the vine, O my son. He shall wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape." <-

These things must be weighed carefully. There is no doubt that these things are said of the Messiah, for when it says absolutely, "he shall be the expectation of the nations," no one else but the Messiah can be that, who is both man and God. For in no one else ought all peoples to hope but in God, because no one is powerful enough to save all except God. But the Messiah was to be a man; therefore, He is also God. A man, so that in his body...

### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK 4

...he might pay the penalty in his body on behalf of all men; and as God, so that he might be powerful enough to save everyone. But a great mystery lies hidden in the word **Shiloh** <note>original: "שילה" (Shiloh). This refers to the prophecy in Genesis 49:10: "The scepter shall not depart from Judah... until Shiloh comes."</note>. The ancient interpreters seem to have read it as *Shiloah* <note>original: "שילוח" (Shiloah), meaning "Sent"</note>, using the letter *Heth* instead of *He*; and therefore they translated it as "he who is to be sent." Or perhaps they translated it that way intentionally, wishing to hide this holy mystery from the pagans. However, that word truly signifies "his son." **David Kimhi** <note>original: "Dauid Chimhí," a famous 12th-13th century Jewish biblical commentator and grammarian</note> says in his exposition that *Shiloh* (שילה) is the same as *beno* (בנו), meaning "his son," and David [Kimhi] suggests this refers to the Messiah. That this should not be understood as referring to King David is shown by the fact that the "scepter" actually began under him, rather than failing or departing. Furthermore, King David was so wealthy, and so far removed from the poverty of riding a donkey, that no king (except his son Solomon) was ever richer in proportion to his kingdom.

But let us look at the mystery. That relative suffix, the letter *He* (ה), encompasses both generations of Jesus Christ. For it is written and read with a *He*, yet understood with a *Vav* (ו) <note>In Hebrew grammar, the letter He at the end of a word can signify a feminine "her," while the Vav signifies a masculine "his." Postel is making a mystical-linguistic argument about Christ’s dual nature.</note>. For this reason, it remains silent about the names of both parents. When it is read as *He*, it is of the feminine gender, and denotes "her son"—that is, the son of the **Virgin Mary**. When it is understood as a *Vav*, it is of the masculine gender, and signifies his eternal progression and generation from the **Father**. This is what is understood first when we speak of him; just as when we speak of a man, we understand his reason before we understand his body. For just as thought is prior to knowledge, the soul prior to the body, and eternal generation prior to temporal generation—and yet we understand nothing except from what comes after—so the prophet wished to subject to our senses what we have seen, rather than writing what we necessarily think of first. He expressed Christ’s humanity through the *He*, but kept his divinity silent within the *Vav*. Nor is there anything else like this in the whole of Scripture, just as no man is like the Messiah in his birth. 

Just as he had to differ infinitely by his most excellent condition, even from the most perfect man, so too in his manner of being born. For if he had been born in the flesh outside the vessels of nature without a woman, by the work of God the Father and the Holy Spirit, he would have had Adam as a companion <note>i.e., he would have been unique in the same way the first man was created directly by God</note>. If he had been born in our usual way, he would have been like all other men. Therefore, he ought to have had nothing in common [with either extreme] except in part, so that by being different from both, he might nevertheless join both together. He had a Father without a mother, and a mother without a father; therefore Moses wished to encompass both generations in a single syllable. God, just as He had inspired it, also preserved it from the impious corruption of the scribes. 

Truly, that good old man <note>referring to the patriarch Jacob, who gives the Shiloh prophecy on his deathbed</note> was not content to say that the Messiah would come when the kingdom and the senate had perished and the priests were stripped of authority, unless he also noted two most excellent qualities in the Messiah: **poverty** and **passion**. When the Messiah binds his donkey to the vine’s trunk, it is due to a lack of space, since he had no place to lay his head. This denotes that he willingly wished to embrace remarkable humility and poverty. Otherwise, could he—who had raised so many men from the dead, and helped centurions, rulers of the synagogue, and men established in the highest authority and great wealth in their moment of greatest crisis—not have obtained any riches he wanted if he had wished to sell his services? There is no one who would not gladly acknowledge as heir and lord the man who had restored them to life. Yet Jesus Christ was, by profession, the poorest of men; he did not wish to be richer than he was. About to enter Jerusalem, he arranged for a donkey—one suited for the use of the poor out of civic piety—to be untied from its post for him. As a gentle and poor king, he entered Jerusalem, that most ungrateful city, which because of his kindness and humility killed its own king, and will eternally pay the penalty for neglecting the Just One.

He mentions the other quality when he says: *He shall wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape.* <note>Genesis 49:11</note> This notes the magnitude of his torments and the bloody outpouring of blood from his whole body. Wishing to suggest this through the mouth of **Isaiah** (chapter 63), the Holy Spirit says:

> Who is this who comes with dyed red garments, etc.? The Messiah responds: It is I, who speak justice, and lead the captive Israel back to safety. Why is your clothing red, and your garments like those of people treading in a winepress? Answer: I have trodden the winepress alone, and of all the nations there was no man with me, etc.

This is the staining of his clothes in his own blood. You cannot deny that these things are said of the Messiah, since he is the one who speaks justice, and who alone can save the captive Israel. But after he spoke of his own blood, he immediately added words concerning yours; of which, as you know, there was such a great outpouring that its rivers flowed from here...

### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...the future Messiah will be such that the law of Moses, and Moses himself, are almost nothing in comparison to him. Yet nothing greater than a Man-God can be given to humanity; this is Jesus, and his law is a spiritual law. In the use of natural things—from which religion seems to differ only slightly to those who consider it lightly—God teaches that the same process occurs daily, by training individual men toward their children in the same way. 

For the sake of virtue and the things to be sought after where they are born, but especially in persuading one toward works of virtue and piety, parents incite their children (who are unskilled in all things due to their age) toward noble things. They give them those things by which they see the children are most captivated, and they soothe them with promises of similar things to come daily if they persist in what they have begun, as if it would always be thus for them. Meanwhile, they cover in silence what will eventually happen: that as another age succeeds, they will no longer seek **little cookies** <note>original: "crustula," a common Latin term for small sweets or treats used as rewards for children</note> or **small gifts** <note>original: "munuscula"</note> as a reward for virtue, but rather fame. Since they consider this most just and believe it with certainty, they cannot fail to attain the most just things from Him (I am speaking here of a man instructed under true religion). Just as in the ages of a man nothing is more certain than change, but nothing is more uncertain than the exact moment of alteration (for it is certain that a child becomes a boy, a boy a youth, a youth a man, and a man an elder; yet hardly anyone knows *when* it happens until after it has already occurred), so it was in the Law. They flourished indeed under **David** and **Solomon**, but when He came who was meant to draw them from the fleeting and empty toward the perfect reward of virtue—after He had lived among them for nearly forty years (the number below the decade pertains to this)—they killed Him most cruelly. Forty years later, they themselves perished in a slaughter, until having been gathered there again, they fell again a little after forty years. And yet, if it please the gods, these people still think they are going to have, and they still expect, their youth and earthly rewards. They do not feel that they are nourishing a plague in their own bosom, even though they have now been without God longer than their youth and the age of their strength lasted.

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK 4

...in his body, he might atone for all men; and as God, he might be powerful enough to save all. But a great mystery lies hidden in the word **Shiloh** <note>Hebrew: שילה. A messianic title from the prophecy in Genesis 49:10</note>. Ancient interpreters seem to have read *Shelah* <note>Hebrew: שלה</note> with the letter *Heth* instead of *He*, and therefore they translated it as "he who is to be sent." Or perhaps, wishing to deliberately hide this holy mystery from the Gentiles, they translated it that way. In truth, that word signifies "his son." David Kimhi <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish rabbi and grammarian, often called the Radak</note> says in his explanation of **Shiloh** <note>שילה</note>, that it means **his son** <note>Hebrew: בנו, *beno*</note>, and he indicates that David, or the Messiah, is meant. That it should not be understood as referring to King David is shown by the fact that the scepter actually *began* under him; it did not fail. Furthermore, King David was so wealthy—and far removed from the poverty of riding a donkey—that no king (except his son Solomon) was ever richer in proportion to his kingdom.

But let us return to the mystery. That relative suffix **He** <note>The Hebrew letter ה</note> encompasses both "generations" (or origins) of Jesus Christ. For it is written and read with the letter *He*, but it is understood as having the letter *Vav* <note>The Hebrew letter ו, which usually signifies the masculine "his"</note>. Because of this, the names of both parents are kept silent. When it is read as *He*, it is of the feminine gender, and it denotes "her son," that is, the son of the Virgin Mary. When it is understood as *Vav*, it is of the masculine gender, and signifies his eternal progression and generation from the Father. This is understood first when we speak of him, just as when we speak of a human being, we first understand their reason before their physical body. For just as thought comes before knowledge, the soul before the body, and eternal generation before temporal birth—and yet we understand nothing except through what comes after—so the prophet wished to subject to our senses what we have seen; he did not write what we necessarily think of first. He expressed Christ's humanity through the *He*, while he kept the divinity silent within the *Vav*. 

Nor is there anything else like this in the whole of Scripture, just as no human is like the Messiah in his birth. Since he had to differ infinitely in his most excellent condition, even from the most perfect man, so too must he differ in the manner of his birth. For if he had been born physically outside the "vessel of nature" <note>i.e., the womb</note> without a woman, by the operation of God the Father and the Holy Spirit, he would have had Adam as a companion. If he were born in our usual way, he would have been like all other men. Therefore, he ought to have nothing in common with them except in part, so that, by being different from both, he might nonetheless join both together. He had a Father without a mother, and a mother without a father; therefore Moses wished to encompass both generations in a single syllable. God, who had inspired this, preserved it even from the wicked corruption of the scribes.

Indeed, the good old man <note>referring to the patriarch Jacob, who gives the prophecy in Genesis 49</note> did not think it enough to have said that the Messiah would come when the kingdom and the high council were perishing and the priests were removed from power, unless he also noted two most excellent qualities in the Messiah: poverty and passion. When he [the Messiah] ties his donkey to the vine-stalk, he notes a lack of place, as he had nowhere to lay his head. It marks that he willingly wished to embrace distinguished humility and poverty. Otherwise, since he had raised so many men from the dead and had helped centurions, leaders of synagogues, and men established in the highest authority and great wealth in their moments of extreme crisis, what riches could he not have obtained if he had wished to sell his services? There is no one who would not have gladly acknowledged as heir and lord the man who had restored their life. 

Jesus Christ was, and was by profession, the poorest of men; he did not wish to be richer than he was. When he was about to enter Jerusalem, he arranged for a young donkey—suited for the uses of the poor out of civic piety—to be untied from its post for him. With it, he entered Jerusalem as a gentle and poor king. He entered that most ungrateful city, which, despite his favors and humility, would destroy its king, and which will forever pay the penalty for neglecting the Just One.

He mentions another quality when he says: *He shall wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape.* For this notes the magnitude of his torments and the bloody outpouring of blood from his whole body. Wishing to indicate this through Isaiah 63, the Holy Spirit speaks thus:

> Who is this who comes with red-dyed garments, etc.? The Messiah responds: It is I, who speak justice, and who lead the captive Israel back to safety. Why is your clothing red, and your garments like those of people treading in a winepress? Response: I have trodden the winepress alone, and of all the nations there was no man with me, etc.

This is the "dipping of garments" in his blood. You cannot deny that these things are said of the Messiah, since he is the one who speaks justice, and who alone can save the captive Israel. But after he spoke of his own blood, he immediately added words concerning yours—of which, as you know, there was such a great outpouring that its rivers from here...

Having previously discussed the linguistic mysteries of the name "Shiloh," he now addresses the Jewish scholars ("Rabbis") directly, interpreting the symbolic language of the Torah—specifically the "washing of garments in wine"—as a reference to the blood of Christ rather than a literal or luxury-related practice.</meta>

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

...at its rising, and from there to its setting, it would flow even into the sea; and yet you do not understand. Otherwise, I ask you, what benefit would there be in washing and dipping garments in wine? For they cannot be cleansed by wine, nor does any pleasant scent or instrument of luxury—the direction in which you drag all interpretations—come from a garment submerged in wine; rather, it leaves a stain. Therefore, that dipping must be understood as referring to the blood of Jesus Christ, as will be discussed more extensively regarding the Passion. I come now to those revelations which Moses had and brought forth concerning the Messiah. In many places—indeed, almost everywhere—there are figures looking toward Christ. Just as the rejection of Moses by his own people matches Christ being rejected and killed; the selling of Joseph matches Christ’s being sold; the crossing of the Red Sea and the sprinkling of blood matches baptism; the eating of the Passover lamb matches the offering of his body for the salvation of all; the raising of the serpent <note>The "Brazen Serpent" from Numbers 21, which healed those who looked at it</note>, at which those who looked were healed, just as those trusting in Christ crucified and raised on high are saved; the leading of Isaac to death while he was innocent, and so forth. But since you hardly believe even in these explicit passages, I do not wish to argue with you using them; I have decided to set forth the most manifest things.

<margin>Deuteronomy 18</margin>
God says to Moses: "I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, like unto you, and I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him. But whoever will not hear my words which he shall speak in my name, I will be the avenger." Now, so that a true prophet might be distinguished from a false one, God adds: "If what he predicted comes to pass, he is a true prophet; otherwise, he is false." These things also must be examined. For I think the stubborn Rabbis will not easily admit these things about the Messiah, because they seem to work against what we believe about Jesus Christ. They will say, "He calls him a prophet, therefore he is not God." They admit that the Messiah must be a most perfect man. But no greater quality can be given to a man than prophecy; therefore, it was necessary for him to possess it so excellently that even the greatest men positioned next to him would be as nothing. There were four major prophets, twelve minor; David, Solomon, Nathan, Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, and many others, such as the disciples of Hillel <note>A famous Jewish sage and scholar from the 1st century BCE</note>, and up to Simon the Just <note>A High Priest during the Second Temple period</note> there were countless most holy men; and yet this one is called "the Prophet" by excellence <note>original Latin: *per antonomasiam* — a rhetorical term for using a title as a proper name</note>, as if the others were nothing. 

It is also necessary to concede divinity in him from what Moses wrote. For when he says, "Whoever will not hear his words," he excludes no one from his law. If he includes all—as he certainly does—then he teaches that all who keep that law are saved through it. But we have shown that by a single law of bodies, or civil law, one cannot rule even the whole world for God. Therefore, he was speaking of one who would be God by these words; otherwise, he could not give a saving law to the whole world, and he ought to have such right only over souls throughout the entire world; but good bodies, or men, follow the movement of souls. 

But you will say: "If he was to be both prophet and God, why did the prophets not say so?" If you thought even once that God could dwell in the person of a prophet, no prophet would have been anything but a Messiah and God to you. For you sought gods so close to you that you preferred to choose a single calf <note>The Golden Calf from Exodus 32</note> by popular consent rather than the God whose fire was so great before your eyes that you could not bear it. Whoever had shown you even the slightest bit of prophecy would immediately have been held as God; since the serpent, raised as a sign on account of the damage from serpents, was impiously preferred by you over the God of heaven, whose present power was in the holier temple. 

However, Christ possessed the most excellent signs of a true prophet. For he foretold so many things that they can scarcely be numbered. He predicted the overturning of your city with tears; he said your captivity would happen shortly; that in Judea, those women who had not given birth would be happy. He predicted his own future resurrection and proved it by the deed; likewise his ascension, and the mission of the Holy Spirit, the deaths of his own followers, the miracles that would happen in his name, and so forth—innumerable things, which brought nothing but bitterness to a wicked nation. All nations believed in him, even when scarcely a few Jews had approached the truth; he is indeed Christ, the supreme man...

[Un]derstandable even to children is that law; he would seem unjust who would bind men to the impossible. Therefore, O Jews, you ought not to rise up against us because we do not observe your ceremonies. On the same day that Jesus was conceived by the Virgin and died <note>Postel follows a tradition that the Annunciation/Conception and the Crucifixion occurred on the same calendar date, March 25.</note>, the fruit of the ceremonies perished; at that same time, Jesus and his law began, which the Spirit hinted at through the mouth of Isaiah, when he said: *Before the child knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land that you detest will be forsaken.* <note>original: "Antequam puer sciret reprobare malum, & eligere bonum, derelinquetur terra quam tu detestaris." Isaiah 7:16.</note> For when Christ was born, the sentence for the overturning of Jerusalem was passed, since God knew it would come to pass that his own citizens would put him to death, and the new law succeeded the old. Yet his power was made manifest after his death, when you no longer saw your signs. Indeed, around the time of his birth, the power of judgment was taken away by King Herod, who had seized the tyranny by killing those of royal blood. The place of his birth must be touched upon. Micah, chapter 5: *You shall be joined to the army, the city to be destroyed by the army; they have laid siege against us, with a rod they shall strike the cheek of the judge of Israel. And you, Bethlehem Ephrata, are a little one among the thousands of Judah. From you shall come forth for me he who is to be ruler in Israel, and his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity.* <note>Micah 5:1–2. Postel uses this to prove both the location of the birth and the Messiah's eternal divinity.</note> Because of this, he will give them up until the time in which she who is in labor shall give birth, and the remnant of his brothers shall be converted to the children of Israel, and (a little later) he shall be magnified even to the ends of the earth. And this man shall be our peace, etc. These things are most clearly said concerning the Messiah, and they mark the place of his birth, his divinity, and his office. Since the city was to be destroyed shortly after the Messiah was killed, he began with a threat of the punishments that were to come upon Israel in Jerusalem. Then he adds that Bethlehem does not lack its own greatness, since from it would be born the leader for the true Israel and for the survivor <unclear>st</unclear>ti after the destruction of the other <note>Likely referring to the spiritual "survivors" or the Church after the fall of the Second Temple.</note>, whose origin would not be like that of men, but would proceed from the Father God from eternity. That these things are understood to be about the Messiah is supported by the <term>Targum</term> <note>The Targums are ancient Aramaic translations and interpretations of the Hebrew Bible which often identify specific passages as messianic.</note>; for it says that this one will be the Messiah. Therefore, the Messiah is God and man; and because he is eternal God, he will give those people up for a time to their own judgment, until she who is in labor gives birth—that is, until Titus comes to the ruin [of the city]. <note>Titus was the Roman general, later Emperor, who destroyed Jerusalem and the Temple in 70 AD.</note> For we have seen that it must be understood in this way from the last chapter of Isaiah. For that it should be understood of the Messiah, the interpreters say: *Before she was in labor, she gave birth, and before the pain of birth came, she brought forth a male child.* <note>Isaiah 66:7.</note> That is, before Titus was born, the Messiah, the Son of God, was born. Because the prophet, understanding by divine inspiration that people would also fight against Christ because he called himself the Son of God, added: *Who has ever heard such a thing? And who has seen the like?* This must be a great miracle, and certainly, according to the letter, it can be understood of the birth by the Virgin, who brought forth a male child without pain. Since the following things seem to be said of the Messiah and his coming in the flesh, it means that God, the author of all generation, also generates the Son from eternity. But I prefer to agree with the Jews by referring all these things to that birth of sorrows. Therefore, God gave seventy-three years from the time he was born in Jerusalem; and forty years of truce from the time of his death, so that those remnants whom Isaiah had said were to be saved might be joined to the apostles and the true Israel, and so that the others might flock to Jerusalem from the whole world as if to a slaughter. Furthermore, he fed his own people with such strength that neither fire, nor iron, nor lions, nor any unheard-of torments could overcome them. For in the loftiness of the name of their God, Jesus Christ, they were capable of all things. For it was necessary for the soldiers to be like their leader: unbroken in spirit, and prepared to receive and endure even evils from everyone after [doing] good deeds. Certainly, just as no man was more humble than Jesus Christ, yet none greater in status, none a greater prophet, none more powerful in virtue, and none more equipped with every perfection; so also it was necessary for him to magnify his followers, equipped with those same arms, even to the ends of the earth, because he is peace—truly peace, not just a peacemaker.

but very peace itself. Therefore Isaiah writes of him as the Prince of Peace, as will soon be seen. For otherwise he would never come, because Bethlehem was utterly destroyed by the Roman army 1,450 years ago <note>Postel, writing around 1544, calculates this duration from the Roman destruction of Judea in the 1st century AD.</note>; thus, one cannot be born from it since it no longer exists. I cannot in this place help but be vehemently enraged at the impudence of Rabbi Solomon <note>original: "Rabi Salomonis," referring to Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent Jewish commentator whose literalist interpretations Postel opposes.</note> and his followers, and say: *O my people, those who call you blessed deceive you, and destroy the way of your steps.* <note>original: "Popule meus, qui te beatum dicunt, ipsi te decipiunt, & uiam gressuum tuorum dissipant." If you became Christians, they would perish. 

This charmer <note>original: "fascinator," used here to mean a deceiver or one who casts a spell of ignorance.</note> says in this place that these things are understood to be about David. But why are prophets called prophets? If they weave a history and predict nothing, they are not prophets. What is divine about relating things already done? Can anyone not do this? David had already died long ago; Micah wrote in the times of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. They so twist and pervert all the sayings of the prophets that they seem to be spoken of past events. What is this, truly, but to drag you into a reprobate sense? Wretched and unhappy ones, who do not have enough affliction from all nations, unless your own also impose upon you and deceive you for so long. But let us hear the qualities of our Jesus, predicted 600 years before he was born. Isaiah, chapter 9, says at the beginning:

> The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; upon those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, light has dawned for them. <note>Isaiah 9:2.</note> And a little later: A child is born to us, and a son is given to us, and the government is placed upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Father of Eternity, Prince of Peace: while his empire shall be multiplied, of peace there shall be no end. He shall sit upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, to confirm it and strengthen it in judgment and justice, from then on and forevermore. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will perform this. <note>Isaiah 9:6–7.</note>

These things apply to God alone. And yet our impious Solomon does not fear to make the most divine prophet into a mere historian, and to attribute the names of God to a mortal man—to Hezekiah, the son of an impious parent, who was purified by fire by his father <note>A reference to King Ahaz passing his son through fire in pagan ritual, from which Hezekiah was said to have been miraculously saved.</note>; yet even the Targum <note>original: "Targum," the Aramaic translations/paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible used in Jewish liturgy and study.</note> understands all these things as referring to the Messiah. Indeed, Jonathan <note>Referring to the Targum Jonathan, the traditional Aramaic paraphrase of the Prophets.</note> says:

> The prophet said to the house of David: because a child, our Lord, is born to us, and a son is given to us, and he shall take the government upon his shoulder, and his name has been called from of old Wonderful in Counsel, God, Mighty, abiding forever, the Messiah of Peace. May his empire be multiplied over us in his days; the empire of his servants is greatly increased, and for those hoping in him, there is no end of peace. Upon the throne of David himself, etc.

Can these things possibly fit Hezekiah? The empires of the princes of this world depend on the consent of the common people; but this one's not at all, because he seeks nothing earthly. Therefore, by his own will, he exercises a happy reign over souls, and carries upon his shoulders the punishments of truth—namely, the cross—by which he broke the power of Satan, redeemed the world, and opened paradise to believers; in whose sign infinite miracles have been done, are done daily, and will be done. The interpreter explained those names which follow. For who can be called "Mighty God" except God himself? Who "Prince of Peace"? Whose empire can be so multiplied that there is no end to his peace? 

Furthermore, it must not be overlooked that in the word <term>for multiplying</term> <note>original Hebrew: לםרבה, *le-marbeh*</note>, the prophet placed a <term>closed mem</term> <note>original: *mem setumah*. In Isaiah 9:6, it appears strangely in the middle of the word *le-marbeh*.</note>, against the usual order of writing, for two reasons. through the throne of David, except the God-man Jesus Christ. I have already shown from various passages that the eternal throne of David is the congregation of the faithful, in which He reigned under Moses, and now under the Gospel, Jesus reigns forever. All these things rightly signify that He is called **Emmanuel**, which means *God with us*. For in Him redemption was completed. For He was, as Isaiah says, a *goel male* <note>original: "goel male," from the Hebrew 'goel' (redeemer/kinsman) and 'male' (full/complete).</note>, that is, an absolute and full redeemer. Furthermore, it is clear that He was born to redeem all people because He is a perfect redeemer, and in Him all nations are blessed. For all people since Adam have been infected by sin and could not be led back except by Him who had formed the first man, as I taught in the first book. But I also wish to confirm with one passage what I have often cited: that Christ was sent to all nations. *It is too small a thing,* says Isaiah in chapter forty-nine, *O Messiah, that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to gather the remnants of Israel. I have given you as a light to the nations, so that you may be my salvation even to the farthest reaches of the earth.*

But I come now to other things to be noted regarding His birth. When He was in Bethlehem—a very small city with a great shortage of inns—and a great multitude had gathered there for the registration of names while Cyrenius <note>The Roman official Quirinius, mentioned in the Gospel of Luke as overseeing the census.</note> was governor in Syria, Mary and Joseph (who was of the family of David) arrived there. Although they were very poor—for you know it was customary for the daily records of all tribes and generations to be kept publicly until Herod destroyed many of them—they came there, compelled to obey the command and the appointed day. There, while they were staying in a stable that was open on all sides, Mary gave birth to Jesus, so named by the angel before He was conceived by the virgin. 

Thus, in His first cradle, He gave proof of the life He was to embrace. For there was never any greater poverty than where the Savior of the world was born; and yet that humility summoned from the regions of the East, from the borders of Persia and the domain of the Magi, three kings. They arrived at that place on the thirteenth day after His birth and began to ask the wise men and the scribes where the King of the Jews had been born. When they learned it was in Bethlehem, they visited the poorest King, guided by a star, and honored Him with gifts so that the saying of the prophet might be fulfilled: *The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts, the kings of the Arabians and of Sheba shall bring presents, and all kings shall adore him, all nations shall serve him.* <note>Postel is quoting Psalm 72:10-11.</note> 

That region is to the east, thirteen days distant from Judea; it is a maritime region having dominion over land and sea, as well as over the islands of the Persian Gulf. These are the lands of the Magi on the borders of the Arabians and Sheba—that is, *Arabia Deserta* and *Arabia Felix* <note>term: Arabia Deserta and Arabia Felix; Latin for "Deserted Arabia" and "Fertile/Happy Arabia," standard geographical divisions in the Renaissance.</note>. There, the princes use dromedary camels, and the journey from that place is through the borders of Midian and Ephah, which are in the western part of Arabia Deserta. Thus, another prophecy of Isaiah (chapter 60) fits perfectly: *Arise,* he says, *be enlightened, O Israel, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you. For behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and a thick mist the peoples; but the Lord shall rise upon you, and His glory shall be seen in you. And the nations shall walk in your light, and kings in the brightness of your rising.* And a little later: *A multitude of camels shall cover you, the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah; all those from Sheba shall come, bringing gold and frankincense, and announcing the praise of the Lord.* 

Just as these things can be understood of no one else but the Messiah, the God-man, so they happened to Jesus the Savior at His birth. For the Messiah was meant to bring light to His people; Jesus gave such great light to His followers that the least of His apostles could turn the faces of all princes toward himself, though he was most lowly, and by greatness of soul could overcome the whole world. The glory of the Lord truly rose in Israel when Jesus was born, and then darkness and mist covered all the peoples—not for lack of light, but by comparison. For those same peoples were in darkness before the birth of Jesus Christ, but since a great light was not yet present, they seemed to be a "luminous darkness,"

That splendor of yours, O *Messiah*, brought kings to you and accompanied them always, until—out of curiosity to see the primary city and to interrogate the leading men about whom they sought—they had left it. Then, entering without delay, these kings adored the most poor infant king and presented him with gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh, with which their region abounded. The gold served as a travel fund <term>viaticum: money or supplies provided for a journey</term> while the impoverished parents fled into *Egypt* to escape the fury of the most wicked and unjust tyrant *Herod*.

For when *Herod* had been informed of the birth of the child and the birth of the King *Messiah* by these King-Magi (who, as is fitting, had come with a very large company of camels and attendants, so that their entrance could not have been hidden even if they had not gone to *Jerusalem* to ask about the matter), he did not wish to openly reveal to them his murderous intent toward the royal blood—as he had already shown before. He dismissed them, but requested that they return to him after they had found the child, so that he too might adore him. He said this not with the intention of adoring, but of killing. 

A few months later, when he realized he had been deceived by the Magi—who had promised they would report what they found concerning the child—he took action. (For after their adoration, an angel had forbidden them from returning to *Herod*). To ensure that this child born in the territory of *Bethlehem* could not escape death, he ordered all children two years old and younger to be killed. He even killed one of his own, lest he might be the *Messiah*, because he was in *Bethlehem*. So great was the man's madness, so great his ferocity, that whatever he heard was of royal blood, he immediately punished with death. From this, he wished not only to destroy all royal blood entirely, but he intended to kill every single senator, sparing only one of the priests. The history of *Herod's* wicked cruelty is well known in the *Roman* annals. *Macrobius* <note>A 5th-century Roman writer; Postel cites him as a "pagan" (ethnicus) source to validate the biblical account.</note>, a pagan, as I have already cited twice, reports that when *Augustus* heard of that crime—that he had ordered all boys from two years old to be killed, and among them one of his own—he said:

> *I would rather be Herod’s pig than his son.* <note>original: "Mallem esse Herodis porcus, quàm filius." This is a famous wordplay: in Greek, "pig" (hys) and "son" (hyios) sound similar. Since Herod followed Jewish customs, he would not eat or kill a pig, but he did kill his own sons.</note>

For he who had killed his son spared the life of a pig. The prophet *Jeremiah* mentions this cruelty in chapter 31, where God speaks of the rejection and recall of His people, saying among other things:

> *A voice was heard in Rama of lamentation, mourning, and weeping; Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more.*

They are called the children of *Rachel* because she is seen as the mother of the entire race, since she gave birth to *Joseph*, from whom all *Jewish* prosperity proceeded. Some write that the city of *Ramah* is a high place—which it is—where *Bethlehem* is situated, in the tribe of *Benjamin* within the borders of the *Gibeonites*.

As a miracle of the event, they show an image of the Virgin and the infant. But we must come to the precursor of Jesus Christ. What kind of man John the Baptist was, I think no Jew is ignorant, unless by choice. For among a Jewish man, one alien to us, mention of him is made with a judgment of this kind: "To some of the Jews," says Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian. This passage is from *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 18.</note>, "it seemed that Herod’s army perished for this reason: because he killed John the Baptist. He was a very good man, who commanded the Jews to apply themselves to virtue, to cultivate justice and piety, and to come together in baptism. For then at last would baptism be health-bringing, when it was observed with the greatest innocence of soul." 

When he had many followers because of these words, Herod, fearing his integrity lest he expose his own crimes, thrust him into prison at Machaerus <note>original: "Macherunta"; a mountaintop fortress in modern-day Jordan.</note>. And so, out of mere suspicion, he killed this excellent man. The Gospel adds that Herodias was the cause, whom he had joined to himself in illegitimate marriage, since she was his brother’s wife, because he [John] had freely rebuked him for such an atrocious crime. For Herodias, who was more pleased with the marriage of Herod the Tetrarch than with the private life of the other Herod, feared that the prophet would dissuade her husband’s brother from what she desired to be done. She saw to it immediately upon Herod’s return from Rome—whose marriage she was soliciting and had already settled upon—that the prophet should be removed from the scene. Josephus pursues this history more extensively in the preceding chapter. 

That precursor was the herald of Jesus Christ, and in him he also brought back the grace of his baptism. The prophets had predicted that a certain prophet must precede as the indicator of the Messiah. Malachi, in the third chapter, has it thus:

> Behold, I send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before my face, and the Lord whom you seek shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire. Behold, he comes, says the Lord, and who shall be able to think of or endure the day of his coming? And who shall stand when he appears? For he himself shall be like a refining fire, and like the soap <note>original: "borith (herba) fullonum"; borith refers to a cleansing herb or vegetable alkali used by fullers/launderers.</note> of fullers. And he shall sit refining and cleansing silver, and he shall purge the sons of Levi, and refine them like gold and like silver, and they shall be offering a gift in justice to the Lord, and it shall be pleasing, etc.

Whether this be the prophecy of Malachi or Ezra <note>Postel notes the scholarly debate over the authorship of the book of Malachi, which some ancient traditions attributed to Ezra the Scribe.</note>, I care little for the author—let the Rabbis doubt and argue—it is certain that it is divinely inspired scripture. Surely it speaks of the Messiah, since He alone is the ruler whom the Jews were seeking. For they knew God the Father before, but to the fulfillment of that law which they observed, it was necessary for the law of the Son of God, the blessed Messiah, to approach. 

Therefore he sent before him an angel—that is, the messenger John the Baptist—who prepared and purged the way before him by baptism and repentance. From this, because John was also sent by him, he [the Messiah] must also be God: for God alone sends prophets. He was not sent much before, but immediately He followed him for whom he prepared the way; and He came to His temple in the sixth month from which John had been conceived, and entered into the womb of the most pure virgin, which was the first temple for the God-man. Secondly, He wished to have the souls of all those who embrace His decrees and follow them in deeds as His temple. For what temple could be more worthy of God than those souls themselves, which encompass heaven and earth? What temple could be built of stones worthy of such majesty, which fills heaven and earth, and surpasses them infinitely? The most worthy and greatest of the whole world...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument for the divinity of Jesus by interpreting Old Testament prophecies. # GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK IV #

->The temple was owed to the Messiah.<- But no temple greater, more august, or more worthy can be given than the soul of holy men itself. Therefore, that Lord whom you seek, and the Messenger of the Covenant whom you expect, was going to come into his own temple—the soul—and into his church. However, since there were two advents <note>Postel refers to the "Two Advents" of Christ: the first as a humble savior and the second as a judge at the end of time.</note> of the Messiah, the prophet confuses one with the other, which happens in many places regarding both the advent and other matters. For since our soul is unequal to the comprehension of divine things and meanings, and being occupied by this mass of the body, it does not judge as freely as when it is separate; it cannot distinctly receive, bear, and bring forth divine impulse without it being far removed from that highest notion before it reaches the organs of the body. Therefore, there is the greatest obscurity in all the prophets, and various interpositions often not fully understood even by the one who brings them forth. This is done by divine providence: so that under a constant fear of God, whatever pious, holy, and just things we have known, we may have peace by subscribing to those prescriptions of divine goodness; and that impious and wicked men may draw poison from that which is actually most soul-healing. 

As I was saying, the prophet includes the two advents of the Messiah together in one. The first period in the sequence, therefore, is about the final advent. For no mortal will be able to bear the day of the second coming of Jesus Christ, for it will be so terrible that no one can stand when he appears. But the following part pertains to both, for he says, *he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap, and he will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver.* <note>Postel is quoting Malachi 3:2–3.</note> When he is said to be like the herb *borith* <note>original: "borith"; a Hebrew term for a cleaning agent or vegetable alkali used by fullers to whiten cloth.</note>, which fullers use to clean and thicken raw cloth to make it fit for use, then this ought to be referred to the first advent. In this coming, he gradually purifies men and renders them fit for the use of the divine will, even though he appears as the lowliest of men. For from the power of his humble rejection, such great strength flows into men who are filthy with sins and devoted to worldly cares, that the cloth becomes far better—without which there would be no good use for it. 

It truly does not matter what *borith* signifies in this place: whether it be soap, or the soapwort herb, or anything else fit for scouring. For by its very appearance (whatever it is) it is lower than the cloth; just as Jesus Christ was even humbler and more abject than any man in his first advent, without whom, however, no one—not even the greatest prince of the world—ever was or will be pleasing to God the Father. 

When he is called a *refiner's fire*, it must be judged as referring to his second and transition-tremendous advent, about which David said: *Fire shall go before him, and shall burn up his enemies on every side. His lightnings enlightened the world: the earth saw and was moved,* etc. <note>Quoting Psalm 97:3–4.</note> But the words that follow—*And he shall sit refining and cleansing*, etc.—pertain to both. For here [in this life] he purges the man who believes in him; there [at the Judgment] there will no longer be a place for individual purging, but for a universal one, so that when his whole flock has been gathered and united, he may give the wicked (separated and destined for fire) to eternal punishments, and the good to perpetual joys. 

Indeed, he makes mention especially of the "sons of Levi" <note>In the biblical tradition, the Levites were the priestly tribe; Postel uses them here as a symbol for the clergy and religious leaders.</note>, upon whose example the people depend. For since they ought to be the most holy, and lead others with the most holy deeds and words, their virtue or vice creeps into those below them; and the vice that proceeds from their example becomes all the worse the greater the dignity they hold over others. Therefore Ezekiel says in chapter 9, when dealing with the great vengeance: *Begin at my sanctuary.* <note>original: "à sanctuario meo incipite"; Ezekiel 9:6.</note> Here certainly are those who must be corrected first, and in judgment, damned first. But where the order was purged, those who followed Christ were most just, until they stained the order with wealth and pride. Certainly Jesus Christ...

This is written in the annals of the Moors <note>original: "Maurorum annalibus". Postel often cites Arabic or Islamic sources to provide "outside" testimony for Christian claims.</note>, as a memory of the event, to the praise and glory of Christ, and as a crime of your people [the Jews], which even the elements themselves shudder at. Consult them on this matter, and ask why entry to that place is forbidden to Jews under penalty of death, if the law passed long ago is still observed. 

But we must come to the precursor of Jesus Christ. I think no Jew, unless by choice, is ignorant of what kind of man John the Baptist was. For mention of him is made by a Jewish man, an outsider to us <note>Postel refers to the historian Flavius Josephus, who was Jewish and not a Christian, making him a "neutral" witness in Postel's eyes.</note>, in a statement of this sort: *To some of the Jews* (says Josephus) *it seemed that Herod’s army perished for this reason: because he killed John the Baptist. That man was very good; he commanded the Jews to strive for virtue, to cultivate justice and piety, and to come together in baptism. For only then would baptism be life-giving, when it was kept with the greatest innocence of soul.* When he had many followers because of these words, Herod, fearing his integrity lest he expose his own crimes, thrust him into prison in Machaerus <note>original: "Macherunta", a fortress palace overlooking the Dead Sea.</note>. And so, out of suspicion alone, he killed that excellent man. 

The Gospel adds that Herodias was the cause, whom he had joined to himself in unlawful marriage, since she was his brother’s wife, because he [John] had freely rebuked him for such a nefarious crime. For Herodias—who preferred marriage to Herod the Tetrarch over marriage to the private citizen Herod <note>Josephus and the Gospels explain that Herodias left her first husband (Herod II) for his half-brother Herod Antipas.</note>—feared that the prophet would dissuade her husband’s brother from the marriage she desired. As soon as Herod returned from Rome, whose marriage she sought and had already bargained for, she saw to it that the prophet was removed from the scene. Josephus follows this history more extensively in the preceding chapter. 

That man was the precursor of Jesus Christ, and he directed his grace of baptism toward him. That a certain prophet, the indicator of the Messiah, was supposed to precede him, the prophets had predicted. Malachi, in the third chapter, has it thus:

> Behold, I send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before my face. And suddenly the Lord whom you seek shall come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire. Behold, he comes, says the Lord. And who can think of bearing the day of his coming? And who shall stand when he appears? For he will be like a refining fire, and like the soap <note>original: "borith (herba) fullonum". Borith is a Hebrew term for a cleansing herb or alkaline lye used by launderers.</note> of fullers. And he shall sit refining and cleansing silver, and he shall purge the sons of Levi, and refine them like gold and silver, and they shall be offering a gift in justice to the Lord, and it shall be pleasing, etc.

Whether this be the prophecy of Malachi or Ezra—I do not dwell on the author; let the Rabbis doubt and argue—it is established that this is divinely inspired scripture. Certainly, it speaks of the Messiah, since he alone is the ruler whom the Jews were seeking. For they knew God the Father before, but to the fulfillment of that law which they kept, it was necessary to add the law of the Son of God, the blessed Messiah. 

Therefore, he sent before him his "angel"—that is, the messenger John the Baptist—who by baptism and repentance prepared and cleansed the way before him. From this, because John was also sent by him, he [the Messiah] must also be God: for only God sends prophets. He was not sent much earlier, but immediately he followed the one for whom he prepared the way. He came to his temple in the sixth month from when John was conceived, and entered into the womb of the purest Virgin, which was the first temple for the God-man. 

Secondly, however, he willed to have the souls of all good men who embrace his decrees and carry them out in deeds as his temple. For what temple could be more worthy of God than the souls themselves, which encompass heaven and earth? What temple built of stones could be built worthy of such majesty, which fills heaven and earth and surpasses them infinitely? The most worthy and greatest of the whole world...

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK 4

...the temple of the Lord <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely completing a thought from the previous page: "the temple of the Lord was owed to the Messiah."</note> was owed to the Messiah. But no greater, more august, or worthier temple can be given than the very soul of holy men. Therefore, that Ruler whom you seek, and the messenger of the Covenant <note>original: "Testamenti"</note> whom you await, was going to come into his own temple—the soul and his church. However, since there were to be two comings of the Messiah, the prophet [Malachi] confuses one with the other, as happens in many places regarding both his coming and other matters. 

For since our soul is unequal to the comprehension of divine things and meanings, and while occupied by this mass of the body it cannot judge as freely as when it is separated, it cannot receive, bear, or put forth the divine impulse so distinctly. Thus, before the impulse reaches the organs of the body, it falls far short of that highest Notion. For this reason, there is the greatest obscurity in all the prophets, and various interpositions that are frequently not fully understood even by the one who utters them. This happens by divine providence: so that under a constant fear of God, we may have peace by submitting to those prescriptions of divine goodness—whatever pious, holy, and just things we have known—while the impious and wicked draw poison from that which is actually most soul-healing. 

As I was saying, the prophet comprehends the two comings of the Messiah as one. The first period in the sequence, therefore, concerns the final coming. For no mortal will be able to endure the day of the second coming of Jesus Christ; it will be so terrible that no one can stand when he appears. The following part, however, pertains to both. He says: **"He is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap <note>original: "herba fullonum", literally "the herb of the fullers," used for cleaning cloth.</note>, and he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver."** 

When he is said to be like the herb *borith* <term>Borith: a Hebrew term (בּוֹרִית) referring to a cleansing vegetable alkali or lye used by fullers to wash clothes.</term>, with which fullers clean and thicken raw cloth to make it fit for use, then this must refer to the first coming. In this coming, he gradually purifies men and makes them fit for the use of the divine will, even though he appears as the lowest of men. From the power of his lowliness, such a force flows into men who are filthy with sins and devoted to worldly cares that the result is far better than the cloth, which without this process would have no good use. 

Truly, it matters little what *borith* signifies in this place: whether it be soap, or the soapwort herb, or anything else suited for scouring; for by its very appearance (whatever it is), it is inferior to the cloth itself. In the same way, Jesus Christ was humbler and more rejected than any man in his first coming; yet without him, no one—not even the greatest prince of the world—ever was or will be pleasing to God the Father. 

When he is called a **"refiner's fire,"** it must be understood as referring to his second and transitionary coming, of which David said: *Fire shall go before him, and shall burn up his enemies on every side. His lightnings enlightened the world: the earth saw, and trembled,* etc. <note>Postel is quoting Psalm 97:3-4.</note> But the words that follow—**"And he shall sit refining and cleansing,"** etc.—pertain to both comings. For here [in the first coming] he purifies the person who believes in him; there [in the second coming], there will no longer be a place for individual purification, but a universal one. When his entire flock has been gathered and united, he shall deliver the wicked, separated and destined for fire, to eternal punishments, and the good to perpetual joys. 

He makes mention especially of the "sons of Levi" <note>The priestly tribe of Israel.</note>, upon whose example the people depend. Since they ought to be the most holy, and lead others with the holiest deeds and words, their virtue or vice creeps into those below them. Indeed, the vice that proceeds from their example is as much worse as their dignity is greater than that of others. Therefore Ezekiel says in chapter 9, when dealing with the great vengeance: **"Begin at my sanctuary."** Certainly, these are the first to be corrected, and the first to be condemned in judgment. Wherever the order was purified, those who followed Christ were most just, until they stained the order with wealth and pride. Certainly Jesus Christ...

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

...[Chri]st never rejected the sacrifices instituted in his name. For the order itself is not the cause of sin. I come now to another prophetic testimony concerning John the precursor. Isaiah says in chapter 40:

> Comfort, comfort my people, says your God. Speak tenderly to Jerusalem, and call out to her: for her time is fulfilled, her iniquity is forgiven. She has received from the hand of the Lord double for all her sins. A voice of one crying in the desert: clear the way of the Lord, make straight in the wilderness the paths of our God.

Here the prophet mixes rewards with punishments; for when her time was fulfilled—that is, when the Messiah came—he brought the remission of sins to all believers, but by the same work he signaled punishments for the impious and faithless, even doubled. For so great a slaughter of the Jews was carried out in their domain that there never was a greater, nor will there be in the future; and a captivity among all nations so long-lasting that none is more memorable. 

Truly, lest they say they were unable to recognize Jesus Christ, there came before him a "voice of one crying in the desert," so that they might purge the ways of their souls for the coming grace of God, and make straight the paths of their God. John the Baptist preached repentance in the desert in the name of Jesus Christ, and showed him to those who came to him, saying: "This is the lamb of God; this is he who was made before me, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to untie; he must increase, but I must decrease." 

The impostor Rabbi Solomon <note>original: "R. Selomoh"; referring to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, 1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> breaks out into certain trifles, referring these things to the [Babylonian] captivity, so that this pest might burn remarkably with the zeal of overturning the truth. From the beginning, he dared to attack every sacred thing to overturn the true sense, because he lived in France <note>original: "Gallia"</note>—the nourisher of most brilliant minds when they are cultivated—and was being attacked by Christians, and could not answer the arguments brought from the prophets. Therefore, so that he might be to all Jews like a Theseus or an Achilles, he referred all the oracles of the prophets to the past. He ensured that if the Jews believe him (which they mostly do), there is plainly no prophet in the entire Old Testament. 

For the prophets are named <term>from "speaking beforehand" <note>original Greek: ἐκ τοῦ προφάναι (ek tou prophanai) or φαῦναι (phaunai).</note></term>, because they foresaw and foretold things long before they happened. If they are prophets only in an allegorical or <term>anagogic <note>Anagogic interpretation seeks the spiritual or mystical sense of a text, often relating to the afterlife or the end of the world.</term> sense, then even the history of the Judges, the Kings, and Genesis would be prophecies. But he does not say this in words; yet he proves it by his very deeds. For I ask: what else is it to drag the literal sense of a prophet entirely to the letter [of history], than to establish him as a mere chronicler <note>original: "historiographum"</note>? 

John the Baptist was also called Elijah because he preceded the first coming of Jesus, just as Enoch and Elijah will truly precede the second coming. Malachi, speaking of both comings interchangeably in the last chapter, called him thus, with Jesus Christ acting as the interpreter of the passage and giving the name of "Elijah" to John the Baptist. Indeed, names are often borrowed in the sacred writings. For the Messiah is called by the names of many who were before him. In the first place, even as a man in the body, he preserved the name <term>Jehovah <note>The Tetragrammaton, the personal name of God.</note></term>, as he had it from eternity. Jeremiah shows this in chapter 23:

> Behold, the days are coming, says God, and I will raise up for David a righteous branch, and a King shall reign, and he shall understand and perform judgment and justice on the earth. In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell confidently, and this is his name by which they shall call him: <insert>The Lord our Righteousness</insert> <note>original Hebrew: יהוה צדקנו (Jehovah Tsidkenu)</note>.

If any doubt that these things are said of Christ, the <term>Targum Jonathan <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the prophetic books of the Hebrew Bible.</note></term> confirms it: "And I will establish for David a righteous branch." Jeremiah confirms it himself in chapter 33: "Behold the days come, says the Lord," etc., and a little later: "And this is he who will call her (that is, the synagogue or the church), 'The Lord...'"

<summary>Postel interprets Isaiah 40 as a prophecy of John the Baptist and the Messiah’s arrival, which brought both salvation and "double" punishment for those who rejected him. He specifically attacks the medieval commentator Rashi for reducing prophecy to mere historical record to avoid Christian interpretations.</summary>

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK IV.

**God our righteousness** <note>original: "Deus iustitia nostra"; a reference to Jeremiah 23:6 and 33:16.</note>. Jonathan <note>referring to Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Prophets.</note> understands this to refer to the Messiah. Rabbi David Kimchi <note>Often called Radak (1160–1235), a prominent medieval rabbi and grammarian.</note> also interprets it this way. But he claims he should be called so because in his time Israel will be justified by God. They have wandered so far into a depraved way of thinking that they wish to strip away what is most excellent in Jesus Christ—his Messianic status—lest he agree with their own views in any point. Yet they ought not to have feared this so greatly. For their Messiah will be the Antichrist, diametrically opposed to Christ and most distant from divinity. Some overturn the passage and try to invert the reading. Others, to deceive those among our people who are ignorant of the Hebrew language, say that Moses, Israel, and Jerusalem are called "God," and that it does not mean they are actually God. But they lie with impunity. For they will never show in the sacred scriptures that the name <term>The Name/There</term> <note>original: "שמה" (Shammah/Shemah)</note> is attributed to anyone other than the Messiah and God, from which it is clear that Jesus is God.

But I cannot cover in silence the impiety of the wicked Rabbis, nor fail to show their zeal in corrupting the scriptures. To show that the Messiah is not God simply because he is called <term>Jehovah</term> <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God.</note>, they corrupt the final word of the prophecy of Ezekiel <note>original: "Iechezchelis"</note> so that they might even try to attribute the sacred name to the city. Where it is read, "And the city shall be called from that day, THE LORD IS THERE," they want it to be read as "The Lord is his name," by changing a vowel point and adding a letter. For where it is "there" <note>original: "יהוה שמה" (Yahweh Shammah)</note>, which is the legitimate writing, they substitute "his name" <note>original: "שמו" (Shemo)</note>. So says Rabbi David Kimchi and Rabbi Solomon <note>referring to Rashi.</note>, following the author of this corruption, Jonathan, who in the book *Bava Batra* <note>A tractate of the Talmud.</note>, in the chapter "The Seller of the Ship" <note>original: "Mocher ha-Sefinah"</note>, judges that it must be read this way. 

Even if this reading were accepted, since the prophet describes the Heavenly Jerusalem in that chapter, nothing prevents it being called <term>Jehovah</term>, since then God will be "all in all" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 15:28.</note> according to his presence and substance, whereas in lower and corruptible things he is present only through power and knowledge. If anyone else committed such acts against the scriptures, they would rightly be pursued; but because these men are now adulterers of the word and estranged from the truth, they are permitted to rage against their mother [the Scripture]. In the 28th and 8th chapters of Isaiah, the same name is given to the Messiah, with the agreement of the <term>Targum</term> <note>The Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>. In some places Jesus the Messiah is called "David," as in Jeremiah 30, with the Targum’s agreement; and in Hosea 3 he is even called "Solomon." In 1 Chronicles 17 <note>original: "Paralip. 17"</note> he is called both "Stone" and "Rock," and by innumerable names due to properties related to the things described.

When Christ was manifested by the voice of John the Herald, he then began to collect the dregs and remnants of Israel. Setting aside the pride and arrogance of the world, he took fishermen into his company, speaking thus: "Come, I will make you fishers of men." The Holy Spirit had not kept silent about persons of that condition many years before; for through the mouth of Jeremiah he said: 

> Therefore behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when it shall no longer be said, "The Lord lives who brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt," but "The Lord lives who brought the children of Israel out of the land of the north, and from all the lands to which I cast them out." And I will bring them back to their own land, which I gave to their fathers. Behold, I will send many fishers, says the Lord, and they shall fish for them, and after this, etc.

These things concern the coming of the Messiah and the gathering of Israel. But we have already seen in many places and arguments that Christ would give salvation to all nations. Therefore, when he speaks of gathering Israel, he means all the faithful, both of the nations and the peoples—but those subjected to the North, that is, those liable to the power of the demon. For from the North all evil proceeds. For in the book of the *Zohar*, Rabbi Eleazar writes that the northern part of the world was made imperfect by God, so that whoever would be God, or call himself God, might come and complete it, and then they would know that he is God. Indeed, Rabbi Recanati <note>An Italian kabbalist and halakhist (1250–1310).</note> says, regarding that passage taken from Ezekiel chapter 8, that the wisdom of God, which is called <term>Attah</term> <note>original: "Attah"; Hebrew for "You" or "Thou."</note>, will rule over the angel of death, that is, the devil. Now the word *Attah*...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

[He] is the wisdom of God; therefore the Messiah, having conquered the devil, the author of evil, began from the north <note>A reference to Jeremiah 1:14-15, where "out of the north an evil shall break forth," which Postel interprets here as the starting point for the restoration of Israel.</note> to restore Israel, which is to say, the church of the faithful. This was accomplished not by the work of kings or great men, nor with battle lines drawn, nor with cohorts and phalanxes of soldiers, but by the fishermen Apostles sent into all the world. They "fished" for the church. The hunters—that is, the Roman soldiers—even in the day of visitation, dragged you from your caves to punishment. Finally, the nations, having abandoned their idols, crossed over to Christ. This is the sum and the sense of this chapter of Jeremiah. Ezekiel also mentions these same fishermen in chapter 47, in his shadowed description of the power of the Gospel and his description of baptism. For it is impossible for all living creatures to have life from the power of [physical] water alone; rather, they take life from baptism, having its origin in Jesus Christ, who receives every kind of human being without any respect of persons. For he becomes for them a fountain of water leading into eternal life.

Indicating even more clearly that he translated the power of the Law proceeding from the Temple into the Gospel, Ezekiel demonstrates the origin of the vigor of this water even more expressly. For he said that the waters, which would heal the others, would come out from eastern Galilee, situated near the Lake of Gennesaret <note>The Sea of Galilee.</note>. For Christ proceeded from Galilee, and from its eastern borders he chose the chief of the apostles—Peter, Andrew, Philip, and others—who were the first fishermen. It is worth hearing from Isaiah, in chapter 2, what kind of dragnet <note>original: "fagenam"; from the Greek *sagēnē*, a large hauling net used by fishermen.</note> Christ gave to his fishermen:

> *And it shall come to pass,* he says, *in the last days, that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills, and all nations shall flow unto it. And many people shall go and say: Come and let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us his ways, and we will walk in his paths; for the law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And he shall judge the nations, and shall rebuke many people; and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they be trained for war anymore. O house of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord. For you have cast away your people, etc.*

The Jews will not deny that these things were said concerning the coming of the Messiah, because they seem to work against Jesus Christ and favor their own future Messiah. Therefore, since we are in agreement on this, the individual points must be examined. *It shall be in the last days:* The Jews say this means in the final days of the world, but we say it means in the last days of the Mosaic Law. We must see who speaks better, by bringing forth arguments from both sides. The word <term>אחרית</term> (*acharit*), which means "last" or "latter," does not signify the absolute extreme end of a thing. For Joel 2 says: *Its extremity [shall reach] even to the last sea.* Likewise, Ezekiel 26 says: *While I shall place deserts in the last land.* But since the earth and the water form one round globe, there is simply no "extreme" part. For in any point of a circle, a beginning and an end can be assigned. Therefore, something is called "last" or "latter" there by necessity [of context]. So also in Isaiah, "last" is said of the Mosaic Law. For in the final constitution of the world, there will be an end to action and corruption. There will be no need for Law when time is stopped. For a law is not usually given except for long-term observation. It would therefore be pointless to establish a law so holy, except for the sake of the longest possible observation. Therefore, it ought to be given at least two thousand years before the end of the world, since you see the saying of Elijah <note>A traditional Jewish and early Christian idea that the world would last 6,000 years: 2,000 of Chaos, 2,000 of Torah, and 2,000 of the Messiah.</note> has already come to pass in two parts—those of Nature and of the Law. For each lasted roughly two thousand years; therefore the Law of Grace, much more excellent than the two preceding ones, ought to last longer rather than shorter. The "last days," therefore, in this place, are the end of the Law of Moses. These were the last days when the scepter was taken away from Judah, as Jacob had predicted. When Jesus came, there perished for you...
