<meta>This page continues Postel’s commentary on the fulfillment of prophecy, moving from the geographical origins of the Gospel (Galilee and Jerusalem) to the spiritual nature of the Messiah's kingdom and a defense against common objections regarding the persistence of war in the Christian era.</meta>

->### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK IV.<-

...the scepter [departed] twice from Judah <note>original: "bis sceptrum de Iuda"; a reference to the prophecy in Genesis 49:10 regarding the timing of the Messiah's coming.</note>, and those were the latter days. By **Mountain**, however, is understood that sublime power, higher than all other powers, which was to be set before all others: namely, the state of the religion and the Church of Jesus Christ. For this is the mountain that grew to a great height, since it is the **stone cut from the mountain, without hands**, and which surpassed all others, as Daniel says <note>See Daniel 2:34-45, where a stone cut without hands destroys worldly kingdoms and grows into a mountain.</note>. To this mountain, therefore (whether we understand it as Christ himself or the Church depending on him, it matters little), all nations were to flow together, and they were to be called by the name of **Jacob** or **Israel**. They flowed toward the highest power, than which none is greater, because the word of God—that is, the Gospel of Jesus Christ—went out from **Zion**. This means that Christ, born from the Jewish lineage, taught the word in Judea and Jerusalem, from whence it spread into the entire world. He therefore judges the nations because that law was given to all; nor can anyone complain of its difficulty, for even children can (regarding what pertains to salvation) become most perfect in the knowledge of it.

But here it is a wonder how loudly the blind people <note>original: "gens caeca"; Postel is referring here to the Jewish community of his time who rejected Jesus as the Messiah.</note> protest. "How can Christ have come, as you say, when wars have not yet ceased, and when swords have not been made into plowshares? Nation rises against nation, and everything burns with wars even among Christians." Listen: Was not the law given by Moses from God, and was it not true? But when were fountains flowing with milk and honey ever literally found in it? Therefore, either he spoke falsely, or it must be understood that for one living well under that law, all things ought to succeed so happily that it would be as if he had fountains of milk and honey at home. The promises, therefore, are made to the **observers** of the precept, not to everyone who merely gives their name to circumcision or baptism. For how many Jews were impious and wicked? Yet they were under the holy law and circumcised. The Priests, who among all others were the most observant of ceremonies, what crimes did they not commit? Scarcely against any others were more threats uttered. They left no stone of avarice unturned; they gnawed the people to the very bone; they suffered from the most powerless gluttony and pleasure; and punishments began with them. Does it follow then that the law of Moses was bad? It does not. 

For humans possess **free will** <term>liberi arbitrij: the theological doctrine that humans have the power to choose between good and evil</term>, and they will until the end of the world. Since nothing is more excellent than liberty according to the human soul, given by God, it will always be permitted to act freely, or not to act. For he who does good unwillingly is neither free nor a good man. Since, however, men shall be free until the end of the world, and the **heart of man is prone to evil from youth**, and is so fraudulent and perverse above all things that no one truly knows it, there will be far more wicked people than good ones until the end of the world. Otherwise, laws would exist in vain if everyone were either all good or all bad. For the just have no need of law, and the wicked are held by none. 

Perhaps, therefore, even under the law of the Messiah, only a few were to be saved, as was the case with **Joshua and Caleb**. But among those who truly and from the heart profess Christ, there is no war, no sword, no spear. For what use is a spear or a sword to one who loves all men from the heart? Against whom would he move for war, who neither possesses anything nor craves the property of others? If he possesses anything, let him be as one who possesses nothing; against whom shall he rise up for the sake of these fleeting goods of fortune? He who regards all men as brothers, how can he wish them ill? These are the prescriptions of the most holy religion: to be in all things most like unto God. It is his way to deserve well of everyone and to expect no repayment in return. For glory belongs to him alone, and he who demands return gives nothing. The greatest philosophers judged this to be the highest good in this life: to be born for other men, not for oneself. No one has achieved this except the Christian, instructed and aided by his leader. That the prophet wished to be understood in this way is proven by the fact that he spoke indefinitely.

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

For if all those who were to give their names to Christ had been foreknown to use this divine precept, he would have said *all shall beat their swords...* <note>original: "omnes conflabunt gladios suos"; referring to the prophecy in Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3 where nations "beat their swords into plowshares."</note> and so forth. But since he knew that depraved man would act wrongly for the most part, even until the day of judgment, he said: *They shall beat...* <note>The "they" refers only to those who truly follow the law of the Messiah.</note> That is to say, those who are truly Christians from the heart shall never have any litigation or hatred toward one another, but shall enjoy a festive and eternal peace both in this life and the future one. For if everyone is to be without swords, what would that great Messiah expected by you do, who—as you believe—is to lead you back without sword or spears or war? 

Certainly you are mistaken, O Hebrews. The world will never be without its plague; never in this life will vice, the opposite of virtue, be absent. No law more holy or greater can be given in this life than that which was given by Christ, because it renders the man who obeys his precepts (as much as he is able) most similar to God. The Apostles spread this law—which takes its origin from Judea—throughout the whole world, and they taught by their most holy deeds that it is impossible for war to arise among the truly good. 

This was evident in Egypt, where at one time for four hundred years, nearly three hundred thousand people lived together in almost continuous succession with absolutely no distinction of fortune, food, or drink—the likes of whom many are found even today. But they were not gathered together as they once were. There was no place among them for either judge or soldier; the sacred magistrate was honored not because of wealth or clothing, but for the sake of order. 

I do not need to labor much over the miracles, since even the Jews agree with us regarding them, though they say they were performed by using the name **Jehovah** <note>original: "Iehouah"; Postel refers to the Jewish tradition (often found in the *Toledot Yeshu*) that Jesus performed miracles by stealing the "Ineffable Name" from the Temple.</note>, not understanding how truly they speak. For in the name **YHWH** <note>original: "יהוה"</note>, which is common to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, Jesus the Son of God performed all his miracles. Indeed, the prophet Micah mentions them in chapter 7: *Feed your people,* he says, *with your rod, the flock of your inheritance, so that they may rest in the forest as well as in the midst of the fields, so that they may be fed in Bashan and Gilead, as in the days of old. According to the day of your coming out of the land of Egypt, I will show him wonders. The nations shall see and be confounded by all their strength.* 

In this passage, God speaks through the prophetic mouth to someone who, by his combined works, must necessarily be like God. For it belongs to God alone, who sees and governs all things, to be able to preserve his own in any "forest"—whether of trees or of the impious—just as well as in the middle of the fields. According to God, Jesus alone could do this. Indeed, he taught that he could know hidden things by this: that he opened the thoughts of many. 

Since these things concern the Messiah, whom God commands as a man, the royal prophet <note>Refers to King David.</note> also taught in these same words: *I have set,* (says David from the mouth of God) *my king (against whom the princes of the world had risen) upon Zion my holy mountain.* And shortly after: *I will give the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.* The conclusion of the phrase, *to the ends of the earth,* shows that all these things are understood to be about the Messiah. For no human can command in such a way, nor even God himself over bodies of free will. 

But wonders were performed by Christ according to the day of the exodus from Egypt—wonders as much greater as God was greater than man. The sea receded at the command of Moses by the power of God, but the solid waters bore Christ as if they were land; and in his name, they bore Peter as well. The sun, the greatest of sensible creatures, felt compassion for its Creator's dying humanity by an eclipse contrary to nature. I pass over the innumerable miracles he performed in every place. 

Yet even here the Jews mutter, saying that Moses, Joshua, Hezekiah, Elijah, and Elisha performed miracles. It is true, but they did so by frequently invoking the name of God and by pouring out prayers for a long time. But Christ, by his own authority <note>original: "proprio imperio"</note>, restored sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, speech to the mute, liberation to those possessed by demons, health to the paralyzed, life to the dead, and calm to the turbulent sea. So that there could be no doubt concerning this matter, his Apostles performed such great things in his name, or by the sign of his cross alone...

### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK 4.

...so great that no one was able to count them. When the pagans saw this, and witnessed men who were insuperable by every kind of torture, they were confounded in their own strength; they saw that their strength, though equipped with every art of doing harm, availed nothing against that race of men. Countless girls and boys, even under the age of ten, rendered the torturers weary from torturing; from this it is clear that they were strengthened by the highest power and depended upon God, since tortures applied to other men usually draw out the very things that bring about death. Seeing these things, the pagans abandoned their idols and came to the true God through Christ. You [Jews] never wished to follow their example, even though salvation was sent to you, and you were worse than the nations <note>The "nations" or "Gentiles" (non-Jewish peoples).</note> whom you ought to have fled from under Moses, but followed under Christ. But because you did not do this, God has shown in you an example that lacks any precedent and shall always lack one, as I have already noted quite often. Such a countless multitude of benefits bestowed upon you stirred up such envy against Jesus Christ, due to the pride and arrogance of the rich and the chief priests, that they judged that the most innocent man should be led to the cross. This deed, you wretches—alas, you wretched Jews—regard as a point of glory, and you are accustomed to insultingly call Jesus *Talui* <note>original Hebrew: תלוי (*talni/talui*), meaning "the hanged one," a derogatory term used in the Middle Ages to refer to the crucified Christ.</note>, that is, "the hanged one," by whose cross the world was saved. Now the prophets had already foreseen all these things, which I shall touch upon lightly one by one, since you acknowledge this horrific deed. But the triumph and procession of Jesus Christ, who entered his primary city with a royal name, must be seen just as it was described by the prophet six hundred years before.

->Rejoice greatly (says Zechariah 9), daughter of Zion, shout for joy, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your king comes to you, righteous and a savior; he is cast down and poor, sitting upon a donkey, and upon the foal of a donkey. And I will destroy the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem, and the bow of war shall be scattered; and he shall speak peace to the nations. and his power shall be from sea to sea, and from the rivers even to the ends of the earth. You also, by the blood of your covenant, have sent forth the prisoners from the pit in which there is no water, etc.<-

In this passage, Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo itzhaki), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> was forced to admit that these things are understood to refer to the Messiah. Rabbi Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, another significant medieval Jewish scholar.</note> also wished to admit that it refers to one of the two Messiahs (for as I said, they expect two, because there are two advents of the one): either the Son of David or the Son of Joseph. Regarding Nehemiah, however, he says a certain Rabbi Moses the Priest understood it that way, but the rest reject that opinion; the Targum <note>The Aramaic translation and commentary of the Hebrew Bible.</note> supports the Messianic view. Therefore, in whomever all these things occurred, he was the Messiah.

Now let us examine everything according to the interpretation. The daughter of Zion ought to rejoice greatly, because the Church could obtain nothing greater than such a prince. King, Righteous, and Savior: these are three qualities of God, for He is the King of kings. But the Messiah ought to be the highest of all kings; therefore, He is God. Furthermore, no living person shall be justified in the sight of God. The righteous man falls seven times a day; "our righteousnesses are as a menstrual rag" <note>A reference to Isaiah 64:6.</note>; there is no one, not even one, who does good. Therefore, the Messiah was God. The word "Savior" belongs to God alone; therefore, the Messiah was God. These are the highest qualities of the Messiah. The name *Hu* <note>Hebrew: הוא, meaning "He."</note>, although it is also attributed to creatures, yet the Commentaries provide assurance that it is a name peculiar to God, always calling God Himself *Hakbe* <note>original: הקבה (*Ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu*), a common Hebrew term for God meaning "The Holy One, Blessed be He."</note>—the Holy One, Blessed be He.

How can one who is humble, cast down, and poor be called a king? If he is greater than worldly kings, where are his attendants? Where are his <term>somatophylakoi</term> <note>original Greek: σωματοφύλακοι, meaning "bodyguards."</note>? Where is his treasury, where are his ranks, where are his satraps, where is his army? Therefore, such a great kingdom is not of this world. For if his kingdom had been of this world, his ministers (as he said) would have fought so that he would not be handed over to the Jews. Therefore, he exercises his kingdom over happy souls and those whom he has made free. For otherwise, kingship and poverty could not meet in one person. But let the triumphal chariot go forth. "Sitting," he says, "or riding upon a donkey"—and not even a donkey well-suited for labor, but...

...still a colt, not yet receiving burdens on its back. These are the ornaments of the Messiah, these are his processions. So great was the poverty <note>original: *tenuitas*, referring to his humble circumstances and lack of worldly means</note> of Jesus Christ that he did not even possess a strong donkey, though the smallest of his miracles could not have been compensated by all the gold in the world. It is certain that he did this by example rather than by strict necessity, so that he might trample upon pride, haughtiness, wealth, glory, and the opinions by which the world is shaken, so that his deeds would speak no differently than his words. Meanwhile, the synagogue of Satan <note>A term drawn from the Book of Revelation (2:9), used here by Postel to refer to the religious authorities who opposed Jesus.</note> grumbles while it sees these things. Children and innocents (since the fathers were unable to forbid them) shout "Io triumphe!" <note>A Roman shout of victory used in triumphal processions.</note> and *Hosanna baramoth*, that is, "Save us in the highest." From the mouths of infants and nurslings, praise denied by the pride of the world proceeds, while the envy of the haughty magistrates of the synagogue gnashes its teeth. Because of this, the prophet adds what shall happen on account of that supreme wickedness: namely, that among the ten tribes of Israel, because they had more numerous chariots in which they abounded, and in Jerusalem, the horses would perish. For it was to happen that those who, having despised the truth and neglected God and his prescriptions, hoped in the multitude and heap of their riches, would be utterly cut off because of their neglected salvation. But the other faithful ones, as we have said, would stir up no war, because they would desire nothing beyond the necessities which can most easily be supplied by nature. He shall speak peace to the nations, he who was and is peace, the Prince of Peace. He urged peace, he removed the fuel for wars, and he wished to cut away all desires from his followers. For unless all lust for dominating and possessing desires is removed, no mortal can be happy or of a quiet mind; and although many know and say this, no one has ever provided it, except him whom Christ helped and instructed. Truly his power is most evident in that which he says: that he would rule in the whole world. For this, as I said, belongs to God alone. But how shall that empire of a poor man be established in the whole world? The prophet reveals: *Even by the blood of your covenant*, says God, *I have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water.* <note>Zechariah 9:11. In medieval theology, this "pit" was often identified with Limbo.</note> This empire is prepared in the blood of his covenant. Nor does it look only toward those to come, but also toward those who were bound in the pit in which there is no water: that is, those who were already being held in the underworld and in limbo since the time of Adam—he has redeemed them even from Adam’s time. For the blood of Jesus Christ prepared salvation for the whole world, for both those past and those to come. Therefore the Messiah had to be killed, and his blood had to be poured out, in which he would establish this Testament. Daniel also noted this: *And Christ shall be killed and cut off, but not for himself*, or for his own sake <note>Daniel 9:26. Postel emphasizes that the Messiah was innocent.</note>; for in him there was no deceit, but it was for the salvation of all and by the service of envy. He subjoins the penalty: once Christ has been killed, the people of a coming leader shall destroy the city. Zechariah does the same in this place: *Return*, he says (after the Just One has been killed), *to the stronghold, you prisoners of hope* (supply: of another Messiah), *even today I declare I will restore double to you.* What those "double" things are, I have already explained in two places: the two destructions and the present exile. Isaiah repeats the same thing; for after he had said this concerning Christ in chapter 40, he repeats the same again in chapter 61, also speaking of Christ; having mixed in the blessings of the faithful, he says of the punishments of the treacherous: *For your confusion you shall receive double*, he says, *and for your ignominy they shall praise in their fields; because of this, they shall possess double in their land, and he has given them everlasting joy.* <note>Isaiah 61:7.</note> The first part of the sentence looks to the treacherous, who are to be punished with a double penalty in the body and a double one in the soul. For, as I said, they feel the penalty of ruin and captivity in the body, and in their souls they experience the penalty of anguish and doubt in this life, and eternal damnation in the future. But the others—the faithful—shall also receive double, but in the soul: they shall receive rest and tranquility in this life, and eternal joy in the future. This injury of the wicked race against their Savior, in many places...

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK IV

The prophets have revealed these things, O Jews, lest by chance you think that those things are to be understood of any other Messiah than Jesus. You have seen, with perfect precision and without any distortion, that the context of the scriptures speaks of those things which were done by Jesus and in Jesus; it would be impossible for everything to align so perfectly unless he were the same one who is the Messiah. But lest I leave you occupied with a weak faith, I add certain oracles of the prophets to confirm what has been said. Isaiah foretold that the synagogue would never hear of anything but a humble Christ: "For Zion’s sake," he said, "I will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem's sake I will not rest, until her righteousness goes forth as brightness, and her salvation is kindled like a lamp." <note>Isaiah 62:1</note> 

The most wicked synagogue <note>Postel uses "synagogue" here to refer to the religious leadership of the time who opposed Jesus's ministry.</note> ordered the prophets to be silent whenever they openly brought forth the humility of Christ. The entire chapter declares that this is to be understood as the righteousness of the Messiah. Indeed, by this word he indicates that the Messiah is God, when he asserts that his church should be called: "My delight is in them" <note>original: *Voluntas mea in eis*, a Latin rendering of the Hebrew name *Hephzibah* from Isaiah 62:4.</note> and further: "A holy people, redeemed by the Lord," and also: "A city sought out, and not forsaken." 

In chapter 53, he says the same: "Who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? For he grew up before him like a young plant, and like a root out of dry ground; he had no form or majesty," etc. These things are said concerning the humility, gentleness, and other virtues of the Messiah, as will be evident in his passion. And the wicked interpreters <note>referring to contemporary Jewish commentators who disagreed with the Christological interpretation</note> are not ashamed to interpret these things as referring to a most lost people, who were led into captivity because of crimes horrendous to heaven and earth. Truly, I shall deal with them in their proper place. 

Yet under that humility—squalid, ragged, and cast down—he dared to undertake a notable deed, more than kingly; because it concerned the glory of God, he showed himself a man there. The greedy crowd of initiates <term>mystarum (ministers or priests of the temple rites)</term> had made the house of God a den of thieves, so that no opportunity for making an offering would be lacking to anyone. Lest anyone should pretend they could not offer because they had not found goods for sale, or did not have gold for exchange, they had brought the marketplace right into the temple—an argument for the unquenchable greed from which they suffered. With a whip, which he had used to drive the young donkey, he drove the men and animals away from the borders of the sacred place. He overturned the tables of the money-changers, scattering their coins, bringing forth the words of Jeremiah before the priests and Pharisees: "Has this house, in which my name is called, become a den of thieves?" <note>Jeremiah 7:11</note> Because of that neglect and the vices of the priests, he threatens destruction and the overturning of the temple, just as happened in Shiloh because of the vices of Hophni and Phinehas. <note>The sons of Eli the priest, whose corruption led to the loss of the Ark of the Covenant; see 1 Samuel 2-4.</note> 

But so that Jesus might be related in some way to the primary author of your wealth, the iniquity of your masters began its crime against him with a sale. Although you trace your lineage from Abraham, O Hebrews, you first gathered both power and wealth by the benefit of Joseph, who had been sold by his brothers. For before him you were only sixty souls, and you went out of Egypt numbering nearly 600,000 men capable of bearing arms; to each of these, at least two household members were added, making the number three times greater. 

Christ corresponds with Joseph in being sold by his own, in his innocence, in the repayment of good in place of evil, and in virginity and chastity. They agree only at the beginning, because Joseph preserved a temporary [salvation], while Christ preserved an eternal one. By a domestic enemy (a plague than which nothing is more deadly), Judas the traitor—while the scribes and Pharisees were agitating a council to seize him without a popular riot—he was sold for thirty silver pieces, with a guarantee given for delivering the man by night. That sum, estimated in our money, would perhaps make twenty-one Tours pounds. <note>original: *libras Turonenfes*, a standard French currency in Postel's 16th-century context.</note> For a silver piece was equal to fourteen sous. The most worthless and weak slave would have sold for four times as much. But it was so ordained by God the Father. 

Zechariah makes mention of that sale in chapter 11, where he spoke of the gates of the temple which opened of their own accord forty years before your ruin (as I noted before), and he touched upon the nefarious crimes of the priests, and dealt with the rejection of the covenant of Moses and the lamentation of the unhappy race of initiates, saying: "And I said to them (God to the priests), 'If it is good in your eyes, bring my reward. But if not;'"

For within a few days, he destroyed the royal, Levite, and judicial powers into one, and established new men in the temple, the court, and the palace: and yet—if it please the gods <note>A sarcastic Latin idiom (*si Dijs placet*) used here to mock those who refused to see that the traditional Jewish leadership had been dissolved.</note>—the scepter did not then fail from Judah. Your misfortune so captures and affects you that you do not even wish to acknowledge it. 

What shall I say of the temple gates? Finally, what was also proven over forty years follows the "selling of the Just One." For the priesthood was instituted by the Roman power, and given to the more favored, or sold to the wealthier; additionally, it was made an annual office. Because each man performing this magistracy wanted to scrape everything together during his own year, they were killing not only the poor (as is the custom everywhere) but even the rich through extortions, which better suited a royal and new power. For nothing of private means was safe from the reign of Herod until the time of Titus. <note>Titus was the Roman general, later Emperor, who destroyed Jerusalem in 70 AD.</note> The following <margin>Chapter 13</margin> chapter continues to pursue your unhappiness, and says that some among you, coming to your senses by the gift of the Holy Spirit, will acknowledge Christ, who was pierced and killed by them.

It opens the fountain of God's grace given through Jesus Christ. And from that time, all your false prophets have been Rabbis, who, predicting the coming of the Messiah at various periods of time, have held you in perdition for a full 1,500 years. Finally, your misfortune followed, heaped up with captivities, so that it seems to weave the history of the future word for word. I do not wish to be any longer in delivering the rest. In writing this, I wish to be like the Pharisees [only] in following the sequence of the condemnation of Jesus Christ’s death. Although in free cities, where law holds its place, even the life <note>original: *de capite*; literally "concerning the head," referring to a capital trial.</note> of a slave or the most abject man is discussed, and the cause is usually weighed among good men for many days: Jesus Christ had only six hours of daylight from the time He was captured until the cross. Let all mortals see how much "maturity" there could have been in that judgment, even if it had been a matter of a wicked man. On that very day, the princes gathered together as one, against the Lord and against His Christ. ...because he had permitted the judicial investigation of Jesus's case—which he knew had been stirred up by the envy of the Pharisees and scribes—the entire cohort of priests, Pharisees, and scribes gathered against the head of an innocent man, rising against the Lord and against Christ, His son. But because that psalm <note>original: "is psalmus"; referring to Psalm 2.</note> presses them hard, the stubborn will say it should be understood as referring to David. But I ask them to listen to how individual points can possibly apply to David. For whoever is spoken of must have a common cause with God. For the phrase:
> Let us break their bonds asunder, etc. <note>original: "dirumpamus uincula eorum"</note>
shows that a law and a common yoke must be imposed upon all men. But David did not have this, for he was not the author of the Law. And other bonds could restrain all the kings of the earth, whereas no such law existed for them. The Law of Moses was intended to have only one people. The Law of the Messiah pertains to all. It follows, therefore, that it was written about Him and His law:
> He who dwells in the heavens: <note>original: "Qui habitat in cælis"; Psalm 2:4.</note>
God would not have laughed at all the princes of the earth on account of the tiny dominion of the petty king David, because the law under which David lived did not pertain to them. Nor should God have been moved to fury against those who did not sin by refusing to receive the bonds of Moses. It was the Messiah whom God appointed as His king over Mount Zion, so that He might proclaim the commandment and the new law. It was true to say of David once:
> today I have begotten you. <note>original: "hodie genui te"; Psalm 2:7.</note>
But it is always true concerning Christ and His generation. For just as the action of fire always proceeds from its power as long as it is fire, so does His wisdom proceed from the power of God from eternity. Furthermore, if this is said of David, when did he possess the ends of the earth? That belongs to God alone. He rules them with the strict laws of their minds, laws harder than iron and adamant, and He shatters them when He wishes; for He is God. The kings of the world must depend on His example and law. It is necessary for all to kiss Him as the Son of God,
> lest the Lord be angry, etc.
Thus, since nothing—or very little—clearly applies to David, it follows that it must be understood as referring to the Messiah, the Son of God. In this way they corrupt and invert all the meanings of the psalms, but they invert Psalm 109 <note>Psalm 110 in modern numbering, beginning "The Lord said to my Lord."</note> most of all, because they are most vehemently pressed by it to acknowledge the divinity of Christ. But I pass on to other things.

Regarding the torments of Jesus Christ, I judge it superfluous to write how great they were, since solid chapters on this matter are found in the prophets. I shall be satisfied with refuting the impiety of the wicked rabbis where they corrupt the 53rd chapter of Isaiah with their dreams. It says:
> Who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? <note>Isaiah 53:1.</note>
These things cannot be understood as a physical deed or a common event like a war. For they ought to have been sufficiently persuaded of what God could do in such things, whether in afflicting or in saving. Therefore, the prophet declares what this "report" is that is so wonderful as to be scarcely believable:
> And he grew up like a sapling before him, <note>Isaiah 53:2.</note>
that is, before God the Father. 
The wealthy, the powerful, those supported by worldly things, and the wicked are exalted like the cedar of Lebanon; but this one, who is the arm and power of God, rises up like a sapling, so that nothing is more humble and abject or less believable than that which is supreme—like God—should be so humble as to seem lower than the lowest. And like a shrub from dry ground: because it tends upward. For the affairs of the Hebrew people were never so cut down that they did not preserve some splendor. I will not mention how impudently they try to make a whole "people" out of a single "man."
> He has no stately form or majesty, it says: and he had no beauty for which we should desire him; he was despised, the outcast of men, a man of sorrows, and one who experienced weakness. And as one from whom men turn their gaze, he was despised, and we esteemed him not. <note>Isaiah 53:2–3.</note>
If this is said of the Jewish people, who says it about them? Not the enemies who afflict them, nor God who sends the punishment—therefore, no one. For no one speaks of themselves in the third person. All these things are about the affliction of Jesus Christ and His lowliness. For He was so disfigured by spit, mud, and His own blood, that He seemed more abject than a leper. Indeed, they did not recognize Him as...

### ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

...then, keep still. 
> And they weighed out my wages as thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me: "Throw it to the potter—the magnificent price at which I was valued by them." And I took the thirty pieces of silver, and I threw them into the house of the Lord for the potter. <note>Postel is quoting Zechariah 11:12–13, which he views as a literal prophecy of Judas Iscariot’s betrayal of Jesus.</note>

These words entirely contain the sequence of what actually happened. For by eternal deliberation, divine providence had determined to give His only-begotten Son for the redemption of the world, and that whatever was done concerning Him should come to pass, since God knew the perversity of that nation. However, so that no one could say that God compels this person or that one toward evil, He said: 
> If it seems right. If not, be quiet. <note>original: "Si ita uidetur. Sin autem, quiefcite"; Zechariah 11:12.</note>

For no force is applied to free will through predestination. The priests gave the thirty pieces of silver to Judas, who delivered Him to them. Finally, when Judas saw Him being afflicted with unheard-of torments, led by a late repentance, he brought the coins back to the priests. When they refused to receive them, saying to him, "That is your responsibility," he threw them down before them and, departing in misery, broke his own neck with a noose. Those men, still remaining in the temple itself, gathered that money and said that because it was the "price of blood," it ought not be placed back with the sacred offerings, which are called <term>Curban</term> <note>Corban: A Hebrew term for an offering or gift consecrated to God.</note>, but should be converted to the use of pilgrims. And so, busying themselves with washing away their impiety with a new kind of "piety," they bought a small field from a potter not far from the city for the burial of pilgrims, and they called it <term>hacaldema</term> <note>Akeldama: Aramaic for "Field of Blood."</note>, that is, the field of blood, which remains to this day as a witness to your perfidy. This is the history. Furthermore, lest you think this is the only evidence of your ruin and of God withdrawing from you contained in this chapter, there is another, far more serious one, a little earlier: 
> And I cut off three shepherds in one month. <note>original: "Et succidi tres pastores in uno mense"; Zechariah 11:8.</note>

Shortly before this, the triple "shepherd" and power by which any republic must be governed was taken away from you by Herod. For in a few days, he destroyed the royal, the Levitical, and the judicial powers into one, and he appointed new men in the temple, the tribunal, and the palace; and yet, if it please the Gods <note>A sarcastic classical idiom meaning "God forbid" or "can you believe it?"</note>, the scepter did not fail from Judah at that time. Your own unhappiness so captures and affects you that you do not even wish to recognize it. What shall I say of the temple doors? Finally, that which was also proven through forty years follows the sale of the Just One. For the priesthood was established by the Roman power, and given to the one who was more favored, or sold to the one who was richer. In addition to this, it was made an annual office; those functioning as magistrates, because each one wanted to scrape everything together in his own year, murdered not only the weak (as is the custom elsewhere) but even the rich through extortions—which is more suited to a royal and "new" power. For nothing of private means was safe from the reign of Herod until the time of Titus. Indeed, the following chapter proceeds to follow your unhappiness, and says that some of you, repenting through the gift of the Holy Spirit, will recognize the Christ who was pierced and killed by them. The 13th chapter opens the fountain of the grace of God given through Jesus Christ. And from that time, all your rabbis have been false prophets, who, by divining the arrival of the Messiah at various periods of time, have kept you in destruction for a full 1,500 years. Finally, your unhappiness followed, heaped up with captivities, so that it seems to weave the history of the future word for word. I do not wish to be longer in handing down the rest. I wish to be similar to the Pharisees in my writing style as they were in carrying out the condemnation of Jesus Christ’s death. While in free cities, where law holds its place, even the life of a slave and the lowliest of men is considered, and the cause is usually weighed among good men for many days—Jesus Christ had only six hours of light from the time he was captured until the cross. Let all mortals see how much "maturity" there could have been in that judgment, even if it had been about a wicked man. On that very day, the princes gathered together against the Lord and against His Christ. For Herod—the second king of that name—was reconciled to Pilate, the governor of Judea in the name of the Roman Senate.

### WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK IV

Because he <note>Referring to Pontius Pilate</note> had permitted the legal investigation of Jesus—which he knew had been stirred up by the envy of the Pharisees and scribes—the entire cohort of priests, Pharisees, and scribes conspired against the head of an innocent man, against the Lord and against Christ His son. But because that Psalm <note>Psalm 2</note> presses upon them, the stubborn will say it is to be understood as referring to David. 

But I ask them to listen to how these individual points could possibly apply to David. For regarding whomever this is said, it is necessary that he have a common cause with God. For the phrase "let us break their bonds," etc. <note>original: "disrumpamus uincula eorum"; Psalm 2:3</note> shows a law and a yoke that is to be common to all men. But David did not have this, for he was not the author of the Law. And what other bonds could hold back all the kings of the earth except for some Law? None. The Law of Moses was intended to have only one people. The Law of the Messiah pertains to everyone. 

It follows, therefore, that it was written concerning Him and His law: "He who dwells in heaven" <note>Psalm 2:4</note>. God would not have laughed at all the princes of the earth on account of the tiny empire of a petty king like David, because that Law under which David lived did not pertain to them. Nor should God have been moved to fury against those who did not sin by not receiving the bonds of Moses. It was the Messiah whom God appointed as His king over Mount Zion, so that He might proclaim the decree and the new law. 

It was true to say of David once, "today I have begotten you" <note>original: "hodie genui te"; Psalm 2:7</note>, but it is *always* true concerning Christ and His generation. For just as the action of fire always proceeds from its power as long as it is fire, so does His Wisdom proceed from the power of God from eternity. Furthermore, if this is said of David, when did he ever possess the ends of the earth? That belongs to God alone. He rules them with the strict laws of the soul, harder than iron or adamant, and He crushes them when He wills. For He is God. It is necessary for the kings of the world to depend on His example and Law. It is necessary for everyone to "kiss the Son," lest the Lord at some time become angry <note>Psalm 2:12</note>. Thus, since these things fit David clearly not at all or very little, it follows that they must be understood as referring to the Messiah, the Son of God. 

Thus they <note>Postel’s Jewish interlocutors</note> distort and invert all the meanings of the Psalms, but they invert Psalm 110 <note>Postel uses the Vulgate numbering, 109</note> most of all, because they are most vehemently pressed by it to acknowledge the divinity of Christ. But I pass on to other things. 

Regarding the torments of Jesus Christ, I judge it superfluous to write how great they were, since solid chapters on this matter are found in the prophets. I will be content to refute the impiety of the wicked rabbis <note>Postel uses the harsh polemical language typical of the 16th century, "sceleratorum rabinorum," to describe the Jewish scholars of his time who disagreed with his Christological readings.</note> where they distort the 53rd chapter of Isaiah with their dreams. It says: 
> Who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? <note>Isaiah 53:1</note> 

These things cannot be understood as a physical deed or a common thing like war. For they ought to have been sufficiently persuaded of what God could do in that regard, whether by afflicting or by saving. The prophet therefore declares what this report is that is so wonderful as to be scarcely believable: "And he grew up like a young plant before him," that is, before God the Father. 

The rich, the great, those supported by worldly things, and the impious are exalted like the cedars of Lebanon; but this one, who is the "arm" and power of God, arises like a young plant, so that nothing is more humble, more dejected, or less believable than that what is highest—even God—should be so humble as to seem lower than the lowest. And "like a root out of dry ground" because he tends upward. For the affairs of the Hebrew people were never so cut down that they did not retain some splendor. I remain silent on how impudently they <note>Jewish commentators</note> try to make a whole "people" out of this one "man." 

"He has no form nor comeliness," he says, "and there was no beauty that we should desire him; he was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity." <note>Isaiah 53:2–3</note> And like one who turns the faces of men away from himself, he was despised, and we did not esteem him. If this is said of the Jewish people, who is saying it about them? Not the enemies who afflict them, nor God who sends the punishment; therefore, no one. For no one speaks of themselves in the third person. All these things are about the affliction of Jesus Christ and His rejection. ...the wicked nation thought. *Truly he has borne our infirmities, and carried our sorrows, and we esteemed him as one struck by leprosy by God and humbled.* <note>original: "Vere languores nostros ipse tulit... reputauimus eū lepra percuſſũ a Deo et humiliatũ"; Isaiah 53:4</note> This passage explains itself well enough; it does not fit the people [of Israel] in any respect, neither today nor during the Babylonian captivity. For although some may waste away from starvation, yet it is nothing like leprosy. And even if it were similar, no people, while being punished themselves, can bear the sorrows of another. Furthermore, what a great and unheard-of miracle it would be—so much so that no one would believe it—to see (what you almost never see) men worn down and afflicted by wars? Certainly, Christ suffered for us, the just for the unjust. For no man, merely as a man, can bear the infirmities and sorrows of another. 

It follows: *But he was wounded for our iniquities, he was crushed for our sins, and the correction was upon him so that we might have peace, and by his stripes we are healed.* <note>Isaiah 53:5</note> What is more wonderful than this? That by the stripes and pain of one innocent, just, poor, and rejected man, the whole world is healed? That one who is both God and man should carry these signs of weakness? *All we like sheep have gone astray, and the Lord laid on him the iniquity of us all.* <note>Isaiah 53:6</note> What has this to do with a whole people? If this is said of the people, then either the Babylonian captivity never happened, or this present exile is not real. But since both occurred, it would follow that no expiation was ever made for all of you. 

Cease your raving, you impious men, and stop seducing this wretched people. All human beings were sinners except for Christ and Mary. <note>Postel here refers to the sinlessness of Jesus and the Virgin Mary, a central point in his theology.</note> Christ died for the sins of all; He alone, on account of His divinity, wished and was able to transmit the fruit of His death—by which He paid the price for our sins—to all people who believe in Him. For a mere man could not do this. The "stripe" <note>The Latin *liuor* refers to the bruising or livid marks of a beating.</note> truly shows the shedding of blood, in which He established a covenant for those who believe. 

Then: *While he was oppressed and afflicted, he opened not his mouth. Like a sheep he is led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is dumb, so he opened not his mouth.* <note>Isaiah 53:7</note> Who would believe such things? That the most innocent one would not even let out a cry, like a lamb being led to execution? O Jesus Christ, how great is your goodness! Consider these things, you blasphemers; He will have mercy on you, He waits for you to turn to His mercy. 

*He was taken away from distress and judgment.* <note>Isaiah 53:8</note> But that people [the Jews], if the gods permit, did not perish, nor were they led to slaughter, but were preserved for servitude. *Who shall declare his generation?* <note>original: "Generationē eius quis enarrabit?"</note> It follows from this passage that He has nothing in common with other men regarding His birth. But everyone knows from where and how the devilish Jewish people were born and generated. There is the eternal generation of Christ, which is unique, and another which is temporal. 

*And yet he was cut off from the land of the living. For the wickedness of my people I struck him.* <note>Isaiah 53:8</note> This is what Daniel writes: *And Christ shall be killed, but not for himself*—that is, not for his own sake, but for the sake of the salvation of all who believe in him. <note>Postel links Isaiah 53 with Daniel 9:26, a common strategy in Renaissance Messianic debate.</note> *His burial was made with evil men*—that is, his death. *The rich were present in his death. Because he did no iniquity, nor was there deceit in his mouth. And the Lord willed to crush him in weakness. When he shall lay down his soul for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed.* <note>Isaiah 53:9–10</note> 

Let the Jews see their delusions in this place. If the prophet is speaking about a mere man or a group of men, how can he see a "long-lived seed" when he is dead? Does a dead man see a long-lived offspring? These are trifles. Behold God, God from God, the Son from the Father, eternal from the eternal. *The will of the Lord shall be directed by his hand. Because his soul labored in death, he shall see and be satisfied. By his knowledge, my righteous servant shall justify many, and he shall bear their iniquities.* <note>Isaiah 53:11</note> No one except God can justify. Therefore, the prophet speaks of God, yet calls him a "servant." Therefore, He is also man, otherwise He would not have been able to die. 

The Messiah, therefore—the blessed God—suffered for us, the just for the unjust, so that by His justice we might return to grace with God. *Therefore I will give him a great multitude for his spoils, and the strong shall be his prey.* <note>Isaiah 53:12</note> All kinds of men have already partly yielded to Him, and partly shall yield, because He delivered His soul—that is, His life—unto death; and He was counted among the wicked. ...he was crucified among robbers, so that he might appear to receive from their company the disgrace that he himself did not deserve. *And he bore the sins of many*—not of all, unless they believe in him—*and he prayed for the transgressors.* <note>Postel is citing Isaiah 53:12 here.</note> When he was driven onto the cross, near to death, he prayed for the impious Jews, saying: *Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.* <note>original: "Pater parce illis, quia nesciūt quid faciunt"; Luke 23:34.</note> O divine mercy! These things are described no more clearly in the Gospels than they were written by Isaiah. Moreover, Zechariah revealed the nature of his death in chapter 13; after he spoke of the false prophets, he says this regarding the true Messiah: *And it shall be said to him* (to the Messiah, of whom he had spoken shortly before), *“What do these wounds in the middle of your hands mean?” And he shall say, “I was struck with these wounds in the house of those who loved me.”* <note>Zechariah 13:6. Postel interprets the "house of those who loved me" as the authorities of Jerusalem.</note> By the judges of Jerusalem, to which he had come to save, I was thus affected. 

That this is said of the Messiah is shown when God says: *Awake, O sword, against my shepherd; strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered. And I will turn my hand to the little ones, and they shall be in all the earth; the Lord says two parts in it shall be cut off and fail, and the third part shall be left in it. And I will lead the third part through the fire, and I will refine them as silver is refined, and I will test them as gold is tested. He shall call upon my name, and I will hear him. I will say, “You are my people,” and he shall say, “The Lord is my God.”* <note>Zechariah 13:7-9.</note> Everything from that passage to the end must be understood as referring to the Messiah. For no other mortal is read of having died from wounds in pierced hands during his punishment. Those who ought to have loved him did this to him, whom he nonetheless always held as friends. When the sword was raised against Christ and persecution came, all his disciples—except for a few following from a distance—were scattered by the fear of death. Indeed, they were not firm in him until the Holy Spirit descended upon them and emboldened them even unto death. Nevertheless, while Jesus was being afflicted, the Lord meanwhile kept his disciples in his love until he should rise again. Finally, from Judea, two parts were afflicted by slaughter and dispersion; the third part, consisting of the Apostles and Christians, remained, but was to be refined and purged by fire. That people, famous everywhere among the nations for their martyrdom and miracles for 300 years and more, was truly called the people of God.

David mentions the piercing of the hands in Psalm 21: *They pierced my hands and my feet, they numbered all my bones.* <note>original: "Foderūt manus meas & pedes meos, dinumerauerūt omnia ossa mea"; Psalm 22:16-17 in modern Bibles, though Postel uses the Vulgate numbering of Psalm 21.</note> He reveals that he was stretched out on the cross, and because of the weight of his body, the joints of his bones were separated. That entire Psalm was written concerning the afflictions of Christ's body and his human nature, by which he was indeed vehemently tormented. It also describes how those passing by mocked him, saying that because he had saved many, he could not save himself. Thus the scoundrels, mocking the afflicted one, moved their heads in sneers and derision. Shortly after, he mentions those who wished to divide his garments, which they finally shared by lot. All these things agree with what was done. 

Nothing more shameful than the cross could have been devised by the Jews against Christ. It was his purpose that, just as he possessed all greatness within himself, he should also undergo the greatest infamy for our salvation. For because the fruit of the whole world, the price and redemption of all, lay in his death, it was necessary for him to undergo a death heaped with the title of infamy (as far as the opinion of the wicked is concerned). How cruel it was, I leave to common estimation to judge. Since no one, not even the strongest man, could balance his body for even a few moments if a nail were snatched upward through both hands, what could Christ our God suffer, hanging alive on the cross for three whole hours—not held by a gripped nail, but by pierced hands and feet—having the entire mass of his body dangling from the fixing of the nails? O soul purged by his blood, think on these things suffered for you!

He is led as a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before his shearer is dumb, so he opens not his mouth.* <note>Isaiah 53:7.</note> Who would believe these things? That the most innocent one would not even let out a cry, but be led like a lamb to the execution? O Jesus Christ, how great is your goodness! Perish, you blasphemers! He will have mercy on you; he awaits you for mercy. *He was taken from distress and from judgment.* <note>Isaiah 53:8.</note> But that people [Israel], if the gods please, did not die, nor was it led to the slaughter, but was preserved for servitude. 

*Who shall declare his generation?* <note>Isaiah 53:8. Postel uses this to argue for Christ's divine nature.</note> It follows from this passage that he has nothing in common with other men regarding his birth. But everyone knows from where and how the Jewish people of the devil were born and how they were generated. The generation of Christ is eternal and unique; the other is temporary. *And yet he was cut off out of the land of the living. For the wickedness of my people, I struck him.* This is what Daniel writes: *And Christ shall be killed, but not for himself*—that is, not for his own sake, but for the sake of the salvation of all who believe in him. <note>Daniel 9:26.</note> *His burial was made with wicked men*—that is, his death. *The rich were in his death.* Because he did no iniquity, nor was there deceit in his mouth. 

*And the Lord willed to crush him in infirmity. When he shall lay down his soul for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed.* <note>Isaiah 53:10.</note> Let the Jews see their delusions in this place. If the prophet is speaking about a man or men, how can he see "long-lived seed" when he is dead? Does a dead man see long-lived offspring? This is nonsense. Behold, God from God, Son from Father, Eternal from Eternal. *The will of the Lord shall be directed by his hand. Because his soul labored in death, he shall see and be satisfied. In his knowledge, my righteous servant shall justify many, and he shall bear their iniquities.* <note>Isaiah 53:11.</note> No one except God can <term>justify</term><note>In theology, the act of being declared or made righteous in the sight of God.</note>. Therefore, he speaks of God, and yet calls the same person a "servant." Therefore, he is also man, for otherwise he could not have died. 

Therefore, the Messiah, the blessed God, suffered for us, the just for the unjust, so that by his justice we might return into grace with God. *Therefore, I will give him a great multitude for spoils, and the strong shall be for his prey.* All types of men have partly yielded to him already, and partly will yield, because *he delivered his soul*—that is, his life—*unto death, and was reputed with the wicked.* Between two...

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK IV.

He was crucified between thieves, so that the shame he lacked in himself might seem to be received from his companions. *And he himself bore the sins of many* <note>original: "Et ipse peccata multorum tulit"—a quote from Isaiah 53:12.</note>, though not of all, unless they believe in him; and he prayed for the transgressors. When he was placed on the cross, near death, he prayed for the wicked Jews saying: *Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.* <note>Luke 23:34.</note> O divine mercy! By your own people you were beaten with whips, defiled with spit, worn down by lashings, and crowned with thorns; the cross was carried by others, yet you bore your own, and you deign to pray for that people who committed such things against you. In the following chapter, Isaiah calls the same one the God of the whole earth, the Lord of hosts, and the redeemer of Israel. These things are not described more clearly in the Gospels than they were written by Isaiah. 

However, Zechariah revealed the nature of his death in chapter 13. After speaking of false prophets, he says this about the true Messiah: *And it shall be said to him* (to the Messiah, of whom he had spoken a little before): *What do these wounds in the middle of your hands mean? And he will say: I was struck with these wounds in the house of those who loved me* <note>Zechariah 13:6.</note>, by the judges of Jerusalem. Coming to save her, I was thus treated. That this is said of the Messiah is shown when God says: *Ho, sword, rise up against my shepherd: strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered.* <note>Zechariah 13:7; quoted by Jesus in Matthew 26:31.</note> *And I will turn my hand toward the little ones, and they shall be in all the land, says the Lord; two parts in it shall be cut off and fail, and the third part shall be left in it. And I will lead the third part through the fire, and I will refine them as silver is refined, and I will test them as gold is tested. He will call upon my name, and I will hear him. I will say, "You are my people," and he will say, "The Lord is my God."* 

What follows from that place to the end must be understood as referring to the Messiah. For no mortal is ever read to have died from wounds in pierced hands during punishments. Those who ought to have loved him did this to him, whom he nevertheless always held as friends. With the sword raised against Christ and persecution coming, all his disciples (except a few following from afar) were scattered for fear of death. For they were not firm in him until the Holy Spirit descended upon them and emboldened them for death. Meanwhile, however, while Jesus was suffering, the Lord kept the disciples in his love until he rose again. Finally, from Judea, two parts were afflicted with slaughter and dispersion; the third part, consisting of the apostles and Christians, remained, but was to be tried and purified by fire. That people, indeed famous through martyrdom and miracles for 300 years and more among all nations, was truly called the "People of God." 

David mentions the piercing of the hands in Psalm 21: *They pierced my hands and my feet, they numbered all my bones.* <note>Psalm 22:16-17 in modern bibles; Psalm 21 in the Latin Vulgate used by Postel.</note> He reveals that he was stretched out on the cross, the joints of his bones being separated by the weight of his body. That entire psalm was written about the afflictions of Christ’s body and his human nature, by which he was indeed violently tortured; and it describes how those passing by mocked him, saying that since he had saved many, he could not save himself. Thus did the scoundrels move their heads with sneers and turned-up noses, laughing at him in his affliction. A little later, the prophet mentions those who wanted to divide his garments, which they finally shared by lot. All things agree with what happened. 

Nothing more shameful than the cross could be devised by the Jews against Christ. It was fitting that, just as he possessed all the highest qualities in himself, he should also undergo the highest infamy for our salvation. For because in his death was the fruit of the whole world, the price and redemption of all, it was necessary for him to undergo a death heaped with the title of infamy (as far as the opinion of the wicked is concerned). How cruel it was, I leave to common estimation. Since no one, even the strongest, could balance his body for even a few moments of time if a nail were driven through both hands while suspended on high: what could Christ our God suffer, hanging alive on the cross for three whole hours, not hanging by a gripped nail but by pierced hands and feet, having the whole weight of his body hanging from the fixing of the nails? O soul, purged by his blood! Think of these things suffered for you. ...they preserved him as a symbol of eternal life. Truly, there was an earthquake so great that no greater has ever been seen in the whole world in any record of history or memory. The sun failed on that day at the time Christ was fastened to the cross, even though it was the fourteenth moon <note>the time of a full moon during Passover</note>, at which time it is naturally impossible for the sun itself to suffer an eclipse. The first coming has this in common with the final coming: that the sun must be deprived of its light. But at the final coming, it will happen for the sake of transformation, for both the moon and the stars will then fail along with the sun. He rose from the dead on the third day, which David noted by saying: *I slept and was heavy with sleep, and I rose up, because the Lord sustained me.* <note>Psalm 3:5.</note> And likewise: *For you will not leave my soul in hell, nor will you allow your Holy One to see corruption.* <note>Psalm 16:10.</note> 

Ascending on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to men—that is, he led with him into heaven the fathers and patriarchs of the Old Testament redeemed from Limbo; and he gave gifts to men by giving his grace and the remission of sins, and finally by sending the Holy Spirit into the faithful on the tenth day from the Ascension. The prophets mention the sending of the Holy Spirit in many places, so I will refrain from citing them. For his apostles sufficiently revealed the grace of Jesus Christ; besides receiving it in the visible form of fiery tongues, they gave it to all believers by the laying on of hands, so that everyone spoke in various languages they had not learned and possessed remarkable knowledge of the Sacred Scriptures. There are many things in the prophets concerning the second coming of Christ which concern everyone equally. Consider them yourself. You Jews have the context of the Gospel drawn from the prophets and from books approved by you, by which everything that could be said of the Messiah is clearly shown to be said of Jesus. Therefore, the Messiah or Christ promised to you in the Law and the Prophets must be one and the same as the Jesus received by us as Christ. If you wish to return to him, God is pious and merciful. Now I shall satisfy the objections you usually make against his coming, so that I do not seem to have failed you in any way.

# THE FOURTH BOOK OF GUILLAUME POSTEL

<page-num>417</page-num>

Because I proceed by reason wherever I can, and I am writing this work so that it may be translated into the Hebrew language, I collect in a few brief chapters what others have written in great heaps of authoritative citations. If my diligence adds any light to these matters, I leave that to be judged by posterity. The Jews lean on twelve primary arguments to prove that the Messiah has not yet come, and therefore that Jesus is not the Messiah.

**First**, because he was to come at the "end of days." But since it is not yet the end, he has not yet come. I have already hissed away <note>original: "exibilaui," meaning to hiss off a stage, indicating Postel's strong dismissal.</note> this absurdity—it is more an absurdity than a reason—in the previous sections when I examined the second chapter of Isaiah using this logic: No one fails to concede that perfection is better than imperfection. The Jews do not deny that the Messiah must be the most excellent of all men; similarly, his law must be so perfect that no greater or holier law could be given. Since this is the case, and since Divine Providence makes things in the best possible way they can exist, and since every law is established to keep men in their duty, the Messiah ought to have come a long time ago.

Otherwise, God would have acted like a fool, making that which is worse <note>the Mosaic Law</note> last longer than that which is good <note>the Law of the Messiah</note>. For according to the **Tradition of Elijah**, and the number of the **six Alephs** <note>In some Cabalistic traditions, the six "Alephs" (the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, representing 1,000) found in the first verse of Genesis signify that the world will last 6,000 years.</note> at the beginning of Genesis, and the natural order of things, it must be accepted that the world will last six thousand years—a point they themselves are most firmly persuaded of. There were two thousand years of the law of nature and *tohu* <note>original: "thohu," the Hebrew word for "formless" or "void" from Genesis 1:2.</note> up until Abraham; the Law of Moses ought to have lasted at least as long, and the Law of the Messiah for the same duration. 

Yet if the Messiah has not yet come, the Law of Moses has lasted three thousand five hundred years—nearly double what is appropriate. Suppose, with the modern Jews, that 260 years have vanished from the annals (for they subtract that many years so they may more freely sell a costly hope to their kinsmen and contradict Christ). Even by that logic, we would be 700 years away from the end of the world (if we are allowed to follow their tradition, for one must not seriously guess about periods of time). 

Therefore, since God rules and ought to rule this world with the most excellent laws (as far as men are capable of them), one must accuse Him of either ignorance or envy if He did not offer the highest means for moderating human behavior, and in the meantime permitted us to be fed on inferior things—as if He saturated us with husks and bran, only to serve the most excellent feast as a dessert that vanishes instantly. To think this of God is impious. 

Thus, according to the Tradition of Elijah and following the Hebrew truth, there are two thousand years from Adam to Abraham, and the same number from him to Christ, with a few years anticipated. And it is now 1,542 years <note>This identifies the date Postel is writing this text.</note> since him. These figures correspond to the truth of things—which consist of six diverse natures—as well as to the sacred words that place rest on the seventh day, the Tradition of Elijah, and the opinions of the **Cabalists**. 

Wherefore it follows that the Jews have been in error and a reprobate sense for fifteen hundred years already. For if what they claim were true, why would they have been deluded to this day by the countless false timelines of the rabbis, since the end of the world has not yet come? I have taught above how the "last days" are to be understood in most passages of the prophets. For when they are spoken of regarding the first coming, they are understood as the last days of the Mosaic Law, whose worship was to be amended under the Messiah. When spoken of regarding the second coming, they are understood truly as the end of the world. But then Jesus Christ will not come to give a law, but to take eternal vengeance on those who neglected the law; the Jews, obstinate until that point, will feel him as a judge and avenger, not a mediator. 

A few years before the second coming, they will be mocked by the **Antichrist**, the son of perdition. He, having loosened the reins on every kind of pleasure and being famous for deceptions and war, will rush headlong with his followers into destruction at the arrival of Christ. For he will be the one they desired—one who busies himself with joining every kind of pleasure to religion. This is easily proven by the fact that they have never followed any holy, humble, and pious man, yet they have approved many wicked men who were similar to the final Antichrist:

<note>Postel lists historical figures claimed as messiahs to show their failure.</note> **Bar Kokhba** <note>original: "Barchozibas"; leader of the Jewish revolt against Rome, 132–136 CE.</note>, two others, **Simon the Samaritan** <note>Simon Magus.</note>, a certain **Egyptian** (whom Josephus mentions, as he does many others), **Julian the Apostate**, and a **false Moses** who mocked and drowned countless people in the waters of Crete. Finally, there is **Muhammad**, who is closest to the **Antichrist** in his character. For if he had joined deceptive wonders to his crimes and cruelty, he would have been the very last one. Indeed, a countless multitude of Jews perished through the works of these "Messiahs," even more than those who died under Julian.

I have also satisfied another objection raised in that same place, in which they say that **Mount Zion** will be higher than all other mountains of the world upon the arrival of the Messiah. They claim that by placing **Mount Sinai** and **Mount Carmel** on top of it, it will reach a height of three leagues or miles, to the summit of which one ascends "flying like a cloud," as **Isaiah** said. I will not speak of how ridiculous these things are, or how unworthy they are to be said or thought; they expose themselves. Such fables are exploded by others. However, because those who rely on authority without reason will subscribe to anything according to their whims, I shall set aside these altercations and come to rational arguments. 

If that physical mountain is to be so high that it is lower than none, it must be for the sake of some great and unheard-of utility or pleasure—either for access to heaven, or for better air, or for a greater and more elegant view. If it is for a closer access to heaven, what are three miles compared to the two hundred and fifty-five miles which **Pliny**, following **Posidonius**, estimates to be the distance of the moon’s heaven from the earth? And how far is the heaven of the moon from the highest heaven? This would be done for such a cause in vain. Nor can it be for the sake of purer air; for whatever is dross is collected in the clouds at twenty-four <term>stadia</term> <note>An ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet.</note>, which is the beginning of the middle region of the atmosphere. Therefore, since no utility but only loss would be gained from this, it would be a poor thing to do. Nor is it done for the sake of a view; for the higher you are, even if the view extends further, the less you can distinguish details, since the function of sight is to represent clear concepts. Even if the field were open on all sides and the widest level plains were all around, the human eye usually does not penetrate beyond a hundred miles. I even grant that it could be higher than the sun, so that your Messiah could see the world in a single glance: he would still only see half of the terrestrial and aquatic globe. Therefore, in every way, that labor of raising a mountain would be useless. It is therefore (as is frequent in the Sacred Scriptures) that **Christ** is called a "mountain" because of properties akin to the thing; the **Church** also, and its members the saints, are called so, along with many other things. Let learned theologians distinguish which of these apply in which places and for what reasons.

Because all nations have not flocked to Jesus, they argue that Jesus is not the Messiah. I have sufficiently taught above that no man—indeed, not even God himself—can rule the whole world (except at the very end of time) as long as **free will** lasts in man, who is subject to <term>corruptible matter</term> <note>A philosophical term referring to the physical world where things change and decay.</note>. The Jews themselves provide proof of this, for they could not endure God because of terror, nor obey him because of his power. Yet the most excellent way of restraining the empire of the wicked is terror. The Messiah, therefore, who must be a man, will never be able to rule the whole world according to their bodies. He will rule, however, according to their souls. He will also gather all nations to his empire—that is, all those from every nation who believe in him. For if there were to be no evil people under him, even among those who received his law, he would have given the law in vain. For one does not serve a law if one does not sin. God does not use force against the will, and much less does Christ. But if God was never able to rule one nation freely without there always being more evil than good people in it, will the Messiah not be greater than God in the whole world?

That argument brings nothing against Christ. Jesus Christ has had, and still has, followers from the whole world. **Moses** had one nation chosen by God, and it was a most stubborn one; Christ calls all without distinction to salvation, and it is set before everyone to follow. If they are unwilling, the fault is not in the law or the lawgiver...

Therefore, those people truly **change swords and spears into scythes and hoes** who do not even take revenge with fists or words. There are, have been, and will be such people from all nations until the second coming, in which there will be no law, since sin will no longer be committed.

God takes the place of everything for him. It can never happen that one who has abolished all desires (except those joined to necessity) does not live in peace. Among men—tyrants, robbers, the wicked, and those driven wild by any number of crimes, who have as if turned into beasts—these shall become allies, brothers, and friends with pious and good men after they have submitted their necks to the **lightest yoke of Christ.** <note>A reference to Matthew 11:30: "For my yoke is easy and my burden is light."</note> Though there will be a difference in gifts and duties, people will recognize each other as equals; those to whom they once used to be a source of harm, they shall now treat as brothers, laying aside their former character. Why would they stop doing what they do by the guidance of nature, without an intent to harm, and in which they do not commit a sin? See, you blind people, where you have fallen: you make brute animals equal to men just so you can follow your own dreams. For if animals were able to sin, they would necessarily possess reason. 

"Why then," one of the <term>circumcised</term> <note>original: "recutitus." A Latin term literally meaning "re-skinned," used historically as a derogatory reference to Jewish people; Postel uses it here to address his Jewish theological opponents.</note> will ask, "did the prophet use such language if he meant something else?" I will tell you. The reason was a proud magistrate, panting for glory, in whose presence the prophet could not speak openly. Thus the prophet was cut through the middle of his head. So it is read in the histories of the Hebrews. The prophets deliberately wove many miracles and famous things before their most stubborn listeners to make room for divine revelations. Therefore, Isaiah changed the names here. Fierce men, from the time of the first coming, will become most gentle, perfect in every part, and equal to the lowest, if they receive the truth from the heart. But from the time of the second coming, there will no longer be a place for laws or social orders. Christ will enter into an accounting of the previous life with everyone.

Tell me, Hebrew, has it not become known to you in at least forty places in the prophets that Israel was to be rejected? If you deny it, reread what I collected above concerning the rejection of your race. You will believe it whether you want to or not. If you admit it, then you were destined to be estranged from both laws. Otherwise, you are still under the Law of Moses. "We are," you will say. Do you believe there is a God? "I believe it." You are also willing to confess Him as merciful, pious, just, holy, and the best, I suppose. "I am." If He is such a God, and yet for fifteen hundred years He has ignored a people living under His law, pouring out prayers to Him from the heart almost every moment, wasting away with fasts, and nourishing brothers with alms so that there is no needy person among the Jews—then it must be that He has become some kind of wicked and impious God who does not look upon these things for so long. For in the time when He was favorable to you, He was ready almost at your beck and call. Or, what is most true, you have fallen away from the law of Him who no longer hears you. For if He approved of His law in you, He would have heard you at least after several generations of men. Indeed, I have shown above what your sin was, by which you fell into the eternal indignation of God. It follows, therefore, that you are no longer the people of God. You are not to be gathered together anymore, except for those who will be converted to Christ, or those who will follow the Antichrist. For either you must have no God (which would be an unjust God who does not hear His own), or the Jews are not the people of Him who has rejected them for so long.
