...you call Syria, which your ancestors once inhabited, and in the center of which sits Jerusalem <note>original: "Hierosolyma"</note>. How could it be possible for that Messiah to gather the bodies of all men dispersed across the entire world to perform sacred rites in one tiny place, which barely occupies a four-hundredth part of the entire globe? It is surely impossible. And yet they shall gather, as it is written. Therefore, they shall gather not by physical location, but by the harmony of minds and mutual benevolence. You wait in vain, then, for something that will never happen to you. For 1,542 years now, your land has been possessed by the nations. This is because faith in the true Messiah—whom your fathers killed—is such that God now demands a penalty from you. For while Pilate did not wish to send Him to the cross because He was innocent (there was so much more justice in the pagans than in you), they said: **"His blood be upon us and upon our children."** <note>A reference to Matthew 27:25, a verse historically used in "blood curse" theology to explain the Jewish diaspora.</note> You are paying for the crimes committed by them; this has separated you from God. Do not hope, therefore, that this land—subject as it is to birth and decay—was the one promised to you. The most wretched man is he who considers the gifts of fortune to be the reward for the highest virtue. Just as nothing in the works of man is greater than virtue, so it can have no other reward than God Himself. Wherever He is, there is the Holy Land, wherever there is faith in Jesus Christ.

What shall I say to your follies? When you are cornered, you say that the Messiah has indeed been born—for He was born when the Temple was destroyed, as is clear from the last chapter of Isaiah: *Before she was in labor, she gave birth,* etc. <note>Isaiah 66:7. Postel is mocking a Rabbinic tradition that the Messiah was born on the day the Second Temple fell but remains hidden.</note>—but you say He has not yet "arrived." Consider how Satan holds you back and mocks you, turning you away from the truth through the instrument of the Rabbis. Was the arrival of the Messiah necessary or not? In my judgment, you will say it was necessary, since God and Nature do nothing in vain. But if nothing is done in vain, where has that Messiah been hiding for so long, while his people are afflicted and slaughtered by nations everywhere? Who was ever born who lived a useless life for 1,500 years, especially when his work is so necessary? I will pass over this unheard-of lifespan, which is nearly double the life of Adam. Where in the world was he born in such a wasteland that at least his father and mother did not find out about him? And if they did not speak, who knows he was even born? These are dreams, delusions, and the mockeries of impostors, more worthy of loud laughter than a serious response.

The next argument concerns the **Third Temple** devised by the modern Rabbis. Because Zechariah speaks of the glory of the Church and the harmony of minds in the sixth chapter, where he says, *And he shall build the Temple of God,* they think the Messiah will build a certain temple out of physical matter and rebuild Jerusalem. But this has not yet happened; therefore, they say the Messiah has not yet come. You expect a Messiah who is more perfect and greater than all other mortals. Therefore, he will build a temple for God out of the most noble material in the entire world. But in all of nature, nothing is more noble than the human soul and the angelic nature, second only to God. He will therefore take the "material" of souls for his construction, and from them, he will make himself a temple greater than the corruptible world itself. For he demands souls, so that they may move their bodies into the work of God. That **Third House** shall be constructed of **living stones**, just as it has been since the death of Jesus Christ. I would reveal the dignity of these stones to you—that is, the miracles of the apostles and martyrs, with which the entire map of the world could be filled, a taste of which I provided at the beginning of this book—but just as you did with Christ, you would only laugh.

As for the objection concerning the salvation of Israel—that the Jews are not yet saved and therefore the Messiah has not come—I have already answered that above. For when the Messiah was sent, He came for the salvation of the nations no less than for the Jews, and from that time there has been no difference in salvation, whether for Jew or pagan <note>original: "ethnici"</note>. For whoever approaches baptism achieves salvation, not by his own merits, but by the pure grace of Jesus Christ. For unless our salvation depended on His benefit, He would have come in vain. Previous works or laws achieve nothing (perhaps something toward preparation); what is needed is faith in Him and the merit of His passion...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...finally by works that confirm faith and show other men that we are indeed the children of God. In this way, we prove ourselves to the Father, who will render to each according to his works. O Jews, you think that you are what you hear yourselves to be—those who confess and praise God—but you have fallen from the grace of God. For this reason, God does not hear you, nor do you currently have any greater access to God than any pagan. He prayed for his persecutors; this will be as profitable for you as it is for the nations. Indeed, I wonder how you dare to promise yourselves such a return, a temple, and a claim to the holy land, since in the book *Sanhedrin* <note>original: "Sandrin," referring to the Talmudic tractate regarding legal and religious courts.</note>, in the chapter *Helek* <note>original: "Helec," the chapter of the Talmud (Sanhedrin 10 or 11) that discusses who has a portion in the world to come.</note>, it is written that the ten tribes are never to enter the holy land and have no portion in the world to come. Truly, none of you can say from which tribe you descend, except by mere opinion. The coming of Gog and Magog <note>Symbolic figures from Ezekiel and Revelation representing the final enemies of God's people.</note> and his slaughter belongs only to the future; and your messiah, O Jews, will be when the remnant of you joins him against the Christians and the people of God. For although all the plagues rising against the Gospel and bringing the force of the multitude are called "Gog and Magog," there will nevertheless be one specific man, the "son of perdition" <note>A title for the Antichrist.</note>, a king of shameless face. He will wear down the world with luxury and portents, and consume the good with unheard-of punishments; but the coming Jesus Christ will slay him with the breath of his mouth <note>original: "spiritu oris sui," a reference to 2 Thessalonians 2:8.</note> and destine him for eternal punishments, immediately bringing the world to an end. That this is not a proper name but an allegory is clear from the fact that in the chapter *Helek* in the book *Sanhedrin*, Sennacherib <note>The ancient Assyrian king who besieged Jerusalem.</note> is called "Gog and Magog" because he had risen against the people of God under King Hezekiah. And in my zeal, in the fire of my wrath, I have spoken: because on that day there shall be a great shaking over the land of Israel, and the fish of the sea, and the birds of the heaven, and the beasts of the field, and every creeping thing that moves upon the ground, and all the men who are upon the face of the earth shall be moved at my presence, and the mountains shall be overturned, and buildings shall fall, and every wall shall crumble to the earth, etc.

By these words, it is most clearly evident that the final judgment is meant. Furthermore, the "land of Israel" signifies the entire world, in which piety will be trampled by impiety until the Lord arrives—terrible to all the impious—to put an end to the miseries of mortal life.

There remains one single argument: that Jesus did not leave a "seed" (offspring) after him, and therefore was not the Messiah. For in Isaiah 53, it is said of the Messiah:

"And the Lord willed to crush him in infirmity; if he lays down his soul for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed," etc. See the impiety of these wicked men of corrupt minds: when the whole chapter refers to Christ (to whom it fits like a recorded history), they then claim it was written about the affliction of the [Jewish] people. But now, when they think they can twist a single word against Him, they ascribe it to him and attribute to him a "seed." If the Messiah is killed so that he may see a long-lived seed, yet once he is dead he cannot procreate or live among his own on earth, then these things must be understood as a **spiritual seed**. For it is a contradiction to be struck by God and lay down one's soul for the crime of the people, and yet to remain a survivor among men—for those who see a long-lived physical seed must themselves be long-lived. But so it is written. It is also written in Numbers 3: "These are the generations of Moses and Aaron," even though the literal text speaks only of the sons of Aaron. # THE FOURTH BOOK OF GUILLAUME POSTEL
### 423

...and in the evening do not let your hand rest <note>original: "vesperum non cesset manus tua"; a reference to Ecclesiastes 11:6</note>: this refers to the doctrine and learning poured from a teacher into a disciple, from which one must not desist. From this, it is clear that the "seed" of doctrine is spoken of in two places. But I prefer to argue by reason. The King Messiah ought to be blessed in every part and most like unto God, as you believe. Yet no greater likeness can exist in a man with God than when he is free from sin. If the Messiah were to have biological offspring, he would also have had sin; for no one can procreate without sin, however small it may be, as David says: *and in sin did my mother conceive me.* <note>Psalm 51:5</note> It is therefore impious to ascribe the act of biological generation to the Messiah, since his generation is spiritual, as we have already taught. For he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. Furthermore, he who is justice, salvation, and liberation must necessarily be God; but Jesus was such as the Messiah was described; therefore he is God and our justice, upon whom no suspicion of sin can fall.

->EPILOGUE TO THE JEWISH OBJECTION<-

Since we have previously written many various things so concisely that they could not be delivered in fewer words, and since they can hardly be reduced into an Epilogue (as they are like a final summary and compendium), nevertheless, so that they may more easily be held and preserved in your memory, I shall touch upon the main points. You must be forced to admit, being taught by your very senses, that you have been rejected for a captivity of fifteen hundred years, if you do not have faith in the innumerable scriptures. Indeed, it is clear that you are outside the law of God and His grace, because you have not been able to move God—who is just, good, merciful, and pious—with such long-lasting prayers, fasts, and rituals. Meanwhile, all the periods for the coming of the Messiah have long since passed, both those certainly predicted by the sacred texts and those falsely dreamed up by the impostor Rabbis. Truly, the cause of your present calamity and rejection has been the killing of the Messiah, Jesus the son of God and Mary, as is clear by these arguments:

By the revelation of Elijah, Christ was to come in the four-thousandth year; he came, and you killed him. In the six-hundredth year from the prophecy of Isaiah—where there is the secret in the *closed Mem* <note>original: "Mem fetuma." This refers to a scribal anomaly in Isaiah 9:6 (9:7 in English bibles) where the Hebrew letter 'Mem' is written in its final, closed form (ם) in the middle of a word, which Postel and other mystics interpreted as a sign of the Virgin Birth or a hidden mystery.</note>—he came, and you killed him. Around the 490th year from the construction of the second house <note>The Second Temple</note>, he came and was killed, as Daniel had predicted. Fifty years earlier, by the disciples of Hillel <note>A famous Jewish sage</note> who hoped they would see him, he was said to be near at hand, as you have in the Talmud; he came when that time had elapsed, and was killed. He came at the time the Egyptian said the Messiah was born in Bethlehem of Judea. He was to come when the scepter should fail from Judah and from your lawgiver <note>Genesis 49:10</note>; he came in the times of Herod, who destroyed the three orders of the Republic by finishing the royal, sacred, and judicial power and instituting other magistrates. He was to come when prophecy and the miracles of the temple should fail; he came and was embraced by Simeon the Just, who was the last of your holy men, under whom the sacred flame ceased to be carried to the right. Miracles failed from the temple forty years before the temple’s destruction; it was forty years earlier that Jesus was crucified by you. Forty years before, the ten miracles vanished; it was then that the Messiah was killed by you. Forty years before, the temple opened of its own accord, which was opened at the death of Christ by the tearing of its veil. The Messiah was to come before Titus <note>The Roman Emperor who destroyed Jerusalem</note> was born; forty years before his arrival, Christ was killed on the cross. Just as Moses waited forty years for the heart of a stiff-necked people to be softened; for just as many years God was favorable to you in the desert, waiting for your repentance—just as a similar number of days spent by the Ninevites in fasting, weeping, and mourning appeased the wrath of God, and just as Moses by fasting for forty days implored pardon for you—so God, after His son Jesus Christ was killed, wished to spare you for forty years, in case you might perhaps repent. You sold the Just One for money, and you were worse than the nations who had already received him in the neighboring cities. In short, no sign...

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD
### 424

...nothing of the future Messiah, whether in time, person, or place, was absent from Jesus. From that time [of his coming], you have lived as exiles; you lack a prophet, you lack miracles, and you lack the mercy of God. To all nations, by the very impulse of nature, you are more hateful than a dog, as if you were enemies to the parent of nature herself. Before Jesus, you accepted no one as the Messiah; since his death, you have had many false ones everywhere among the nations, besides Bar Kokhba <note>original: "Barcozbas." Simon bar Kokhba led the Jewish revolt against Rome (132–136 CE) and was hailed as a Messiah by some, but his defeat led to his being called "Bar Koziba" (Son of a Lie).</note>. Jesus was most perfect and most like unto God; for that very reason, he was hateful to you. I shall not repeat the prophetic Gospel, in which the words of the prophets agree word-for-word with the Gospel. *Jerusalem, Jerusalem, return to the Lord your God* <note>A common liturgical and biblical refrain, primarily from Hosea 14:1.</note>; *look upon him whom you have pierced* <note>Zechariah 12:10.</note>; grieve over him, as one grieves over the death of an only son. If certain things in our traditions displease you, you are not bound by all of them; we worship the same God. We preserve the books of Moses, except for the ceremonial precepts which were to be abolished. You are not being drawn toward idolatry; your most holy Messiah offers himself: who in truth, even if he were not yours and promised in the Law, is nevertheless superior to all men, and like God in every way within a human body. For—to return the discourse to where it began—he treated enemies just as he did friends, he strove to help men in all things, he never harmed anyone, and he was and is of benefit to the whole world. In short, nothing was lacking in him that you could judge as great in God; wherefore he is both man and God, the Son of God, the wisdom of the Father, living with him and the Holy Spirit forever and ever: Amen.

->THE IMPIOUS OBJECTIONS OF THE JEWS AGAINST CHRIST AND HIS<-
->Gospel, and their refutation.<-

Since to have routed and put an enemy to flight, while leaving him the weapons with which he is accustomed to attack you, is not to win a victory but rather to provoke and irritate him—lest he ever perform what is commanded so long as there is any hope of evasion—I wish to wring from their hands even those weapons with which the Jews attack us and strive to pervert the Gospel. I intend to carry out a complete treatment of those things which serve for their refutation. I have undertaken this work not for a display of wit or for the sake of attaining a little glory, but so that a Hebrew version might eventually reach the leaders of the Jews living everywhere. This will, most importantly, make our own people ready, who are sometimes unable to satisfy the objections of the Jews on the spot. Therefore, if I am permitted after the Arabic version of the first, second, and the beginning of this third part <note>Postel refers here to his massive project of translating Christian texts into Eastern languages to facilitate global conversion.</note>, I shall also translate this one in earnest. But if death or some misfortune prevents me from completing this, I pray and entreat by the most holy name of Jesus Christ the professors and those skilled in the Hebrew language: if they approve of this work, let them translate it into that language, whether they include or remove my name. Since Paris <note>original: "Lutetia."</note> possesses a man who is easily the leader in the knowledge of this language, François Vatable <note>original: "F. Vatablum." A renowned humanist and Regius Professor of Hebrew at Paris.</note>—far superior even to the most excellent of the Jews (whose grandsons are his students in the same institution with singular erudition)—along with Paul Canossa, Alain Caligin (who is excellent beyond his years even in familiar conversation), all of whom are Royal Professors; and since there are countless others who have come from their schools; and since in Germany there are very many, the most famous and easily the first being Widmanstetter, Masius, Welteficius, and Fagius <note>Postel lists the leading Hebraists of the 16th century, including Johann Albrecht Widmanstetter, Andreas Masius, and Paul Fagius.</note>; I would wish them all to be asked that, if they judge this worthy of their translation, they do not deny their labor to the perishing Jews, for they will receive ample rewards for this labor from Christ. In all things, I have seen fit to follow the objections of the Jews which Sebastian Münster <note>original: "Munsterus." A famous German cartographer and Hebraist.</note> attached to his edition of the Gospel of Matthew; although I do not think that specific copy of the Gospel is ancient, as I have seen the same text in many places in Constantinople, and I brought back a transcript with those same objections and left it at Venice in the hands of my dearest friend, Marcantonio Giustiniani, a man of patrician rank and most adorned in both learning and virtue, from whom whatever can be bestowed from a friend to a friend...

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK IV. 425

...[it] can [be], while we were once received among the Turks. But I begin to run through everything in such a way as to proceed according to those things I have already written. For I shall only touch upon those points that have not previously occurred in passing, repeating the rest. I do not wish to refute the insults they bring against Christ, Mary, and Joseph according to their own impiety, since the whole world cries out against them; indeed, to be reviled by the wicked is no less praiseworthy than to be praised by the best. 

In the first chapter they say that the genealogy of Christ was described in vain through the line of Joseph, since he himself is not the father of Christ, but it ought to have been traced to Mary. Therefore, they argue, Christ is not the "son of David" because he is not the son of Joseph. This was done for two reasons by the Evangelists: first, following the usage of Scripture, and second, because of the law established for the Hebrews, which I will speak of immediately after repeating the excellence of the Messiah. 

The Jews also still expect that the Messiah must be the most excellent of all men and as similar to God as possible—this is agreed among them. Therefore, more excellently than other men, and differing as much as can be, he ought to have been conceived, born, lived, reigned, and died. For otherwise, if he were similar to other men in all things, he would have many companions in his virtue and excellence; and since the pinnacle of virtue cannot be held among mortals by one to whom many are equal, a superior could always be found. Let him therefore be such that, when compared to him, Moses, his law, and his happiness are as nothing—most worthy, indeed, as he who was promised to Abraham to reign forever, whom Jacob, Moses, David, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets rightly predicted, as one than whom no greater would come for the salvation of all nations. 

He ought, therefore, to have been conceived and born in a manner unlike others. Thus, not from a seed common to others, nor from a woman who has been "corrupted" <note>In this context, Postel uses "corrupta" to mean a woman who has known a man physically, contrasting her with a virgin.</note>, but rather to be sown by divine inspiration and born of a virgin—greater than which nothing can be given. The prophets predicted this in the places noted by me: "God will give a sign," namely when "a virgin shall conceive" <note>Isaiah 7:14</note>; "The Lord will do a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man" <note>Jeremiah 31:22</note>. 

To the point, then: the Messiah had to be born of a virgin, but the genealogies of women are not usually woven into the sacred texts, except to connect them to a father. This is the usage of Holy Scripture; the Holy Spirit wished to accommodate himself through the Evangelist to the style of the Old Testament, lest he weave a genealogy in an unusual manner. Furthermore, since divinely inspired letters ought to have nothing superfluous, it was sufficient to provide the genealogy of the husband. What woman was more famous than Sarah, from whom you trace your lineage? Not even her father’s name is recorded in her own genealogy. From where was Ruth, from whom the royal line comes? Huldah, Deborah, and countless other most famous women were never celebrated with their own genealogies. Even if some were noted for a remarkable deed, Scripture sufficiently indicates the tribe of the woman from the tribe of her husband. 

As for what the Jews say in response to us—that they were not bound to take wives from their own tribes—if they mean today, when they have fallen away from God and can no longer show which tribe they are from due to captivities and afflictions, I would certainly concede that easily. But I will deny it if they mean as it was once under the Law. For they either kept the law of God, or they did not. If they did not keep it, they were wicked; if they did keep it, they lie when they say they were not bound. For it is written in the last part of Numbers <note>Numbers 36:6–9</note>: "Let them marry whom they wish, only that it be to men of their own tribe, lest the possession of the children of Israel be mixed from tribe to tribe. For all men shall take wives from their own tribe and kinship, and all women shall receive husbands from the same tribe, so that the inheritance may remain in the families." 

Are these writings to be kept or not? Although wicked interpreters have perverted these things, and princes and nobles have acted against them, and your current calamity does not prove it, nevertheless the divine law was to be kept. For a law ought not to be abolished because it is inconvenient. Therefore, since Mary and Joseph were most righteous, they wished to subscribe even to the law, although the marriage was a "shadowy" one <note>original: "umbratile," meaning a formal or legal marriage that was not physically consummated, protecting the Virgin Birth.</note>. Lest the divine conception be turned into a reproach for the virgin, Mary married a man who would assist her in her needs. As for what they raise regarding Adam’s fault...

# ON WORLD CONCORD

...and they diminish the sins of men, so that it might be permitted to sin abundantly in the hope of God's abundant mercy, and so that it might seem there was no need for a mediator. To wash away the stain admitted into our nature—since they have far more teachers of the contrary opinion—I do not wish to tear this down except by natural argument. For they fight against themselves and mutually cut their own throats with various authorities. When God created all things, they were "very good," and more perfect things could not be given. For the philosophers affirm that along with Moses: God is not the author of evil. Truly, all men are born from Adam; if his sin was small, as the <term>Nizzahon<note>A reference to the *Sefer Nizzahon*, a famous medieval Jewish polemical work used to critique Christian interpretations of the Bible.</note></term> says, how can it be that the heart of man, proceeding from the seed of Adam, is prone to evil from his youth? Why are all our righteousnesses like a "menstrual cloth"? Why is there no one who does good, no one justified in the sight of God? Why does God repent having made man? All are sinners; all meet in sin, as if from a principle common and innate to all from the first parent. This is not only handed down in the sacred letters but is also proven by the authors of humanity <note>i.e., secular philosophers and poets</note>. For all are so affected that there is no one who does not delight in his own miseries; all seek the good, but do not achieve it. Therefore, it cannot be that they all agree in this unless it proceeds from the first spring. No one created from Adam was more perfect than he; truly, a sin is considered more serious the greater the person who sins is held to be. Therefore, no one ever sinned more gravely than he, since no one was more noble. Thus, his sin infected the whole mass. Nor could this loss, poured into all men, be repaired except by the Author of nature, who, having received that mass into Himself, might reform it. Therefore, Jesus the Messiah saves His people—that is, those who wish to believe in Him—from their sins. Otherwise, if God seemed unjust for one fault by raging for eternity in inflicting punishment, let them see how, by the same reasoning, they wish the devil (who admitted one guilt of thought) to be saved by God and to be punished unjustly. For it is established from the scriptures that there are devils and evil spirits bound by perpetual punishments. Justly, indeed, God is incensed forever against that foul nature, because it sinned more gravely insofar as it was far more excellent than man; therefore, it became the most harmful of all pests, cast down into the lower world. He <note>the devil</note> leaves no stone unturned here to prevent man from returning to his first happiness. To the objection concerning the virgin and the word <term>Almah<note>original Hebrew: עלמה (*almah*). Postel is debating whether this word in Isaiah 7:14 means specifically a "virgin" or simply a "young woman."</note></term>, I say nothing else except what the prophet himself said: it is a sign and a miracle that a virgin shall conceive; and it would not be a miracle if it were a common thing. Furthermore, it was fitting for the highest of men—as He was God and man (for otherwise one could be greater than He)—to be born of a virgin, in a chastity common with the angels.

### ON CHAPTER TWO.

As for the objection concerning the leader from Bethlehem, that he is not the Messiah because he only saves Israel, it does nothing against us. For as many as were to give their names to Christ from whatever tribe, nation, or region, were to be the "Israelites"—that is, they were truly to see God in man, who is otherwise invisible in His essence. For the Messiah ought to reign forever and in the whole world, and over the Israel of God. Truly, this cannot be done by a mere man; it follows that it is done by a God-man. That objection—that God performing a miracle in a thirteen-year-old virgin was not so great as if He had shown His power in a three or four-year-old—what else does it do but reveal a mind for mere slander? God, who made things exist out of nothing, could make the forms of things change daily; must He therefore do so just so that the <term>circumcised<note>Latin: *recutiti*. A common, often disparaging, Renaissance term for Jews, referring to circumcision.</note></term> might believe? God performs miracles, but not absurdities. God could have shown a greater force of divinity if...

...when He granted to Elisha <note>original: Heliseo; a reference to 2 Kings 4, where the prophet Elisha raises a child from the dead</note> that by his prayers an infant might be raised, it would have been possible for God to do so not just with the body that had died, but with any other matter whatsoever; therefore, He ought to have done it.

Who would believe that Christ learned magic in Egypt, since he spent only four years of his infancy there? What boy at that age is capable of any discipline—let alone that supreme one which contains within itself the very apex and circle of all sciences? These are trifles; right up until his thirtieth year of age, Christ practiced nothing other than the trade of a craftsman with his father Joseph, which was held against him as a disgrace. For everyone wondered, saying: "How does this man know letters, since he has not learned?" <note>John 7:15</note> and, "Is this not the carpenter, the son of the carpenter?" <note>Matthew 13:55</note> and, "From where does this man get wisdom and power?" Christ had to be like his own in all things. Born in humility, he was the Lord of all; though educated in no disciplines or letters, he was knowledgeable in all things. Acting in the most humble condition, he showed, when it seemed right, how great he was, whom the sea, the winds, the demons, and all of nature obeyed. Nothing is more excellent or more rare than when that which is thought abject, ignorant, and humble, appears—beyond everyone's expectation—to be sublime, most wise, and supreme. Such is the course of Christ’s life.

## ON CHAPTER III.

Concerning the baptism instituted by Christ, and that infants <note>original: paruulis</note> must also necessarily be dipped <note>the Latin 'intingendis' refers to the act of immersion or ritual washing</note>, there is nothing in these things that they can disapprove of. Since the Messiah was to be the most excellent of mortals, with an excellence common to no one else, he did not have to adopt his own followers or rule them in any way common to other men or preceding prophets. Therefore, he did not have to be noble through the empty noise, pride, pomp, ruins, or slaughter of the princes of the world, but rather to exercise his right over the most noble possession of men: the soul. But nothing is greater than the soul; therefore, he had to exercise his command over souls. Since he was truly to be a King of Peace, not of war, and was to receive the names of those who would swear by his words in the manner of other princes, he also had to do this with a sign and a sacrament <term>sacramentum<note>In Latin, this word means both a "sacred rite" and a "military oath of allegiance." Postel is playing on both meanings here.</note></term> unlike all others. He was, therefore, to institute a new law and also sacraments, not according to that law which was given in Egypt, but one entirely new and different. Indeed, those signs which the Messiah was to give as a sacrament of faith were to be similar in their effects. Therefore, just as he was to wash souls by the power of his death and the flesh he assumed, so he willed that bodies be drenched with water as the nearest sign, in the name of God the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit—who, as we have seen before, is one God, whose single person the Messiah was to hold within himself. For unless the man were God, a greater could be given to him. Since, therefore, infants are subject to the sin of Adam as soon as the soul is conceived, they must also be washed, so that through the faith of their parents they may swear their oaths to the words of their leader—not differently than circumcision given to boys on the eighth day was the cause of salvation for them. Truly, as to why Christ was circumcised, that was done for a double reason: to prove the law was from God and was good, and to become subject in all things to that law, which He had given to bodies rather than to souls; and finally, so that he who was to be the God-man might receive the sacraments of both laws in one man, just as he joined his entirely spiritual law to the corporal one, and the New Testament to the Old. I do not wish to bring up here how God willed the Jews to act in the first steps of baptism, when he willed them to be purified of their failings by frequent washings. No element is more suited for cleansing than water itself, nor one in which God has shown more miracles, or shows in the creation of things—as may be seen in the first book. Therefore, the Messiah, being about to give a new law, willed that supreme instrument of washing to be the sign of the supreme washing of souls.

->ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD<-

### ON CHAPTER IV.

How truly it has been said that nothing can be more unjust than an ignorant man. The Jews, out of a desire to find fault, do not hesitate to minimize the faith in Christ’s fast, even though they approve of the same in Moses and Elijah. They say: "If he fasted for forty days, why was he hungry afterward?" For they argue he could not have fasted so long as a man; it follows, therefore, that he abstained only insofar as he was God. O, you empty-headed men! Was Moses then a god for forty-eight days <note>original: "quadraginta octo diebus"; although the biblical account in Exodus 34:28 specifies forty days and forty nights, Postel here writes forty-eight, perhaps including the periods of transit or a specific exegetical calculation</note>? Was Elijah a god for the same number? Was Daniel a god for twenty-one days? See where your logic fails. Christ willed to be hungry and to experience in himself all the imperfections of our body, except for sin. There should be no doubt concerning the power of the Word of God. Christ certainly could have shown his divinity to the demon (which is what the demon was fishing for), but he did not wish to. For as to what the Jews say—that in the following objection the demon was so powerful in intelligence that he could have recognized Christ—that must be firmly denied. For there is no separate substance, whether good or evil, that can know the essence of God and comprehend Him as He is. For God would be finite if He could be comprehended by a finite power. Therefore, the demon could not have known the divinity in Christ unless Christ himself permitted it; but He did not wish to give him any sign of Himself, nor to proceed to miracles when there was a place for the order of nature. Bread could have been obtained from elsewhere than through a miracle, and the material to be converted into bread could have come from elsewhere than from the devil. Therefore, the objection is vain.

And although Münster <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a noted German Hebraist and scholar whom Postel frequently engages with regarding Jewish-Christian dialogue</note> responded learnedly to the question in which the Jews ask why God did not reveal His Son in the Law if He has a Son, something must nevertheless be added to his response. Münster responds thus: God did not want to manifest to the children of Israel that He had a Son because they were so prone to idolatry. For they gave an example of idolatry in worshipping the calf, and later Baal-Peor <note>A Moabite deity; the Israelites' worship of this god is recorded in Numbers 25 as a moment of great apostasy</note>. Therefore, they would have said there were two gods and two principles, and they would have perverted the Law by ascribing individual precepts now to the Father, now to the Son, according to their own whims. 

Truly, these points do not fully satisfy the question; for one must not admit to them that nothing is written in the Law concerning the Son of God, since in many places in the Law God speaks to God, mention is made of the Wisdom of God, and He who makes all animals able to give birth is certainly able to give birth Himself. But the knot <note>original: "nodus"; a difficult problem or crux</note> lies in this: why was it written so obscurely and hiddenly concerning Him, so that a matter which pertained to everyone was not most clearly set forth? 

What is most excellent in man is the use of the mind, namely <term>free will (liberum arbitrium): the capacity of the human soul to choose between good and evil</term>, for if this were taken away, the world would have been created in vain, nor would there be a God. Therefore, holy religion—in order to exercise the faith of the good and to condemn the wicked who do not acquiesce to good and just things—does not openly and clearly reveal the things it promises. If, therefore, the Holy Spirit had wished to clearly reveal through the prophets all the qualities and times of the Messiah, the merit of believing would have been taken away, since he would have been so obvious from his birth that no one but a madman could have refused him. And if they had spoken openly, without the context of time and description, saying that God the Son of God would act among men in human form, undoubtedly whoever had seen the slightest sign of divinity in the prophets, or rather in miracles, would have immediately accepted as many Messiahs as there were men famous for rare miracles. Therefore, for the sake of hope, faith, and the stubbornness of the people, God willed to reveal His Son to the world through light hints, so that before his advent he might be sketched out by the conjectures of the pious; but after he arrived, all things written about him would appear clearly.

It is a wonder what made a man so learned and well-versed in every kind of discipline as Münster so perplexed that he has nothing to answer the Jews when they object to us concerning the worship of the saints, claiming we even act against our own Gospel. For in it is written, "The Lord your God shall you worship," <note>Matthew 4:10; Postel is addressing the Jewish critique of the Catholic practice of venerating saints as a violation of monotheism</note>

### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK IV.

"...and Him only shalt thou serve." <note>A reference to Matthew 4:10, concluding the previous page's discussion on the temptation of Christ.</note> Was it really so difficult for a man educated in the primary teachings of sacred matters—and even in the stricter practice of the Gospel—to answer the Jewish objection: that the Church does indeed celebrate the memories of the martyrs and holy men in honor of Him who bestowed His gifts upon them, but that it does not worship them *to receive something from them* <note>original Greek: "εἰς τὸ λαβεῖν" (eis to labein), implying a transactional or pagan form of worship</note> nor adore them? If Münster <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a famous Christian Hebraist whose works Postel is critiquing here</note> is ignorant of the fact that this has been the institution since the time of the Apostles, it is a case of gross and lazy ignorance. For as many as wrote within the first three hundred years after the birth of Christ record that this was the custom in the Church. If the men closest to Christ did not understand the Scriptures, and if everyone universally erred, then there was never any Church of Christ. 

That holy men can obtain more from God through their prayers than those who are still living is stated and hinted at by the Holy Spirit through the prophet, when he says: "Even if Moses and Samuel stood before me," etc. <note>Jeremiah 15:1</note>; for he shows that they had more power with God than other mortals. Since they are powerful in the name of the holy one, through Jesus Christ who blessed them, why is it a wonder that they can be called upon for our necessities, and that in his name healings are performed through their relics or even through their memory alone? For countless miracles have been done in this way, and even the "handkerchiefs" of Paul performed healings <note>A reference to Acts 19:12</note>. 

Furthermore, if God is to be praised with frequent remembrance of his benefits, what can be proposed or repeated to Him that is greater or more pleasing than those things which he performed in man—the greatest of his creations? Thus, in all commemorations of the saints, the Church refers everything back to Christ and God, beginning from Him and ending in Him. To be sure, one might wish that a limit had been placed on images, that *deifications* <note>original Greek: "ἀποθεώσεις" (apotheoseis)</note> of many had not been made rashly, and that no fictional miracles were read. But what can you do? Nothing is so good that men will not abuse it; the tares must be left with the wheat until the harvest. Indeed, nothing—not even God himself—fails to become poison to ruinous men. Yet things are not evil simply because some people abuse them. 

Certainly, holy men—as they are the greatest part of this whole corruptible world—must be held in memory foremost after God. God is to be praised in them, and He is to be entreated through His benefits toward them; even though this equally displeases the Jews and the Muslims <note>original: "Muhamedicīs"</note> who now live in a false religion. Those who have long observed their own laws in these matters ought not to dictate laws to us. If it were only this one thing that prevented them from accepting the truth, then images could be removed for a time and worship suspended. But they propose these things with a mind for contradicting, not for learning. 

Why then did this man, so very skilled in the <term>Talmudic traditions</term> <note>Postel refers to Münster's knowledge of Jewish law</note>, along with many others, not object to the fast of the ten impious doctors who had favored the apostate Barcoziba <note>Simon bar Kokhba, leader of the Jewish revolt (132–136 AD). The "ten doctors" likely refers to the "Ten Martyrs" of Jewish tradition executed by the Romans.</note>? What does the memory of the prophets, of Moses, David, and the Maccabees mean, if it is not a commemoration of them as those to whom God was favorable? I cannot judge otherwise in this place except that it ill suits Münster that those to whom Christ gave power while living (to perform all kinds of miracles in his name, and even greater ones than he did) should have those same things occur after their death—so that a certain faith in their blessedness, eternal life, and God's mercy might be established. These objections of his savor of that "sleep of the soul" <note>Psychopannychism, the belief that the soul sleeps between death and resurrection, which Postel views as a precursor to atheism</note> from which our impious men have derived the mortality of souls. Certainly, it becomes a greater sign of divine piety toward us when a manifest and necessary miracle occurs after death, than when it occurred during this present and doubtful life. 

Therefore, although there are many saints who are not recorded in the <term>calendar of saints</term> <note>original: "diariū ſanctorū"</note>, the holy congregation has never enrolled anyone among the "divine" <note>the saints in heaven</note> except for Martyrs, or those clearly famous after death for miracles performed in the sight of many. Suppose that some have crept into the reputation of holiness through ambition; are all the others the same? The veneration of holy men must not be yielded to the Jews, since even when God was present and terrifying them, they preferred a calf to Him; they never ceased worshipping idols amidst God’s frequent miracles, even sacrificing their own children. 

Regarding the entry into Paradise before the death and redemption of the Messiah, Münster answered well: that no one ought to have entered Paradise before the coming of the Messiah. For since it is confessed that Adam was exiled from both <note>likely referring to both the earthly and heavenly paradise</note> through sin, and since there is no greater joy or happiness of which a man can be a participant...

...to become human than the contemplation of God and the First Cause. It remains, then, that the supreme man, the Messiah, revealed this to his followers, and did so through love—or rather, in a manner like no other: namely, through death. For while other men preserve life through living, Christ does so through death. If any other man besides Him could have secured such a great inheritance for his subjects, he would have been His superior or His equal; but such a thing is inconsistent with the majesty of so great a man. The Gospel text is a parable, not a historical event. The pious were in a certain place unknown to mortals before the time of Christ, in "a lake in which there is no water," <note>original Latin: "in lacu in quo nō est aqua," quoting Zechariah 9:11. In the 16th century, this was often interpreted as Limbo or a state of waiting for the Messiah.</note> as Zechariah says. For He, by the blood of His covenant, led the prisoners out of the lake in which there is no water—that is, from a certain place outside of paradise. As for those wicked distorters who, in their commentaries, refer these things to the departure from Egypt, I read of no blood shed there by the lawgiver <note>Moses</note>. Furthermore, there is a promise that brings immediate joy because of the coming King; for it says: "Behold, your King comes," or "is coming," etc. They also say in the traditions of the <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>A Jewish mystical tradition that Postel studied deeply, believing it contained hidden Christian truths.</note> that Abraham, with his servant Eliezer, and the souls of the righteous are "under the leaf of majesty" <note>original: "sub folio maiestatis," likely referring to the protective shadow of the Divine Presence or Shekhinah.</note>. This contradicts the wicked opinion of the <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, which Postel frequently criticized while simultaneously mining it for support of his own theories.</note> which claims that Abraham holds authority over both hell and paradise.

As for the fact that Christ did not wish to become known through miracles and the Gospel before his thirtieth year, that was determined by His own will. That is the mature age at which He chose to adorn His life with miracles. Furthermore, He did this so that one who had for a long time practiced the craft of a carpenter <note>original: "fabrilem artem"</note>—and had not previously been engaged in letters or formal disciplines—might suddenly bring forth the works of a hidden divinity, even while being regarded as the lowest of mortals. I have said before: if He had arrived with human power and glory, known to everyone, He undoubtedly would not have lived three years among that stubborn nation without them declaring war on the whole world by exalting Him through seditions, even though He was intended to be the Prince of Peace.

### ON CHAPTER V.

I have already abundantly satisfied the objection of this chapter, as I have shown from the prophets that the ceremonies of the Law of Moses were to be removed so that they might be joined to the Law of the Messiah. Furthermore, Münster <note>Sebastian Münster, the Hebraist scholar Postel is debating.</note> recites almost the same points. See the passages concerning the abrogation of ceremonies and circumcision in Deuteronomy, Isaiah, David, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, etc. Regarding the sixth chapter, Münster offers nothing, and I follow his example for that reason, as those objections might cause offense to some. Otherwise, there is no need to know these things except when they are raised as objections, so that one may refute them and satisfy the Jews. There are no objections to the seventh chapter. But the example Münster brought from the Hebrews is not without error when he discusses the nature of evil—namely, how we are evil, whether in body, in soul, or in both. I gather from this very passage by the adversaries themselves that our whole nature is corrupted. The parable is as follows: They say, "If the flesh sins without the spirit, why is the spirit afflicted? Since the one sins and the other is punished, it follows that they sin together." This is clear from the following example. A certain King had planted a garden in which there were the most excellent fruits of all kinds; however, he could not appoint any guards over it without them stealing the fruit. Therefore, having entered into a plan, he assigned the guarding of the garden to one blind man who could not see, and one lame man who was unable to climb the trees. But they committed a fraud together: for the blind man, supporting the lame man on his shoulders, stretched him up to the fruit, so that the theft became common to both. By this, they wish to imply that the principle of evil is in both natures <note>both body and soul</note>, which should not be asserted thoughtlessly. Therefore, the soul and the parts of the mind must be distinguished. For it is admitted that there is vice in the flesh. Truly, it possesses a vital soul, an animal soul, and a sensitive soul; these three are one thing, resulting from and depending upon the nature and temperament of the body. If, therefore, the Jews say that this "spirit" is corrupted along with the body, we do not deny it. But if they mean that highest mind, which comes into the human body from heaven—which the Prince of Philosophers <note>Aristotle</note> in the third part of his book *On the Soul* calls the "abstract and immortal intellect"—

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK 4

...understand that this assertion carries danger. For if evil were to proceed even from the **abstract intellect** <note>The higher, rational part of the human soul, separate from physical desires.</note>, without a doubt, **free will** <term>liberum arbitrium</term> in man would entirely perish. Indeed, if those two wills by which we are driven in opposite directions were both depraved, there would certainly be no accusation of conscience to resist evil. Therefore, since we do the evil that we do not want, it is clear that our reason perceives things differently than the bodily spirit. Thus, when that intellect, so full of life within the body, allows itself to be conquered and drawn toward the pleasures of the bodily soul, it is deservedly punished—not as the author of the act, but as an accomplice and one who complied. Therefore, the analogy of the "blind and the maimed" <note>A common medieval analogy where the soul is a blind man carrying a lame body, or vice versa; here Postel argues it is a poor comparison for the immortal soul.</note> is a poor one if it is understood to represent the immortal part and the body.

In Chapter 8, they raise this objection: Why did Christ send the leper, once cleansed, to the priest after his healing? Christ made both into one; he joined the works of his divinity to the observation of the Law for this reason: to show that its precepts were holy. For it was not necessary for the sake of health, but for the sake of distinguishing between different types of leprosy <note>Referring to the priestly duty in Leviticus to certify a healing.</note>. For He himself never violated the Law unless necessity compelled it: such as when He approved of rubbing the ears of grain on the Sabbath, or healed on that same day. As for his neglect of the washings of the traditions, and other matters, they are unworthy of a response.

It follows: Since Jesus in many places calls himself the **Son of Man**, it is indicated to us therein that we should not worship the Son of Man, because Balaam said, "God is not a man that he should lie," nor like a man that he should change. "Do not put your hope in the generous, in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation," says David; and even more so: "Cursed is he who trusts in man, and makes flesh his arm." We confess that Christ frequently calls himself the **Son of Man**. Therefore, we deny that one should not hope in him. If the Messiah had been a mere man, he would not have been worthy of worship. But because he is the highest of all men—that is, the **God-Man**—he was to be worshiped. Nor is it an evil thing to hope in him. For Scripture says, "In him the nations shall hope," when it speaks of the Messiah. Therefore, even if he had only been a man, one ought to have hoped in him, which is what your fathers did. For since you Jews trust in a man, and expect a butcher and a tyrant most unlike God to be your Messiah, you are all cursed. You cut your own throats, you **circumcised ones** <note>original: "recutiti," a contemporary, often polemical term for Jews.</note>. By embracing the highest of men as God and man together, we follow the truth. Your butcher Messiah—or rather, the **Anti-messiah** <term>Antimessias</term>—will be the blight and ruin of the world. Since God is desirous of preserving nature, your Messiah is going to overturn the world for the sake of the pleasure of a few men.

->### ON CHAPTER IX.<-

I truly wish the occasion for this perplexity had not been presented to me, since I do not know well enough whether I am refuting the opinion of the Jews or that of the translator. Therefore, since **Münster** <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a famous Christian Hebraist whose translations and commentaries Postel often critiqued.</note> harms the accepted faith regarding good works more than the Jews do, both must be rebuked. The Jews disapprove of our **fasts** <term>ieíunía</term> because we eat during the day, whereas they are not accustomed to take food before evening—which the ancient **Church** <term>Ecclesía</term> used to do. Furthermore, they claim we do not begin the day of fasting well because we eat meat on the night preceding the fast day. But they are disparaging the method of acting, not the thing itself. For them, the day begins from evening to evening; for us, from **midnight** <term>mesonyctío</term> to midnight; for others from sunrise to sunrise; for some from midday to midday. However, since there is a deprivation in things, it seems that eternal night preceded the light; but if we take night as a condition, the day precedes it in dignity. Yet these things are irrelevant. For it matters little at what point you begin to do well, provided that you do well. As for what they add ironically—that we fast unworthily on the sixth day <note>Friday</note> in memory of the **Passion of Christ**, when we ought rather to be joyful because of our liberation—this is a matter unworthy of a response. For because of His pains and our misery, which crucified Him through the work of those Jewish executioners, one must weep and fast, both daily and especially on that day; yet one must also rejoice because of the certain hope of salvation, which we do together with the pious and holy...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...is possible. For a true Christian must always weep and always rejoice. By the knowledge of our misery, the flesh and the "old man" <note>A Pauline concept referring to the unregenerate human nature prone to sin.</note> are weighed down and die; yet through the certain hope of salvation, one is invited to continual joy. Thus, true hope in God relies first on humility of self.

But I wonder greatly what came into the mind of Münster <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a famous German Hebraist and scholar whom Postel often critiques for his interpretations of Jewish texts.</note>, a man otherwise prudent and wise, that he would assert that we and the Jews have falsely believed fasting <term>ieiunium</term> to be a "good work." If fasting is not a good work, Münster, then God—who commanded it and approved of it in countless places—is imprudent and empty. Certainly, no greater impiety regarding good works could be brought forward. But he makes the excuse that one ought to fast "always," as if indeed the Apostles and their successors, who pre-ordained certain days for greater abstinence, did not understand that in this world we must live soberly, justly, and piously. Truly, Christ, who said, "When you fast," etc. <note>Matthew 6:16.</note>, not implying that one must always fast equally, did not understand the Gospel in that way. It is indeed true that one must always live soberly, but on certain days more than just soberly—to the point that you barely even yield to the laws of necessity. I do not wish to recount the praises of fasting here, or how many times the Lord turned away his wrath because of a fast, or how demons and wild beasts are conquered by it, for that would be another work entirely.

Thus, the Jews write poorly when they observe the fast of Friday; but you, Münster, write impiously, because you desire nothing to be prescribed for men except their own lust. For if things were done better without a prescription than with one, God would have been a fool to give laws to men. Certainly, the modern faction <note>Likely referring to radical reformers or those Postel views as discarding tradition.</note> seems more plausible to you than the Apostolic life, and you prefer to call Christ a liar rather than anyone else like yourself.

In his response to the following objection, he has hit the mark <note>original: "rem acu tetigit," literally "touched the matter with a needle," meaning to be precisely correct.</note> against the Jews who affirm that whatever miracles Christ performed had already been performed by the ancients. For the difference lies in this: Christ alone did what all the saints did, but He did it in His own name, whereas they did it by invoking God. Furthermore, many things were performed by Him that were never done before Him: the Transfiguration, the Resurrection, His conduct after the Resurrection, the sending of the Holy Spirit, and the granting of similar miracles to His true followers—in which matter His divinity is most clearly seen.

I have already responded to the objection regarding the eternal peace among true Christians, which Münster also satisfies well in his annotations on Chapter 10. It is impossible, as long as human free will <term>arbitrium</term> lasts, for evil men to ever be lacking in the world, by whose occasion war arises daily. For if there were to be no evil people under the Messiah, He would give the Law in vain. But since He was going to give a Law, and one by far the most perfect, it is necessary that there be the wicked and the dishonest under it, for whom He might prescribe rules. Therefore, that peace is understood not as a peace of bodies, but of souls, and that only among the good. Thus, the Gospel does not conflict with the Law when Christ says He will "send a sword into the world" <note>Matthew 10:34.</note>. For however many good people there are, the better they are, the more they are afflicted by the impious; and the more they are harassed, the greater the peace they exercise toward all men. For virtue, the more it is exercised—even though it is undertaken for the sake of rest—the less it enjoys its goal in this life. For if it wished to enjoy rest in this life, it would cease to be virtue. For the present life consists in the action of the good; the future life consists in the perception of the reward.

Who does not see the impudent slander of the Jews regarding Chapter 12, where the Sabbath <term>sabbatum</term> is discussed? For they say that in our exposition of the Sabbath, it is said that one must especially cease from sins—suggesting that we are advising that on other days one should persist in sin. Who is so impious as to have ever even thought this? A Christian must indeed always beware of all sins more than death, but most attentively on a feast day or Sunday, so that we may labor to wash away the faults committed on other days through tears, confession, good works, and every kind of expiation before God. The common tenor of human life cannot always be in the same order, yet a good man must never act wickedly.

He clarifies that while Christians strive for holiness daily, the Sabbath and fast days are specific times for heightened devotion and expiation.</summary>

# BOOK IV OF GUILLAUME POSTEL

...good. And so, although he should strive for good works throughout the whole course of his life, nevertheless on certain prescribed days he ought most attentively either to resist sins or to persist in good works. **To** their objection against Christ's response to the Pharisees—that people are accustomed to help both humans and beasts whose lives are in danger on the Sabbath—nothing else needs to be brought forward than this: if physical action violates the Sabbath, then it would be violated most of all by its guardians, the Levites <note>The priestly tribe of Israel responsible for temple sacrifices.</note>, who work most with their hands on that day. From this it follows that the violation of the Sabbath does not lie in necessary work, but in the neglect of the commandment. For otherwise God would not have "hated your Sabbaths" <note>A reference to Isaiah 1:13-14, where God rejects rituals performed without a pure heart.</note>, O circumcised ones <note>original: "recutiti," a term for the circumcised, here used polemically.</note>, if you had performed all works of mercy in them through whatever physical service was required. As for the story Münster <note>Sebastian Münster, a contemporary Hebraist whom Postel frequently debates.</note> brings up about the Saxon Jew—though it seems to suggest the habits of all, because he spent the Sabbath and the Lord's Day <note>Sunday</note> in the latrine <note>An allusion to a popular anecdote where a Jew falls into a pit on a Saturday and refuses to be rescued to avoid breaking the Sabbath, only to have the Christian prince refuse him rescue on Sunday.</note>—nevertheless, those same customs of Sabbath observation do not exist in Africa, or in Asia, especially among the Karaites <note>A Jewish sect that follows the written Torah and rejects the oral traditions of the Talmud.</note>, who reject the traditions and the Talmud <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central body of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note>. They always have this grumbling in their mouths: that we do not observe the Law, even though Christ came to fulfill it and said that "not one jot or tittle" <note>Matthew 5:18.</note> of it would perish until all things are accomplished. This point has already been abundantly satisfied. For the new law was not intended to be like the old one, except in those things pertaining to morals.

But a difficult question follows. "If he is God," they say, "why did he hide himself in the flesh? And why did he not come with boldness to proclaim his law and to explain it in public, so that the people of that age would not be deceived, nor mortals stumble over him? He ought to have done his works in the open, for both the known and the unknown, so that all might believe in him. For the loss of those who perished because of this concealment is greater than the redemption itself; because people hesitate to believe in one who is hidden." These objections are translated word-for-word so that they may understand. I have already answered them in many places, yet I will repeat my answer briefly. In all things, God wishes to exercise our free will <term>arbitrium</term> <note>The capacity for choice, essential for moral merit in Postel's theology.</note>. Just as all the miracles he performs rouse us to obedience and virtue, so too he allows us the capacity and choice in carrying things out, so that those who are proven and upright might be revealed. For just as God under Moses could, with no more difficulty than a blink of an eye, have transferred you all from Egypt—striking down the Canaanites—into the Holy Land without any need for the diligence of faith, just as he showed power above nature before Pharaoh, in the sea, in the desert, in the river, in the sun, among the Philistines, in Sennacherib <note>An Assyrian king whose army was miraculously defeated.</note>, in Habakkuk, in Daniel, and the youths; yet he willed that he should test the faithful by having them arrive there through human labor. Likewise, when the Messiah came, whose law was most excellent, in order to leave the choice of believing [to us], he—as the Preserver of nature—did not wish to join his power with bloodshed in the manner of tyrants, lest it should force all, even the unwilling, to swear by his words. For he would have been most unlike God if he had acted in such a way. The power of believing was given to all through the freedom of faith, which would have been taken away—along with its merit—had it been more manifest in the beginning. Furthermore, if Christ had been known immediately from his birth, you would have driven him, even against his will, into wars and the ruin of the world. Certainly, if he had come with physical power, he would have either brought disaster to the entire world (which he had come to save) or he would have had many rivals. He could hardly have been a match for Ninus <note>The legendary founder of Nineveh.</note>, who led fifteen hundred thousand men into war and slaughtered countless numbers; or for Semiramis <note>A legendary queen of Assyria known for her conquests.</note>, who led eighteen hundred thousand; or for Xerxes <note>The Persian king who invaded Greece with a massive army.</note>, who led ten times as many; nor could he have been wealthier or more splendid than Solomon. Therefore, it is not his fault that many perished and stumbled, just as it is not the fault of water if many die of thirst because they are unwilling to come to the spring. That more are lost than saved is no surprise. For few are good; and as you have it in your Talmud, the situation at the coming of the Messiah will be just as it was at the entry into the Holy Land. For only two out of at least fifteen hundred thousand men entered the Holy Land—Joshua and Caleb <note>Numbers 14:30; the only two adults of the generation that left Egypt who reached the Promised Land.</note>. This was not the fault of God, nor of Moses, nor of the Holy Land; so also when Christ came, very few were to be saved, as it happened. He was sent for the salvation of Israel throughout the whole world, yet so...

...it is possible. For the true Christian must always weep, and always rejoice. By the knowledge of misery, the flesh and the **old man** <note>A biblical concept from St. Paul referring to the sinful human nature before spiritual renewal.</note> are weighed down and die, while through the certain hope of salvation, one is invited to perpetual joy. Thus, true hope in God rests first upon humility of self. Furthermore, I wonder greatly what came into the mind of *Münster* <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a famous German Hebraist and mapmaker whose interpretations Postel often disputes.</note>—a man otherwise prudent and wise—that he should assert that we and the *Jews* have falsely believed fasting to be a good work. If fasting is not a good work, *Münster*, then God would be unwise and vain, for He commanded it and approved of it in countless places.

Certainly, no greater impiety regarding good works could be brought forward. But he uses the pretext that one ought to fast always: as if indeed the apostles and their successors, who appointed certain days for greater abstinence, did not understand that in this world one must live soberly, justly, and piously. Truly, Christ, who said, "When you fast," etc. <note>Matthew 6:16.</note>, did not imply that one must always fast in the same way, and would not have understood the Gospel in that manner. Indeed, one must certainly always live soberly, and on certain days more than soberly, so that you hardly even satisfy the laws of necessity. I do not wish to recount here the praises of fasting, nor how many times the Lord turned away His anger because of fasting, or how demons and wild beasts are conquered by it, etc.; for that would be another work entirely. Therefore, the *Jews* write poorly when they observe the fast of Friday; but you [Münster] act impiously, because you desire nothing to be prescribed for men except their own lust.

For if things were better done without a prescription than with one, God would be a fool to have given laws to men. Certainly, the modern faction <note>Likely referring to Protestant Reformers who rejected mandatory fast days.</note> seems more plausible to you than the apostolic life, and you would rather call Christ a liar than anyone else like yourself. In the response to the following objection, he has hit the nail on the head <note>original: "rem acu tetigit," literally "touched the matter with a needle."</note> against the *Jews* who affirm that whatever miracles Christ performed had been performed by the ancients. For in this he differs: what Christ alone did, compared to what all the saints did—He did in His own name, while they did so by invoking God. Although many things were performed by Him that were not done before Him: the Transfiguration, the Resurrection, His conversation after the resurrection, the sending of the Holy Spirit, and the granting of similar miracles to true followers—in which matter His divinity is most clearly seen.

I have already responded before to the objection concerning the eternal peace among true Christians, which *Münster* also adequately addresses in his annotations on chapter 10. It is impossible, as long as human free will lasts, that there should ever be a lack of evil people in the world, whose presence causes war to arise daily. For if there were to be no evil people under the Messiah, He would give the Law in vain. But since He was to give a law, and by far the most perfect one, it is necessary that there be wicked and shameless men under it for whom He may prescribe rules. Therefore, that peace is understood not as a peace of bodies, but of souls, and that only among the good. Thus, the Gospel does not conflict with the Law when Christ says He will "send a sword into the world" <note>Matthew 10:34.</note>. For however many good people there are, the better they are, the more they are afflicted by the impious; and the more they are harassed, the greater the peace they exercise toward all men. For virtue, the more it is exercised—though it is undertaken for the sake of rest—the less it enjoys its target in this life. For if it wished to enjoy rest in this life, it would cease to be virtue. For the present life consists in the action of good, while the future life consists in the receiving of the reward.

Who does not see the shameless calumny of the *Jews* in chapter 12, where the Sabbath is discussed? For they say that because it is stated in our exposition of the Sabbath that one must especially cease from sins on that day, we are suggesting that on other days one should persist in sin. Who is so impious as to have ever even thought this? Indeed, a Christian must always guard against all sins more than against death, but most attentively on a feast day or the Lord's Day [Sunday], so that we may labor to wash away the faults committed on other days before God with tears, confession, good works, and every kind of expiation. The general course of human life cannot always be of the same tenor or the same order; nevertheless, a good man must never act wickedly.

...good. Therefore, although one should strive for good works throughout the entire course of life, on certain prescribed days, one must most attentively either resist sins or persist in good works. **Regarding** their objection against Christ’s response to the Pharisees—that it is customary to aid both humans and beasts whose lives are in danger on the Sabbath—nothing else needs to be said except that if a physical action violates the Sabbath, then it would be most violated by its own preservers, the *Levites* <note>The priestly tribe of Israel responsible for temple sacrifices, which involved significant physical labor even on the Sabbath.</note>, who work most heavily with their hands on that day. From this it follows that the violation of the Sabbath lies not in a necessary work, but in the neglect of the commandment. For otherwise, God would not have "hated your sabbaths" <note>A reference to Isaiah 1:13.</note>, O circumcised ones <note>Original: *recutiti*. A common, often polemical, Latin term for Jews.</note>, if you had performed all works of mercy through any bodily duty upon those days. 

As for the story *Münster* <note>Sebastian Münster, mentioned on the previous page.</note> brings forward regarding the Jew of *Saxony*—although it seems to suggest the character of all Jews, because he remained in the latrines on the Sabbath day even when the Lord’s day followed <note>A famous medieval anecdote where a Jew falls into a cesspool on a Saturday and refuses to be rescued to avoid breaking the Sabbath; the local Bishop then refuses to let him out on Sunday, the Christian Sabbath.</note>—nevertheless, these same customs of Sabbath observation are not found in Africa or Asia, especially among the *Karaites* <note>Original: *Carainos*. A Jewish movement characterized by the recognition of the Tanakh (Hebrew Bible) alone as supreme authority, rejecting the Oral Law or Talmud.</note>, who reject the traditions and the **Talmud**.

They are always muttering and have it in their mouths that we do not observe the Law, even though Christ came to fulfill it and said that not one jot or tittle of it would perish until all things are done. This part has now been abundantly satisfied. For the New Law was not to be like the old, except in those matters pertaining to morals. 

But a difficult question follows. "If he is God," they say, "why did he hide himself in the flesh? And why did he not come with audacity to proclaim his law and to explain it in public, so that the people of that age would not be seduced, nor mortals stumble because of him? He ought to have performed his works in the open, for the known and the unknown, so that all might believe in him. For the loss of those who perished because of this concealment is greater than the redemption itself; because he was hidden, they hesitate to believe." These words are translated literally so that they may be understood. 

I have already satisfied these points in many places, yet I will repeat it briefly. In all things, God wishes to exercise our free choice <note>Original: *arbitrium*. Postel emphasizes that faith must be a voluntary act of the will rather than forced by overwhelming evidence.</note>. Just as He performs all the miracles by which we are stirred to obedience and virtue, so He allows us the power and choice to carry things out, so that those who are proven and upright may be made manifest. For God could have transferred you all from Egypt in the blink of an eye under Moses—striking down the Canaanites without any need for your diligent faith—just as He showed power beyond nature before Pharaoh, in the sea, in the desert, in the river, in the sun, among the Philistines, against Sennacherib, through Habakkuk, in Daniel and the youths. Yet He willed that the faithful be tested by human labor to reach that goal. 

So too when the Messiah came, whose law was most excellent: to leave the choice of believing, the Preserver of nature did not wish to join His power with blood in the manner of tyrants, lest He compel everyone to swear to His words even against their will. He would have been most unlike God had He acted so. The power of believing was given to all through the freedom of faith; this merit would have been removed had He been more manifest in the beginning. Certainly, if he had come with physical power, he would have either brought slaughter to the whole world (which he came to save), or he would have had many equals. Nor could he have been richer or more splendid than Solomon.
