It also pertains to the matter that he gave an example, lest we boast of ourselves on account of divine benefits. <margin>In chapter 13</margin> <note>Likely referring to Matthew 13, which contains the Parable of the Sower and other comparisons.</note> They <note>The Jewish interlocutors or critics Postel is addressing.</note> debate the parables of Christ using the likeness of Aaron’s rod, which we apply to the Virgin Mother, as if every likeness must agree in all respects with the thing it is compared to—a principle that not even secular authors grant. I would ask them: if parables must be fitted to their likenesses in all respects, then when Hosea compares an adulterous wife to the synagogue <note>Original: *synagogæ*. Postel refers to Hosea 1-3, where the prophet's marriage to Gomer is a metaphor for God's relationship with Israel.</note>, it would be necessary for the synagogue to have worshipped all the gods of the entire world, just as a harlot admits all men. It would be necessary for it to be shaved like hair and implanted in the body, since the Jews are compared to hair by Ezekiel; and six hundred things of this kind. For all things are full of parables; yet in the prophets, there is none that fits perfectly in every detail of comparison.

I do not refute the futility of the Jews regarding the fire of hell, since it refutes itself. For they say that the bodies of the wicked are to be consumed by fire like chaff, so that no memory of their name remains. But what purpose would the future resurrection serve if the destruction <note>Original: *corruptio*.</note> of the one rising could occur? Why would those perish entirely whose name and body ought to endure eternally for their disgrace, so that the action of divine justice may be known? In the future age, there will be no consumption of bodies. The matter of the human body alone will be able to suffer, not be destroyed, with an eternal bond holding the bodies themselves together. Thus, just as in their obstinate lust for sinning they thought God was nothing, or did not care for human affairs, or possess justice, so they may feel him to be the avenger forever, whom they believed did not exist.

The objection of the Jews is false when they say Christ had brothers and sisters because the Jews of his time said, "Is this not the carpenter <note>Original: *faber*. In Latin, this can mean a smith or craftsman, traditionally translated as carpenter in the context of Joseph.</note>, the son of the carpenter? Is not his mother called Mary, and his brothers James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas?" For they say things that are partly true—that he was believed to be the carpenter, the son of a carpenter, born of Mary—but that he truly had a biological father, or brothers and sisters, they said falsely. For it is not written in the Gospel as a true and proven thing, but as an objection <note>Postel argues that the Gospel records the *claims* of the townspeople, not the factual reality of Christ’s genealogy.</note>. But suppose they spoke from the heart: it is the custom of Scripture that a relative is placed in the position of a brother by that very name. This is also commonly said in all languages out of friendship, beyond kinship, concerning those most closely joined—that they are "brothers" in this manner. 

If they force the meaning of things from words in this way, if the modern Jews <note>Original: *neoterici*.</note> believe the ancient Jews—who, scarcely recognizing Christ before his miracles, spoke out of ignorance—they should much more believe Christ himself, who said that his mother was his brother and sister. He claimed as his kin not only her, but as many as do the will of the Father. Christ became all things to all good people, so that he might win them all; therefore, he affirmed that blessed souls were bound to him by every kind of kinship. He called these people "brothers" for a twofold reason: by reason of kinship and by reason of goodness. Truly, he calls his disciples and the poor his brothers, not by reason of the flesh—to which the wretched Jews refer everything. They are therefore driven into a perverse sense because they twist the force of words to the literal meaning even in the prophets, which overturns the truth. 

Although I have already spoken of the excellence of the Messiah, yet for the sake of this objection, those things that were said must be recounted briefly and enriched. We said at the beginning that all supreme things, and things common to no one except in a human body, are owed to the Messiah. All those things happened to Jesus Christ: for as he was God and man, than whom nothing greater can be given, so also he ought to have been conceived and born and have kinship differently from all other men of the whole world. Nothing is more distinct than man and God, yet he has both in himself alone. Nothing is more different than seed and the absence of seed; both were present in his conception. A virgin and mother does not exist in nature; yet above nature, Mary is a perpetual virgin and mother. She married, and did not marry, so that she might satisfy the civil constitution <note>The legal requirements of marriage in society.</note> and hide such a great mystery until the appointed time. Joseph was called her husband and Christ's father, yet he was never truly father or husband. Other men are accustomed to and able to have brothers; Christ ought not to agree with them in any respect: therefore, she who is his mother remained a perpetual virgin. ### BOOK IV OF GUILLAUME POSTEL

It is an admirable thing that God gave when the virgin conceived. It is a new thing that God did upon the earth, because a woman surrounded a man in an unusual way. <note>Original: *fœmina circūdedit uirū*. A reference to Jeremiah 31:22, traditionally interpreted by Christians as a prophecy of the Virgin Birth.</note> It is the eastern gate of the mystical temple (which is human nature) described by Ezekiel, which shall not be opened, nor shall any of the mortals enter through it, but only God, who, contrary to the dimensions of bodies, can pass through closed places no differently than through open ones. For if God is understood there in His own nature, without a body, what need has He of the opening of a gate? If He has a body and enters through a closed gate which shall never be opened, that gate by which the Redeemer first came among men is the eastern one, and it is the prince, the Virgin Mary. Otherwise, the prophet would have lied—which is a sin to suggest—if he had understood this to mean any other gate of either the first or second Temple. For there was none that was not opened. Indeed, there is no third material Temple. Therefore, the eastern gate of this temple of humanity is Mary, the virgin and mother of God alone, and daughter and sister of man, the one who gave birth and was herself born, immune from every stain. <note>Postel emphasizes Mary’s "Immaculate" nature here, a point of significant theological debate in the 16th century.</note> If, therefore, Jesus possessed that most excellent thing which the Messiah ought to have, there is no doubt that He is the one promised in the Law, since a greater cannot be given. Thus, Christ had no brothers and no father according to the flesh.

I set aside the insane opinions concerning demons and traditions, and I address you briefly, friend Münster. <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552) was a German Hebraist and reformer whom Postel frequently challenged on his interpretations of Jewish texts.</note> I implore you by the holy name of Jesus Christ: do you think that no mortal until this day has understood the Sacred Scriptures, or would have left behind a record of their true sense? If you say "no one," I will not argue with you; but if you say "some," then where all have agreed, it is certain they followed the rule of the prescribed Gospel and pious institution. Regarding the "choice of foods" <note>Referring to fasting and dietary restrictions.</note> discussed by you in Chapter 15: when it was introduced (which was immediately from the time of the Apostles), did the Fathers not understand it so as to think there was some inherent evil in the foods themselves? Did they think, like the Jews regarding swine's blood and strangled meat, that there was a vice infecting the souls of believers? Far be it from us to even suspect this of their piety. Therefore, the choice [of food] was not approved by the Church and prescribed for certain days for the same reason as it was for the Jews. Rather, it was so that the wanton flesh, accustomed to its usual foods, should not resist the spirit. Thus, the sacred institutions do not conflict with that passage in Matthew, *This people*, etc. <note>Matthew 15:8-11, where Jesus says it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person.</note>

Act piously: has the Lord’s Day not been introduced? But where do you find it in the Sacred Scriptures? Do you not believe that John the Baptist, the Apostles, and the disciples of Christ were baptized? But this is not [explicitly detailed] in the Sacred Scriptures. How many and various things are to be held and kept as most holy which consist of traditions? What is this madness and childish assertion of one's own wisdom, to prefer one’s own judgment to the whole world? Therefore, the sacred statutes introduced by the observers of the Gospel do not collapse. Suppose there are hypocrites under them; what does that matter? There would be hypocrites even if there were no traditions. Pious statutes that bring perfection to the saints are not at fault. Otherwise, the Gospel—which through distorted interpretation has produced as many <term>Epicureans</term> <note>Postel uses "Epicureans" as a slur for those who live for pleasure or deny the providence of God, a common 16th-century polemic.</note> and impious people as it has followers—would be evil. The Gospel is good; it is the interpretation of certain people that is evil and impious, those most wicked men who twist it toward their belly, their lust, and their glory. You ought to have been satisfied with bringing forward the objections of the Jews, with whom you often seem allied. You should never have preferred a new opinion and <term>philautia</term> <note>Original Greek: $\phi\iota\lambda\alpha\upsilon\tau\iota\alpha$, meaning self-love or conceit.</note> to Christ and His Church, which has already been confirmed in these matters for 1540 years.

Concerning the rejection of the Jews, and that as many as believe in Christ are the true Israel, I have written enough above. It was not Christ who made those who crucified and rejected Him sin and stumble, but rather their own treacherous mind, which did not rest in the truth known to it. For God left man in the hand of his own counsel. Thus it was decreed by God that while some were the authors of His death, they brought death upon themselves, but to others they brought a providential cause of life. So, in the death of Jesus, all things were unlike the deaths of other men. Other men receive benefits from their own people; He was destroyed [by His]. By their death, a loss comes to the State; but salvation depends upon His death. The generation of the dead is altogether cut off, but because Jesus "laid down His life for His brothers," He "sees a long-lived seed." <note>A reference to Isaiah 53:10.</note> He who kills a good man brings harm to himself and others. # ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

...chapter 16, regarding the comparison of Jonah and the resurrection of Christ. The objection is that they do not match in all respects, since Jonah was in the belly of the fish for three days and three nights, whereas Christ was in the heart of the earth for only three days and two nights. Certainly, in one place Münster <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a famous German Hebraist and cartographer whose works Postel frequently consulted.</note> demonstrated entirely that those who slander these things do so falsely, since there are many similar instances in Scripture that hardly match the thing being compared. For example, when God said, "Let us make man in our image and likeness." <note>Genesis 1:26</note> Man has clearly nothing in common with God except for the invisible spirit—unless the Jews are "anthropomorphites" <note>Those who believe God possesses a physical human form.</note> and think the parable must match in every physical detail. The Scriptures are full of such similarities. 

The three-day period of Christ's resurrection—lasting one full day and parts of two others, along with two nights—is calculated in the manner of "tertian fevers." <note>In ancient medicine, a fever that recurred every second day was called "tertian" (third-day) because the Greeks and Romans counted inclusively (Day 1: Fever, Day 2: Clear, Day 3: Fever).</note> There is no language that does not call these "thirds," which are specifically caused by yellow bile ignited in the veins. For it is enough that they skip one full day, from the cessation of the attack to the next paroxysm, for them to be said to recur on the "third day."

As for the literal truth of the statement that Christ would be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights, it should be understood through "anticipation" <note>Original: *anticipationem*. A rhetorical device (prolepsis) where an event is treated as having started earlier than it physically did.</note>—specifically, starting immediately from the decree of His death made by the scribes and Pharisees, before He was captured on the day of the Last Supper. For it is commonly said, "That man is dead," from the moment the sentence is passed against him. For although Pilate issued the formal decree, they had already prepared the slanders for His death on Thursday. Thus, He was dead (or as good as dead, and called "dead" in common speech) on Thursday night, Friday night, and Saturday night. Regarding the days, there is no controversy, for neither full days nor full nights are required, but only certain hours of them. 

If the Jews should say that this style of writing is unusual in the Sacred Scriptures—that a space of time is described through anticipation—I will bring forth one passage where there is a far greater use of this device. It is written in Exodus 12: "Now the sojourn of the children of Israel, who dwelt in Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years." Yet it is clearly evident through the ages of the patriarchs that the Israelites were in the land of Egypt for only two hundred and thirty years. Therefore, two hundred years must necessarily be referred back to the times of Abraham for the number to be correct. We shall therefore take "Egypt" in that passage to mean a region of "affliction." For from the time Abraham was chosen and left all his resources for God's sake, he was certainly afflicted "among the straits" <note>Original: *ben mezarim*. Postel is playing on the Hebrew word for Egypt, *Mizraim*, and the word for "straits" or "distress," *Metzarim*.</note>, not just in Egypt. For that word, if you remove the vowel points, signifies both equally: one is pronounced *mezzarim*, the other *mizraim*. 

Indeed, "God disciplines every son whom He loves." <note>Hebrews 12:6</note> With respect to the happiness he left behind, Abraham was never so wealthy that he was not in distress—in Egypt with Pharaoh, in Gerar with Abimelech, and with the servants of his brother Lot. For the entire life of the righteous must be a continuous affliction, either voluntary or through patient endurance, so that they may always remember God, whose memory is often lost in times of prosperity. Thus, there are 400 years from the exodus of Israel back to the birth of Isaac, and 30 years from then to the calling of Abraham. That this should be understood as the affliction of the godly starting immediately from the calling of Abraham was indicated by Stephen the Protomartyr in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 7; for Luke records his sermon thus:

> But God spoke to Abraham in this way: that his descendants would be dwellers in a foreign land, and they would bring them into bondage and afflict them for four hundred years, etc.

I believe this error in interpretation arose from the time when "All things were added to the sacred rites" shortly after Ezra. <note>Postel suggests a period of historical or textual corruption in Jewish tradition following the time of Ezra.</note> Therefore, there is an anticipation based on the power and effect of Christ’s death, just as here there is one from the calling of Abraham. Rabbi Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish biblical exegete and philosopher.</note> collects many such numbers in this place, lest the Jews say that this is merely my own groundless invention.

I cannot pass over with a "dry foot" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to pass over something quickly or without getting involved.</note> the madness—I might even say the impiety—of our translator. Who could ignore such notable slanders? As if indeed in the sacred constitutions of the Church (those which men call such) he had suggested that the Law and works profit anyone without faith and Christ. Produce one writer, of whatever kind you wish, in whom that impiety is held, and I will submit.

<meta>This page continues Postel’s defense of traditional Christian practice and his critique of both the Protestant Reformers and Jewish anti-Christian polemics. # GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK IV.

The Church knows that we can do nothing good without faith, without Christ, hope, and charity. Yet it also knows that man is so indebted to God—both because of the benefits he has received and the sins he has committed—that there is absolutely no good work he should not continually perform, repenting throughout his entire life. But who are those who are supposedly accustomed to "selling" their surplus good works to others? Absolutely no one. <note>Postel is refuting the Protestant critique of "indulgences" or "works of supererogation," where it was claimed that saints had extra merit they could sell or distribute.</note> Certainly, it has been accepted since the times of the apostles that the prayer of a certain saint is beneficial, that the members of the church help one another with mutual prayers, and that what one person cannot achieve, many can. Otherwise, if it were not permitted to be helped by mutual prayers, what is the use of a congregation? Even if some are as poor as the apostles were, is it not a great thing if they "reap carnal things" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 9:11, regarding spiritual leaders receiving material support.</note> for the sake of common prayers and good works, both for themselves and others? There are wicked people everywhere, unworthy of their rank; should everyone therefore be treated the same? If this reasoning holds, then all these "New-Evangelists" <note>original: "cæneuangelistæ," a derogatory term Postel uses for the Reformers.</note> are godless <note>original Greek: "ἄθεοι" (atheoi).</note>. For the greatest part of them, under the pretext of "Gospel liberty," has preferred Epicurus and Lucretius <note>Ancient philosophers associated with materialism and the pursuit of pleasure rather than divine law.</note> to Christ. You should not defame an entire order just because some members are wicked; that "great liberty" of yours is merely a way for you to praise yourself and your own as the only "good" ones while you seek to suppress everyone else. There are no longer any Pharisees; Jewish affairs were cut down long ago. The weeds and the tares must grow with the crop; God will choose from the net which fish He himself will approve. <note>References to the parables in Matthew 13.</note> Whence comes this arrogance? Why do you—as if you were a second Aristarchus <note>Aristarchus of Samothrace was a famous ancient critic known for being exceptionally harsh.</note>—snatch judgment away from God in matters that could be interpreted for good rather than for evil? Why do you judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master. <note>Romans 14:4</note> If you were displeased by your monastic cowl, your celibacy, your fasts, and the pious works which God prepared for us to walk in, to the point that you said goodbye to all of them so as not to "insult the merit of Christ," remember that not everyone is of the same temperament. Even if they believe they can do nothing worthy of God, and even if they are "useless servants" as Christians, they nevertheless strive to prove themselves to God in those things they are able to do.

He <note>Referring to Sebastian Münster, mentioned on the previous page.</note> is consistent with himself in his interpretation of the "Keys." <note>The "Power of the Keys" refers to the authority to forgive or retain sins (Matthew 16:19).</note> He says that "binding and loosing" is nothing other than believing or not believing in the remission of sins. How then did Peter abuse this power when he "bound" Ananias and Sapphira, who were believers? <note>Acts 5:1–11; Postel argues that Peter’s judgment was a physical/authoritative act, not just a matter of belief.</note> Or how did Paul, who handed the Corinthian believer over to Satan? Furthermore, since according to Münster all Christians are equal in authority, who will be the presiding officer in councils? To whom will matters regarding daily doubts that arise be referred between two councils? Those who are of equal authority do not have to yield to one another. Therefore, one will have to feel however one pleases—for that is where such ideas lead. Under an arbitrary interpretation of the Gospel, you may live as you wish; all things are "free."

I return to the Jews. In their exposition of the passage in Genesis, they speak in this manner: It is written, *Behold, Adam has become like one of us, etc., so that he might live forever.* <note>Genesis 3:22</note> In this way, you [the Jew] will question the heretic: "Does God not care if man lives forever? Is it not customary that any author wants the work he produced to last as long as possible? But because God saw that in the future Jesus would seduce the world and claim to be God, He ordained it better that men should die, and that Jesus be hung on a single piece of wood, so that he would not eat from the Tree of Life; thus it is clear to all that he is not God." These are the words of the impious Jews—exceptional theologians indeed, who attribute *fear* to their own God! They claim that death was brought upon everyone, and upon Christ himself, specifically so they would not live forever. In truth, death had already been imposed because of the sin committed, but God expelled them so they would not persist in doing evil. Therefore, death is not from God, but from sin. As for the claim that Jesus himself "seduced the world," they cannot prove this with a single wicked word. Let them take whatever they want from the Gospel or its examples; if there is anything there that is not perfectly just, we will admit defeat. <note>original: "herbā porrigemus," literally "we shall proffer the grass," a Roman idiom for surrendering.</note> Christ certainly caused many to go astray—not as the Jews write, but in the manner of a law being established: for before the law, there is no sin. Thus, before Christ was incarnated, one did not err by not believing in Him while He was unknown. But after He arrived, as many as heard of Him and did not believe are in error, and in the far greater sin of infidelity—especially the Jews, to whom He was sent. Let the Jews believe Jesus to be whatever they wish...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK IV.

The Church knows that we can do nothing of any good without faith, without Christ, hope, and charity. However, it also knows that man is so indebted to God—both because of the benefits he has received and because of the sins he has committed—that there is no good work he should not be doing constantly, and his entire life should be spent in repentance. But who are these people who are accustomed to selling their own good works, in which they supposedly abound, to others? Plainly, there are none. Certainly, it has been an accepted practice since the times of the Apostles that the prayer of some holy person may be of benefit, that the members of the Church should help one another with mutual prayers, and that what one person cannot achieve alone, many might achieve together. Otherwise, if it were not permitted to be helped by mutual prayers, what would be the point of a congregation? Even if some are of the poorest means, as the Apostles were, is it not a great thing if they reap carnal support through the common prayers and good works they perform for themselves and others? There are wicked men everywhere, and those unworthy of their rank; should everyone be judged the same because of them? He certainly possessed all the qualities owed to the most perfect of men, the Messiah, and those attributed to him by the prophets. Nor can they <note>Referring to Jewish critics.</note> hurl any insult or reproach at him with their taunts. It happened to the Jews regarding Jesus just as it does to those with night-blindness <note>original: *nyctilopibus*. Those who can see at night but are blinded by bright daylight.</note> when they are confronted by the greatest light. For that light which serves others so well that they see nothing without it, actually deprives these others of their sight. There is no need for a defense when they object that God cannot be seen, and claim that we therefore speak falsely when we say Christ saw God. No Christian has ever asserted that they have seen the divinity itself, whether of Christ or of God. For it is so invisible that even those who are glorified are better able to wonder at it than to comprehend it. So far as his appearance <note>original: *spectrum*</note> can be conceived, Moses, Isaiah, and Micah saw him. But truly, no one has seen God and lived. Divinity is sought by the mind alone, and can scarcely be conceived—even in a faint image—except by the most perfect.

Regarding their objection that the saints have not moved mountains: Christians are not street-performers, tightrope walkers, or acrobats <note>original: *circulatores, funambuli, aut petauristae*</note> who turn the faces of all toward themselves with miracles, unless it concerns the salvation of men. Countless dead have been raised by them in the name of Jesus, which is indeed a greater thing than moving a mountain from its place. It is necessary for faith to be at its greatest, and to proceed from a heart that is most innocent and purified. Indeed, the apostles had their own imperfections while Christ was living.

It is surely a shame to call [Sebastian] Münster <note>A famous Hebraist and Reformer whose work Postel often critiqued for being too influenced by rabbinic tradition.</note> a Jew in many of his opinions, yet the facts themselves compel it. Since the monastic and eremitic life is, and has always been since the times of the apostles, a most holy institution from which the greatest lights of the world have come forth—men and women of exceptional holiness—nevertheless, as if all were most wicked and admitted every kind of foulness, they are all censured with a single word by the Jews, with Münster’s support. It was certainly to be lamented that not a few parents, unworthy of their offspring and wealth, drive young people to take up that kind of life before they have experienced the vanity of the world (from which a certain constancy usually arises), just so the inheritance might be kept intact. Yet not a few of those come to a fruitful life even from such coerced beginnings. For Christ also compels those lingering on the road to approach his already prepared banquet.

No form of life lacks its own plagues, and they are more serious the greater the dignity of mind or body they profess. But truly the world has had far more good than evil from those orders of monks; otherwise, Germany would not be the only place sensing this "evil." The Templars taught Christians that they are not bound by superstitions whenever the State <note>original: *Resp.* (Respublica)</note> receives more damage than benefit from a single order. The State would do the same in other cases if things were as the Jews—I meant to say the "flesh-evangelists" <note>original: *carneuangelistæ*. A derogatory term for Reformers who Postel believed focused on carnal or worldly liberty rather than spiritual discipline.</note>—mutter. We all know that chastity is a gift from God, but because it is most pleasing to God, it is likely that he grants it to many, since he can do all things in us. 

It is the custom of wicked men to begin their agitation against religious orders by focusing on the vices of individuals, and thus they persuade the unrefined common folk to rise up against the sacred orders. If the matter is weighed more carefully, scarcely every twentieth person will seem unworthy of their order. If the wickedness of some infects the whole flock, then all the angels are treacherous from whose company the spirits of the demon <note>original: *kakodaimonos*</note> fell; the law of the Jews was wicked, under which so many evil men perished for their crimes; the apostles are to be called worthless because one among them was a treacherous betrayer of the Lord; and Christians are impious because they have many impious people among them.

In Chapter 21, they say that our Messiah, if he is God, ought not to have mounted a donkey, because it is an unclean animal. He was able to make all things clean. The prophet had foretold that he who was to be King would ride a donkey for the sake of humility, in which no one can be his equal. I have already addressed this above in the prophetic gospel. ...the third, as I have shown above. For after the first and second <note>The first temple was built by Solomon; the second was rebuilt after the Babylonian exile.</note>, no other temple is read of, except for that which Josephus writes: that Herod the Ascalonite <note>Herod the Great, who expanded the Second Temple complex.</note> constructed a most beautiful temple to capture the favor of the Jewish people; but it did not last except until the destruction brought about by Titus. As for their claim that a third, eternal house has been established by God as incorruptible, that is truer than they themselves say. For the soul and the church of the faithful is the truly eternal house in which God dwells, and it is the image of the higher reality, in which there shall be no stain or wrinkle. It shall not be on a mountain or in a field, nor shall it belong to Abraham or Isaac alone, but truly to all Israelites. However, because it is to be eternal, there will be no need for the Law. Therefore, there will no longer be a difference between nations. For that shall be after the resurrection. Ezekiel saw a type of it in the spirit and wrote of it; the Evangelist John also wrote of it in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>. In this current state of corruption, nothing will ever be eternal. 

The argument concerning the hunger of Christ has already been resolved by me. For Jesus possessed both natures—namely, the divine and the human—in such a way that, although he had made one composite and one subject in himself, nevertheless each nature held its own aptitude without the hindrance of the other, whenever he willed. The divinity did not hinder the imperfections of the body, just as those imperfections did not hinder the divinity. He fasted for forty days, with the divinity supporting the body in that middle state of the composite; finally, the body, returning as if separately to its own functions, became hungry. There was no external glory of God present to strengthen him, such as the manifestation <note>original: *spectrum*</note> of God to Moses, or the angelic manifestation to Elijah. By the power of those manifestations, although the seventh day of fasting is usually fatal to a man, both of them fasted for forty days. He, therefore, who by his own power had caused both to fast within themselves, taught both that he had given that power which he exercised through himself, and he showed the humanity within himself in such a way that, being driven by its necessities, he created faith in both natures; for if he had not felt need, he would be believed to be a ghost <note>original: *spectrum*</note>, not a man. 

Regarding the fig tree which he struck with a curse because it was barren, he could have done the same while absent, for his physical approach was not the primary consideration. Just as God’s approach and calling to Adam after the sin, the descent to the Tower of Babel, the visitation of Sodom and Gomorrah, and countless other instances are not signs of God’s ignorance, so too this act of Christ was not. Just as God accommodates himself to the weakness of our intellect in those stories, so Christ looked after his disciples in this deed, to show both his omnipotence and that all barren deeds (or the undone deeds of men) are to be exterminated and punished with eternal penalties. As for the claim that he acted against the precept of love by becoming inflamed against an unfeeling tree—who is so mad as to believe that? Love, hatred, and anger are directed from one human to another. For other things, which lack both will and judgment, deserve neither hatred, nor envy, nor anger. 

Another objection: The Jews say, "We are in captivity because of the death or killing of Christ, according to the Christians; but we were in captivity before him." I respond: Before Jesus, no captivity took away your dominion over the affairs of Syria, except for the Babylonian captivity, which was predicted and limited by the prophets before it happened. In that captivity, indeed, there were not lacking <term>mehocecim</term> <note>Hebrew: *mechoqeqim*, meaning lawgivers, leaders, or scribes.</note> or legislators. For Jeremiah, Daniel, and many other most holy men were with you, who made you certain that you would be liberated after 70 years. In this current state, despite the highest observation of your worship, as I have already said, you have now lived for 1,500 years, more hated by the pagans than by the Christians. I have seen the condition of your affairs in Africa, in Asia, and in the most famous cities of Europe. Why do you not raise your head? Why does your Messiah defraud you so greatly of his presence? For what reason has he slept for 1,500 years since his birth? As for your wish to be protected ironically by the prayer Christ made on the cross for you: certainly Christ the Son of God, God from God, the wisdom of the Father, prayed seriously to the Father for you, and obtained it for the good. But whatever the nature of divine prayers, unless a person acquiesces through <term>free will</term> <note>original: *liberũ arbitriũ*</note>, he is not saved. For God does not bring force upon our will; it stands with the person...

He further interprets the 1,500-year Jewish diaspora as evidence of a deeper spiritual exile compared to the brief Babylonian captivity.</summary>

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

<page-num>440</page-num>

...less saved. Therefore, Christ says: *How often I wanted to gather you as a hen gathers her chicks, and you were unwilling* <note>original: "Quoties uolui te cõgregare sicut gallina congregat pullos suos, et noluisti"; a reference to Matthew 23:37.</note>. It belongs to Him to will, and to Him to whom it belongs not to will. God calls all who are thirsty to the waters and invites them of his own accord; and although all mortals thirst, nevertheless very few are saved. God wanted to lead the people brought out of Egypt safely into the holy land; yet because they did not acquiesce to God, out of countless thousands, only two were saved <note>Joshua and Caleb were the only adults from the Exodus generation allowed to enter the Promised Land.</note>. A forced servant is no better than an evil one, even if he seems to act well; for this reason, that which God gave as the highest gift to man <note>referring to free will</note>, He wishes to be in man's own power, and He is not accustomed to bringing force upon it.

What they <note>Postel's Jewish interlocutors</note> concede mockingly in chapter 22, I seriously embrace and approve: that there is a Son to God, namely His very wisdom and Word, to whom God said, as to his own Lord and equal: *Sit at my right hand.* <note>Psalm 110:1. This is a central text in Christian-Jewish polemics regarding the identity of the Messiah.</note> However, as for what follows—that these things were said on account of the Jews who would hatefully kill the Son—that is not true, although no nation was ever more hostile to God. That phrase expressed by the prophet is an explanation of the divine nature and its condition, so that the equality of the persons might be proved, and a similar deity that does not lack a place. Although this deity, as I showed in the beginning, is entirely in the Son, entirely in the Father, and entirely in the Holy Spirit—just as a whole thing exists in thought, the whole in the word, and the whole in the effect—nevertheless it ought neither be confounded nor separated. Therefore, the Son did not leave the right hand of the Father when he came in the flesh; he is also the arbiter of the whole world. Nor was he disobedient and rebellious toward the Father, whose will he performed, since without his death humanity could not be redeemed.

That saying, *Sit at my right hand*, cannot be understood as referring to David or Abraham. For David does not have the kingdom of heaven in his power to give to Abraham, who was (according to your traditions) at the gate of the underworld <note>original: "porta inferi"</note> resisting God and preventing the wicked Jews whom God was sending into Gehenna <note>Hell or the place of punishment</note> from entering it. Sane interpretations of that passage are to be brought forward, for which thanks must certainly be given to Münster <note>Sebastian Münster, a famous Christian Hebraist and contemporary of Postel.</note>. Thus the paraphrast Jonathan, son of Uzziel <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Prophets.</note>, translates it: *Jehovah said to his lord, sit at my right hand.* In the book *Kibuzin* <note>Likely referring to a "Kibbutz" or collection of Midrashic sayings.</note> it is written: *The best and greatest God is to come, establishing the King Messiah at his right hand.* For it is said: *The Lord said to my lord, sit at my right hand.* Rabbi Isaac writes thus concerning Genesis: *Before the creation of the sun, the name of our Messiah was flourishing and subsisting, and he sat at the right hand of God.* And this is what the prophe<gloss>t</gloss> says: *Sit at my right hand.* In this way that passage is usually explained; thus the ancient teachers understood it.

Now, in the first refutations of the Jews, I taught how Christ said he was ignorant of the day of judgment. For he said that the Son does not know. Certainly, as they saw Jesus <note>i.e., in his human form</note>, he truly did not know concerning that day, because it is not profitable for any mortal to know about the future. God wishes to keep us in our duty through fear. There is no reason to care what the Jews bark about <note>original: "oblatrẽt," a common polemical verb meaning to bark or snarl like a dog.</note> regarding the imperfection of the nature that was in Christ—in the mother's womb, in his birth, and in his infancy. For that which happens without the fault of the one acting or suffering contains no evil. Indeed, they contend that the verse of Psalm 19 is poorly applied, in which it is written: *In the sun he set his tabernacle like a bridegroom* <note>Psalm 19:4-5.</note>, etc., as if it were hardly suitable for Christ himself; yet truly it can suit no one better. Let that which God touches be foul, filthy, or in any way stained—He cleanses and sanctifies it, never touching the blemish, just as light illuminates all dark things and conceives no darkness. The tabernacle of the Messiah was heaven, and this entire temple of nature, after the world was created. When he wished to become man, the tabernacle was the Virgin; now it is the souls of the faithful. And so, you Jews, when you think you defile Christ with words prepared from the necessity of nature, you immerse yourselves in filth; not unlike one who strives to obstruct the lights—he can indeed take the light away from himself, but he cannot infect the nature of light.

I would not dare to involve Münster further in Jewish impieties, unless he so impiously took away free choice <term>arbitrium: free will or the power of choice</term> from man, so that he judges him to be held lower than the other animals, for as if nothing...

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK 4

<page-num>441</page-num>

...man possesses free choice <note>original: "arbitrij," referring to *liberum arbitrium* or free will.</note>, then all good and evil works are done necessarily out of predestination; therefore, God would be unjust. Thus, no one would exist who commands that which He wishes to remain undone. Oh, what blasphemy! I will not hesitate to affirm one thing: that certain people fall more foully into error in this matter than **Arius**, than **Eunomius**, than **Nestorius**, and as many impious heretics as have ever existed <note>These are early Christian figures whose teachings were condemned as heretical; Postel uses them as a benchmark for severe theological error.</note>. For whoever denies that free choice resides in man—especially one initiated into the sacred rites of Jesus Christ—and denies that good works contribute anything toward salvation, denies the existence of God. It is no wonder if those so formed pass daily into impiety, since it matters nothing to them what they shall become in the future. Therefore, those impious ones have this saying in their mouths: *I cannot act otherwise; God compels me.*

The passage usually cited by the Jews from **Deuteronomy, chapter 13**, is so violently twisted against Christ that anyone can see it. It goes like this: *If your brother, the son of your mother, or your son or daughter, or the wife in your embrace, or your companion who is dear to you as your own soul, should entice you in secret, saying: "Let us go and serve foreign gods whom neither you nor your fathers have known," etc.* At the end of the sentence it says: *You shall not yield to him; he shall be put to death, and your hand shall be the first against him to kill him.* <note>Postel is quoting the law against enticement to idolatry.</note> That is the verse. But taking only two expressions, they claim it is understood to be about Christ. They explain "the son of your mother" as meaning "he who is said to be born without the seed of a father," whereas the entire passage intended to indicate nothing other than that even one's closest relatives must not be spared in such a crime. Furthermore, Christ never taught about God in secret, nor about a "foreign god," but about the Creator of the universe whom your fathers worshipped, O Jews! I truly pity such unheard-of blindness, or perhaps I should call it stubborn persistence. For nothing is less fitting for such a description than Jesus Christ. 

With equal impudence, they affirm that Christ did not know his own betrayer, whom he nevertheless so often said was destined for this task. And again: "If he was God, why did he allow himself to be bound?" Let them ask **Isaiah 53**: *Who is he upon whom God placed the iniquities of us all? Who, like a sheep, shall be led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer shall be silent, and shall not open his mouth?* <note>original: "Esaia 53... sicut ouis ad occisionem ducetur." This is a foundational "Suffering Servant" prophecy used by Christians to explain the Passion.</note> Is his death not pleasing to him? It certainly is. His humanity, in its own way, shuddered at and recoiled from death; his divinity sought it—not for its own sake, but as an instrument of the treacherous—to be offered as a sacrifice for the salvation of the world by that death. And therefore, Judas did evil by betraying him, and the Jews by destroying him, since they perpetrated this act not for the sake of the world's salvation, but driven—he by greed and envy, and they by envy and wrath. If Christ had revealed himself more clearly to the world, as he certainly could have, the redemption, which had to be achieved through a most violent death, could never have been consummated. For even though it was necessary for the **God-man** <note>original: "homo Deus"</note> to be put to death—as he told everyone, for otherwise it would never happen that man would return to favor with God—certainly no one would have wished to be the executioner of such a pious and holy man. Indeed, even some of his apostles were in doubt about his divinity until he rose again and gave them the Holy Spirit.

Regarding the **Passover lamb**, they say that just as there were many lambs to be offered, so it would be necessary, if they pointed to Christ, for him to be born and hanged more often, so that the reality might correspond to the figure. I said from the beginning that the **Messiah** <note>original: "Messiam"</note> would be so excellent that he would exceed all human excellence and would agree with no one in establishing his own things. For his law was to be new, not according to the one God gave in Egypt or to Moses, but one that would be written on the heart. Therefore, just as atonements were made in the Law through the external blood of many innocent animals, so the sins of all believers are forgiven by the power of the blood of the one Lamb slain once. He was both the Lamb and was offered once for all, and he made [the bread] parts of his own body when he gave it to his disciples. This is a matter that the Jews do not agitate as much as our **Gospel-Supperists** <note>original: "cenneuangelistæ." A polemical term for reformers (like Zwingli or Calvin) who viewed the Eucharist as a symbolic meal rather than the literal body of Christ.</note>, since they judge Christ to be powerless to distribute his body anywhere on earth, and affirm it is taken only by faith; even though we see...

# DE ORBIS CONCORDIA
### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

<page-num>442</page-num>

In nature, there are even countless physical things that can be entirely in one and the same moment of time in one place, and entirely in others, yet remain only one thing in the whole. Who does not know that in any tree suitable for transplanting—whether from a stake or a cutting—there is only one nature in both body and soul? Make as many cuttings and willow plants as you wish; each possesses as much of that nature as the first. Shall I bring an example from spiritual things? The image of a single object is present in its entirety in the eyes of everyone, in countless mirrors, and in every power of sight. Scents hit the nostrils of all people equally in their entirety. Light is equal in both small and large quantities, as far as the nature of the thing is concerned. The nature of Christ’s glorified body can be everywhere, no differently than his divinity. It was in his own hands <note>Postel refers to the Last Supper, where Christ held the bread—his body—in his own hands.</note>, no differently than if a willow tree could speak and, embracing branch to branch, were to say: "This is my body."

The impiety of the **New Evangelists** <note>Postel uses this term for Reformers like Zwingli or Oecolampadius, who argued that the bread and wine were merely symbols, not the literal body and blood.</note> does not grasp this, because it believes the Creator to be less powerful than his creation. The same impiety that **Munster** <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a famous Hebraist and Reformer whose translations Postel often critiqued.</note> dares not vomit forth in Latin, he teaches to the Jews: that the sacrament is nothing other than a memory of Christ’s death. He writes this in Hebrew—as if, forsooth, by asserting the presence of Jesus’s body, the Church denies the memory of his passion.

The objection regarding the hour of the slaughter of the lamb is false, when the Jews say the lamb was usually eaten in the evening, but Christ was crucified in the morning. They claim that until the lamb was eaten, no one received the power of the Passover. However, even though Jesus was crucified at noon, he did not expire before the ninth hour, which is three in the afternoon <note>original: "nonam, quæ est tertia uespertina." In the ancient world, the "ninth hour" of daylight corresponds to roughly 3:00 PM.</note>. Thus, on the same day the symbolic lamb was eaten by the Jews in the evening, Christ gave himself. For as he gave up his spirit, salvation was restored to the whole world. Therefore, he wished to eat the symbolic lamb on Thursday, contrary to the Jewish custom, and substituted his sacrosanct body for it. Let us not think this is received only by faith and not in reality <note>original: "re," meaning the physical reality of the body.</note>; for whoever takes it unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself. For this reason, many in the early church died, and others were very gravely ill, because they did not "discern the body of the Lord"—that is, they did not believe it differed from other foods.

As for the different manner of the killing of Jesus and the lamb, what is the point of speaking? For a man and a lamb are not the same thing. It is enough that they agree in innocence. "Why," says the circumcised **Nizahon** <note>A reference to the *Sefer Nizzahon* (Book of Victory), a famous Jewish polemical text used to argue against Christian interpretations of the Bible.</note>, "was his soul sorrowful even unto death? If you say he speaks according to the flesh, which fears, does he not say: 'My soul is sorrowful'?" You say "according to the flesh" in every instance, though everyone knows the flesh can neither speak nor know, any more than a stone.

See, treacherous Jew, where your obstinacy and your vow of blaspheming Christ lead you: that which you can grant and see daily in all men, you desire to take away from Christ alone. At the very least, Christ was a man; but no man exists who cannot, in the very same matter, both want and not want, and be both sorrowful and joyful. What makes a person allow a doctor to treat "figs" <note>An archaic term for hemorrhoids or external growths.</note>, fistulas, cancers, or stones with the harshest iron remedies for the sake of obtaining health? Does not reason judge one way, while the sense of nature wants another? Reason leads most willingly to the butchery <note>original: "carnificinam," referring here to the painful "butchery" of surgery without anesthesia.</note>, but the nature of the body shrinks back—not from health, but from health bought at such a high price. Thus, the same man wants to be cut and not to be cut. Meanwhile, he implores the doctor, whom he knows will not spare him; and if the doctor wanted to spare him, reason would not want it. 

So many, willing, rush into death when nature is not equal to the torments. With the same mind, for the sake of the fatherland or for profit, the leader and the soldier undergo dangers, willing to obtain peace through torments. Thus, virtue laboriously struggles against the corporeal soul—that is, the vital, natural, and animal part. For that part seeks luxury and pleasure, while the other, led by reason, seeks the greatest dangers. Christians are not so foolish as to think that inanimate flesh feels or speaks for itself. Therefore, even if Christ had been a pure man, his soul attached to a body and subject to death could have struggled through his mind and reason. For those things differ most widely. But how much more so when in him, along with reason, he was with us...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s defense of the dual nature of Christ—fully human and fully divine. Following his discussion on the Eucharist, he now addresses a common theological objection: if Christ was God, why did he show fear, sorrow, and physical weakness during his Passion? Postel frames this as a rebuttal to Jewish polemics of his time.</meta>

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK IV

<page-num>443</page-num>

His shared divinity was able to both desire death for the salvation of all with its whole will, and yet shrink from it with its whole will. He did not wish, through the union of divinity with humanity, to remove any corporeal imperfection of our fallen nature, lest he diminish the full penalties owed to it. Therefore, his soul was **sorrowful even unto death**, the bitterness of which his divinity had already placed before his eyes. Yet, that ardor for saving mankind conquered. The prayer made to the Father pertains to this same point. For the human man implores the divinity in his own fragility, even though reason does not wish to spare the body; he acts no differently than one who must be cut or burned by a doctor, who asks and entreats the doctor if it can be done otherwise, and yet desires not his own will, but that of the doctor and of reason to be done. 

Nor for that reason are the two states of mind unequal—namely, that of the sufferer and that of the *impassible* <note>original Greek: *ἀπαθοῦς* (apathous), referring to a being incapable of suffering or changing, a standard philosophical description of God</note>. For both decreed the cutting or the cautery. Therefore, what that impious Jew says—that Christ is not God, nor has a will equal to God the Father—is false. For both the power of the Father, the wisdom of the Son, and the love of the Holy Spirit, which is the unique divinity before the world was founded, had established this remedy for man (who was lost by his own choice): that a body connected to divinity should pay the penalties for fallen human nature. Thus, that will was accomplished, even while the fragile nature of the man shrank from it and was driven by sorrow even to a sweat of blood. I have taught copiously through human reasoning in the first book that nature could be repaired in no other way than by the death of a man joined to God. 

All other objections raised by our "triumphing" opponent are pierced by the aforementioned reasons. As for what he adds—that the flesh could not have fasted for forty days except by the grace of the Holy Spirit—it is certainly true that such a capacity is not in the flesh to remain fasting for so long. But just as the vision of divinity gave this to **Moses**, as I said, and angelic comfort gave it to **Elijah**, so the divinity, possessing its fullness within him, conferred it upon Jesus Christ for as long as it willed. 

But if divinity worked this in him, why did it not make it so that he did not fear? I respond: so that absolutely none of those imperfections and passions (except sin) which are placed in the nature of all people would be lacking in the flesh paying the penalties for everyone. Christ certainly could have stripped his flesh of feeling and emotion before death, and died an imaginary death; but he willed to truly suffer and truly give signs of all human passions. For it would have been a mere theatrical act, unworthy of him, if he had come to suffer but had only suffered in imagination. 

O faithless and lost Jews, how could it be possible—unless Christ were God giving his grace to whom he wills—that infinite thousands of saints have been placed among the blessed in his name, which you object to us? Certainly, one man cannot give holiness and the grace of miracles to another man. Jesus was therefore offered because he willed it. The objection of the Jews regarding the **three boys** <note>Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego from the Book of Daniel, who survived the fiery furnace</note>, who are not read to have been vexed by sorrow because of the fiery furnace they entered, falls by the same reasoning. There are also countless Martyrs (to grant the Jews more than they might wish) who rushed not sadly, but eagerly into all kinds of unheard-of tortures. 

But, as I have already said, the logic in Christ’s suffering was different. For the three boys, comforted by God through his angel, were encouraged for their torments; and what the nature of the body could not bear, divine consolation provided, so that the pain was diminished in those torments which fragile nature is unequal to bearing. But in Christ, whatever can happen that is simply sad and troublesome without any supernatural help happened precisely because he was washing away the sins of all in himself. He would have done less so if he had been encouraged by the same privilege as the others. Yet, so that there might also be faith in his divinity and his friendship with God, his human nature received consolation from an angel in word; for it would not have been possible for nature, left so abandoned in its capable-of-suffering condition, to have endured—a nature which divinity did not wish to relieve with its infinite perfection before death—unless it had been helped by some "breathing room."

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

<page-num>444</page-num>

God willed to comfort His Son through the service of a minister <note>original: *ministri*—referring to the angel who comforted Christ in the Garden of Gethsemane</note> rather than through divine support, so that the consolations of divinity—which had ordained that His death would be most bitter—might not lessen the pangs of punishment. Just as the death of the Messiah was arranged for the sake of all mankind, so it had to be remote from the common experience of dying. As we have seen that all His qualities were most excellent, so it was most just that He should differ from others in His death. This most outstanding of the best of men bore the most bitter reward of virtue: death in a body tormented by every kind of calamity, without any privilege of moderated punishment, as is evident even in His crucifixion. For, as I taught above, that a living body was suspended by the piercings of the hands for three hours surpasses whatever torments can be devised.

But here the Jews snarl <note>original: *ogganniunt*—literally "to growl" or "to mutter like a dog," reflecting the polemical tone of the period</note>, though they call Christ "the hanged one" <note>original: *talui*—from the Hebrew *Talui* (תלוי)</note> for the sake of insult, and call His cross "the upright and transverse wood." They say He was not crucified but simply killed, arguing that such a type of punishment was unusual among the Jews. For they claim the Great Sanhedrin <note>original: *summus senatus*</note> used to stone, burn, behead, or strangle. As if, indeed, judicial matters were then conducted according to their ancient constitution (even if we grant their objections), when already sixty years or so earlier the Sanhedrin <note>original: *Syneddrin*</note> had been abolished by Herod. He had killed, as I taught before, "three shepherds in one month," by destroying the sacred, profane, and mixed orders, and by establishing laws, constitutions, and magistrates at his own whim. Therefore, O Jews, it was not lawful for you to kill anyone when Christ was captured—though it certainly was lawful under the Leaders, Kings, and Heads of the Exile <note>original: *capitibus captiuitatis*—referring to the Exilarchs who led the Jewish community in Babylon</note> when you were free. The Cross was the mystery of redemption and a sign of eternal life in hieroglyphic symbols <note>original: *notis Hieroglyphicis*—Postel often viewed the shape of the cross as an ancient mystical symbol found in many cultures</note>. On it, He died with His arms spread wide in an embrace, He who was to embrace all those willing to believe in Him.

But now a heap of insults and slanders presents itself. From the version of the Seventy Interpreters <note>the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> and the Latin version derived from it, they wish to infer that Jesus was even a sinner, because in Psalm 22 He cried out: *Eli, Eli, lama azabtani, rahoc misuathi dibre hatati* <note>Postel provides a transliteration of the Hebrew for Psalm 22:1: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? [Why are you so] far from my salvation [and from] the words of my sins?"</note>. That is: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Far from my salvation are the words of my sins." So the Greek text has it. But the Hebrew has *dibre shaagati* <note>OCR: *faagati*. This refers to the Hebrew *shaagati* (שַׁאֲגָתִי), meaning "my groaning" or "my roaring."</note>, that is, "the words of my roaring." They prefer to pervert their own scriptures to insult the truth rather than embrace it by accepting and defending the truth. 

But lest we seem to flee from our own version—since that Psalm is said to be about the Messiah—I admit that even there one may read *hattati* <note>Hebrew: *hattati* (חַטָּאתִי), "my sin"</note>, that is, "my sin," and that Christ "had sin." But we must see in what way He had it. For we have things and call them "ours" either as our own property (like a body, a soul, a field, or a crime)—in that way Christ never had sin—or we call something "ours" because it is committed to our trust or received in another's name. In this way, Christ did not have a single sin of His own, but He received the sins of the whole world into Himself in potential. This is what the prophet said: "For the wickedness of my people I struck Him." And elsewhere: "The Lord laid on Him the iniquities of us all." And: "He was wounded for our iniquities, bruised for our crimes." And: "If He shall lay down His soul for sin, He shall see a long-lived seed." And: "By His knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many, and He Himself shall bear their iniquities." <note>These are references to the "Suffering Servant" in Isaiah 53</note> You cannot deny that these things are said of a certain supreme man to whom divinity is joined. For a man cannot justify men. In that way, therefore, He had the sins of all who believe in God through Him—and yours as well, O Jews, if you would believe in Him and repent of your blasphemies. For He wishes all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

As for the fact that they stitch together blasphemies in a heap after their fashion, saying He was not righteous whom God wished to be forsaken—since it says (not in Solomon’s Ecclesiastes, as they wrongly cite, but in David’s Psalm 37 <note>Text cites Psalm 36, following the Vulgate numbering; in modern Bibles it is Psalm 37:25</note>): "I have not seen the righteous forsaken," etc. I have already provided the reason above why He was left in that sorrow...

<summary>Postel defends the unique nature of Christ's crucifixion against Jewish critiques, explaining that Christ "bore sin" not as a sinner, but by taking the world's transgressions upon Himself. He also provides a historical-legal argument that the Sanhedrin had lost the power of capital punishment under Roman/Herodian rule, necessitating the Cross.</summary>

### BOOK IV OF GUILLAUME POSTEL

<page-num>445</page-num>

...was not exempt, because both reason and divinity were opposed to the human petition. It is just as the reason for cutting or cauterizing a sick person conflicts with the surgeon’s <note>Postel uses the analogy of a patient's physical instinct to flee pain versus the rational understanding that surgery is necessary for health.</note> sensitive appetite which flees from pain, even though the patient implores his trust that, if it can be done otherwise, he might be allowed his health. Therefore, for the sake of salvation, the humanity of Jesus Christ itself did not cry out so much for its own sake, but rather asked by a certain vow, as if already obeying the divinity, for the sake of the salvation of all. For when He uttered the aforementioned words, Jesus was very near to death.

Our "circumcised victor" <note>original: *apella*—a Latin slur for a Jewish person, referencing circumcision, used here in a polemical sense</note> repeatedly presses this point: "If He was God, and by His own will and love He wished to suffer, why did He pray sadly?" I have already responded more than enough: it was to show that the human nature, although it was joined to the divinity, nevertheless suffered neither falsely nor through an image, but without any protection coming from the divine nature. For as I said, if He had wished, He could have eluded all the torments of the Jews without punishment, as He showed more than once before His passion when they wanted to throw Him down or seize Him.

Finally, the filth and the plague <note>Postel refers here to those he considers heretics or blasphemers.</note> mock the sacred mysteries and their interpretation. They say—the *Hamimin* <note>original: *hamimin*—from the Hebrew *ha-minim* (the heretics), a term often used in Jewish literature to refer to Christians, which Postel here turns back against them</note>, that is, the Christian heretics—that when God said, "Let us make man in our image," the Father was saying to the Son, "Help me to make man," and the Son did not want to obey; thus the Father alone made Adam. Then the Father said to the Son, "You did not want to help me just now; someday I will not help you when you ask me," and that this is why He refused to hear the Son in death. These are old wives' delusions. The divine goodness is most unified in the Trinity, as we said before; it cannot have conflict in the will, nor can anything be done unless power, wisdom, and love concur as one. May such plagues perish miserably—men so thick and lazy that they can conceive of nothing regarding divine matters.

Indeed, who could bear the impious words by which they overturn all sacred things? "If," they say, "the spirit was united with the body, and divinity was also united into one, then the divinity died." Are you not ashamed, you beast? Even if Christ had been a pure man, would His soul not have survived? For what purpose are laws and rights, piety and virtue, if the soul perishes with the body? If the soul survives death (as it certainly does), how does the unhappy "circumcised one" dare to place divinity behind it and call it mortal? Let the wretch perish.

They also strive to attack the divinity of Jesus Christ from what is written in the last chapter of Matthew: "All power is given to me in heaven and on earth." "What does this mean?" says the *Nizahon* <note>original: *Nizahon*—referring to the *Sefer Nizzahon* (Book of Victory), a famous medieval Jewish polemical text that critiqued Christian interpretations of the Bible</note>. "Who gave it to Him, if He is the Son of God? What need was there for a gift? Is not the whole world His? If you say that His Father gave it to Him, and that He and the Father are two, then is not each one part of a whole? One is not greater than the other, neither in dominion, nor in virtue, nor in intelligence."

Listen, you circumcised one <note>original: *recutite*—another polemical reference to circumcision</note>: does not wisdom always proceed from the singular power of God, and love from both? If Wisdom—which is called the "Son" by analogy to lower things—should say, "I have all things from my Father," would He not speak the truth, since power and wisdom are one? Thus Christ says, "All things are delivered to me by my Father." "If they are delivered, and if common power belongs to both, what then was 'given' in the way of power?" asks the follower of Moses <note>original: *Mosaicus*</note>. It is not the same thing to be God through Himself, and to be God joined to human nature. Therefore, after death was conquered through the glorious resurrection, since Christ is a "new composite" consisting of both natures, the Father gives to Him the power which He had from eternity in His divinity. For once the condition was changed, it was necessary to assert the inheritance anew. Thus, power in heaven and on earth was given to the God-man, so that He might draw there those whom He redeemed, whereas before Him they had nothing in heaven.

I give no answer to the nonsense of that scoundrel, in which he says that Christ would be with his own until the end of the age, but would not be in the age to come. They feel that even to this day He is in heaven, because wherever the Jew acts—even at the furthest distance from Christian rule—Christ brings it about that he is in the harshest servitude. At the very least, He is either God, or He is able to stand in the way of the God of Israel so that He is neither able nor willing, for these past fifteen hundred years now, to hear the Jews in all their worship and...

<summary>In this page, Postel defends the reality of Christ's human suffering and the unity of the Trinity against Jewish polemical texts like the Nizzahon. He argues that Christ's "received" power after the resurrection refers to His status as a "new composite" of God and man, rather than a lack of eternal divinity.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the polemical arguments of Guillaume Postel's fourth book and begins the comprehensive Index of Chapters for the entire work, "On the Harmony of the World." Postel has been arguing against Jewish and Muslim objections to Christianity, and here he provides a summary defense before transitioning to the table of contents.</meta>

worshipping Him in every kind of affliction, God shut His ears to them. I bring forward nothing concerning the comparison of the partridge <note>original: *perdicis*. Postel likely refers to a common medieval belief that the partridge was a deceptive bird that stole eggs, often used as a metaphor for the devil or heretics trying to steal "children" from the Church.</note>, since that is merely an arbitrary slander. That Jesus leaves none of His own is clear enough from the "catastrophe" <note>The "catastrophe" here refers to the final movement or conclusion of a drama—in this case, the final earthly moments and deaths of the martyrs.</note> of the martyrs' lives. For it is not within the power of a human being to not only endure so many and such great torments, but even to seek them out voluntarily; and even more so that after death their remains continue to shine with miracles. 

As for their judgment that we are in error because of our small numbers, they themselves lack judgment. For if a small number made a law void, then Moses would have given a false law, because out of at least fifteen hundred thousand men, we read that only two <note>Referring to Joshua and Caleb, the only two adults from the generation of the Exodus permitted to enter the Promised Land.</note> reached the place to which God had called them. Once, Christianity occupied the entire world; now, it has been diminished by our own wickedness. What does it take away from Christ that the Jews do not confess Him to be God? What does it matter that they bring forward the Muslims <note>original: *Muhametanos*</note> as witnesses to the same thing, since that plague arose from Jewish instruction six hundred years after the death of Christ? Or is it that because something is rare, it is not good *because* it is rare? Truly beautiful, honorable, and good things are rare. Indeed, we testify that the [Mosaic] law was good and entirely to be kept before Christ; now we say it is abrogated, except for what pertains to morals. Therefore, two false witnesses are not witnesses at all, and especially not against the truth, which they keep suppressed in a lie. These are the things I had to propose to our people who are unskilled in Jewish matters, so that they may finish off the Jews when engaging them and know how to respond to them.
